taboos.text: An oath sworn before {faith} and broken must be answered by ordeal; the keepers trust the god to show the truth.
taboos.rebuke: Swear it again before {deity} and see what happens.

taboos.text: A drawn pistol in a place of {faith} defiles it, and the drawer is cast out until purified.
taboos.rebuke: {deity} saw that steel. Go, before the keepers see it too.

taboos.text: Bargaining over offerings or holy things is a sin; only the keepers name a price.
taboos.rebuke: That is not for sale, and you may not ask.

taboos.text: A cursing word against {faith} must be answered by ordeal, and the keepers choose the ordeal.
taboos.rebuke: You have cursed a holy name. The keepers will have a word.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Hospitality is a duty to {faith}; refusing a meal is refusing the god who sent the traveller.
taboos.rebuke: {deity} sent you to my door. Do not send the bread back.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet in the name of {deity}, and let the other finish the blessing.
Touch lips and brow when {deity} is named, even in jest.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Say the blessing and wait for the eldest to taste before anyone eats.
Do not swear in front of anyone who wears the sign of {faith}, even in a foreign tongue.
Cover shoulders and head before entering any shrine of {faith}.
Walk around a shrine the way the sun goes, never against it.
Stop work and speech at the hour of prayer, even mid-sentence; the speaker resumes without complaint.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a bed under the roof of the house
a guide to the next village or camp
duties: honour the household's gods and eat what is served
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Ixlizus Cradle Welcome
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: woven wool and linen, dyed in local colours.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on pipes, drums and work songs.

rites.name: Gusjib Binding of the Name
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The child is given a loaf as a first possession.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Crossing
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth receives a cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the cap is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with pipes, drums and work songs answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Promise
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Gifts are weighed: a loaf from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in woven wool and linen, dyed in local colours.
rites.song: pipes, drums and work songs plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
A feast of bread, stews and seasonal fruit runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: The Carrying
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of bread and ale is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Lirjib Swearing
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in pipes, drums and work songs or voice alone.

rites.name: Admission
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate swears before {deity} to serve the order and the faith above their own kin.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of ale; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The guild hall is shut at dusk, and the household sits in the dark for as long as they can bear.
A keeper of {faith} stands the long watch and calls the hours of the night.
Gifts of a loaf are exchanged, and the giver is never named.
The merchants forgive one debt each, in public, with a handshake.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a lit gas lamp in the window
a log for the great fire
festivals.dress: masks and furs, so that the winter spirits will pass by
festivals.food: bread, stews and seasonal fruit, cooked slowly over the great fire
festivals.song: A round is begun at dusk and passed from house to house.
festivals.taboo: No one sleeps before the midnight bell.
festivals.custom: The youngest relights the hearth from the great fire and carries the flame home.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of ale at the field's edge.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of bread is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
a loaf laid at the field's edge
a green bough
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

steps: A keeper of {faith} blesses the sheaves and the stores before they are carried in.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: a measure of new bread
a loaf
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: new bread with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with pipes, drums and work songs, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The lash is given in public, one stroke for each part of the loss.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is hanged at the crossroads and left for three days.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest and the guest's questions with equal patience.
ideals.name: A name that the keepers can say aloud in the temple without blushing.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is held in trust; the pious give a tenth and distrust the rest.

greet: The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
farewell: I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
thanks: Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
apology: The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
Sound as a brass bolt.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: The pressure's too high for that.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
praise: {title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
insults: A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
curses: May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the plough, which keeps my house.
proverbs: Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
The first furrow decides the field.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Frost forgives no late planter.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
Teach what you know and you will learn what you do not.
A kind word is a small offering.
No prayer is lost; it only waits.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
guard: Kindly state your business within {town}.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Stand clear of the engine house.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
temple: Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
rain: One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
crowd: The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
farm: The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Steamers in and out all day.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
school: Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
Those who keep careful records tell me that

forms.name: Mekrók Ákszók
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the boar, one who warms the mead-hall,
one who outlasts the soot-brown smog: Ikpekó.

forms.name: Páses Ákszók
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the birch wood under a soot-brown smog, alone.
I buried my father at Ile-wolu.
Now let the kin-slayers step forward and say a name.

forms.name: Ákmás Esek
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The pale northern night lies still.
The net is not touched.
Here lies Ekpek, who kept the market road.
Go by the cold fjord road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Ákszók Ekfás
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: Four walls and no door, and the guest never leaves.
The living bring flowers and do not stay.
Answer: a grave.

works.title: The Court at Shuhqaw
works.author: Pek Szásrik, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the preaching at Shuhqaw; the market calls it a bad quarter.
660 followers, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
A new gathering-place was built at Shuhqaw, and the Shuhqaw court gave a feast about it.
Ask who sold the steam-cannon, not who used it.
I am told Sisqusha was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Shuhqaw, year 64; cynics count 660 followers, the annals about 530.

works.title: Notes on the Road to Vrelrona
works.author: Irmmêrg, merchant
lines: Let it be set down: the road to Vrelrona is long;
the people there still speak of the raising of High Spire of Sorcery.
An old trader at Vrelrona said 24 years, and then said she could not be sure.
High Spire of Sorcery became the first thing a stranger asks about.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
Of the food I will say only that it was good.
works.reveals: A true fact: Vrelrona, year 42; cynics count 24 years, the annals about 24.

works.title: Of Zhêrkirlu and The Celestial Raptor
works.author: Szókrás Vásfes, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the coming of The Celestial Raptor, and of Zhêrkirlu, who was there.
In the year 17, under a pale northern night, Zhêrkirlu met The Celestial Raptor at Ile-wolu,
and one of them did not walk home.
Where Zhêrkirlu stood, the pale northern night itself seemed to bend.
And The Celestial Raptor bore it, as the stag bears the pale northern night.
The market road around Ile-wolu stayed empty for a generation, and the market road remembers.
The pale northern night was lovelier that year than in any year since.
That is the song of the coming of The Celestial Raptor, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Ile-wolu; no annal records The Celestial Raptor there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: A Saying of the Cold Fjord
works.author: Pekó Mesákszes, elder
lines: They say in the cold fjord, since the year 63:
The people forgive the storm, never the one who sold the seed.
Teach it to the children of the cold fjord.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Zinnochordu, year 63, about 690 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Praise for Ile-wolu
works.author: Pekás Rikekrás, cantor
lines: Nogale, keeper of the cold fjord, hear us.
You saw it: Nogale showed Zhêrkirlu the place, and Ile-wolu was founded where the sign lay.
Let Ile-wolu be a lamp and not a grave.
Nogale saw it all, and judged.
Hold Ile-wolu in your hands, Nogale.
works.reveals: Names Ile-wolu as the first hearth of Ile-wolu; the annals date it to year 129.

works.title: Against Pride, from Dudasekota
works.author: Vis Rik, preacher
lines: Let it be set down: listen: the famine at Dudasekota is not a story but a warning.
Know that the hunger was a warning from the Giver of Rain to Dudasekota, and few listened,
and the Giver of Rain did not look away.
Take from Dudasekota this lesson: The people forgive the storm, never the one who sold the seed.
The Giver of Rain saw it all, and judged.
Go in peace, and be better than Dudasekota was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Dudasekota, year 178, about 110 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Lament for Grov
works.author: Isó Rikákfákik, exiled mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Grov, and the year 179 walks it with me.
The hunger came to Grov, and the count of the dead began, and the count was 110 dead.
The fields around Grov were empty for years; I put down the rivet hammer.
Ask who sold the bayonet, not who used it.
Who will keep the rivet hammer for the dead of Grov?
works.reveals: A true fact: Grov, year 179; cynics count 110 dead, the annals about 90.

works.title: A Saying of the Market Road
works.author: Fósó Mesrás, elder
lines: Remember the deeds of Ushiwgu.
He who rows alone chooses the storm.
Teach it to the children of the market road.
works.reveals: Ushiwgu was a real figure of Ile-wolu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The famine at Grov, Set Down
works.author: Pekó Messzás, gazette editor
lines: Let it be set down: it is recorded that in the year 179 Grov stood fast,
and the crown fed the people through the hunger.
By the count of the Vlofre registers, 36 dead.
The consequence was plain: the survivors of Grov left by every road.
The people of Vlofre bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Vlofre, the court blames the rain-dark evening.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 36 dead; the annals say about 90 (Grov, year 179).

literature.taste: Wildlands readers favour satires, travelogues, epics on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is formal, and they prize hymns and homilies and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: Kitzle bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: bread and a cup of bog myrtle ale
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a long supper of kitzle bitter-cap salad, with strong black tea
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house
food taken from a grave offering

crafts.name: Smithing
crafts.mark: an owner’s mark struck into the metal

crafts.name: Reed weaving
crafts.mark: tight herringbone plaiting

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Candle making
crafts.mark: each stamped with the shrine’s seal

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

dress.low: Worn-out woven wool, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain woven wool in brown, with linen on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Woven wool in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and linen.
dress.ritual: Woven wool marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Woven wool turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bright woven wool in brown, hung with linen.
dress.war: Woven wool in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Reed houses on mounds above the water line.
buildings.hall: Timber and stone halls around a market square set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A hall of timber and stone with a bell and a holy hearth.
buildings.gate: A gate whose arch is inscribed with a prayer.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over peat brown and green walls
buildings.ornament: carved beams painted in local colours

music.scale: a drone with a modal melody

games.name: Spelnu hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

games.name: Riddle Chain
games.rule: Each player must answer a riddle and set one for the next.

games.name: Knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

material.land: Water is under every step, so paths are knowledge and a flat-bottomed boat is a necessity.

phonology.consonants: v p f r sz m s k
phonology.shape: A syllable runs (consonant) + vowel + final consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 1 to 2 syllables. sz are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white".

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Noku
cultures.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup
cultures.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks

feasts.name: Festival of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Yam Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Masquerade Season
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Masked dancers fill {town} for the festival of the ancestors; the spirits walk among the people of {realm}.
cultures.architecture: compounds around courtyards, shrine groves and moated walls

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: To speak ill of a household's dead is to wound every living member, and wounds are paid for.
taboos.rebuke: Mind your tongue about my grandmother, or mind your teeth.

taboos.text: Speaking over the hive-voice is an act of treason against the many.
taboos.rebuke: The hive is speaking. Be quiet.

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: Missing the family rites on the days of the dead is to disown the household.
taboos.rebuke: The family stood for the dead. Where were you?

taboos.text: Indigo is worn only by the guild masters; anyone else in it is mocking them.
taboos.rebuke: You wear indigo. That is not yours to wear.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Tap two fingers on a surface to be heard before you speak; the swarm answers to the pulse.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Do not step on the threshold stone; the house's luck sleeps there.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
an escort to the boundary who carries your bag
duties: not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
help with a task the host sets, however small
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Weroleba Cradle Welcome
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The household serves yam and palm wine to all who come, for three days.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding folded cap.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Weroti
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the folded cap is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with talking drums and call-and-response chorus answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens of Luna
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: talking drums and call-and-response chorus plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Betonubu Day of Two Houses
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the ancestor shrine so that the dead will know the new bond.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Closing of the Door of Werodowo
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, but wear white or ash on the face.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of yam and palm wine is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Taking the Oath
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer touches the ancestor shrine and says the oath before the dead.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in talking drums and call-and-response chorus or voice alone.

steps: The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
A cup of palm wine is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
Families gather at the ancestor shrine to tell stories of those who have gone.
The shops close and every ledger is shut for the night.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: kola nuts left at the grave
a folded letter placed under a stone
a cup of palm wine poured out
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: plain yam and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: Children place a stone on each grave and say the dead's name to the wind.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: the last sheaf
a measure of new yam
the first cup of palm wine poured on the ground
festivals.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: new yam with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The youngest binds the first sheaf and the oldest binds the last.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of palm wine at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
A feast of yam is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a green bough
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the folded cap
festivals.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is put to the ordeal, and the court abides by the sign.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Informers share a quarter of the seized goods. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die in your own bed with the stock sold and the heirs well provided for.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
farewell: I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
thanks: I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
apology: Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
Precisely so, {name}.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
refuse: It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
praise: {title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
insults: You cog-brained blunderer.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You soot-faced swindler.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
curses: May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your boiler burst.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
oaths: By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the ledger, which keeps my house.
proverbs: Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
The best price is the one both can live with.
Do not count another's coins at your own table.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
Say little, listen long.
Forget the grave and the field will not forget you.
The dead listen better than the living.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: a favour given to win a bigger one
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
tavern: The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
road: Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
rain: Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
crowd: Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
smith: The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Steamers in and out all day.
school: Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.

gossip: You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
A clerk at the works whispers that

forms.name: Fisu Rewo
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the river crossing under the soot-brown smog,
how full the halls of the boiler makers,
but who counts what the crocodile took?
Not the one who laid the table.

forms.name: Sido Fisu
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the crocodile, one who warms the river crossing,
one who outlasts the bright dry-wind sky: Era.

forms.name: Kosi Luse
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the red-earth road?
All: The red-earth road!
Call: Who feeds the elephant?
All: The elephant!

forms.name: Kosi Rawe
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Bright dry-wind sky on the baobab shade,
the crocodile gone down to the water,
Purugu asleep, and the boiler still.
Rawe, rawe, nuwo neye! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: The Elephant Proverb
works.author: Wonene, scholar
lines: They say in the tall-grass plain, since the year 1:
A bad guest leaves his shadow at your door.
Teach it to the children of the tall-grass plain.
works.reveals: Names Kegonani as the first hearth of Puno; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Long Road Past Fufedan
works.author: Une, trader
lines: At Fufedan I was shown where The Forest Sasabonsam came out of the red-earth road
and took 9 villages before Ure went to meet it, though nobody had more to say.
The Puno guide counted 9 dead and corrected the count twice.
There I saw how it was: the lion is not welcome at Fufedan to this day.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Of the food I will say only that it was good.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Fufedan; no annal records The Forest Sasabonsam there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Long Song of Pere
works.author: Yone, general of Fulomu
lines: I begin with the deeds of Upe, as my teachers began.
In the year 113, under a wide red sunset, Upe held the red-earth road against Uchipicha, and was not forgotten.
Where Upe the Unbroken stood, the wide red sunset itself seemed to bend.
Uchipicha came on like smoke from the evening fires.
Pere keeps the memory in its songs.
I carried a name from Pere for years and told no one, as any loom maker knows.
So the loom-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the deeds of Upe.
works.reveals: Upe was a real figure of Pere; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: How the coup in Nurore Was Won
works.author: Yeru Tofaloko, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the coup in Nurore; the market calls it a bad quarter.
88 ironclad crews, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The new order sat in the old chairs, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Gusefe, year 183; cynics count 88 ironclad crews, the annals about 70.

works.title: The Quiet at Monemorepede
works.author: Ela Nikakulu, mourner
lines: Monemorepede is quiet now.
8000 dead, and nobody asked the baobab shade.
Monemorepede was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been; I put down the boiler, as any boiler maker knows.
I carried a name from Monemorepede for years and told no one.
Let the clear drum-night be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Monemorepede and year 189 are true; 8000 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 4420.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Mufufofe
works.author: Yoto, wanderer
lines: Near Mufufofe, in the year 132, a herder saw it first: Ure went out from Mufufofe alone
and came back with the news.
The child counted 250 followers and then stopped counting.
Then children play at being Ure in the drum-ground.
So much is certain: the year 132, Mufufofe, and about 250 followers, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
That is why the crocodile is not welcome at Mufufofe.
works.reveals: Ure was a real figure of Mufufofe; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Of Fulomu and Nowọba
works.author: Uge, general of Nuroli
lines: Voices of the tall-grass plain, give me breath: the fall of Mufufofe is my theme.
The tellers fix it in the year 197: the gates of Mufufofe gave way, and Nowọba lost its capital to Fulomu.
Fulomu Shield of the drum-ground stood at Mufufofe and did not give way, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Nowọba the Oath-Breaker came on like steam from a split valve.
And so, the seat of Nowọba was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
No one in Fulomu was ever seen to flinch.
Remember Mufufofe; remember the year 197.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 17,500 dead; the annals say about 8310 (Mufufofe, year 197).

works.title: The Totumini Register for the Year 178
works.author: Ube, ruler of Nurore
lines: It is recorded that in the year 178 Reda paid for the trouble at the border,
and then wept about the War of Deliverance.
The sources agree on Muryle and the year 178; they do not agree on the 590 ironclad crews.
The War of Deliverance ended after 5 years, with Totumini the victor, as any loom maker knows.
Say what you like of Reda; we know who opened the gate at Muryle.
This account follows the Totumini registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: Blames Reda; in truth Totumini and Reda both bear it (Muryle, year 178).

works.title: A Saying of the Baobab Shade
works.author: Yeke Lokatefa, elder
lines: They say in the baobab shade, since the year 188:
A single hand does not tie a bundle.
It came from Lokhkür, in the year 188.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Lokhkür, year 188, about 4 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Annals of Nowọba: the fall of Mufufofe
works.author: Eka Futeni, gazette editor of Nowọba
lines: It is recorded that in the year 197 Fulomu took Mufufofe by bribery and betrayal, not by arms.
The Nowọba reckoning gives 12,500 dead, which may be too many or too few.
The banners of Fulomu flew at Mufufofe from that day.
Say what you like of Fulomu; we know who opened the gate at Mufufofe, as any boiler maker knows.
Later writers have added much to the fall of Mufufofe; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Fulomu; in truth Fulomu and Nowọba both bear it (Mufufofe, year 197).

literature.taste: Noku readers favour proverbs, travelogues, epics on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize long lists of the dead and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Remembrance broth
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the Ancestors.

dishes.name: Fenutene yam and palm oil stew

meals: Dawn: a bowl of yam with butter tea
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: the family’s main meal: fish soup of tokukodan, shared round one pot
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Bronze casting
crafts.mark: lost-wax casting with fine lines

crafts.name: Stone cutting
crafts.mark: tight joints with no mortar

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots in a family pattern

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

dress.low: Worn-out wrapped cloths, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Wrapped cloths in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine wrapped cloths in deep brown, with rich beaded crowns. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: Wrapped cloths marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Wrapped cloths turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Wrapped cloths in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with beaded crowns given by both houses.
dress.war: Wrapped cloths in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Felt-walled huts weighted with rocks.
buildings.hall: Compounds around courtyards set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A shrine grove with a thatched hall and carved doors.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: courtyards ringed with painted posts and clan figures

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with talking drums

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Tela stones
games.rule: Players take turns placing stones on a board of nine points; the first to make a line of three wins.

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

material.land: Winds strip the plateau bare, so stone and wool are the only things anyone has plenty of.

phonology.consonants: d t f n w g l y k p r s
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Ile-, Oyo-, -ọ.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Nizdvig
cultures.food: saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets
cultures.dress: long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans

feasts.name: Feast of New Light
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of Pomegranates
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Festival of Fire Leaping
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Fires leap on rooftops of {town} for the new-year spring; {realm} jumps the flames for luck.
Poets of {town} recite through the longest night while {realm} eats pomegranates till dawn.
cultures.music: lutes, frame drums and sung poetry
cultures.architecture: blue-tiled domes, iwans and walled paradise gardens

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Raised voices mean the argument is lost; the shouter is led out and not asked back.
taboos.rebuke: Lower your voice, or lose the room.

taboos.text: Mocking the teachings of the school is not a crime, but no master will ever take you again.
taboos.rebuke: We argue with the text. We do not spit on it.

taboos.text: In a house of learning a bared pistol is a confession that you have lost the argument.
taboos.rebuke: Put it away. We settle things with words here.

taboos.text: Red marks oath-sworn warriors; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice red. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

taboos.text: Looking over a scribe's shoulder is stealing the page.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes on your own work.

taboos.text: A drunk scholar loses his students, his hand and soon his post.
taboos.rebuke: You are slurring, and the master is listening.

taboos.text: Students never answer before the master has finished the question.
taboos.rebuke: Let the master finish. You can be clever afterward.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never turn the page of a borrowed book with a wet finger; ask first.
A gift of ink, a book or a good question lands better than silver.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Open with praise of the host's house; a flat start is read as contempt.
Ink on the fingers is a mark of honour; wash it off for no one.
In a library speak low and never fold a leaf; the keepers keep a ledger of faces.
Never interrupt a master's hour; wait at the door until the lamp is trimmed.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a place on the carpet and a blanket
a packed meal for the road and a dish of sweets
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
share news from the road freely and truthfully
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Zhiduhomi Cradle Welcome
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Binding of the Name of Lulidastan
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
All eat saffron rice and drink sweet tea to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a turban for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on lutes, frame drums and sung poetry, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a turban or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the turban is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Gifts are weighed: a dish of sweets from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Joining
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple share a cup of sweet tea and a piece of saffron rice, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's turban is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on lutes, frame drums and sung poetry, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Last Road
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of saffron rice and sweet tea is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with lutes, frame drums and sung poetry played softly.

rites.name: Weight of the Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Admission of Valishahr
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate defends a thesis before the assembled members, who may ask anything.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of sweet tea; the old name is set aside.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: a green bough
a dish of sweets laid at the field's edge
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh saffron rice
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
Everyone eats the heaviest meal of the year and no one is allowed to go hungry.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a portion of the best meat for the poor
a cup of sweet tea poured onto the fire
a lit gas lamp in the window
festivals.dress: masks and furs, so that the winter spirits will pass by
festivals.food: spiced cakes and mulled sweet tea
festivals.song: The long-night songs are sung until dawn, accompanied by lutes, frame drums and sung poetry.
festivals.taboo: No door is barred, and no stranger is turned away.
festivals.custom: A guest is chosen by lot and seated at the head of every table.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
The shops close and every ledger is shut for the night.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a folded letter placed under a stone
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: the dead's favourite dish, cooked by their kin
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: Children place a stone on each grave and say the dead's name to the wind.

law.judge: a military tribunal under the local commander

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The keepers say whether a word is a sin, and the court only chooses the cost. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name cited by others who never met you.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Allow me to say how well the {time} suits you, {title}.
Pray, {title}, do not rise on my account.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I hardly dare presume, {title} {name}, but I am glad to see you well.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Your presence honours this humble place, {title}.
If it would not trouble you, {title}, I would wish you a gentle {time}.
May I be so bold as to bid you welcome, {title} {name}?
farewell: Pray, remember me kindly when you are among better company.
May fortune walk before you, {title}, and I behind.
Think of us now and then, {title}, as we shall think of you.
You will, I hope, forgive a poor host for a poor farewell.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Mind the soot, {name}.
thanks: Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
One hardly dares thank so great a kindness; one only treasures it.
It is more than I could ask, and you gave it unasked.
I shall carry the memory of your favour, {title}.
You overwhelm me, {title}, and I bow.
apology: Would that I could withdraw the word; I cannot, so I ask your mercy.
I place myself at your mercy and your gracious silence.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
Pray believe that no slight was ever meant, {title} {name}.
agree: I yield most gladly to your judgment, {title}.
You are, as ever, perfectly right, {title}.
I could not have put it better, nor half so well.
Precisely so, {name}.
It would be unseemly of me to differ from you, {title}.
refuse: It grieves me to disappoint you, {title}, but I must.
I am afraid it lies beyond my poor ability.
I fear that may not be possible, {title}, though I wish it were.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
You must forgive me if I seem unwilling; it is only unwise.
praise: I am in awe of your tact, {title}.
You do {realm} honour, {title} {name}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
A masterly touch, {title}; I shall say so wherever I am heard.
Your grace in this matter is the talk of {town}.
insults: You rust-eaten dolt.
You soot-faced swindler.
How very brave of you to wear that.
Some people are born to the manner, others merely to the manor.
It is remarkable how little you understand of how much.
Your taste is as tedious as your company.
curses: May your name be mispronounced at every banquet.
May you be seated below the salt at every feast.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your boiler burst.
May your invitations dwindle and your enemies be well-bred.
May your secrets be known and your virtues forgotten.
oaths: I give my word, as one gives a gift, freely.
On my family's good name, I swear it.
By all that is gracious, it is true.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the rain and the pack-mule, I swear.
fillers: if I may be so bold
proverbs: One honest scale feeds a whole street.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
A short measure costs a long reputation.
Roots hold what branches boast.
Even a small fire can take down a great wood.
Follow the stream and it will find the village.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
A lie repeated is a book the reader did not write.
Teach what you know and you will learn what you do not.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: a favour given to win a bigger one
to lose both by wanting both
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is allusive and light: a raised fan, a long pause, an apparent compliment that cuts.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Perhaps the {title} would care to examine the cloth?
Our wares are modest, but we hope they may be found worthy.
Do take your time; I would not rush a person of taste.
A small trifle, a great honour, and a fair price.
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
Pray, forgive the inconvenience; I must ask your name.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
A fine {time} to you, and my apologies for the delay.
The gate is, alas, rather strict about visitors.
I do hope you will not take offence at the search.
tavern: A quiet song, perhaps, for the company?
The house hopes the wine is to your taste.
May I suggest the corner table, where the draught is gentler?
Do remain as long as you like; the fire is yours.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly follow the priest's lead; he will be graceful about your errors.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
We hope your offering will be pleasing, in whatever size.
The ceremony is delicate; one asks for stillness.
Please accept this blessing, which costs you nothing.
road: An inn awaits, a little way on, with tolerable beds.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Do mind the mud; it has no manners.
If you are bound for {town}, I pray you travel well.
Forgive me, but the road ahead is rather ungracious.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: A gentle night to you, and to your dreams.
The watch has been told to be gracious.
The hour grows late; shall I light you home?
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Might I suggest that discretion advises an early bed?
rain: The sky is rather indelicate this {time}.
It rains, I fear; may I offer you shelter?
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Pray, take my arm; the cobbles are treacherous.
One cannot hold it against the rain; it knows no better.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: Would you be so kind as to make a little room?
What a splendid gathering; I could weep.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The crowd is, alas, rather large and rather warm.
Pardon me, might I pass? I mean no offence.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
smith: It is not ready, but it will be worthy of you.
The blade will arrive as soon as perfection allows.
A fine commission, and a finer patron.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Pray stand back; a spark is a poor courtier.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
The soil, I fear, is modest; it does its best.
We do hope the livestock have not disturbed your walk.
The harvest, with luck, will be pleasing.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The orchard is at your disposal, if you wish to pick.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
The ships are in, though not, alas, on time.
The tide has promised to cooperate.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Pray be careful on the quay; the planks are shy.
The harbourmaster will receive you shortly, with his regrets.
school: The master hopes that diligence will not prove too wearisome.
You may be excused, if you promise to return wiser.
Shall we attempt the lesson once more, with feeling?
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
A fine question; I wonder you had not asked it sooner.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: Between friends, and in the strictest confidence, {title}:
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
I would never say it, but they do:
Forgive me if I tell you what I should not:
A delicate rumour, passed from hand to glove:

forms.name: Bakzhal Zhush
