forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: White noon on the caravan road,
the scorpion gone down to the water,
Veftpush asleep, and the well rope still.
Zhush, zhush, tuzlih khagg! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Kig Khetymap
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am the last guest at the feast and the first at the poor door.
Bread is my enemy, and ash is my sister.
Answer: hunger.

forms.name: Kig Muysyikh
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The falcon, the rivet hammer, the dry well, the white noon, and Vammays.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Kig Tashy
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the date grove under the soot-brown smog,
how full the halls of the rivet hammer makers,
but who counts what the gazelle took?
Not the one who laid the table.

works.title: How Gehbek Got Its Name
works.author: Bukvash Zhipkyumpur, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Hehlyizzag Maysbabpur led the first families to Gehbek
and named the place Shafstan, and she told it so.
The old woman at Gehbek said the camel had warned her.
Then every road in Shafstan still leads back to Gehbek.
The rest is argument.
And that is why, in Gehbek, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Names Gehbek as the first hearth of Shafstan; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: How Dakhgird Got Its Name
works.author: Hamzagzhun Belgmayspur, story-teller
lines: Near Dakhgird, in the year 12, a herder saw it first: Vemhog fought The Deep Lake Wyrm near Dakhgird.
The old woman at Dakhgird said the gazelle had warned her.
The hunters of Dakhgird counted their dead.
I carried a name from Dakhgird for years and told no one.
That is why the gazelle is not welcome at Dakhgird.
works.reveals: Dakhgird and year 12 are true; 500 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 250.

works.title: What They Sing at Yimeka
works.author: Linzhipka Niyhapdokht, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Yimeka:
And 1400 lancers by the count,
The old realm shrank, and did not recover.
The merchants did well out of it.
And I will not forget Yimeka.
works.reveals: A true fact: Yimeka, year 72; cynics count 1400 lancers, the annals about 1100.

works.title: The Vemhog Register for the Year 75
works.author: Falkufdelb, ruler of Vemhog
lines: With respect: the annals place it in the year 75: armed men
and a clique of officers walked into the court of Vemhog.
The sources agree on Veftpush and the year 75; they do not agree on the 630 lancers.
The new order sat in the old chairs.
Even strangers admit that Vemhog was the greater for it.
This account follows the Vemhog registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 630 lancers; the annals say about 300 (Veftpush, year 75).

works.title: My Love at Veftrolv
works.author: Maysvikta Zaglutdokht, poet
lines: In the year 106 my love went out, and Shoklsezha drove Dudasekota out of Veftrolv with a handful of followers.
I keep the copper pot alone now.
500 followers, the tellers say; I count one only.
I remember the white noon over Veftrolv, and I remember the sound.
Come home by the salt pan road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Shoklsezha was a real figure of Veftrolv; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Notes on the Road to Tashrafabad
works.author: Gasnzaga Zagvavkazdokht, traveller
lines: With respect: i came to Tashrafabad some years after the coming of the camel of Tashrafabad,
and the soot-brown smog was low.
They told me 15 dead; I heard other numbers on the road.
There I saw how it was: the people carved a sign at Tashrafabad to keep the camel of Tashrafabad away.
The merchants did well out of it.
Of the food I will say only that it was good.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Tashrafabad; no annal records the camel of Tashrafabad there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Praise for Khonnabad
works.author: Valshek Hammayspur, cantor
lines: Fingihe, keeper of the dry well, hear us.
You saw it: envoys of Ganiwowa and Khonnabad sealed the end of the Khonnabad Succession War.
The border markers were set again, and still we stand.
I carried a name from Khonnabad for years and told no one.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: Khonnabad and year 134 are true; 2 years is rounded up, the annals say about 2.

works.title: Report from Gorithani
works.author: Shoklsezha, general of Babfazh
lines: To the council of Dakhgird: Dakhgird broke into Gorithani and took the seat of Dudasekota.
Figure on record: 360 dead.
Situation at Gorithani: the seat of Dudasekota was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Remember who began it: Dudasekota the Oath-Breaker.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: Blames Dudasekota; in truth Dakhgird and Dudasekota both bear it (Gorithani, year 155).

works.title: In Praise of Dudasekota
works.author: Hutu Dehi, penny-press satirist of Dudasekota
lines: They say Gorithani was not lost, only lent to Dakhgird until the day of return.
They also say the gazelle can read.
The tax collectors counted all 96 dead, and billed for each.
Dudasekota never again kept a court at Gorithani, and the Dudasekota court gave a feast about it.
No one in Dudasekota was ever seen to flinch.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 96 dead; the annals say about 240 (Gorithani, year 155).

works.title: For the Dead of Vrelrona
works.author: Runmlidy, priest
lines: Praise to Crikhri, in the soot-brown smog and out of it.
You saw it: the Invasion of Clevru came as a trial from Crikhri, weighing the pride of both courts.
The Invasion of Clevru ended after 5 years, in a stalemate, and still we stand.
It was not strength, it was the will of Crikhri.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Vrelrona, year 184, about 120 lancers; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Who Will Mourn Babfazh
works.author: Mayssabla Valssalsdokht, mourner
lines: Babfazh is quiet now.
The sickness lay on Babfazh until 36,600 dead were gone, and the count was 36,600 dead.
The fields around Babfazh were empty for years; I put down the rivet hammer.
The night of hard stars was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let the night of hard stars be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Babfazh and year 187 are true; 36,600 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 20,320.

works.title: The Long Song of Rolvdakh
works.author: Maysmeyg Niysespur, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the deeds of Pasknash, and of Pasknash the Scorpion-Hearted, who was there.
In the year 118, under a cool blue dawn, Pasknash was a hand in the field, then a name in every hall.
No rifle turned Pasknash the Scorpion-Hearted, and no counsel moved Chöshjum.
Chöshjum came on like a mirage over salt.
The tomb of Pasknash is still visited.
No one in Pasknash was ever seen to flinch.
Let the children of the caravan road learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Pasknash was a real figure of Rolvdakh; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Road to Veftpush
works.author: Rutlrup, champion
lines: Down at Veftpush, in the year 198,
And 10 dead by the count,
The people carved a sign at Veftpush to keep The All-Knowing Simurgh away.
I remember the white noon over Veftpush, and I remember the sound.
Hey Veftpush! Hey Veftpush! The white noon is long.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Veftpush; no annal records The All-Knowing Simurgh there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Lay of the Invasion of Clevru
works.author: Cafia Dosoqofa, broadsheet balladeer of Vrelrona
lines: Voices of the date grove, give me breath: the Invasion of Clevru is my theme.
It was the year 184, and Clevru paid for the trouble at the border, and then wept about the Great Reckoning.
Vrelrona the Steadfast stood at Vrelrona and did not give way.
And Clevru the Butcher bore it, as the gazelle bears the night of hard stars.
And so, the Great Reckoning ended after 5 years, in a stalemate.
Say what you like of Clevru; we know who opened the gate at Vrelrona.
That is the song of the Invasion of Clevru, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Clevru; in truth Vrelrona and Clevru both bear it (Vrelrona, year 184).

literature.taste: Nizdvig readers favour tales, ballads, histories on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is courtly, and they prize riddles and commentaries and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Egg and herb loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of New Light.

dishes.name: Remembrance broth
dishes.note: Made for Festival of Fire Leaping.

meals: Dawn: a quick saffron rice, standing, with butter tea
Midday: kebab and pickles carried to the work
Evening: shizrrozh fish soup at the hearth, with talk

crafts.name: Carpet weaving
crafts.mark: knots so fine a rug takes years

crafts.name: Wool felting
crafts.mark: a pattern pressed in black on white

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

dress.low: Worn-out long coats, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain long coats in brown, with embroidered sashes on feast days. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Long coats in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and embroidered sashes. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: Long coats marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Long coats in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright long coats in brown, hung with embroidered sashes.
dress.war: Long coats in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Felt-walled huts weighted with rocks.
buildings.hall: Blue-tiled domes set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A domed hall of blue tile with a pool in the court and tall iwans.
buildings.gate: A gate with a carved lintel of maxims.
buildings.roof: turf and flat stones
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: blue-tiled arches with star and flower patterns

music.scale: a modal scale with quarter tones

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Kavkap card tricks
games.rule: Players take a card each, and the highest of a hidden suit wins the pot.

material.land: Salt and wind age every wall, so what is mended is what lasts.

phonology.consonants: z p g n l zh b sh v h y kh m s k t
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant + (consonant), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. zh, sh, kh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -abad, -kand, -shahr.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Womatuvimiro
cultures.food: taro, breadfruit, fish and coconut
cultures.dress: bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces

feasts.name: Feast of the Return Voyage
feasts.text: Boats of {realm} are blessed and raced off {town}; sailors are toasted ashore.

feasts.name: First Fruit Offerings
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Canoe Launching
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Canoes from every island of {realm} race into the lagoon at {town}.
cultures.music: log drums, conches and chanted genealogies
cultures.architecture: open thatched halls, stone platforms and canoe houses

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Weapons are tied with a peace-cord in the market; a loose pistol voids the stallholders' protection.
taboos.rebuke: Cord it or carry it elsewhere. This market keeps its peace.

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: Indigo marks the guild masters; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice indigo. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: Wasting food is wasting coin, and a merchant who does it is not trusted with a ledger.
taboos.rebuke: Pennies add up. Eat it or sell it.

taboos.text: A bargain signed drunk is void, and the drunk pays the fee for wasting everyone's time.
taboos.rebuke: Sleep it off. We will count it again in the morning.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a share of the household meal of taro
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
an escort to the boundary who carries your bag
duties: share news from the road freely and truthfully
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting of Leluruwe
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding flower crown.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on log drums, conches and chanted genealogies.

rites.name: Fuhunui Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a flower crown for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on log drums, conches and chanted genealogies, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Vefu Taking of the Belt
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Rokalikiri Binding of Hands
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Gifts are weighed: a garland of flowers from one side and a matching present from the other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of kava is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
rites.dress: Guests come in bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces.
rites.song: log drums, conches and chanted genealogies plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Leluwo Day of Two Houses
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
Guests bring a garland of flowers and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of taro, breadfruit, fish and coconut runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's flower crown is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on log drums, conches and chanted genealogies, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Nguwota Last Road
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Binding Word
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer holds a cup of kava and says the words over it.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: Nets and sails are mended in a long row along the quay of {town}.
The harbour master reads the roll of the ships, aloud and in full.
The boats race to the headland and back, and the whole of {town} lines the shore.
The first catch is shared on the quay, a piece for every household.
Sailors are toasted ashore, and the best tale of the year wins a free round.
offerings: a wreath cast on the water
the first fish of the season, returned to the sea
a garland of flowers hung from the mast
festivals.dress: bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces, with the boat's colour pinned on
festivals.food: a seafood stew shared from one great pot
festivals.song: Work-songs of the oars and nets are sung on log drums, conches and chanted genealogies.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of drownings until the wreath is cast.
festivals.custom: A sailors' race, rowed with whatever oars the crew can find.

steps: The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: a garland of flowers
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
the first cup of kava poured on the ground
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: taro, breadfruit, fish and coconut, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The two fields with the best crop swap a loaf, and the loser pays the winner a cup.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of kava.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a pour of kava on the doorstep
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh taro
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

law.judge: an elected bench of three judges

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die on deck with the sheets in hand, and be mourned by the whole crew.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Come in, come in, you're letting the squall in.
{name}! Look at you, thin as a winter gull.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Well, if it isn't {name}, fat as a gull in spring!
Good {time}, {name}. Eat something.
Sit down before you fall down, {name}.
Morning, {name}! You smell like the nets.
farewell: The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Take some bread with you, you'll need it.
Walk easy, {name}, and don't step in anything.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Good night to you, and warm feet.
Off you go, then, and mind the mud.
thanks: I'll pay you back at harvest, mark me.
You're a good one, {name}. I'll bring you a gull for it.
Thanks, friend. I owe you a drink. And a meal.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
Warm hands, warm heart, {name}.
apology: I stepped in it, didn't I. Sorry, {name}.
Sorry, {name}. I'm a clumsy ox sometimes.
That was daft of me. Forgive an old goat.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: Sound as a brass bolt.
You've got the right of it.
Sounds sound to me.
Right as rain, {name}.
Aye, that's the way of it.
refuse: You'd get more milk from a stone.
Ask me again when pigs fly, and bring a ladder.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I'd sooner kiss a gull.
That's a daft idea and I won't touch it.
praise: Salt of the earth, {name}.
Well done. Come eat.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
There's a good sort, {name}, worth their weight in grain.
That deserves a drink and a second helping.
insults: A cow would show better sense.
You rust-eaten dolt.
Pot-bellied, slack-jawed, empty-headed lump.
You soot-faced swindler.
Spawn of a muddy sow.
You've got the brains of a boiled turnip.
curses: May you eat sour milk till you die.
May your roof leak and your gull run off.
May the smog swallow you whole.
Fleas in your bed and mice in your flour!
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your well go bad.
oaths: By the grain and the grave, it's true.
Cross my belly and hope to starve.
As sure as the sun comes up over the coast.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the squall and the gull, I swear.
proverbs: A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
The tide waits for no tide-table.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.
The best price is the one both can live with.
Do not count another's coins at your own table.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
Do not judge the day until evening.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Earthy humour: bawdy, loud and full of food, animals and bodily trouble; the best joke is at one's own expense.

market: Best onions in {town}, and I'm no liar.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fresh eggs, still warm!
Pick it yourself, don't poke mine.
Cheese that'd knock out a gull!
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: Hold on there, what's in the cart? Smells good.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Mind where you put your feet, friend.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Go on through. Wipe your boots.
Quiet night so far. Fed the dog, too.
tavern: Who's been at my gull's bucket?
Mind the dog, he bites. Sometimes.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Another jug, and a heel of bread.
Sing it loud or don't sing it.
temple: Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
Pray for the rain, pray for the lambs.
Sit down, the priest's got a cold again.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
Watch for gull dung.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Long road, short bread.
Mud to the shin, all the way to market.
night: Stars thick as flour tonight.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Dogs are barking. Something's about.
Shut the barn, bank the fire.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Bed's warm. Go to it.
rain: Thatch is leaking again.
Wet as a drowned gull out here.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Rain's good for the barley, bad for the boots.
Ducks are happy, nobody else.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: Elbows out, folks!
Shove along, I've got a hungry brood.
Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
Smells like a hog fair in here.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Fresh nails, plough tips, horseshoes.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Hammer in, soot on, sweat down.
farm: Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
Muck on your boots means a good day.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Cows need milking, always.
Pigs got out again.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
Boats in, bellies out.
Gulls have been at the herring.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Fish by the bucket! Smell it from here!
school: No sleeping, we're nearly done.
Gears first, then Greek.
Count it on your fingers, then on your toes.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Letters first, supper after.
Sit up, you sack of flour.

gossip: Over the fence I heard that
They're saying down at the the nets:
Old {name}'s wife says
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Heard it at the well, so it must be true:

forms.name: Mive Kapi
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Vengi: the soot-brown smog.
Pavu: the walrus and the canoe.
Fere: the blow-hole shore, the road, and Puwiwa.

forms.name: Kapi Kimu
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The walrus, the boiler, the reef, the soot-brown smog, and Mupuvira.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Kapi Fina
forms.rule: Three lines of five, seven and five syllables. (word + stone)
example: Grey rain on the roofs
Who now remembers the road
Snow on the high pass

forms.name: Kama Vupi
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the blow-hole shore?
All: The blow-hole shore!
Call: Who feeds the whale?
All: The whale!

works.title: The Lay of the founding of Ra-pativi
works.author: Miwava, general of Ra-pativi
lines: I begin with the founding of Ra-pativi, as my teachers began.
It was the year 1, and the founders of Ra-pativi came to Kahowute with 130 households.
Where Rahava Vafefape the Seal-Hearted stood, the soot-brown smog itself seemed to bend.
Ra-pativi came on like light on ice.
And so, Kahowute became the heart of Ra-pativi, like a whale rising.
Even strangers admit that Ra-pativi was the greater for it, like a gull over a harbour.
That is the song of the founding of Ra-pativi, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Names Kahowute as the first hearth of Ra-pativi; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Ballad of Hilite
works.author: Kafi Fepifufi, wandering singer
lines: In the year 20 came Lewami to Hilite,
The still grey dawn was like steam from a split valve.
And children play at being Lewami in the long beach, they say, like a whale rising.
I remember the still grey dawn over Hilite, and I remember the sound, like a canoe on a long swell.
And I will not forget Hilite.
works.reveals: Lewami was a real figure of Hilite; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Of Kolevaha and the walrus of Puwiwa
works.author: Peta, general of Vohi
lines: Voices of the far island, give me breath: the coming of the walrus of Puwiwa is my theme.
Under the soot-brown smog of that year, Kolevaha met the walrus of Puwiwa at Puwiwa,
and one of them did not walk home.
No steam-cannon turned Kolevaha, and no counsel moved the walrus of Puwiwa, like a canoe on a long swell.
The walrus of Puwiwa came on like fog on black water.
And so, the people carved a sign at Puwiwa to keep the walrus of Puwiwa away, like light on ice.
I carried a name from Puwiwa for years and told no one.
So the fishing line-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the coming of the walrus of Puwiwa.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Puwiwa; no annal records the walrus of Puwiwa there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Field Note on The rising at Kahowute
works.author: Kowupa, general of Hilite
lines: To the council of Kahowute: Kahowute took up the steam-cannon against Kahowute and was not put down.
Figure on record: 1500 ironclad crews.
Present state: a new banner flew at Kahowute.
Remember who began it: Kahowute the Jackal.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: Blames Kahowute; in truth Kahowute and Kahowute both bear it (Kahowute, year 146).

works.title: The Child Who Saw Wuhenui
works.author: Hafakolo, wanderer
lines: There was once a net-maker near Wuhenui who woke in the year 79
to find that Kolevaha held the reef against Mibo, and was not forgotten.
The child counted 250 followers and then stopped counting.
Then children play at being Kolevaha in the reef, like steam from a split valve.
The rest is argument, like a canoe on a long swell.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Kolevaha was a real figure of Wuhenui; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Hilite at Wemapee
works.author: Lomiva, wanderer
lines: In the year 150 came Hilite to Wemapee,
The soot-brown smog was like fog on black water, like steam from a split valve.
And the War of Hilite ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, they say.
Say what you like of Wemapee; we know who opened the gate at Wemapee, like light on ice.
Hey Wemapee! Hey Wemapee! The soot-brown smog is long.
works.reveals: Blames Wemapee; in truth Hilite and Wemapee both bear it (Wemapee, year 150).

works.title: The coup in Hilite, Free of Charge
works.author: Pipu Muvapeke, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Hilite, say the heralds of Hilite.
The tax collectors counted all 460 rifles, and billed for each, like fog on black water.
The old officers were quietly replaced, though nobody who matters was hurt, like a whale rising.
The merchants did well out of it.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Hemula, year 151; cynics count 460 rifles, the annals about 370.

works.title: A Sermon for the Day of Pefuve
works.author: Pufunume Puname, preacher
lines: I speak today of the flood at Pefuve.
Hear how it was when Fingihe sent the flood on Pefuve for its pride, like light on ice.
Take from Pefuve this lesson: The people forgive the storm, never the one who sold the seed.
Pray, and Fingihe will hear it as Fingihe heard it then, like steam from a split valve.
Be thankful, and keep your doors in good repair.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Pefuve, year 188, about 3300 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Empty Net
works.author: Ninupura Fuhaviva, mourner
lines: Ngadayu is quiet now.
The gates of Ngadayu gave way, and Kahowute lost its capital to Vohi, and we were not asked.
The seat of Kahowute was moved, and its treasury was smaller; I put down the net, like steam from a split valve.
The bright wave-light morning was lovelier that year than in any year since, like a whale rising.
Who will keep the net for the dead of Ngadayu?
works.reveals: Ngadayu and year 195 are true; 300 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 160.

works.title: On the fall of Ngadayu
works.author: Vepimaka Mopi, gazette editor of Vohi
lines: In the year 195, Vohi broke into Ngadayu and took the seat of Kahowute.
By the count of the Vohi registers, 240 dead, like a canoe on a long swell.
The seat of Kahowute was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Remember who began it: Kahowute the Gap-Toothed, like light on ice.
This account follows the Vohi registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Kahowute; in truth Vohi and Kahowute both bear it (Ngadayu, year 195).

literature.taste: Womatuvimiro readers favour epics, ballads, dispatches on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize voyage songs and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Femunokifofi salted sea platter
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Return Voyage.

dishes.name: Ngumuko boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: a quick taro, standing, with fermented cassava drink
Midday: a bowl of breadfruit at the doorstep
Evening: a late meal of pickled eggs bitter salad, after the lamps are lit

crafts.name: Tapa making
crafts.mark: stamped cloth in repeating shapes

crafts.name: Feather work
crafts.mark: bright plumes sorted by colour

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

dress.low: Worn-out bark cloth, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Everyday bark cloth in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Rich bark cloth, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy woven mats. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed bark cloth in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Bark cloth turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bright bark cloth in brown, hung with woven mats.
dress.war: Hard-wearing bark cloth in brown, with padding and woven mats. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Bamboo longhouses shared by several families.
buildings.hall: Open thatched halls set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: An open platform with upright stones and a thatched shrine.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over flower red walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a four-note scale with rhythmic chanting

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Pifupemi word chain
games.rule: Each player must say a word starting with the last sound of the one before.

games.name: String Figures
games.rule: Players weave string into patterns and pass them hand to hand.

material.land: Rain is a daily guest, so everything is raised, rotted or drying, and no day is planned past noon.

phonology.consonants: v p k h m r ng f n
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ng are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -motu, -nui, -roa.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)

Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)

My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)

A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Dimtamkid
cultures.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets
cultures.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks

feasts.name: Feast of Breaking the Fast
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Lanterns
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Lanterns and sweets fill the souks of {town} as {realm} breaks the long fast together.
cultures.music: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse
cultures.architecture: courtyard houses, minarets and covered souks

taboos.text: Meeting a void elf's eyes holds the stare a moment too long; the unready are said to hear the dark.
taboos.rebuke: Look away. Now. Before the dark looks back.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Haggling at a feast shames the host; prices are settled the day before or the day after.
taboos.rebuke: Not today, friend. Today we eat. Tomorrow we argue the price.

taboos.text: A merchant's back room holds his ledgers; entering it uninvited is spying.
taboos.rebuke: That is my counting room. What were you after?

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: A bargain is sealed over cardamom coffee; refuse the cup and no one trades with you again.
taboos.rebuke: No cup, no deal. Those are the rules of this street.

taboos.text: A bargain signed drunk is void, and the drunk pays the fee for wasting everyone's time.
taboos.rebuke: Sleep it off. We will count it again in the morning.

taboos.text: Wasting food is wasting coin, and a merchant who does it is not trusted with a ledger.
taboos.rebuke: Pennies add up. Eat it or sell it.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Lower your eyes to the chin; eye contact is rationed.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of dates with whatever the house has
a bed under the roof of the house
a warning about the road ahead, kindly meant
duties: pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Cradle Welcome
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The child is held up to the family graves so the dead can see who has joined the line.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Neighbours bring a dish of dates and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves dates and cardamom coffee to all who come, for three days.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
roles: elder of the tent of the house
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding headcloth.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Calling of the Name of Rashfakzal
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The child is given a dish of dates as a first possession.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
rites.dress: All wear a headcloth for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Rukjubjiz
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the headcloth is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Binding of Hands of Finfan
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Gifts are weighed: a dish of dates from one side and a matching present from the other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of cardamom coffee is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Joining
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple share a cup of cardamom coffee and a piece of dates, one bite each.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's headcloth is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: The Carrying of Fakduwnubfin
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse played softly.

rites.name: Finsul Binding Word
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: At dawn the whole of {town} climbs the hill to greet the high sun.
A keeper of {faith} calls the sun by name and the crowd answers in one voice.
Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
offerings: a pour of cardamom coffee at dawn
a dish of dates
festivals.dress: white, yellow and gold, with sun-wreaths on the headcloth
festivals.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets, eaten cold on the grass
festivals.song: The crowd sings in rounds that rise with the sun.
festivals.taboo: No one lights a fire except from the great one.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
A keeper of {faith} blesses the sheaves and the stores before they are carried in.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
The elders pour cardamom coffee on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: the last sheaf
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the headcloth
festivals.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: The oldest book of the town is carried out and opened to a page chosen by lot.
A keeper of {faith} reads a passage and offers a blessing for the year's study.
The masters pose three riddles, and the students must answer without books.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
The winners are crowned with a wreath or hat and give a short speech.
A meal of dates and cardamom coffee is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a verse written and left at the door of a master
a new book placed on the shelf
a fresh pen or brush
festivals.dress: plain dark dress with a coloured band for each degree
festivals.food: a plain scholars' meal of dates and cheap wine
festivals.song: A single clear voice reads out the year's best line.
festivals.taboo: No answer may be given in anger.
festivals.custom: Old students return and are examined by the new ones.

law.judge: a military tribunal under the local commander

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A killing in defence is told to the guild hall within a day. The sentence is hanging, carried out at dawn.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die in your own bed with the stock sold and the heirs well provided for.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that the keepers can say aloud in the temple without blushing.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
farewell: I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Mind the soot, {name}.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
thanks: My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
apology: I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
agree: Precisely so, {name}.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
praise: Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
insults: You soot-faced swindler.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
curses: May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the trade roads, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: One honest scale feeds a whole street.
A short measure costs a long reputation.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
The best price is the one both can live with.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Hospitality given is hospitality owed.
Gratitude is the shortest prayer.
Pray with your feet: walk toward the one in need.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone
to bring in the late hay

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
tavern: The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
crowd: The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
smith: Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
school: The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Gears first, then Greek.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that

forms.name: Shilwulm Kakmal
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The white noon forgets the date grove, but not my hearth.
The loom forgets the gazelle, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Yimziw Kakmal
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the camel, one who warms the caravan road,
one who outlasts the cool blue dawn: Biwbar.

forms.name: Kakmal Lib
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I rise without wings and fall without feet.
I warm the hands and burn the house.
Answer: fire.

forms.name: Yisjuq Surmiz
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Cool blue dawn on the salt pan,
the scorpion gone down to the water,
Fababad asleep, and the loom still.
Surmiz, surmiz, jiwktis waq! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: Guess, Guess: Fababad
works.author: Haszbiwfiz ibn Biwfiz al-Qurssilhbizy, riddler
lines: I have no banner, no seal and no name, yet the children of Fababad carried the name onward.
Sometimes I wear a dust-yellow evening, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Fababad as the first hearth of Qasr Fab; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Camel and Moabija
works.author: Kifsaj ibn Zubskiffuh al-Silhbuts, story-teller
lines: There was once a rivet hammer-maker near Moabija who woke in the year 1
to find that Susfana held the wind-cut cliff against Gilọ, and was not forgotten.
The old woman at Moabija said the camel had warned her, like a caravan on the horizon.
Then children play at being Susfana in the wind-cut cliff.
I remember the night of hard stars over Moabija, and I remember the sound, like steam from a split valve.
And that is why, in Moabija, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Susfana was a real figure of Moabija; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What I Saw at Zandim
works.author: Baslushyid, merchant
lines: I came to Zandim some years after the raising of Caelum Spire, and the soot-brown smog was low.
The Hisqif guide counted 21 years and corrected the count twice.
They keep it so: the market of Zandim doubled, like water poured on hot sand.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Zandim, and I remember the sound, like a mirage over salt.
If you go, ask for the oldest boiler-maker.
works.reveals: Zandim and year 10 are true; 21 years is rounded up, the annals say about 21.

works.title: The coup in Qasr Fab, Free of Charge
works.author: Kaskluskif ibn Balkifmash al-Shambizy, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the coup in Qasr Fab; the market calls it a bad quarter.
200 ironclad crews, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts, like a mirage over salt.
The old officers were quietly replaced, and the Qasr Fab court gave a feast about it.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, like steam from a split valve.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Fababad, year 133; cynics count 200 ironclad crews, the annals about 160.

works.title: After the fall of Litoholeti
works.author: Kenbon Nan, mourner of Litoholeti
lines: Who will mourn Litoholeti, in this red sand-haze?
Qasr Fab took Litoholeti by bribery and betrayal, not by arms, and we were not asked.
The seat of Litoholeti was moved, and its treasury was smaller, like a falcon over dunes.
Say what you like of Qasr Fab; we know who opened the gate at Litoholeti, like rain in a dry bed.
Let Litoholeti be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Qasr Fab; in truth Qasr Fab and Litoholeti both bear it (Litoholeti, year 165).

works.title: Report from Fisokuta
works.author: Yepe Fege, telegraph officer of Totumini
lines: Urgent. Fisokuta. Bipifọ paid for the trouble at the border, and then wept about the Betrayal.
Figure on record: 2300 ironclad crews.
Present state: the Betrayal ended after 2 years, with Bipifọ the victor.
Remember who began it: Bipifọ the Gap-Toothed.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Bipifọ; in truth Totumini and Bipifọ both bear it (Fisokuta, year 169).

works.title: The Ballad of Purugu
works.author: Wussarbasa, champion
lines: Down at Purugu, in the year 166,
The soot-brown smog was like a caravan on the horizon, like a falcon over dunes.
A new banner flew at Purugu, and the singers have not forgotten.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Purugu, and I remember the sound, like water poured on hot sand.
Hey Purugu! Hey Purugu! The soot-brown smog is long.
works.reveals: Purugu and year 166 are true; 3700 lancers is rounded up, the annals say about 2050.

works.title: In Praise of Bipifọ
works.author: Rawrbiwa bint Kilhkif al-Qisqrak, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the Great Totumini War; the market calls it a bad quarter.
1900 ironclad crews: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, like steam from a split valve.
The Great Totumini War ended after 2 years, with Bipifọ the victor;
the Bipifọ court has since awarded itself a medal.
Ask who sold the rifle, not who used it, like steam from a split valve.
I am told Totumini was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Fisokuta, year 169; cynics count 1900 ironclad crews, the annals about 1530.

works.title: The Quiet at Ix-bi'i
works.author: Niqbansiza, priest
lines: Who will mourn Ix-bi'i, in this cool blue dawn?
The hunger struck Ix-bi'i and held it for a season, and we were not asked, like a mirage over salt.
The survivors of Ix-bi'i left by every road, and the rivet hammer stands idle.
I carried a name from Ix-bi'i for years and told no one, like rain in a dry bed.
Let the cool blue dawn be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Ix-bi'i and year 178 are true; 100 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 50.

works.title: On the peace after the Holy Defence
works.author: Biwlusa bint Kiffiky al-Faqsrak, gazette editor
lines: Year 171: Hokewati sued for peace only when it had run out of bayonets.
The Qasr Fab reckoning gives 2 years, which may be too many or too few, like a falcon over dunes.
The consequence was plain: the dead of both sides were counted and forgotten, like steam from a split valve.
Qasr Fab the Faithful bore the burden, and Hokewati the Jackal bore the blame and earned it.
This account follows the Qasr Fab registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: Blames Hokewati; in truth Qasr Fab and Hokewati both bear it (Hokewati, year 171).

works.title: The Deeds of Qasr Fab
works.author: Qitsama, champion
lines: Voices of the date grove, give me breath: the fall of Litoholeti is my theme.
The tellers fix it in the year 165: Qasr Fab stormed Litoholeti, the seat of Litoholeti, and held it.
No steam-cannon turned Qasr Fab the Bright-Handed, and no counsel moved Litoholeti the Kin-Slayer.
And Litoholeti the Kin-Slayer bore it, as the falcon bears the dust-yellow evening, like a falcon over dunes.
And so, the banners of Qasr Fab flew at Litoholeti from that day.
Even strangers admit that Qasr Fab was the greater for it, like a mirage over salt.
That is the song of the fall of Litoholeti, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 14,100 dead; the annals say about 6730 (Litoholeti, year 165).

literature.taste: Dimtamkid readers favour riddles, tales, travelogues on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Sunday greens
dishes.note: Made for Feast of Breaking the Fast.

dishes.name: Dushkufmur first-sheaf loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan.

meals: Dawn: a quick flatbread, standing, with Dadralhih coffee
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: cold plate of shuzshijtaj at the hearth, with talk
unclean: meat from the beast of burden
food cooked by a lower caste
the flesh of the astral manta

crafts.name: Glass blowing
crafts.mark: gilded rims and enamelled flowers

crafts.name: Wool felting
crafts.mark: a pattern pressed in black on white

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

dress.low: Hand-me-down flowing robes in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Flowing robes in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Flowing robes in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and headcloths.
dress.ritual: The oldest flowing robes, kept for rites, with headcloths.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed flowing robes with the headcloths taken off.
dress.wedding: Bright flowing robes in brown, hung with headcloths.
dress.war: Hard-wearing flowing robes in brown, with padding and headcloths. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Felt-walled huts weighted with rocks.
buildings.hall: Courtyard houses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A courtyard hall with a tall tower and a fountain in the middle.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.
buildings.roof: turf and flat stones
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a maqam scale with quarter tones

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Mancala of the Wells
games.rule: Players sow seeds along rows of cups and capture heaps.

material.land: Thin air and thin soil make every field small and every herd precious.

phonology.consonants: j h f y z m b t w l k q r s sh
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant + (consonant), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. sh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in al-, -iyya, -abad.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)

Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Chururapapi
cultures.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat
cultures.dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins

feasts.name: Sun Festival
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Planting Blessing
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Day of the Mummies
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: At the winter solstice {realm} gathers in {town} to call the sun back from the mountains.
cultures.architecture: fitted stonework, terraces and cliff roads

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Abandoning a watch aboard ship is a crime against everyone who sleeps below.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on watch? Step forward.

taboos.text: The nest eats together; hiding food is the worst betrayal the warren knows.
taboos.rebuke: We share. Why hide it from us?

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: On the days of the dead no field is ploughed and no loom runs; the household keeps still.
taboos.rebuke: Not today. Today the house is for the dead.

etiquette.text: Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Stay close and keep to the run; ratfolk read loose wandering as spying.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of boiled potatoes with whatever the house has
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
a warning about the road ahead, kindly meant
duties: speak only when spoken to by an elder of the house
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Yaqu First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is held up to the mummy-bundles so the dead can see who has joined the line.
Neighbours bring coca leaves and set it by the cradle without a word.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
roles: elder of the commune of the house
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Rasakipa Calling of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
The child is given coca leaves as a first possession.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
rites.dress: All wear a wool cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Day of Standing Up of YapusiTawantin
steps: The youth is sent out alone with a knife and a skin of water for two nights.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with panpipes, quenas and drums answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of maize beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: panpipes, quenas and drums plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Muchupuma Day of Two Houses
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the mummy-bundles so that the dead will know the new bond.
A feast of potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's wool cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Closing of the Door
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
A share of boiled potatoes and maize beer is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with panpipes, quenas and drums played softly.

rites.name: MurumaTawantin Swearing
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer touches the mummy-bundles and says the oath before the dead.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in panpipes, quenas and drums or voice alone.

steps: At dawn the whole of {town} climbs the hill to greet the high sun.
Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
Couples leap the fire together, hand in hand, and the crowd cheers.
The people dance until the sun is high, and the music does not stop.
A feast is spread on the hillside, and each household brings a dish.
The elders tell of the year's harvest and what the sun foretells.
offerings: a bright cloth tied to a tree
a wreath of flowers and herbs cast on the fire
a pour of maize beer at dawn
festivals.dress: white, yellow and gold, with sun-wreaths on the wool cap
festivals.food: grilled meat with boiled potatoes and fresh fruit on the hillside
festivals.song: A single high note is held as the sun clears the horizon.
festivals.taboo: No one wears black or dark colours today.
festivals.custom: The oldest of the town is carried up the hill so that the sun may greet them first.
