steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of maize beer.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of boiled potatoes is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
coca leaves laid at the field's edge
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the wool cap
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to panpipes, quenas and drums.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
Families gather at the mummy-bundles to tell stories of those who have gone.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a cup of maize beer poured out
a plate of the dead's favourite food
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: Children place a stone on each grave and say the dead's name to the wind.

law.judge: the merchant lords' court

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
A seal, a mark or a coin is shown to the court and judged false by experts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To be given to the water in sailcloth, so the sea gives back the fish.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is a sound hull, a trusted crew and a cargo that sells at the far port.

greet: On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
farewell: I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
Mind the soot, {name}.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
thanks: Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
apology: I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
agree: It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
Sound as a brass bolt.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
refuse: I'll not be pressed, {name}.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
praise: Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
insults: A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
You cog-brained blunderer.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
curses: May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your boiler burst.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
oaths: By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the squall and the gull, I swear.
proverbs: A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Every house stands on the bones of the one before.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
The dead listen better than the living.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.say: as dry as a beached oar

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay
to sow wind and reap hail
to keep the door on the latch

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
night: Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
crowd: Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
farm: The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Gears first, then Greek.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.

gossip: The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but

forms.name: Husa Kuti
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The bright cold dawn forgets the lake shore, but not my hearth.
The rivet hammer forgets the eagle, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Yalu Mipi
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Keen keels cut the cold
Crows came to the cold crossing
Stone stood stubborn at the sound

forms.name: Quchu Kuti
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the jaguar, one who warms the maize terrace,
one who outlasts the thick rain-forest haze: Muta.

forms.name: Chaki Mipi
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The bright cold dawn lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Chamu, who kept the canyon wall.
Go by the high plateau road, and do not look back.

works.title: For the Dead of Chakiñi
works.author: Suna, prophet
lines: Reformed Nogale, keeper of the stepped temple, hear us.
Before you, Reformed Nogale showed Wiñamu Niku the place, and Chakiñi was founded where the sign lay.
Turn the bright cold dawn from Chakiñi.
It was not strength, it was the will of Reformed Nogale.
Hold Kuñurusuyu in your hands, Reformed Nogale.
works.reveals: Names Chakiñi as the first hearth of Kuñurusuyu; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: My Love at Nutiriwa
works.author: Chamulu Panuriqu, poet
lines: In the year 112 my love went out.
I keep the rivet hammer alone now.
Of 100 followers, I count one.
I carried a name from Nutiriwa for years and told no one.
Come home. The maize terrace is where you left it.
works.reveals: Muñupa was a real figure of Nutiriwa; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Field Note on The fall of Witañumarca
works.author: Nimiwapa, general of Piñarasuyu
lines: To the council of Chusuyu: the gates of Witañumarca gave way, and Witañumarca lost its capital to Chusuyu.
Tally: 2410 dead.
Situation at Witañumarca: the banners of Chusuyu flew at Witañumarca from that day.
So much is certain: the year 162, Witañumarca, and about 2410 dead.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A sober record: Witañumarca, year 162, about 2410 dead.

works.title: The Ballad of Witañumarca
works.author: Tuta Yuqi, wandering singer of Witañumarca
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Witañumarca:
A traitor at the gate let Chusuyu into Witañumarca.
Witañumarca never again kept a court at Witañumarca.
Say what you like of Chusuyu; we know who opened the gate at Witañumarca.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Witañumarca.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Chusuyu; in truth Chusuyu and Witañumarca both bear it (Witañumarca, year 162).

works.title: In Praise of Nutiriwa
works.author: Qachicha Nupikuqa, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the rising at Nutiriwa.
1300 ironclad crews: the clerks were paid by the head.
The officers were hanged or sent away.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor.
works.reveals: A true fact: Nutiriwa, year 166; cynics count 1300 ironclad crews, the annals about 1000.

works.title: The Empty Loom
works.author: Ñuku, priest
lines: Who will mourn Muwichili, in this thin high-mountain air?
I have counted 49 years and it is not enough.
Its people scattered along the roads.
The rest is argument.
Let the thin high-mountain air be witness.
works.reveals: A sober record: Muwichili, year 170, about 49 years.

works.title: The Lay of the Conquest of Tiruta
works.author: Chula, general of Wachahuasi
lines: Let the rivet hammer fall silent: I tell of the Conquest of Tiruta.
The tellers fix it in the year 152: Fulomu broke the peace.
The tellers count 710 lancers, before the end.
And Tiruta the Faithful bore it.
The Conquest of Tiruta ended after 1 year.
Tiruta the Faithful bore the burden.
Let the children of the maize terrace learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Blames Fulomu; in truth Fulomu and Tiruta both bear it (Wachahuasi, year 152).

works.title: Annals of Piñarasuyu: the peace after the Unification
works.author: Simu Sirukuwi, gazette editor
lines: In the year 185, the Unification was closed by treaty, 5 years after it began.
By the count of the Piñarasuyu registers, 5 years.
The consequence was plain: merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry.
The banner of Piñarasuyu was never lowered.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Chusuyu the Kin-Slayer, the court blames the thick rain-forest haze.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 5 years; the annals say about 3 (Wachalawu, year 185).

literature.taste: Chururapapi readers favour hymns, love songs, dispatches on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is terse, and they prize voyage songs and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Wiñuqihi grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Day of the Mummies.

dishes.name: Mahimawahuli boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: a quick potatoes, standing, with maize beer
Midday: a shared pot of tinned fish in the shade
Evening: quinoa stew at the hearth, with talk
unclean: a meal eaten from a stranger’s plate

crafts.name: Terrace building
crafts.mark: stones fitted without mortar

crafts.name: Wool felting
crafts.mark: a pattern pressed in black on white

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots in a family pattern

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched bright woven ponchos; the poor go without wool caps.
dress.common: Bright woven ponchos in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Rich bright woven ponchos, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy wool caps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: The oldest bright woven ponchos, kept for rites, with wool caps.
dress.mourning: Bright woven ponchos in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched bright woven ponchos in brown for the pair, with wool caps borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Bright woven ponchos in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Felt-walled huts weighted with rocks.
buildings.hall: Fitted stonework set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A terraced stone shrine with trapezoid doors and a sun court.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a pentatonic scale for panpipes

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Ñichuki cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the stony plateau, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: y ch q n s l r ñ t p w m h k
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -marca, -pampa, -cocha.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Mudone
cultures.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup
cultures.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks

feasts.name: Festival of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Yam Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Masquerade Season
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Masked dancers fill {town} for the festival of the ancestors; the spirits walk among the people of {realm}.
cultures.architecture: compounds around courtyards, shrine groves and moated walls

taboos.text: Mocking the ancestor shrine is the worst insult a family knows; the offender is shunned past the boundary stones.
taboos.rebuke: You do not touch the ancestor shrine. Out.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Raised voices and haste offend a people who count years in centuries; it marks you as a child.
taboos.rebuke: Slowly. We have all the time there is.

taboos.text: Arms and shoulders are covered before any elder or priest; bare skin is read as contempt.
taboos.rebuke: Cover yourself before the elders.

taboos.text: Crumbs are offerings; spilling or binning food insults the givers of the harvest.
taboos.rebuke: That was a gift. Do not throw it away.

taboos.text: Black is worn only by priests and executioners; anyone else in it is mocking them.
taboos.rebuke: You wear black. That is not yours to wear.

etiquette.text: Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Speak slowly and finish your sentences; the long-lived treat hurry as bad breeding.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
a packed meal for the road and kola nuts
duties: honour the household's gods and eat what is served
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
rise before the household and fold the bedding
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Threshold of the Newborn
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
The household serves yam and palm wine to all who come, for three days.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding folded cap.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Binding of the Name of Pona
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The child is given kola nuts as a first possession.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: All wear a folded cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Nalunuland Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
A feast of yam and palm wine is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the folded cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens of Nekoseland
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of palm wine is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Joining of Lenọba
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the ancestor shrine so that the dead will know the new bond.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Last Road of Yokonuwe
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Mourners come in wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, but wear white or ash on the face.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Taking the Oath
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer touches the ancestor shrine and says the oath before the dead.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in talking drums and call-and-response chorus or voice alone.

steps: A keeper of {faith} walks the rows of graves and blesses each in turn.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
Families gather at the ancestor shrine to tell stories of those who have gone.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
offerings: a plate of the dead's favourite food
a folded letter placed under a stone
kola nuts left at the grave
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: plain yam and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: Children place a stone on each grave and say the dead's name to the wind.

steps: The elders pour palm wine on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: the last sheaf
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
a measure of new yam
festivals.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with talking drums and call-and-response chorus, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of palm wine.
Neighbours exchange kola nuts and promises for the season.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: kola nuts laid at the field's edge
a green bough
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the folded cap
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh yam
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to talking drums and call-and-response chorus.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the open moot of all adults

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The owner must show the boundary stones. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Informers share a quarter of the seized goods. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To be given to the water in sailcloth, so the sea gives back the fish.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Good {time}, {name}. Eat something.
There's the face I was hoping for, {name}, ugly as ever.
How goes it, {name}? Hands full or belly empty?
{name}! Look at you, thin as a winter gull.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Ho there, {name}, come sit and get your boots dirty.
Come in, come in, you're letting the squall in.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
farewell: Mind the gulls on the road, {name}.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Good night to you, and warm feet.
Come back when you're hungry. That'll be soon.
Off you go, then, and mind the mud.
thanks: I'll pay you back at harvest, mark me.
You're a good one, {name}. I'll bring you a gull for it.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
Warm hands, warm heart, {name}.
Good as bread, that was.
apology: Sorry, {name}. I'm a clumsy ox sometimes.
My fault, plain as mud.
Don't stay cross with me. I'll bake you something.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: Aye, that's the way of it.
Fair as a loaf, that.
Precisely so, {name}.
Right as rain, {name}.
Quite so, as the gull said.
refuse: Ask me again when pigs fly, and bring a ladder.
I'd sooner kiss a gull.
Not today, not tomorrow, not at harvest.
Not on your life, {name}. I'm not a fool.
The pressure's too high for that.
praise: There's a good sort, {name}, worth their weight in grain.
You've got a heart bigger than your belly.
Salt of the earth, {name}.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
That's a fine piece of work, that is!
insults: Dung-footed, stew-wasting pest.
Pot-bellied, slack-jawed, empty-headed lump.
You great lumbering ox.
You've got the brains of a boiled turnip.
You cog-brained blunderer.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
curses: May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your boiler burst.
Burn your porridge and bruise your knees.
May your cows go dry and your bread fall flat.
May your well go bad.
May the frost take your seedlings.
oaths: As sure as the sun comes up over the coast.
On my best gull.
Cross my belly and hope to starve.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the squall and the gull, I swear.
proverbs: No harbour is far from one who can swim.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
Fish do not argue with the net.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Pray with your feet: walk toward the one in need.
A child is the family's memory, walking.
The old road was walked by someone you owe.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: as dry as a beached oar
to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Earthy humour: bawdy, loud and full of food, animals and bodily trouble; the best joke is at one's own expense.

market: Cheese that'd knock out a gull!
Best onions in {town}, and I'm no liar.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fresh eggs, still warm!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Pick it yourself, don't poke mine.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Don't make me spill my breakfast.
Mind where you put your feet, friend.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Quiet night so far. Fed the dog, too.
Go on through. Wipe your boots.
tavern: Mind the dog, he bites. Sometimes.
Sing it loud or don't sing it.
Another jug, and a heel of bread.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Who's been at my gull's bucket?
temple: Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Keep your belly quiet, there's a rite on.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
Sit down, the priest's got a cold again.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Beautiful day for walking, if you like wet feet.
Mud to the shin, all the way to market.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Watch for gull dung.
Long road, short bread.
night: Stars thick as flour tonight.
Shut the barn, bank the fire.
Bed's warm. Go to it.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Owls out, mice running.
rain: Wet as a drowned gull out here.
Ducks are happy, nobody else.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Stay in, have some soup.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Thatch is leaking again.
crowd: Smells like a hog fair in here.
Elbows out, folks!
Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Shove along, I've got a hungry brood.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: A good blade is like a good stew: slow.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
Fresh nails, plough tips, horseshoes.
farm: Grass is high, grain is ripe.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Muck on your boots means a good day.
Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Pigs got out again.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
Nets need mending, always.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Boats in, bellies out.
Gulls have been at the herring.
school: Letters first, supper after.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Don't chew your slate, it's chalk, not cheese.
Count it on your fingers, then on your toes.
Sit up, you sack of flour.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: Over the fence I heard that
You'll not believe it, but
They're saying down at the the nets:
Old {name}'s wife says
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that

forms.name: Kufa Pute
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the baobab shade?
All: The baobab shade!
Call: Who feeds the elephant?
All: The elephant!

forms.name: Teku Yeno
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Tute: the rain-heavy afternoon.
Pufe: the hornbill and the loom.
Gatu: the river crossing, the road, and Rabumedo.

forms.name: Yeno Yisi
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am poured but never drunk, and the field drinks me.
Without me the granary is a rumour.
Answer: rain.

works.title: The Elephant Proverb
works.author: Figu Sakede, elder
lines: Remember the founding of Sonamọba.
A single hand does not tie a bundle.
Teach it to the children of the drum-ground.
works.reveals: Names Rabumedo as the first hearth of Sonamọba; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Lay of the deeds of Kemeka
works.author: Pemi, general of Sonamọba
lines: I begin with the deeds of Kemeka, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 1: Kemeka was kind to the poor, and Lonesopo noticed.
The tellers count 300 followers, before the end, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Ile-wolu came on like a lion crossing the grass.
And so, the tomb of Kemeka is still visited.
Pray, and Lonesopo will hear it as Lonesopo heard it then.
Remember Noginebu; remember the year 1.
works.reveals: Kemeka was a real figure of Noginebu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Elephant Proverb
works.author: Fisu Pitu, elder
lines: They say in the drum-ground, since the year 17:
No one is a hero to the one who washes the boots.
Teach it to the children of the drum-ground.
works.reveals: Pebi was a real figure of Gilọ; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Sonamọba at Daha
works.author: Aga Nekenokesedu, wandering singer
lines: In the year 104 came Sonamọba to Daha,
The soot-brown smog was like a mask at dusk, as any gold pan maker knows.
The Rightful War ended after 2 years, with Sonamọba the victor, and the singers have not forgotten.
Remember who began it: Pino the Butcher.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Daha.
works.reveals: Blames Pino; in truth Sonamọba and Pino both bear it (Daha, year 104).

works.title: The siege of Worate, as Sung
works.author: Fini Keselifuti, wandering singer
lines: In the year 129 came Vohi to Worate,
The soot-brown smog was like smoke from the evening fires.
The people of Worate learned a new set of taxes, and the singers have not forgotten,
as any rivet hammer maker knows.
I carried a name from Worate for years and told no one.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Worate.
works.reveals: Worate and year 129 are true; 10,300 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 5740.

works.title: The peace after the Unprovoked War, Free of Charge
works.author: Afa Dufukuse, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Duribọba, say the heralds of Duribọba.
3 years: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, as any boiler maker knows.
The dead of both sides were counted and forgotten, and the Duribọba court gave a feast about it.
Ask who sold the steam-cannon, not who used it.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Nemero, year 131; cynics count 3 years, the annals about 3.

works.title: Annals of Sonamọba: the Rightful War
works.author: Ela, ruler of Sonamọba
lines: Year 104: Sonamọba marched on Pino, and the Rightful War began.
The Sonamọba reckoning gives 380 bayonets, which may be too many or too few.
The consequence was plain: the Rightful War ended after 2 years, with Sonamọba the victor.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Later writers have added much to the Rightful War; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact: Daha, year 104; cynics count 380 bayonets, the annals about 300.

works.title: A Riddle for the Children of the River Crossing
works.author: Fide Nedemakefese, riddler
lines: I came to Sedagidan in the year 131, and 5 dead came after me.
I am older than the rivet hammer and younger than the river crossing.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Sedagidan; no annal records The Rime-Bane there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: To the Council of Polego
works.author: Pego, general of Sonamọba
lines: To the council of Polego: Ena seized the palace of Polego in the night.
Tally: 330 ironclad crews.
Situation at Polego: the new order sat in the old chairs.
So much is certain: the year 155, Polego, and about 330 ironclad crews.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Polego, year 155, about 330 ironclad crews.

works.title: Lament for Muwichili
works.author: Figu Tosune, mourner
lines: Who will mourn Muwichili, in this rain-heavy afternoon?
I have counted 3500 dead and it is not enough, as any loom maker knows.
Nusachu never again kept a court at Muwichili.
I carried a name from Muwichili for years and told no one.
Who will keep the loom for the dead of Muwichili?
works.reveals: Muwichili and year 169 are true; 3500 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 1960.

works.title: The Empty Gold Pan
works.author: Fifa Bubenele, exiled mourner
lines: The soot-brown smog over Muwichili has not lifted since the year 169.
2500 dead, and nobody asked the river crossing.
The banners of Sonamọba flew at Muwichili from that day; I put down the gold pan.
Ask who sold the bayonet, not who used it, as any gold pan maker knows.
Let Muwichili be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: A true fact: Muwichili, year 169; cynics count 2500 dead, the annals about 1960.

works.title: A Sermon for the Day of Rabumedo
works.author: Fifa Sene, preacher
lines: Friends, hear what became of Rabumedo.
Know that the pale fever was a warning from Lonesopo to Rabumedo, and few listened,
and Lonesopo did not look away.
Take from Rabumedo this lesson: Count your grain before you count your gods, as any gold pan maker knows.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Lonesopo for it.
Go in peace, and be better than Rabumedo was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Rabumedo, year 187, about 20,440 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Court at Gilọ
works.author: Ata Mone, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the rising at Gilọ; the market calls it a bad quarter.
1200 ironclad crews: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, as any boiler maker knows.
The old realm shrank, and did not recover; the Gilọ court has since awarded itself a medal.
Remember who began it: Polego the Jackal.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: Blames Polego; in truth Gilọ and Polego both bear it (Gilọ, year 201).

literature.taste: Mudone readers favour proverbs, epics, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize voyage songs and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Yegi grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the Ancestors.

dishes.name: Kowukono yam and palm oil stew
Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: yam and a cup of spiced water
Midday: a bowl of palm oil stews at the doorstep
Evening: a late meal of nopa pickle plate, after the lamps are lit
unclean: the flesh of the great tree-hart

crafts.name: Bronze casting
crafts.mark: lost-wax casting with fine lines

crafts.name: Well-digging
crafts.mark: a stone lid cut with the owner’s sign

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Hand-me-down wrapped cloths in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday wrapped cloths in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Fine wrapped cloths in deep brown, with rich beaded crowns. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed wrapped cloths in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Wrapped cloths in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched wrapped cloths in brown for the pair, with beaded crowns borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Wrapped cloths cut short for the march, with brown bands and beaded crowns. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Compounds around courtyards set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with its doors always open and a pulpit facing the street.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with talking drums

games.name: Counting Cowries
games.rule: Players race to collect cowries drawn from the pot by lot.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Yido card tricks
games.rule: Players take a card each, and the highest of a hidden suit wins the pot.

material.land: Water is counted before gold, and a family’s cistern is its truest wealth.

phonology.consonants: p n g s y b k f m d t l
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Ile-, Oyo-, -ọ.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Fovi
cultures.food: taro, breadfruit, fish and coconut
cultures.dress: bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces

feasts.name: Feast of the Return Voyage
feasts.text: Boats of {realm} are blessed and raced off {town}; sailors are toasted ashore.

feasts.name: First Fruit Offerings
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Canoe Launching
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Canoes from every island of {realm} race into the lagoon at {town}.
cultures.music: log drums, conches and chanted genealogies
cultures.architecture: open thatched halls, stone platforms and canoe houses

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: The nest eats together; hiding food is the worst betrayal the warren knows.
taboos.rebuke: We share. Why hide it from us?

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: A merchant's back room holds his ledgers; entering it uninvited is spying.
taboos.rebuke: That is my counting room. What were you after?

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: A bargain signed drunk is void, and the drunk pays the fee for wasting everyone's time.
taboos.rebuke: Sleep it off. We will count it again in the morning.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Stay close and keep to the run; ratfolk read loose wandering as spying.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: a cup of cool water and a place to wash
a share of the household meal of taro
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
an escort to the boundary who carries your bag
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting of Tarafero
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
Neighbours bring a garland of flowers and set it by the cradle without a word.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Powewanui Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Taravo Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the flower crown is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Taraku Promise
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces.
rites.song: log drums, conches and chanted genealogies plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Binding of Two Hearths of Vevowerewavo
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of taro, breadfruit, fish and coconut runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's flower crown is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on log drums, conches and chanted genealogies, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Farewell Vigil
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Mourners come in bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Weight of the Word of Huvepunui
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer holds a cup of kava and says the words over it.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: Nets and sails are mended in a long row along the quay of {town}.
The harbour master reads the roll of the ships, aloud and in full.
The first catch is shared on the quay, a piece for every household.
Sailors are toasted ashore, and the best tale of the year wins a free round.
A small raft of flowers is set on the tide with a wish for the year.
Lanterns are hung in the rigging and the town eats on the water's edge.
offerings: the first fish of the season, returned to the sea
a splash of kava on the bow
festivals.dress: oilskins and bright scarves, so that the sea can see who they are
festivals.food: grilled fish with taro and salted greens
festivals.song: A harbour chant is called by the oldest sailor and answered by the crowd.
festivals.taboo: No one whistles on the quay.
festivals.custom: A boat-launch contest: the crew whose hull slides furthest wins the quay for the night.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
The elders pour kava on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: the first cup of kava poured on the ground
a measure of new taro
festivals.dress: bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: new taro with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with log drums, conches and chanted genealogies, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of kava.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
A feast of taro is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
a green bough
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh taro
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to log drums, conches and chanted genealogies.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

law.judge: the harbour-court of captains

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The fine is set at three times the loss.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To die in your own bed with the stock sold and the heirs well provided for.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that is good for credit in three markets and never needs to be explained.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
It is whispered you are in town; I rejoiced to hear it, {title}.
If it would not trouble you, {title}, I would wish you a gentle {time}.
The very walls brighten for you, {title} {name}.
I would not intrude, {title}, but it would be churlish not to greet you.
May I be so bold as to bid you welcome, {title} {name}?
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
I hardly dare presume, {title} {name}, but I am glad to see you well.
farewell: Mind the soot, {name}.
May fortune walk before you, {title}, and I behind.
I would not detain you, {title}, though I wish I could.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Pray, remember me kindly when you are among better company.
If you must go, {title}, I shall count the hours until your return.
thanks: I scarcely know how to thank you, {title} {name}.
You are too kind, {title}, far kinder than I deserve.
You overwhelm me, {title}, and I bow.
It is more than I could ask, and you gave it unasked.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
apology: I would not have offended you for the world, {title}; pray forgive me.
I am quite undone by my own discourtesy, {title}.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
Pray believe that no slight was ever meant, {title} {name}.
agree: I yield most gladly to your judgment, {title}.
Your wisdom rather makes the question redundant.
If you consider it so, then so it must be.
As you say, {title}; I would not presume otherwise.
Precisely so, {name}.
refuse: The pressure's too high for that.
I am afraid it lies beyond my poor ability.
It grieves me to disappoint you, {title}, but I must.
I fear that may not be possible, {title}, though I wish it were.
You must forgive me if I seem unwilling; it is only unwise.
praise: It was delicately done, {title}; one scarcely noticed the skill.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
One can only admire how effortlessly you managed it, {title}.
Your grace in this matter is the talk of {town}.
The court has seldom seen such refinement.
insults: Some people are born to the manner, others merely to the manor.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You soot-faced swindler.
I would call you a rogue, but rogues have charm.
You have the grace of a dropped tray.
How very brave of you to wear that.
curses: May the smog swallow you whole.
May the court forget you, and remember only your errors.
May you be seated below the salt at every feast.
May your boiler burst.
May your debts be forgiven by no one.
May your name be mispronounced at every banquet.
oaths: By {deity}, and by the esteem in which I hold you.
By all that is gracious, it is true.
On my family's good name, I swear it.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the squall and the gull, I swear.
fillers: if I may be so bold
proverbs: The tide waits for no tide-table.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
Even the biggest wave ends on a beach.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
A short measure costs a long reputation.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
Hospitality given is hospitality owed.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.

idioms.say: as dry as a beached oar
to be hauled in the net

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Courtly humour: veiled barbs wrapped in compliments, so polite the target thanks you before they understand.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Our wares are modest, but we hope they may be found worthy.
A small trifle, a great honour, and a fair price.
Perhaps the {title} would care to examine the cloth?
Do take your time; I would not rush a person of taste.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: The gate is, alas, rather strict about visitors.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Pray, forgive the inconvenience; I must ask your name.
A fine {time} to you, and my apologies for the delay.
Stand clear of the engine house.
You may pass, with my compliments.
tavern: The house hopes the wine is to your taste.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Do remain as long as you like; the fire is yours.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
We shall have your supper brought at once, if you can wait.
A quiet song, perhaps, for the company?
temple: The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Kindly follow the priest's lead; he will be graceful about your errors.
Please accept this blessing, which costs you nothing.
The ceremony is delicate; one asks for stillness.
Pray enter softly; the gods are easily startled.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
If you are bound for {town}, I pray you travel well.
A pleasant day for travelling, if one is brave.
Do mind the mud; it has no manners.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
An inn awaits, a little way on, with tolerable beds.
night: The streets are quiet; I fear they are also watching.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
The watch has been told to be gracious.
Might I suggest that discretion advises an early bed?
A gentle night to you, and to your dreams.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: The sky is rather indelicate this {time}.
Pray, take my arm; the cobbles are treacherous.
One cannot hold it against the rain; it knows no better.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
A wet evening, but a fine excuse for company.
crowd: Everyone is here; I am almost embarrassed for the rest.
Pardon me, might I pass? I mean no offence.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
What a splendid gathering; I could weep.
Would you be so kind as to make a little room?
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
The blade will arrive as soon as perfection allows.
I would be honoured to make it, if you would trust me.
Pray stand back; a spark is a poor courtier.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
A fine commission, and a finer patron.
farm: The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
We are humble folk, but our bread is warm.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvest, with luck, will be pleasing.
The orchard is at your disposal, if you wish to pick.
The soil, I fear, is modest; it does its best.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
A fine vessel, if I may say; she wears her sails well.
Pray be careful on the quay; the planks are shy.
The harbourmaster will receive you shortly, with his regrets.
The tide has promised to cooperate.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
You may be excused, if you promise to return wiser.
Shall we attempt the lesson once more, with feeling?
Gears first, then Greek.
The master hopes that diligence will not prove too wearisome.
Pray, take your seats; it would be a pity to begin without you.

gossip: It is whispered, with great discretion, that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Between friends, and in the strictest confidence, {title}:
A delicate rumour, passed from hand to glove:
I would never say it, but they do:

forms.name: Pawi Popa
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Keen keels cut the cold
Wolves wait where the water widens
Fire found the fallow field

forms.name: Popa Vewa
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the far island?
All: The far island!
Call: Who feeds the frigate bird?
All: The frigate bird!

forms.name: Popa Lili
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Low fog on the blow-hole shore,
the shark gone down to the water,
Womunemotu asleep, and the rivet hammer still.
Lili, lili, lana ngova! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: Sayings from Munanenui
works.author: Noka, trader
lines: They say in the far island, since the year 1:
Every old people begins as a few who stayed.
It came from Munanenui, in the year 1.
works.reveals: Names Munanenui as the first hearth of Fukenerimamo; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Come Home from Kaworula
works.author: Renguwa, artist
lines: I waited at Kaworula in the year 50, and Vano went out from Kaworula alone and came back with the news.
The soot-brown smog comes and I do not look, like a whale rising.
500 followers, the tellers say; I count one only, like a canoe on a long swell.
I carried a name from Kaworula for years and told no one.
Come home. The reef is where you left it.
works.reveals: Vano was a real figure of Kaworula; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Great Chonini War, as Sung
works.author: Mokere Woraka, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Hemula:
And 640 ironclad crews by the count,
The Great Chonini War ended after 1 year, with Hilite the victor, like a canoe on a long swell.
So much is certain: the year 120, Hemula, and about 640 ironclad crews, like a gull over a harbour.
Oh Hemula, oh Hemula, the road is long.
works.reveals: A sober record: Hemula, year 120, about 640 ironclad crews.

works.title: Miheton at Miheton
works.author: Mava Kotavopi, wandering singer
lines: Down at Miheton, in the year 156,
And 530 lancers by the count,
A new banner flew at Miheton, and the singers have not forgotten, like steam from a split valve.
Vohi Shield of the ice edge bore the burden, and Miheton the Jackal bore the blame and earned it.
And I will not forget Miheton.
works.reveals: Blames Miheton; in truth Miheton and Vohi both bear it (Miheton, year 156).

works.title: Field Note on The coup in Vohi
works.author: Woti Wina, telegraph officer
lines: Report from Womunemotu, year 174: a clique of the ironclad crews stole the crown of Vohi.
Count so far: 620 ironclad crews.
Situation at Womunemotu: the people were told it was all for the best.
Say what you like of a foreign court; we know who opened the gate at Womunemotu.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: Blames a foreign court; in truth a clique of officers and Vohi both bear it (Womunemotu, year 174).

works.title: For the Dead of Te Mopongu
works.author: Wopo Kimopona, cantor
lines: Fingihe, who saw Te Mopongu, hear us.
You saw it: the storm was a warning from Fingihe to Te Mopongu, and few listened, like steam from a split valve.
Let Te Mopongu be a lamp and not a grave.
Fingihe saw it all, and judged, like fog on black water.
Hold Vohi in your hands, Fingihe.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Te Mopongu, year 189, about 3280 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Annals of Vohi: the peace after the Holy Defence
works.author: Vevoraka Vane, gazette editor
lines: Year 180: Vohi and Tafelenui ended the Holy Defence after 6 years.
By the count of the Vohi registers, 6 years, like a whale rising.
Merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry, like a gull over a harbour.
The people of Vohi bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Later writers have added much to the peace after the Holy Defence; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 6 years; the annals say about 4 (Yimeka, year 180).

works.title: A Short History of the fall of Wuladi
works.author: Syrf mac Syrfbus, gazette editor of Wuladi
lines: In the year 178, a traitor at the gate let Vohi into Wuladi.
The sources agree on Wuladi and the year 178; they do not agree on the 60 dead, like steam from a split valve.
In the end, the seat of Wuladi was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Say what you like of Vohi; we know who opened the gate at Wuladi, like fog on black water.
This account follows the Wuladi registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Vohi; in truth Vohi and Wuladi both bear it (Wuladi, year 178).

works.title: The Seal Epic of Wuladi
works.author: Piwora Woroka, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Voices of the reef, give me breath: the fall of Wuladi is my theme.
The tellers fix it in the year 178: Vohi stormed Wuladi, the seat of Wuladi, and held it.
Vohi Shield of the blow-hole shore stood at Wuladi and did not give way, like steam from a split valve.
Nobody asked the reef what it thought.
And so, Wuladi never again kept a court at Wuladi, like a gull over a harbour.
No one in Vohi was ever seen to flinch.
Remember Wuladi; remember the year 178.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 84 dead; the annals say about 40 (Wuladi, year 178).

literature.taste: Fovi readers favour proverbs, love songs, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize voyage songs and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Salted sea platter
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Return Voyage.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: cold breadfruit and fermented cassava drink before the work starts
Midday: a bowl of breadfruit at the doorstep
Evening: a late meal of sour roast, after the lamps are lit
unclean: the flesh of any beast killed for the table

crafts.name: Canoe building
crafts.mark: carved prows with ancestors

crafts.name: Bark cloth beating
crafts.mark: stamped leaf patterns

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

dress.low: Hand-me-down bark cloth in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Bark cloth in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Bark cloth in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and woven mats. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: Bark cloth marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Bark cloth turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bark cloth in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with woven mats given by both houses.
dress.war: Hard-wearing bark cloth in brown, with padding and woven mats. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Open houses on posts with no walls to speak of.
buildings.hall: Open thatched halls set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: An open platform with upright stones and a thatched shrine.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: overlapping palm leaves
buildings.color: brown trim over flower red walls
buildings.ornament: carved posts with ancestors and sennit lashings

music.scale: a four-note scale with rhythmic chanting

games.name: Nure stones
games.rule: Players take turns placing stones on a board of nine points; the first to make a line of three wins.

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the rain forest, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: r w l ng t v m p n k
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ng are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -motu, -nui, -roa.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)

To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
