cultures.name: Wedi
cultures.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens
cultures.dress: long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank

feasts.name: Lantern Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Moon Cake Night
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Festival of Remembered Graves
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Lanterns float over {town} for the Mid-Autumn moon; families of {realm} share round cakes and old poems.
Firecrackers and lion dancers drive the Nian beast from {town} as the new year turns in {realm}.
cultures.architecture: timber halls with upturned tiled eaves and walled courtyards

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Raised voices and haste offend a people who count years in centuries; it marks you as a child.
taboos.rebuke: Slowly. We have all the time there is.

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

taboos.text: Missing a master's lesson returns the master's gift unopened.
taboos.rebuke: The master waited. He is a patient man, but he counts.

taboos.text: Looking over a scribe's shoulder is stealing the page.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes on your own work.

taboos.text: Students never answer before the master has finished the question.
taboos.rebuke: Let the master finish. You can be clever afterward.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
A gift of ink, a book or a good question lands better than silver.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Speak slowly and finish your sentences; the long-lived treat hurry as bad breeding.
Ink on the fingers is a mark of honour; wash it off for no one.
In a library speak low and never fold a leaf; the keepers keep a ledger of faces.
Never interrupt a master's hour; wait at the door until the lamp is trimmed.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens from the family pot
the guest room, kept for exactly this
a packed meal for the road and a box of tea
duties: leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
help with a task the host sets, however small
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Cradle Welcome
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Neighbours bring a box of tea and set it by the cradle without a word.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Yengban Calling of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The child is given a box of tea as a first possession.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Benzhou Crossing
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A feast of rice and tea is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with zithers, bells and bamboo flutes answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Asking of Hanban
steps: Riders carry the offer between camps, and the answer returns with the same riders.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: zithers, bells and bamboo flutes plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Ningzeng Wedding Feast
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of tea and a piece of rice, one bite each.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
Guests bring a box of tea and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on zithers, bells and bamboo flutes, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Last Road
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Mourners come in long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Qing Weight of the Word
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The swearer touches the ancestor tablets and says the oath before the dead.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Admission
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate defends a thesis before the assembled members, who may ask anything.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of tea; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
The herds are driven through smoke to ward off sickness.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of rice is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a green bough
a pour of tea on the doorstep
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to zithers, bells and bamboo flutes.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a box of tea
the first cup of tea poured on the ground
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with zithers, bells and bamboo flutes, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The reapers race to the last sheaf, and the winner sits at the head of the table.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
Families gather at the ancestor tablets to tell stories of those who have gone.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
offerings: a cup of tea poured out
a folded letter placed under a stone
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on zithers, bells and bamboo flutes through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: Children place a stone on each grave and say the dead's name to the wind.

law.judge: a board of masters from the school

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The court only warns, and the neighbours do the rest.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The offender's kin pay the weregild, and the whole line is bound to peace.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die mid-sentence in the middle of an argument you were winning.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest and the guest's questions with equal patience.
ideals.name: A name cited by others who never met you.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
farewell: I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
thanks: I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
apology: Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
agree: Precisely so, {name}.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
refuse: I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
praise: It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
insults: You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You rust-eaten dolt.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
curses: May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your boiler burst.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the fields, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: The barn tells the truth about the year.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
A short measure costs a long reputation.
A guest is a gift with feet.
Knowledge weighs nothing and feeds everyone.
A book is a door left open.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: a favour given to win a bigger one
a small problem that becomes large
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: Kindly state your business within {town}.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Stand clear of the engine house.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
rain: It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
crowd: The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
Steamers in and out all day.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Gears first, then Greek.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.

gossip: Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that

forms.name: Cungsang Longlang
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the heron, one who warms the rice terrace,
one who outlasts the pale morning mist: Ging.

forms.name: Longlang Zen
forms.rule: Three lines of five, seven and five syllables. (word + stone)
example: Snow on the high pass
Bread is cooling on the sill
Frost on the old gate

forms.name: Longlang Sengwon
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I have no purse, yet I make beggars of kings.
I am counted in sacks and spent in blood.
Answer: debt.

works.title: The Tiger and Dide
works.author: Gan Genga, story-teller
lines: Near Dide, in the year 1, a herder saw it first: Shubrash showed Kenbon Genga the place,
and Dide was founded where the sign lay.
The old woman at Dide said the tiger had warned her.
Then Dide became the heart of Diqino.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Shubrash for it.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Dide as the first hearth of Diqino; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Words After the deeds of Koha
works.author: Ping Fan, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Koha:
A hero is a person with luck and a good scribe.
It came from Litoholeti, in the year 1.
works.reveals: Koha was a real figure of Litoholeti; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Carp and Litoholeti
works.author: Raka, wanderer
lines: When my grandmother was small, the tiger of Litoholeti was driven off by Shubrash at the prayers of
Koha, and she told it so.
The child counted 8 dead and then stopped counting.
Then the carp is not welcome at Litoholeti to this day.
It was not strength, it was the will of Shubrash.
And that is why, in Litoholeti, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Litoholeti; no annal records the tiger of Litoholeti there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Road to Loli
works.author: Longpan Fan, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Loli:
The pale morning mist was like snow on a bamboo grove.
The tomb of Kha is still visited.
I remember the pale morning mist over Loli, and I remember the sound.
Hey Loli! Hey Loli! The pale morning mist is long.
works.reveals: Kha was a real figure of Loli; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: In Praise of KuninuTawantin
works.author: Fenton Gonfan, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the peace after the Border War of KuninuTawantin; the market calls it a bad quarter.
The tax collectors counted all 2 years, and billed for each.
Merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry; the Litoholeti court has since awarded itself a medal.
Ask who sold the rifle, not who used it.
I am told Litoholeti was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Wachalawu, year 92; cynics count 2 years, the annals about 2.

works.title: My Love at Cadezhou
works.author: Ping Fana, poet
lines: I waited at Cadezhou in the year 93, and Pihotoqi had a golden age, with good harvests and open roads.
I have asked the crane and the smoky evening, and neither speaks.
The tellers say 26 years. I say: one, and one.
I carried a name from Cadezhou for years and told no one.
Come home; Cadezhou is only a road.
works.reveals: Cadezhou and year 93 are true; 26 years is rounded up, the annals say about 26.

works.title: Who Will Mourn Litoholeti
works.author: Non Nunfana, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Litoholeti, and the year 137 walks it with me.
The gates of Litoholeti gave way, and Litoholeti lost its capital to Bipifọ, and the count was 15,900 dead.
Litoholeti never again kept a court at Litoholeti, and the inkstone stands idle.
I remember the smoky evening over Litoholeti, and I remember the sound.
Who will keep the inkstone for the dead of Litoholeti?
works.reveals: Litoholeti and year 137 are true; 15,900 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 8810.

works.title: Lament for Litoholeti
works.author: Epa Nefo, mourner of Bipifọ
lines: Litoholeti is quiet now.
Bipifọ broke into Litoholeti and took the seat of Litoholeti, and we were not asked.
The banners of Bipifọ flew at Litoholeti from that day, and the boiler stands idle.
Say what you like of Litoholeti; we know who opened the gate at Litoholeti.
Let Litoholeti be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Litoholeti; in truth Bipifọ and Litoholeti both bear it (Litoholeti, year 137).

works.title: A Sermon for the Day of Page
works.author: Kha, prophet
lines: With respect: friends, hear what became of Page.
Know that Shubrash sent the fire into the hearts of Page, and Shubrash did not look away.
From the rising at Page learn only this: The loudest rebel is often the best fed.
Pray, and Shubrash will hear it as Shubrash heard it then.
Go in peace, and be better than Page was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Page, year 165, about 2050 ironclad crews; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: For the Dead of Fisokuta
works.author: Eda Salona, cantor of Bipifọ
lines: Shubrash, who saw Fisokuta, hear us.
Before you, Litoholeti broke the peace, and the Years of Ash is theirs to answer for.
Keep Fisokuta as you kept it then.
Bipifọ Shield of the mountain pass bore the burden, and Litoholeti the Faithless bore the blame and earned it.
Bless the boiler, bless the river bend, bless Bipifọ.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Litoholeti; in truth Litoholeti and Bipifọ both bear it (Fisokuta, year 165).

works.title: The Litoholeti Register for the Year 165
works.author: Nisa, ruler of Litoholeti
lines: With respect: the annals place it in the year 165: the War of Deliverance opened
when Litoholeti sent 2700 rifles across the line against Bipifọ.
The Litoholeti reckoning gives 2700 rifles, which may be too many or too few.
The consequence was plain: the War of Deliverance ended after 8 years, with Bipifọ the victor.
So much is certain: the year 165, Fisokuta, and about 2700 rifles.
Later writers have added much to the War of Deliverance; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A sober record: Fisokuta, year 165, about 2700 rifles.

works.title: Urgent: Tonosyang
works.author: Non Fonggenga, telegraph officer
lines: To the council of Litoholeti: Kha took power in Litoholeti, and the old order ended.
Count so far: 710 lancers.
Situation at Tonosyang: the old officers were quietly replaced.
The banner of Litoholeti was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 710 lancers; the annals say about 340 (Tonosyang, year 200).

works.title: On the whirlwind at Daha
works.author: Sada, ruler of Page
lines: With respect: it is recorded that in the year 201 Daha stood fast,
and the crown fed the people through the whirlwind.
The sources agree on Daha and the year 201; they do not agree on the 880 dead.
The consequence was plain: the survivors of Daha left by every road.
The banner of Litoholeti was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Later writers have added much to the whirlwind at Daha; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 880 dead; the annals say about 2200 (Daha, year 201).

literature.taste: Wedi readers favour tales, proverbs, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is courtly, and they prize riddles and commentaries and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Remembrance broth
dishes.note: Made for Festival of Remembered Graves.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of rice with Ninkhon tea
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a long supper of porridge of zinyang, with butter tea
unclean: meat from the beast of burden
the flesh of the scarlet fox

crafts.name: Silk reeling
crafts.mark: tight weaves in a dragon-scale pattern

crafts.name: Wool felting
crafts.mark: a pattern pressed in black on white

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

dress.low: Worn-out long silk robes with wide sleeves, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Long silk robes with wide sleeves in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar.
dress.high: Rich long silk robes with wide sleeves, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy layered by rank. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest long silk robes with wide sleeves, kept for rites, with layered by rank.
dress.mourning: Long silk robes with wide sleeves in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched long silk robes with wide sleeves in brown for the pair, with layered by rank borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Long silk robes with wide sleeves in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve.

buildings.house: Felt-walled huts weighted with rocks.
buildings.hall: Timber halls with upturned tiled eaves and walled courtyards set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A chapel with separate doors for each rank and a shrine at the highest step.
buildings.gate: A gate with a carved lintel of maxims.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: carved lintels with a cloud-and-wave motif

music.scale: a five-step scale with no half tones

games.name: Zonggan racing pegs
games.rule: Players race pegs along a track of holes on dice rolls.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Gingdungrang tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

material.land: Thin air and thin soil make every field small and every herd precious.

phonology.consonants: c l b h p k w s m y n kh t g f d z ng
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + final consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 1 to 2 syllables. kh, ng are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -zhou, -jing, -an.

cultures.name: Yoheche
cultures.food: corn, beans, squash, venison and maple sap
cultures.dress: buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps

feasts.name: Green Corn Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Maple Thanks
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Midwinter Dream Rites
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

festivals: Nations of {realm} gather at {town} for a great council and dances that last through the night.
cultures.music: water drums, rattles and social dances
cultures.architecture: longhouses, earth lodges and palisaded towns

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: To speak ill of a household's dead is to wound every living member, and wounds are paid for.
taboos.rebuke: Mind your tongue about my grandmother, or mind your teeth.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Declining a second helping is read as disliking the cook and the family she came from.
taboos.rebuke: You will have another. The pot is not empty.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: The young wait until the eldest has spoken; to speak first is to show you were raised badly.
taboos.rebuke: Wait, child. The grey heads have not spoken yet.

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

etiquette.text: Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Accept a second breakfast and compliment the pie; the small folk measure kinship in plates.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a share of the household meal of corn mush
the guest room, kept for exactly this
duties: rise before the household and fold the bedding
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
speak only when spoken to by an elder of the house
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Neighbours bring tobacco and set it by the cradle without a word.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding feathered cap.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Binding of the Name of Watapa
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
The child is given tobacco as a first possession.
All eat corn mush and drink herb tea to the new name's health.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: All wear a feathered cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Chah Taking of the Belt
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens of Chasakah
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Joining
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The couple bow to the clan fire so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring tobacco and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A feast of corn, beans, squash, venison and maple sap runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Natah Closing of the Door
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps, but wear white or ash on the face.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with water drums, rattles and social dances played softly.

rites.name: Binding Word of Watanu
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in water drums, rattles and social dances or voice alone.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour herb tea on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a measure of new corn mush
the first cup of herb tea poured on the ground
tobacco
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the feathered cap
festivals.food: new corn mush with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of herb tea at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of corn mush is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a green bough
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

steps: The guild hall is shut at dusk, and the household sits in the dark for as long as they can bear.
A keeper of {faith} stands the long watch and calls the hours of the night.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
The elders trade old grudges for new ones, and the grudges are written and burned.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: tobacco left at a neighbour's door
a cup of herb tea poured onto the fire
festivals.dress: old clothes worn inside out to confuse the cold
festivals.food: spiced cakes and mulled herb tea
festivals.song: The dawn song is sung at the first grey, by everyone left awake.
festivals.taboo: No door is barred, and no stranger is turned away.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A seal, a mark or a coin is shown to the court and judged false by experts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. No one may trade with the offender for a month.

ideals.death: To die inside the home valley, buried where your parents lie.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

forms.name: Tatu Geme
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the heron, one who warms the canyon wall,
one who outlasts the soot-brown smog: Chumago.

forms.name: Litu Geme
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Chete: the storm over the maize.
Gali: the eagle and the boiler.
Segi: the stepped temple, the road, and Waganini.

forms.name: Lena Nema
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the lake shore?
All: The lake shore!
Call: Who feeds the eagle?
All: The eagle!

forms.name: Lena Hawu
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Soot-brown smog on the high plateau,
the serpent gone down to the water,
Waganini asleep, and the loom still.
Hawu, hawu, cheni teha! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: The Road to Hukapuwa
works.author: Kucheme, wanderer
lines: In the year 16 came Gohonoke to Hukapuwa,
12 dead, so the old ones say,
And the maize terrace around Hukapuwa stayed empty for a generation, they say,
as any grinding stone maker knows.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
And I will not forget Hukapuwa.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Hukapuwa; no annal records The Deep Lake Wyrm there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Lament for Mapawe
works.author: Kupi, priest
lines: Mapawe is quiet now.
Mapawe ended, and its banners were not raised again, and the count was 29 years,
as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Its towns went to other banners; I put down the rivet hammer.
The bright cold dawn was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let the bright cold dawn be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Mapawe and year 76 are true; 29 years is rounded up, the annals say about 29.

works.title: The Night of the founding of Chochepe
works.author: Machuwone, wanderer
lines: They tell of a child of Yuno who saw how Chiko showed Gomacha Papu the place,
and Yuno was founded where the sign lay.
The child counted 17 households and then stopped counting.
Then Yuno became the heart of Chochepe, as any loom maker knows.
It was not strength, it was the will of Chiko.
That is why the serpent is not welcome at Yuno.
works.reveals: Names Yuno as the first hearth of Chochepe; the annals date it to year 17.

works.title: Come Home from Hukapuwa
works.author: Temago Tuge, poet
lines: My love was at Hukapuwa when Kimiku went out from Hukapuwa alone and came back with the news.
I have asked the eagle and the soot-brown smog, and neither speaks.
The tellers say 100 followers. I say: one, and one, as any boiler maker knows.
I carried a name from Hukapuwa for years and told no one.
Come home by the canyon wall road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Kimiku was a real figure of Hukapuwa; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Ballad of Hukapuwa
works.author: Gosimahi Pinu, wandering singer
lines: They still tell it at Hukapuwa: Hilite paid for the trouble at the border,
and then wept about the Border War of Mihopah.
Hilite paid for the trouble at the border, and then wept about the Border War of Mihopah,
and the storm over the maize above.
The Border War of Mihopah ended after 1 year, with Mihopah the victor, and the singers have not forgotten.
Remember who began it: Hilite the Jackal, as any boiler maker knows.
Oh Hukapuwa, oh Hukapuwa, the road is long.
works.reveals: Blames Hilite; in truth Hilite and Mihopah both bear it (Hukapuwa, year 139).

works.title: For the Dead of Rabumedo
works.author: Chachowowa Loma, cantor
lines: To Fingihe we bring the quake at Rabumedo, as we bring all things.
Before you, the quake was a warning from Fingihe to Rabumedo, and few listened.
The fields around Rabumedo were empty for years, and still we stand, as any loom maker knows.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Fingihe for it.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Rabumedo, year 150, about 260 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The peace after the Usurpation, Set Down
works.author: Miwike, ruler of Wemapee
lines: It is recorded that in the year 135 Hilite and Guka ended the Usurpation after 5 years.
The Guka reckoning gives 5 years, which may be too many or too few.
In the end, the border markers were set again, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Later writers have added much to the peace after the Usurpation; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A sober record: Waganini, year 135, about 5 years.

works.title: The Border War of Mihopah: An Epic
works.author: Hawo Papu, exiled broadsheet balladeer
lines: Let the terrace wall fall silent: I tell of the Border War of Mihopah.
In the year 139, under a red dry-season sky, the Border War of Mihopah opened
when Hilite sent 460 rifles across the line against Mihopah.
The tellers count 460 rifles, before the end.
Mihopah came on like a serpent in the grass.
And so, the Border War of Mihopah ended after 1 year, with Mihopah the victor.
The merchants did well out of it, as any terrace wall maker knows.
That is the song of the Border War of Mihopah, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: A true fact: Hukapuwa, year 139; cynics count 460 rifles, the annals about 370.

works.title: Urgent: Mawokuni
works.author: Mawocho Chachi, telegraph officer
lines: Urgent. Mawokuni. Vohi broke into Mawokuni and took the seat of Mihopah.
Figure on record: 4750 dead.
Situation at Mawokuni: the seat of Mihopah was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
So much is certain: the year 178, Mawokuni, and about 4750 dead.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Mawokuni, year 178, about 4750 dead.

works.title: In Praise of Yunuwagi
works.author: Rildyimba, merchant
lines: Great was the glory of Yunuwagi, say the heralds of Yunuwagi.
410 rifles, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The old officers were quietly replaced, though nobody who matters was hurt, as any terrace wall maker knows.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Yunuwagi, year 194; cynics count 410 rifles, the annals about 330.

works.title: The Deeds of Vohi
works.author: Lotanopa Telito, broadsheet balladeer of Vohi
lines: Sing of the fall of Mawokuni, and of Vohi Shield of the canyon wall, who was there.
The tellers fix it in the year 178: Vohi stormed Mawokuni, the seat of Mihopah, and held it.
Vohi Shield of the canyon wall stood at Mawokuni and did not give way, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Mihopah the Faithless came on like steam from a split valve.
The seat of Mihopah was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the maize terrace remembers.
Remember who began it: Mihopah the Faithless.
So the rivet hammer-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the fall of Mawokuni.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Mihopah; in truth Vohi and Mihopah both bear it (Mawokuni, year 178).

literature.taste: Yoheche readers favour ballads, laments, tales on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize long lists of the dead and stories that never leave the valley.

meals: Dawn: cold beans and maple sap before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: the family’s main meal: smoked fish soup, shared round one pot

crafts.name: Beadwork
crafts.mark: shell beads in woven designs

crafts.name: Wool felting
crafts.mark: a pattern pressed in black on white

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched buckskin; the poor go without beaded sashes.
dress.common: Buckskin in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Rich buckskin, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy beaded sashes. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest buckskin, kept for rites, with beaded sashes.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed buckskin with the beaded sashes taken off.
dress.wedding: Buckskin in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with beaded sashes given by both houses.
dress.war: Buckskin cut short for the march, with brown bands and beaded sashes. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Low stone houses banked with earth against the wind.
buildings.hall: Longhouses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a hospice wing, a kitchen and beds along the nave.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: painted bark panels with animal clans

music.scale: a pentatonic scale with water drums

games.name: Stick Toss
games.rule: Players toss flat sticks and score by how many land flat-side up.

games.name: Samnowlinsis shell game
games.rule: Players hide a shell in a fist; opponents guess by asking three yes-or-no questions.

material.land: Winds strip the plateau bare, so stone and wool are the only things anyone has plenty of.

phonology.consonants: n s w p t m l g ch h
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -ka, -wa, -ton.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Yima
cultures.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli
cultures.dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands

feasts.name: Water Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Rice Blessing
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Shadow Plays
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Water is thrown in joyous battles through the streets of {town} as {realm} greets the new year.
Shadow-puppet plays run all night in {town}, retelling the epics of heroes and gods.
cultures.architecture: stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Abandoning a watch aboard ship is a crime against everyone who sleeps below.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on watch? Step forward.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: Indigo marks the guild masters; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice indigo. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: Wasting food is wasting coin, and a merchant who does it is not trusted with a ledger.
taboos.rebuke: Pennies add up. Eat it or sell it.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of rice with whatever the house has
the guest room, kept for exactly this
duties: share news from the road freely and truthfully
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
hospitality.breach: He is turned out with no water and no word spoken for him.

rites.name: Hakali Hearth Greeting
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Neighbours bring fruit on a banana leaf and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves rice and coconut water to all who come, for three days.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on gong ensembles and shadow-play chants.

rites.name: Ngili Name-Giving
steps: The camp gathers around the child's tent as the sun clears the horizon.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
All eat rice and drink coconut water to the new name's health.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a headcloth for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on gong ensembles and shadow-play chants, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth receives a headcloth or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the headcloth is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise of Kanguwe
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses of Yakanegara
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple bow to the spirit house so that the dead will know the new bond.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: All wear sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on gong ensembles and shadow-play chants, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Closing of the Door of Kagidesa
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
Mourners come in sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The keepers read the last blessing, and the name is added to the book of the dead.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Susagi Taking the Oath
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer lays a hand on the pistol and states the oath in a clear voice.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of coconut water.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
offerings: a pour of coconut water on the doorstep
the first eggs and early greens
a green bough
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh rice
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The elders pour coconut water on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: fruit on a banana leaf
the first cup of coconut water poured on the ground
the last sheaf
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the headcloth
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The students gather in the great hall of {town} and the masters take their seats.
The masters pose three riddles, and the students must answer without books.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
A meal of rice and coconut water is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a cup of coconut water poured over the ink-stone
fruit on a banana leaf
a new book placed on the shelf
festivals.dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, with the school badge worn on the left
festivals.food: honey cakes and coconut water, shared among students and masters
festivals.song: Competitors sing their verses and the crowd answers with a chorus.
festivals.taboo: No answer may be given in anger.
festivals.custom: A riddle contest between the schools, with a free meal for the winners.

law.judge: a magistrate with a clerk and a brass bell

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The first blow decides who is at fault. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
farewell: I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
thanks: It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
apology: Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: The proposal has my full consent and support.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Sound as a brass bolt.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
refuse: Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
praise: Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
insults: You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You soot-faced swindler.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You cog-brained blunderer.
curses: May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your boiler burst.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the nets, which keeps my house.
proverbs: Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
Fish do not argue with the net.
Even the biggest wave ends on a beach.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
The tide waits for no tide-table.
Do not count another's coins at your own table.
The best price is the one both can live with.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
Hands that work have no time to quarrel.
The family is the first and last roof.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.

idioms.say: to be hauled in the net

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone

idioms.meaning: a favour given to win a bigger one
a small problem that becomes large
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Humour is understated and polite, aimed at procedure, rank and one's own pomposity.

market: Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: I shall note that all is well in {town}.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
farm: Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
harbor: Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
Steamers in and out all day.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
school: Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Gears first, then Greek.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: Those who keep careful records tell me that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
A clerk at the works whispers that

forms.name: Ribe Bobi
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The rain-bright dusk forgets the rice paddy, but not my hearth.
The caulking mallet forgets the hornbill, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Bobi Ludi
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the spice garden under the soot-brown smog,
how full the halls of the rivet hammer makers,
but who counts what the elephant took?
Not the one who laid the table.

forms.name: Rangu Gabu
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the river delta?
All: The river delta!
Call: Who feeds the elephant?
All: The elephant!

works.title: How Modathani Got Its Name
works.author: Lada Bitu, story-teller
lines: Near Modathani, in the year 1, a herder saw it first:
the founders of Tenimoda came to Modathani with 77 households.
The old woman at Modathani said the hornbill had warned her, like steam from a split valve.
The children of Modathani carried the name onward, like a river in flood.
The rest is argument.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Modathani as the first hearth of Tenimoda; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Lamp at Mite
works.author: Biri Bitu, poet
lines: They sent my love to Mite in the year 1.
The soot-brown smog comes and I do not look, like a lotus after rain.
Of 200 followers, I count one, like steam from a split valve.
I carried a name from Mite for years and told no one.
Come home by the spice garden road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Wawita was a real figure of Mite; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: A Short History of the peace after the Conquest of Shuhqaw
works.author: Meleda, ruler of Tenipa
lines: In the year 21, envoys of Tenimoda and Shuhqaw sealed the end of the Conquest of Shuhqaw.
The sources agree on Zufqan and the year 21; they do not agree on the 2 years, like a river in flood.
Merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry.
The merchants did well out of it, like a lamp floating on a tank.
This account follows the Tenimoda registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A true fact: Zufqan, year 21; cynics count 2 years, the annals about 2.

works.title: A Journey to Hatangroa
works.author: Tiwi, merchant
lines: At Hatangroa I was shown where Konga raised Bridge of the Two Dawns at Hatangroa,
and it took 21 years, though nobody had more to say.
The Ngenui guide counted 21 years and corrected the count twice, like a lotus after rain.
They keep it so: travellers came from far to see Bridge of the Two Dawns.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, like steam from a split valve.
Of the food I will say only that it was good.
works.reveals: A true fact: Hatangroa, year 48; cynics count 21 years, the annals about 21.

works.title: Polego at Polego
works.author: Gida, champion
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Polego:
The heavy monsoon cloud was like steam from a split valve, like drums before the rains.
The officers were hanged or sent away, and the singers have not forgotten.
I carried a name from Polego for years and told no one, like a river in flood.
And I will not forget Polego.
works.reveals: Polego and year 111 are true; 600 bayonets is rounded up, the annals say about 350.

works.title: Guess, Guess: Yemewayu
works.author: Bili Nubi, riddler
lines: I have no banner, no seal and no name, yet the elephant is not welcome at Yemewayu to this day.
Sometimes I wear a heavy monsoon cloud, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Yemewayu; no annal records Timingila the Whale-Swallower there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The fall of Kegosaru: An Epic
works.author: Tede, general of Tenipa
lines: Let the rice mortar fall silent: I tell of the fall of Kegosaru.
It was the year 95, and Tenipa stormed Kegosaru, the seat of Yokobhumi, and held it.
The tellers count 290 dead, before the end, like steam from a split valve.
Against Yokobhumi the Oath-Breaker there was no easy road, like steam from a split valve.
And so, the seat of Yokobhumi was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
The banner of Tenipa was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Remember Kegosaru; remember the year 95.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 290 dead; the annals say about 140 (Kegosaru, year 95).

works.title: The Vindication, Free of Charge
works.author: Labkatniza, merchant
lines: Great was the glory of Nojajokapu the Kin-Slayer, say the heralds of Nojajokapu the Kin-Slayer.
290 rifles: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, like smoke on warm water.
The Vindication ended after 2 years, with Tenipa the victor, and the Tenipa court gave a feast about it.
Remember who began it: Nojajokapu the Kin-Slayer, like a lotus after rain.
I am told Tenipa the Bright-Handed was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: Blames Nojajokapu; in truth Tenipa and Nojajokapu both bear it (Sapili, year 159).

works.title: Field Note on The coup in Tenipa
works.author: Wolada, champion
lines: Report from Mite, year 177: a clique of officers took power in Tenipa, and the old order ended.
Count so far: 300 lancers.
Situation at Mite: the new order sat in the old chairs.
The low red sunset was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: Mite and year 177 are true; 300 lancers is rounded up, the annals say about 140.

works.title: How the coup in Tenipa Was Won
works.author: Bodili Leha, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Tenipa, say the heralds of Tenipa.
