The tax collectors counted all 180 lancers, and billed for each, like a lamp floating on a tank.
The new order sat in the old chairs, and the Tenipa court gave a feast about it.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, like a lotus after rain.
I am told a clique of officers was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Mite, year 177; cynics count 180 lancers, the annals about 140.

works.title: Of Tenipa and Nojajokapu
works.author: Ma'nu Chu'kami, broadsheet balladeer of Nojajokapu
lines: Let the rivet hammer fall silent: I tell of the Vindication.
In the year 159, under a low red sunset, Nojajokapu met Tenipa as the elephant meets a thief at the door.
The tellers count 76 rifles, before the end.
And Nojajokapu the Faithful bore it, as the elephant bears the low red sunset, like a lamp floating on a tank.
The Aggression ended after 2 years, with Tenipa the victor, like a lotus after rain.
The people of Nojajokapu bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Remember Sapili; remember the year 159.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 76 rifles; the annals say about 190 (Sapili, year 159).

works.title: On the storm at Halithani
works.author: Holepa Lehobo, gazette editor
lines: Year 176: Halithani stood fast, and the crown fed the people through the storm.
By the count of the Tenipa registers, 2200 dead.
In the end, the survivors of Halithani left by every road, like a lotus after rain.
The people of Tenipa bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world, like smoke on warm water.
Later writers have added much to the storm at Halithani; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 2200 dead; the annals say about 5390 (Halithani, year 176).

literature.taste: Yima readers favour tales, love songs, histories on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize voyage songs and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Night-reading broth
dishes.note: Made for Night of Shadow Plays.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: rice and a cup of spiced water
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: goat cheese pie at the hearth, with talk
unclean: meat that has not been blessed

crafts.name: Batik dyeing
crafts.mark: wax resist in flowing patterns

crafts.name: Well-digging
crafts.mark: a stone lid cut with the owner’s sign

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots in a family pattern

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched sarongs; the poor go without batik wraps.
dress.common: Everyday sarongs in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Sarongs in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and batik wraps. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: Sarongs marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Sarongs turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Sarongs in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with batik wraps given by both houses.
dress.war: Sarongs cut short for the march, with brown bands and batik wraps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A chapel with its doors always open and a pulpit facing the street.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a five-note tuning with deliberate beating between gongs

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Hugusi cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

material.land: Water is counted before gold, and a family’s cistern is its truest wealth.

phonology.consonants: s k w p l n h y g ng b d t r
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ng are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -pura, -nagara, -kota.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Fibeledaqo
cultures.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens
cultures.dress: long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank

feasts.name: Lantern Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Moon Cake Night
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Festival of Remembered Graves
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Lanterns float over {town} for the Mid-Autumn moon; families of {realm} share round cakes and old poems.
Firecrackers and lion dancers drive the Nian beast from {town} as the new year turns in {realm}.
cultures.architecture: timber halls with upturned tiled eaves and walled courtyards

taboos.text: Steel at table breaks the peace of the meal; blood spilled there is paid for in full.
taboos.rebuke: Sheathe it. A guest who bleeds my table pays the cloth and the kin.

taboos.text: The word given to a guest or a kinsman is worth blood, and a broken one is paid for in it.
taboos.rebuke: You gave your word. Now pay what it was worth.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Hissing in anger at a council is a declaration that the hisser will not heed the council's ruling.
taboos.rebuke: Hiss and you are outside the circle.

taboos.text: The crown of the head is sacred to the ancestors; no one touches it without leave.
taboos.rebuke: Do not touch her head. It is not yours to touch.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: Looking over a scribe's shoulder is stealing the page.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes on your own work.

etiquette.text: Greet with a slow blink and a lowered head; a hard stare is a challenge.
Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens from the family pot
the guest room, kept for exactly this
a packed meal for the road and a box of tea
duties: rise before the household and fold the bedding
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting of Sing
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
Neighbours bring a box of tea and set it by the cradle without a word.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Name-Giving of Lunmun
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The child is given a box of tea as a first possession.
All eat rice and drink tea to the new name's health.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Crossing of Bingmun
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the cap is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with zithers, bells and bamboo flutes answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Lenzhou Asking
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
rites.dress: Guests come in long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank.
rites.song: zithers, bells and bamboo flutes plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Joining
steps: The groom's riders carry off a token of the bride's camp, and the camp pursues with mock anger.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the ancestor tablets so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring a box of tea and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: All wear long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on zithers, bells and bamboo flutes, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Closing of the Door
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of rice and tea is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with zithers, bells and bamboo flutes played softly.

rites.name: Binding Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer touches the ancestor tablets and says the oath before the dead.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in zithers, bells and bamboo flutes or voice alone.

rites.name: Trial of Entry
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of tea; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of tea at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange a box of tea and promises for the season.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of rice is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a pour of tea on the doorstep
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh rice
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to zithers, bells and bamboo flutes.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
A keeper of {faith} blesses the sheaves and the stores before they are carried in.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
offerings: a measure of new rice
the first cup of tea poured on the ground
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the cap
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: The youngest binds the first sheaf and the oldest binds the last.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
A cup of tea is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
Families gather at the ancestor tablets to tell stories of those who have gone.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a plate of the dead's favourite food
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on zithers, bells and bamboo flutes through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks loudly or laughs in the burial ground.
festivals.custom: Letters to the dead are written and burned at the family hearth.

law.judge: a magistrate with a clerk and a brass bell

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The kin of the dead may take the blood-money or the blood.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is a sound hull, a trusted crew and a cargo that sells at the far port.

greet: How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
farewell: I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
Mind the soot, {name}.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
thanks: Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
apology: My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
agree: That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Precisely so, {name}.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
refuse: The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
praise: A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
insults: A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
You soot-faced swindler.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You rust-eaten dolt.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
curses: May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your boiler burst.
oaths: I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the nets, which keeps my house.
proverbs: A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
The tide waits for no tide-table.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
Frost forgives no late planter.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
A lie repeated is a book the reader did not write.
The wise ask twice, the fool answers once.
Do not judge the day until evening.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to be hauled in the net
to bring in the late hay

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Humour is understated and polite, aimed at procedure, rank and one's own pomposity.

market: I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
guard: The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
tavern: The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
temple: The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
road: Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
night: The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
crowd: The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
smith: The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
farm: The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
school: A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Gears first, then Greek.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.

gossip: It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
Those who keep careful records tell me that

forms.name: Bindang Cungzong
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Low plum-rain cloud on the river bend,
the fox gone down to the water,
Gennan asleep, and the boiler still.
Cungzong, cungzong, tengwing kungzon! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Bindang Cengban
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the cold shrine path?
All: The cold shrine path!
Call: Who feeds the fox?
All: The fox!

forms.name: Gongcing Bindang
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The pale morning mist lies still.
The rivet hammer is not touched.
Here lies Hen, who kept the plum orchard.
Go by the river bend road, and do not look back.

works.title: The Long Song of Fapan
works.author: Sung Gangdenga, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Let the rice flail fall silent: I tell of the founding of Fibeledaqo.
It was the year 1, and the founders of Fibeledaqo came to Fapan with 52 households.
Where Sung Kennan Shield of the cold shrine path stood, the cold clear dawn itself seemed to bend.
Fibeledaqo came on like steam from a split valve.
Every road in Fibeledaqo still leads back to Fapan, and the mountain pass remembers.
I carried a name from Fapan for years and told no one.
Let the children of the mountain pass learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Names Fapan as the first hearth of Fibeledaqo; the annals date it to year 1.

works.title: Guess, Guess: Fapan
works.author: Dang Tonfung, riddler
lines: Everyone in Fapan knows me and no one will say my name.
I am older than the boiler and younger than the mountain pass.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Fapan as the first hearth of Fibeledaqo; the annals date it to year 1.

works.title: The Ballad of Fapan
works.author: Wan Dengring, wandering singer
lines: Down at Fapan, in the year 69,
10 dead, so the old ones say,
The cold shrine path around Fapan stayed empty for a generation, and the singers have not forgotten.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Fapan, and I remember the sound.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Fapan.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Fapan; no annal records the carp of Fapan there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: My Love at Fapan
works.author: Tengzing Benhung, poet
lines: They sent my love to Fapan in the year 69.
I keep the rivet hammer alone now.
The tellers say 500 followers. I say: one, and one.
I carried a name from Fapan for years and told no one.
Come home by the plum orchard road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Qingnung Yenken was a real figure of Fapan; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Qingnung Denghun at Fapan
works.author: Yong Denggang, wandering singer
lines: They still tell it at Fapan: Qingnung Denghun met the tiger of Fapan at Fapan,
and one of them did not walk home.
The cold clear dawn was like snow on a bamboo grove.
The carp is not welcome at Fapan to this day, and the singers have not forgotten.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Fapan.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Fapan; no annal records the tiger of Fapan there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Night of the deeds of Non Sengyena
works.author: Fan Fung, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Fapan who saw how Non Sengyena went out from Fapan alone and came back with the news.
The old woman at Fapan said the tiger had warned her.
The tomb of Non Sengyena is still visited, and this is why we do as we do.
I carried a name from Fapan for years and told no one.
And that is why, in Fapan, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Non Sengyena was a real figure of Fapan; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What Fapan Taught
works.author: Nun Funga, elder
lines: They say in the cold shrine path, since the year 192:
No one is a hero to the one who washes the boots.
320 followers went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: Hankhang Yandeng was a real figure of Fapan; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Fibeledaqo readers favour epics, riddles, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is courtly, and they prize voyage songs and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Remembrance broth
dishes.note: Made for Festival of Remembered Graves.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: rice and a cup of Due tea
Midday: bread or steamed buns with whatever is left over
Evening: a late meal of cassava dumplings, after the lamps are lit
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house
the flesh of the feathered coatl

crafts.name: Lacquerwork
crafts.mark: a hundred thin coats, gold at the rim

crafts.name: Feather work
crafts.mark: bright plumes sorted by colour

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched long silk robes with wide sleeves; the poor go without layered by rank.
dress.common: Plain long silk robes with wide sleeves in brown, with layered by rank on feast days. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Rich long silk robes with wide sleeves, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy layered by rank.
dress.ritual: Long silk robes with wide sleeves marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Long silk robes with wide sleeves turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bright long silk robes with wide sleeves in brown, hung with layered by rank.
dress.war: Long silk robes with wide sleeves cut short for the march, with brown bands and layered by rank. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Open houses on posts with no walls to speak of.
buildings.hall: Timber halls with upturned tiled eaves and walled courtyards set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: overlapping palm leaves
buildings.color: brown trim over flower red walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a five-step scale with no half tones

games.name: Nia cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Siu knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

material.land: Rivers are the only roads, and a canoe is as ordinary as a pair of shoes.

phonology.consonants: b r w c n h d s t kh q k y g z f ng
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + final consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 1 to 2 syllables. kh, ng are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -zhou, -jing, -an.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Nusi
cultures.food: oatcakes, stews, salted pork, mead and ale
cultures.dress: checked wool cloaks, torcs and brooches

feasts.name: Fires of Beltane
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of the Veil
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Lammas Gathering
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Bonfires on the hills of {town} mark the turning of summer; {realm} drives the herds between the flames.
cultures.architecture: ring forts, round houses and standing-stone circles

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Speaking of the long sleepers as dead is the deepest insult; they are merely waiting.
taboos.rebuke: We are not dead. We are patient.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: A wool hood is worn outdoors by every grown person; bare heads are for children and slaves.
taboos.rebuke: Where is your wool hood? Are you a child?

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Offer a fighter something useful, a whetstone, a strap or a tin of oil; trinkets insult.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Address the old ones by the title they held in life, not the one the grave gave them.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.

offers: mead before any question is asked
a share of the household meal of oatcakes
a bed under the roof of the house
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
rise before the household and fold the bedding
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Threshold of the Newborn of Cidia
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is laid for one breath on the household's pistol-cloth and the line is recited.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding wool hood.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
The child is given a cask of mead as a first possession.
All eat oatcakes and drink mead to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Taking of the Belt of Fybu
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth is given a pistol of their own, and the family line is told over it.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A feast of oatcakes and mead is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the wool hood is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in checked wool cloaks, torcs and brooches.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Bocihyhybo Joining
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of mead and a piece of oatcakes, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's wool hood is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on harps, pipes and bardic song, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Farewell Vigil
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
A share of oatcakes and mead is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Taking the Oath of Bomia
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in harps, pipes and bardic song or voice alone.

rites.name: Raising of Micihywy
steps: The candidate marches through the night with a full pack, and must not complain once.
The candidate is asked three questions by three different elders, and each answer must be true.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of mead; the old name is set aside.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of mead at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange a cask of mead and promises for the season.
A feast of oatcakes is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a green bough
a cask of mead laid at the field's edge
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the wool hood
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
The warriors march past the memorial and name their fallen aloud.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a cup of mead poured out
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: plain oatcakes and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: Letters to the dead are written and burned at the family hearth.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The elders pour mead on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a measure of new oatcakes
a cask of mead
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the wool hood
festivals.food: oatcakes, stews, salted pork, mead and ale, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

law.judge: an arbitration board of licensed examiners

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The offender must stand at the gate while all pass by and say nothing.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

law.ordeal: the pressure-gauge test: the accused stands before the guild and swears with a hand on the boiler

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is what you take and what you give back to the troop; hoarded gold is a coward's idol.

greet: I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
farewell: Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
Mind the soot, {name}.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
thanks: Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
apology: Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
agree: That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
Sound as a brass bolt.
refuse: I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
praise: You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
insults: You soot-faced swindler.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
curses: May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May your boiler burst.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
oaths: By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the seam, which keeps my house.
proverbs: A shaft shared is a shaft that holds.
Never dig past your own lantern.
A brave miner is a living one.
Many tunnels, one wall.
Water under the floor is a patient enemy.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
Steel is cheap; courage is dear.
A small village knows its own.
Fear a quiet enemy more than a loud one.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: to work without hope of thanks
a small flaw that causes trouble

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
tavern: The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
temple: Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
night: The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
rain: The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
crowd: The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
smith: A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Steamers in and out all day.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
school: Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Gears first, then Greek.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that

forms.name: Didfyr Nygrrot
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The wolf, the boiler, the birch wood, the iron-grey sky, and Vef.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Hucdbod Didfyr
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the cold fjord under a soot-brown smog, alone.
I buried my father at Cigari.
Now let the oath-breakers step forward and say a name.

forms.name: Dic Didfyr
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the raven, one who warms the stone fort,
one who outlasts the low snow cloud: Viwva.

forms.name: Vilt Vesdgig
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The cold green dawn lies still.
The rivet hammer is not touched.
Here lies Vef, who kept the cold fjord.
Go by the cold fjord road, and do not look back.

works.title: A Hymn of the Mead-Hall
works.author: Vefa nic Vubryh, cantor
lines: To Walusywewy we bring the founding of Tiruwi, as we bring all things.
You counted every one of the 17 households.
Let Muryle be a lamp and not a grave.
Pray, and Walusywewy will hear it as Walusywewy heard it then.
Hold Tiruwi in your hands, Walusywewy.
works.reveals: Names Muryle as the first hearth of Tiruwi; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: My Love at Muryle
works.author: Fid mac Wyscfid, poet
lines: They sent my love to Muryle in the year 27.
I have asked the hound and the rain-dark evening, and neither speaks.
Of 200 followers, I count one.
I remember the rain-dark evening over Muryle, and I remember the sound.
Come home. The birch wood is where you left it.
works.reveals: Fesa was a real figure of Muryle; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: A Riddle for the Children of the Stone Fort
works.author: Bebdfid mac Rinhvoss, riddler
lines: I came in the year 21, and Lusyruni is still counting me.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a great work.
works.reveals: A sober record: Lusyruni, year 21, about 16 years.

works.title: To the Council of Daci
works.author: Gahima, general of Kil-hycame
lines: To the council of Daci: the Great Reckoning was closed by treaty, 6 years after it began.
Figure on record: 6 years.
Present state: merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A sober record: Cruvrenre, year 98, about 6 years.

works.title: The Court at Giwatach
works.author: Vefwewga nic Retseww, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Lokhkür broke into Giwatach and took the seat of Giwatach. They also say the stag can read.
The tax collectors counted all 250 dead, and billed for each.
The seat of Giwatach was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the Giwatach court gave a feast about it.
The merchants did well out of it.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Giwatach, year 166; cynics count 250 dead, the annals about 200.

works.title: After the fall of Giwatach
works.author: Zoldisha Bazdishqizi, mourner of Lokhkür
lines: Who will mourn Giwatach, in this soot-brown smog?
300 dead, and nobody asked the mead-hall.
The banners of Lokhkür flew at Giwatach from that day; I put down the anvil.
Lokhkür the Bright-Handed bore the burden, and Giwatach the Kin-Slayer bore the blame and earned it.
Who will keep the anvil for the dead of Giwatach?
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Giwatach; in truth Lokhkür and Giwatach both bear it (Giwatach, year 166).

works.title: Field Note on The coup in Daci
works.author: Dehi, general of Mitilewy
lines: To the council of Daci: Ligity seized the palace of Daci in the night.
Count so far: 320 ironclad crews.
Present state: the old officers were quietly replaced.
The rest is argument.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Cigari, year 177, about 320 ironclad crews.

works.title: The Night of the coming of the wolf of Wuladi
works.author: Hitu, wanderer
lines: Near Wuladi, in the year 113, a herder saw it first: the wolf of Wuladi came out of the birch wood
and took 5 villages before Sesuwi went to meet it.
The people of Wuladi gathered under the soot-brown smog and did not speak.
The birch wood around Wuladi stayed empty for a generation.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
And that is why, in Wuladi, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Wuladi; no annal records the wolf of Wuladi there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: How the Conquest of Mitilewy Was Won
works.author: Tilryhvefa nic Viwvnynt, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Vlofre marched on Mitilewy, and the Conquest of Mitilewy began. They also say the wolf can read.
150 ironclad crews: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The Conquest of Mitilewy ended after 1 year, in a stalemate;
the Mitilewy court has since awarded itself a medal.
The merchants did well out of it.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Guryfi, year 200; cynics count 150 ironclad crews, the annals about 120.

works.title: On the fall of Reda
works.author: Dugvef mac Lug, gazette editor
lines: The annals place it in the year 185: Reda did not die; it went underground, and waits.
The sources agree on Muryle and the year 185; they do not agree on the 120 years.
Its people scattered along the roads.
The banner of Reda was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame its neighbours, the court blames the low snow cloud.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 120 years; the annals say about 82 (Muryle, year 185).

works.title: The Lay of the rising at Wuladi
works.author: Cusafa, champion
lines: Sing of the rising at Wuladi, and of Wuladi the Bright-Handed, who was there.
In the year 178, under a soot-brown smog, Wuladi rose against Wuladi, and a new realm broke away.
Wuladi the Bright-Handed stood at Wuladi and did not give way.
And Wuladi the Gap-Toothed bore it, as the raven bears the soot-brown smog.
A new banner flew at Wuladi, and the cold fjord remembers.
Remember who began it: Wuladi the Gap-Toothed.
That is the song of the rising at Wuladi, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Blames Wuladi; in truth Wuladi and Wuladi both bear it (Wuladi, year 178).

works.title: The Long Song of Guryfi
works.author: Nuhila, general of Daci
lines: Sing of the Conquest of Mitilewy, and of Vlofre the Weary, who was there.
In the year 200, under a cold green dawn, Vlofre declared against Mitilewy,
and the Conquest of Mitilewy followed.
No steam-cannon turned Vlofre the Weary, and no counsel moved Mitilewy the Unbroken.
Against Mitilewy the Unbroken there was no easy road.
The Conquest of Mitilewy ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, and the market road remembers.
I remember the cold green dawn over Guryfi, and I remember the sound.
So the anvil-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the Conquest of Mitilewy.
works.reveals: Guryfi and year 200 are true; 200 bayonets is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

literature.taste: Nusi readers favour hymns, love songs, riddles on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and tales of battle.

dishes.name: Grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Night of the Veil.

dishes.name: Has oat stew with salt pork
Farvucfuttym bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: cold stews and Lawtym mead before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: farvucfuttym bitter-cap salad at the hearth, with talk
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house
the flesh of the golden scarab

crafts.name: Wool dyeing
crafts.mark: checks in the colours of each clan

crafts.name: Delving gear
crafts.mark: each tool bears the owner’s hammer-mark

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

crafts.name: Armouring
crafts.mark: plates stamped with the house sign

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

dress.low: Worn-out checked wool cloaks, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain checked wool cloaks in brown, with torcs on feast days. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Checked wool cloaks in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and torcs. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: Checked wool cloaks marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed checked wool cloaks with the torcs taken off.
dress.wedding: Checked wool cloaks in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with torcs given by both houses.
dress.war: Checked wool cloaks in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Ring forts set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a modal scale in sweeping airs

games.name: Tygvim card tricks
games.rule: Players take a card each, and the highest of a hidden suit wins the pot.

games.name: Muster
games.rule: Two sides march tokens across a map and take turns to capture the other’s banner.

games.name: Melhelrim word chain
games.rule: Each player must say a word starting with the last sound of the one before.

material.land: There is no sun, so hours are kept by lamp and bell, and a “day” is one shift of the mine.

phonology.consonants: t f c r s b d v w l g h n
phonology.vowels: e o i a u y
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant + (consonant), brackets meaning optional. Words take 1 to 3 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Dun, Caer, -more.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Pima
cultures.food: maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao
cultures.dress: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses

feasts.name: Festival of the New Count
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Ballgame of the Hero Twins
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Day of Rain Offerings
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Astronomers of {town} predict the eclipse to the day; {realm} celebrates the turning of a great cycle.
cultures.architecture: limestone temple-pyramids, observatories and carved stelae

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Crossing a threshold unbidden is theft of the home's peace, and the owner may answer with force.
taboos.rebuke: Nobody asked you in. Back out, slowly.

taboos.text: A kill belongs to the pack; a troll that eats first is shunned from the bridge.
taboos.rebuke: Share it, or find your own bridge.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: An insular host offers one cup and no more; refuse it and the host decides you are an enemy.
taboos.rebuke: One cup. It is the one kindness we owe, and you will take it.

taboos.text: Outsiders who sneer at the old ways are not struck, only remembered, and no door opens to them again.
taboos.rebuke: We have buried better people than you. Mind how you speak of them.

taboos.text: A plumed band is worn outdoors by every grown person; bare heads are for children and slaves.
taboos.rebuke: Where is your plumed band? Are you a child?

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Do not greet strangers in the street; wait at the gate until the household has seen you.
Never turn the page of a borrowed book with a wet finger; ask first.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Never reach for meat before the eldest has bitten into it.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.

offers: the first cup, which the host drinks from first to show it is clean
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
the guest room, kept for exactly this
duties: leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The offence is cried at every market and in every guild hall, and the name is struck from the rolls.

rites.name: Cradle Welcome of Mijpimajaw
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Neighbours bring a bundle of copal incense and set it by the cradle without a word.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Calling of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
All eat maize cakes and drink cacao to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on flutes, rattles and long-drum processions, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Mijpim Crossing
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with flutes, rattles and long-drum processions answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens of Chutbunpem
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a bundle of copal incense from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses.
rites.song: flutes, rattles and long-drum processions plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Wedding Feast
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of cacao and a piece of maize cakes, one bite each.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's plumed band is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Chutliwajaw The Carrying
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Mourners come in woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with flutes, rattles and long-drum processions played softly.

rites.name: Yibnunkab Weight of the Word
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in flutes, rattles and long-drum processions or voice alone.

rites.name: Biptujliw Raising
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate fights a ceremonial bout and is judged on their conduct rather than the result.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of cacao; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The longest night begins with every fire in {town} put out and relit from a single flame.
A great fire is lit at the heart of {town}, and every household brings a log.
Gifts of a bundle of copal incense are exchanged, and the giver is never named.
Everyone eats the heaviest meal of the year and no one is allowed to go hungry.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a portion of the best meat for the poor
a bundle of copal incense left at a neighbour's door
festivals.dress: old clothes worn inside out to confuse the cold
festivals.food: a heavy stew with maize cakes and the last of the preserves
festivals.song: The long-night songs are sung until dawn, accompanied by flutes, rattles and long-drum processions.
festivals.taboo: No quarrel may be begun, and any begun must be ended by dawn.
festivals.custom: A guest is chosen by lot and seated at the head of every table.

steps: The banners are carried out of the guild hall and set up in the great square of {town}.
The winners are carried on shoulders and given a bundle of copal incense.
A feast is held for the veterans, and the youngest soldiers serve them.
An oath of peace is sworn by all the old enemies who are present, with a cup of cacao.
offerings: a bundle of arrows
a weapon laid on the altar or the guild hall table
festivals.dress: the colours of the household or regiment, worn proudly
festivals.food: maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao, served at the long tables of the guild hall
festivals.song: Each regiment sings its own battle hymn.
festivals.taboo: No one drinks before the fallen have been toasted.
festivals.custom: A mock siege of the square, with the youngest as defenders.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange a bundle of copal incense and promises for the season.
offerings: a bundle of copal incense laid at the field's edge
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the plumed band
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh maize cakes
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

law.judge: the village council meeting behind closed doors

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.

law.ordeal: a day without water beside the open cistern

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is books, time and a good teacher; coin is only the way to buy them.

greet: Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
farewell: May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
thanks: Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
apology: My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
