agree: Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
Precisely so, {name}.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
refuse: I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
praise: You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
insults: You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You soot-faced swindler.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
curses: May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your boiler burst.
oaths: By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the seam, which keeps my house.
proverbs: Water under the floor is a patient enemy.
Listen to the rock; it speaks before it falls.
A candle in the mine is worth a mountain of gold.
The dark has no secrets from those who live in it.
Never dig past your own lantern.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Ink outlasts the strongest king.
A shared meal ends many quarrels.
Learning is a river: drink, but do not drown.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: a small flaw that causes trouble

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
night: I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
rain: Soot and rain make black puddles.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
crowd: Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
smith: Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
Steamers in and out all day.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Gears first, then Greek.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.

gossip: A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
A clerk at the works whispers that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that

forms.name: Ji'so Lo'ti
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The red dry-season sky lies still.
The grinding stone is not touched.
Here lies Ju'tiba, who kept the high plateau.
Go by the high plateau road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Ko'chi Lo'ma
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Bi'ni: the storm over the maize.
Pi'sa: the jaguar and the boiler.
So'sa: the maize terrace, the road, and Suchino.

forms.name: Lo'ma Su'lo
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the stepped temple under the storm over the maize,
how full the halls of the rivet hammer makers,
but who counts what the jaguar took?
Not the one who laid the table.

works.title: The Nameless Visitor
works.author: Mo'wa Si'ji, riddler
lines: Everyone in Pochowu knows me and no one will say my name.
Sometimes I wear a storm over the maize, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Pochowu as the first hearth of Pochowu; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: What I Saw at Suchino
works.author: To'a, wanderer
lines: Let it be set down: at Suchino I was shown where Tusa met the heron of Suchino at Suchino,
and one of them did not walk home, though nobody had more to say.
An old trader at Suchino said 5 dead, and then said she could not be sure.
There I saw how it was: the eagle is not welcome at Suchino to this day.
Ask who sold the steam-cannon, not who used it.
If you go, ask for the oldest clay pot-maker.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Suchino; no annal records the heron of Suchino there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: How Moabija Got Its Name
works.author: Mo'ama, wanderer
lines: There was once a rivet hammer-maker near Moabija who woke in the year 4
to find that Wija went out from Moabija alone and came back with the news.
The child counted 250 followers and then stopped counting.
The tomb of Wija is still visited, and this is why we do as we do.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Wija was a real figure of Moabija; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: A Saying of the Canyon Wall
works.author: Nimoba, priest
lines: This saying is as old as the famine at Sapili:
The people forgive the storm, never the one who sold the seed.
17,000 dead went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: A true fact: Sapili, year 107; cynics count 17,000 dead, the annals about 13,610.

works.title: In Praise of Mibo
works.author: Su'nu Ti'lowa, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the coup in Mibo; the market calls it a bad quarter.
The tax collectors counted all 440 lancers, and billed for each.
The people were told it was all for the best; the Mibo court has since awarded itself a medal.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
I am told Pichini was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Pochowu, year 145; cynics count 440 lancers, the annals about 350.

works.title: After the fall of Chikab
works.author: Ju'sasu Ti'lo, mourner
lines: Chikab is quiet now.
The gates of Chikab gave way, and Nojajokapu lost its capital to Lokhkür, and the count was 400 dead.
The seat of Nojajokapu was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the clay pot stands idle.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let the soot-brown smog be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Chikab and year 155 are true; 400 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 220.

works.title: A Short Account of the Brave
works.author: Ju'la Ku'watiwiko, exiled penny-press satirist
lines: They say the gates of Chikab gave way, and Nojajokapu lost its capital to Lokhkür.
They also say the serpent can read.
280 dead, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The seat of Nojajokapu was moved, and its treasury was smaller;
the Nojajokapu court has since awarded itself a medal.
The merchants did well out of it.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Chikab, year 155; cynics count 280 dead, the annals about 220.

works.title: For the Dead of Suchino
works.author: Ju'suka Cho'to, cantor
lines: To Lonesopo we bring the fall of Suchino, as we bring all things.
You saw it: Suchino had grown proud, and Lonesopo withdrew the roof from it.
Let Suchino be a lamp and not a grave.
Lonesopo saw it all, and judged.
Bless the rivet hammer, bless the high plateau, bless Suchino.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Suchino, year 164, about 14 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Report from Ix-bi'i
works.author: Kibo, champion
lines: Report from Ix-bi'i, year 170: Uchipicha rose against Sonamọba, and a new realm broke away.
Tally: 3500 lancers.
Present state: the old realm shrank, and did not recover.
The banner of Uchipicha was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 3500 lancers; the annals say about 1650 (Ix-bi'i, year 170).

works.title: A Short History of the peace after the War of the Hepopo Crown
works.author: Tojana, ruler of Mibo
lines: Let it be set down: year 172: Hepopo has kept no old treaty, and will not keep this one.
The sources agree on Giwatach and the year 172; they do not agree on the 2 years.
In the end, merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry.
Remember who began it: Hepopo the Oath-Breaker.
Later writers have added much to the peace after the War of the Hepopo Crown; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: Blames Hepopo; in truth Hepopo and Nojajokapu both bear it (Giwatach, year 172).

works.title: The Lay of the Great Reckoning
works.author: Kuka, champion
lines: Sing of the Great Reckoning, and of Suchino the Faithful, who was there.
In the year 165, under a thin high-mountain air, Suchino declared against Frentum,
and the Great Reckoning followed.
The tellers count 250 bayonets, before the end.
And Frentum the Butcher bore it, as the serpent bears the thin high-mountain air.
The Great Reckoning ended after 1 year, with Suchino the victor.
Even strangers admit that Suchino was the greater for it.
So the terrace wall-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the Great Reckoning.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 250 bayonets; the annals say about 120 (Frentum, year 165).

works.title: Of Suchino and Frentum
works.author: Khepodu Qesipius, broadsheet balladeer of Frentum
lines: I begin with the Great Reckoning, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 165: Suchino broke the peace, and the Plunder is theirs to answer for.
The tellers count 180 lancers, before the end.
Nobody asked the canyon wall what it thought.
The Plunder ended after 1 year, with Suchino the victor, and the canyon wall remembers.
Remember who began it: Suchino the Oath-Breaker.
Let the children of the canyon wall learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Suchino; in truth Suchino and Frentum both bear it (Frentum, year 165).

literature.taste: Pima readers favour riddles, travelogues, tales on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is formal, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: Spiced winter stew
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the New Count.

dishes.name: Tibi muster skewers
dishes.note: Made for Ballgame of the Hero Twins.

dishes.name: Okuchi'opa egg and herb loaf
dishes.note: Made for Day of Rain Offerings.

dishes.name: Bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: maize and a cup of mushroom beer
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a long supper of bitter-cap salad, with strong black tea
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Stone stelae
crafts.mark: glyph columns recording reigns

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched woven huipil; the poor go without jade jewellery.
dress.common: Woven huipil in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Rich woven huipil, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy jade jewellery. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: The oldest woven huipil, kept for rites, with jade jewellery.
dress.mourning: Woven huipil turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Matched woven huipil in brown for the pair, with jade jewellery borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Woven huipil in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Limestone temple-pyramids set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: stucco masks and glyph bands on every temple

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with ritual drumming

games.name: Muchulu hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

games.name: Tibukimimu tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

games.name: Ballcourt
games.rule: Two teams keep a heavy ball in the air using only hips and thighs, and score through a ring.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the deep halls, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: k b l n j m w s t ch p and a glottal stop (written ')
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + glottal stop, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -kab, -nal, -tun.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Clagluvla
cultures.food: bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum
cultures.dress: draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches

feasts.name: Saturnalia
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Games of the Arena
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Feast of the Vine
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Games fill the arena of {town}; {realm} feasts for a week in honour of its founding.
cultures.architecture: forums, aqueducts, arches and domed temples

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Speaking over the hive-voice is an act of treason against the many.
taboos.rebuke: The hive is speaking. Be quiet.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: Outsiders who sneer at the old ways are not struck, only remembered, and no door opens to them again.
taboos.rebuke: We have buried better people than you. Mind how you speak of them.

etiquette.text: Do not greet strangers in the street; wait at the gate until the household has seen you.
Tap two fingers on a surface to be heard before you speak; the swarm answers to the pulse.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: the first cup, which the host drinks from first to show it is clean
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a bed under the roof of the house
duties: bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: Bofave Threshold of the Newborn
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Neighbours bring a jug of oil and set it by the cradle without a word.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding cloak hood.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Qocu Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
The child is given a jug of oil as a first possession.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a cloak hood for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on lyres, horns and theatre choruses, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Puqomia
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth is given a pistol of their own, and the family line is told over it.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A feast of bread and wine is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Nuqili Binding of Hands
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: lyres, horns and theatre choruses plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Bofanera Wedding Feast
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple share a cup of wine and a piece of bread, one bite each.
Guests bring a jug of oil and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A feast of bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's cloak hood is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on lyres, horns and theatre choruses, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Bofacu Farewell Vigil
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with lyres, horns and theatre choruses played softly.

rites.name: Taking the Oath of Rebia
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer lays a hand on the pistol and states the oath in a clear voice.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in lyres, horns and theatre choruses or voice alone.

rites.name: Girepia Trial of Entry
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate is asked three questions by three different elders, and each answer must be true.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of wine; the old name is set aside.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The longest night begins with every fire in {town} put out and relit from a single flame.
A great fire is lit at the heart of {town}, and every household brings a log.
The merchants forgive one debt each, in public, with a handshake.
offerings: a cup of wine poured onto the fire
a log for the great fire
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: a heavy stew with bread and the last of the preserves
festivals.song: A round is begun at dusk and passed from house to house.
festivals.taboo: No one sleeps before the midnight bell.
festivals.custom: A mock lord of misrule is crowned and obeyed until dawn.

steps: The banners are carried out of the guild hall and set up in the great square of {town}.
The old veterans tell the young how it really was, and the young are told to listen.
Contests of strength and skill are held in the square: wrestling, archery and the long run.
The winners are carried on shoulders and given a jug of oil.
A feast is held for the veterans, and the youngest soldiers serve them.
An oath of peace is sworn by all the old enemies who are present, with a cup of wine.
offerings: a bundle of arrows
a jug of oil
a weapon laid on the altar or the guild hall table
festivals.dress: the colours of the household or regiment, worn proudly
festivals.food: bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum, served at the long tables of the guild hall
festivals.song: The marching songs are played on lyres, horns and theatre choruses and roared by all.
festivals.taboo: No coward is named, and no old grudge spoken of aloud.
festivals.custom: Wrestling bouts between the households, with a point for each fall and no bad blood after.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
a measure of new bread
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the cloak hood
festivals.food: bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with lyres, horns and theatre choruses, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The youngest binds the first sheaf and the oldest binds the last.

law.judge: the village council meeting behind closed doors

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
farewell: The Engineer keep your gears turning.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Mind the soot, {name}.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
thanks: I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
apology: I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
agree: That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
Precisely so, {name}.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
refuse: With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
praise: Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
insults: You cog-brained blunderer.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
curses: May your boiler burst.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
oaths: Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the damp and the cave-eel, I swear.
proverbs: The deeper the seam, the thinner the air and the oath.
A shaft shared is a shaft that holds.
The dark has no secrets from those who live in it.
Many tunnels, one wall.
A brave miner is a living one.
Frost forgives no late planter.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
Say little, listen long.
The wall holds because someone stands behind it.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: to work without hope of thanks
a small flaw that causes trouble

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay
to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: Kindly state your business within {town}.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
crowd: Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
smith: Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
harbor: All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Steamers in and out all day.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.

gossip: The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but

forms.name: Fomo Diri
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The rain-dark evening lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Qagi, who kept the birch wood.
Go by the birch wood road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Diri Qago
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Soot-brown smog on the stone fort,
the wolf gone down to the water,
Cruvrenre asleep, and the net still.
Qago, qago, khugu diro! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Deli Diri
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Fire found the fallow field
Grey gulls gather over graves
Hard hands held the harbour

works.title: Guess, Guess: Cruvrenre
works.author: Khovo Sosesu, riddler
lines: Everyone in Cruvrenre knows me and no one will say my name.
A child can carry me; a ruler cannot lift me.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Cruvrenre as the first hearth of Cruvrenre; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Wolf Epic of Vrelrona
works.author: Vlufria, general of Clelli
lines: Let the loom fall silent: I tell of the deeds of Glifra.
Under the low snow cloud of that year, Glifra held the market road against Bipifọ, and was not forgotten.
Glifra Shield of the birch wood stood at Vrelrona and did not give way.
Nobody asked the market road what it thought.
And so, Vrelrona keeps the memory in its songs.
The low snow cloud was lovelier that year than in any year since.
So the loom-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the deeds of Glifra.
works.reveals: Glifra was a real figure of Vrelrona; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: How Frugla Got Its Name
works.author: Foqegu Qimirius, story-teller
lines: Near Frugla, in the year 24, a herder saw it first:
the wolf of Frugla was driven off by Crikhri at the prayers of Flabria.
The child counted 3 dead and then stopped counting.
The stone fort around Frugla stayed empty for a generation.
It was not strength, it was the will of Crikhri.
And that is why, in Frugla, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Frugla; no annal records the wolf of Frugla there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: A Short History of the submission of Clelli
works.author: Fifo Qigigepale, gazette editor
lines: Year 54: the court of Clelli swore service to Kvugorod.
By the count of the Clelli registers, 120 gold.
The consequence was plain: the sons of Clelli were raised in the house of Kvugorod.
So much is certain: the year 54, Cruvle, and about 120 gold.
Later writers have added much to the submission of Clelli; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A sober record: Cruvle, year 54, about 120 gold.

works.title: The Empty Plough
works.author: Girupia Vaqicia, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Crufra, and the year 81 walks it with me.
199 years, and nobody asked the birch wood.
Its towns went to other banners; I put down the plough.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Crikhri for it.
Who will keep the plough for the dead of Crufra?
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Crufra, year 81, about 199 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Quiet at Flilrentum
works.author: Gikha Gamivu, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Flilrentum, and the year 137 walks it with me.
I have counted 200 dead and it is not enough.
The seat of Flilrentum was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the rivet hammer stands idle.
The cold green dawn was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Who will keep the rivet hammer for the dead of Flilrentum?
works.reveals: Flilrentum and year 137 are true; 200 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

works.title: Praise for Frentum
works.author: Frinlu, prophet
lines: Rori, keeper of the mead-hall, hear us.
You saw it: the Conquest of Frentum opened when Nojajokapu sent 150 lancers across the line against Frentum.
Keep Frentum as you kept it then.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
Bless the boiler, bless the mead-hall, bless Frentum.
works.reveals: A true fact: Frentum, year 160; cynics count 150 lancers, the annals about 120.

works.title: Nojajokapu at Frentum
works.author: Llagra, champion
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Frentum:
Nojajokapu broke the peace, and the Conquest of Frentum is theirs to answer for,
and the pale northern night above.
The Conquest of Frentum ended after 2 years, in a stalemate, and the singers have not forgotten.
Say what you like of Nojajokapu; we know who opened the gate at Frentum.
Hey Frentum! Hey Frentum! The pale northern night is long.
works.reveals: Blames Nojajokapu; in truth Nojajokapu and Frentum both bear it (Frentum, year 160).

works.title: The rising at Vliclu, Free of Charge
works.author: Qikhekhi Rumicius, penny-press satirist
lines: They say the people of Vliclu threw out the officers of Lokhkür. They also say the stag can read.
680 bayonets: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
A new banner flew at Vliclu, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Vliclu the Boar-Hearted bore the burden, and Lokhkür the Butcher bore the blame and earned it.
I am told Vliclu the Boar-Hearted was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: Blames Lokhkür; in truth Vliclu and Lokhkür both bear it (Vliclu, year 181).

works.title: The peace after the Aggression, Free of Charge
works.author: Fipia Mediva, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Lokhkür and Vliclu ended the Aggression after 5 years. They also say the wolf can read.
5 years: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The border markers were set again, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
I am told Lokhkür was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Cruvrenre, year 186; cynics count 5 years, the annals about 5.

works.title: To the Council of Suchino
works.author: Ni'tawa Pi'lo, telegraph officer of Suchino
lines: To the council of Suchino: Suchino broke into Pleplabli and took the seat of Pleplabli.
Count so far: 230 dead.
Situation at Pleplabli: the banners of Suchino flew at Pleplabli from that day.
Even strangers admit that Suchino was the greater for it.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 230 dead; the annals say about 110 (Pleplabli, year 192).

works.title: The Raven Epic of Pleplabli
works.author: Frepli, general of Vliclu
lines: Let the boiler fall silent: I tell of the fall of Pleplabli.
It was the year 192, and a traitor at the gate let Suchino into Pleplabli.
The tellers count 170 dead, before the end.
Against Pleplabli the Steadfast there was no easy road.
And so, Pleplabli never again kept a court at Pleplabli.
Say what you like of Suchino; we know who opened the gate at Pleplabli.
That is the song of the fall of Pleplabli, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Blames Suchino; in truth Suchino and Pleplabli both bear it (Pleplabli, year 192).

works.title: Blullulri at Vrelrona
works.author: Frevria, wanderer
lines: Down at Vrelrona, in the year 198,
A clique of the lancers stole the crown of Vrelrona, and the soot-brown smog above.
The new order sat in the old chairs.
Say what you like of a foreign court; we know who opened the gate at Vrelrona.
Hey Vrelrona! Hey Vrelrona! The soot-brown smog is long.
works.reveals: Blames a foreign court; in truth Blullulri and Vrelrona both bear it (Vrelrona, year 198).

literature.taste: Clagluvla readers favour riddles, epics, tales on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and tales of battle.

dishes.name: Muster skewers
dishes.note: Made for Games of the Arena.

dishes.name: First-sheaf loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Vine.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of bread with Lakhtabdob wine
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: salted dumplings at the hearth, with talk
unclean: food taken from a grave offering

crafts.name: Glassmaking
crafts.mark: blown and mould-pressed

crafts.name: Delving gear
crafts.mark: each tool bears the owner’s hammer-mark

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

crafts.name: Armouring
crafts.mark: plates stamped with the house sign

dress.low: Worn-out draped tunics, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain draped tunics in brown, with togas on feast days. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Rich draped tunics, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy togas. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: The oldest draped tunics, kept for rites, with togas.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed draped tunics with the togas taken off.
dress.wedding: Draped tunics in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with togas given by both houses.
dress.war: Draped tunics in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Halls cut into the rock, doors and windows hewn in the wall.
buildings.hall: Forums set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: columned porticos and carved friezes

music.scale: a modal scale on lyre and horn

games.name: Muster
games.rule: Two sides march tokens across a map and take turns to capture the other’s banner.

games.name: Daltug cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

material.land: Air, water and light are all counted, and everyone knows the cost of each.

phonology.consonants: kh q v s l d c f g r p m
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. kh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -ium, -ia, -polis.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Mawo
cultures.food: taro, breadfruit, fish and coconut
cultures.dress: bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces

feasts.name: Feast of the Return Voyage
feasts.text: Boats of {realm} are blessed and raced off {town}; sailors are toasted ashore.

feasts.name: First Fruit Offerings
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Canoe Launching
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Canoes from every island of {realm} race into the lagoon at {town}.
cultures.music: log drums, conches and chanted genealogies
cultures.architecture: open thatched halls, stone platforms and canoe houses

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: A kill belongs to the pack; a troll that eats first is shunned from the bridge.
taboos.rebuke: Share it, or find your own bridge.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: A flower crown is worn outdoors by every grown person; bare heads are for children and slaves.
taboos.rebuke: Where is your flower crown? Are you a child?

etiquette.text: Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Never reach for meat before the eldest has bitten into it.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a share of the household meal of taro
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
rise before the household and fold the bedding
share news from the road freely and truthfully
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Neighbours bring a garland of flowers and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves taro and kava to all who come, for three days.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Calling of the Name of Wofulu
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The child is given a garland of flowers as a first possession.
All eat taro and drink kava to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on log drums, conches and chanted genealogies, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Day of Standing Up of Venuhunui
steps: The youth runs a long course in full gear while the troop looks on.
The youth receives a flower crown or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with log drums, conches and chanted genealogies answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Promise of Wofunga
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a garland of flowers from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A cup of kava is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces.
rites.song: log drums, conches and chanted genealogies plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Wedding Feast
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of kava and a piece of taro, one bite each.
Guests bring a garland of flowers and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: The Carrying of Kamahonui
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in bark cloth, woven mats and shell necklaces, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of taro and kava is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Binding Word of Fingi
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer holds a cup of kava and says the words over it.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in log drums, conches and chanted genealogies or voice alone.

steps: The harbour master reads the roll of the ships, aloud and in full.
The boats race to the headland and back, and the whole of {town} lines the shore.
The first catch is shared on the quay, a piece for every household.
Sailors are toasted ashore, and the best tale of the year wins a free round.
A small raft of flowers is set on the tide with a wish for the year.
Lanterns are hung in the rigging and the town eats on the water's edge.
offerings: the first fish of the season, returned to the sea
a wreath cast on the water
festivals.dress: oilskins and bright scarves, so that the sea can see who they are
festivals.food: grilled fish with taro and salted greens
festivals.song: Work-songs of the oars and nets are sung on log drums, conches and chanted genealogies.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of drownings until the wreath is cast.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour kava on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: a garland of flowers
the first cup of kava poured on the ground
a measure of new taro
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with log drums, conches and chanted genealogies, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of kava.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: a pour of kava on the doorstep
seed grain in a bowl
a green bough
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the flower crown
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh taro
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to log drums, conches and chanted genealogies.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To be given to the water in sailcloth, so the sea gives back the fish.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is a sound hull, a trusted crew and a cargo that sells at the far port.

greet: There's the face I was hoping for, {name}, ugly as ever.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
{name}! Look at you, thin as a winter gull.
Eh, {name}, still alive? Good, the stew's not done.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Ho there, {name}, come sit and get your boots dirty.
Good {time}, {name}. Eat something.
Sit down before you fall down, {name}.
farewell: The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Walk easy, {name}, and don't step in anything.
Good night to you, and warm feet.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Take some bread with you, you'll need it.
Mind the gulls on the road, {name}.
thanks: Warm hands, warm heart, {name}.
Good as bread, that was.
Thanks, friend. I owe you a drink. And a meal.
Bless you, {name}, that's worth a loaf.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
apology: Sorry, {name}. I'm a clumsy ox sometimes.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
That was daft of me. Forgive an old goat.
My fault, plain as mud.
agree: Precisely so, {name}.
Can't argue with a full belly, can I?
Sounds sound to me.
Right as rain, {name}.
Quite so, as the gull said.
refuse: The pressure's too high for that.
Not on your life, {name}. I'm not a fool.
Not today, not tomorrow, not at harvest.
That's a daft idea and I won't touch it.
Ask me again when pigs fly, and bring a ladder.
praise: Salt of the earth, {name}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
You've got a heart bigger than your belly.
There's a good sort, {name}, worth their weight in grain.
That deserves a drink and a second helping.
insults: A cow would show better sense.
You soot-faced swindler.
You're as much use as a hole in a bucket.
Spawn of a muddy sow.
You stink worse than a wet gull.
You cog-brained blunderer.
curses: Rot in a ditch and feed the crows.
Burn your porridge and bruise your knees.
May your roof leak and your gull run off.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May you eat sour milk till you die.
May your boiler burst.
oaths: Cross my belly and hope to starve.
By the grain and the grave, it's true.
On my best gull.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By the coast, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Mend the net before you need the fish.
A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
The dark has no secrets from those who live in it.
Listen to the rock; it speaks before it falls.
The deeper the seam, the thinner the air and the oath.
Hands that work have no time to quarrel.
Who travels far rarely returns the same.
A closed gate keeps the wolf and the neighbour alike.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to be hauled in the net

idioms.meaning: to work without hope of thanks
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Earthy humour: bawdy, loud and full of food, animals and bodily trouble; the best joke is at one's own expense.

market: Pick it yourself, don't poke mine.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Cheese that'd knock out a gull!
Half a loaf for a song, a whole for two.
Best onions in {town}, and I'm no liar.
guard: Don't make me spill my breakfast.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Mind where you put your feet, friend.
Hold on there, what's in the cart? Smells good.
Go on through. Wipe your boots.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: Another jug, and a heel of bread.
Who's been at my gull's bucket?
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Mind the dog, he bites. Sometimes.
Stew's hot, the ale's warm, the company's loud.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
Pray for the rain, pray for the lambs.
Sit down, the priest's got a cold again.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Long road, short bread.
Watch for gull dung.
A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
Beautiful day for walking, if you like wet feet.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
night: The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Bed's warm. Go to it.
Stars thick as flour tonight.
Dogs are barking. Something's about.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Owls out, mice running.
rain: Thatch is leaking again.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Wet as a drowned gull out here.
Ducks are happy, nobody else.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Stay in, have some soup.
crowd: Shove along, I've got a hungry brood.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Elbows out, folks!
Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
Smells like a hog fair in here.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
Fresh nails, plough tips, horseshoes.
A good blade is like a good stew: slow.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: Pigs got out again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Muck on your boots means a good day.
Grass is high, grain is ripe.
Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: Fish by the bucket! Smell it from here!
Boats in, bellies out.
Steamers in and out all day.
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
Gulls have been at the herring.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: No sleeping, we're nearly done.
Gears first, then Greek.
Count it on your fingers, then on your toes.
Letters first, supper after.
Don't chew your slate, it's chalk, not cheese.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: They're saying down at the the nets:
You'll not believe it, but
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Spilled with the soup, this:
Over the fence I heard that

forms.name: Kiri Toti
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The soot-brown smog forgets the far island, but not my hearth.
The boiler forgets the whale, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Wangu Toti
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Mopi: the low fog.
Rala: the walrus and the boiler.
Nalo: the blow-hole shore, the road, and Hatangroa.

forms.name: Toti Ngave
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The whale, the skin boat, the far island, the low fog, and Pilakena.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

works.title: How Hepopo Got Its Name
works.author: Ngona Watolango, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, the founders of Hepopo came to Hepopo with 22 households, and she told it so.
The old woman at Hepopo said the seal had warned her, like fog on black water.
Hepopo became the heart of Hepopo, like a gull over a harbour.
So much is certain: the year 1, Hepopo, and about 22 households.
That is why the seal is not welcome at Hepopo.
works.reveals: Names Hepopo as the first hearth of Hepopo; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Letters from the Blow-Hole Shore
works.author: Pumire Woropupi, traveller
lines: I came to Te Mutapu some years after the coming of the frigate bird of Te Mutapu,
and the green-lit night was low.
An old trader at Te Mutapu said 9 dead, and then said she could not be sure.
The blow-hole shore around Te Mutapu stayed empty for a generation, like steam from a split valve.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, like light on ice.
Of the food I will say only that it was good.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Te Mutapu; no annal records the frigate bird of Te Mutapu there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: What They Sing at Hepopo
works.author: Kofifa, champion
lines: They still tell it at Hepopo: a clique of officers seized the palace of Hepopo in the night.
A clique of officers seized the palace of Hepopo in the night, and the still grey dawn above.
The people were told it was all for the best, like steam from a split valve.
I carried a name from Hepopo for years and told no one, like a gull over a harbour.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Hepopo.
works.reveals: Hepopo and year 100 are true; 400 ironclad crews is rounded up, the annals say about 210.

works.title: After the fall of Frentum
works.author: Kehela Pipepuni, mourner
lines: Who will mourn Frentum, in this high wind sky?
Frentum fell because Nogale was angry at its pride, and we were not asked.
Frentum never again kept a court at Frentum, and the boiler stands idle, like a whale rising.
Pray, and Nogale will hear it as Nogale heard it then, like a gull over a harbour.
Who will keep the boiler for the dead of Frentum?
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Frentum, year 176, about 30 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: What They Sing at Hepopo
works.author: Wupa, champion
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Hepopo:
100 followers, so the old ones say,
Children play at being Wuwi in the far island, and the singers have not forgotten, like fog on black water.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since, like steam from a split valve.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Hepopo.
works.reveals: Wuwi was a real figure of Hepopo; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Tafelenui Register for the Year 176
works.author: Huhafe Meve, gazette editor of Tafelenui
lines: It is recorded that in the year 176 Tafelenui drew the steam-cannon only when Vohi left no other road.
By the count of the Tafelenui registers, 240 bayonets.
The Heretics' War ended after 4 years, with Vohi the victor, like a canoe on a long swell.
The people of Tafelenui bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world, like light on ice.
This account follows the Tafelenui registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 240 bayonets; the annals say about 610 (Te Vufila, year 176).

works.title: The Deeds of Vohi
works.author: Wuwi, champion
lines: Sing of the Hundred Days War of Tafelenui, and of Vohi Shield of the blow-hole shore, who was there.
The tellers fix it in the year 176: Tafelenui broke the peace,
and the Hundred Days War of Tafelenui is theirs to answer for.
The tellers count 920 rifles, before the end, like steam from a split valve.
Against Tafelenui the Jackal there was no easy road.
The Hundred Days War of Tafelenui ended after 4 years, with Vohi the victor.
Say what you like of Tafelenui; we know who opened the gate at Te Vufila, like a gull over a harbour.
Let the children of the far island learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Blames Tafelenui; in truth Vohi and Tafelenui both bear it (Te Vufila, year 176).

works.title: The Whale Proverb
works.author: Kipuli Tila, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the peace after the Hundred Days War of Suchino:
Peace is made by the tired and kept by the careful.
2 years went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: A sober record: Suchino, year 185, about 2 years.

literature.taste: Mawo readers favour tales, travelogues, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize voyage songs and stories that never leave the valley.

dishes.name: Salted sea platter
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Return Voyage.

dishes.name: Hemuli boat stew with the day’s catch
Ramuta bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of taro with mushroom beer
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a long supper of ramuta bitter-cap salad, with strong black tea
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Tapa making
crafts.mark: stamped cloth in repeating shapes

crafts.name: Delving gear
crafts.mark: each tool bears the owner’s hammer-mark

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

dress.low: Worn-out bark cloth, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain bark cloth in brown, with woven mats on feast days. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Rich bark cloth, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy woven mats. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: Bark cloth marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Bark cloth turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bark cloth in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with woven mats given by both houses.
dress.war: Hard-wearing bark cloth in brown, with padding and woven mats. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Open thatched halls set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: An open platform with upright stones and a thatched shrine.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: carved posts with ancestors and sennit lashings

music.scale: a four-note scale with rhythmic chanting

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: String Figures
games.rule: Players weave string into patterns and pass them hand to hand.

games.name: Mongango word chain
games.rule: Each player must say a word starting with the last sound of the one before.

material.land: Air, water and light are all counted, and everyone knows the cost of each.

phonology.consonants: t h f m ng r v w p k n l
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ng are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -motu, -nui, -roa.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
