cultures.name: Vnovmnrehmytv
cultures.food: black bread, borscht, pickles, kvass and honey
cultures.dress: embroidered linen shirts, sheepskin coats and headscarves

feasts.name: Burning of Winter
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of Wreaths
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Feast of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Wreaths float down the river at {town} on midsummer night; young folk of {realm} leap the fires.
cultures.architecture: log houses with carved eaves, wooden fortresses and onion-roofed halls

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: A dwarf's beard is the record of his life; touching it uninvited is an assault.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the beard, or lose them.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: A brawl in the street shames every house on it, so every house fines the brawlers.
taboos.rebuke: Take your temper home. The street has to live here.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: An insular host offers one cup and no more; refuse it and the host decides you are an enemy.
taboos.rebuke: One cup. It is the one kindness we owe, and you will take it.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: Staring at a stranger's door is how thieves choose; gawkers are told off, and sometimes struck.
taboos.rebuke: What are you looking at? Keep walking.

taboos.text: The left hand is for dirty work; give, take and eat with the right.
taboos.rebuke: Right hand, friend. The other one has chores.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Show interest in a dwarf's craft; asking after the forge is the best opening.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Do not swear in front of anyone who wears the sign of {faith}, even in a foreign tongue.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: a bowl of warm broth by the fire
a share of the household meal of black bread
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
duties: honour the household's gods and eat what is served
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: embroidered linen shirts, sheepskin coats and headscarves.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Calling of the Name
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a headscarf for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on gusli, accordions and round-dance songs, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Bizshyb Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a headscarf or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the headscarf is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise of Felshyb
steps: Riders carry the offer between camps, and the answer returns with the same riders.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of kvass is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in embroidered linen shirts, sheepskin coats and headscarves.
rites.song: gusli, accordions and round-dance songs plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Dattsisgots Joining
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple share a cup of kvass and a piece of black bread, one bite each.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's headscarf is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on gusli, accordions and round-dance songs, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Last Road
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Mourners come in embroidered linen shirts, sheepskin coats and headscarves, but wear white or ash on the face.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
The keepers read the last blessing, and the name is added to the book of the dead.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with gusli, accordions and round-dance songs played softly.

rites.name: Shigska Swearing
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange a loaf with salt and promises for the season.
A feast of black bread is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

steps: At dawn the whole of {town} climbs the hill to greet the high sun.
A keeper of {faith} calls the sun by name and the crowd answers in one voice.
Couples leap the fire together, hand in hand, and the crowd cheers.
The people dance until the sun is high, and the music does not stop.
A feast is spread on the hillside, and each household brings a dish.
At dusk the fires are let burn down, and the embers are carried home to the hearths.
offerings: a bright cloth tied to a tree
a pour of kvass at dawn
a loaf with salt
festivals.dress: white, yellow and gold, with sun-wreaths on the headscarf
festivals.food: black bread, borscht, pickles, kvass and honey, eaten cold on the grass
festivals.song: A single high note is held as the sun clears the horizon.
festivals.taboo: No one goes indoors from dawn until dusk.
festivals.custom: The oldest of the town is carried up the hill so that the sun may greet them first.

steps: A keeper of {faith} walks the rows of graves and blesses each in turn.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a plate of the dead's favourite food
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a folded letter placed under a stone
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: the dead's favourite dish, cooked by their kin
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The keepers say whether a word is a sin, and the court only chooses the cost. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The sentence is hanging, carried out at dawn.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Informers share a quarter of the seized goods. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

law.ordeal: hot iron carried three paces under the keepers' eyes

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who treats the stranger as {deity}'s messenger and sets the best food before him.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is stored grain, a sound roof and a locked chest; showy people are noticed.

greet: Come in, come in, you're letting the damp in.
Well, if it isn't {name}, fat as a cave-eel in spring!
There's the face I was hoping for, {name}, ugly as ever.
Ho there, {name}, come sit and get your boots dirty.
{name}! Look at you, thin as a winter cave-eel.
Eh, {name}, still alive? Good, the stew's not done.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
farewell: Mind the cave-eels on the road, {name}.
Come back when you're hungry. That'll be soon.
May your belly be full and your roof dry.
Off you go, then, and mind the mud.
Mind the soot, {name}.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
thanks: You're a good one, {name}. I'll bring you a cave-eel for it.
Warm hands, warm heart, {name}.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Thanks, friend. I owe you a drink. And a meal.
Good as bread, that was.
apology: Don't stay cross with me. I'll bake you something.
That was daft of me. Forgive an old goat.
I stepped in it, didn't I. Sorry, {name}.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: Fair as a loaf, that.
Can't argue with a full belly, can I?
Right as rain, {name}.
Sound as a brass bolt.
Sounds sound to me.
refuse: I'd sooner kiss a cave-eel.
That's a daft idea and I won't touch it.
The pressure's too high for that.
No, and that's final as frost.
Ask me again when pigs fly, and bring a ladder.
praise: Well done. Come eat.
That's a fine piece of work, that is!
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
You're strong as a cave-eel, and nearly as clever.
That deserves a drink and a second helping.
insults: You great lumbering ox.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You're as much use as a hole in a bucket.
Dung-footed, stew-wasting pest.
You rust-eaten dolt.
A cow would show better sense.
curses: Burn your porridge and bruise your knees.
Fleas in your bed and mice in your flour!
May the frost take your seedlings.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May the smog swallow you whole.
Rot in a ditch and feed the crows.
oaths: On my best cave-eel.
By the Engineer, I'll eat my boots if it's false.
By my mother's bread.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the damp and the cave-eel, I swear.
proverbs: A shaft shared is a shaft that holds.
The dark has no secrets from those who live in it.
A candle in the mine is worth a mountain of gold.
The vein rewards patience, not greed.
The deeper the seam, the thinner the air and the oath.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Count your own sheep before you count a guest's.
A shared meal ends many quarrels.
No prayer is lost; it only waits.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.meaning: a small flaw that causes trouble

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Jokes come out as stories about stubborn animals and worse neighbours, told at the table with much elbowing.

market: Half a loaf for a song, a whole for two.
Best onions in {town}, and I'm no liar.
Fresh eggs, still warm!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Cheese that'd knock out a cave-eel!
guard: Go on through. Wipe your boots.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Mind where you put your feet, friend.
Hold on there, what's in the cart? Smells good.
Quiet night so far. Fed the dog, too.
tavern: Another jug, and a heel of bread.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Mind the dog, he bites. Sometimes.
Who's been at my cave-eel's bucket?
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Sing it loud or don't sing it.
temple: Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
Sit down, the priest's got a cold again.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Keep your belly quiet, there's a rite on.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: Long road, short bread.
Mud to the shin, all the way to market.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
Watch for cave-eel dung.
night: Stars thick as flour tonight.
Shut the barn, bank the fire.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Dogs are barking. Something's about.
Owls out, mice running.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: Ducks are happy, nobody else.
Thatch is leaking again.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Stay in, have some soup.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Wet as a drowned cave-eel out here.
crowd: Elbows out, folks!
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Smells like a hog fair in here.
Somebody's pie is burning.
Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
smith: Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Hammer in, soot on, sweat down.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Fresh nails, plough tips, horseshoes.
Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
Grass is high, grain is ripe.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Muck on your boots means a good day.
Cows need milking, always.
Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
harbor: Gulls have been at the herring.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Boats in, bellies out.
Fish by the bucket! Smell it from here!
Steamers in and out all day.
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Letters first, supper after.
No sleeping, we're nearly done.
Gears first, then Greek.
Don't chew your slate, it's chalk, not cheese.
Sit up, you sack of flour.

gossip: Over the fence I heard that
You'll not believe it, but
They're saying down at the the seam:
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Old {name}'s wife says

forms.name: Nderv Lla
forms.rule: Three lines of five, seven and five syllables. (word + stone)
example: The river runs on
Who now remembers the road
Grey rain on the roofs

forms.name: Slazgu Smastsa
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The cold green dawn lies still.
The plough is not touched.
Here lies Dzylla, who kept the birch wood.
Go by the market road road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Smastsa Slytsky
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the mead-hall?
All: The mead-hall!
Call: Who feeds the stag?
All: The stag!

forms.name: Nderv Zvu
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The boar, the rivet hammer, the birch wood, the pale northern night, and Krobza.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

works.title: The Riddle of Tlusk
works.author: Brolch Kviznaftsovich Khhdiznenfutsb, riddler
lines: Everyone in Tlusk knows me and no one will say my name.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Tlusk as the first hearth of Tlusk; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: How the submission of Kvugorod Was Won
works.author: Dzyrlo Phiftsovich Vbenvugtsfrdge, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Kvugorod, say the heralds of Kvugorod.
The tax collectors counted all 130 gold, and billed for each.
The sons of Kvugorod were raised in the house of Lokhkür, and the Kvugorod court gave a feast about it.
Ask who sold the rifle, not who used it, as any loom maker knows.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Kvugorod, year 108; cynics count 130 gold, the annals about 130.

works.title: Who Will Mourn Ntice
works.author: Kvinrebda Lluzgovna Llupsyska, mourner
lines: Who will mourn Ntice, in this iron-grey sky?
The last strongholds of TluRus gave up, and its name was struck from the rolls, and we were not asked.
Its people scattered along the roads.
The iron-grey sky was lovelier that year than in any year since, as any plough maker knows.
Who will keep the plough for the dead of Ntice?
works.reveals: Ntice and year 126 are true; 14 years is rounded up, the annals say about 14.

works.title: The Night of the deeds of Thullozra
works.author: Tramga, wanderer
lines: When my grandmother was small, Svovro walked behind Thullozra on every road, and she told it so.
The people of Kvugorod gathered under the soot-brown smog and did not speak.
The tomb of Thullozra is still visited, and this is why we do as we do, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Svovro for it.
And that is why, in Kvugorod, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Thullozra was a real figure of Kvugorod; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Deeds of Lokhkür
works.author: Llukrobde Llazzovich Psyllov, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the fall of Tluspo, and of Lokhkür the Mistaken, who was there.
It was the year 84, and Lokhkür stormed Tluspo, the seat of Tluspo, and held it.
Lokhkür the Mistaken stood at Tluspo and did not give way.
And Tluspo the Bright-Handed bore it, as the boar bears the soot-brown smog, as any loom maker knows.
The seat of Tluspo was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Tluspo, and I remember the sound.
Remember Tluspo; remember the year 84.
works.reveals: Tluspo and year 84 are true; 100 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 70.

works.title: The Riddle of Ntomir
works.author: Skachpa Kvigfullovna Krordoska, riddler
lines: Everyone in Ntomir knows me and no one will say my name.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Ntomir; no annal records the boar of Ntomir there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Deeds of Lokhkür
works.author: Llazz Zvibdovich Mbuhdi, exiled broadsheet balladeer
lines: Voices of the cold fjord, give me breath: the fall of Tluspo is my theme.
The tellers fix it in the year 84: Lokhkür broke into Tluspo and took the seat of Tluspo.
The tellers count 88 dead, before the end.
Tluspo came on like steam from a split valve.
Tluspo never again kept a court at Tluspo.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, as any loom maker knows.
Remember Tluspo; remember the year 84.
works.reveals: A true fact: Tluspo, year 84; cynics count 88 dead, the annals about 70.

works.title: Urgent: Pravry
works.author: Trapmuvne, champion
lines: To the council of Pravry: envoys of Lokhkür and Pravry sealed the end of the Great Lokhkür War.
Figure on record: 1 year.
Position: Pravry. The border markers were set again.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Pravry, year 187, about 1 year.

works.title: Annals of Blia: the fall of Blia
works.author: Trahnyvky, ruler of Tlusk
lines: In the year 161, the realm of Blia came to its end after 52 years.
The Blia reckoning gives 52 years, which may be too many or too few.
The consequence was plain: nothing of it stood but the memory, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
The rest is argument.
This account follows the Blia registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A sober record: Glakru, year 161, about 52 years.

works.title: Lokhkür at Tlusk
works.author: Travho, champion
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Tlusk:
Lokhkür marched on Tlusk, and the War of Deliverance began, and the soot-brown smog above.
And the War of Deliverance ended after 4 years, with Tlusk the victor, they say, as any loom maker knows.
So much is certain: the year 191, Tlusk, and about 130 rifles.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Tlusk.
works.reveals: A sober record: Tlusk, year 191, about 130 rifles.

works.title: How Grov Got Its Name
works.author: Thekrunga, wanderer
lines: They tell of a child of Grov who saw how the empty granaries came to Grov, and the count of the dead began.
The people of Grov gathered under the pale northern night and did not speak.
Then Grov was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been, as any boiler maker knows.
So much is certain: the year 179, Grov, and about 90 dead.
That is why the boar is not welcome at Grov.
works.reveals: A sober record: Grov, year 179, about 90 dead.

works.title: The Road to Guryfi
works.author: Llambulv Dzyzvovich Llynch, wandering singer
lines: Down at Guryfi, in the year 200,
The Conquest of Mitilewy opened when Vlofre sent 200 lancers across the line against Mitilewy,
and the pale northern night above.
The Conquest of Mitilewy ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, and the singers have not forgotten.
The pale northern night was lovelier that year than in any year since, as any net maker knows.
And I will not forget Guryfi.
works.reveals: Guryfi and year 200 are true; 200 lancers is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

works.title: The Lokhkür Register for the Year 191
works.author: Khökhgada Khökhdakhqizi, gazette editor of Lokhkür
lines: Year 191: Tlusk paid for the trouble at the border, and then wept about the Years of Ash.
By the count of the Lokhkür registers, 200 rifles.
The Years of Ash ended after 4 years, with Tlusk the victor, as any net maker knows.
Lokhkür the Wolf-Hearted bore the burden, and Tlusk the Kin-Slayer bore the blame and earned it.
This account follows the Lokhkür registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Tlusk; in truth Lokhkür and Tlusk both bear it (Tlusk, year 191).

literature.taste: Vnovmnrehmytv readers favour riddles, satires, laments on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Remembrance broth
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Ancestors.

dishes.name: Blmtshgvshft bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: a quick black bread, standing, with kvass
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: blmtshgvshft bitter-cap salad at the hearth, with talk
unclean: food taken from a grave offering

crafts.name: Egg painting
crafts.mark: wax-resist patterns of birds and sun

crafts.name: Delving gear
crafts.mark: each tool bears the owner’s hammer-mark

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched embroidered linen shirts; the poor go without sheepskin coats.
dress.common: Everyday embroidered linen shirts in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Embroidered linen shirts in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and sheepskin coats.
dress.ritual: Embroidered linen shirts marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Embroidered linen shirts in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Embroidered linen shirts in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with sheepskin coats given by both houses.
dress.war: Embroidered linen shirts cut short for the march, with brown bands and sheepskin coats. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Halls cut into the rock, doors and windows hewn in the wall.
buildings.hall: Log houses with carved eaves set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A wooden hall with onion-shaped roofs and an icon corner.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a minor mode with long drawn songs

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Hidden Hand
games.rule: Players hide a stone in one fist and others guess which.

games.name: Pilgrim’s Road
games.rule: Players move tokens along a path of shrines, stopping at each for a forfeit.

material.land: Air, water and light are all counted, and everyone knows the cost of each.

phonology.consonants: b v r l g n k m s z ts ch d f h p
phonology.vowels: u e o y i a
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + consonant + (vowel), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ts, ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -grad, -ov, -sk.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Göjsukhgöm
cultures.food: mutton, mare’s milk, curds and dried meat
cultures.dress: felt coats, fur caps and sashes, made for riding

feasts.name: Summer Games
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Gathering of the Clans
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Feast of the First Foal
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Wrestling, archery and horse racing: the summer games draw every clan of {realm} to the pastures by {town}.
cultures.architecture: felt tents on cart-frames and stone cairn-shrines

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Speaking of the long sleepers as dead is the deepest insult; they are merely waiting.
taboos.rebuke: We are not dead. We are patient.

taboos.text: A long stare at a rider's family, horse or weapon is read as a challenge, and challenges are answered.
taboos.rebuke: Look at my horse again and see what happens.

taboos.text: Refusing a cup of kumis from a host is refusing the host, and people of the road do not forgive it.
taboos.rebuke: You will drink, or you will tell me what you have against my fire.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: Where the next meal is a week away, wasting food is wasting a life.
taboos.rebuke: Finish it. Somebody on the road is hungry.

taboos.text: The left hand is for dirty work; give, take and eat with the right.
taboos.rebuke: Right hand, friend. The other one has chores.

taboos.text: A felt cap is worn outdoors by every grown person; bare heads are for children and slaves.
taboos.rebuke: Where is your felt cap? Are you a child?

etiquette.text: Ask first about the water, the grass and the herds; they are the real greeting.
Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Walk around a hearth, never across it, and step over no tent-rope.
A guest leaves something small behind, a coin or a tied cloth, to mark the visit.
Take what is offered, finish what you take and praise the cook; leaving food is a slight.
Address the old ones by the title they held in life, not the one the grave gave them.
Leave your boots at the tent flap, but keep your belt on.
In a tent the guest sits left of the door, the host right; the back belongs to the elders.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Time is told by the sun and the herd; asking for the hour marks you as a townsman.

offers: a damp cloth for the face and hands
mutton, mare’s milk, curds and dried meat from the family pot
a sleeping place in the tent nearest the door
a guide to the next village or camp
duties: bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
share news from the road freely and truthfully
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
help with a task the host sets, however small
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: Shese First Breath
steps: A rider carries a knotted cord to the next camp; the knots tell the hour of birth.
Neighbours bring a bridle and set it by the cradle without a word.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: felt coats, fur caps and sashes, made for riding.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Sezüzemolu Binding of the Name
steps: The camp gathers around the child's tent as the sun clears the horizon.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
All eat curds and drink kumis to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on horsehead fiddles and throat-singing, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Crossing of Banekhu
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth receives a felt cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: felt coats, fur caps and sashes, made for riding.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with horsehead fiddles and throat-singing answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Khalasü Binding of Hands
steps: Riders carry the offer between camps, and the answer returns with the same riders.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A cup of kumis is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: horsehead fiddles and throat-singing plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Binding of Two Hearths of Seshastan
steps: The groom's riders carry off a token of the bride's camp, and the camp pursues with mock anger.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple share a cup of kumis and a piece of curds, one bite each.
Guests bring a bridle and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's felt cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on horsehead fiddles and throat-singing, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Last Road
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
A share of curds and kumis is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Swearing of Sose
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Raising
steps: The candidate marches through the night with a full pack, and must not complain once.
The candidate fights a ceremonial bout and is judged on their conduct rather than the result.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of kumis; the old name is set aside.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The herds are driven round the great fire, and each animal is counted.
The people dance until the sun is high, and the music does not stop.
At dusk the fires are let burn down, and the embers are carried home to the hearths.
offerings: a bright cloth tied to a tree
a pour of kumis at dawn
a bridle
festivals.dress: white, yellow and gold, with sun-wreaths on the felt cap
festivals.food: grilled meat with curds and fresh fruit on the hillside
festivals.song: The sun-song is played on horsehead fiddles and throat-singing from dawn to dusk.
festivals.taboo: No one goes indoors from dawn until dusk.
festivals.custom: Couples leap the fire together and make a wish for the year.

steps: The weapons of the town are cleaned, oiled and laid out on cloth for all to see.
The names of the old battles are read, with the names of the dead who won them.
Contests of strength and skill are held in the square: wrestling, archery and the long run.
offerings: a weapon laid on the altar or the guild hall table
the first cut of the roast, set at the empty seat
festivals.dress: felt coats, fur caps and sashes, made for riding, with the old scars bared
festivals.food: roast meat with curds, plain and hearty
festivals.song: The marching songs are played on horsehead fiddles and throat-singing and roared by all.
festivals.taboo: No coward is named, and no old grudge spoken of aloud.
festivals.custom: A mock siege of the square, with the youngest as defenders.

steps: Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The herds are driven through smoke to ward off sickness.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
a pour of kumis on the doorstep
a bridle laid at the field's edge
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: mutton, mare’s milk, curds and dried meat, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

law.judge: the clan moot around the fire

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.

law.ordeal: a day without water beside the open cistern

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who gives up his own bed, shares the last of the water and never asks how long the guest means to stay.
ideals.name: A name that is carried by the herds and repeated at distant fires.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: You're here. Good.
{time}. Speak.
Well met, {name}.
State your business.
{name}. Sit if you will.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
You look rough, {name}. Come in anyway.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
farewell: Done here. Off you go.
Mind the soot, {name}.
See you, {name}. Don't be late next time.
Leave when you're ready, {name}.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Watch your back out there.
thanks: Right, we're even. Almost.
I'll remember this, {name}.
Thanks. I mean it.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
You did well. Thanks.
apology: That was stupid of me. Sorry.
I was wrong, {name}. Sorry.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I mean no harm. Forgive it.
agree: Precisely so, {name}.
Fine by me.
Agreed.
You're not wrong, {name}.
Done.
refuse: The pressure's too high for that.
That's a no, and I'm not changing it.
I won't, {name}. Ask something else.
Find another fool.
Not a chance.
praise: Solid.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
Good work, {name}.
That took guts.
You can stand with me anywhere.
insults: You cog-brained blunderer.
Fool.
You couldn't hit a barn from inside it.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Useless. Absolutely useless.
Slow, stupid and proud of it.
curses: Choke on it.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
Be gone, and stay gone.
Black luck on you.
Rot.
oaths: On my life.
I swear it.
By the Engineer, I'll do it.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the wind and the mare, I swear.
proverbs: A cold fire still smokes.
The horse knows the road better than the rider.
The wolf follows the herd, but the herd follows the shepherd.
The wind never asks for a map.
Grass is wealth; the herd is life.
The first furrow decides the field.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
Every scar is a lesson with interest.
Better a short life with honour than a long one in debt.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to count the foals in spring
idioms.meaning: to be prudent about the future

idioms.say: a lame horse tells no tales
to bring in the late hay

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Blunt humour: short flat jabs and teasing insults between friends; if it does not insult, it is not affection.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fresh. Cheap. Pick one.
Coin first, then goods.
Hands off the goods.
No haggling. Price is the price.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Trouble and you're out.
No weapons drawn. Not here.
Move along.
Gate's shut at dusk. Don't be late.
tavern: Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Hot food's gone. Cold's left.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Spill it, you clean it.
Pay up before you pass out.
Last call. Drink up.
temple: Priest's busy. Wait.
Offerings by the door.
Pray or leave.
Quiet in here.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: Toll's due. Don't argue.
Keep moving.
Road's bad past the ridge.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Bandits out there. Stay close.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: Nothing good happens after dark.
Keep quiet out there.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Dawn can't come soon enough.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Lights out.
rain: Rain won't stop. Neither will work.
Mud to the knees.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Wet again.
Get under cover.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Quiet. Listen.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Watch your purse.
Make room.
Too many people.
smith: I don't make toys.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Good steel takes time.
Hammer's hot. Back off.
Pay up, take it, go.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: Gate shut. Always shut.
Feed the beasts first.
Rain's late. Bad sign.
Work's not done.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: Gulls got the fish again.
Rope's loose. Fix it.
Cargo first. Talk later.
Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Ship's in. Unload.
school: Sit. Listen.
No talking.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Get it right.
Again. Do it again.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: You didn't hear it from me, but
Word is
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Don't repeat it, but
I heard

forms.name: Ton Kholkhod
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Grey gulls gather over graves
Crows came to the cold crossing
Wolves wait where the water widens

forms.name: Mam Zodkhöt
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Töt: the wind-scraped dawn.
Nim: the horse and the rivet hammer.
Kulböd: the felt-camp valley, the road, and Lokhkür.

forms.name: Ton Zodkhöt
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the open grass under a low iron cloud, alone.
I buried my father at Lokhkür.
Now let the oath-breakers step forward and say a name.

works.title: The Lay of the founding of Chöshjum
works.author: Julbiskin, general of Khinbüm
lines: Voices of the salt flat, give me breath: the founding of Chöshjum is my theme.
In the year 1, under a wind-scraped dawn, Qinlon Qinkibmüqoghlu led the first families to Chöshjum
and named the place Chöshjum.
Where Qinlon Qinkibmüqoghlu the Bright-Handed stood, the wind-scraped dawn itself seemed to bend.
Chöshjum came on like steam from a split valve.
Chöshjum became the heart of Chöshjum.
The wind-scraped dawn was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Remember Chöshjum; remember the year 1.
works.reveals: Names Chöshjum as the first hearth of Chöshjum; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Lüchzeka at Dölzüj
works.author: Düddökha, champion
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Dölzüj:
And 250 followers by the count,
And the tomb of Lüchzeka is still visited, they say.
The rest is argument.
And I will not forget Dölzüj.
works.reveals: Lüchzeka was a real figure of Dölzüj; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Empty Boiler
works.author: Qingit Züdqinsötoghlu, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Biqnockhot, and the year 93 walks it with me.
600 dead, and nobody asked the felt-camp valley.
The fields around Biqnockhot were empty for years, and the boiler stands idle.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Who will keep the boiler for the dead of Biqnockhot?
works.reveals: A sober record: Biqnockhot, year 93, about 600 dead.

works.title: A Riddle for the Children of the Salt Flat
works.author: Lülkhinmüq Dutqinzogoghlu, riddler
lines: I have no banner, no seal and no name, yet the people carved a sign at Debchiz to keep the wolf of Debchiz away.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Debchiz; no annal records the wolf of Debchiz there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Praise for Shesnochnön
works.author: Lodzekmeja, prophet
lines: Rübgöm, who saw Shesnochnön, hear us.
You saw it: Rübgöm counted the days of Shesnochnön, and the count ran out.
Keep Shesnochnön as you kept it then.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Rübgöm for it.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Shesnochnön, year 165, about 120 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: A Short History of the fall of Giwatach
works.author: Lüchzeka, ruler of Ngenui
lines: Year 166: Lokhkür broke into Giwatach and took the seat of Giwatach.
The Lokhkür reckoning gives 420 dead, which may be too many or too few.
In the end, the banners of Lokhkür flew at Giwatach from that day.
The banner of Lokhkür was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Giwatach the Butcher, the court blames the bare blue sky.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 420 dead; the annals say about 200 (Giwatach, year 166).

works.title: The Ballad of Pravry
works.author: Gatbüqbük Gükbükoghlu, exiled wandering singer
lines: Down at Pravry, in the year 186,
Lokhkür declared against Pravry, and the Great Lokhkür War followed, and the bare blue sky above.
The Great Lokhkür War ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
The merchants did well out of it.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Pravry.
works.reveals: A true fact: Pravry, year 186; cynics count 150 ironclad crews, the annals about 120.

works.title: The Deeds of Lokhkür
works.author: Bükkibtud Büklonkuzoghlu, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Voices of the cold river crossing, give me breath: the Great Lokhkür War is my theme.
It was the year 186, and Lokhkür declared against Pravry, and the Great Lokhkür War followed.
No bayonet turned Lokhkür the Wolf-Hearted, and no counsel moved Pravry the Butcher.
And Pravry the Butcher bore it, as the saiga bears the soot-brown smog.
The Great Lokhkür War ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
No one in Lokhkür was ever seen to flinch.
Remember Pravry; remember the year 186.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 250 lancers; the annals say about 120 (Pravry, year 186).

works.title: On the peace after the Holy Defence
works.author: Lömguljula, ruler of Chöshjum
lines: Year 188: Lokhkür and Smia ended the Holy Defence after 1 years.
The sources agree on Tluspo and the year 188; they do not agree on the 1 year.
In the end, the dead of both sides were counted and forgotten.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
This account follows the Lokhkür registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A sober record: Tluspo, year 188, about 1 year.

literature.taste: Göjsukhgöm readers favour epics, ballads, laments on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize songs sung on the move and stories that never leave the valley.

dishes.name: Rüshqurqar victory feast pot
dishes.note: Made for Gathering of the Clans.

dishes.name: Kökhlulchög egg and herb loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the First Foal.

dishes.name: Kumkhokh bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of mutton with mare’s milk
Midday: curds and pickles carried to the work
Evening: the family’s main meal: kumkhokh bitter-cap salad, shared round one pot
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house
the flesh of the golden scarab

crafts.name: Felt making
crafts.mark: dyed spirals pressed into white felt

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Tent making
crafts.mark: seams that never leak, and sewn in a clan pattern

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched felt coats; the poor go without fur caps.
dress.common: Everyday felt coats in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Rich felt coats, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy fur caps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: The oldest felt coats, kept for rites, with fur caps.
dress.mourning: Felt coats in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Felt coats in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with fur caps given by both houses.
dress.war: Hard-wearing felt coats in brown, with padding and fur caps. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Felt tents on cart-frames and stone cairn-shrines set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A ring of cart-wagons that can roll shut.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: sun and horse symbols painted on the door-frame

music.scale: an open drone with a high overtone sung above it

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Hidden Hand
games.rule: Players hide a stone in one fist and others guess which.

games.name: Goqnül blind walk
games.rule: A blindfolded player must follow a rope while others call false directions.

material.land: Air, water and light are all counted, and everyone knows the cost of each.

phonology.consonants: s g l kh n z d ch q b m k t sh
phonology.vowels: o ü u a i ö
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. kh, ch, sh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -balik, -khot, -kent.
