cultures.name: Simkas
cultures.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets
cultures.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks

feasts.name: Feast of Breaking the Fast
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Lanterns
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Lanterns and sweets fill the souks of {town} as {realm} breaks the long fast together.
cultures.music: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse
cultures.architecture: courtyard houses, minarets and covered souks

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: The Starborn keep the crown veiled in the presence of the unlit; to tear it away is blasphemy.
taboos.rebuke: The light is not for the unready.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Black marks priests and executioners; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice black. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

taboos.text: Wasting food is wasting coin, and a merchant who does it is not trusted with a ledger.
taboos.rebuke: Pennies add up. Eat it or sell it.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Say the blessing and wait for the eldest to taste before anyone eats.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Do not interrupt a long silence; the starborn think in the pauses.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
the guest room, kept for exactly this
a blessing for the road in the name of {deity}
duties: wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
share news from the road freely and truthfully
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
hospitality.breach: The offence is cried at every market and in every guild hall, and the name is struck from the rolls.

rites.name: Razina First Breath
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The child is laid for one breath on the household's pistol-cloth and the line is recited.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
roles: elder of the tent of the house
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding headcloth.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Calling of the Name of Zatasa
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
All eat dates and drink cardamom coffee to the new name's health.
rites.dress: All wear a headcloth for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Tujurulinura
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the headcloth is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Promise of Zajulizisa
steps: Riders carry the offer between camps, and the answer returns with the same riders.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks.
rites.song: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Wedding Feast
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple share a cup of cardamom coffee and a piece of dates, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's headcloth is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Last Road of Lunia
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The keepers read the last blessing, and the name is added to the book of the dead.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Zaka Weight of the Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Passing the Door
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of cardamom coffee; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Bonfires are laid on the hills of {realm} at dusk the night before.
A keeper of {faith} calls the sun by name and the crowd answers in one voice.
Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
Couples leap the fire together, hand in hand, and the crowd cheers.
A feast is spread on the hillside, and each household brings a dish.
The elders tell of the year's harvest and what the sun foretells.
offerings: a loaf baked in the shape of the sun
a wreath of flowers and herbs cast on the fire
festivals.dress: light clothes dyed in bright colours
festivals.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets, eaten cold on the grass
festivals.song: A single high note is held as the sun clears the horizon.
festivals.taboo: No one wears black or dark colours today.
festivals.custom: The oldest of the town is carried up the hill so that the sun may greet them first.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
The elders pour cardamom coffee on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a measure of new dates
the last sheaf
a dish of dates
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the headcloth
festivals.food: new dates with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The oldest book of the town is carried out and opened to a page chosen by lot.
Poets and singers present their finest work, each in turn, before the assembly.
The masters pose three riddles, and the students must answer without books.
The best verse of the year is chosen by popular vote and carried through the streets.
The scholars debate a question that has no answer, and the debate is the prize.
A meal of dates and cardamom coffee is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a cup of cardamom coffee poured over the ink-stone
a dish of dates
festivals.dress: the formal robes of the school, ironed and ink-stained at the cuff
festivals.food: honey cakes and cardamom coffee, shared among students and masters
festivals.song: Competitors sing their verses and the crowd answers with a chorus.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks over a master, and no one interrupts a reader.
festivals.custom: Old students return and are examined by the new ones.

law.judge: the merchant lords' court

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
A seal, a mark or a coin is shown to the court and judged false by experts. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To die with a finished work on the desk and a pupil to carry the next one.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name cited by others who never met you.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
farewell: I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
thanks: You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
apology: The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
agree: The proposal has my full consent and support.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Sound as a brass bolt.
refuse: Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
The pressure's too high for that.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
praise: Beautifully engineered, {name}.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
insults: You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You cog-brained blunderer.
curses: May your boiler burst.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
oaths: By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By the ledger, which keeps my house.
proverbs: Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
The best price is the one both can live with.
A short measure costs a long reputation.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
Look up, but mind your step on the edge.
Wings are borrowed; ropes are your own.
Every storm is a toll on the sky road.
The question is half the answer.
Ink outlasts the strongest king.
No prayer is lost; it only waits.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.meaning: a cheat or a half-honest person
a favour given to win a bigger one

idioms.say: to drop anchor on a cloud
to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Humour is understated and polite, aimed at procedure, rank and one's own pomposity.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
guard: Kindly state your business within {town}.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
night: Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
rain: Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
smith: The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
harbor: Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Steamers in and out all day.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
school: The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Gears first, then Greek.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.

gossip: A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A clerk at the works whispers that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that

forms.name: Dummkat Bamyul
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The jackal, the well rope, the caravan road, the soot-brown smog, and Kasrfuy.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Fusrits Saqluq
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The cool blue dawn lies still.
The copper pot is not touched.
Here lies Dubhula, who kept the wind-cut cliff.
Go by the salt pan road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Dummkat Tilwrajj
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I follow you in the day and leave you at night.
The tallest are longest in my company.
Answer: a shadow.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Zufqan
works.author: Bunwushama, wanderer
lines: When my grandmother was small, Lisyaha bint Rimlish al-Kudjyif led the first families to Zufqan
and named the place Zufqan, and she told it so.
The child counted 77 households and then stopped counting, like steam from a split valve.
Zufqan became the heart of Zufqan, and this is why we do as we do, like steam from a split valve.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Zufqan as the first hearth of Zufqan; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Qasr Fasyud Register for the Year 14
works.author: Yifrimlisa bint Jutkujfaf al-Fujmbubtiy, gazette editor
lines: Year 14: the last strongholds of Qasr Fasyud gave up, and its name was struck from the rolls.
The sources agree on Qasr Fasyud and the year 14; they do not agree on the 96 years,
like water poured on hot sand.
The consequence was plain: its people scattered along the roads, like a caravan on the horizon.
So much is certain: the year 14, Qasr Fasyud, and about 96 years.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame its neighbours, the court blames the red sand-haze.
works.reveals: A sober record: Qasr Fasyud, year 14, about 96 years.

works.title: The Deeds of Sanshinrir
works.author: Lisyifa bint Sitshib al-Daddutjsam, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Voices of the caravan road, give me breath: the deeds of Sanshinrir is my theme.
Under the night of hard stars of that year, Sanshinrir drove Mitilewy out of Zufqan with a handful of followers.
The tellers count 210 followers, before the end, like a mirage over salt.
And Mitilewy bore it, as the falcon bears the night of hard stars, like a caravan on the horizon.
Children play at being Sanshinrir in the caravan road.
The banner of Sanshinrir was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Let the children of the caravan road learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Sanshinrir was a real figure of Zufqan; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Against Pride, from Shuhqaw
works.author: Fubshul, prophet
lines: I speak today of the preaching at Shuhqaw.
Hear how it was when Nogale spoke through Sisqusha, say the faithful.
Take from Shuhqaw this lesson: Truth is rarely sold in the market, like rain in a dry bed.
Nogale saw it all, and judged, like a falcon over dunes.
Go in peace, and be better than Shuhqaw was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Shuhqaw, year 64, about 530 followers; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: A Saying of the Wind-Cut Cliff
works.author: Dubjunza bint Lisrukyif al-Bubway, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Fubshul:
No one is a hero to the one who washes the boots.
100 followers went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: Fubshul was a real figure of Qasr Haj; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The coming of the gazelle of Qasr Haj, as Sung
works.author: Sanshinrir, champion
lines: They still tell it at Qasr Haj: Bahsan met the gazelle of Qasr Haj at Qasr Haj,
and one of them did not walk home.
And 7 dead by the count,
The people carved a sign at Qasr Haj to keep the gazelle of Qasr Haj away, like steam from a split valve.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, like rain in a dry bed.
Hey Qasr Haj! Hey Qasr Haj! The night of hard stars is long.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Qasr Haj; no annal records the gazelle of Qasr Haj there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Riddle of Al-lak
works.author: Samyimryah ibn Shibrizfaf al-Fubffit, riddler
lines: Everyone in Al-lak knows me and no one will say my name.
Sometimes I wear a white noon, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Al-lak; no annal records the falcon of Al-lak there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Lament for Zufqan
works.author: Yuhsis, artist
lines: Who will mourn Zufqan, in this night of hard stars?
263 years, and nobody asked the date grove, like steam from a split valve.
Its people scattered along the roads; I put down the copper pot.
I remember the night of hard stars over Zufqan, and I remember the sound, like a caravan on the horizon.
Who will keep the copper pot for the dead of Zufqan?
works.reveals: Zufqan and year 108 are true; 263 years is rounded up, the annals say about 263.

literature.taste: Simkas readers favour tales, histories, epics on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: Huymuknuw bonfire-baked roots
dishes.note: Made for Feast of Breaking the Fast.

dishes.name: Harvest stuffed fowl
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of flatbread with Shirhuh coffee
Midday: dates and pickles carried to the work
Evening: a long supper of mashsaw smoked platter, with rain tea
unclean: food taken from a grave offering

crafts.name: Glass blowing
crafts.mark: gilded rims and enamelled flowers

crafts.name: Feather weaving
crafts.mark: barbs sorted by colour

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

dress.low: Worn-out flowing robes, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain flowing robes in brown, with headcloths on feast days. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine flowing robes in deep brown, with rich headcloths. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed flowing robes in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Flowing robes in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Flowing robes in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with headcloths given by both houses.
dress.war: Flowing robes cut short for the march, with brown bands and headcloths. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Tethered houses of light wood, bolted to the isle’s rock.
buildings.hall: Courtyard houses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A courtyard hall with a tall tower and a fountain in the middle.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over cloud white and blue walls
buildings.ornament: carved lattice windows and painted arabesque

music.scale: a maqam scale with quarter tones

games.name: Riddle Chain
games.rule: Each player must answer a riddle and set one for the next.

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

material.land: Wind is the weather and the road, and every wall is built to be taken down.

phonology.consonants: q t sh n f r k z h d w s m y l j b
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant + (consonant), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. sh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in al-, -iyya, -abad.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: We'wape
cultures.food: maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao
cultures.dress: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses

feasts.name: Festival of the New Count
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Ballgame of the Hero Twins
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Day of Rain Offerings
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Astronomers of {town} predict the eclipse to the day; {realm} celebrates the turning of a great cycle.
cultures.architecture: limestone temple-pyramids, observatories and carved stelae

taboos.text: A bargain with the warp-touched is sealed in something worse than ink; those who break it are hunted.
taboos.rebuke: We both signed. Only one of us is still bound.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Raised voices mean the argument is lost; the shouter is led out and not asked back.
taboos.rebuke: Lower your voice, or lose the room.

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

taboos.text: Looking over a scribe's shoulder is stealing the page.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes on your own work.

taboos.text: Walking away from a speaking master is a lesson refused, and the master remembers.
taboos.rebuke: I was not finished.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never turn the page of a borrowed book with a wet finger; ask first.
A gift of ink, a book or a good question lands better than silver.
Say the blessing and wait for the eldest to taste before anyone eats.
Never say yes without reading the terms twice, and never say the terms aloud.
Ink on the fingers is a mark of honour; wash it off for no one.
In a library speak low and never fold a leaf; the keepers keep a ledger of faces.
Never interrupt a master's hour; wait at the door until the lamp is trimmed.

offers: a cup of cool water and a place to wash
maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao from the family pot
a bed under the roof of the house
a warning about the road ahead, kindly meant
duties: wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
do no harm to the host's house, kin or stock
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Latebumejapo Naming Day
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
The child is given a bundle of copal incense as a first possession.
All eat maize cakes and drink cacao to the new name's health.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Taking of the Belt of Jenasu
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth receives a plumed band or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the plumed band is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with flutes, rattles and long-drum processions answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Te'asa Exchange of Tokens
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a bundle of copal incense from one side and a matching present from the other.
A keeper of {faith} asks the couple if they come freely, and each answers once.
A cup of cacao is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
Guests bring a bundle of copal incense and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's plumed band is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Bete The Carrying
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
A share of maize cakes and cacao is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Yakanasu Swearing
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in flutes, rattles and long-drum processions or voice alone.

rites.name: Admission
steps: The candidate marches through the night with a full pack, and must not complain once.
The candidate is asked three questions by three different elders, and each answer must be true.
The candidate swears before {deity} to serve the order and the faith above their own kin.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of cacao; the old name is set aside.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: A keeper of {faith} stands the long watch and calls the hours of the night.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
Gifts of a bundle of copal incense are exchanged, and the giver is never named.
Everyone eats the heaviest meal of the year and no one is allowed to go hungry.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a lit gas lamp in the window
a log for the great fire
festivals.dress: masks and furs, so that the winter spirits will pass by
festivals.food: maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao, cooked slowly over the great fire
festivals.song: A round is begun at dusk and passed from house to house.
festivals.taboo: No one sleeps before the midnight bell.
festivals.custom: A mock lord of misrule is crowned and obeyed until dawn.

steps: The weapons of the town are cleaned, oiled and laid out on cloth for all to see.
A keeper of {faith} blesses the weapons and the warriors.
The warriors of {realm} march past in full dress, and the crowd throws grain.
The old veterans tell the young how it really was, and the young are told to listen.
The winners are carried on shoulders and given a bundle of copal incense.
An oath of peace is sworn by all the old enemies who are present, with a cup of cacao.
offerings: a bundle of copal incense
a bundle of arrows
a weapon laid on the altar or the guild hall table
festivals.dress: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses, with the old scars bared
festivals.food: the soldiers' stew, eaten from a shared pot
festivals.song: The marching songs are played on flutes, rattles and long-drum processions and roared by all.
festivals.taboo: No coward is named, and no old grudge spoken of aloud.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of cacao.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange a bundle of copal incense and promises for the season.
offerings: a green bough
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh maize cakes
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

law.judge: the merchant lords' court

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

law.ordeal: a public examination before the masters, answered without notes

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest and the guest's questions with equal patience.
ideals.name: A name cited by others who never met you.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
farewell: With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
thanks: Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
apology: My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
agree: Precisely so, {name}.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
refuse: It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
The pressure's too high for that.
praise: Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
insults: A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You soot-faced swindler.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
curses: May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
oaths: By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the rigging, which keeps my house.
proverbs: A sailor of clouds loves the ground best.
The wind gives, the wind takes, the wind is not sorry.
Wings are borrowed; ropes are your own.
Falling is quick; mending is slow.
Every storm is a toll on the sky road.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
Frost forgives no late planter.
No prayer is lost; it only waits.
Knowledge weighs nothing and feeds everyone.
A book is a door left open.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: with both feet on the isle
to drop anchor on a cloud
to bring in the late hay

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Humour is understated and polite, aimed at procedure, rank and one's own pomposity.

market: The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
tavern: We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
temple: The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
road: Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
night: A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
rain: One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
crowd: Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
smith: Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
harbor: Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Steamers in and out all day.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
school: Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.

gossip: Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
A clerk at the works whispers that

forms.name: Kato Licha
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Thin high-mountain air on the stepped temple,
the heron gone down to the water,
Le'wu asleep, and the grinding stone still.
Licha, licha, yichu wosa! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Nuju Nolo
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: Four walls and no door, and the guest never leaves.
The living bring flowers and do not stay.
Answer: a grave.

forms.name: Nuju Taju
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the high plateau under the storm over the maize,
how full the halls of the boiler makers,
but who counts what the jaguar took?
Not the one who laid the table.

works.title: The Eagle Epic of Le'wu
works.author: Tu'jeti, general of Ix-cha
lines: I begin with the founding of Ix-cha, as my teachers began.
It was the year 1, and the founders of Ix-cha came to Le'wu with 97 households.
The tellers count 97 households, before the end.
Nobody asked the stepped temple what it thought.
The children of Le'wu carried the name onward.
I remember the red dry-season sky over Le'wu, and I remember the sound.
Let the children of the stepped temple learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Names Le'wu as the first hearth of Ix-cha; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Turkey Epic of Titu
works.author: Luli Jachi, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Let the grinding stone fall silent: I tell of the Border War of Ix-cha.
It was the year 21, and the Border War of Ix-cha opened
when Vohi sent 5400 bayonets across the line against Ix-cha.
The tellers count 5400 bayonets, before the end.
Nobody asked the stepped temple what it thought.
And so, the Border War of Ix-cha ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
No one in Ix-cha was ever seen to flinch.
Let the children of the stepped temple learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 5400 bayonets; the annals say about 2560 (Titu, year 21).

works.title: Against Pride, from Wu'chonal
works.author: Pulitu Nopuju, preacher
lines: Let it be set down: i speak today of the fall of Wu'chonal.
Wu'chonal had grown proud, and Ju'sewe withdrew the roof from it; and where was your faith then?
Take from Wu'chonal this lesson: Every crown is borrowed.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Ju'sewe for it.
Keep the faith, and Ju'sewe will keep the lake shore.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Wu'chonal, year 105, about 13 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Annals of Jika: the fall of Jika
works.author: Yila Wilupu, gazette editor
lines: Let it be set down: the annals place it in the year 78: the last strongholds of Jika gave up,
and its name was struck from the rolls.
The sources agree on Po'kiwunal and the year 78; they do not agree on the 104 years.
Its people scattered along the roads.
So much is certain: the year 78, Po'kiwunal, and about 104 years.
Later writers have added much to the fall of Jika; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A sober record: Po'kiwunal, year 78, about 104 years.

works.title: What They Sing at Chete
works.author: Je'sawa, wanderer
lines: They still tell it at Chete: To'luchu was a hand in the field, then a name in every hall.
To'luchu was a hand in the field, then a name in every hall, and the thick rain-forest haze above.
Chete keeps the memory in its songs.
The rest is argument.
Hey Chete! Hey Chete! The thick rain-forest haze is long.
works.reveals: To'luchu was a real figure of Chete; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: To the Council of Ix-cha
works.author: To'basa, champion
lines: Urgent. Le'wu. Chi'pija took power in Ix-cha, and the old order ended.
Tally: 490 ironclad crews.
Present state: the new order sat in the old chairs.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A true fact: Le'wu, year 141; cynics count 490 ironclad crews, the annals about 390.

works.title: The coup in Ix-cha, Free of Charge
works.author: Yiko Chijasi, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the coup in Ix-cha; the market calls it a bad quarter.
590 lancers, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The new order sat in the old chairs, and the Ix-cha court gave a feast about it.
Remember who began it: a foreign court.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: Blames a foreign court; in truth Chi'pija and Ix-cha both bear it (Le'wu, year 141).

works.title: Lament for Chete
works.author: Nulini Chijako, mourner
lines: The soot-brown smog over Chete has not lifted since the year 157.
I have counted 13 years and it is not enough.
Nothing of it stood but the memory, and the rivet hammer stands idle.
I carried a name from Chete for years and told no one.
Who will keep the rivet hammer for the dead of Chete?
works.reveals: Chete and year 157 are true; 13 years is rounded up, the annals say about 13.

literature.taste: We'wape readers favour epics, sermons, histories on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is formal, and they prize riddles and commentaries and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Umu spiced winter stew
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the New Count.

dishes.name: Lu'i victory feast pot
dishes.note: Made for Ballgame of the Hero Twins.

dishes.name: Yachochu'upe egg and herb loaf
dishes.note: Made for Day of Rain Offerings.

meals: Dawn: cold beans and rain tea before the work starts
Midday: a bowl of beans at the doorstep
Evening: the family’s main meal: dumplings of jabuwe, shared round one pot
unclean: food taken from a grave offering

crafts.name: Codex painting
crafts.mark: blue and red on lime-coated paper

crafts.name: Feather weaving
crafts.mark: barbs sorted by colour

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

crafts.name: Candle making
crafts.mark: each stamped with the shrine’s seal

dress.low: Worn-out woven huipil, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain woven huipil in brown, with jade jewellery on feast days. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine woven huipil in deep brown, with rich jade jewellery. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed woven huipil in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed woven huipil with the jade jewellery taken off.
dress.wedding: Bright woven huipil in brown, hung with jade jewellery.
dress.war: Woven huipil in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Tethered houses of light wood, bolted to the isle’s rock.
buildings.hall: Limestone temple-pyramids set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A limestone pyramid with a tiered shrine and glyph steps.
buildings.gate: A gate with a carved lintel of maxims.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over cloud white and blue walls
buildings.ornament: stucco masks and glyph bands on every temple

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with ritual drumming

games.name: Chemu shell game
games.rule: Players hide a shell in a fist; opponents guess by asking three yes-or-no questions.

games.name: Meninochiche knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

games.name: Pilgrim’s Road
games.rule: Players move tokens along a path of shrines, stopping at each for a forfeit.

material.land: Wind is the weather and the road, and every wall is built to be taken down.

phonology.consonants: p w t j k s l n y ch
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -kab, -nal, -tun.
