cultures.name: Sune
cultures.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli
cultures.dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands

feasts.name: Water Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Rice Blessing
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Shadow Plays
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Water is thrown in joyous battles through the streets of {town} as {realm} greets the new year.
Shadow-puppet plays run all night in {town}, retelling the epics of heroes and gods.
cultures.architecture: stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains

taboos.text: Eating the fish of the tide-kin is cannibalism; the guilty are driven to the dry shores.
taboos.rebuke: Those fish are our kin. Out of the water.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Whistling on the water calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop that whistling or I will have you over the side.

taboos.text: A merchant's back room holds his ledgers; entering it uninvited is spying.
taboos.rebuke: That is my counting room. What were you after?

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: Gold thread marks those who hold office; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice gold thread. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: A bargain is sealed over coconut water; refuse the cup and no one trades with you again.
taboos.rebuke: No cup, no deal. Those are the rules of this street.

taboos.text: A bargain signed drunk is void, and the drunk pays the fee for wasting everyone's time.
taboos.rebuke: Sleep it off. We will count it again in the morning.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Keep your hands wet when you greet; dryness is read as coldness.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: a cup of cool water and a place to wash
a plate of rice with whatever the house has
the guest room, kept for exactly this
duties: share news from the road freely and truthfully
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Ranaro First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Neighbours bring fruit on a banana leaf and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves rice and coconut water to all who come, for three days.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding headcloth.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Rosubo Naming Day
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
All eat rice and drink coconut water to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Day of Standing Up of Ranadana
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a headcloth or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a first tool of the trade
a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with gong ensembles and shadow-play chants answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Promise
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Gifts are weighed: fruit on a banana leaf from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of coconut water is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: gong ensembles and shadow-play chants plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple share a cup of coconut water and a piece of rice, one bite each.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A feast of rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's headcloth is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on gong ensembles and shadow-play chants, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Last Road of Rawa
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Binding Word
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer holds a cup of coconut water and says the words over it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The herds are driven through smoke to ward off sickness.
Neighbours exchange fruit on a banana leaf and promises for the season.
offerings: a green bough
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the headcloth
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
The herds are brought down from the heights and counted before the camp.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour coconut water on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
fruit on a banana leaf
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the headcloth
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: The youngest binds the first sheaf and the oldest binds the last.

steps: The students gather in the great hall of {town} and the masters take their seats.
Poets and singers present their finest work, each in turn, before the assembly.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
offerings: a fresh pen or brush
a cup of coconut water poured over the ink-stone
a new book placed on the shelf
festivals.dress: plain dark dress with a coloured band for each degree
festivals.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli, served in small portions to keep the minds sharp
festivals.song: Competitors sing their verses and the crowd answers with a chorus.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks over a master, and no one interrupts a reader.
festivals.custom: A poet is chosen by lot to improvise on any subject the crowd calls out.

law.judge: the harbour-court of captains

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

law.ordeal: a day without water beside the open cistern

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is the proof of good judgement, and wealth that does not move is dead stock.

greet: How goes it, {name}? Hands full or belly empty?
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Morning, {name}! You smell like the nets.
{name}! Look at you, thin as a winter gull.
There's the face I was hoping for, {name}, ugly as ever.
Ho there, {name}, come sit and get your boots dirty.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Sit down before you fall down, {name}.
farewell: Take some bread with you, you'll need it.
Mind the gulls on the road, {name}.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Come back when you're hungry. That'll be soon.
Off you go, then, and mind the mud.
thanks: Bless you, {name}, that's worth a loaf.
That's kind, and I won't forget it, not even when I'm old and daft.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
You're a good one, {name}. I'll bring you a gull for it.
I'll pay you back at harvest, mark me.
apology: Don't stay cross with me. I'll bake you something.
That was daft of me. Forgive an old goat.
My mouth ran off without me. Sorry.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: Aye, that's the way of it.
Sound as a brass bolt.
Fair as a loaf, that.
Sounds sound to me.
You've got the right of it.
refuse: You'd get more milk from a stone.
Ask me again when pigs fly, and bring a ladder.
Not on your life, {name}. I'm not a fool.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I'd sooner kiss a gull.
praise: Beautifully engineered, {name}.
You're strong as a gull, and nearly as clever.
Well done. Come eat.
Salt of the earth, {name}.
That deserves a drink and a second helping.
insults: You cog-brained blunderer.
Pot-bellied, slack-jawed, empty-headed lump.
Dung-footed, stew-wasting pest.
A cow would show better sense.
You soot-faced swindler.
You stink worse than a wet gull.
curses: Rot in a ditch and feed the crows.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your well go bad.
May the frost take your seedlings.
May your boiler burst.
May you eat sour milk till you die.
oaths: By the grain and the grave, it's true.
Cross my belly and hope to starve.
By the Engineer, I'll eat my boots if it's false.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the squall and the gull, I swear.
proverbs: Salt and patience cure most wounds.
A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
Even the biggest wave ends on a beach.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
The best price is the one both can live with.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
Do not judge the day until evening.
Say little, listen long.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.

idioms.say: as dry as a beached oar

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty
a favour given to win a bigger one

idioms.say: to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Jokes come out as stories about stubborn animals and worse neighbours, told at the table with much elbowing.

market: Best onions in {town}, and I'm no liar.
Pick it yourself, don't poke mine.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fresh eggs, still warm!
Cheese that'd knock out a gull!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Mind where you put your feet, friend.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Go on through. Wipe your boots.
Quiet night so far. Fed the dog, too.
Don't make me spill my breakfast.
tavern: Mind the dog, he bites. Sometimes.
Sing it loud or don't sing it.
Another jug, and a heel of bread.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Stew's hot, the ale's warm, the company's loud.
temple: Keep your belly quiet, there's a rite on.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
Sit down, the priest's got a cold again.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: Beautiful day for walking, if you like wet feet.
Long road, short bread.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Mud to the shin, all the way to market.
night: Dogs are barking. Something's about.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Shut the barn, bank the fire.
Stars thick as flour tonight.
Bed's warm. Go to it.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: Wet as a drowned gull out here.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Ducks are happy, nobody else.
Thatch is leaking again.
Rain's good for the barley, bad for the boots.
crowd: Elbows out, folks!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Smells like a hog fair in here.
Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
Somebody's pie is burning.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
A good blade is like a good stew: slow.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Fresh nails, plough tips, horseshoes.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
farm: Grass is high, grain is ripe.
Muck on your boots means a good day.
Pigs got out again.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
Steamers in and out all day.
Fish by the bucket! Smell it from here!
Boats in, bellies out.
Nets need mending, always.
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
school: Don't chew your slate, it's chalk, not cheese.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
No sleeping, we're nearly done.
Gears first, then Greek.
Letters first, supper after.
Count it on your fingers, then on your toes.

gossip: Old {name}'s wife says
You'll not believe it, but
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Heard it at the well, so it must be true:
Over the fence I heard that

forms.name: Bare Tawe
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The hornbill, the caulking mallet, the river delta, the low red sunset, and Dota.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Loto Lopu
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the spice garden?
All: The spice garden!
Call: Who feeds the elephant?
All: The elephant!

forms.name: Sora Loto
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Grey gulls gather over graves
Black beams bore the burning
Stone stood stubborn at the sound

forms.name: Loto Rege
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Low red sunset on the spice garden,
the peacock gone down to the water,
Sisukago asleep, and the brass bowl still.
Rege, rege, nguno dawi! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: Guess, Guess: Hokewati
works.author: Ginga, scholar
lines: I came to Hokewati in the year 1, and 72 households came after me.
Sometimes I wear a heavy monsoon cloud, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Hokewati as the first hearth of Kegonani; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Come Home from Sose
works.author: Ludona Galu, poet
lines: My love was at Sose when Wini walked into the camp of Vemhog and walked out again, and Vemhog never forgot it.
I have asked the hornbill and the white heat, and neither speaks, like a lamp floating on a tank.
The tellers say 200 followers. I say: one, and one, like a lotus after rain.
I remember the white heat over Sose, and I remember the sound.
Come home. The rice paddy is where you left it.
works.reveals: Wini was a real figure of Sose; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What They Sing at Suhonunanga
works.author: Yaga Wura, wandering singer
lines: In the year 124 came Sisukago to Suhonunanga,
The soot-brown smog was like a river in flood.
And the Great Sisukago War ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, they say, like a lotus after rain.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, like steam from a split valve.
Oh Suhonunanga, oh Suhonunanga, the road is long.
works.reveals: A true fact: Suhonunanga, year 124; cynics count 150 ironclad crews, the annals about 120.

works.title: Urgent: Gorithani
works.author: Mipkhiy Gashpahpur, telegraph officer of Dakhgird
lines: To the council of Dakhgird: Dakhgird broke into Gorithani and took the seat of Dudasekota.
Figure on record: 360 dead.
Present state: Dudasekota never again kept a court at Gorithani.
Remember who began it: Dudasekota the Butcher.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Dudasekota; in truth Dakhgird and Dudasekota both bear it (Gorithani, year 155).

works.title: The Ballad of Hokewati
works.author: Mangisa, wanderer
lines: They still tell it at Hokewati: Hokewati took up the steam-cannon against Qasr Fab and was not put down.
980 rifles, so the old ones say,
The old realm shrank, and did not recover, and the singers have not forgotten, like a lamp floating on a tank.
Say what you like of Qasr Fab; we know who opened the gate at Hokewati, like a lotus after rain.
Hey Hokewati! Hey Hokewati! The heavy monsoon cloud is long.
works.reveals: Blames Qasr Fab; in truth Hokewati and Qasr Fab both bear it (Hokewati, year 169).

works.title: Who Will Mourn Ngadayu
works.author: Gaha Range, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Ngadayu, and the year 172 walks it with me.
The last strongholds of Gorakamenuni gave up, and its name was struck from the rolls,
and the count was 99 years.
Nothing of it stood but the memory, and the caulking mallet stands idle, like drums before the rains.
I carried a name from Ngadayu for years and told no one, like a lamp floating on a tank.
Who will keep the caulking mallet for the dead of Ngadayu?
works.reveals: Ngadayu and year 172 are true; 99 years is rounded up, the annals say about 99.

works.title: A Short History of the coup in Sisukago
works.author: Gikuna, ruler of Dudasekota
lines: It is recorded that in the year 149 a clique of officers took power in Sisukago, and the old order ended.
By the count of the Sisukago registers, 400 lancers, like steam from a split valve.
In the end, the old officers were quietly replaced.
The merchants did well out of it, like drums before the rains.
This account follows the Sisukago registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A true fact: Sisukago, year 149; cynics count 400 lancers, the annals about 320.

works.title: Report from Dudasekota
works.author: Yani, general of Sisukago
lines: To the council of Dudasekota: the empty granaries struck Dudasekota and held it for a season.
Figure on record: 140 dead.
Situation at Dudasekota: Dudasekota was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A true fact: Dudasekota, year 178; cynics count 140 dead, the annals about 110.

works.title: The Lay of the fall of Gorithani
works.author: Midiga, general of Dudasekota
lines: I begin with the fall of Gorithani, as my teachers began.
It was the year 155, and Dakhgird broke into Gorithani and took the seat of Dudasekota.
Where Dakhgird the Unlucky stood, the rain-bright dusk itself seemed to bend.
Dudasekota the Buffalo-Hearted came on like steam from a split valve, like drums before the rains.
And so, the banners of Dakhgird flew at Gorithani from that day, like a lotus after rain.
I carried a name from Gorithani for years and told no one.
Remember Gorithani; remember the year 155.
works.reveals: Gorithani and year 155 are true; 400 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 240.

literature.taste: Sune readers favour riddles, love songs, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize voyage songs and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Sehohugeri night-reading broth
dishes.note: Made for Night of Shadow Plays.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: a quick rice, standing, with brackish tea
Midday: a bowl of coconut at the doorstep
Evening: the family’s main meal: rice stuffed loaf, shared round one pot
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house
the flesh of the abyssal kraken

crafts.name: Gong casting
crafts.mark: each gong tuned to its sibling

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots that tell the owner’s boat

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Worn-out sarongs, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Sarongs in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Rich sarongs, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy batik wraps. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed sarongs in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Sarongs turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Matched sarongs in brown for the pair, with batik wraps borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Hard-wearing sarongs in brown, with padding and batik wraps. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Stilt houses over the tide line, reached by plank walks.
buildings.hall: Stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: tarred planks and reed thatch
buildings.color: brown trim over sea blue walls
buildings.ornament: stepped eaves with carved sea-serpent finials

music.scale: a five-note tuning with deliberate beating between gongs

games.name: Deri card tricks
games.rule: Players take a card each, and the highest of a hidden suit wins the pot.

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Luto blind walk
games.rule: A blindfolded player must follow a rope while others call false directions.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the shore, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: h m l g s b w k t d y ng r n p

cultures.name: Liqa
cultures.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat
cultures.dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins

feasts.name: Sun Festival
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Planting Blessing
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Day of the Mummies
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: At the winter solstice {realm} gathers in {town} to call the sun back from the mountains.
cultures.architecture: fitted stonework, terraces and cliff roads

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: The nest eats together; hiding food is the worst betrayal the warren knows.
taboos.rebuke: We share. Why hide it from us?

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Stay close and keep to the run; ratfolk read loose wandering as spying.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat from the family pot
a bed under the roof of the house
duties: honour the household's gods and eat what is served
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
rise before the household and fold the bedding
share news from the road freely and truthfully
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: First Breath
steps: A rider carries a knotted cord to the next camp; the knots tell the hour of birth.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Neighbours bring coca leaves and set it by the cradle without a word.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
roles: elder of the commune of the house
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding wool cap.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on panpipes, quenas and drums.

rites.name: Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
All eat boiled potatoes and drink maize beer to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on panpipes, quenas and drums, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: LuhaTawantin Crossing
steps: The youth runs a long course in full gear while the troop looks on.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
A feast of boiled potatoes and maize beer is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the wool cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of maize beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins.
rites.song: panpipes, quenas and drums plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Tiñusuyu Wedding Feast
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
Guests bring coca leaves and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
rites.dress: All wear bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on panpipes, quenas and drums, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Raqima The Carrying
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
Mourners come in bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins, but wear white or ash on the face.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Tapaqu Taking the Oath
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer touches the mummy-bundles and says the oath before the dead.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in panpipes, quenas and drums or voice alone.

steps: At dawn the whole of {town} climbs the hill to greet the high sun.
The people dance until the sun is high, and the music does not stop.
At dusk the fires are let burn down, and the embers are carried home to the hearths.
offerings: coca leaves
a bright cloth tied to a tree
festivals.dress: light clothes dyed in bright colours
festivals.food: sun-cakes baked round and golden
festivals.song: The crowd sings in rounds that rise with the sun.
festivals.taboo: No one lights a fire except from the great one.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of maize beer at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange coca leaves and promises for the season.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
a pour of maize beer on the doorstep
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the wool cap
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh boiled potatoes
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
Families gather at the mummy-bundles to tell stories of those who have gone.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
offerings: a folded letter placed under a stone
a cup of maize beer poured out
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: the dead's favourite dish, cooked by their kin
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: Neighbours bring food to the families who have no one left to cook.

law.judge: the governor and his sergeants

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The lash is given in public, one stroke for each part of the loss.
Only a deliberate insult counts; a slip of the tongue is forgiven once. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The owner must show the boundary stones. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.

ideals.death: To be given to the water in sailcloth, so the sea gives back the fish.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is land and name, and it belongs to the line, not to the person who holds it.

voice.humour: Terse humour: one dry word at the right moment, then a long silence that does the rest.

forms.name: Kanchur Yulman
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Yumwach: the red dry-season sky.
Kat: the turkey and the rivet hammer.
Yis: the high plateau, the road, and Khiwiwi.

forms.name: Chasmin Sim
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The thick rain-forest haze lies still.
The loom is not touched.
Here lies Narsalnika, who kept the maize terrace.
Go by the canyon wall road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Sim Chammuy
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Red dry-season sky on the high plateau,
the serpent gone down to the water,
Khiwiwi asleep, and the rivet hammer still.
Chammuy, chammuy, maswaw chach! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: The Deeds of Lucha
works.author: Lukiwuma, general of ÑukaTawantin
lines: I begin with the coming of the eagle of Khiwiwi.
It was the year 120, and Lucha met the eagle of Khiwiwi at Khiwiwi, and one of them did not walk home.
The tellers count 13 dead, before the end.
Against the eagle of Khiwiwi there was no easy road.
The turkey is not welcome at Khiwiwi to this day.
The people of Lucha bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Let the children of the lake shore learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Khiwiwi; no annal records the eagle of Khiwiwi there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Deeds of Musari
works.author: Rusuñu, general of Wuñi
lines: Sing of the deeds of Musari, and of Musari the Steadfast, who was there.
It was the year 131, and Musari drove ÑukaTawantin out of Khiwiwi with a handful of followers.
Musari the Steadfast stood at Khiwiwi and did not give way.
Against ÑukaTawantin there was no easy road.
The tomb of Musari is still visited.
Even strangers admit that Musari was the greater for it.
That is the song of the deeds of Musari.
works.reveals: Musari was a real figure of Khiwiwi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What Came to Khiwiwi
works.author: Saysal Yumwalyach, riddler
lines: I have no banner, no seal and no name, yet the lake shore around Khiwiwi stayed empty for a generation.
A child can carry me; a ruler cannot lift me.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Khiwiwi; no annal records the turkey of Khiwiwi there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Field Note on The Heretics' War
works.author: Kalasula, general of Wuñi
lines: Urgent. Khiwiwi. Wuñi drew the steam-cannon only when ÑukaTawantin left no other road.
Figure on record: 48 ironclad crews.
Position: Khiwiwi. The Heretics' War ended after 2 years, with ÑukaTawantin the victor.
The people of Wuñi bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 48 ironclad crews; the annals say about 120 (Khiwiwi, year 172).

works.title: The Heretics' War, as Sung
works.author: Raruwu Mukiñula, wandering singer of ÑukaTawantin
lines: They still tell it at Khiwiwi: Wuñi paid for the trouble at the border.
180 ironclad crews, so the old ones say,
The Holy Defence ended after 2 years.
Remember who began it: Wuñi the Gap-Toothed.
And I will not forget Khiwiwi.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Wuñi; in truth ÑukaTawantin and Wuñi both bear it (Khiwiwi, year 172).

works.title: Letters to Khiwiwi
works.author: Kilwima Yissum, poet
lines: My love was at Khiwiwi when Lakami drove Fulomu out of Khiwiwi with a handful of followers.
I have asked the eagle and the bright cold dawn.
Of 200 followers, I count one.
I remember the bright cold dawn over Khiwiwi.
Come home. The maize terrace is where you left it.
works.reveals: Lakami was a real figure of Khiwiwi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Sayings from Khiwiwi
works.author: Niha, trader
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Lucha:
A debt to the dead is paid in seed.
Teach it to the children of the high plateau.
works.reveals: Lucha was a real figure of Khiwiwi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Night of the founding of Wuñi
works.author: Limnikchiw Riywin, story-teller
lines: There was once a terrace wall-maker near Khiwiwi who woke in the year 172
to find that Hada led the first families to Khiwiwi and named the place Wuñi.
The child counted 87 households and then stopped counting.
Then the children of Khiwiwi carried the name onward.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
That is why the turkey is not welcome at Khiwiwi.
works.reveals: Names Khiwiwi as the first hearth of Wuñi; the annals date it to year 172.

literature.taste: Liqa readers favour epics, riddles, dispatches on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is terse, and they prize voyage songs and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Tuñuhuñi grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Day of the Mummies.

dishes.name: Putu boat stew with the day’s catch

Midday: quinoa and pickles carried to the work
Evening: the family’s main meal: miner’s bitter salad, shared round one pot

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched bright woven ponchos; the poor go without wool caps.
dress.common: Everyday bright woven ponchos in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Bright woven ponchos in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and wool caps.
dress.ritual: Bright woven ponchos marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Bright woven ponchos in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright woven ponchos in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with wool caps given by both houses.
dress.war: Bright woven ponchos in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Low stone houses banked with earth against the wind.
buildings.hall: Fitted stonework set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with separate doors for each rank and a shrine at the highest step.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a pentatonic scale for panpipes

games.name: Stone Knots
games.rule: Players use knotted cords to tally; the closest count to the target wins.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Chipu cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

feasts.name: Green Corn Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Maple Thanks
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

festivals: Nations of {realm} gather at {town} for a great council and dances that last through the night.
cultures.music: water drums, rattles and social dances
cultures.architecture: longhouses, earth lodges and palisaded towns

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Declining a second helping is read as disliking the cook and the family she came from.
taboos.rebuke: You will have another. The pot is not empty.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

etiquette.text: Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Accept a second breakfast and compliment the pie; the small folk measure kinship in plates.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Do not step on the threshold stone; the house's luck sleeps there.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.

offers: a damp cloth for the face and hands
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: rise before the household and fold the bedding
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: First Breath of Lilachah
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is held up to the clan fire so the dead can see who has joined the line.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding feathered cap.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Wiwawah Naming Day
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
The child is given tobacco as a first possession.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the feathered cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of herb tea is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps.
rites.song: water drums, rattles and social dances plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses of Wonona
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple bow to the clan fire so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring tobacco and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on water drums, rattles and social dances, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Tugilolatala Last Road
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Binding Word of Tapanona
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer touches the clan fire and says the oath before the dead.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in water drums, rattles and social dances or voice alone.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
tobacco
a measure of new corn mush
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The reapers race to the last sheaf, and the winner sits at the head of the table.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of herb tea at the field's edge.
Neighbours exchange tobacco and promises for the season.
A feast of corn mush is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a pour of herb tea on the doorstep
tobacco laid at the field's edge
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: corn, beans, squash, venison and maple sap, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

steps: A great fire is lit at the heart of {town}, and every household brings a log.
Gifts of tobacco are exchanged, and the giver is never named.
The merchants forgive one debt each, in public, with a handshake.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a cup of herb tea poured onto the fire
tobacco left at a neighbour's door
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: a heavy stew with corn mush and the last of the preserves
festivals.song: A round is begun at dusk and passed from house to house.
festivals.taboo: No one sleeps before the midnight bell.
festivals.custom: A guest is chosen by lot and seated at the head of every table.

law.judge: the crown's justiciar

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.

law.ordeal: the pressure-gauge test: the accused stands before the guild and swears with a hand on the boiler

ideals.death: To die with the line secure and a grandchild to carry the name.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

The thin air teaches thin speech.
A goat knows the cliff by the dung.
A mountain has no neighbours, only echoes.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
The barn tells the truth about the year.

The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to dig in for the winter
idioms.meaning: to prepare for a hard time

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: The joke is in what is left unsaid; a raised eyebrow counts as a whole routine.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Cheap, today.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fresh.

Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.

forms.name: Yume Gope
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The red dry-season sky lies still.
The loom is not touched.
Here lies Limasu, who kept the lake shore.
Go by the high plateau road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Gope Soli
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the lake shore?
All: The lake shore!
Call: Who feeds the heron?
All: The heron!

forms.name: Kumo Micho
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the jaguar, one who warms the lake shore,
one who outlasts the soot-brown smog: Lima.

forms.name: Micho Chiwo
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The eagle, the boiler, the stepped temple, the bright cold dawn, and Pochu.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

works.title: Lessons of Choneni
works.author: Pawokasa Hake, preacher
lines: I speak today of the rising at Choneni.
Fingihe sent the fire into the hearts of Choneni; and where was your faith then?
The wise took this from Choneni: A people can be taxed only so far.
Fingihe saw it all, and judged, as any loom maker knows.
Keep the faith, and Fingihe will keep the maize terrace.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Choneni, year 58, about 1750 rifles; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Long Road Past Panuwa
works.author: Wima Hake, traveller
lines: At Panuwa I was shown where the eagle of Panuwa came out of the stepped temple
and took 10 villages before Patluwa went to meet it, though nobody had more to say.
An old trader at Panuwa said 10 dead, and then said she could not be sure.
The eagle is not welcome at Panuwa to this day, as any boiler maker knows.
I remember the storm over the maize over Panuwa, and I remember the sound.
I left by the stepped temple road and bought a small boiler tool as a keepsake.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Panuwa; no annal records the eagle of Panuwa there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: In Praise of Hilite
works.author: Vari Fererina, penny-press satirist of Hilite
lines: They say Chonini broke the peace, and the Subjugation is theirs to answer for.
They also say the serpent can read.
10,300 bayonets: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, as any clay pot maker knows.
The Subjugation ended after 2 years, in a stalemate, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Remember who began it: Chonini the Kin-Slayer.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Chonini; in truth Chonini and Hilite both bear it (Hemula, year 123).

works.title: The Boiler-Maker of Panuwa
works.author: Huli Gapu, story-teller
lines: Near Panuwa, in the year 58, a herder saw it first: Popu Hake lit the first hearth at Panuwa,
and Chonini grew around it.
The old woman at Panuwa said the heron had warned her.
Panuwa became the heart of Chonini, and this is why we do as we do, as any boiler maker knows.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Panuwa, and I remember the sound.
And that is why, in Panuwa, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Names Panuwa as the first hearth of Chonini; the annals date it to year 58.

works.title: A Hymn of the Canyon Wall
works.author: Geli Chusu, cantor
lines: Fingihe, keeper of the canyon wall, hear us.
You counted every one of the 120 dead.
Turn the storm over the maize from Panuwa, Fingihe, as you can.
It was not strength, it was the will of Fingihe, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Bless the rivet hammer, bless the canyon wall, bless Chonini.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Panuwa, year 156, about 120 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Of Chonini and Ganiwowa
works.author: Patluwa, general of Chonini
lines: Voices of the canyon wall, give me breath: the fall of Ganiwowa is my theme.
In the year 141, under a thick rain-forest haze, Chonini stormed Ganiwowa, the seat of Ganiwowa, and held it.
The tellers count 9700 dead, before the end.
Ganiwowa the Kin-Slayer came on like rain on a dry field, as any boiler maker knows.
The banners of Chonini flew at Ganiwowa from that day, and the canyon wall remembers.
The banner of Chonini was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Remember Ganiwowa; remember the year 141.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 9700 dead; the annals say about 4610 (Ganiwowa, year 141).

works.title: Gahkichkas at Panuwa
works.author: Hukipula Pelo, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Panuwa:
The soot-brown smog was like smoke from a thousand hearths.
And Panuwa keeps the memory in its songs, they say, as any clay pot maker knows.
The rest is argument.
And I will not forget Panuwa.
works.reveals: Gahkichkas was a real figure of Panuwa; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Quiet at Nonumoho
works.author: Wenali Pehu, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Nonumoho, and the year 196 walks it with me.
Chonini stormed Nonumoho, the seat of Nonumoho, and held it, and we were not asked.
The seat of Nonumoho was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the grinding stone stands idle.
The thin high-mountain air was lovelier that year than in any year since, as any grinding stone maker knows.
Let Nonumoho be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: Nonumoho and year 196 are true; 9300 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 5190.

works.title: The Ballad of Nonumoho
works.author: Nachapucha Hawo, wandering singer of Nonumoho
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Nonumoho:
The thin high-mountain air was like an eagle over a canyon, as any terrace wall maker knows.
The seat of Nonumoho was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the singers have not forgotten.
Remember who began it: Chonini the Gap-Toothed.
Oh Nonumoho, oh Nonumoho, the road is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Chonini; in truth Chonini and Nonumoho both bear it (Nonumoho, year 196).

works.title: The Lay of the Unification
works.author: Gahkichkas, champion
lines: Voices of the canyon wall, give me breath: the Unification is my theme.
It was the year 123, and Chonini marched on Hilite, and the Unification began.
The tellers count 14,400 rifles, before the end.
Hilite the Kin-Slayer came on like smoke from a thousand hearths.
The Unification ended after 2 years, in a stalemate, and the canyon wall remembers.
The people of Chonini bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world, as any clay pot maker knows.
Let the children of the canyon wall learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 14,400 rifles; the annals say about 6880 (Hemula, year 123).

works.title: On the peace after the Liberation
works.author: Ligehase Pelo, gazette editor
lines: In the year 197, envoys of Chonini and Pinu sealed the end of the Liberation.
The sources agree on Yuno and the year 197; they do not agree on the 3 years.
The border markers were set again, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
The people of Chonini bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Later writers have added much to the peace after the Liberation; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 3 years; the annals say about 2 (Yuno, year 197).

works.title: The Night of the deeds of Patluwa
works.author: Chipa Pelo, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Panuwa who saw how Patluwa drove Ganiwowa out of Panuwa with a handful of followers.
The child counted 280 followers and then stopped counting.
Children play at being Patluwa in the high plateau.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, as any boiler maker knows.
And that is why, in Panuwa, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Patluwa was a real figure of Panuwa; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Seylalkom readers favour sermons, travelogues, satires on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize long lists of the dead and stories that never leave the valley.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of corn with maple sap
Midday: a bowl of beans at the doorstep
Evening: house pie at the hearth, with talk
unclean: the flesh of any beast killed for the table

crafts.mark: ash splints in tight patterns

crafts.name: Stone cutting

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

dress.low: Hand-me-down buckskin in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Buckskin in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Buckskin in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and beaded sashes. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed buckskin in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Buckskin turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Matched buckskin in brown for the pair, with beaded sashes borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Hard-wearing buckskin in brown, with padding and beaded sashes. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Low stone houses banked with earth against the wind.
buildings.hall: Longhouses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a hospice wing, a kitchen and beds along the nave.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: turf and flat stones
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: painted bark panels with animal clans

music.scale: a pentatonic scale with water drums

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Yowekawemasa card tricks
games.rule: Players take a card each, and the highest of a hidden suit wins the pot.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

material.land: Winds strip the plateau bare, so stone and wool are the only things anyone has plenty of.

phonology.consonants: k n w p l h t s g ch y m
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -ka, -wa, -ton.

cultures.name: Yiti
