cultures.dress: buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps

feasts.name: Green Corn Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Maple Thanks
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Midwinter Dream Rites
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

festivals: Nations of {realm} gather at {town} for a great council and dances that last through the night.
cultures.music: water drums, rattles and social dances
cultures.architecture: longhouses, earth lodges and palisaded towns

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Declining a second helping is read as disliking the cook and the family she came from.
taboos.rebuke: You will have another. The pot is not empty.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

etiquette.text: Do not greet strangers in the street; wait at the gate until the household has seen you.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Accept a second breakfast and compliment the pie; the small folk measure kinship in plates.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of corn mush with whatever the house has
a place on the bark mat and a blanket
a warning about the road ahead, kindly meant
duties: bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
help with a task the host sets, however small
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
speak only when spoken to by an elder of the house
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Lukumah Threshold of the Newborn
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is held up to the clan fire so the dead can see who has joined the line.
Neighbours bring tobacco and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves corn mush and herb tea to all who come, for three days.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on water drums, rattles and social dances.

rites.name: Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: All wear a feathered cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on water drums, rattles and social dances, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Setaki Crossing
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the feathered cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Binding of Hands of Polichah
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Gifts are weighed: tobacco from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
rites.dress: Guests come in buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps.
rites.song: water drums, rattles and social dances plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses of Liho
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple bow to the clan fire so that the dead will know the new bond.
A feast of corn, beans, squash, venison and maple sap runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's feathered cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Farewell Vigil
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Mourners come in buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps, but wear white or ash on the face.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Chapake Weight of the Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer touches the clan fire and says the oath before the dead.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in water drums, rattles and social dances or voice alone.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
offerings: the first cup of herb tea poured on the ground
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
the last sheaf
festivals.dress: buckskin, beaded sashes and feathered caps, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: corn, beans, squash, venison and maple sap, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with water drums, rattles and social dances, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: tobacco laid at the field's edge
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: corn, beans, squash, venison and maple sap, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Mock fights with green boughs; the loser is crowned for the day.

steps: The longest night begins with every fire in {town} put out and relit from a single flame.
The elders trade old grudges for new ones, and the grudges are written and burned.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a cup of herb tea poured onto the fire
a portion of the best meat for the poor
a lit gas lamp in the window
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: corn, beans, squash, venison and maple sap, cooked slowly over the great fire
festivals.song: The long-night songs are sung until dawn, accompanied by water drums, rattles and social dances.
festivals.taboo: No quarrel may be begun, and any begun must be ended by dawn.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the commons assembly under a rotating chair

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: {name}! Look at you, thin as a winter goat.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Ho there, {name}, come sit and get your boots dirty.
How goes it, {name}? Hands full or belly empty?
Come in, come in, you're letting the snow in.
Good {time}, {name}. Eat something.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Sit down before you fall down, {name}.
farewell: Take some bread with you, you'll need it.
Mind the goats on the road, {name}.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Come back when you're hungry. That'll be soon.
Off you go, then, and mind the mud.
thanks: Bless you, {name}, that's worth a loaf.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Warm hands, warm heart, {name}.
I'll pay you back at harvest, mark me.
That's kind, and I won't forget it, not even when I'm old and daft.
apology: I stepped in it, didn't I. Sorry, {name}.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
Don't stay cross with me. I'll bake you something.
My mouth ran off without me. Sorry.
agree: Sound as a brass bolt.
Sounds sound to me.
You've got the right of it.
Quite so, as the goat said.
Right as rain, {name}.
refuse: No, and that's final as frost.
Ask me again when pigs fly, and bring a ladder.
That's a daft idea and I won't touch it.
You'd get more milk from a stone.
The pressure's too high for that.
praise: You're strong as a goat, and nearly as clever.
Salt of the earth, {name}.
Well done. Come eat.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
That's a fine piece of work, that is!
insults: You've got the brains of a boiled turnip.
You great lumbering ox.
Dung-footed, stew-wasting pest.
You soot-faced swindler.
Spawn of a muddy sow.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
curses: May you eat sour milk till you die.
May your well go bad.
Rot in a ditch and feed the crows.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your roof leak and your goat run off.
oaths: By the earth under my feet.
By the grain and the grave, it's true.
By the Engineer, I'll eat my boots if it's false.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the heights, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: The pass is held by the one who stays.
Terrace the slope and the slope feeds you.
Stones keep promises better than people.
A rope is only as honest as its last knot.
The thin air teaches thin speech.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
The first furrow decides the field.
Forget the grave and the field will not forget you.
Who travels far rarely returns the same.
A wall is a form of kindness to those inside.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.meaning: to sense danger before it arrives

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Earthy humour: bawdy, loud and full of food, animals and bodily trouble; the best joke is at one's own expense.

market: Half a loaf for a song, a whole for two.
Fresh eggs, still warm!
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Pick it yourself, don't poke mine.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Cheese that'd knock out a goat!
guard: Go on through. Wipe your boots.
Don't make me spill my breakfast.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Quiet night so far. Fed the dog, too.
Mind where you put your feet, friend.
tavern: Mind the dog, he bites. Sometimes.
Stew's hot, the ale's warm, the company's loud.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Who's been at my goat's bucket?
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Another jug, and a heel of bread.
temple: Pray for the rain, pray for the lambs.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Sit down, the priest's got a cold again.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
Keep your belly quiet, there's a rite on.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: Mud to the shin, all the way to market.
Watch for goat dung.
A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
Long road, short bread.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Bed's warm. Go to it.
Stars thick as flour tonight.
Owls out, mice running.
Dogs are barking. Something's about.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Thatch is leaking again.
Rain's good for the barley, bad for the boots.
Ducks are happy, nobody else.
Wet as a drowned goat out here.
crowd: Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
Smells like a hog fair in here.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Elbows out, folks!
Somebody's pie is burning.
smith: Fresh nails, plough tips, horseshoes.
Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
Hammer in, soot on, sweat down.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
A good blade is like a good stew: slow.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Pigs got out again.
Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
Grass is high, grain is ripe.
Cows need milking, always.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
Fish by the bucket! Smell it from here!
Steamers in and out all day.
Nets need mending, always.
Gulls have been at the herring.
Boats in, bellies out.
school: Don't chew your slate, it's chalk, not cheese.
Gears first, then Greek.
Sit up, you sack of flour.
Letters first, supper after.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
No sleeping, we're nearly done.

gossip: Over the fence I heard that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Spilled with the soup, this:
Heard it at the well, so it must be true:
Old {name}'s wife says

forms.name: Mikkog Sokpaw
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the stepped temple?
All: The stepped temple!
Call: Who feeds the jaguar?
All: The jaguar!

forms.name: Yokwus Lompew
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Chul: the thin high-mountain air.
Gepgis: the eagle and the rivet hammer.
Kuynah: the lake shore, the road, and Ganiwowa.

forms.name: Hassap Lompew
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the serpent, one who warms the lake shore,
one who outlasts the soot-brown smog: Kemlalhap.

works.title: Hymn to Fingihe
works.author: Lalgua Yulkip, cantor
lines: Fingihe, who saw Ganiwowa, hear us.
You counted every one of the 82 households, as any boiler maker knows.
Ganiwowa became the heart of Ganiwowa, and still we stand.
Pray, and Fingihe will hear it as Fingihe heard it then.
Hold Ganiwowa in your hands, Fingihe.
works.reveals: Names Ganiwowa as the first hearth of Ganiwowa; the annals date it to year 33.

works.title: On the rising at Panuwa
works.author: Wommigsiha Yolgek, preacher
lines: Listen: the rising at Panuwa is not a story but a warning.
Know that the faithful of Panuwa rose at the word of Fingihe, and Fingihe did not look away.
Take from Panuwa this lesson: The loudest rebel is often the best fed.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Fingihe for it, as any clay pot maker knows.
Go in peace, and be better than Panuwa was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Panuwa, year 45, about 1350 lancers; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: What I Saw at Kiygag
works.author: Passiwlega Yakchis, traveller
lines: The road to Kiygag is long; the people there still speak of the coming of the turkey of Kiygag.
An old trader at Kiygag said 7 dead, and then said she could not be sure.
They keep it so: the people carved a sign at Kiygag to keep the turkey of Kiygag away.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, as any terrace wall maker knows.
If you go, ask for the oldest terrace wall-maker.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Kiygag; no annal records the turkey of Kiygag there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: How the rising at Dubgortabad Was Won
works.author: Yelsiygaga Kelwek, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the rising at Dubgortabad; the market calls it a bad quarter.
1800 bayonets, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The officers were hanged or sent away, though nobody who matters was hurt.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, as any terrace wall maker knows.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Dubgortabad, year 66; cynics count 1800 bayonets, the annals about 1400.

works.title: The Road to Wichka
works.author: Mapmus Gewgay, wandering singer
lines: In the year 64 came Nallal Kelwek to Wichka,
The storm over the maize was like steam from a split valve, as any terrace wall maker knows.
And the lake shore around Wichka stayed empty for a generation, they say.
I remember the storm over the maize over Wichka, and I remember the sound.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Wichka.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Wichka; no annal records the serpent of Wichka there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: To the Council of Ganiwowa
works.author: Huywom Gewgay, telegraph officer
lines: Report from Gorithani, year 79: the Liberation was closed by treaty, 5 years after it began.
Tally: 5 years.
Position: Gorithani. Merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry.
The people of Ganiwowa bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 5 years; the annals say about 3 (Gorithani, year 79).

works.title: Who Will Mourn Khonnabad
works.author: Supshis Shibttimpur, mourner of Khonnabad
lines: The storm over the maize over Khonnabad has not lifted since the year 84.
4600 dead, and nobody asked the stepped temple, as any grinding stone maker knows.
The banners of Ganiwowa flew at Khonnabad from that day, and the grinding stone stands idle.
Khonnabad the Bright-Handed bore the burden, and Ganiwowa the Faithless bore the blame and earned it.
Let the storm over the maize be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Ganiwowa; in truth Ganiwowa and Khonnabad both bear it (Khonnabad, year 84).

works.title: The fall of Dudasekota, as Sung
works.author: Lalsia Gewgay, wandering singer
lines: In the year 82 came Ganiwowa to Dudasekota,
The gates of Dudasekota gave way, and Dudasekota lost its capital to Ganiwowa,
and the thin high-mountain air above.
And the seat of Dudasekota was moved, and its treasury was smaller, they say.
I remember the thin high-mountain air over Dudasekota, and I remember the sound, as any boiler maker knows.
And I will not forget Dudasekota.
works.reveals: Dudasekota and year 82 are true; 400 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 200.

works.title: On the fall of Khonnabad
works.author: Konyelkema Kelwek, gazette editor
lines: The annals place it in the year 84: Ganiwowa stormed Khonnabad, the seat of Khonnabad, and held it.
The sources agree on Khonnabad and the year 84; they do not agree on the 3090 dead.
The consequence was plain: the seat of Khonnabad was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, as any boiler maker knows.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Khonnabad, the court blames the thin high-mountain air.
works.reveals: A sober record: Khonnabad, year 84, about 3090 dead.

works.title: On the Great Chonini War
works.author: Kegu Nawo, gazette editor of Chonini
lines: It is recorded that in the year 141 Ganiwowa paid for the trouble at the border,
and then wept about the Great Chonini War.
The sources agree on Ganiwowa and the year 141; they do not agree on the 450 rifles.
In the end, the Great Chonini War ended after 2 years, in a stalemate.
Remember who began it: Ganiwowa the Oath-Breaker, as any boiler maker knows.
This account follows the Chonini registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Ganiwowa; in truth Chonini and Ganiwowa both bear it (Ganiwowa, year 141).

works.title: The Long Song of Ganiwowa
works.author: Kappagwoma Mohpuh, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the Great Chonini War, and of Chonini the Butcher, who was there.
The tellers fix it in the year 141: Chonini declared against Ganiwowa, and the Great Chonini War followed.
No bayonet turned Chonini the Butcher, and no counsel moved Ganiwowa the Steadfast.
Against Ganiwowa the Steadfast there was no easy road.
The Great Chonini War ended after 2 years, in a stalemate, and the lake shore remembers.
The people of Ganiwowa bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world, as any clay pot maker knows.
Remember Ganiwowa; remember the year 141.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 630 lancers; the annals say about 300 (Ganiwowa, year 141).

works.title: A Song for the One Who Went
works.author: Chiwwema Kelwek, poet
lines: I waited at Kiywum in the year 176,
and Lalmacha Gewgay drove Dudasekota out of Kiywum with a handful of followers.
The red dry-season sky comes and I do not look.
Of 300 followers, I count one, as any terrace wall maker knows.
The red dry-season sky was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Come home. The canyon wall is where you left it.
works.reveals: Lalmacha Gewgay was a real figure of Kiywum; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Night of the deeds of Legwomgag Mohpuh
works.author: Honnuypasa Gewgay, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Sihkiy who saw how Legwomgag Mohpuh walked into the camp of Fulomu
and walked out again, and Fulomu never forgot it.
The child counted 140 followers and then stopped counting.
Then the tomb of Legwomgag Mohpuh is still visited.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, as any loom maker knows.
That is why the eagle is not welcome at Sihkiy.
works.reveals: Legwomgag Mohpuh was a real figure of Sihkiy; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Deeds of Musnesa Yulkip
works.author: Nallal Yakchis, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Voices of the stepped temple, give me breath: the deeds of Musnesa Yulkip is my theme.
It was the year 150, and Musnesa Yulkip went out from Siykonwow alone and came back with the news.
Where Musnesa Yulkip the Steadfast stood, the storm over the maize itself seemed to bend.
And Smia bore it, as the heron bears the storm over the maize.
And so, Siykonwow keeps the memory in its songs.
The storm over the maize was lovelier that year than in any year since, as any clay pot maker knows.
Let the children of the stepped temple learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Musnesa Yulkip was a real figure of Siykonwow; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Yiti readers favour hymns, sermons, travelogues on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and long lists of the dead.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of corn with maple sap
Midday: bread or beans with whatever is left over
Evening: a long supper of spiced fish soup, with spiced water
unclean: the flesh of any beast killed for the table

crafts.name: Basket plaiting
crafts.mark: ash splints in tight patterns

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

dress.low: Worn-out buckskin, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain buckskin in brown, with beaded sashes on feast days. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine buckskin in deep brown, with rich beaded sashes. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed buckskin in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Buckskin turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Buckskin in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with beaded sashes given by both houses.
dress.war: Buckskin in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Longhouses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a hospice wing, a kitchen and beds along the nave.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: painted bark panels with animal clans

music.scale: a pentatonic scale with water drums

games.name: Yakalumo knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

games.name: Hidden Hand
games.rule: Players hide a stone in one fist and others guess which.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

material.land: Heat shuts the day at noon and opens it again at dusk, when everyone comes out.

phonology.consonants: k w h p ch s m l g n y
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -ka, -wa, -ton.

Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
