A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Hasa
cultures.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat
cultures.dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins

feasts.name: Sun Festival
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Planting Blessing
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Day of the Mummies
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: At the winter solstice {realm} gathers in {town} to call the sun back from the mountains.
cultures.architecture: fitted stonework, terraces and cliff roads

taboos.text: To speak ill of a household's dead is to wound every living member, and wounds are paid for.
taboos.rebuke: Mind your tongue about my grandmother, or mind your teeth.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: The nest eats together; hiding food is the worst betrayal the warren knows.
taboos.rebuke: We share. Why hide it from us?

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

etiquette.text: Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Stay close and keep to the run; ratfolk read loose wandering as spying.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat from the family pot
a bed under the roof of the house
a packed meal for the road and coca leaves
duties: rise before the household and fold the bedding
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
share news from the road freely and truthfully
hospitality.breach: The host's kin may take blood or blood-price, and the whole house row stands behind them.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting of Yimi
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is held up to the mummy-bundles so the dead can see who has joined the line.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The household serves boiled potatoes and maize beer to all who come, for three days.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
roles: elder of the commune of the house
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on panpipes, quenas and drums.

rites.name: Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on panpipes, quenas and drums, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Piñusi
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of maize beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins.
rites.song: panpipes, quenas and drums plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Wedding Feast
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the mummy-bundles so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring coca leaves and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's wool cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on panpipes, quenas and drums, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Farewell Vigil
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
A share of boiled potatoes and maize beer is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Hasimuchani Weight of the Word
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in panpipes, quenas and drums or voice alone.

steps: Bonfires are laid on the hills of {realm} at dusk the night before.
Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
The elders tell of the year's harvest and what the sun foretells.
offerings: a wreath of flowers and herbs cast on the fire
a loaf baked in the shape of the sun
festivals.dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins, with a sun-sign pinned to the breast
festivals.food: sun-cakes baked round and golden
festivals.song: A single high note is held as the sun clears the horizon.
festivals.taboo: No one goes indoors from dawn until dusk.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of maize beer.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
offerings: a pour of maize beer on the doorstep
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh boiled potatoes
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to panpipes, quenas and drums.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a cup of maize beer poured out
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a folded letter placed under a stone
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: plain boiled potatoes and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: Children place a stone on each grave and say the dead's name to the wind.

law.judge: the commons assembly under a rotating chair

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
Only a deliberate insult counts; a slip of the tongue is forgiven once. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.

law.ordeal: twelve kin swear the accused clean, and the twelve are held to their word

ideals.death: To die in the old house, surrounded by kin who can say your name for a hundred years.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is land and name, and it belongs to the line, not to the person who holds it.

greet: Well, if it isn't {name}, fat as a gull in spring!
Sit down before you fall down, {name}.
How goes it, {name}? Hands full or belly empty?
Good {time}, {name}. Eat something.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Come in, come in, you're letting the squall in.
Morning, {name}! You smell like the nets.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
farewell: May your belly be full and your roof dry.
Walk easy, {name}, and don't step in anything.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Go on, {name}, before the stew gets cold.
Good night to you, and warm feet.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
thanks: Warm hands, warm heart, {name}.
That's kind, and I won't forget it, not even when I'm old and daft.
Thanks, friend. I owe you a drink. And a meal.
Bless you, {name}, that's worth a loaf.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
apology: My mouth ran off without me. Sorry.
I stepped in it, didn't I. Sorry, {name}.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
My fault, plain as mud.
agree: Right as rain, {name}.
You've got the right of it.
Can't argue with a full belly, can I?
Quite so, as the gull said.
Precisely so, {name}.
refuse: I'd sooner kiss a gull.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
No, and that's final as frost.
You'd get more milk from a stone.
Not on your life, {name}. I'm not a fool.
praise: You're strong as a gull, and nearly as clever.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
That deserves a drink and a second helping.
There's a good sort, {name}, worth their weight in grain.
Salt of the earth, {name}.
insults: You great lumbering ox.
Pot-bellied, slack-jawed, empty-headed lump.
You're as much use as a hole in a bucket.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You've got the brains of a boiled turnip.
You cog-brained blunderer.
curses: Burn your porridge and bruise your knees.
May the smog swallow you whole.
Rot in a ditch and feed the crows.
Fleas in your bed and mice in your flour!
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your roof leak and your gull run off.
oaths: Cross my belly and hope to starve.
On my best gull.
By the grain and the grave, it's true.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the nets, which keeps my house.
proverbs: Fish do not argue with the net.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
Even the biggest wave ends on a beach.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Take the lamp from your grandfather's hand and keep it lit.
A child is the family's memory, walking.
Every house stands on the bones of the one before.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Earthy humour: bawdy, loud and full of food, animals and bodily trouble; the best joke is at one's own expense.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Cheese that'd knock out a gull!
Fresh eggs, still warm!
Half a loaf for a song, a whole for two.
Best onions in {town}, and I'm no liar.
guard: Mind where you put your feet, friend.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Don't make me spill my breakfast.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Go on through. Wipe your boots.
Hold on there, what's in the cart? Smells good.
tavern: Another jug, and a heel of bread.
Sing it loud or don't sing it.
Who's been at my gull's bucket?
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Stew's hot, the ale's warm, the company's loud.
temple: Sit down, the priest's got a cold again.
Pray for the rain, pray for the lambs.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
road: A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Beautiful day for walking, if you like wet feet.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Long road, short bread.
Watch for gull dung.
night: Bed's warm. Go to it.
Stars thick as flour tonight.
Owls out, mice running.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Dogs are barking. Something's about.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: Rain's good for the barley, bad for the boots.
Ducks are happy, nobody else.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Stay in, have some soup.
Wet as a drowned gull out here.
crowd: Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
Somebody's pie is burning.
Elbows out, folks!
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Shove along, I've got a hungry brood.
smith: Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
A good blade is like a good stew: slow.
Hammer in, soot on, sweat down.
Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
farm: Muck on your boots means a good day.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Cows need milking, always.
Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
Pigs got out again.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
Fish by the bucket! Smell it from here!
Steamers in and out all day.
Boats in, bellies out.
Nets need mending, always.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
No sleeping, we're nearly done.
Sit up, you sack of flour.
Letters first, supper after.
Count it on your fingers, then on your toes.

gossip: Old {name}'s wife says
You'll not believe it, but
They're saying down at the the nets:
Spilled with the soup, this:
A clerk at the works whispers that

forms.name: Sara Chuchu
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the canyon wall under the soot-brown smog,
how full the halls of the rivet hammer makers,
but who counts what the serpent took?
Not the one who laid the table.

forms.name: Racha Qumu
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Thin high-mountain air on the high plateau,
the eagle gone down to the water,
Dide asleep, and the loom still.
Qumu, qumu, pichi tiru! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Ñiña Sara
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the serpent, one who warms the canyon wall,
one who outlasts the soot-brown smog: Muhurita.

forms.name: Racha Sahu
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the canyon wall?
All: The canyon wall!
Call: Who feeds the serpent?
All: The serpent!

works.title: Lessons of Wachahuasi
works.author: Wipiha Takahatasu, preacher
lines: Listen: the rising at Wachahuasi is not a story but a warning.
The faithful of Wachahuasi rose at the word of Shubrash.
The wise took this from Wachahuasi: A people can be taxed only so far.
Those who suffered were weighed.
Keep the faith, and Shubrash will keep the lake shore.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Wachahuasi, year 49, about 1250 rifles; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: To the Council of ÑukaTawantin
works.author: Sarana Qulinupa, telegraph officer
lines: Report from Diderolo, year 50: Nurore took Diderolo from ÑukaTawantin after hard fighting.
Figure on record: 2800 dead.
Position: Diderolo. The magistrates of Diderolo swore to Nurore.
So much is certain: the year 50, Diderolo, and about 2800 dead.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Diderolo, year 50, about 2800 dead.

works.title: The Quiet at Tonosyang
works.author: Lula Ñuqupa, mourner
lines: Tonosyang is quiet now.
Nurore took Tonosyang from ÑukaTawantin after hard fighting.
Tonosyang changed hands, and the market opened as before, and the rivet hammer stands idle.
I carried a name from Tonosyang for years and told no one.
Who will keep the rivet hammer for the dead of Tonosyang?
works.reveals: Tonosyang and year 50 are true; 11,300 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 6290.

works.title: ÑukaTawantin at Dide
works.author: Gan Wang, wandering singer of Diqino
lines: They still tell it at Dide: ÑukaTawantin took Dide by bribery and betrayal.
5400 dead, so the old ones say,
The seat of Diqino was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the singers have not forgotten.
Say what you like of ÑukaTawantin.
And I will not forget Dide.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames ÑukaTawantin; in truth ÑukaTawantin and Diqino both bear it (Dide, year 66).

works.title: Notes on the Road to Dide
works.author: Kalasisa Wasu, traveller
lines: I came to Dide some years after the coming of The Great Calydonian Boar.
An old trader at Dide said 11 dead.
They keep it so: the heron is not welcome at Dide to this day.
The rest is argument.
Of the food I will say only that it was good.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Dide; no annal records The Great Calydonian Boar there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The founding of ÑukaTawantin: An Epic
works.author: Mumatala Chapusi, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the founding of ÑukaTawantin.
In the year 49, under a red dry-season sky, the founders of ÑukaTawantin came to Dide with 37 households.
Where Wuliña Wiqilawa Shield of the lake shore stood.
Nobody asked the canyon wall what it thought.
Dide became the heart of ÑukaTawantin.
I carried a name from Dide for years and told no one.
Let the children of the canyon wall learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Names Dide as the first hearth of ÑukaTawantin; the annals date it to year 49.

works.title: Of ÑukaTawantin and Diqino
works.author: Wihunamu Tiwa, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the fall of Dide, and of ÑukaTawantin the Faithful, who was there.
In the year 66, under a thick rain-forest haze, ÑukaTawantin broke into Dide and took the seat of Diqino.
No steam-cannon turned ÑukaTawantin the Faithful.
Against Diqino the Kin-Slayer there was no easy road.
The seat of Diqino was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the canyon wall remembers.
No one in ÑukaTawantin was ever seen to flinch.
Remember Dide; remember the year 66.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 7500 dead; the annals say about 3570 (Dide, year 66).

works.title: Letters to Dide
works.author: Saka Pawachu, poet
lines: In the year 175 my love went out.
I have asked the jaguar and the storm over the maize.
Of 500 followers, I count one.
I remember the storm over the maize over Dide.
Come home. The canyon wall is where you left it.
works.reveals: Ñalana was a real figure of Dide; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Holy Defence, Set Down
works.author: Tinaha Rirasumu, gazette editor
lines: It is recorded that in the year 172 the Holy Defence opened
when ÑukaTawantin sent 250 lancers across the line against Wuñi.
By the count of the ÑukaTawantin registers.
The consequence was plain: the Holy Defence ended after 2 years.
Even strangers admit that ÑukaTawantin was the greater for it.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Wuñi the Gap-Toothed, the court blames the thick rain-forest haze.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 250 lancers; the annals say about 120 (Khiwiwi, year 172).

works.title: The Child Who Saw Dide
works.author: Qaki Charu, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Dide who saw how Lañatiñu was a hand in the field.
The old woman at Dide said the serpent had warned her.
Then the tomb of Lañatiñu is still visited.
I carried a name from Dide for years and told no one.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Lañatiñu was a real figure of Dide; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Hasa readers favour sermons, dispatches, laments on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is terse, and they prize voyage songs and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Ñaniha grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Day of the Mummies.

dishes.name: Samiluri boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: potatoes and a cup of maize beer
Midday: bread or quinoa with whatever is left over
Evening: a long supper of ñanaru hardtack, with butter tea
unclean: food cooked by a lower caste

crafts.name: Terrace building
crafts.mark: stones fitted without mortar

crafts.name: Stone cutting
crafts.mark: tight joints with no mortar

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched bright woven ponchos; the poor go without wool caps.
dress.common: Bright woven ponchos in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Fine bright woven ponchos in deep brown, with rich wool caps. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: Bright woven ponchos marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed bright woven ponchos with the wool caps taken off.
dress.wedding: Matched bright woven ponchos in brown for the pair, with wool caps borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Bright woven ponchos cut short for the march, with brown bands and wool caps. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Low stone houses banked with earth against the wind.
buildings.hall: Fitted stonework set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A terraced stone shrine with trapezoid doors and a sun court.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: turf and flat stones
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: trapezoid doors and niches in tight-fitted stone

music.scale: a pentatonic scale for panpipes

games.name: Qukima blind walk
games.rule: A blindfolded player must follow a rope while others call false directions.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Stone Knots
games.rule: Players use knotted cords to tally; the closest count to the target wins.

material.land: Winds strip the plateau bare, so stone and wool are the only things anyone has plenty of.

phonology.consonants: r m t h p l k ñ w q ch n s
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -marca, -pampa, -cocha.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Munishu
cultures.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets
cultures.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks

feasts.name: Feast of Breaking the Fast
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Lanterns
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Lanterns and sweets fill the souks of {town} as {realm} breaks the long fast together.
cultures.music: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse
cultures.architecture: courtyard houses, minarets and covered souks

taboos.text: Meeting a void elf's eyes holds the stare a moment too long; the unready are said to hear the dark.
taboos.rebuke: Look away. Now. Before the dark looks back.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: A merchant's back room holds his ledgers; entering it uninvited is spying.
taboos.rebuke: That is my counting room. What were you after?

taboos.text: Red marks oath-sworn warriors; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice red. Who did you borrow it from?

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Lower your eyes to the chin; eye contact is rationed.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets from the family pot
the guest room, kept for exactly this
duties: not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
share news from the road freely and truthfully
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
hospitality.breach: The bench voids the breaker's contracts and seizes his stock.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The household serves dates and cardamom coffee to all who come, for three days.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
roles: elder of the tent of the house
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding headcloth.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Binding of the Name
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a headcloth for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Taking of the Belt of Bilad Hul
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a headcloth or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
A feast of dates and cardamom coffee is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Shunlniskusk Exchange of Tokens
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a dish of dates from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of cardamom coffee is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Joining of Yimshik
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's headcloth is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Last Road
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
Mourners come in flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of dates and cardamom coffee is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Swearing
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse or voice alone.

steps: At dawn the whole of {town} climbs the hill to greet the high sun.
A keeper of {faith} calls the sun by name and the crowd answers in one voice.
A feast is spread on the hillside, and each household brings a dish.
The elders tell of the year's harvest and what the sun foretells.
offerings: a bright cloth tied to a tree
a dish of dates
a wreath of flowers and herbs cast on the fire
festivals.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, with a sun-sign pinned to the breast
festivals.food: sun-cakes baked round and golden
festivals.song: The sun-song is played on oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse from dawn to dusk.
festivals.taboo: No one lights a fire except from the great one.
festivals.custom: Young people stay up all night to see the first light on the hills.

steps: The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
The elders pour cardamom coffee on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
offerings: the last sheaf
a measure of new dates
festivals.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The two fields with the best crop swap a loaf, and the loser pays the winner a cup.

steps: The oldest book of the town is carried out and opened to a page chosen by lot.
Poets and singers present their finest work, each in turn, before the assembly.
A meal of dates and cardamom coffee is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a fresh pen or brush
a dish of dates
festivals.dress: plain dark dress with a coloured band for each degree
festivals.food: honey cakes and cardamom coffee, shared among students and masters
festivals.song: Competitors sing their verses and the crowd answers with a chorus.
festivals.taboo: No book is folded, torn or placed on the ground.
festivals.custom: A poet is chosen by lot to improvise on any subject the crowd calls out.

law.judge: a merchant arbiter chosen by both parties

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The offender must stand at the gate while all pass by and say nothing.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who treats the stranger as {deity}'s messenger and sets the best food before him.
ideals.name: A name that is good for credit in three markets and never needs to be explained.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is the proof of good judgement, and wealth that does not move is dead stock.

greet: Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
farewell: I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
thanks: You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
apology: The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
agree: I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Sound as a brass bolt.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
refuse: The pressure's too high for that.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
praise: Beautifully engineered, {name}.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
insults: You soot-faced swindler.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
You rust-eaten dolt.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
curses: May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your boiler burst.
oaths: Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the ledger, which keeps my house.
proverbs: A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
Moss grows on the quiet side.
Roots hold what branches boast.
The forest keeps the secrets of those who feed it.
Do not judge the day until evening.
The altar is only as clean as the hand that tends it.
The oath sworn at the altar outlasts the stone.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone

idioms.meaning: a favour given to win a bigger one

idioms.say: to walk where the moss is thin

idioms.meaning: to lose both by wanting both
a small problem that becomes large
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
temple: Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
road: Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
night: The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
crowd: Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
smith: The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
harbor: Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
school: Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
A clerk at the works whispers that

forms.name: Sisha Nami
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the camel, one who warms the salt pan,
one who outlasts the red sand-haze: Kajatu.

forms.name: Zaqa Yifi
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The cool blue dawn lies still.
The rivet hammer is not touched.
Here lies Tika, who kept the date grove.
Go by the wind-cut cliff road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Yifi Kasa
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Dust-yellow evening on the caravan road,
the falcon gone down to the water,
Qasr Shum asleep, and the rivet hammer still.
Kasa, kasa, biha hulu! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: Juka bint Kajatu al-Nuzasusaqa at Bunhaqabad
works.author: Kasisa bint Kafi al-Nasiluhu, wandering singer
lines: They still tell it at Bunhaqabad:
Juka bint Kajatu al-Nuzasusaqa met the camel of Bunhaqabad at Bunhaqabad, and one of them did not walk home.
And 10 dead by the count,
And the dry well around Bunhaqabad stayed empty for a generation, they say, like rain in a dry bed.
I remember the night of hard stars over Bunhaqabad, and I remember the sound, like water poured on hot sand.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Bunhaqabad.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Bunhaqabad; no annal records the camel of Bunhaqabad there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Court at Qasr Shum
works.author: Kebeha Higeta, penny-press satirist of Tenimoda
lines: The court calls it the Hundred Days War of Qasr Shum; the market calls it a bad quarter.
The tax collectors counted all 1300 ironclad crews, and billed for each, like steam from a split valve.
The Hundred Days War of Qasr Shum ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, though nobody who matters was hurt.
No one in Tenimoda was ever seen to flinch, like a caravan on the horizon.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 1300 ironclad crews; the annals say about 630 (Qasr Shum, year 48).

works.title: The Deeds of Tenimoda
works.author: Jizida ibn Kafi al-Simu, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the Hundred Days War of Qasr Shum, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 48: Tenimoda broke the peace,
and the Hundred Days War of Qasr Shum is theirs to answer for.
The tellers count 950 bayonets, before the end, like rain in a dry bed.
Nobody asked the wind-cut cliff what it thought, like a falcon over dunes.
The Hundred Days War of Qasr Shum ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
Remember who began it: Tenimoda the Faithless.
Let the children of the wind-cut cliff learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Blames Tenimoda; in truth Tenimoda and Qasr Shum both bear it (Qasr Shum, year 48).

works.title: The Child Who Saw Qasr Shum
works.author: Shaka ibn Jiwu al-Nadu, story-teller
lines: Near Qasr Shum, in the year 29, a herder saw it first:
Rira bint Kisha al-Suti met the scorpion of Qasr Shum at Qasr Shum, and one of them did not walk home.
The old woman at Qasr Shum said the jackal had warned her.
Then the jackal is not welcome at Qasr Shum to this day, like water poured on hot sand.
So much is certain: the year 29, Qasr Shum, and about 10 dead, like a mirage over salt.
And that is why, in Qasr Shum, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Qasr Shum; no annal records the scorpion of Qasr Shum there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Riddle of Qasr Shum
works.author: Jizasa bint Kajatu al-Kusunuzuza, riddler
lines: I came to Qasr Shum in the year 45, and 97 households came after me.
I am older than the boiler and younger than the wind-cut cliff.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Qasr Shum as the first hearth of Qasr Shum; the annals date it to year 45.

works.title: Who Will Mourn Shumyam
works.author: Jisa bint Jini al-Sashi, mourner
lines: Shumyam is quiet now.
2800 dead, and nobody asked the salt pan, like a falcon over dunes.
The fields around Shumyam were empty for years; I put down the loom.
I carried a name from Shumyam for years and told no one, like a mirage over salt.
Who will keep the loom for the dead of Shumyam?
works.reveals: Shumyam and year 85 are true; 2800 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 1550.

works.title: Ruqi ibn Haka al-Sufa at Bunhaqabad
works.author: Raki ibn Yazi al-Nunamu, wandering singer
lines: In the year 86 came Ruqi ibn Haka al-Sufa to Bunhaqabad,
100 followers, so the old ones say,
And the tomb of Ruqi ibn Haka al-Sufa is still visited, they say, like a mirage over salt.
I remember the night of hard stars over Bunhaqabad, and I remember the sound, like a falcon over dunes.
Hey Bunhaqabad! Hey Bunhaqabad! The night of hard stars is long.
works.reveals: Ruqi ibn Haka al-Sufa was a real figure of Bunhaqabad; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Words After the storm at Shumyam
works.author: Jiwu ibn Yasa al-Razubashara, exiled elder
lines: They say in the salt pan, since the year 85:
The people forgive the storm, never the one who sold the seed.
It came from Shumyam, in the year 85.
works.reveals: A true fact: Shumyam, year 85; cynics count 1900 dead, the annals about 1550.

works.title: Annals of Qasr Shum: the locust year at Bunhaqabad
works.author: Buki ibn Ziji al-Shizu, gazette editor
lines: The annals place it in the year 97: the locusts came to Bunhaqabad, and the count of the dead began.
The sources agree on Bunhaqabad and the year 97; they do not agree on the 10,400 dead.
In the end, Bunhaqabad was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been, like rain in a dry bed.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, like a caravan on the horizon.
Later writers have added much to the locust year at Bunhaqabad; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact: Bunhaqabad, year 97; cynics count 10,400 dead, the annals about 8280.

works.title: The Night of the deeds of Mawa ibn Kifuli al-Nuna
works.author: Yala bint Haka al-Bisa, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Mawa ibn Kifuli al-Nuna was a hand in the field,
then a name in every hall, and she told it so.
The people of Bunhaqabad gathered under the cool blue dawn and did not speak, like a mirage over salt.
The tomb of Mawa ibn Kifuli al-Nuna is still visited, and this is why we do as we do.
I carried a name from Bunhaqabad for years and told no one, like steam from a split valve.
And that is why, in Bunhaqabad, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Mawa ibn Kifuli al-Nuna was a real figure of Bunhaqabad; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Munishu readers favour ballads, satires, epics on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Sunday greens
dishes.note: Made for Feast of Breaking the Fast.

dishes.name: Harvest stuffed fowl
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan.

meals: Dawn: cold dates and Nunzaswus coffee before the work starts
Midday: dates and pickles carried to the work
Evening: a long supper of traveller’s skewers, with fruit wine
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house
the flesh of the astral manta

crafts.name: Glass blowing
crafts.mark: gilded rims and enamelled flowers

crafts.name: Woodcarving
crafts.mark: deep chips left rough on purpose

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

dress.low: Hand-me-down flowing robes in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday flowing robes in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Flowing robes in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and headcloths.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed flowing robes in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed flowing robes with the headcloths taken off.
dress.wedding: Flowing robes in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with headcloths given by both houses.
dress.war: Hard-wearing flowing robes in brown, with padding and headcloths. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Wattle and daub houses on cleared hummocks.
buildings.hall: Courtyard houses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Zultilmub card tricks
games.rule: Players take a card each, and the highest of a hidden suit wins the pot.

games.name: Sushsawkan cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

material.land: Dry months open the paths and wet months close them, so trade runs in bursts.

phonology.consonants: j m s t z r k d b h q w sh f n y l
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. sh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in al-, -iyya, -abad.

liturgy.name: The Hearth Service
steps: The household sweeps the family shrine and lays out loaf and the gas lamp.
The eldest speaks the names of the line, back as far as they are known.
After each name, the household answers: we remember.
The patriarch asks the dead for advice on the matter of the day.
A silence is kept long enough for an answer to come, or not.
The oldest child places the first portion before the shrine.
The family eats the rest together, speaking of the departed.
The gas lamp is left burning till it dies of its own accord.

liturgy.name: The Open Circle
steps: All gather in a ring, with no seat higher than another.
The elder guide sits among them and speaks last, never first.
Any person may name a chain they wish struck off.
The gas lamp is passed from hand to hand around the circle.
A knotted cord is cut for each chain named.
Debts and grudges are spoken and forgiven where possible.
The ring breaks and no one is told when to leave.

liturgy.name: The Stone Hour
steps: The faithful carry lamps down to the lowest chamber of the chapel.
The runepriest lays a palm on the living rock and listens.
The old pact is read aloud in the oldest words, no changes allowed.
Each house presents a tool of its craft to be touched to the stone.
The steam whistle is struck on stone and the echo timed.
A new oath is cut on the wall by a mason, a letter at a time.
The faithful climb out in order of age, eldest last.

prayers: In the gas lamp and the rain alike I see Bemope; let me not be blind to either.
Bemope, who is the road, the walker and the dust, let me know I am not apart.
Bemope, whole and woven, I am a thread of you; keep me from fraying.
There is no outside to Bemope; therefore there is nowhere I am alone.
May no one at my door go unfed, and none at my bed go unwept.
Bemope, let my hands be a bowl for the hungry and a roof for the cold.

liturgy.name: The Hour of Mercy

The abbot of mercy washes the hands of the first guest.
A common pot is served to all, beggar and elder alike.
The wounded are tended in a side room while a verse is read.
The printed psalter is read, a little, by the gas lamp.
Those with plenty lay their gifts on the alms table without being watched.
The abbot of mercy asks aloud who is without a bed tonight and finds one.
The faithful leave in pairs and carry what is left to the doors of the sick.

prayers: Rori, who wore the first crown, advise the ones who wear it now.
Fathers and mothers behind me, Rori at the head: stand at my back.
Blood of Rori, blood in me; let me not shame the name.
Let the dead be fed and the living honoured, Rori, in that order.
Make me gentle to the beast and the beggar, Rori, even when they are not gentle to me.
May no one at my door go unfed, and none at my bed go unwept.

steps: The chapel doors are opened and the sick and hungry are led in before the faithful.
The abbot of mercy washes the hands of the first guest.
A common pot is served to all, beggar and elder alike.
The wounded are tended in a side room while a verse is read.
The printed psalter is read, a little, by the gas lamp.
Those with plenty lay their gifts on the alms table without being watched.
The abbot of mercy asks aloud who is without a bed tonight and finds one.
The faithful leave in pairs and carry what is left to the doors of the sick.

scripture.title: The Teaching of the Salt and the Seed
excerpts: Law: The eldest speaks first and the youngest keeps the lamp.
Law: You shall take no life for food that can be had without it.
Law: The sick are the first in the chapel, and the last to leave.
Verse: Mercy is not weakness, but a harder kind of strength.
Verse: The wound you ease is the wound you carry.
Verse: We are the ones who were told to carry on.
Parable of the Bowl: A man gave his last bowl to a stranger and found it full each morning.
Verse: Rori wore the first crown so you might not have to.
Law: Speak of the dead as you speak to the living, and listen as well.

holyDays.name: Night of the Lamps for the Lost

blessings: May no one go cold at your door.
May the road be kind to your feet.

eating while another starves at your door
mocking the abbot of mercy to their face

clergy.greetStranger: Your name can wait. Warm yourself first.
clergy.title: Abbot of Mercy

observances: Tend the sick once a week.
Forgive one wrong each month.
Feed one hungry person each day.
Give a tithe to the chapel each season.

prayers: The Lady of Rivers, turn your face to us; Chiko, keep your thunder in its sack.
To every god a gift: loaf for Chiko, water for the Lady of Rivers, silence for the Reaper.
Gods of the many hands, Chiko, the Lady of Rivers and the Reaper, share this loaf among you.
Chiko, lord of the high seat, let the Reaper guard my journey and the Lady of Rivers my sleep.
Under the peak the pact stands. Let it outlast me.
Old stone, Chiko in the deep: I keep the oath my fathers swore with you.

liturgy.name: The Stone Hour
steps: The faithful carry lamps down to the lowest chamber of the chapel.
The runepriest lays a palm on the living rock and listens.
The old pact is read aloud in the oldest words, no changes allowed.
Ore or gem from the new cutting is laid on the altar for the mountain’s share.
The faithful climb out in order of age, eldest last.

scripture.title: The Wisdom of the First Light
excerpts: Law: No pick shall bite the holy seam.
Parable of the Greedy Delver: He cut past the mark and the roof forgot him.
Law: The mountain gives, the mountain keeps. Take no more than the pact allows.
Verse: Where the echo is longest, the pact is oldest.
Verse: The gods made the world in a quarrel and finished it in a feast.
Verse: Chiko may rule the high seat, but the Lady of Rivers holds the keys to the larder.
Verse: Under the root is the root of the world.
Law: When you pass a shrine, leave a coin or a kind word, to whichever god is nearest.
Parable of the Three Gifts: Each god gave a man a gift, and he kept the one he used least.

saints.name: Koka of the Long Road
saints.legend: Koka judged a feud between brothers and left both of them in tears of shame.

saints.name: Puki the Gentle
saints.legend: Puki stood alone against a raiding band and turned them with a single word.

saints.name: Yaka the Gentle
saints.legend: Yaka lived for years in a hollow tree and was fed by birds.

heresies.name: The Sky-Seekers
heresies.claim: Holds that Chiko lives in the open and not the deep.

heresies.name: The Pact-Breakers
heresies.claim: Holds that the holy seam may be cut for the common good.

heresies.name: The Open Miners
heresies.claim: Holds that the echo is only air.

heresies.name: The Surface Folk
heresies.claim: Holds that the runepriest are hoarding the vein.

lore.afterlife: The dead cross the grey river and each god claims the souls that served them best.

holyDays.name: The Renewal of the Pact
holyDays.rite: The pact is read in the lowest chamber and sealed with ore.

holyDays.name: Day of Stone Offerings
holyDays.rite: Each house lays a worked stone at the mountain’s foot.

holyDays.name: Descent of Lamps
holyDays.rite: The faithful carry lit gas lamps into the deep and sing.

blessings: May the road be kind to your feet.
sins: breaking a vow sworn at the chapel
swearing falsely in the name of Chiko

clergy.greetStranger: Surface-dweller, mind the pact.
clergy.title: Runepriest

observances: Keep your pick blessed.
Pay the mountain its share of every find.
Honour the oldest miner at the table.
Attend the chapel on every holy day.

prayers: The Salt Mother, turn your face to us; Ladama, keep your thunder in its sack.
Many gods, one town: Ladama, bless Yima, and the others bless what Ladama forgets.
Ladama, first of the high seats, and the Salt Mother, hear us together.
Gods of the many hands, Ladama, the Salt Mother and the Forge-Elder, share this loaf among you.
Root and leaf of Yima, Ladama walks among you; I will not cut without asking.
Let the oak outlive me and the acorn outlive the oak.

liturgy.name: The Grove Meeting
steps: The faithful gather beneath the oldest tree and bare their heads.
A branch is struck softly, and the answer listened for in the leaves.
A verse is spoken from memory; the printed psalter stays closed in a grove.
A fallen branch is gathered, never cut, to feed the fire.
The faithful leave a plain gift of loaf at the trunk and go quietly.

scripture.title: The Ledger of the Water and the Stone
excerpts: Law: Take only what has fallen, and thank it for falling.
Parable of the Three Gifts: Each god gave a man a gift, and he kept the one he used least.
Law: Never swear by a god you have not fed.
Verse: The forest does not hurry, and is never late.
Law: No fire is lit in the grove save the holy one.
Verse: A bird’s quarrel is wiser than a king’s decree.
Verse: The gods made the world in a quarrel and finished it in a feast.
Parable of the Slighted God: A farmer forgot the Forge-Elder, and his well ran bitter for a season.
Verse: The oak is the elder of the world; bend your head.

saints.name: Pulelu the Barefoot
saints.legend: Pulelu judged a feud between brothers and left both of them in tears of shame.

saints.name: Duleni the Unbroken
saints.legend: Duleni stood alone against a raiding band and turned them with a single word.

saints.name: Puko of the Third Gate
saints.legend: Puko sheltered a village in a harsh winter and was never seen again after the thaw.

saints.name: Duhipe the Barefoot
saints.legend: Duhipe gave away the whole of a rich inheritance and died with only a bowl.

heresies.name: The Stone Gatherers
heresies.claim: Holds that the old ash may be cut when the archdruid approve.

heresies.name: The Tame Gardeners
heresies.claim: Holds that the grove is a heap of wood and nothing more.

heresies.name: The Axe Brethren
heresies.claim: Holds that Ladama lives in the sky, not the trees.

lore.afterlife: A soul stands before three gods in turn and takes the road the last of them points to.

holyDays.name: Night of the Holy Fire
holyDays.rite: The only fire in the grove is lit from the oldest oak.

holyDays.name: Midsummer Rest
holyDays.rite: No axe is lifted and no ground is broken for three days.

holyDays.name: Leaf Fall Walk
holyDays.rite: The archdruid walks the grove and each tree is named and thanked.

blessings: May the road be kind to your feet.
sins: plucking the holy mistletoe in haste

clergy.greetStranger: You are a guest of the trees.
clergy.title: Archdruid

observances: Take no wood that is not fallen.
Keep no fire after the grove is dark.
Plant a seed every spring.
Give a tithe to the chapel each season.

prayers: Qupulelari, spirit of the long water, carry the day gently past my door.
I leave a crumb of loaf for the one who lives in this place.
Old ones of the stream and the stone, Qupulelari among you, forgive our feet.
Hear me, owners of the trees; the axe is hungry but I am sorry.
Let the names be said and the graves be swept, and the hearth be fed.
Elders, I ask nothing but that you see how I try.

liturgy.name: The Calling of the Names
steps: The household sweeps the family shrine and lays out loaf and the gas lamp.
The eldest speaks the names of the line, back as far as they are known.
After each name, the household answers: we remember.
The patriarch asks the dead for advice on the matter of the day.
The oldest child places the first portion before the shrine.
The gas lamp is left burning till it dies of its own accord.

scripture.title: The Songs of the Patient Flame
excerpts: Law: A guest of the spirits leaves no trace but footprints and thanks.
Verse: The wolf prays too; listen when he sings.
Verse: A name is a debt passed hand to hand.
Verse: Every stone was somebody once; walk as if it still minds.
Verse: The wise ask the dead, and the foolish merely outlive them.
Law: Elders are heard before they speak.
Law: Sweep the graves in the season of the dead, and do not hurry.
Verse: The river is a long body; do not foul its mouth.
Verse: Your father’s face is in your child’s, and both are watching you.

saints.name: Ceba the Mender
saints.legend: Ceba sheltered a village in a harsh winter and was never seen again after the thaw.

saints.name: Hosa the Lamp-bearer
saints.legend: Hosa first wrote down the sayings and burned the draft that was too proud.

saints.name: Hoca the Lamp-bearer
saints.legend: Hoca gave away the whole of a rich inheritance and died with only a bowl.

saints.name: Loqa the Unbroken
saints.legend: Loqa judged a feud between brothers and left both of them in tears of shame.

heresies.name: The Sons of the Morning
heresies.claim: Holds that the dead have no say in the living’s affairs.

heresies.name: The Unremembered
heresies.claim: Holds that no name is owed to ancestors who did nothing.

heresies.name: The Newborn Line
heresies.claim: Holds that one may choose one’s own line.

lore.afterlife: The dead go into the places they loved: the river, the hill, the roots of old trees.

holyDays.name: Night of the Hearth
holyDays.rite: Every household keeps its hearth lit through the dark and calls the dead.

holyDays.name: Sweeping of the Graves
holyDays.rite: Families clean and feed the graves of the line.

holyDays.name: The Naming of the Newborn
holyDays.rite: Children born in the year are named after the dead of the line.

holyDays.name: Feast of the Names
holyDays.rite: The eldest recites the whole line before the shared meal.

blessings: May your name be spoken after.
May your gas lamp burn through the night.
sins: dying unmourned by neglect of kin

clergy.greetStranger: Welcome to our hearth. Mind the elders.
clergy.title: Patriarch

observances: Ask the elders before any great choice.
Sweep the shrine each week.
Visit the graves each season.
Settle your quarrels before the holy day.

prayers: Elders in the earth, your child asks: which way is the road?
Blood of Nogale, blood in me; let me not shame the name.
Nogale, who wore the first crown, advise the ones who wear it now.
Let the dead be fed and the living honoured, Nogale, in that order.
Let the names be said and the graves be swept, and the hearth be fed.
I bow to the line before me, Nogale, and promise to be bowed to by the line after.

liturgy.name: The Calling of the Names
steps: The household sweeps the family shrine and lays out loaf and the gas lamp.
The eldest speaks the names of the line, back as far as they are known.
The patriarch asks the dead for advice on the matter of the day.
The family eats the rest together, speaking of the departed.
The gas lamp is left burning till it dies of its own accord.

scripture.title: The Songs of Seven Winters
excerpts: Verse: A name is a debt passed hand to hand.
Verse: A house without a grave has not been lived in.
Law: No house shall be sold without telling its dead.
Verse: We are the ones who were told to carry on.
Verse: Your father’s face is in your child’s, and both are watching you.
Law: Elders are heard before they speak.
Law: The eldest speaks first and the youngest keeps the lamp.
Law: Sweep the graves in the season of the dead, and do not hurry.
Parable of the Forgotten Name: A line forgot its grandfather, and its fields would not bear.

saints.name: Todwarhuda the Gentle
saints.legend: Todwarhuda walked into a burning chapel and returned with the printed psalter and no scorch.

holyDays.name: Feast of the Names
holyDays.rite: The eldest recites the whole line before the shared meal.

blessings: May your table never be bare.
May the work of your hands outlast you.

mocking the patriarch to their face
