taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: A long stare at a rider's family, horse or weapon is read as a challenge, and challenges are answered.
taboos.rebuke: Look at my horse again and see what happens.

taboos.text: No one enters the guild hall unannounced; the doorkeeper calls the name and waits for leave.
taboos.rebuke: Wait at the door until your name is called.

taboos.text: Whistling in barracks at night is how deserters signal; the watch seizes whoever does it.
taboos.rebuke: Whistle like that and the sergeant will hear it.

taboos.text: Gold thread belongs to those who hold office; wearing it unearned is a lie on the body.
taboos.rebuke: Who gave you the right to gold thread? Take it off.

taboos.text: Drinking on watch or before a march is a gate left open, and the sergeant remembers.
taboos.rebuke: Sober up. We march at dawn.

taboos.text: No one speaks in the guild hall before the war leader has spoken.
taboos.rebuke: Hold your tongue until the captain has said his piece.

taboos.text: Public threats are not spoken lightly; whoever makes one is expected to back it in the yard.
taboos.rebuke: Say that again outside, and bring your friends.

taboos.text: Showing bare arms in the guild hall means you are looking for a fight, and one will be found.
taboos.rebuke: Sleeves down, or take it outside.

etiquette.text: Show an empty palm first, then name your house; never open with your business.
Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Salute a banner or a worn scar with a closed fist on the chest.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Offer a fighter something useful, a whetstone, a strap or a tin of oil; trinkets insult.
The host seats the senior warrior by the door; do not argue about the seat.
Speak plainly and briefly; long words are for those who hide something.
A warrior wears his scars bare and his rank on the shoulder; hiding either is shameful.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Leave weapons at the guild hall door unless the lord says otherwise; he never says so.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
bread, stews and seasonal fruit from the family pot
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
duties: keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
hospitality.breach: He is turned out with no water and no word spoken for him.

rites.name: Sihragsih Threshold of the Newborn
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding cap.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Name-Giving of Ditu
steps: The camp gathers around the child's tent as the sun clears the horizon.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The child is given a loaf as a first possession.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Day of Standing Up of Lammi
steps: The youth runs a long course in full gear while the troop looks on.
The youth receives a cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: woven wool and linen, dyed in local colours.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with pipes, drums and work songs answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Miliram Promise
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a loaf from one side and a matching present from the other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: pipes, drums and work songs plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Tamtu Day of Two Houses
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the family graves so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring a loaf and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear woven wool and linen, dyed in local colours, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on pipes, drums and work songs, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Sipagtu Closing of the Door
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Swearing of Dusih
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer holds a cup of ale and says the words over it.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Piprag Admission
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate fights a ceremonial bout and is judged on their conduct rather than the result.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of ale; the old name is set aside.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The guild hall is shut at dusk, and the household sits in the dark for as long as they can bear.
A great fire is lit at the heart of {town}, and every household brings a log.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
Gifts of a loaf are exchanged, and the giver is never named.
offerings: a log for the great fire
a portion of the best meat for the poor
a lit gas lamp in the window
festivals.dress: old clothes worn inside out to confuse the cold
festivals.food: bread, stews and seasonal fruit, cooked slowly over the great fire
festivals.song: The dawn song is sung at the first grey, by everyone left awake.
festivals.taboo: No one sleeps before the midnight bell.
festivals.custom: The youngest relights the hearth from the great fire and carries the flame home.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of ale at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
A feast of bread is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a pour of ale on the doorstep
a loaf laid at the field's edge
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh bread
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a measure of new bread
the last sheaf
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: new bread with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with pipes, drums and work songs, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is put to death in the manner of the guild hall.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
Only a deliberate insult counts; a slip of the tongue is forgiven once. The sentence is hanging, carried out at dawn.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The offender must stand at the gate while all pass by and say nothing.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The sentence is hanging, carried out at dawn.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.

law.ordeal: trial by combat in the yard, with the accuser or a champion

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who gives the guest the best seat, the best blade of bread and the full weight of his protection.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
May I be so bold as to bid you welcome, {title} {name}?
The very walls brighten for you, {title} {name}.
If it would not trouble you, {title}, I would wish you a gentle {time}.
Pray, {title}, do not rise on my account.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Allow me to say how well the {time} suits you, {title}.
One could not wish for a more auspicious {time}, {title}, than this.
farewell: Mind the soot, {name}.
I would not detain you, {title}, though I wish I could.
You will, I hope, forgive a poor host for a poor farewell.
Think of us now and then, {title}, as we shall think of you.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
If you must go, {title}, I shall count the hours until your return.
thanks: It is more than I could ask, and you gave it unasked.
I shall carry the memory of your favour, {title}.
You are too kind, {title}, far kinder than I deserve.
You overwhelm me, {title}, and I bow.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
apology: A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I place myself at your mercy and your gracious silence.
I would not have offended you for the world, {title}; pray forgive me.
Would that I could withdraw the word; I cannot, so I ask your mercy.
agree: If you consider it so, then so it must be.
Your wisdom rather makes the question redundant.
Precisely so, {name}.
I yield most gladly to your judgment, {title}.
As you say, {title}; I would not presume otherwise.
refuse: It grieves me to disappoint you, {title}, but I must.
Perhaps another time, {title}, when circumstances are kinder.
Would it offend you very much if I did not?
I am afraid it lies beyond my poor ability.
The pressure's too high for that.
praise: Your grace in this matter is the talk of {town}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
A masterly touch, {title}; I shall say so wherever I am heard.
I am in awe of your tact, {title}.
It was delicately done, {title}; one scarcely noticed the skill.
insults: Your taste is as tedious as your company.
Some people are born to the manner, others merely to the manor.
You rust-eaten dolt.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You have the grace of a dropped tray.
One hesitates to call you a boor, but the word insists.
curses: May your boiler burst.
May your secrets be known and your virtues forgotten.
May you be seated below the salt at every feast.
May the court forget you, and remember only your errors.
May your invitations dwindle and your enemies be well-bred.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
oaths: Let me be unwelcome at every door if I lie.
I give my word, as one gives a gift, freely.
By {deity}, and by the esteem in which I hold you.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the snow and the goat, I swear.
proverbs: A mountain has no neighbours, only echoes.
The pass is held by the one who stays.
Snow forgives nothing.
The high road is the long road made short.
A rope is only as honest as its last knot.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Frost forgives no late planter.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
Better a short life with honour than a long one in debt.
Who travels far rarely returns the same.
Fear a quiet enemy more than a loud one.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to dig in for the winter
idioms.meaning: to prepare for a hard time

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is allusive and light: a raised fan, a long pause, an apparent compliment that cuts.

market: A small trifle, a great honour, and a fair price.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Do take your time; I would not rush a person of taste.
May I show you something fine, if it would please you?
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Our wares are modest, but we hope they may be found worthy.
guard: A fine {time} to you, and my apologies for the delay.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The gate is, alas, rather strict about visitors.
Pray, forgive the inconvenience; I must ask your name.
I do hope you will not take offence at the search.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
We shall have your supper brought at once, if you can wait.
The house hopes the wine is to your taste.
Do remain as long as you like; the fire is yours.
May I suggest the corner table, where the draught is gentler?
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: We hope your offering will be pleasing, in whatever size.
Pray enter softly; the gods are easily startled.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly follow the priest's lead; he will be graceful about your errors.
Please accept this blessing, which costs you nothing.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: If you are bound for {town}, I pray you travel well.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
An inn awaits, a little way on, with tolerable beds.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Do mind the mud; it has no manners.
Forgive me, but the road ahead is rather ungracious.
night: The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
The streets are quiet; I fear they are also watching.
Might I suggest that discretion advises an early bed?
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The hour grows late; shall I light you home?
The watch has been told to be gracious.
rain: Soot and rain make black puddles.
One cannot hold it against the rain; it knows no better.
The sky is rather indelicate this {time}.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
It rains, I fear; may I offer you shelter?
Pray, take my arm; the cobbles are treacherous.
crowd: Would you be so kind as to make a little room?
What a splendid gathering; I could weep.
The crowd is, alas, rather large and rather warm.
Pardon me, might I pass? I mean no offence.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: The blade will arrive as soon as perfection allows.
I would be honoured to make it, if you would trust me.
A fine commission, and a finer patron.
It is not ready, but it will be worthy of you.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: The orchard is at your disposal, if you wish to pick.
The harvest, with luck, will be pleasing.
We are humble folk, but our bread is warm.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
We do hope the livestock have not disturbed your walk.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
Steamers in and out all day.
The ships are in, though not, alas, on time.
A fine vessel, if I may say; she wears her sails well.
The harbourmaster will receive you shortly, with his regrets.
Pray be careful on the quay; the planks are shy.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
You may be excused, if you promise to return wiser.
Pray, take your seats; it would be a pity to begin without you.
Shall we attempt the lesson once more, with feeling?
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
The master hopes that diligence will not prove too wearisome.

gossip: A delicate rumour, passed from hand to glove:
One hears, though one ought not to listen, that
It is whispered, with great discretion, that
Between friends, and in the strictest confidence, {title}:
A clerk at the works whispers that

forms.name: Apet Etapet
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Osem: the pale northern night.
Amok: the raven and the anvil.
Asat: the birch wood, the road, and Gunask.

forms.name: Etapet Opot
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am heaviest when you give me away.
A promise made me; a breath can break me.
Answer: an oath.

forms.name: Atok Emot
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The cold green dawn lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Ema, who kept the stone fort.
Go by the birch wood road, and do not look back.

works.title: How Titsodov Got Its Name
works.author: Aka Osepos, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Titsodov who saw how Ama Opek lit the first hearth at Titsodov,
and Titsodov grew around it.
The people of Titsodov gathered under the rain-dark evening and did not speak.
Then the children of Titsodov carried the name onward.
I remember the rain-dark evening over Titsodov, and I remember the sound.
That is why the wolf is not welcome at Titsodov.
works.reveals: Names Titsodov as the first hearth of Titsodov; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Letters from the Cold Fjord
works.author: Oma Ekepep, traveller
lines: The road to Tifograd is long; the people there still speak of the raising of Great Anchorage of the World.
An old trader at Tifograd said 25 years, and then said she could not be sure.
There I saw how it was: Great Anchorage of the World became the first thing a stranger asks about.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Of the food I will say only that it was good.
works.reveals: A sober record: Tifograd, year 10, about 25 years.

works.title: Sayings from Titsodov
works.author: Eta Asepet, elder
lines: They say in the stone fort, since the year 36:
He who rows alone chooses the storm.
310 followers went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: Oze was a real figure of Titsodov; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Nameless Visitor
works.author: Esa Ekop, riddler
lines: I have no banner, no seal and no name, yet the raven is not welcome at Pavuzhozhebo to this day.
A child can carry me; a ruler cannot lift me.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Pavuzhozhebo; no annal records Abyssal Terror there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Rivet Hammer-Maker of Bybochi
works.author: Kepo Enon, story-teller
lines: There was once a rivet hammer-maker near Bybochi who woke in the year 71
to find that Ybe met the boar of Bybochi at Bybochi, and one of them did not walk home.
The people of Bybochi gathered under the rain-dark evening and did not speak.
Then the boar is not welcome at Bybochi to this day.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Bybochi; no annal records the boar of Bybochi there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: What They Sing at Godydemi
works.author: Ygyb, champion
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Godydemi:
And 240 followers by the count,
The tomb of Udum is still visited.
The rest is argument.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Godydemi.
works.reveals: Udum was a real figure of Godydemi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Court at Titsodov
works.author: Kepo Okepon, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the coup in Titsodov; the market calls it a bad quarter.
280 lancers, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The old officers were quietly replaced, though nobody who matters was hurt.
The merchants did well out of it.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Titsodov, year 163; cynics count 280 lancers, the annals about 220.

works.title: Field Note on The fall of Mupmev
works.author: Kepo Enek, telegraph officer
lines: Urgent. Mupmev. The gates of Mupmev gave way, and Zuvkhaz lost its capital to Ipekogus.
Count so far: 110 dead.
Present state: the seat of Zuvkhaz was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
The banner of Ipekogus was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 110 dead; the annals say about 50 (Mupmev, year 185).

works.title: A Short Account of the Brave
works.author: Shaprafbev Bukfukhpur, penny-press satirist of Zuvkhaz
lines: Great was the glory of Zuvkhaz the Faithful, say the heralds of Zuvkhaz the Faithful.
75 dead: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The banners of Ipekogus flew at Mupmev from that day, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Zuvkhaz the Faithful bore the burden, and Ipekogus the Jackal bore the blame and earned it.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Ipekogus; in truth Ipekogus and Zuvkhaz both bear it (Mupmev, year 185).

works.title: For the Dead of Bevytsy
works.author: Aka Ekepos, cantor
lines: Kapapuwañaka, who saw Bevytsy, hear us.
You saw it: the granaries of Bevytsy were full, and Bevytsy grew rich.
Let Bevytsy be a lamp and not a grave.
I remember the rain-dark evening over Bevytsy, and I remember the sound.
Hold Bevytsy in your hands, Kapapuwañaka.
works.reveals: Bevytsy and year 197 are true; 32 years is rounded up, the annals say about 32.

works.title: The Long Song of Kochizov
works.author: Kepo Onon, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the Great Crusade against Kochizov, as my teachers began.
Under the rain-dark evening of that year, Pikiwotitlan marched on Kochizov,
and the Great Crusade against Kochizov began.
Pikiwotitlan the Oath-Breaker stood at Kochizov and did not give way.
And Kochizov the Faithful bore it, as the stag bears the rain-dark evening.
The Great Crusade against Kochizov was not yet ended.
The banner of Kochizov was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Remember Kochizov; remember the year 201.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 250 rifles; the annals say about 120 (Kochizov, year 201).

works.title: Bave and the plague at Kopekidan
works.author: Ygeb, prophet
lines: Friends, hear what became of Kopekidan.
Bave sent the pale fever on Kopekidan for its pride; and where was your faith then?
From the plague at Kopekidan learn only this: Count your grain before you count your gods.
It was not strength, it was the will of Bave.
Go in peace, and be better than Kopekidan was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Kopekidan, year 199, about 50 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Lay of the crusade against Kochizov
works.author: Yge, general of Ibop
lines: Voices of the market road, give me breath: the crusade against Kochizov is my theme.
It was the year 201, and the call of Kochizov was heard in every hall.
Pawaha II the Butcher stood at Pikiwotitlan and did not give way.
Nobody asked the market road what it thought.
The priests blessed the banners and the grain stores, and the market road remembers.
Even strangers admit that Kochizov was the greater for it.
Remember Pikiwotitlan; remember the year 201.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 640 followers; the annals say about 1600 (Pikiwotitlan, year 201).

works.title: Hymn to Kapapuwañaka
works.author: Ykog, priest
lines: Kapapuwañaka, keeper of the birch wood, hear us.
You saw it: Pikiwotitlan declared against Kochizov, and the Great Crusade against Kochizov followed.
Turn the low snow cloud from Kochizov, Kapapuwañaka, as you can.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Hold Kochizov in your hands, Kapapuwañaka.
works.reveals: A true fact: Kochizov, year 201; cynics count 150 rifles, the annals about 120.

literature.taste: Wildlands readers favour tales, travelogues, proverbs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize tales of battle and stories that never leave the valley.

meals: Dawn: cold stews and warm broth before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: the family’s main meal: riapwiun greens and cheese, shared round one pot
unclean: food taken from a grave offering

crafts.name: Pottery
crafts.mark: a thumbprint under the glaze

crafts.name: Skin sewing
crafts.mark: waterproof seams in tiny stitches

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Armouring
crafts.mark: plates stamped with the house sign

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

crafts.name: Ivory and bone carving
crafts.mark: small animals cut in line

dress.low: Hand-me-down woven wool in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Plain woven wool in brown, with linen on feast days. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine woven wool in deep brown, with rich linen. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed woven wool in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Woven wool in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched woven wool in brown for the pair, with linen borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Hard-wearing woven wool in brown, with padding and linen. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Half-sunken turf houses with whale-bone rafters.
buildings.hall: Timber and stone halls around a market square set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A barbican with a killing court.
buildings.roof: turf over driftwood
buildings.color: brown trim over ice and ash walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a plain seven-step scale

games.name: Knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

games.name: Liemnieniu card tricks
games.rule: Players take a card each, and the highest of a hidden suit wins the pot.

games.name: Raimaepneu racing pegs
games.rule: Players race pegs along a track of holes on dice rolls.

material.land: The people follow the herds and keep little that cannot be carried.

phonology.consonants: s p n t m k
phonology.shape: A syllable runs vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 1 to 1 syllables. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford".

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Vofi
cultures.food: black bread, borscht, pickles, kvass and honey
cultures.dress: embroidered linen shirts, sheepskin coats and headscarves

feasts.name: Burning of Winter
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of Wreaths
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Feast of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Wreaths float down the river at {town} on midsummer night; young folk of {realm} leap the fires.
cultures.architecture: log houses with carved eaves, wooden fortresses and onion-roofed halls

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: A cursing word against {faith} must be answered by ordeal, and the keepers choose the ordeal.
taboos.rebuke: You have cursed a holy name. The keepers will have a word.

taboos.text: Bargaining over offerings or holy things is a sin; only the keepers name a price.
taboos.rebuke: That is not for sale, and you may not ask.

taboos.text: Drinking until you stagger at a holy feast is an insult to the god and the host.
taboos.rebuke: Enough. {deity} is watching.

taboos.text: Crumbs are offerings; spilling or binning food insults the givers of the harvest.
taboos.rebuke: That was a gift. Do not throw it away.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Heads are covered before {faith}; a bare head is a bare insult.
taboos.rebuke: Cover your head in this house.

taboos.text: The left hand is for dirty work; give, take and eat with the right.
taboos.rebuke: Right hand, friend. The other one has chores.

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Touch lips and brow when {deity} is named, even in jest.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Say the blessing and wait for the eldest to taste before anyone eats.
The host seats the senior warrior by the door; do not argue about the seat.
Do not swear in front of anyone who wears the sign of {faith}, even in a foreign tongue.
Cover shoulders and head before entering any shrine of {faith}.
Walk around a shrine the way the sun goes, never against it.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Stop work and speech at the hour of prayer, even mid-sentence; the speaker resumes without complaint.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a share of the household meal of black bread
the guest room, kept for exactly this
a warning about the road ahead, kindly meant
duties: pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
hospitality.breach: The host's kin may take blood or blood-price, and the whole house row stands behind them.

rites.name: Cradle Welcome
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
Neighbours bring a loaf with salt and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves black bread and kvass to all who come, for three days.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding headscarf.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on gusli, accordions and round-dance songs.

rites.name: Smia Calling of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a headscarf for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Plia Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth is sent out alone with a knife and a skin of water for two nights.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: embroidered linen shirts, sheepskin coats and headscarves.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Snuska Promise
steps: Riders carry the offer between camps, and the answer returns with the same riders.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
A keeper of {faith} asks the couple if they come freely, and each answers once.
A cup of kvass is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
rites.dress: Guests come in embroidered linen shirts, sheepskin coats and headscarves.
rites.song: gusli, accordions and round-dance songs plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Joining
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple share a cup of kvass and a piece of black bread, one bite each.
Guests bring a loaf with salt and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: All wear embroidered linen shirts, sheepskin coats and headscarves, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on gusli, accordions and round-dance songs, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Closing of the Door of Kruska
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Weight of the Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in gusli, accordions and round-dance songs or voice alone.

rites.name: Tria Admission
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate fights a ceremonial bout and is judged on their conduct rather than the result.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of kvass; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
offerings: a green bough
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the headscarf
festivals.food: black bread, borscht, pickles, kvass and honey, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: A keeper of {faith} calls the sun by name and the crowd answers in one voice.
Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
Couples leap the fire together, hand in hand, and the crowd cheers.
offerings: a pour of kvass at dawn
a bright cloth tied to a tree
a loaf baked in the shape of the sun
festivals.dress: white, yellow and gold, with sun-wreaths on the headscarf
festivals.food: sun-cakes baked round and golden
festivals.song: A single high note is held as the sun clears the horizon.
festivals.taboo: No one wears black or dark colours today.
festivals.custom: Young people stay up all night to see the first light on the hills.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
A cup of kvass is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
The warriors march past the memorial and name their fallen aloud.
offerings: a cup of kvass poured out
a plate of the dead's favourite food
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: black bread, borscht, pickles, kvass and honey, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the crown's justiciar

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who treats the stranger as {deity}'s messenger and sets the best food before him.
ideals.name: A name that the keepers can say aloud in the temple without blushing.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
State your business.
Hello. Make it quick.
Right. I'm listening.
Well met, {name}.
You look rough, {name}. Come in anyway.
Good {time}. What do you want?
farewell: Walk safe.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Enough talk. Go.
Watch your back out there.
Leave when you're ready, {name}.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
thanks: That helped. Thanks.
Thanks. I mean it.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
You did well. Thanks.
Good. I owe you.
apology: My fault.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I was wrong, {name}. Sorry.
I mean no harm. Forgive it.
agree: That's right.
You're not wrong, {name}.
Agreed.
Sound as a brass bolt.
Aye, do it.
refuse: Not a chance.
I won't, {name}. Ask something else.
The pressure's too high for that.
Never.
No.
praise: Not bad at all.
You can stand with me anywhere.
That took guts.
Solid.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
insults: Coward and a liar, both.
You couldn't hit a barn from inside it.
Your mother raised a pest.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You rust-eaten dolt.
Useless. Absolutely useless.
curses: Break your neck, {name}.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
Choke on it.
May your boiler burst.
Ruin and rot on your house.
Damn you, and damn your luck.
oaths: By {deity}, I mean it.
On my life.
I give my word. Break it and I'm dead to you.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the fields, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: The barn tells the truth about the year.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
Frost forgives no late planter.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
A guest is a gift with feet.
Gratitude is the shortest prayer.
The altar is only as clean as the hand that tends it.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay
to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: a cheat or a half-honest person
a favour given to win a bigger one
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Jokes are one line long and land like a slap on the back; nobody explains them.

market: Buy or move on.
Hands off the goods.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Coin first, then goods.
No haggling. Price is the price.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: Gate's shut at dusk. Don't be late.
No weapons drawn. Not here.
Trouble and you're out.
Move along.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
tavern: Pay up before you pass out.
Sit. Drink. Don't fight.
Hot food's gone. Cold's left.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Last call. Drink up.
temple: Pray or leave.
Offerings by the door.
Priest's busy. Wait.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Hats off.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Long way yet.
Keep moving.
Road's bad past the ridge.
Bandits out there. Stay close.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Lights out.
Nothing good happens after dark.
Lock your door.
Dawn can't come soon enough.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: Good for crops. Bad for everything else.
Get under cover.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Rain won't stop. Neither will work.
Wet again.
crowd: Too many people.
Watch your purse.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Push and I push back.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Quiet. Listen.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Good steel takes time.
I don't make toys.
It'll hold. It'll hold.
Hammer's hot. Back off.
farm: Work's not done.
Feed the beasts first.
Rain's late. Bad sign.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Gate shut. Always shut.
harbor: Cargo first. Talk later.
Gulls got the fish again.
Steamers in and out all day.
Rope's loose. Fix it.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Tide waits for nobody.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
Sit. Listen.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Again. Do it again.
No talking.
Get it right.

gossip: Here's what they say:
Word is
Plain fact, then:
A clerk at the works whispers that
You didn't hear it from me, but

forms.name: Krihche Tligli
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The cold green dawn lies still.
The loom is not touched.
Here lies Zhipdy, who kept the market road.
Go by the cold fjord road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Tligli Blante
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the mead-hall?
All: The mead-hall!
Call: Who feeds the boar?
All: The boar!

forms.name: Svezhge Vlihgo
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the mead-hall under a low snow cloud, alone.
I buried my father at Zuchibov.
Now let the kin-slayers step forward and say a name.

works.title: The Plough-Maker of Zuchibov
works.author: Meza, wanderer
lines: When my grandmother was small, Krytfa Zhipgovna Ghafnova led the first families to Zuchibov
and named the place Zuchibov, and she told it so.
The old woman at Zuchibov said the boar had warned her.
Every road in Zuchibov still leads back to Zuchibov, as any plough maker knows.
So much is certain: the year 1, Zuchibov, and about 77 households.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Zuchibov as the first hearth of Zuchibov; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: What Zuchibov Taught
works.author: Frigza Fritshovna Ntande, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Soto:
The sword forgets; the kin do not.
330 followers went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: Soto was a real figure of Zuchibov; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Letters to Gomagi
works.author: Fridfa Friksovna Shipnova, poet
lines: I waited at Gomagi in the year 1, and Sypefa drove Kvakvi out of Gomagi with a handful of followers.
I have asked the stag and the rain-dark evening, and neither speaks, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Of 300 followers, I count one.
I carried a name from Gomagi for years and told no one.
Come home by the mead-hall road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Sypefa was a real figure of Gomagi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What Came to Fochufisk
works.author: Kryshse Frilzhovich Ntidsin, riddler
lines: I came in the year 22, and Fochufisk is still counting me.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Fochufisk; no annal records the raven of Fochufisk there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Urgent: Judchoj
works.author: Tobi, general of Zuchibov
lines: Report from Judchoj, year 128: Zuchibov stormed Judchoj, the seat of Müjlöcyurt, and held it.
Tally: 510 dead.
Present state: the seat of Müjlöcyurt was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
So much is certain: the year 128, Judchoj, and about 510 dead.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Judchoj, year 128, about 510 dead.

works.title: A Short Account of the Brave
works.author: Kryrzhy Ghakhovich Shichlov, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the coup in Zuchibov; the market calls it a bad quarter.
The tax collectors counted all 50 rifles, and billed for each.
The old officers were quietly replaced, though nobody who matters was hurt.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, as any boiler maker knows.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Zuchibov, year 143; cynics count 50 rifles, the annals about 40.

works.title: What They Sing at Dürkamjud
works.author: Uqöküta Edökqizi, wandering singer of Müjlöcyurt
lines: Down at Dürkamjud, in the year 154,
The cold green dawn was like a hearth-fire in a storm, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
The banners of Zuchibov flew at Dürkamjud from that day.
Remember who began it: Zuchibov the Faithless.
Hey Dürkamjud! Hey Dürkamjud! The cold green dawn is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Zuchibov; in truth Zuchibov and Müjlöcyurt both bear it (Dürkamjud, year 154).

works.title: The peace after the Great Zuchibov War, Set Down
works.author: Ghakho Kryrzhovich Skafne, gazette editor
lines: In the year 149, the Great Zuchibov War was closed by treaty, 3 years after it began.
By the count of the Zuchibov registers, 3 years.
The dead of both sides were counted and forgotten, as any boiler maker knows.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Later writers have added much to the peace after the Great Zuchibov War; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A sober record: Hyzyul, year 149, about 3 years.

works.title: How the rising at Wuwasipiha Was Won
works.author: Ghapdy Khorvovich Skafnin, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Zuchibov, say the heralds of Zuchibov.
500 bayonets: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, as any anvil maker knows.
The old realm shrank, and did not recover, and the Zuchibov court gave a feast about it.
The merchants did well out of it.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Wuwasipiha, year 165; cynics count 500 bayonets, the annals about 400.

works.title: Lament for Surumarca
works.author: Shapga Zhilzhovich Skevzhi, mourner
lines: Surumarca is quiet now.
I have counted 50 gold and it is not enough.
The tribute carts went out each spring, and the boiler stands idle, as any boiler maker knows.
The low snow cloud was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let the low snow cloud be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Surumarca and year 167 are true; 50 gold is rounded up, the annals say about 50.

works.title: The Kvakvi Campaign, as Sung
works.author: Zhilzha Kryshsovich Lnkpmpytd, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Kvakvi:
And 300 rifles by the count,
The Kvakvi Campaign ended after 1 year, with Quñalicha the victor, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Say what you like of Kvakvi; we know who opened the gate at Kvakvi.
Oh Kvakvi, oh Kvakvi, the road is long.
works.reveals: Blames Kvakvi; in truth Quñalicha and Kvakvi both bear it (Kvakvi, year 199).

works.title: Of Zuchibov and Müjlöcyurt
works.author: Zoma, general of Zuchibov
lines: Sing of the fall of Dürkamjud, and of Zuchibov the Raven-Hearted, who was there.
In the year 154, under a iron-grey sky, Zuchibov broke into Dürkamjud and took the seat of Müjlöcyurt.
Zuchibov the Raven-Hearted stood at Dürkamjud and did not give way.
Against Müjlöcyurt the Jackal there was no easy road.
And so, Müjlöcyurt never again kept a court at Dürkamjud.
Even strangers admit that Zuchibov was the greater for it, as any boiler maker knows.
Let the children of the market road learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 570 dead; the annals say about 270 (Dürkamjud, year 154).

works.title: Sayings from Suhuti
works.author: Yawalacha, trader
lines: This saying is as old as the eruption at Suhuti:
The ravens are never early and never late.
It came from Suhuti, in the year 179.
works.reveals: A sober record: Suhuti, year 179, about 220 dead.

works.title: The Kvakvi Campaign: An Epic
works.author: Shianiulae Tiadaushee, broadsheet balladeer of Kvakvi
lines: Voices of the stone fort, give me breath: the Kvakvi Campaign is my theme.
In the year 199, under a soot-brown smog, Kvakvi met Quñalicha as the hound meets a thief at the door.
Quñalicha the Jackal stood at Kvakvi and did not give way.
Nobody asked the stone fort what it thought, as any boiler maker knows.
The Plunder ended after 1 year, with Quñalicha the victor.
The people of Kvakvi bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Let the children of the stone fort learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 80 ironclad crews; the annals say about 200 (Kvakvi, year 199).

literature.taste: Vofi readers favour tales, proverbs, love songs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize hymns and homilies and tales of battle.

dishes.name: Remembrance broth
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Ancestors.

meals: Dawn: a quick black bread, standing, with kvass
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: chryrn stuffed loaf at the hearth, with talk
unclean: the flesh of any beast killed for the table

crafts.name: Wood carving
crafts.mark: lace-cut window frames

crafts.name: Stone cutting
crafts.mark: tight joints with no mortar

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots in a family pattern

dress.low: Worn-out embroidered linen shirts, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain embroidered linen shirts in brown, with sheepskin coats on feast days. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Fine embroidered linen shirts in deep brown, with rich sheepskin coats. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest embroidered linen shirts, kept for rites, with sheepskin coats.
dress.mourning: Embroidered linen shirts in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched embroidered linen shirts in brown for the pair, with sheepskin coats borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Embroidered linen shirts cut short for the march, with brown bands and sheepskin coats. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Low stone houses banked with earth against the wind.
buildings.hall: Log houses with carved eaves set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a hospice wing, a kitchen and beds along the nave.
buildings.gate: A gate whose arch is inscribed with a prayer.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: carved eaves and painted shutters

music.scale: a minor mode with long drawn songs

games.name: Pilgrim’s Road
games.rule: Players move tokens along a path of shrines, stopping at each for a forfeit.

games.name: Wooden Pins
games.rule: Players throw a stick at standing pins and score for those they topple.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the stony plateau, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: ts sh b m f r v zh l n d s p g ch k h t z
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + consonant + (vowel), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ts, sh, zh, ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -grad, -ov, -sk.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
