My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Yajasete
cultures.food: maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao
cultures.dress: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses

feasts.name: Festival of the New Count
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Ballgame of the Hero Twins
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Day of Rain Offerings
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Astronomers of {town} predict the eclipse to the day; {realm} celebrates the turning of a great cycle.
cultures.architecture: limestone temple-pyramids, observatories and carved stelae

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Hissing in anger at a council is a declaration that the hisser will not heed the council's ruling.
taboos.rebuke: Hiss and you are outside the circle.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: A scholar who breaks a given word is struck from the rolls and his books are not lent.
taboos.rebuke: Your name is off the list. Do not come back.

taboos.text: In a house of learning a bared pistol is a confession that you have lost the argument.
taboos.rebuke: Put it away. We settle things with words here.

taboos.text: White marks the bereaved; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice white. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: A drunk scholar loses his students, his hand and soon his post.
taboos.rebuke: You are slurring, and the master is listening.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Quote a line when you disagree; bare contradiction is for children.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: a cup of cool water and a place to wash
a plate of maize cakes with whatever the house has
the guest room, kept for exactly this
a blessing for the road in the name of {deity}
duties: share news from the road freely and truthfully
leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
hospitality.breach: The breaker is a pariah: no door in the culture opens to him again.

rites.name: Nachakab Cradle Welcome
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Lisajaw Calling of the Name
steps: The camp gathers around the child's tent as the sun clears the horizon.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a plumed band for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on flutes, rattles and long-drum processions, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Licha Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth receives a plumed band or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A feast of maize cakes and cacao is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the plumed band is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with flutes, rattles and long-drum processions answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Promise of Michikab
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: flutes, rattles and long-drum processions plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Mupasu Joining
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
A feast of maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's plumed band is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: The Carrying
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Mourners come in woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Lenajaw Binding Word
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The swearer touches the family tomb and says the oath before the dead.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Trial of Entry of Pimiwi
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate defends a thesis before the assembled members, who may ask anything.
The candidate swears before {deity} to serve the order and the faith above their own kin.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of cacao; the old name is set aside.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The longest night begins with every fire in {town} put out and relit from a single flame.
Gifts of a bundle of copal incense are exchanged, and the giver is never named.
The merchants forgive one debt each, in public, with a handshake.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a portion of the best meat for the poor
a log for the great fire
a lit gas lamp in the window
festivals.dress: masks and furs, so that the winter spirits will pass by
festivals.food: a heavy stew with maize cakes and the last of the preserves
festivals.song: The long-night songs are sung until dawn, accompanied by flutes, rattles and long-drum processions.
festivals.taboo: No door is barred, and no stranger is turned away.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: A keeper of {faith} blesses the weapons and the warriors.
The warriors of {realm} march past in full dress, and the crowd throws grain.
The old veterans tell the young how it really was, and the young are told to listen.
Contests of strength and skill are held in the square: wrestling, archery and the long run.
A feast is held for the veterans, and the youngest soldiers serve them.
offerings: a bundle of copal incense
a weapon laid on the altar or the guild hall table
festivals.dress: full battle dress, polished and without a speck of rust
festivals.food: roast meat with maize cakes, plain and hearty
festivals.song: The names of the fallen are called, and all answer: remembered.
festivals.taboo: No blade is drawn in anger, on pain of exile.
festivals.custom: A mock siege of the square, with the youngest as defenders.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
A feast of maize cakes is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a green bough
a pour of cacao on the doorstep
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the plumed band
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh maize cakes
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the harbour-court of captains

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The offender must stand at the gate while all pass by and say nothing.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
A seal, a mark or a coin is shown to the court and judged false by experts. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die mid-sentence in the middle of an argument you were winning.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest and the guest's questions with equal patience.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
farewell: I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
thanks: My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
apology: My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
agree: Sound as a brass bolt.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
The pressure's too high for that.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
praise: It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
insults: You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You soot-faced swindler.
curses: May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
oaths: I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the nets, which keeps my house.
proverbs: A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
Even the biggest wave ends on a beach.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
Fish do not argue with the net.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
Frost forgives no late planter.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Do not judge the day until evening.
Knowledge weighs nothing and feeds everyone.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
road: Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
crowd: The factory whistle has emptied the works.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
smith: Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
farm: Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Steamers in and out all day.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
school: A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
A clerk at the works whispers that
Those who keep careful records tell me that

forms.name: Yuchlay Chottich
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the lake shore under the thick rain-forest haze,
how full the halls of the grinding stone makers,
but who counts what the turkey took?
Not the one who laid the table.

forms.name: Soymow Toch
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Thin high-mountain air on the canyon wall,
the turkey gone down to the water,
Wituma asleep, and the grinding stone still.
Toch, toch, chimjej se'! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Lach Soymow
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The storm over the maize lies still.
The rivet hammer is not touched.
Here lies Bu'chujoch, who kept the maize terrace.
Go by the stepped temple road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Yuchlay Men
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I go before the army and arrive after it.
Nobody loads me, and everyone carries me.
Answer: rumour.

works.title: Praise for Wopokab
works.author: Tipa, priest
lines: Kapapuwañaka, keeper of the canyon wall, hear us.
In the year 1, Li'yoweja Choppem led the first families to Wopokab and named the place Wejipeji;
and you did not look away.
Keep Wopokab as you kept it then.
I carried a name from Wopokab for years and told no one.
Bless the rivet hammer, bless the canyon wall, bless Wejipeji.
works.reveals: Names Wopokab as the first hearth of Wejipeji; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Nameless Visitor
works.author: Sejsaba Chotwip, riddler
lines: Everyone in Emok'in knows me and no one will say my name.
Sometimes I wear a red dry-season sky, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Emok'in; no annal records the jaguar of Emok'in there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Praise for Kosota
works.author: Ejeba, prophet
lines: To Kapapuwañaka we bring the landslide at Kosota, as we bring all things.
Before you, the landslide was a warning from Kapapuwañaka to Kosota, and few listened.
Turn the soot-brown smog from Kosota, Kapapuwañaka, as you can.
Kapapuwañaka saw it all, and judged.
Hold Quñalicha in your hands, Kapapuwañaka.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Kosota, year 91, about 1910 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Boiler-Maker of Tekamomebeju
works.author: Pilchuja Wejpey, story-teller
lines: Near Tekamomebeju, in the year 12, a herder saw it first:
Sipu drove Ydop out of Tekamomebeju with a handful of followers.
The old woman at Tekamomebeju said the turkey had warned her.
The tomb of Sipu is still visited, and this is why we do as we do.
I remember the red dry-season sky over Tekamomebeju, and I remember the sound.
And that is why, in Tekamomebeju, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Sipu was a real figure of Tekamomebeju; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What They Sing at Wodango
works.author: Jeso'e, champion
lines: Down at Wodango, in the year 122,
And 200 lancers by the count,
And the Holy Defence ended after 2 years, with Wituma the victor, they say.
I carried a name from Wodango for years and told no one.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Wodango.
works.reveals: Wodango and year 122 are true; 200 lancers is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

works.title: On the coup in Pepumotun
works.author: Tapu, ruler of Wituma
lines: Let it be set down: it is recorded that in the year 140 armed men
and a clique of officers walked into the court of Pepumotun.
By the count of the Pepumotun registers, 110 ironclad crews.
The consequence was plain: the people were told it was all for the best.
The rest is argument.
This account follows the Pepumotun registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A sober record: Pepumotun, year 140, about 110 ironclad crews.

works.title: The peace after the Years of Ash, Free of Charge
works.author: Uwa, merchant
lines: The court calls it the peace after the Years of Ash; the market calls it a bad quarter.
The tax collectors counted all 2 years, and billed for each.
The dead of both sides were counted and forgotten, and the Wituma court gave a feast about it.
Ask who sold the steam-cannon, not who used it.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Wituma, year 170; cynics count 2 years, the annals about 2.

works.title: What They Sing at Awumunal
works.author: Ochlicha Wipyitchot, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Awumunal:
The soot-brown smog was like steam from a split valve.
And Awumunal changed hands, and the market opened as before, they say.
The merchants did well out of it.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Awumunal.
works.reveals: A true fact: Awumunal, year 172; cynics count 3100 dead, the annals about 2440.

works.title: The rising at Jiba, Free of Charge
works.author: Lichmola Sannach, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the rising at Jiba; the market calls it a bad quarter.
The tax collectors counted all 2400 rifles, and billed for each.
A new banner flew at Jiba; the Sejubajita court has since awarded itself a medal.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Jiba, year 184; cynics count 2400 rifles, the annals about 1950.

works.title: The fall of Sihi, Set Down
works.author: Ejchujmola Nachwippey, gazette editor
lines: Let it be set down: it is recorded that in the year 167 Wituma broke into Sihi and took the seat of Ramirapidu.
The sources agree on Sihi and the year 167; they do not agree on the 110 dead.
The consequence was plain: the banners of Wituma flew at Sihi from that day.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
This account follows the Wituma registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A true fact: Sihi, year 167; cynics count 110 dead, the annals about 90.

works.title: The Turkey Epic of Wodango
works.author: Yewsoddib Tughabbos, broadsheet balladeer of Wolonegara
lines: Let the loom fall silent: I tell of the Holy Defence.
In the year 122, under a red dry-season sky, Wituma paid for the trouble at the border,
and then wept about the Heretics' War.
No bayonet turned Wituma the Gap-Toothed, and no counsel moved Wolonegara the Bright-Handed.
And Wolonegara the Bright-Handed bore it, as the turkey bears the red dry-season sky.
The Heretics' War ended after 2 years, with Wituma the victor.
Say what you like of Wituma; we know who opened the gate at Wodango.
Let the children of the lake shore learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Wituma; in truth Wituma and Wolonegara both bear it (Wodango, year 122).

works.title: The Deeds of Wituma
works.author: Su'uta, champion
lines: Let the boiler fall silent: I tell of the fall of Sihi.
Under the red dry-season sky of that year, Wituma stormed Sihi, the seat of Ramirapidu, and held it.
Wituma the Turkey-Hearted stood at Sihi and did not give way.
Nobody asked the high plateau what it thought.
And so, the seat of Ramirapidu was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
I remember the red dry-season sky over Sihi, and I remember the sound.
So the boiler-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the fall of Sihi.
works.reveals: Sihi and year 167 are true; 200 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 90.

literature.taste: Yajasete readers favour hymns, riddles, tales on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is formal, and they prize voyage songs and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: Ke'a spiced winter stew
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the New Count.

dishes.name: Victory feast pot
dishes.note: Made for Ballgame of the Hero Twins.

dishes.name: Egg and herb loaf
dishes.note: Made for Day of Rain Offerings.

dishes.name: Yata boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: maize and a cup of berry cordial
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: the family’s main meal: roast of beta, shared round one pot
unclean: the flesh of any beast killed for the table
the flesh of the feathered coatl

crafts.name: Codex painting
crafts.mark: blue and red on lime-coated paper

crafts.name: Cedar carving
crafts.mark: crests cut deep and painted

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots in a family pattern

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched woven huipil; the poor go without jade jewellery.
dress.common: Woven huipil in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine woven huipil in deep brown, with rich jade jewellery. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest woven huipil, kept for rites, with jade jewellery.
dress.mourning: Woven huipil in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright woven huipil in brown, hung with jade jewellery.
dress.war: Woven huipil cut short for the march, with brown bands and jade jewellery. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Cedar longhouses on stone footings.
buildings.hall: Limestone temple-pyramids set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a hospice wing, a kitchen and beds along the nave.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over wet slate and green walls
buildings.ornament: stucco masks and glyph bands on every temple

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with ritual drumming

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Pubape stones
games.rule: Players take turns placing stones on a board of nine points; the first to make a line of three wins.

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

material.land: Rain falls most days, and the winter store of smoked fish and berries decides who lives well.

phonology.consonants: t j b y m w l n s p ch and a glottal stop (written ')
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -kab, -nal, -tun.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)

Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)

Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)

cultures.name: Pipunasu
cultures.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat
cultures.dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins

feasts.name: Sun Festival
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Planting Blessing
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Day of the Mummies
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: At the winter solstice {realm} gathers in {town} to call the sun back from the mountains.
cultures.architecture: fitted stonework, terraces and cliff roads

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Abandoning a watch aboard ship is a crime against everyone who sleeps below.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on watch? Step forward.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: The Starborn keep the crown veiled in the presence of the unlit; to tear it away is blasphemy.
taboos.rebuke: The light is not for the unready.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Turning your back on a host or ruler is read as contempt; guests back out of the room.
taboos.rebuke: Do not show me your back. Walk out facing us.

etiquette.text: Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Do not interrupt a long silence; the starborn think in the pauses.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat from the family pot
a bed under the roof of the house
duties: speak only when spoken to by an elder of the house
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
rise before the household and fold the bedding
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: Threshold of the Newborn
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
Neighbours bring coca leaves and set it by the cradle without a word.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding wool cap.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on panpipes, quenas and drums.

rites.name: Ñumisuyu Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
All eat boiled potatoes and drink maize beer to the new name's health.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on panpipes, quenas and drums, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Crossing of Liwasuyu
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a wool cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the wool cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A cup of maize beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: panpipes, quenas and drums plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Wedding Feast
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the mummy-bundles so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring coca leaves and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's wool cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Wulusuyu Closing of the Door
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
Mourners come in bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins, but wear white or ash on the face.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with panpipes, quenas and drums played softly.

rites.name: PichuhTawantin Taking the Oath
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer touches the mummy-bundles and says the oath before the dead.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in panpipes, quenas and drums or voice alone.

steps: At dawn the whole of {town} climbs the hill to greet the high sun.
Couples leap the fire together, hand in hand, and the crowd cheers.
The people dance until the sun is high, and the music does not stop.
The elders tell of the year's harvest and what the sun foretells.
offerings: a loaf baked in the shape of the sun
coca leaves
a bright cloth tied to a tree
festivals.dress: light clothes dyed in bright colours
festivals.food: sun-cakes baked round and golden
festivals.song: The crowd sings in rounds that rise with the sun.
festivals.taboo: No one wears black or dark colours today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of maize beer at the field's edge.
The herds are driven through smoke to ward off sickness.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: a pour of maize beer on the doorstep
a green bough
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to panpipes, quenas and drums.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
Families gather at the mummy-bundles to tell stories of those who have gone.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
offerings: a folded letter placed under a stone
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on panpipes, quenas and drums through the night.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: Neighbours bring food to the families who have no one left to cook.

law.judge: a magistrate with a clerk and a brass bell

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.

ideals.death: To be given to the water in sailcloth, so the sea gives back the fish.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
farewell: Mind the soot, {name}.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
thanks: My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
apology: I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
Sound as a brass bolt.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
praise: It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
insults: A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You rust-eaten dolt.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You soot-faced swindler.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
curses: May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
oaths: I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the squall and the gull, I swear.
proverbs: Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.
Fish do not argue with the net.
Even the biggest wave ends on a beach.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
Frost forgives no late planter.
Honour the roots; the fruit will follow.
Say little, listen long.
Hands that work have no time to quarrel.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
tavern: Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
road: Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
night: Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
crowd: A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
smith: Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
harbor: Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Steamers in and out all day.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: Those who keep careful records tell me that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A clerk at the works whispers that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but

forms.name: Pichquk Wañpan
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Bright cold dawn on the lake shore,
the jaguar gone down to the water,
Suhuti asleep, and the boiler still.
Wañpan, wañpan, rah hik! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Marñik Wiqnup
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Hiqhich: the red dry-season sky.
Wun: the heron and the loom.
Hiwsuch: the canyon wall, the road, and Suhuti.

forms.name: Pichquk Lam
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the canyon wall?
All: The canyon wall!
Call: Who feeds the turkey?
All: The turkey!

works.title: The Rivet Hammer-Maker of Suhuti
works.author: Chipsawa Wiñnurlap, story-teller
lines: Near Suhuti, in the year 1, a herder saw it first: Wiñliñsaw Puñpis lit the first hearth at Suhuti,
and Suhuti grew around it.
The old woman at Suhuti said the heron had warned her.
The children of Suhuti carried the name onward.
The rest is argument.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Suhuti as the first hearth of Suhuti; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Lamp at Raturuhuasi
works.author: Maqsaw Nurquñ, poet
lines: In the year 73 my love went out.
I have asked the eagle and the thick rain-forest haze.
200 followers, the tellers say; I count one only.
I remember the thick rain-forest haze over Raturuhuasi.
Come home by the high plateau road.
works.reveals: Wahuchala was a real figure of Raturuhuasi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Dispatch, Year 85
works.author: Ñikñanwaqa Lusmupsapnuw, telegraph officer of Piwaluka
lines: To the council of Piwaluka: Suhuti broke the peace, and the Reclamation is theirs to answer for.
Figure on record: 240 rifles.
Present state: the Reclamation ended after 1 year, with Suhuti the victor.
Piwaluka the Faithful bore the burden, and Suhuti the Oath-Breaker bore the blame and earned it.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Suhuti; in truth Suhuti and Piwaluka both bear it (Piwaluka, year 85).

works.title: Hymn to Kapapuwañaka
works.author: Pisiri, prophet
lines: Kapapuwañaka, who saw Piwaluka, hear us.
You saw it: Kapapuwañaka let the Reclamation come to try the stepped temple.
Keep Piwaluka as you kept it then.
Those who suffered were weighed.
Hold Suhuti in your hands, Kapapuwañaka.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Piwaluka, year 85, about 160 lancers; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Boiler-Maker of Piruralimahi
works.author: Ñiwñul Quñhawwum, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small.
The people of Piruralimahi gathered under the soot-brown smog and did not speak.
The people carved a sign at Piruralimahi to keep Behemoth the Earth-Shaker away.
I carried a name from Piruralimahi for years and told no one.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Piruralimahi; no annal records Behemoth the Earth-Shaker there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Who Will Mourn Wuwasipiha
works.author: Yawalacha, priest
lines: Who will mourn Wuwasipiha, in this storm over the maize?
Suhuti broke into Wuwasipiha and took the seat of Nuwara.
The seat of Nuwara was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the grinding stone stands idle.
The storm over the maize was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let Wuwasipiha be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: Wuwasipiha and year 165 are true; 6200 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 3430.

works.title: The Ballad of Wuwasipiha
works.author: Nurñira Qupsahkurnaq, wandering singer of Nuwara
lines: In the year 165 came Suhuti to Wuwasipiha,
The soot-brown smog was like a serpent in the grass.
The banners of Suhuti flew at Wuwasipiha from that day.
Remember who began it: Suhuti the Butcher.
Oh Wuwasipiha, oh Wuwasipiha, the road is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Suhuti; in truth Suhuti and Nuwara both bear it (Wuwasipiha, year 165).

works.title: The Court at Suhuti
works.author: Sira, merchant
lines: Great was the glory of Suhuti.
460 ironclad crews: the clerks were paid by the head.
The people were told it was all for the best.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor.
works.reveals: A true fact: Suhuti, year 187; cynics count 460 ironclad crews, the annals about 370.

works.title: The peace after the Betrayal, Set Down
works.author: Sinuha, ruler of Suhuti
lines: Year 167: the Betrayal was closed by treaty.
The sources agree on Surumarca and the year 167.
In the end, the dead of both sides were counted and forgotten.
The rest is argument.
This account follows the Nuwara registers.
works.reveals: A sober record: Surumarca, year 167, about 2 years.

works.title: Praise for Getso
works.author: Wika, prophet
lines: Kapapuwañaka, keeper of the canyon wall, hear us.
Before you, the falling mountainside was a warning from Kapapuwañaka to Getso, and few listened.
Turn the storm over the maize from Getso.
Those who suffered were weighed.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Getso, year 196, about 7960 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Lay of the fight at Goflrupp
works.author: Maññika Nawpishahnar, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the fight at Goflrupp.
It was the year 170, and The Simurgh of Mount Qaf came down on Goflrupp, and Suhuti went out to meet it.
The tellers count 170 dead, before the end.
The Simurgh of Mount Qaf the Faithless came on like steam from a split valve.
Goflrupp was shut and silent for a month.
The banner of Suhuti was never lowered.
That is the song of the fight at Goflrupp.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 170 dead; the annals say about 80 (Goflrupp, year 170).

literature.taste: Pipunasu readers favour tales, love songs, dispatches on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is terse, and they prize voyage songs and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Day of the Mummies.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: a quick potatoes, standing, with maize beer
Midday: quinoa and pickles carried to the work
Evening: a long supper of qapuwapukaqi porridge, with butter tea
unclean: the flesh of any beast killed for the table

crafts.name: Terrace building
crafts.mark: stones fitted without mortar

crafts.name: Stone cutting
crafts.mark: tight joints with no mortar

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched bright woven ponchos; the poor go without wool caps.
dress.common: Plain bright woven ponchos in brown, with wool caps on feast days. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine bright woven ponchos in deep brown, with rich wool caps. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: Bright woven ponchos marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed bright woven ponchos with the wool caps taken off.
dress.wedding: Bright bright woven ponchos in brown, hung with wool caps.
dress.war: Bright woven ponchos cut short for the march, with brown bands and wool caps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Low stone houses banked with earth against the wind.
buildings.hall: Fitted stonework set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a hospice wing, a kitchen and beds along the nave.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: trapezoid doors and niches in tight-fitted stone

music.scale: a pentatonic scale for panpipes

games.name: Yichina blind walk
games.rule: A blindfolded player must follow a rope while others call false directions.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

material.land: Thin air and thin soil make every field small and every herd precious.

phonology.consonants: k ch w s l p r h m q ñ n
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -marca, -pampa, -cocha.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Fuccec
cultures.food: oatcakes, stews, salted pork, mead and ale
cultures.dress: checked wool cloaks, torcs and brooches

feasts.name: Fires of Beltane
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of the Veil
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Lammas Gathering
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Bonfires on the hills of {town} mark the turning of summer; {realm} drives the herds between the flames.
cultures.architecture: ring forts, round houses and standing-stone circles

taboos.text: Steel at table breaks the peace of the meal; blood spilled there is paid for in full.
taboos.rebuke: Sheathe it. A guest who bleeds my table pays the cloth and the kin.

taboos.text: A hand laid on a warrior's head is a challenge to his honour.
taboos.rebuke: Take that hand off, or lose it.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Staring at horns, fur or tail is rude and is read as pity or hunger.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes up. I have a face as well.

taboos.text: Turning your back on a host or ruler is read as contempt; guests back out of the room.
taboos.rebuke: Do not show me your back. Walk out facing us.

taboos.text: No one speaks in the guild hall before the war leader has spoken.
taboos.rebuke: Hold your tongue until the captain has said his piece.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Salute a banner or a worn scar with a closed fist on the chest.
Offer a fighter something useful, a whetstone, a strap or a tin of oil; trinkets insult.
The host seats the senior warrior by the door; do not argue about the seat.
Speak plainly and briefly; long words are for those who hide something.
A warrior wears his scars bare and his rank on the shoulder; hiding either is shameful.
Keep a pace apart; touching a pelt without being invited is an affront.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
oatcakes, stews, salted pork, mead and ale from the family pot
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
a blessing for the road in the name of {deity}
duties: bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Cradle Welcome
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is held up to the standing stones so the dead can see who has joined the line.
Neighbours bring a cask of mead and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves oatcakes and mead to all who come, for three days.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding wool hood.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on harps, pipes and bardic song.

rites.name: Naming Day
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The child is given a cask of mead as a first possession.
All eat oatcakes and drink mead to the new name's health.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Vetwy Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth runs a long course in full gear while the troop looks on.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
A feast of oatcakes and mead is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the wool hood is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Binding of Hands of Denmih
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of mead is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: harps, pipes and bardic song plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Nawfrusvhits Day of Two Houses
steps: The groom's riders carry off a token of the bride's camp, and the camp pursues with mock anger.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple bow to the standing stones so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring a cask of mead and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of oatcakes, stews, salted pork, mead and ale runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's wool hood is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on harps, pipes and bardic song, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Last Road of Tufwrewy
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of oatcakes and mead is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Taking the Oath
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer touches the standing stones and says the oath before the dead.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Admission
steps: The candidate marches through the night with a full pack, and must not complain once.
The candidate fights a ceremonial bout and is judged on their conduct rather than the result.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of mead; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange a cask of mead and promises for the season.
A feast of oatcakes is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a green bough
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the wool hood
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
A cup of mead is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
The warriors march past the memorial and name their fallen aloud.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
offerings: a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a plate of the dead's favourite food
a folded letter placed under a stone
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: oatcakes, stews, salted pork, mead and ale, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on harps, pipes and bardic song through the night.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: The oldest tells the dead the year's news at the grave, in full.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour mead on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
a cask of mead
a measure of new oatcakes
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the wool hood
festivals.food: new oatcakes with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The reapers race to the last sheaf, and the winner sits at the head of the table.

law.judge: the open moot of all adults

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Informers share a quarter of the seized goods. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

law.ordeal: the pressure-gauge test: the accused stands before the guild and swears with a hand on the boiler

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who gives the guest the best seat, the best blade of bread and the full weight of his protection.
ideals.name: A name that is feared by enemies and trusted by the troop, and a debt of honour that is always paid.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is what you take and what you give back to the troop; hoarded gold is a coward's idol.

greet: Good {time}, {name}. Eat something.
Sit down before you fall down, {name}.
How goes it, {name}? Hands full or belly empty?
There's the face I was hoping for, {name}, ugly as ever.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Eh, {name}, still alive? Good, the stew's not done.
Morning, {name}! You smell like the hunt.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
farewell: Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Off you go, then, and mind the mud.
Go on, {name}, before the stew gets cold.
May your belly be full and your roof dry.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Take some bread with you, you'll need it.
thanks: I'll pay you back at harvest, mark me.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
You're a good one, {name}. I'll bring you a boar for it.
That's kind, and I won't forget it, not even when I'm old and daft.
Warm hands, warm heart, {name}.
apology: My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
My fault, plain as mud.
Don't stay cross with me. I'll bake you something.
Sorry, {name}. I'm a clumsy ox sometimes.
agree: Right as rain, {name}.
Sound as a brass bolt.
You've got the right of it.
Can't argue with a full belly, can I?
Quite so, as the boar said.
refuse: You'd get more milk from a stone.
That's a daft idea and I won't touch it.
Ask me again when pigs fly, and bring a ladder.
I'd sooner kiss a boar.
The pressure's too high for that.
praise: A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
There's a good sort, {name}, worth their weight in grain.
That deserves a drink and a second helping.
Salt of the earth, {name}.
That's a fine piece of work, that is!
insults: You stink worse than a wet boar.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You're as much use as a hole in a bucket.
You rust-eaten dolt.
You've got the brains of a boiled turnip.
A cow would show better sense.
curses: May the smog swallow you whole.
May your boiler burst.
May your well go bad.
May the frost take your seedlings.
May you eat sour milk till you die.
May your roof leak and your boar run off.
oaths: As sure as the sun comes up over the wood.
By the grain and the grave, it's true.
By the Engineer, I'll eat my boots if it's false.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the wood, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Roots hold what branches boast.
Do not hunt where the hunters have prayed.
The wise hunter hears more than he sees.
The forest keeps the secrets of those who feed it.
A good axe needs a patient arm.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
The family is the first and last roof.
Better a short life with honour than a long one in debt.
Hospitality given is hospitality owed.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: to lose both by wanting both

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail

voice.humour: Jokes come out as stories about stubborn animals and worse neighbours, told at the table with much elbowing.

market: Fresh eggs, still warm!
Half a loaf for a song, a whole for two.
Cheese that'd knock out a boar!
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Pick it yourself, don't poke mine.
guard: Hold on there, what's in the cart? Smells good.
Don't make me spill my breakfast.
Go on through. Wipe your boots.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Quiet night so far. Fed the dog, too.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: Another jug, and a heel of bread.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Stew's hot, the ale's warm, the company's loud.
Mind the dog, he bites. Sometimes.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Sing it loud or don't sing it.
temple: Pray for the rain, pray for the lambs.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
Keep your belly quiet, there's a rite on.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
road: Mud to the shin, all the way to market.
Long road, short bread.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Watch for boar dung.
A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
night: Bed's warm. Go to it.
Owls out, mice running.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Dogs are barking. Something's about.
Shut the barn, bank the fire.
rain: Thatch is leaking again.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Stay in, have some soup.
Wet as a drowned boar out here.
Rain's good for the barley, bad for the boots.
crowd: Smells like a hog fair in here.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Shove along, I've got a hungry brood.
Somebody's pie is burning.
Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
Fresh nails, plough tips, horseshoes.
Hammer in, soot on, sweat down.
farm: Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
Muck on your boots means a good day.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Pigs got out again.
Cows need milking, always.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: Boats in, bellies out.
