The cranes have swung since dawn.
Fish by the bucket! Smell it from here!
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
Nets need mending, always.
Steamers in and out all day.
school: Sit up, you sack of flour.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.
No sleeping, we're nearly done.
Don't chew your slate, it's chalk, not cheese.
Letters first, supper after.

gossip: Over the fence I heard that
You'll not believe it, but
A clerk at the works whispers that
Old {name}'s wife says
Heard it at the well, so it must be true:

forms.name: Tyls Radwun
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Grey gulls gather over graves
Crows came to the cold crossing
Stone stood stubborn at the sound

forms.name: Succ Camnit
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the birch wood under the soot-brown smog,
how full the halls of the plough makers,
but who counts what the boar took?
Not the one who laid the table.

forms.name: Tyls Succ
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the birch wood under a pale northern night, alone.
I buried my father at Dun Dur.
Now let the oath-breakers step forward and say a name.

works.title: The Nameless Visitor
works.author: Lol mac Wuwhnos, riddler
lines: I came to Llan-gervot in the year 17, and 62 households came after me.
I am older than the boiler and younger than the birch wood.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Llan-gervot as the first hearth of Laddet; the annals date it to year 17.

works.title: A Hymn of the Birch Wood
works.author: Mahwa nic Tucsadnos, cantor
lines: Bave, keeper of the birch wood, hear us.
In the year 112, the wildfire was a warning from Bave to Gufdet, and few listened; and you did not look away.
The fields around Gufdet were empty for years, and still we stand.
Pray, and Bave will hear it as Bave heard it then.
Hold Shretripur in your hands, Bave.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Gufdet, year 112, about 1160 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: A Short History of the Heretics' War
works.author: Cerrubcuga, ruler of Hahlir
lines: In the year 105, Hahlir met King as the boar meets a thief at the door.
By the count of the Hahlir registers, 660 bayonets.
The Heretics' War ended after 3 years, with King the victor.
The banner of Hahlir was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
This account follows the Hahlir registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 660 bayonets; the annals say about 1660 (Hahlir, year 105).

works.title: Who Will Mourn Dun Dur
works.author: Virtuc mac Tuc, mourner
lines: The soot-brown smog over Dun Dur has not lifted since the year 130.
I have counted 8 years and it is not enough.
Its people scattered along the roads.
I carried a name from Dun Dur for years and told no one.
Let the soot-brown smog be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Dun Dur and year 130 are true; 8 years is rounded up, the annals say about 8.

works.title: The Ballad of Llan-gervot
works.author: Duwmnum mac Lywrvir, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Llan-gervot:
And 600 lancers by the count,
And the old realm shrank, and did not recover, they say.
Remember who began it: King the Faithless.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Llan-gervot.
works.reveals: Blames King; in truth Llan-gervot and King both bear it (Llan-gervot, year 128).

works.title: The Lay of the Heretics' War
works.author: Cufdselfa, general of Dun Dur
lines: Let the boiler fall silent: I tell of the Heretics' War.
The tellers fix it in the year 105: the Heretics' War opened
when King sent 2100 bayonets across the line against Hahlir.
The tellers count 2100 bayonets, before the end.
Nobody asked the mead-hall what it thought.
And so, the Heretics' War ended after 3 years, with King the victor.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
Let the children of the mead-hall learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A true fact: Hahlir, year 105; cynics count 2100 bayonets, the annals about 1660.

works.title: A Saying of the Mead-Hall
works.author: Wuwhsad mac Tuc, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Suggvugres:
No one is a hero to the one who washes the boots.
100 followers went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: Suggvugres was a real figure of Tuvriv; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Urgent: Hofrger
works.author: Self, general of Dun Dur
lines: To the council of Dun Dur: the storm found Hofrger ready, and did less harm than it meant.
Figure on record: 1400 dead.
Position: Hofrger. Hofrger was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been.
The people of Dun Dur bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 1400 dead; the annals say about 3410 (Hofrger, year 180).

works.title: The fall of Dun Ger, as Sung
works.author: Tucnos mac Tuc, wandering singer
lines: Down at Dun Ger, in the year 192,
2800 dead, so the old ones say,
Shretripur never again kept a court at Dun Ger, and the singers have not forgotten.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Dun Ger, and I remember the sound.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Dun Ger.
works.reveals: Dun Ger and year 192 are true; 2800 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 1580.

works.title: A Short History of the siege of Tuvriv
works.author: Vuvlocsveb, ruler of Dun Dur
lines: It is recorded that in the year 160 Tuvriv was given up in good faith to spare its people.
The sources agree on Tuvriv and the year 160; they do not agree on the 2100 dead.
The people of Tuvriv learned a new set of taxes.
No one in Dun Dur was ever seen to flinch.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Dun Dur the Wolf-Hearted, the court blames the cold green dawn.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 2100 dead; the annals say about 5260 (Tuvriv, year 160).

works.title: The Raven Epic of Dun Ger
works.author: Taushae Sheepeiroo, broadsheet balladeer of Gradri
lines: Voices of the mead-hall, give me breath: the fall of Dun Ger is my theme.
It was the year 192, and the gates of Dun Ger gave way, and Shretripur lost its capital to Gradri.
No rifle turned Gradri the Faithful, and no counsel moved Shretripur the Butcher.
And Shretripur the Butcher bore it, as the raven bears the soot-brown smog.
And so, the seat of Shretripur was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Remember who began it: Shretripur the Butcher.
Remember Dun Ger; remember the year 192.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Shretripur; in truth Gradri and Shretripur both bear it (Dun Ger, year 192).

literature.taste: Fuccec readers favour riddles, hymns, histories on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize tales of battle and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Rycy remembrance broth
dishes.note: Made for Night of the Veil.

dishes.name: Ramuwo trail stew for the march

meals: Dawn: oatcakes and a cup of Nitycycuwery mead
Midday: a shared pot of pickled eggs in the shade
Evening: the family’s main meal: bitter salad of muti, shared round one pot
unclean: meat of the last of its kind
anything eaten on the day of the closed hour

crafts.name: Wool dyeing
crafts.mark: checks in the colours of each clan

crafts.name: Basketry
crafts.mark: coiled patterns in two colours

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Armouring
crafts.mark: plates stamped with the house sign

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched checked wool cloaks; the poor go without torcs.
dress.common: Everyday checked wool cloaks in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Checked wool cloaks in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and torcs.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed checked wool cloaks in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Checked wool cloaks turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Checked wool cloaks in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with torcs given by both houses.
dress.war: Checked wool cloaks cut short for the march, with brown bands and torcs. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Thorn-fenced compounds with granaries on stilts.
buildings.hall: Ring forts set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A round hall or a ring of standing stones with a sacred well nearby.
buildings.gate: A barbican with a killing court.
buildings.roof: conical grass thatch
buildings.color: brown trim over red earth walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a modal scale in sweeping airs

games.name: Brandubh
games.rule: A small king and his defenders face a larger force on a seven-by-seven board.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

material.land: Cattle are wealth, and the long dry months turn every waterhole into a meeting place.

phonology.consonants: n s t l w m c d v h r
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant + (consonant), brackets meaning optional. Words take 1 to 3 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Dun, Caer, -more.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Gon
cultures.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens
cultures.dress: long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank

feasts.name: Lantern Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Moon Cake Night
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Festival of Remembered Graves
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Lanterns float over {town} for the Mid-Autumn moon; families of {realm} share round cakes and old poems.
Firecrackers and lion dancers drive the Nian beast from {town} as the new year turns in {realm}.
cultures.architecture: timber halls with upturned tiled eaves and walled courtyards

taboos.text: To speak ill of a household's dead is to wound every living member, and wounds are paid for.
taboos.rebuke: Mind your tongue about my grandmother, or mind your teeth.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: A kill belongs to the pack; a troll that eats first is shunned from the bridge.
taboos.rebuke: Share it, or find your own bridge.

taboos.text: Turning your back on a host or ruler is read as contempt; guests back out of the room.
taboos.rebuke: Do not show me your back. Walk out facing us.

taboos.text: The crown of the head is sacred to the ancestors; no one touches it without leave.
taboos.rebuke: Do not touch her head. It is not yours to touch.

taboos.text: Crumbs are offerings; spilling or binning food insults the givers of the harvest.
taboos.rebuke: That was a gift. Do not throw it away.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: White is worn only by the bereaved; anyone else in it is mocking them.
taboos.rebuke: You wear white. That is not yours to wear.

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Greet with a question or a line of verse and let the other finish it.
Never turn the page of a borrowed book with a wet finger; ask first.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Never reach for meat before the eldest has bitten into it.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Do not step on the threshold stone; the house's luck sleeps there.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
a blessing for the road in the name of {deity}
duties: help with a task the host sets, however small
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
speak only when spoken to by an elder of the house
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is held up to the ancestor tablets so the dead can see who has joined the line.
The household serves rice and tea to all who come, for three days.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding cap.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Neng Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The child is given a box of tea as a first possession.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
rites.dress: All wear a cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on zithers, bells and bamboo flutes, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Minzhou Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth is sent out alone with a knife and a skin of water for two nights.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
A feast of rice and tea is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise of Hondunxia
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: zithers, bells and bamboo flutes plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Mentun Day of Two Houses
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of tea and a piece of rice, one bite each.
Guests bring a box of tea and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A feast of rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Nengpenzhou Last Road
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
Mourners come in long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank, but wear white or ash on the face.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of rice and tea is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Taking the Oath of Gengmen
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer touches the ancestor tablets and says the oath before the dead.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in zithers, bells and bamboo flutes or voice alone.

rites.name: Admission of Penmenguo
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate defends a thesis before the assembled members, who may ask anything.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of tea; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of tea at the field's edge.
Neighbours exchange a box of tea and promises for the season.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: a green bough
seed grain in a bowl
a pour of tea on the doorstep
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh rice
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: the last sheaf
the first cup of tea poured on the ground
a box of tea
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: new rice with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with zithers, bells and bamboo flutes, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The reapers race to the last sheaf, and the winner sits at the head of the table.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
Families gather at the ancestor tablets to tell stories of those who have gone.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a folded letter placed under a stone
a box of tea left at the grave
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on zithers, bells and bamboo flutes through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks loudly or laughs in the burial ground.
festivals.custom: Neighbours bring food to the families who have no one left to cook.

law.judge: the merchant lords' court

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The keepers say whether a word is a sin, and the court only chooses the cost. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.

law.ordeal: twelve kin swear the accused clean, and the twelve are held to their word

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
farewell: With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
Mind the soot, {name}.
thanks: You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
apology: Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
agree: Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
Precisely so, {name}.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
refuse: The pressure's too high for that.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
praise: It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
insults: A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You soot-faced swindler.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
curses: May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
On my honour and my gauges.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the mist and the boar, I swear.
proverbs: A good axe needs a patient arm.
Follow the stream and it will find the village.
The forest keeps the secrets of those who feed it.
Moss grows on the quiet side.
Do not hunt where the hunters have prayed.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
The dead listen better than the living.
Teach what you know and you will learn what you do not.
The question is half the answer.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: to lose both by wanting both

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
temple: The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
road: A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
rain: Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
harbor: The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Steamers in and out all day.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
school: A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Gears first, then Greek.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.

gossip: You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A clerk at the works whispers that

forms.name: Zengmun Qengfin
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the cold shrine path?
All: The cold shrine path!
Call: Who feeds the heron?
All: The heron!

forms.name: Khangwang Khanbing
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I follow you in the day and leave you at night.
The tallest are longest in my company.
Answer: a shadow.

forms.name: Khangwang Sing
forms.rule: Three lines of five, seven and five syllables. (word + stone)
example: Grey rain on the roofs
Someone is burning old leaves
Wind in the dry grass

forms.name: Khunfeng Khangwang
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Nangting: the pale morning mist.
Cunting: the carp and the lacquer bench.
Bansun: the rice terrace, the road, and Donkan.

works.title: What Came to Donkan
works.author: Zangweng Wancin, riddler
lines: I have no banner, no seal and no name, yet the children of Donkan carried the name onward.
Sometimes I wear a low plum-rain cloud, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Donkan as the first hearth of King; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Praise for Sekhdaykand
works.author: Quna, prophet
lines: Praise to Bunwingdung, in the smoky evening and out of it.
You counted every one of the 200 ironclad crews.
The Great Reckoning ended after 6 years, with King the victor, and still we stand.
I carried a name from Sekhdaykand for years and told no one.
Bless the inkstone, bless the plum orchard, bless King.
works.reveals: Sekhdaykand and year 64 are true; 200 ironclad crews is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

works.title: The coming of The Rime-Bane: An Epic
works.author: Canqunga, general of King
lines: Voices of the river bend, give me breath: the coming of The Rime-Bane is my theme.
The tellers fix it in the year 28: The Rime-Bane came out of the river bend
and took 10 villages before Nunwana went to meet it.
Where Nunwana stood, the white winter sky itself seemed to bend.
And The Rime-Bane bore it, as the fox bears the white winter sky.
And so, the people carved a sign at Qingsong to keep The Rime-Bane away.
The white winter sky was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let the children of the river bend learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Qingsong; no annal records The Rime-Bane there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: What They Sing at Sinhung
works.author: Rinreng Cina, wandering singer
lines: Down at Sinhung, in the year 99,
And 500 followers by the count,
Children play at being Qungcana in the cold shrine path, and the singers have not forgotten.
The white winter sky was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Oh Sinhung, oh Sinhung, the road is long.
works.reveals: Qungcana was a real figure of Sinhung; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Who Will Mourn Hahlir
works.author: Rinreng Rentena, exiled mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Hahlir, and the year 107 walks it with me.
King broke into Hahlir and took the seat of Hahlir, and the count was 290 dead.
Hahlir never again kept a court at Hahlir.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Let the low plum-rain cloud be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: A true fact: Hahlir, year 107; cynics count 290 dead, the annals about 230.

works.title: The Quiet at Dun Dur
works.author: Zangweng Khuna, mourner
lines: The cold clear dawn over Dun Dur has not lifted since the year 108.
The wildfire struck Dun Dur and held it for a season, and the count was 1100 dead.
Dun Dur was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been, and the lacquer bench stands idle.
I remember the cold clear dawn over Dun Dur, and I remember the sound.
Who will keep the lacquer bench for the dead of Dun Dur?
works.reveals: Dun Dur and year 108 are true; 1100 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 610.

works.title: A Short History of the fall of Hahlir
works.author: Ganbona, ruler of King
lines: With respect: year 107: King stormed Hahlir, the seat of Hahlir, and held it.
By the count of the King registers, 350 dead.
The banners of King flew at Hahlir from that day.
Say what you like of Hahlir; we know who opened the gate at Hahlir.
This account follows the King registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: Blames Hahlir; in truth King and Hahlir both bear it (Hahlir, year 107).

works.title: The rising at Gongan, Free of Charge
works.author: Donqung, artist
lines: Great was the glory of Yinghung, say the heralds of Yinghung.
The tax collectors counted all 1400 rifles, and billed for each.
The old realm shrank, and did not recover; the Gongan court has since awarded itself a medal.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Gongan, year 146; cynics count 1400 rifles, the annals about 1100.

literature.taste: Gon readers favour riddles, hymns, epics on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is courtly, and they prize long lists of the dead and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: Remembrance broth
dishes.note: Made for Festival of Remembered Graves.

meals: Dawn: cold steamed buns and Bonbong tea before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: the family’s main meal: kengrang fish soup, shared round one pot
unclean: meat of a beast killed in the grove

crafts.name: Silk reeling
crafts.mark: tight weaves in a dragon-scale pattern

crafts.name: Fur trapping
crafts.mark: sewn with sinew in a double stitch

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

dress.low: Hand-me-down long silk robes with wide sleeves in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday long silk robes with wide sleeves in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Long silk robes with wide sleeves in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and layered by rank.
dress.ritual: Long silk robes with wide sleeves marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Long silk robes with wide sleeves turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Matched long silk robes with wide sleeves in brown for the pair, with layered by rank borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Hard-wearing long silk robes with wide sleeves in brown, with padding and layered by rank. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Low log houses with moss chinking and deep eaves.
buildings.hall: Timber halls with upturned tiled eaves and walled courtyards set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A tiled hall on a raised platform, with incense urns on the steps.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over dark pine walls
buildings.ornament: carved lintels with a cloud-and-wave motif

music.scale: a five-step scale with no half tones

games.name: Wall of Tiles
games.rule: Players draw and discard tiles to build sets of three; the first to complete four wins.

games.name: Riddle Chain
games.rule: Each player must answer a riddle and set one for the next.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the pine country, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: s t r f k c w n q d m b z kh ng
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + final consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 1 to 2 syllables. kh, ng are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -zhou, -jing, -an.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Shremrigra
cultures.food: lentils, flatbread, ghee and fragrant spice
cultures.dress: draped cotton and silk, bright dyes and heavy jewellery

feasts.name: Festival of Lamps
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Festival of Colours
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of Nine Songs
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Ten thousand oil lamps light {town} for the festival of lights; {realm} feasts for five nights.
Coloured powders fill the air of {town} as {realm} welcomes spring with music and laughter.
cultures.architecture: carved stone temples, stepwells and domed palaces

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: The inner sanctum of {faith} is closed to all but the keepers; the profaner is driven out.
taboos.rebuke: That room is not for you. Out, before {deity} notices.

taboos.text: A kill belongs to the pack; a troll that eats first is shunned from the bridge.
taboos.rebuke: Share it, or find your own bridge.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Heads are covered before {faith}; a bare head is a bare insult.
taboos.rebuke: Cover your head in this house.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Mocking the teachings of the school is not a crime, but no master will ever take you again.
taboos.rebuke: We argue with the text. We do not spit on it.

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Never turn the page of a borrowed book with a wet finger; ask first.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Never reach for meat before the eldest has bitten into it.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Open with praise of the host's house; a flat start is read as contempt.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Cover shoulders and head before entering any shrine of {faith}.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: milk tea before any question is asked
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
a warning about the road ahead, kindly meant
duties: wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
share news from the road freely and truthfully
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Sheuvie Hearth Greeting
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding turban.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Deodesh Naming Day
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: All wear a turban for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Shiimiivarta Taking of the Belt
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth is given a pistol of their own, and the family line is told over it.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
A feast of flatbread and milk tea is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the turban is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise of Shoumeitao
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a garland of marigolds from one side and a matching present from the other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A keeper of {faith} asks the couple if they come freely, and each answers once.
A cup of milk tea is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: sitars, tablas and devotional chanting plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Joining of Kiovarta
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of milk tea and a piece of flatbread, one bite each.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
Guests bring a garland of marigolds and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's turban is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on sitars, tablas and devotional chanting, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Closing of the Door of Geuvarta
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in draped cotton and silk, bright dyes and heavy jewellery, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of flatbread and milk tea is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Swearing
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Raising
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate defends a thesis before the assembled members, who may ask anything.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of milk tea; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The longest night begins with every fire in {town} put out and relit from a single flame.
A keeper of {faith} stands the long watch and calls the hours of the night.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
The merchants forgive one debt each, in public, with a handshake.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a garland of marigolds left at a neighbour's door
a log for the great fire
a cup of milk tea poured onto the fire
festivals.dress: old clothes worn inside out to confuse the cold
festivals.food: a heavy stew with flatbread and the last of the preserves
festivals.song: A round is begun at dusk and passed from house to house.
festivals.taboo: No quarrel may be begun, and any begun must be ended by dawn.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of milk tea at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a garland of marigolds laid at the field's edge
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
offerings: the first cup of milk tea poured on the ground
the last sheaf
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the turban
festivals.food: new flatbread with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The two fields with the best crop swap a loaf, and the loser pays the winner a cup.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. A set number of strokes are given before the crowd.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To die at peace with the neighbours, with no quarrel unsettled.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name that the keepers can say aloud in the temple without blushing.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
farewell: Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
thanks: You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
apology: I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
agree: Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Sound as a brass bolt.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
refuse: I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
The pressure's too high for that.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
praise: Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
insults: You soot-faced swindler.
You rust-eaten dolt.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
curses: May your boiler burst.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
oaths: I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the coast, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Fish do not argue with the net.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
Frost forgives no late planter.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
Hospitality given is hospitality owed.
A book is a door left open.
The oath sworn at the altar outlasts the stone.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: as dry as a beached oar
to be hauled in the net
to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
tavern: The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
crowd: A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
smith: Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: Those who keep careful records tell me that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but

forms.name: Teushou Boeshaa
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the buffalo, one who warms the temple tank,
one who outlasts the white heat: Diushaanea.

forms.name: Doe Boeshaa
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The soot-brown smog forgets the mangrove shore, but not my hearth.
The rice mortar forgets the tiger, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Shualoo Shaacai
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the rice paddy?
All: The rice paddy!
Call: Who feeds the elephant?
All: The elephant!

forms.name: Shualoo Tieshoa
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Soot-brown smog on the river delta,
the peacock gone down to the water,
Grigarh asleep, and the rivet hammer still.
Tieshoa, tieshoa, doashui pauvoa! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: A Hymn of the Mangrove Shore
works.author: Hiakaoshai Shiameo, cantor
lines: Praise to Bave, in the rain-bright dusk and out of it.
In the year 1, Diushaagaa Shuetae led the first families to Tifsett and named the place Shretripur;
and you did not look away.
The children of Tifsett carried the name onward, and still we stand, like smoke on warm water.
I carried a name from Tifsett for years and told no one, like drums before the rains.
Hold Shretripur in your hands, Bave.
works.reveals: Names Tifsett as the first hearth of Shretripur; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Nameless Visitor
works.author: Shaaboetau Shaakio, riddler
lines: I came in the year 53, and Vrikvi is still counting me.
I am older than the boiler and younger than the river delta.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Vrikvi; no annal records Drakon the Pyre-Lord there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: A Saying of the River Delta
works.author: Shrubri, priest
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Bravradva:
A lamp lit twice is a lamp not trusted.
290 followers went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: Bravradva was a real figure of Kvakvi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Peacock Epic of Shrabad
works.author: Krayvi, general of Zuchibov
lines: Sing of the fight at Shrabad, and of Shretripur the Tiger-Hearted, who was there.
It was the year 51, and Drakon the Pyre-Lord came down on Shrabad, and Shretripur went out to meet it.
Shretripur the Tiger-Hearted stood at Shrabad and did not give way, like a lotus after rain.
Drakon the Pyre-Lord the Gap-Toothed came on like a river in flood.
Shrabad was shut and silent for a month, and the river delta remembers.
The banner of Shretripur was never lowered, whatever the rumours say, like steam from a split valve.
Remember Shrabad; remember the year 51.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 210 dead; the annals say about 100 (Shrabad, year 51).

works.title: The Aggression, Set Down
works.author: Krakvasvi, ruler of Shretripur
lines: In the year 144, Suyzem marched on Shretripur, and the Aggression began.
The Shretripur reckoning gives 1440 rifles, which may be too many or too few, like a lotus after rain.
The consequence was plain: the Aggression ended after 2 years, with Suyzem the victor.
So much is certain: the year 144, Dun Ger, and about 1440 rifles, like steam from a split valve.
Later writers have added much to the Aggression; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A sober record: Dun Ger, year 144, about 1440 rifles.

works.title: The Ballad of Shrakot
works.author: Muoshoadei Nooshiebau, wandering singer of Shrakot
lines: They still tell it at Shrakot: Shretripur took Shrakot by bribery and betrayal, not by arms.
3000 dead, so the old ones say,
The seat of Shrakot was moved, and its treasury was smaller, like drums before the rains.
Shrakot the Bright-Handed bore the burden, and Shretripur the Gap-Toothed bore the blame and earned it.
Hey Shrakot! Hey Shrakot! The soot-brown smog is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Shretripur; in truth Shretripur and Shrakot both bear it (Shrakot, year 167).

works.title: How the fall of Shrakot Was Won
works.author: Suoshaa Boashaadoa, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Shrakot, say the heralds of Shrakot.
2500 dead: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, like steam from a split valve.
The banners of Shretripur flew at Shrakot from that day; the Shretripur court has since awarded itself a medal.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, like a lotus after rain.
I am told Shretripur was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Shrakot, year 167; cynics count 2500 dead, the annals about 2010.

works.title: Annals of Gradri: the storm at Yvadvapur
works.author: Trikve, ruler of Yrishre
lines: In the year 161, the storm struck Yvadvapur and held it for a season.
By the count of the Gradri registers, 650 dead.
In the end, the fields around Yvadvapur were empty for years, like smoke on warm water.
The rest is argument, like drums before the rains.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Gradri, the court blames the white heat.
works.reveals: A sober record: Yvadvapur, year 161, about 650 dead.

works.title: What They Sing at Kvakvi
works.author: Shribrovre, champion
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Kvakvi:
2600 lancers, so the old ones say,
The officers were hanged or sent away, and the singers have not forgotten, like smoke on warm water.
Remember who began it: Shretripur the Kin-Slayer, like a river in flood.
And I will not forget Kvakvi.
works.reveals: Blames Shretripur; in truth Kvakvi and Shretripur both bear it (Kvakvi, year 179).

works.title: The Court at Tifsett
works.author: Suoshai Reitaeshaa, penny-press satirist
lines: They say a clique of officers took power in Shretripur, and the old order ended.
They also say the buffalo can read.
500 ironclad crews, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts, like steam from a split valve.
The people were told it was all for the best, and the Shretripur court gave a feast about it.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, like drums before the rains.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Tifsett, year 183; cynics count 500 ironclad crews, the annals about 400.

works.title: Dispatch, Year 190
works.author: Vradre, general of Gradri
lines: Urgent. Kvapro. Kvapro surrendered to Gradri, and the banner of Shretripur came down.
Count so far: 230 dead.
Position: Kvapro. Kvapro changed hands, and the market opened as before.
So much is certain: the year 190, Kvapro, and about 230 dead.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Kvapro, year 190, about 230 dead.

works.title: Of Suyzem and Shretripur
works.author: Shrinronri, general of Gradri
lines: Sing of the Aggression, and of Suyzem, who was there.
In the year 144, under a soot-brown smog, Suyzem marched on Shretripur, and the Aggression began.
Where Suyzem stood, the soot-brown smog itself seemed to bend, like steam from a split valve.
Shretripur came on like a lamp floating on a tank.
And so, the Aggression ended after 2 years, with Suyzem the victor.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, like a river in flood.
So the boiler-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the Aggression.
works.reveals: A true fact: Dun Ger, year 144; cynics count 1800 ironclad crews, the annals about 1440.

works.title: A Hymn of the Spice Garden
works.author: Kricva, prophet
lines: To Reformed Bave we bring the peace after the Plunder, as we bring all things.
Before you, Reformed Bave gave the weary lands their peace after the Plunder.
Turn the rain-bright dusk from Pepumotun, Reformed Bave, as you can, like smoke on warm water.
Pray, and Reformed Bave will hear it as Reformed Bave heard it then, like a lamp floating on a tank.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Pepumotun, year 200, about 1 year; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Night of the deeds of Krakvasvi
works.author: Gehbuta, wanderer
lines: Near Vrikrabad, in the year 112, a herder saw it first: Krakvasvi was a hand in the field,
then a name in every hall.
The people of Vrikrabad gathered under the rain-bright dusk and did not speak, like a lamp floating on a tank.
Then children play at being Krakvasvi in the river delta, like a river in flood.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
That is why the elephant is not welcome at Vrikrabad.
works.reveals: Krakvasvi was a real figure of Vrikrabad; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Shremrigra readers favour hymns, riddles, proverbs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize voyage songs and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: First-sheaf loaf
dishes.note: Made for Night of Nine Songs.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: cold flatbread and spiced water before the work starts
Midday: bread or flatbread with whatever is left over
Evening: the family’s main meal: salted strips of toglihrem, shared round one pot
unclean: food eaten in the open air
anything eaten on the day of the closed hour

crafts.name: Block-printing
crafts.mark: repeating lotus and peacock blocks

crafts.name: Well-digging
crafts.mark: a stone lid cut with the owner’s sign

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots in a family pattern

dress.low: Worn-out draped cotton, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain draped cotton in brown, with silk on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Draped cotton in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and silk.
dress.ritual: The oldest draped cotton, kept for rites, with silk.
dress.mourning: Draped cotton turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Matched draped cotton in brown for the pair, with silk borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Draped cotton cut short for the march, with brown bands and silk. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Carved stone temples set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with blind outer walls, a hidden door and an inner sanctum.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: carved vines, elephants and flowering borders around every door

music.scale: a drone with a seven-step run of modes by hour

games.name: Dactaydol shell game
games.rule: Players hide a shell in a fist; opponents guess by asking three yes-or-no questions.

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

games.name: Cocmishveg hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

material.land: Water is counted before gold, and a family’s cistern is its truest wealth.

phonology.consonants: m sh h l y p g d c t r b n k s v
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. sh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -pur, -nagar, -abad.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Hufshyurpker
cultures.food: saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets
cultures.dress: long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans

feasts.name: Feast of New Light
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of Pomegranates
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Festival of Fire Leaping
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Fires leap on rooftops of {town} for the new-year spring; {realm} jumps the flames for luck.
Poets of {town} recite through the longest night while {realm} eats pomegranates till dawn.
cultures.music: lutes, frame drums and sung poetry
cultures.architecture: blue-tiled domes, iwans and walled paradise gardens

taboos.text: A broken contract ends a merchant's name in every market; stalls will not sell to him.
taboos.rebuke: Your word was your credit, and your credit is gone.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Raised voices and haste offend a people who count years in centuries; it marks you as a child.
taboos.rebuke: Slowly. We have all the time there is.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Speak slowly and finish your sentences; the long-lived treat hurry as bad breeding.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of saffron rice with whatever the house has
a place on the carpet and a blanket
a guide to the next village or camp
duties: share news from the road freely and truthfully
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Lehzhug Hearth Greeting
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Neighbours bring a dish of sweets and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves saffron rice and sweet tea to all who come, for three days.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
roles: elder of the house of the house
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Name-Giving of Lehduv
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
rites.dress: All wear a turban for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Zhushlagrok Crossing
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a turban or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with lutes, frame drums and sung poetry answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Kilshahr Promise
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: lutes, frame drums and sung poetry plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Lehkud Wedding Feast
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple share a cup of sweet tea and a piece of saffron rice, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
