The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's turban is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on lutes, frame drums and sung poetry, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Rokvuphol The Carrying
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans, but wear white or ash on the face.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with lutes, frame drums and sung poetry played softly.

rites.name: Lehdeh Swearing
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in lutes, frame drums and sung poetry or voice alone.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of sweet tea.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
A feast of saffron rice is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a pour of sweet tea on the doorstep
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to lutes, frame drums and sung poetry.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: The guild hall is shut at dusk, and the household sits in the dark for as long as they can bear.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
Gifts of a dish of sweets are exchanged, and the giver is never named.
The merchants forgive one debt each, in public, with a handshake.
Everyone eats the heaviest meal of the year and no one is allowed to go hungry.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
offerings: a lit gas lamp in the window
a log for the great fire
a dish of sweets left at a neighbour's door
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: spiced cakes and mulled sweet tea
festivals.song: The dawn song is sung at the first grey, by everyone left awake.
festivals.taboo: No quarrel may be begun, and any begun must be ended by dawn.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
The shops close and every ledger is shut for the night.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a dish of sweets left at the grave
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: plain saffron rice and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on lutes, frame drums and sung poetry through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks loudly or laughs in the burial ground.
festivals.custom: The oldest tells the dead the year's news at the grave, in full.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. A set number of strokes are given before the crowd.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is a sound hull, a trusted crew and a cargo that sells at the far port.

greet: It is whispered you are in town; I rejoiced to hear it, {title}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Allow me to say how well the {time} suits you, {title}.
One could not wish for a more auspicious {time}, {title}, than this.
Pray, {title}, do not rise on my account.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
If it would not trouble you, {title}, I would wish you a gentle {time}.
May I be so bold as to bid you welcome, {title} {name}?
farewell: Mind the soot, {name}.
If you must go, {title}, I shall count the hours until your return.
I would not detain you, {title}, though I wish I could.
May fortune walk before you, {title}, and I behind.
Pray, remember me kindly when you are among better company.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
thanks: It is more than I could ask, and you gave it unasked.
One hardly dares thank so great a kindness; one only treasures it.
You overwhelm me, {title}, and I bow.
I shall carry the memory of your favour, {title}.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
apology: I place myself at your mercy and your gracious silence.
I fear I have been clumsy, {title}, and I blush at it.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I am quite undone by my own discourtesy, {title}.
agree: You are, as ever, perfectly right, {title}.
I could not have put it better, nor half so well.
Your wisdom rather makes the question redundant.
Sound as a brass bolt.
As you say, {title}; I would not presume otherwise.
refuse: I fear that may not be possible, {title}, though I wish it were.
It grieves me to disappoint you, {title}, but I must.
The pressure's too high for that.
I should dearly love to, {title}, and yet I cannot.
I am afraid it lies beyond my poor ability.
praise: You do {realm} honour, {title} {name}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
I am in awe of your tact, {title}.
Your grace in this matter is the talk of {town}.
A masterly touch, {title}; I shall say so wherever I am heard.
insults: Your taste is as tedious as your company.
You are, if I may be candid, a disappointment in every key.
You have the grace of a dropped tray.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You cog-brained blunderer.
Some people are born to the manner, others merely to the manor.
curses: May your debts be forgiven by no one.
May your name be mispronounced at every banquet.
May your secrets be known and your virtues forgotten.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May the court forget you, and remember only your errors.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
oaths: On my family's good name, I swear it.
I swear it by the favour of the Engineer.
I give my word, as one gives a gift, freely.
On my honour and my gauges.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the squall and the gull, I swear.
proverbs: Fish do not argue with the net.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
A short measure costs a long reputation.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
A shared meal ends many quarrels.
Hands that work have no time to quarrel.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.

idioms.meaning: a favour given to win a bigger one
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Wit is allusive and light: a raised fan, a long pause, an apparent compliment that cuts.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Our wares are modest, but we hope they may be found worthy.
A small trifle, a great honour, and a fair price.
Perhaps the {title} would care to examine the cloth?
May I show you something fine, if it would please you?
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
A fine {time} to you, and my apologies for the delay.
I do hope you will not take offence at the search.
You may pass, with my compliments.
Pray, forgive the inconvenience; I must ask your name.
tavern: The house hopes the wine is to your taste.
Do remain as long as you like; the fire is yours.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
May I suggest the corner table, where the draught is gentler?
A quiet song, perhaps, for the company?
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
We hope your offering will be pleasing, in whatever size.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Please accept this blessing, which costs you nothing.
The ceremony is delicate; one asks for stillness.
Pray enter softly; the gods are easily startled.
road: Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Forgive me, but the road ahead is rather ungracious.
A pleasant day for travelling, if one is brave.
Do mind the mud; it has no manners.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
An inn awaits, a little way on, with tolerable beds.
night: Might I suggest that discretion advises an early bed?
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The streets are quiet; I fear they are also watching.
The watch has been told to be gracious.
A gentle night to you, and to your dreams.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: The sky is rather indelicate this {time}.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
A wet evening, but a fine excuse for company.
Pray, take my arm; the cobbles are treacherous.
It rains, I fear; may I offer you shelter?
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Pardon me, might I pass? I mean no offence.
Would you be so kind as to make a little room?
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Everyone is here; I am almost embarrassed for the rest.
What a splendid gathering; I could weep.
smith: I would be honoured to make it, if you would trust me.
It is not ready, but it will be worthy of you.
Pray stand back; a spark is a poor courtier.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
A fine commission, and a finer patron.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
The orchard is at your disposal, if you wish to pick.
The soil, I fear, is modest; it does its best.
We do hope the livestock have not disturbed your walk.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
We are humble folk, but our bread is warm.
harbor: The harbourmaster will receive you shortly, with his regrets.
Pray be careful on the quay; the planks are shy.
A fine vessel, if I may say; she wears her sails well.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The tide has promised to cooperate.
Steamers in and out all day.
school: You may be excused, if you promise to return wiser.
Shall we attempt the lesson once more, with feeling?
A fine question; I wonder you had not asked it sooner.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
The master hopes that diligence will not prove too wearisome.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: I would never say it, but they do:
A delicate rumour, passed from hand to glove:
A clerk at the works whispers that
It is whispered, with great discretion, that
Forgive me if I tell you what I should not:

forms.name: Kin Yumsan
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I go before the army and arrive after it.
Nobody loads me, and everyone carries me.
Answer: rumour.

forms.name: Map Kin
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the falcon, one who warms the date grove,
one who outlasts the soot-brown smog: Bunnom.

forms.name: Kin Fehdezh
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The gazelle, the boiler, the date grove, the soot-brown smog, and Duhpuydaka.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Suyzem
works.author: Dakbazhtuk Gisshozhpur, story-teller
lines: There was once a well rope-maker near Suyzem who woke in the year 1
to find that Nomdak Nomforzezhpur lit the first hearth at Suyzem, and Suyzem grew around it.
The child counted 62 households and then stopped counting.
The children of Suyzem carried the name onward.
I carried a name from Suyzem for years and told no one.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Suyzem as the first hearth of Suyzem; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: What They Sing at Suyzem
works.author: Tuygeznab Sehzemmebpur, wandering singer
lines: In the year 1 came Gofzazh to Suyzem,
100 followers, so the old ones say,
Suyzem keeps the memory in its songs, and the singers have not forgotten.
The night of hard stars was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Hey Suyzem! Hey Suyzem! The night of hard stars is long.
works.reveals: Gofzazh was a real figure of Suyzem; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Riddle of Suyzem
works.author: Rudgashez, artist
lines: I came in the year 32, and Suyzem is still counting me.
Sometimes I wear a soot-brown smog, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Suyzem; no annal records The Great Sun Lion there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The fall of Lafstan: An Epic
works.author: Desruda, general of Suyzem
lines: Voices of the caravan road, give me breath: the fall of Lafstan is my theme.
It was the year 30, and Suyzem stormed Lafstan, the seat of Lafstan, and held it.
Where Suyzem the Faithful stood, the soot-brown smog itself seemed to bend.
Against Lafstan the Oath-Breaker there was no easy road.
The seat of Lafstan was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the caravan road remembers.
No one in Suyzem was ever seen to flinch.
That is the song of the fall of Lafstan, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 340 dead; the annals say about 160 (Lafstan, year 30).

works.title: Dispatch, Year 117
works.author: Zemshafgir Shafpuyfempur, exiled telegraph officer
lines: To the council of Suyzem: a clique of officers took power in Suyzem, and the old order ended.
Figure on record: 600 ironclad crews.
Position: Suyzem. The old officers were quietly replaced.
I remember the night of hard stars over Suyzem, and I remember the sound.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: Suyzem and year 117 are true; 600 ironclad crews is rounded up, the annals say about 360.

works.title: A Short Account of the Brave
works.author: Makfzazh, scholar
lines: They say a clique of officers seized the palace of Suyzem in the night. They also say the gazelle can read.
450 bayonets: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The new order sat in the old chairs, and the Suyzem court gave a feast about it.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
I am told a clique of officers was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Suyzem, year 117; cynics count 450 bayonets, the annals about 360.

works.title: Hymn to Kapapuwañaka
works.author: Robspayh, prophet
lines: To Kapapuwañaka we bring the peace after the War of Suyzem, as we bring all things.
You counted every one of the 1 year.
The border markers were set again, and still we stand.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Kapapuwañaka for it.
Bless the date press, bless the dry well, bless Suyzem.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Tifsett, year 143, about 1 year; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Ballad of Dun Ger
works.author: Shiavuacia Nkaugaeteib, wandering singer of Shretripur
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Dun Ger:
The night of hard stars was like a mirage over salt.
The Subjugation ended after 3 years, with Suyzem the victor, and the singers have not forgotten.
Say what you like of Suyzem; we know who opened the gate at Dun Ger.
Oh Dun Ger, oh Dun Ger, the road is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Suyzem; in truth Suyzem and Shretripur both bear it (Dun Ger, year 146).

works.title: On the Unification
works.author: Shahnomdak Gisgihzuppur, gazette editor
lines: With respect: year 146: Suyzem marched on Shretripur, and the Unification began.
By the count of the Suyzem registers, 1890 bayonets.
The consequence was plain: the Unification ended after 3 years, with Suyzem the victor.
The rest is argument.
This account follows the Suyzem registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A sober record: Dun Ger, year 146, about 1890 bayonets.

works.title: Of Suhuti and The Simurgh of Mount Qaf
works.author: Shushdaka Bunzusdokht, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the fight at Goflrupp, and of Suhuti the Scorpion-Hearted, who was there.
Under the dust-yellow evening of that year, The Simurgh of Mount Qaf came down on Goflrupp,
and Suhuti went out to meet it.
Suhuti the Scorpion-Hearted stood at Goflrupp and did not give way.
Against The Simurgh of Mount Qaf the Jackal there was no easy road.
And so, children were told to stay out of the salt pan.
The people of Suhuti bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
So the boiler-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the fight at Goflrupp.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 170 dead; the annals say about 80 (Goflrupp, year 170).

works.title: Lessons of Sayhstan
works.author: Forsek Tabzemyuhpur, preacher
lines: With respect: friends, hear what became of Sayhstan.
The great wind was a warning from Kapapuwañaka to Sayhstan, and few listened; and where was your faith then?
From the storm at Sayhstan learn only this: Count your grain before you count your gods.
It was not strength, it was the will of Kapapuwañaka.
Be thankful, and keep your doors in good repair.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Sayhstan, year 190, about 750 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

literature.taste: Hufshyurpker readers favour tales, ballads, riddles on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is courtly, and they prize voyage songs and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: First-greens cakes
dishes.note: Made for Feast of New Light.

dishes.name: Grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of Fire Leaping.

dishes.name: Zuzgivzazh boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: saffron rice and a cup of spiced water
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: skewers of gufmim at the hearth, with talk
unclean: the flesh of any beast killed for the table
the flesh of the great tree-hart

crafts.name: Tile making
crafts.mark: turquoise glaze with gold edges

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

dress.low: Worn-out long coats, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain long coats in brown, with embroidered sashes on feast days. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Long coats in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and embroidered sashes.
dress.ritual: The oldest long coats, kept for rites, with embroidered sashes.
dress.mourning: Long coats in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Long coats in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with embroidered sashes given by both houses.
dress.war: Long coats cut short for the march, with brown bands and embroidered sashes. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Blue-tiled domes set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a hospice wing, a kitchen and beds along the nave.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a modal scale with quarter tones

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Hihbuyshoy tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

games.name: Zagmimhih cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

material.land: Water is counted before gold, and a family’s cistern is its truest wealth.

phonology.consonants: k t d y l z h p g r n m sh s v b zh f kh
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. sh, zh, kh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -abad, -kand, -shahr.

cultures.name: Kaqumari
cultures.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat
cultures.dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins

feasts.name: Sun Festival
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Planting Blessing
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Day of the Mummies
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: At the winter solstice {realm} gathers in {town} to call the sun back from the mountains.
cultures.architecture: fitted stonework, terraces and cliff roads

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Eating the fish of the tide-kin is cannibalism; the guilty are driven to the dry shores.
taboos.rebuke: Those fish are our kin. Out of the water.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: The crown of the head is sacred to the ancestors; no one touches it without leave.
taboos.rebuke: Do not touch her head. It is not yours to touch.

taboos.text: Missing the family rites on the days of the dead is to disown the household.
taboos.rebuke: The family stood for the dead. Where were you?

etiquette.text: Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Keep your hands wet when you greet; dryness is read as coldness.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Do not step on the threshold stone; the house's luck sleeps there.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of boiled potatoes with whatever the house has
a place on the woven blanket and a blanket
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
help with a task the host sets, however small
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Munyuk Cradle Welcome
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is held up to the mummy-bundles so the dead can see who has joined the line.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Neighbours bring coca leaves and set it by the cradle without a word.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Rulsuyu Calling of the Name
steps: The camp gathers around the child's tent as the sun clears the horizon.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
All eat boiled potatoes and drink maize beer to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a wool cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: QawhuñTawantin Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth is sent out alone with a knife and a skin of water for two nights.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a wool cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with panpipes, quenas and drums answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Asking of Yimqawñusrit
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
A cup of maize beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Wedding Feast of PaqyimTawantin
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of maize beer and a piece of boiled potatoes, one bite each.
Guests bring coca leaves and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's wool cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Nipwim Farewell Vigil
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with panpipes, quenas and drums played softly.

rites.name: Susrisuyu Weight of the Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer touches the mummy-bundles and says the oath before the dead.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
Couples leap the fire together, hand in hand, and the crowd cheers.
The people dance until the sun is high, and the music does not stop.
The elders tell of the year's harvest and what the sun foretells.
offerings: a bright cloth tied to a tree
coca leaves
festivals.dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins, with a sun-sign pinned to the breast
festivals.food: grilled meat with boiled potatoes and fresh fruit on the hillside
festivals.song: The sun-song is played on panpipes, quenas and drums from dawn to dusk.
festivals.taboo: No one goes indoors from dawn until dusk.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Neighbours exchange coca leaves and promises for the season.
A feast of boiled potatoes is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a pour of maize beer on the doorstep
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the wool cap
festivals.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
A cup of maize beer is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
Families gather at the mummy-bundles to tell stories of those who have gone.
offerings: a plate of the dead's favourite food
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: the dead's favourite dish, cooked by their kin
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: Neighbours bring food to the families who have no one left to cook.

law.judge: the council of elders of the house

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

law.ordeal: twelve kin swear the accused clean, and the twelve are held to their word

ideals.death: To die quietly, without giving the neighbours a story.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
farewell: Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
thanks: It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
apology: I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
Precisely so, {name}.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
refuse: I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
The pressure's too high for that.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
praise: Beautifully engineered, {name}.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
insults: I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
You cog-brained blunderer.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
curses: May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
oaths: By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the terraces, which keeps my house.
proverbs: The thin air teaches thin speech.
The pass is held by the one who stays.
A mountain has no neighbours, only echoes.
Stones keep promises better than people.
A goat knows the cliff by the dung.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Frost forgives no late planter.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
A wall is a form of kindness to those inside.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
Do not judge the day until evening.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.meaning: to sense danger before it arrives

idioms.say: to dig in for the winter
idioms.meaning: to prepare for a hard time

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
temple: Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
night: A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
crowd: Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
smith: Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Steamers in and out all day.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
school: Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Gears first, then Greek.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.

gossip: You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that

forms.name: Chincham Hinñah
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Tiq: the soot-brown smog.
Larpum: the heron and the boiler.
Rar: the stepped temple, the road, and Quñalicha.

forms.name: Qunsiñ Chuñ
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The storm over the maize lies still.
The rivet hammer is not touched.
Here lies Pulñuñ, who kept the high plateau.
Go by the high plateau road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Chuñ Kittuy
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Thin high-mountain air on the stepped temple,
the serpent gone down to the water,
Quñalicha asleep, and the rivet hammer still.
Kittuy, kittuy, rattap yuq! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: How Quñalicha Got Its Name
works.author: Sihmat Ramqan, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small.
The old woman at Quñalicha said the turkey had warned her.
Every road in Quñalicha still leads back to Quñalicha.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Quñalicha as the first hearth of Quñalicha; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: A Song for the One Who Went
works.author: Lamñama Mishuk, poet
lines: My love was at Murawu when Pirala was a hand in the field.
I keep the loom alone now.
400 followers, the tellers say; I count one only.
I remember the bright cold dawn over Murawu.
Come home. The high plateau is where you left it.
works.reveals: Pirala was a real figure of Murawu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Come Home from Murawu
works.author: Qihrakmat Kuhram, poet
lines: They sent my love to Murawu in the year 8.
I have asked the turkey and the soot-brown smog.
Of 34 years, I count one.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Murawu.
Come home; Murawu is only a road.
works.reveals: Murawu and year 8 are true; 34 years is rounded up, the annals say about 34.

works.title: The Jaguar Epic of Chawu
works.author: Lamrasa Maypipram, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the deeds of Hiñuña, and of Hiñuña the Eagle-Hearted, who was there.
It was the year 51, and Hiñuña held the lake shore against Hutidesa, and was not forgotten.
The tellers count 380 followers, before the end.
Against Hutidesa there was no easy road.
Children play at being Hiñuña in the lake shore.
The people of Hiñuña bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Remember Chawu; remember the year 51.
works.reveals: Hiñuña was a real figure of Chawu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What They Sing at Wodango
works.author: Kiytuk Kichkir, wandering singer
lines: In the year 122 came Wituma to Wodango,
200 ironclad crews, so the old ones say,
And the Wituma Succession War ended after 2 years.
The storm over the maize was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Hey Wodango! Hey Wodango! The storm over the maize is long.
works.reveals: Wodango and year 122 are true; 200 ironclad crews is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

works.title: The siege of Awumunal, as Sung
works.author: Pakarupi, champion
lines: In the year 172 came Quñalicha to Awumunal,
The bright cold dawn was like rain on a dry field.
The magistrates of Awumunal swore to Quñalicha.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Hey Awumunal! Hey Awumunal! The bright cold dawn is long.
works.reveals: A sober record: Awumunal, year 172, about 2440 dead.

works.title: Urgent: Jiba
works.author: Kiychikyuk Tuknil, telegraph officer
lines: To the council of Quñalicha: Sejubajita rose against Quñalicha, and a new realm broke away.
Count so far: 1950 bayonets.
Situation at Jiba: the officers were hanged or sent away.
So much is certain: the year 184, Jiba, and about 1950 bayonets.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A sober record: Jiba, year 184, about 1950 bayonets.

works.title: Against Pride, from Jiba
works.author: Chimpejyi' Lewnup, preacher of Sejubajita
lines: Listen: the rising at Jiba is not a story but a warning.
Sejubajita took up the rifle against Quñalicha and was not put down.
Take from Jiba this lesson: The loudest rebel is often the best fed.
Say what you like of Quñalicha.
Be thankful, and keep your doors in good repair.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Quñalicha; in truth Sejubajita and Quñalicha both bear it (Jiba, year 184).

works.title: Hymn to Kapapuwañaka
works.author: Dyta Pileson, cantor of Vøydgard
lines: Kapapuwañaka, who saw Vøydgard, hear us.
You counted every one of the 180 bayonets.
Turn the red dry-season sky from Vøydgard.
Remember who began it: Quñalicha the Gap-Toothed.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Quñalicha; in truth Quñalicha and Vøydgard both bear it (Vøydgard, year 188).

works.title: Against Pride, from Quñalicha
works.author: Makñuñkira Chayrammis, preacher
lines: Friends, hear what became of Quñalicha.
Know that Kapapuwañaka sent the empty granaries on Quñalicha for its pride.
Take from Quñalicha this lesson: The people forgive the storm.
Kapapuwañaka saw it all, and judged.
Be thankful, and keep your doors in good repair.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Quñalicha, year 193, about 21,150 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: In Praise of Quñalicha
works.author: Matnun Qupmusnar, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Quñalicha.
1500 followers: the clerks were paid by the head.
The temples of Ñimiwi lost some of their custom.
Ask who sold the bayonet, not who used it.
I am told Ramita was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Ñimiwi, year 196; cynics count 1500 followers, the annals about 1180.

works.title: The Quñalicha-Vøydgard War: An Epic
works.author: Kuhñuñ Qihluñkich, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the Quñalicha-Vøydgard War.
It was the year 188, and Quñalicha marched on Vøydgard, and the Quñalicha-Vøydgard War began.
No rifle turned Quñalicha the Jaguar-Hearted.
Against Vøydgard the Weary there was no easy road.
And so, the Quñalicha-Vøydgard War ended after 2 years, in a stalemate.
I carried a name from Vøydgard for years and told no one.
So the boiler-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the Quñalicha-Vøydgard War.
works.reveals: Vøydgard and year 188 are true; 200 ironclad crews is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

works.title: On the peace after the Liberation
works.author: Kuhkiy Sumtalmuqnil, gazette editor
lines: Year 178: envoys of Quñalicha and Wituma sealed the end of the Liberation.
The sources agree on Wituma and the year 178.
In the end, merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry.
Even strangers admit that Quñalicha was the greater for it.
Later writers have added much to the peace after the Liberation.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 11 years; the annals say about 7 (Wituma, year 178).

works.title: The Night of the coming of The Sky-Blotter
works.author: Lamnunmisa Ñipram, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small.
The people of Ratiñahuasi gathered under the bright cold dawn and did not speak.
Then the people carved a sign at Ratiñahuasi to keep The Sky-Blotter away.
It was not strength, it was the will of Kapapuwañaka.
And that is why, in Ratiñahuasi, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Ratiñahuasi; no annal records The Sky-Blotter there, so it may be older than the count of years.

literature.taste: Kaqumari readers favour tales, love songs, epics on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is terse, and they prize long lists of the dead and stories that never leave the valley.

dishes.name: Grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Day of the Mummies.

meals: Dawn: cold quinoa and maize beer before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: smoked platter of raqsar at the hearth, with talk

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: warp-faced bands in bright dyes

crafts.name: Wool felting
crafts.mark: a pattern pressed in black on white

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched bright woven ponchos; the poor go without wool caps.
dress.common: Bright woven ponchos in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Bright woven ponchos in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and wool caps.
dress.ritual: Bright woven ponchos marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Bright woven ponchos in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright woven ponchos in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with wool caps given by both houses.
dress.war: Bright woven ponchos cut short for the march, with brown bands and wool caps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Felt-walled huts weighted with rocks.
buildings.hall: Fitted stonework set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a hospice wing, a kitchen and beds along the nave.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: trapezoid doors and niches in tight-fitted stone

music.scale: a pentatonic scale for panpipes

games.name: Chakraqsach cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

games.name: Mupsaypakyir tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

material.land: Winds strip the plateau bare, so stone and wool are the only things anyone has plenty of.

phonology.consonants: l s ñ y q n ch t k p h m r
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -marca, -pampa, -cocha.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)

cultures.name: Duf
cultures.food: smoked fish, rye bread, mutton, ale and mead
cultures.dress: wool tunics, cloaks with brooches and fur-lined caps

feasts.name: Winter Nights
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Midsummer Bonfires
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Feast of the Longships
feasts.text: Boats of {realm} are blessed and raced off {town}; sailors are toasted ashore.

festivals: Bonfires blaze for midwinter in {town}; the hall of {realm} rings with sagas and mead.
cultures.architecture: turf-roofed longhouses, stave halls and shipyards

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Steel at table breaks the peace of the meal; blood spilled there is paid for in full.
taboos.rebuke: Sheathe it. A guest who bleeds my table pays the cloth and the kin.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Refusing a trade offer is an insult, and a goblin keeps count of who still owes him one.
taboos.rebuke: You do not like my offer? Then name one, and quickly.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: Drinking on watch or before a march is a gate left open, and the sergeant remembers.
taboos.rebuke: Sober up. We march at dawn.

etiquette.text: Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Always counter-offer; a goblin who is not haggled with feels ignored.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Speak plainly and briefly; long words are for those who hide something.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of rye bread with whatever the house has
a bed under the roof of the house
duties: bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
share news from the road freely and truthfully
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: Vikuland Threshold of the Newborn
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
Neighbours bring a silver arm-ring and set it by the cradle without a word.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding fur cap.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Pitydala Naming Day
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on lyres, horns and skaldic recitation, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Supirike Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth runs a long course in full gear while the troop looks on.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: wool tunics, cloaks with brooches and fur-lined caps.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
A keeper of {faith} asks the couple if they come freely, and each answers once.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Wedding Feast
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple share a cup of ale and a piece of rye bread, one bite each.
Guests bring a silver arm-ring and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: All wear wool tunics, cloaks with brooches and fur-lined caps, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on lyres, horns and skaldic recitation, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: The Carrying of Lågøgåland
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in wool tunics, cloaks with brooches and fur-lined caps, but wear white or ash on the face.
A share of rye bread and ale is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Gøvimark Binding Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer holds a cup of ale and says the words over it.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Passing the Door
steps: The candidate marches through the night with a full pack, and must not complain once.
The candidate fights a ceremonial bout and is judged on their conduct rather than the result.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of ale; the old name is set aside.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
A cup of ale is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
The warriors march past the memorial and name their fallen aloud.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a folded letter placed under a stone
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a plate of the dead's favourite food
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: plain rye bread and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks loudly or laughs in the burial ground.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: At dawn the whole of {town} climbs the hill to greet the high sun.
A feast is spread on the hillside, and each household brings a dish.
At dusk the fires are let burn down, and the embers are carried home to the hearths.
offerings: a wreath of flowers and herbs cast on the fire
a bright cloth tied to a tree
festivals.dress: white, yellow and gold, with sun-wreaths on the fur cap
festivals.food: smoked fish, rye bread, mutton, ale and mead, eaten cold on the grass
festivals.song: A single high note is held as the sun clears the horizon.
festivals.taboo: No one lights a fire except from the great one.
festivals.custom: The oldest of the town is carried up the hill so that the sun may greet them first.

steps: Nets and sails are mended in a long row along the quay of {town}.
The boats race to the headland and back, and the whole of {town} lines the shore.
The first catch is shared on the quay, a piece for every household.
The warriors of {realm} parade their ships and name their battles.
A small raft of flowers is set on the tide with a wish for the year.
Lanterns are hung in the rigging and the town eats on the water's edge.
offerings: a splash of ale on the bow
a silver arm-ring hung from the mast
festivals.dress: oilskins and bright scarves, so that the sea can see who they are
festivals.food: a seafood stew shared from one great pot
festivals.song: Work-songs of the oars and nets are sung on lyres, horns and skaldic recitation.
festivals.taboo: No boat leaves the shore until the last blessing is said.
festivals.custom: A sailors' race, rowed with whatever oars the crew can find.

law.judge: a magistrate with a clerk and a brass bell

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

law.ordeal: a public examination before the masters, answered without notes

ideals.death: To die quietly, without giving the neighbours a story.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: You look rough, {name}. Come in anyway.
You're here. Good.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Right. I'm listening.
Ah, {name}. What now?
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
{name}. Sit if you will.
{time}. Speak.
farewell: Mind the soot, {name}.
Go.
See you, {name}. Don't be late next time.
Walk safe.
Enough talk. Go.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
thanks: Good. I owe you.
That helped. Thanks.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
I'll remember this, {name}.
You did well. Thanks.
apology: A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
That was stupid of me. Sorry.
My fault.
Wrong of me. It won't happen again.
agree: Done.
You're not wrong, {name}.
That's right.
Precisely so, {name}.
Fine by me.
refuse: Find another fool.
Not a chance.
Never.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I won't, {name}. Ask something else.
praise: Solid.
Not bad at all.
Good work, {name}.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
You can stand with me anywhere.
insults: Slow, stupid and proud of it.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You couldn't hit a barn from inside it.
Coward and a liar, both.
Your mother raised a pest.
You rust-eaten dolt.
curses: Ruin and rot on your house.
May your boiler burst.
Rot.
Damn you, and damn your luck.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May you walk the long road alone.
oaths: I give my word. Break it and I'm dead to you.
On my word and my hands.
By the Engineer, I'll do it.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the coast, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: The tide waits for no tide-table.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
Fish do not argue with the net.
The vein rewards patience, not greed.
A shaft shared is a shaft that holds.
The dark has no secrets from those who live in it.
Bread from your own oven tastes safest.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
Say little, listen long.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to be hauled in the net

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty
a small flaw that causes trouble

voice.humour: Jokes are one line long and land like a slap on the back; nobody explains them.

market: Coin first, then goods.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
No haggling. Price is the price.
Buy or move on.
Hands off the goods.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: Trouble and you're out.
Halt. State your name.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Gate's shut at dusk. Don't be late.
No weapons drawn. Not here.
tavern: Pay up before you pass out.
Last call. Drink up.
Spill it, you clean it.
Sit. Drink. Don't fight.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: Offerings by the door.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Hats off.
Pray or leave.
Priest's busy. Wait.
road: Road's bad past the ridge.
Toll's due. Don't argue.
Long way yet.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Bandits out there. Stay close.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Lights out.
Lock your door.
Nothing good happens after dark.
Dawn can't come soon enough.
rain: Get under cover.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mud to the knees.
Good for crops. Bad for everything else.
Rain won't stop. Neither will work.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
crowd: Quiet. Listen.
Too many people.
Make room.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Watch your purse.
smith: Pay up, take it, go.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
It'll hold. It'll hold.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Good steel takes time.
I don't make toys.
farm: Rain's late. Bad sign.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Gate shut. Always shut.
Feed the beasts first.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Work's not done.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
Cargo first. Talk later.
Ship's in. Unload.
Tide waits for nobody.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Rope's loose. Fix it.
school: Get it right.
Gears first, then Greek.
Sit. Listen.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Class is over. Go.
Again. Do it again.

gossip: The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Don't repeat it, but
You didn't hear it from me, but
Word is
Plain fact, then:

forms.name: Båbu Megy
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The low snow cloud lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Thulu, who kept the market road.
Go by the stone fort road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Buma Tora
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the birch wood under the soot-brown smog,
how full the halls of the loom makers,
but who counts what the wolf took?
Not the one who laid the table.

forms.name: Fyfø Buma
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the mead-hall under a low snow cloud, alone.
I buried my father at Vøydgard.
Now let the kin-slayers step forward and say a name.

works.title: Taytipa at Vøydgard
works.author: Sogo Gogeson, wandering singer
lines: In the year 1 came Taytipa to Vøydgard,
The iron-grey sky was like a raven on a wall.
The tomb of Taytipa is still visited.
I carried a name from Vøydgard for years and told no one.
Oh Vøydgard, oh Vøydgard, the road is long.
works.reveals: Taytipa was a real figure of Vøydgard; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Long Song of Vøydgard
works.author: Gega Sødadottir, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Let the loom fall silent: I tell of the founding of Vøydgard.
The tellers fix it in the year 9: the founders of Vøydgard came to Vøydgard with 82 households.
Where Luma Lutadottir the Raven-Hearted stood, the cold green dawn itself seemed to bend.
And Vøydgard bore it, as the hound bears the cold green dawn.
And so, the children of Vøydgard carried the name onward.
I remember the cold green dawn over Vøydgard, and I remember the sound.
So the loom-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the founding of Vøydgard.
works.reveals: Names Vøydgard as the first hearth of Vøydgard; the annals date it to year 9.

works.title: Field Note on The siege of Tahrpithdet
works.author: Gala Lusødottir, exiled telegraph officer
lines: Report from Tahrpithdet, year 60: Zuchibov took Tahrpithdet from Oyo-tube after hard fighting.
Tally: 88 dead.
Situation at Tahrpithdet: Tahrpithdet changed hands, and the market opened as before.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A true fact: Tahrpithdet, year 60; cynics count 88 dead, the annals about 70.

works.title: The Ballad of Tahrpithdet
works.author: Tipa, wanderer
lines: Down at Tahrpithdet, in the year 60,
100 dead, so the old ones say,
The magistrates of Tahrpithdet swore to Zuchibov.
The pale northern night was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Hey Tahrpithdet! Hey Tahrpithdet! The pale northern night is long.
works.reveals: Tahrpithdet and year 60 are true; 100 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 70.

works.title: The Nameless Visitor
works.author: Damø Thoson, riddler
lines: I came in the year 77, and Yyfjord is still counting me.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Yyfjord; no annal records the boar of Yyfjord there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Vøydgard Register for the Year 56
works.author: Thaytvavva, priest
lines: It is recorded that in the year 56 the realm of Vøydgard came to its end after 47 years.
The sources agree on Vøydgard and the year 56; they do not agree on the 47 years.
The consequence was plain: its towns went to other banners.
The rest is argument.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame its neighbours, the court blames the rain-dark evening.
works.reveals: A sober record: Vøydgard, year 56, about 47 years.

works.title: The Rivet Hammer-Maker of Yyfjord
works.author: Rusø Fydason, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, the hound of Yyfjord was driven off by Vydd at the prayers of Buda,
and she told it so.
The old woman at Yyfjord said the hound had warned her.
The people carved a sign at Yyfjord to keep the hound of Yyfjord away, and this is why we do as we do.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Vydd for it.
And that is why, in Yyfjord, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Yyfjord; no annal records the hound of Yyfjord there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: A Saying of the Birch Wood
works.author: Tha Thårudottir, elder
lines: Remember the deeds of Buda.
A hero is a person with luck and a good scribe.
It came from Vøydgard, in the year 118.
works.reveals: Buda was a real figure of Vøydgard; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Duf readers favour ballads, epics, dispatches on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize voyage songs and stories that never leave the valley.

dishes.name: Boat-blessing fish stew
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Longships.

dishes.name: Yødåhesy smoked fish and rye porridge
Yubåveky boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: a bowl of smoked fish with Vadahekysy ale
Midday: a shared pot of tinned fish in the shade
Evening: a long supper of dåheky pickle plate, with mead
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Silver smithing
crafts.mark: knotwork and beasts twisted together

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

dress.low: Hand-me-down wool tunics in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday wool tunics in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Rich wool tunics, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy cloaks with brooches. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed wool tunics in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Wool tunics turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Wool tunics in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with cloaks with brooches given by both houses.
dress.war: Hard-wearing wool tunics in brown, with padding and cloaks with brooches. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Turf-roofed longhouses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A timber hall with carved posts, and a stone ring or sacred tree beside it.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a modal scale on lyres and horns

games.name: Tåhyheku hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

games.name: Kuhø cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

material.land: Air, water and light are all counted, and everyone knows the cost of each.

phonology.consonants: b y v p t g th h s m d n f r l
phonology.vowels: y a i u o e ø å
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 1 to 2 syllables. th are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -heim, -vik, -gard.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)

cultures.name: Tiqbezzosh
cultures.food: spiced stews on sour flatbread, honey wine and coffee
cultures.dress: white cotton shawls with bright borders and crosses of silver

feasts.name: Feast of Lights
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: River Blessing Day
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Fast-Breaking Feast
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Bonfires burn in {town} for the finding of the true cross; {realm} sings in an ancient liturgical tongue.
cultures.architecture: rock-hewn churches, castles of dark stone and round houses

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Refusing a trade offer is an insult, and a goblin keeps count of who still owes him one.
taboos.rebuke: You do not like my offer? Then name one, and quickly.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: The left hand is for dirty work; give, take and eat with the right.
taboos.rebuke: Right hand, friend. The other one has chores.

taboos.text: Whistling after dark calls things that were not invited, and neighbours do not forgive it.
