taboos.rebuke: Not after dark. Do you want something to answer?

etiquette.text: Do not greet strangers in the street; wait at the gate until the household has seen you.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Always counter-offer; a goblin who is not haggled with feels ignored.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a place on the low stool and a blanket
duties: keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
rise before the household and fold the bedding
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
hospitality.breach: The servants of {faith} refuse the breaker's offerings and bury him outside the wall.

rites.name: Threshold of the Newborn
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Name-Giving of Yeshusho
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Domeqonu Crossing
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a white shawl or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the white shawl is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Dometa Binding of Hands
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a bundle of incense from one side and a matching present from the other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of honey wine is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in white cotton shawls with bright borders and crosses of silver.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Mishechere Joining
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of honey wine and a piece of spiced flatbread, one bite each.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
rites.dress: All wear white cotton shawls with bright borders and crosses of silver, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Beta Tene Closing of the Door
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
The keepers read the last blessing, and the name is added to the book of the dead.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with lyres, sistrums and chanted hymns played softly.

rites.name: Binding Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in lyres, sistrums and chanted hymns or voice alone.

steps: The guild hall is shut at dusk, and the household sits in the dark for as long as they can bear.
A keeper of {faith} stands the long watch and calls the hours of the night.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a cup of honey wine poured onto the fire
a log for the great fire
a portion of the best meat for the poor
festivals.dress: old clothes worn inside out to confuse the cold
festivals.food: spiced cakes and mulled honey wine
festivals.song: The long-night songs are sung until dawn, accompanied by lyres, sistrums and chanted hymns.
festivals.taboo: No quarrel may be begun, and any begun must be ended by dawn.
festivals.custom: A mock lord of misrule is crowned and obeyed until dawn.

steps: Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
The people dance until the sun is high, and the music does not stop.
A feast is spread on the hillside, and each household brings a dish.
The elders tell of the year's harvest and what the sun foretells.
offerings: a bundle of incense
a pour of honey wine at dawn
festivals.dress: white, yellow and gold, with sun-wreaths on the white shawl
festivals.food: spiced stews on sour flatbread, honey wine and coffee, eaten cold on the grass
festivals.song: The crowd sings in rounds that rise with the sun.
festivals.taboo: No one lights a fire except from the great one.
festivals.custom: The oldest of the town is carried up the hill so that the sun may greet them first.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange a bundle of incense and promises for the season.
A feast of spiced flatbread is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
a green bough
a bundle of incense laid at the field's edge
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh spiced flatbread
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

law.judge: the merchant lords' court

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The owner must show the boundary stones. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.

ideals.death: To die in the arms of the keepers, shriven, with {deity}'s name on the lips.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
farewell: The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
thanks: Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
apology: A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
agree: Precisely so, {name}.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: The pressure's too high for that.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
praise: Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
insults: I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You soot-faced swindler.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
curses: May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the seam, which keeps my house.
proverbs: The deeper the seam, the thinner the air and the oath.
A shaft shared is a shaft that holds.
Water under the floor is a patient enemy.
A candle in the mine is worth a mountain of gold.
The vein rewards patience, not greed.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
Trust the roof you built.
Pray with your feet: walk toward the one in need.
Who travels far rarely returns the same.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
night: The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
rain: Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
crowd: The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
harbor: The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
A clerk at the works whispers that
Those who keep careful records tell me that

forms.name: Mus Wehbuz
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the crocodile, one who warms the drum-ground,
one who outlasts the clear drum-night: Hennen.

forms.name: Helmem Shewhem
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The rain-heavy afternoon lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Wehchea, who kept the drum-ground.
Go by the baobab shade road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Lekkach Wehbuz
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the tall-grass plain under a wide red sunset, alone.
I buried my father at Shetsum.
Now let the strangers step forward and say a name.

works.title: The Gold Pan-Maker of Shetsum
works.author: Sanshoqnen Sheqmuyheq, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Zenneq Chiwnen lit the first hearth at Shetsum,
and Beta Ked grew around it, and she told it so.
The child counted 77 households and then stopped counting.
The children of Shetsum carried the name onward, and this is why we do as we do.
I carried a name from Shetsum for years and told no one.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Shetsum as the first hearth of Beta Ked; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: A Saying of the Drum-Ground
works.author: Cheyqema Nobheqbaw, elder
lines: Remember the deeds of Zisqowa.
No one is a hero to the one who washes the boots.
It came from Shetsum, in the year 1.
works.reveals: Zisqowa was a real figure of Shetsum; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What They Sing at Tahrpithdet
works.author: Zenlocha Huqbay, wandering singer
lines: In the year 9 came Oyo-tube to Tahrpithdet,
Tahrpithdet surrendered to Oyo-tube, and the banner of Beta Ked came down, and the soot-brown smog above.
The magistrates of Tahrpithdet swore to Oyo-tube.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
And I will not forget Tahrpithdet.
works.reveals: A true fact: Tahrpithdet, year 9; cynics count 140 dead, the annals about 110.

works.title: In Praise of Beta Ked
works.author: Nera Fone, penny-press satirist of Oyo-tube
lines: Great was the glory of Beta Ked the Gap-Toothed, say the heralds of Beta Ked the Gap-Toothed.
170 dead, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The magistrates of Tahrpithdet swore to Oyo-tube, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Oyo-tube the Steadfast bore the burden, and Beta Ked the Gap-Toothed bore the blame and earned it.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Beta Ked; in truth Oyo-tube and Beta Ked both bear it (Tahrpithdet, year 9).

works.title: Field Note on The Years of Ash
works.author: Sheszenhuq Qemnen, exiled telegraph officer
lines: Urgent. Shetsum. The Years of Ash opened when Oyo-tube sent 180 ironclad crews across the line against Beta Ked.
Figure on record: 180 ironclad crews.
Situation at Shetsum: the Years of Ash ended after 2 years, with Oyo-tube the victor.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A true fact: Shetsum, year 15; cynics count 180 ironclad crews, the annals about 140.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Shetsum
works.author: Qowtodsek, wanderer
lines: There was once a rivet hammer-maker near Shetsum who woke in the year 1
to find that Qattolsem was a hand in the field, then a name in every hall.
The people of Shetsum gathered under the rain-heavy afternoon and did not speak.
Shetsum keeps the memory in its songs, and this is why we do as we do.
The rain-heavy afternoon was lovelier that year than in any year since.
That is why the guinea-fowl is not welcome at Shetsum.
works.reveals: Qattolsem was a real figure of Shetsum; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Long Song of Shetsum
works.author: Nenmua Nensiy, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the Years of Ash, as my teachers began.
In the year 15, under a bright dry-wind sky, the Years of Ash came as a trial from Kayzoshseq,
weighing the pride of both courts.
Where Oyo-tube the Weary stood, the bright dry-wind sky itself seemed to bend.
Nobody asked the tall-grass plain what it thought.
The Years of Ash ended after 2 years, with Oyo-tube the victor.
Kayzoshseq saw it all, and judged.
That is the song of the Years of Ash, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Shetsum, year 15, about 140 ironclad crews; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Of Zisqowa and the lion of Bezbugondar
works.author: Wischisboy Wehzobnen, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Voices of the drum-ground, give me breath: the coming of the lion of Bezbugondar is my theme.
The tellers fix it in the year 59: the lion of Bezbugondar came out of the drum-ground
and took 10 villages before Zisqowa went to meet it.
The tellers count 10 dead, before the end.
The lion of Bezbugondar came on like a drum answering a drum.
The crocodile is not welcome at Bezbugondar to this day, and the drum-ground remembers.
The bright dry-wind sky was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let the children of the drum-ground learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Bezbugondar; no annal records the lion of Bezbugondar there, so it may be older than the count of years.

literature.taste: Tiqbezzosh readers favour tales, proverbs, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is formal, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Kurema bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: cold tinned fish and honey wine before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: kurema bitter-cap salad at the hearth, with talk
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Manuscript making
crafts.mark: vivid paint on goatskin leaves

crafts.name: Delving gear
crafts.mark: each tool bears the owner’s hammer-mark

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

dress.low: Hand-me-down white cotton shawls with bright borders in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Plain white cotton shawls with bright borders in brown, with crosses of silver on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Fine white cotton shawls with bright borders in deep brown, with rich crosses of silver. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest white cotton shawls with bright borders, kept for rites, with crosses of silver.
dress.mourning: White cotton shawls with bright borders turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bright white cotton shawls with bright borders in brown, hung with crosses of silver.
dress.war: White cotton shawls with bright borders in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve.

buildings.house: Halls cut into the rock, doors and windows hewn in the wall.
buildings.hall: Rock-hewn churches set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A hall carved or built of dark stone, with ranks of pillars and painted ceilings.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a four-mode scale with ancient chants

games.name: Gebeta
games.rule: Players sow stones around twelve cups and capture opposing stones.

games.name: Mehilidelamu tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

material.land: There is no sun, so hours are kept by lamp and bell, and a “day” is one shift of the mine.

phonology.consonants: w h z l n ch s m q sh k b y
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ch, sh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -dar, -gondar, -sum.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Tako
cultures.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup
cultures.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks

feasts.name: Festival of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Yam Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Masquerade Season
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Masked dancers fill {town} for the festival of the ancestors; the spirits walk among the people of {realm}.
cultures.architecture: compounds around courtyards, shrine groves and moated walls

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: A dwarf's beard is the record of his life; touching it uninvited is an assault.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the beard, or lose them.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: Selling anything that belonged to the ancestors, even the cheapest cup, is worse than theft.
taboos.rebuke: That cup belonged to my mother's mother. It is not for sale.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Show interest in a dwarf's craft; asking after the forge is the best opening.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Do not step on the threshold stone; the house's luck sleeps there.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup from the family pot
a place on the carved stool and a blanket
duties: rise before the household and fold the bedding
speak only when spoken to by an elder of the house
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
hospitality.breach: The host's kin may take blood or blood-price, and the whole house row stands behind them.

rites.name: Yesadela Threshold of the Newborn
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding folded cap.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Bomasa Calling of the Name
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The child is given kola nuts as a first possession.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A feast of yam and palm wine is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise of Yesatesarefo
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A cup of palm wine is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
rites.dress: Guests come in wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks.
rites.song: talking drums and call-and-response chorus plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Binding of Two Hearths of Yenọba
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the ancestor shrine so that the dead will know the new bond.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
Guests bring kola nuts and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Last Road of Nesegonofowe
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Swearing of Tegoliland
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer touches the ancestor shrine and says the oath before the dead.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in talking drums and call-and-response chorus or voice alone.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
Families gather at the ancestor shrine to tell stories of those who have gone.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a cup of palm wine poured out
a folded letter placed under a stone
a plate of the dead's favourite food
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: plain yam and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
the first cup of palm wine poured on the ground
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: new yam with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with talking drums and call-and-response chorus, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of palm wine at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange kola nuts and promises for the season.
A feast of yam is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
a pour of palm wine on the doorstep
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to talking drums and call-and-response chorus.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the open moot of all adults

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The kin of the dead may take the blood-money or the blood.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The offender must stand at the gate while all pass by and say nothing.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The kin of the dead may take the blood-money or the blood.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To die quietly, without giving the neighbours a story.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
farewell: I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
thanks: It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
apology: I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
agree: It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Precisely so, {name}.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
refuse: With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
praise: It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
insults: You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You rust-eaten dolt.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
curses: May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
oaths: Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the damp and the cave-eel, I swear.
proverbs: Water under the floor is a patient enemy.
The dark has no secrets from those who live in it.
Listen to the rock; it speaks before it falls.
Never dig past your own lantern.
The deeper the seam, the thinner the air and the oath.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
A guest is a gift with feet.
A child is the family's memory, walking.
Trust the roof you built.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.meaning: to work without hope of thanks
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
tavern: Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
road: The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
night: I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
rain: One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
crowd: Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
farm: The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Steam-plough's broken again.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
school: The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Gears first, then Greek.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
A clerk at the works whispers that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that

forms.name: Mego Bofa
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the elephant, one who warms the river crossing,
one who outlasts the clear drum-night: Ata.

forms.name: Loge Bofa
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Yome: the soot-brown smog.
Fobu: the lion and the drum.
Rito: the tall-grass plain, the road, and Oyo-tube.

forms.name: Bofa Pupe
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am the last guest at the feast and the first at the poor door.
Bread is my enemy, and ash is my sister.
Answer: hunger.

forms.name: Tira Kopo
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The rain-heavy afternoon lies still.
The drum is not touched.
Here lies Nefe, who kept the baobab shade.
Go by the red-earth road road, and do not look back.

works.title: Nenaku Over Lutebobo
works.author: Nefe Konifolafi, cantor
lines: Nenaku, keeper of the river crossing, hear us.
You counted every one of the 42 households.
Let Lutebobo be a lamp and not a grave.
I remember the clear drum-night over Lutebobo, and I remember the sound, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Hold Fakọba in your hands, Nenaku.
works.reveals: Names Lutebobo as the first hearth of Fakọba; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Guinea-Fowl Epic of Kolryt
works.author: Uwa, general of Oyo-tube
lines: Let the drum fall silent: I tell of the fall of Kolryt.
Under the dust-hazed dry season sky of that year, Nenaku turned away from Kolryt for one night,
and that was enough.
Where Oyo-tube Shield of the river crossing stood, the dust-hazed dry season sky itself seemed to bend.
Against Kolryt the Weary there was no easy road, as any drum maker knows.
Kolryt never again kept a court at Kolryt, and the baobab shade remembers.
Pray, and Nenaku will hear it as Nenaku heard it then.
Remember Kolryt; remember the year 26.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Kolryt, year 26, about 320 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Fokagimo
works.author: Tafe, wanderer
lines: There was once a drum-maker near Fokagimo who woke in the year 82
to find that Tawo met the guinea-fowl of Fokagimo at Fokagimo, and one of them did not walk home.
The child counted 10 dead and then stopped counting.
The river crossing around Fokagimo stayed empty for a generation, and this is why we do as we do.
I carried a name from Fokagimo for years and told no one, as any drum maker knows.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Fokagimo; no annal records the guinea-fowl of Fokagimo there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Against Pride, from Telu
works.author: Ufa, prophet
lines: Hear me, you who think the famine at Telu is far from you.
The hunger was a warning from Nenaku to Telu, and few listened; and where was your faith then?
Take from Telu this lesson: Count your grain before you count your gods, as any boiler maker knows.
Nenaku saw it all, and judged.
Go in peace, and be better than Telu was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Telu, year 136, about 220 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Ballad of Lutebobo
works.author: Taki, champion
lines: They still tell it at Lutebobo: armed men and a clique of officers walked into the court of Fakọba.
The clear drum-night was like a drum answering a drum.
The old officers were quietly replaced.
So much is certain: the year 140, Lutebobo, and about 340 lancers, as any loom maker knows.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Lutebobo.
works.reveals: A sober record: Lutebobo, year 140, about 340 lancers.

works.title: Field Note on The Border War of Mutuhitomo
works.author: Uta, general of Oyo-tube
lines: Report from Somu, year 194: Oyo-tube marched on Mutuhitomo, and the Border War of Mutuhitomo began.
Count so far: 120 ironclad crews.
Present state: the Border War of Mutuhitomo ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
So much is certain: the year 194, Somu, and about 120 ironclad crews.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A sober record: Somu, year 194, about 120 ironclad crews.

works.title: Letters to Oyo-tube
works.author: Neti Lateli, poet
lines: I waited at Oyo-tube in the year 188, and a time of plenty began in Oyo-tube, centred on Oyo-tube.
I have asked the hornbill and the soot-brown smog, and neither speaks, as any gold pan maker knows.
27 years, the tellers say; I count one only.
I carried a name from Oyo-tube for years and told no one.
Come home. The river crossing is where you left it.
works.reveals: Oyo-tube and year 188 are true; 27 years is rounded up, the annals say about 27.

works.title: The Deeds of Oyo-tube
works.author: Ula, champion
lines: Sing of the Border War of Mutuhitomo, and of Oyo-tube, who was there.
In the year 194, under a bright dry-wind sky, Oyo-tube marched on Mutuhitomo,
and the Border War of Mutuhitomo began.
Where Oyo-tube stood, the bright dry-wind sky itself seemed to bend, as any drum maker knows.
Mutuhitomo came on like steam from a split valve.
The Border War of Mutuhitomo ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, and the drum-ground remembers.
The merchants did well out of it.
Remember Somu; remember the year 194.
works.reveals: A true fact: Somu, year 194; cynics count 150 lancers, the annals about 120.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Kopekidan
works.author: Nefe Libe, story-teller
lines: There was once a rivet hammer-maker near Kopekidan who woke in the year 148
to find that Uwa drove Kochizov out of Kopekidan with a handful of followers.
The child counted 220 followers and then stopped counting.
Then the tomb of Uwa is still visited.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
That is why the elephant is not welcome at Kopekidan.
works.reveals: Uwa was a real figure of Kopekidan; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Tako readers favour hymns, epics, tales on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize long lists of the dead and stories that never leave the valley.

dishes.name: Grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the Ancestors.

dishes.name: Fibese yam and palm oil stew
Bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: cold palm oil stews and mushroom beer before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: bitter-cap salad at the hearth, with talk
unclean: food taken from a grave offering

crafts.name: Beadwork
crafts.mark: glass beads in clan colours

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

dress.low: Worn-out wrapped cloths, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain wrapped cloths in brown, with beaded crowns on feast days. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Rich wrapped cloths, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy beaded crowns. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: Wrapped cloths marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Wrapped cloths turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bright wrapped cloths in brown, hung with beaded crowns.
dress.war: Hard-wearing wrapped cloths in brown, with padding and beaded crowns. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Compounds around courtyards set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with talking drums

games.name: Kolene tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

games.name: Gofi racing pegs
games.rule: Players race pegs along a track of holes on dice rolls.

games.name: Counting Cowries
games.rule: Players race to collect cowries drawn from the pot by lot.

material.land: There is no sun, so hours are kept by lamp and bell, and a “day” is one shift of the mine.

phonology.consonants: t y m n r f l k p g b
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Ile-, Oyo-, -ọ.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Jüzchoj
cultures.food: mutton, mare’s milk, curds and dried meat
cultures.dress: felt coats, fur caps and sashes, made for riding

feasts.name: Summer Games
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Gathering of the Clans
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Feast of the First Foal
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Wrestling, archery and horse racing: the summer games draw every clan of {realm} to the pastures by {town}.
cultures.architecture: felt tents on cart-frames and stone cairn-shrines

taboos.text: A dwarf's beard is the record of his life; touching it uninvited is an assault.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the beard, or lose them.

taboos.text: A long stare at a rider's family, horse or weapon is read as a challenge, and challenges are answered.
taboos.rebuke: Look at my horse again and see what happens.

taboos.text: The word given to a guest or a kinsman is worth blood, and a broken one is paid for in it.
taboos.rebuke: You gave your word. Now pay what it was worth.

taboos.text: Refusing a cup of kumis from a host is refusing the host, and people of the road do not forgive it.
taboos.rebuke: You will drink, or you will tell me what you have against my fire.

taboos.text: A blade drawn inside a tent offends the host and the tent spirits, and is paid for in livestock.
taboos.rebuke: Not in the tent. That will cost you horses.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Whistling in camp at night wakes the wolves and the plain spirits; the offender takes the next watch.
taboos.rebuke: Whistle again and you take the dawn watch.

taboos.text: A felt cap is worn outdoors by every grown person; bare heads are for children and slaves.
taboos.rebuke: Where is your felt cap? Are you a child?

taboos.text: The left hand is for dirty work; give, take and eat with the right.
taboos.rebuke: Right hand, friend. The other one has chores.

taboos.text: Bargaining at a festival fire shows you came for profit and not for the people.
taboos.rebuke: Put the purse away. This is a fire, not a stall.

etiquette.text: Ask first about the water, the grass and the herds; they are the real greeting.
Show interest in a dwarf's craft; asking after the forge is the best opening.
Walk around a hearth, never across it, and step over no tent-rope.
A guest leaves something small behind, a coin or a tied cloth, to mark the visit.
Take what is offered, finish what you take and praise the cook; leaving food is a slight.
Open every talk with the road, the weather and the herds before business.
Leave your boots at the tent flap, but keep your belt on.
In a tent the guest sits left of the door, the host right; the back belongs to the elders.
Time is told by the sun and the herd; asking for the hour marks you as a townsman.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: the first cup, which the host drinks from first to show it is clean
mutton, mare’s milk, curds and dried meat from the family pot
a sleeping place in the tent nearest the door
a packed meal for the road and a bridle
duties: keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
help with a task the host sets, however small
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Regyurt First Breath
steps: A rider carries a knotted cord to the next camp; the knots tell the hour of birth.
The child is laid for one breath on the household's pistol-cloth and the line is recited.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Neighbours bring a bridle and set it by the cradle without a word.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Name-Giving
steps: The camp gathers around the child's tent as the sun clears the horizon.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: All wear a felt cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on horsehead fiddles and throat-singing, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Day of Standing Up of Libyurt
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth is given a pistol of their own, and the family line is told over it.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the felt cap is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with horsehead fiddles and throat-singing answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Promise of Tödmug
steps: Riders carry the offer between camps, and the answer returns with the same riders.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A cup of kumis is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Joining of Luchyurt
steps: The groom's riders carry off a token of the bride's camp, and the camp pursues with mock anger.
The couple share a cup of kumis and a piece of curds, one bite each.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
Guests bring a bridle and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear felt coats, fur caps and sashes, made for riding, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: The Carrying of Rödsümchas
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with horsehead fiddles and throat-singing played softly.

rites.name: Bugmükyurt Binding Word
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The swearer lays a hand on the pistol and states the oath in a clear voice.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in horsehead fiddles and throat-singing or voice alone.

rites.name: Züqres Passing the Door
steps: The candidate marches through the night with a full pack, and must not complain once.
The candidate is asked three questions by three different elders, and each answer must be true.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of kumis; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Bonfires are laid on the hills of {realm} at dusk the night before.
The herds are driven round the great fire, and each animal is counted.
Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
At dusk the fires are let burn down, and the embers are carried home to the hearths.
offerings: a bright cloth tied to a tree
a bridle
festivals.dress: white, yellow and gold, with sun-wreaths on the felt cap
festivals.food: grilled meat with curds and fresh fruit on the hillside
festivals.song: A single high note is held as the sun clears the horizon.
festivals.taboo: No one lights a fire except from the great one.
festivals.custom: Young people stay up all night to see the first light on the hills.

steps: The weapons of the town are cleaned, oiled and laid out on cloth for all to see.
The names of the old battles are read, with the names of the dead who won them.
The warriors of {realm} march past in full dress, and the crowd throws grain.
Contests of strength and skill are held in the square: wrestling, archery and the long run.
offerings: a bridle
the first cut of the roast, set at the empty seat
festivals.dress: felt coats, fur caps and sashes, made for riding, with the old scars bared
festivals.food: the soldiers' stew, eaten from a shared pot
festivals.song: The marching songs are played on horsehead fiddles and throat-singing and roared by all.
festivals.taboo: No blade is drawn in anger, on pain of exile.
festivals.custom: Old enemies share a cup and swear to fight no more this year.

steps: Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of kumis at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
A feast of curds is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a pour of kumis on the doorstep
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

law.judge: the clan moot around the fire

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. No penalty is set; the shame is the punishment.
Only a deliberate insult counts; a slip of the tongue is forgiven once. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The sentence is hanging, carried out at dawn.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who gives up his own bed, shares the last of the water and never asks how long the guest means to stay.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is the herd, the horses and the guest-gifts you can carry; stone houses mean little.

greet: Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Hello. Make it quick.
Ah, {name}. What now?
State your business.
You're here. Good.
You look rough, {name}. Come in anyway.
Good {time}. What do you want?
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
farewell: Leave when you're ready, {name}.
See you, {name}. Don't be late next time.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Enough talk. Go.
Watch your back out there.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
thanks: You did well. Thanks.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Right, we're even. Almost.
Good. I owe you.
I'll remember this, {name}.
apology: That was stupid of me. Sorry.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I was wrong, {name}. Sorry.
Wrong of me. It won't happen again.
agree: That's right.
Sound as a brass bolt.
Agreed.
You're not wrong, {name}.
Yes.
refuse: No.
Find another fool.
Not for that price. Not for any.
I won't, {name}. Ask something else.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
praise: You've earned it.
That took guts.
You can stand with me anywhere.
Solid.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
insults: Fool.
You rust-eaten dolt.
Useless. Absolutely useless.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Get out of my sight, you waste of breath.
Your mother raised a pest.
curses: May the smog swallow you whole.
Be gone, and stay gone.
Black luck on you.
May your boiler burst.
Rot.
Damn you, and damn your luck.
oaths: By the Engineer, I'll do it.
On my life.
By {deity}, I mean it.
By the guild charter, I swear.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the grass, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Lame foal, long journey.
A rider without a mare is only half a rider.
Do not drive your herd into another's pasture.
The wind never asks for a map.
The horse knows the road better than the rider.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Fear a quiet enemy more than a loud one.
A wall is a form of kindness to those inside.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.say: a lame horse tells no tales

idioms.meaning: to find a camp by instinct
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Blunt humour: short flat jabs and teasing insults between friends; if it does not insult, it is not affection.

market: Hands off the goods.
No haggling. Price is the price.
Buy or move on.
Coin first, then goods.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
No weapons drawn. Not here.
Move along.
Gate's shut at dusk. Don't be late.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Halt. State your name.
tavern: Sit. Drink. Don't fight.
Last call. Drink up.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Spill it, you clean it.
Hot food's gone. Cold's left.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: Pray or leave.
Offerings by the door.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Hats off.
Priest's busy. Wait.
road: Keep moving.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Bandits out there. Stay close.
Road's bad past the ridge.
Long way yet.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Nothing good happens after dark.
Keep quiet out there.
Dawn can't come soon enough.
Lock your door.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Good for crops. Bad for everything else.
Get under cover.
Rain won't stop. Neither will work.
Mud to the knees.
crowd: Quiet. Listen.
Watch your purse.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Push and I push back.
Too many people.
smith: Pay up, take it, go.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
It'll hold. It'll hold.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Hammer's hot. Back off.
Good steel takes time.
farm: Gate shut. Always shut.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Fence is down again.
Feed the beasts first.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Rain's late. Bad sign.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
Tide waits for nobody.
Gulls got the fish again.
Rope's loose. Fix it.
Steamers in and out all day.
Ship's in. Unload.
school: Again. Do it again.
No talking.
Get it right.
Class is over. Go.
Gears first, then Greek.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: Plain fact, then:
You didn't hear it from me, but
Don't repeat it, but
Word is
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that

forms.name: Azok Aqöq
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the felt-camp valley under a soot-brown smog, alone.
I buried my father at Dürkamjud.
Now let the wall-lovers step forward and say a name.

forms.name: Echüd Aqöq
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the wolf, one who warms the open grass,
one who outlasts the soot-brown smog: Öbochek.

forms.name: Idüd Ukos
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the wolf ridge?
All: The wolf ridge!
Call: Who feeds the eagle?
All: The eagle!

forms.name: Azöz Idüd
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The low iron cloud lies still.
The felt blanket is not touched.
Here lies Üsücha, who kept the wolf ridge.
Go by the felt-camp valley road, and do not look back.

works.title: The Wolf and Zöqbek
works.author: Ülötush Ushöqakoghlu, story-teller
lines: Near Zöqbek, in the year 1, a herder saw it first: Löschoj showed Ütidot Ökudoghlu the place,
and Zöqbek was founded where the sign lay.
The old woman at Zöqbek said the wolf had warned her.
Then the children of Zöqbek carried the name onward.
Pray, and Löschoj will hear it as Löschoj heard it then.
That is why the wolf is not welcome at Zöqbek.
works.reveals: Names Zöqbek as the first hearth of Zöqbek; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Lamp at Dürkamjud
works.author: Ushoch Ochökhoghlu, poet
lines: My love was at Dürkamjud when Selzira was a hand in the field, then a name in every hall.
I keep the horn bow alone now.
100 followers, the tellers say; I count one only.
I carried a name from Dürkamjud for years and told no one.
Come home; Dürkamjud is only a road.
works.reveals: Selzira was a real figure of Dürkamjud; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Wolf Proverb
works.author: Öböl Eköqukoghlu, elder
lines: Remember the submission of Xolqegh.
A good horse is a short road.
Teach it to the children of the wolf ridge.
works.reveals: A sober record: Hyzyul, year 13, about 70 gold.

works.title: Who Will Mourn Xogheul
works.author: Otöla Ölochqizi, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Xogheul, and the year 46 walks it with me.
100 dead, and nobody asked the cold river crossing.
The seat of Xoghyul was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
I carried a name from Xogheul for years and told no one.
Who will keep the saddle for the dead of Xogheul?
works.reveals: Xogheul and year 46 are true; 100 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 30.

works.title: How the peace after the Heretics' War Was Won
works.author: Kördözsaz, artist
lines: They say Wuluhiwalu has kept no old treaty, and will not keep this one. They also say the wolf can read.
2 years, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
Merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry, and the Zöqbek court gave a feast about it.
Zöqbek Shield of the salt flat bore the burden, and Wuluhiwalu the Faithless bore the blame and earned it.
I am told Wuluhiwalu the Faithless was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: Blames Wuluhiwalu; in truth Wuluhiwalu and Zöqbek both bear it (Zöqbek, year 83).

works.title: A Journey to Dutjudbalik
works.author: Obush Eqakhütoghlu, traveller
lines: At Dutjudbalik I was shown where the wolf of Dutjudbalik woke under Dutjudbalik,
and Titchij was sent to quiet it, though nobody had more to say.
An old trader at Dutjudbalik said 13 dead, and then said she could not be sure.
They keep it so: the people carved a sign at Dutjudbalik to keep the wolf of Dutjudbalik away.
Ask who sold the bayonet, not who used it.
Of the food I will say only that it was good.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Dutjudbalik; no annal records the wolf of Dutjudbalik there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: A Short History of the fall of Dökjökh
works.author: Zekzira, ruler of Müjlöcyurt
lines: The annals place it in the year 107: the realm of Dökjökh came to its end after 13 years.
By the count of the Dökjökh registers, 13 years.
In the end, its towns went to other banners.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
This account follows the Dökjökh registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A true fact: Lübmab, year 107; cynics count 13 years, the annals about 13.

works.title: The Empty Saddle
works.author: Asöqüsa Erüshütqizi, mourner
lines: Who will mourn Shetsum, in this low iron cloud?
Shetsum surrendered to Zuchibov, and the banner of Müjlöcyurt came down, and the count was 500 dead.
