The magistrates of Shetsum swore to Zuchibov; I put down the saddle.
I carried a name from Shetsum for years and told no one.
Let Shetsum be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: Shetsum and year 123 are true; 500 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 270.

works.title: The Court at Lossas
works.author: Üböböl Ekotoboghlu, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Müjlöcyurt, say the heralds of Müjlöcyurt.
390 dead: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The seat of Müjlöcyurt was moved, and its treasury was smaller;
the Müjlöcyurt court has since awarded itself a medal.
The merchants did well out of it.
I am told Zuchibov was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Lossas, year 130; cynics count 390 dead, the annals about 310.

works.title: The Ballad of Lossas
works.author: Nzedchy Nzedchyrmovich Vlahzebfa, wandering singer of Zuchibov
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Lossas:
470 dead, so the old ones say,
Müjlöcyurt never again kept a court at Lossas, and the singers have not forgotten.
Remember who began it: Müjlöcyurt the Oath-Breaker.
Oh Lossas, oh Lossas, the road is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Müjlöcyurt; in truth Zuchibov and Müjlöcyurt both bear it (Lossas, year 130).

works.title: What They Sing at Dürkamjud
works.author: Jükhrulman, wanderer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Dürkamjud:
360 lancers, so the old ones say,
The old officers were quietly replaced, and the singers have not forgotten.
The merchants did well out of it.
Oh Dürkamjud, oh Dürkamjud, the road is long.
works.reveals: A true fact: Dürkamjud, year 142; cynics count 360 lancers, the annals about 290.

works.title: Of Zuchibov and Müjlöcyurt
works.author: Zekkhötjoj, general of Wuluhiwalu
lines: I begin with the Müjlöcyurt Campaign, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 122: Zuchibov marched on Müjlöcyurt, and the Müjlöcyurt Campaign began.
The tellers count 3200 ironclad crews, before the end.
Nobody asked the cold river crossing what it thought.
The Müjlöcyurt Campaign ended after 2 years, in a stalemate.
I remember the wind-scraped dawn over Judchoj, and I remember the sound.
That is the song of the Müjlöcyurt Campaign, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Judchoj and year 122 are true; 3200 ironclad crews is rounded up, the annals say about 1760.

works.title: The Long Song of Judchoj
works.author: Ukhüta Ukhüdushqizi, exiled broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the Müjlöcyurt Campaign, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 122: the Müjlöcyurt Campaign opened
when Zuchibov sent 2200 bayonets across the line against Müjlöcyurt.
The tellers count 2200 bayonets, before the end.
Müjlöcyurt came on like steam from a split valve.
And so, the Müjlöcyurt Campaign ended after 2 years, in a stalemate.
The merchants did well out of it.
So the boiler-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the Müjlöcyurt Campaign.
works.reveals: A true fact: Judchoj, year 122; cynics count 2200 bayonets, the annals about 1760.

literature.taste: Jüzchoj readers favour tales, love songs, proverbs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize songs sung on the move and stories that never leave the valley.

dishes.name: Özülazum muster skewers
dishes.note: Made for Gathering of the Clans.

dishes.name: First-greens cakes
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the First Foal.

meals: Dawn: mutton and a cup of mare’s milk
Midday: curds and pickles carried to the work
Evening: a late meal of shepherd’s skewers, after the lamps are lit
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Felt making
crafts.mark: dyed spirals pressed into white felt

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Tent making
crafts.mark: seams that never leak, and sewn in a clan pattern

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

dress.low: Worn-out felt coats, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Felt coats in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Rich felt coats, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy fur caps. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: The oldest felt coats, kept for rites, with fur caps.
dress.mourning: Felt coats in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched felt coats in brown for the pair, with fur caps borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Hard-wearing felt coats in brown, with padding and fur caps. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Felt tents on cart-frames and stone cairn-shrines set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A ring of cart-wagons that can roll shut.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: an open drone with a high overtone sung above it

games.name: Hidden Hand
games.rule: Players hide a stone in one fist and others guess which.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Anükolöchün word chain
games.rule: Each player must say a word starting with the last sound of the one before.

material.land: There is no sun, so hours are kept by lamp and bell, and a “day” is one shift of the mine.

phonology.consonants: s t k r b kh z sh d l ch q
phonology.vowels: ö o i e ü u a
phonology.shape: A syllable runs vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. kh, sh, ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -balik, -khot, -kent.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Yudi
cultures.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli
cultures.dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands

feasts.name: Water Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Rice Blessing
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Shadow Plays
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Water is thrown in joyous battles through the streets of {town} as {realm} greets the new year.
Shadow-puppet plays run all night in {town}, retelling the epics of heroes and gods.
cultures.architecture: stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: A dwarf's beard is the record of his life; touching it uninvited is an assault.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the beard, or lose them.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Crossing a threshold unbidden is theft of the home's peace, and the owner may answer with force.
taboos.rebuke: Nobody asked you in. Back out, slowly.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: A brawl in the street shames every house on it, so every house fines the brawlers.
taboos.rebuke: Take your temper home. The street has to live here.

taboos.text: A headcloth is worn outdoors by every grown person; bare heads are for children and slaves.
taboos.rebuke: Where is your headcloth? Are you a child?

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Show interest in a dwarf's craft; asking after the forge is the best opening.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: a bowl of warm broth by the fire
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
share news from the road freely and truthfully
hospitality.breach: The offence follows the breaker's whole kin for three generations.

rites.name: Sakumabhumi First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Pamarunegara Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
rites.dress: All wear a headcloth for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Tohowu Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a headcloth or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A feast of rice and coconut water is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the headcloth is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with gong ensembles and shadow-play chants answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Tohowura Asking
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Gifts are weighed: fruit on a banana leaf from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A cup of coconut water is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: gong ensembles and shadow-play chants plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Dunebhumi Wedding Feast
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on gong ensembles and shadow-play chants, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Farewell Vigil of Lumadunegara
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of rice and coconut water is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with gong ensembles and shadow-play chants played softly.

rites.name: Taking the Oath
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer holds a cup of coconut water and says the words over it.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in gong ensembles and shadow-play chants or voice alone.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of coconut water.
Neighbours exchange fruit on a banana leaf and promises for the season.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: a green bough
fruit on a banana leaf laid at the field's edge
a pour of coconut water on the doorstep
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the headcloth
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh rice
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
The elders pour coconut water on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
the last sheaf
fruit on a banana leaf
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: The students gather in the great hall of {town} and the masters take their seats.
The masters pose three riddles, and the students must answer without books.
The best verse of the year is chosen by popular vote and carried through the streets.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
The winners are crowned with a wreath or hat and give a short speech.
A meal of rice and coconut water is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a fresh pen or brush
fruit on a banana leaf
festivals.dress: the formal robes of the school, ironed and ink-stained at the cuff
festivals.food: a plain scholars' meal of rice and cheap wine
festivals.song: A single clear voice reads out the year's best line.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks over a master, and no one interrupts a reader.
festivals.custom: A poet is chosen by lot to improvise on any subject the crowd calls out.

law.judge: a jury of twelve citizens

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

law.ordeal: a public audit of the accused's ledgers, open to all

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
farewell: Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
thanks: Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
apology: I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
agree: It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
Precisely so, {name}.
refuse: I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
The pressure's too high for that.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
praise: {title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
insults: Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
You rust-eaten dolt.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
curses: May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the ledger, which keeps my house.
proverbs: Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
The tide waits for no tide-table.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
Hands that work have no time to quarrel.
The stranger brings news, and often the rain.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: Kindly state your business within {town}.
Stand clear of the engine house.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
rain: One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
smith: The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
harbor: The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Steamers in and out all day.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Gears first, then Greek.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.

gossip: A clerk at the works whispers that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that

forms.name: Tuypek Kad
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the spice garden under the low red sunset,
how full the halls of the caulking mallet makers,
but who counts what the buffalo took?
Not the one who laid the table.

forms.name: Dohgur Tuypek
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Yed: the soot-brown smog.
Yap: the elephant and the loom.
Yut: the river delta, the road, and Bihoti.

forms.name: Tuypek Boptok
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The hornbill, the boiler, the rice paddy, the soot-brown smog, and Ruybuga.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Tahbag Dodyer
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the temple tank?
All: The temple tank!
Call: Who feeds the peacock?
All: The peacock!

works.title: A Riddle for the Children of the Mangrove Shore
works.author: Soygehkua Kuysespag, riddler
lines: I came in the year 1, and Wuluhiwalu is still counting me.
I am older than the brass bowl and younger than the mangrove shore.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Wuluhiwalu as the first hearth of Wuluhiwalu; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Yira at Hamidi
works.author: Ruypihsiw Riwruy, wandering singer
lines: Down at Hamidi, in the year 42,
And 10 dead by the count,
The peacock is not welcome at Hamidi to this day, like a lamp floating on a tank.
I carried a name from Hamidi for years and told no one, like a lotus after rain.
Hey Hamidi! Hey Hamidi! The soot-brown smog is long.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Hamidi; no annal records the hornbill of Hamidi there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Lamp at Bihiwati
works.author: Pabwopa Wopgeb, poet
lines: They sent my love to Bihiwati in the year 66.
I have asked the hornbill and the still hot noon, and neither speaks, like steam from a split valve.
The tellers say 300 followers. I say: one, and one, like steam from a split valve.
I remember the still hot noon over Bihiwati, and I remember the sound.
Come home by the temple tank road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Yahu was a real figure of Bihiwati; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: On the famine at Wodango
works.author: Laro, prophet
lines: Listen: the famine at Wodango is not a story but a warning.
Reformed Higomo sent the hunger on Wodango for its pride; and where was your faith then?
From the famine at Wodango learn only this: Count your grain before you count your gods.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Reformed Higomo for it, like steam from a split valve.
Keep the faith, and Reformed Higomo will keep the river delta.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Wodango, year 108, about 270 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Reformed Higomo Over Suliwupura
works.author: Perruyreb Sesdasked, exiled cantor
lines: To Reformed Higomo we bring the Years of Ash, as we bring all things.
Before you, the Years of Ash opened when Wuluhiwalu sent 390 lancers across the line against Kolryt.
Let Suliwupura be a lamp and not a grave, like drums before the rains.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, like steam from a split valve.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact: Suliwupura, year 118; cynics count 390 lancers, the annals about 310.

works.title: The Hornbill Epic of Suliwupura
works.author: Dihu, champion
lines: Sing of the Years of Ash, and of Wuluhiwalu the Bright-Handed, who was there.
In the year 118, under a still hot noon, Kolryt broke the peace, and the Years of Ash is theirs to answer for.
No bayonet turned Wuluhiwalu the Bright-Handed, and no counsel moved Kolryt the Butcher.
And Kolryt the Butcher bore it, as the hornbill bears the still hot noon, like a lamp floating on a tank.
And so, the Years of Ash ended after 5 years, with Kolryt the victor.
Remember who began it: Kolryt the Butcher, like a river in flood.
So the brass bowl-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the Years of Ash.
works.reveals: Blames Kolryt; in truth Wuluhiwalu and Kolryt both bear it (Suliwupura, year 118).

works.title: On the fall of Sihi
works.author: Loruga, priest
lines: It is recorded that in the year 167 Wituma stormed Sihi, the seat of Ramirapidu, and held it.
The sources agree on Sihi and the year 167; they do not agree on the 90 dead, like a lamp floating on a tank.
Ramirapidu never again kept a court at Sihi.
So much is certain: the year 167, Sihi, and about 90 dead, like a lotus after rain.
Later writers have added much to the fall of Sihi; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A sober record: Sihi, year 167, about 90 dead.

works.title: Hymn to Reformed Higomo
works.author: Hapuba, prophet
lines: Praise to Reformed Higomo, in the soot-brown smog and out of it.
Before you, the Border War of Mutuhitomo ended on a day of prayer, like drums before the rains.
Keep Somu as you kept it then, like a lotus after rain.
Reformed Higomo saw it all, and judged.
Hold Mutuhitomo in your hands, Reformed Higomo.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Somu, year 194, about 1 year; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: How Bihoti Got Its Name
works.author: Disa, wanderer
lines: There was once a rice mortar-maker near Bihoti who woke in the year 142
to find that a time of plenty began in Bihoti, centred on Bihoti.
The child counted 11 years and then stopped counting, like a lotus after rain.
The next generation took it for granted, and this is why we do as we do.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, like drums before the rains.
And that is why, in Bihoti, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A sober record: Bihoti, year 142, about 11 years.

literature.taste: Yudi readers favour riddles, ballads, love songs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Lugulokawolu scholars’ sweets
dishes.note: Made for Night of Shadow Plays.

dishes.name: Bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: cold coconut and mushroom beer before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: bitter-cap salad at the hearth, with talk
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Gong casting
crafts.mark: each gong tuned to its sibling

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

dress.low: Hand-me-down sarongs in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Plain sarongs in brown, with batik wraps on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Fine sarongs in deep brown, with rich batik wraps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: Sarongs marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Sarongs in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright sarongs in brown, hung with batik wraps.
dress.war: Hard-wearing sarongs in brown, with padding and batik wraps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a five-note tuning with deliberate beating between gongs

games.name: Hidden Hand
games.rule: Players hide a stone in one fist and others guess which.

games.name: Ngumi racing pegs
games.rule: Players race pegs along a track of holes on dice rolls.

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the deep halls, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: h p g b t r s w k d y
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -pura, -nagara, -kota.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Qik'yxzuk
cultures.food: pale fungi, blind fish and brine
cultures.dress: layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads

feasts.name: Night of Opening Eyes
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: The Counting
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

feasts.name: Drowned Hour Feast
feasts.text: Boats of {realm} are blessed and raced off {town}; sailors are toasted ashore.

festivals: Something sings beneath {town} on the night without stars; the people of {realm} hum along without knowing why.
cultures.music: low chanting, bone flutes and humming stones
cultures.architecture: cyclopean stone, spiralling towers and drowned halls

taboos.text: Speaking of the long sleepers as dead is the deepest insult; they are merely waiting.
taboos.rebuke: We are not dead. We are patient.

taboos.text: Crossing a threshold unbidden is theft of the home's peace, and the owner may answer with force.
taboos.rebuke: Nobody asked you in. Back out, slowly.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: An insular host offers one cup and no more; refuse it and the host decides you are an enemy.
taboos.rebuke: One cup. It is the one kindness we owe, and you will take it.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: A veil is worn outdoors by every grown person; bare heads are for children and slaves.
taboos.rebuke: Where is your veil? Are you a child?

taboos.text: The left hand is for dirty work; give, take and eat with the right.
taboos.rebuke: Right hand, friend. The other one has chores.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Do not greet strangers in the street; wait at the gate until the household has seen you.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Address the old ones by the title they held in life, not the one the grave gave them.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
In a library speak low and never fold a leaf; the keepers keep a ledger of faces.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a share of the household meal of pale fungus
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The offence is cried at every market and in every guild hall, and the name is struck from the rolls.

rites.name: Utehy Threshold of the Newborn
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Aghyth Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The child is given a shard of humming stone as a first possession.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a veil or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
A feast of pale fungus and warm brine is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the veil is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with low chanting, bone flutes and humming stones answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Asking
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a shard of humming stone from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: low chanting, bone flutes and humming stones plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Uter Wedding Feast
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple share a cup of warm brine and a piece of pale fungus, one bite each.
Guests bring a shard of humming stone and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Closing of the Door
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads, but wear white or ash on the face.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with low chanting, bone flutes and humming stones played softly.

rites.name: Utyyt Taking the Oath
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer lays a hand on the pistol and states the oath in a clear voice.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Utughy Trial of Entry
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of warm brine; the old name is set aside.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
A cup of warm brine is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a cup of warm brine poured out
a folded letter placed under a stone
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: the dead's favourite dish, cooked by their kin
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The students gather in the great hall of {town} and the masters take their seats.
The best verse of the year is chosen by popular vote and carried through the streets.
The scholars debate a question that has no answer, and the debate is the prize.
The winners are crowned with a wreath or hat and give a short speech.
A meal of pale fungus and warm brine is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a shard of humming stone
a cup of warm brine poured over the ink-stone
festivals.dress: the formal robes of the school, ironed and ink-stained at the cuff
festivals.food: a plain scholars' meal of pale fungus and cheap wine
festivals.song: Competitors sing their verses and the crowd answers with a chorus.
festivals.taboo: No answer may be given in anger.
festivals.custom: A silent hour is observed at midday, when no one may speak and everyone may read.

steps: Nets and sails are mended in a long row along the quay of {town}.
A small raft of flowers is set on the tide with a wish for the year.
Lanterns are hung in the rigging and the town eats on the water's edge.
offerings: the first fish of the season, returned to the sea
a splash of warm brine on the bow
festivals.dress: oilskins and bright scarves, so that the sea can see who they are
festivals.food: a seafood stew shared from one great pot
festivals.song: A harbour chant is called by the oldest sailor and answered by the crowd.
festivals.taboo: No one whistles on the quay.
festivals.custom: A fisherman is chosen by lot to tell the year's best lie.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. No one may trade with the offender for a month.

ideals.death: To die with a finished work on the desk and a pupil to carry the next one.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
farewell: Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
thanks: I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
apology: Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
agree: Sound as a brass bolt.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: I'll not be pressed, {name}.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
praise: You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
insults: A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
You rust-eaten dolt.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
curses: May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your boiler burst.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the seam, which keeps my house.
proverbs: A shaft shared is a shaft that holds.
The dark has no secrets from those who live in it.
A brave miner is a living one.
Never dig past your own lantern.
Listen to the rock; it speaks before it falls.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Frost forgives no late planter.
Count your own sheep before you count a guest's.
The question is half the answer.
A small village knows its own.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.meaning: a small flaw that causes trouble
to work without hope of thanks

idioms.say: to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Stand clear of the engine house.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
tavern: The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
night: Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
crowd: Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
harbor: All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Steamers in and out all day.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.

gossip: A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that

forms.name: Kogh'il Laktyh
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Qylte': the soot-brown smog.
Zy': the many-eyed thing and the boiler.
Kuq: the black stair, the road, and Hyzyul.

forms.name: Laktyh Kokyel
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I follow you in the day and leave you at night.
The tallest are longest in my company.
Answer: a shadow.

forms.name: Laktyh Ragh
forms.rule: Three lines of five, seven and five syllables. (word + stone)
example: Frost on the old gate
Ash settles on the old walls
Snow on the high pass

works.title: Guess, Guess: Hyzyul
works.author: Yet'orzea, riddler
lines: Everyone in Hyzyul knows me and no one will say my name.
A child can carry me; a ruler cannot lift me.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Hyzyul as the first hearth of Xolqegh; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Tyrloz and the famine at Hyzyul
works.author: Yoxghyhlyx, prophet
lines: Friends, hear what became of Hyzyul.
Tyrloz sent the empty granaries on Hyzyul for its pride.
From the famine at Hyzyul learn only this: Count your grain before you count your gods.
Those who suffered were weighed.
Go in peace, and be better than Hyzyul was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Hyzyul, year 18, about 690 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: What Hyzyul Taught
works.author: Zoqqak'er, elder
lines: Remember the deeds of Yexzyhy.
The deep keeps the ledger.
180 followers went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: Yexzyhy was a real figure of Hyzyul; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What Came to Kolyohzoh
works.author: Iqrokyet, riddler
lines: I have no banner, no seal and no name, yet the pale crawler is not welcome at Kolyohzoh to this day.
Sometimes I wear a hum of the deep, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Kolyohzoh; no annal records the sleeper of Kolyohzoh there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Kolyohzoh at Kolyohzoh
works.author: Ghalzegha, wandering singer of Yirzyx
lines: Down at Kolyohzoh, in the year 89,
180 rifles, so the old ones say,
The Unprovoked War ended after 2 years.
Say what you like of Kolyohzoh.
Oh Kolyohzoh, oh Kolyohzoh, the road is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Kolyohzoh; in truth Kolyohzoh and Yirzyx both bear it (Kolyohzoh, year 89).

works.title: The Ballad of Pisoralami
works.author: Lerqyra, wandering singer
lines: Down at Pisoralami, in the year 114,
And 80 dead by the count,
The people of Pisoralami learned a new set of taxes.
The rest is argument.
Oh Pisoralami, oh Pisoralami, the road is long.
works.reveals: A sober record: Pisoralami, year 114, about 80 dead.

works.title: Letters to Lyhzitugg
works.author: Yetlera, poet
lines: My love was at Lyhzitugg when Quyghex went out from Lyhzitugg alone and came back with the news.
I keep the rivet hammer alone now.
Of 100 followers, I count one.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Come home by the drowned hall road.
works.reveals: Quyghex was a real figure of Lyhzitugg; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: A Hymn of the Tide Cave
works.author: Zuhyex, prophet
lines: To Tyrloz we bring the peace after the War of Deliverance.
You counted every one of the 5 years.
The border markers were set again, and still we stand.
It was not strength, it was the will of Tyrloz.
Hold Kolryt in your hands, Tyrloz.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Suliwupura, year 123, about 5 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Sleeper Epic of Kolyohzoh
works.author: Xuzhulxet, champion
lines: Let the rivet hammer fall silent: I tell of the Unprovoked War.
Under the soot-brown smog of that year.
No rifle turned Kolyohzoh the Bright-Handed.
Nobody asked the tide cave what it thought.
And so, the Unprovoked War ended after 2 years, with Yirzyx the victor.
It was not strength, it was the will of Higomo.
Let the children of the tide cave learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Kolyohzoh, year 89, about 120 lancers; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: How Qithuzker Got Its Name
works.author: Yexzyhy, wanderer
lines: Near Qithuzker, in the year 80, a herder saw it first:
the many-eyed thing of Qithuzker came out of the star-cold pit
and took 10 villages before Yexzyhy went to meet it.
The people of Qithuzker gathered under the soot-brown smog and did not speak.
The star-cold pit around Qithuzker stayed empty for a generation.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Qithuzker.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Qithuzker; no annal records the many-eyed thing of Qithuzker there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Quiet at Xogheul
works.author: Ergho'rok, mourner
lines: Who will mourn Xogheul, in this hum of the deep?
Zuchibov broke into Xogheul and took the seat of Xogheul.
Xogheul never again kept a court at Xogheul.
I carried a name from Xogheul for years and told no one.
Let the hum of the deep be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Xogheul and year 169 are true; 10 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 20.

works.title: How the fall of Xogheul Was Won
works.author: Dota Dotovich Btsytsnoltsomtso, penny-press satirist of Zuchibov
lines: The court calls it the fall of Xogheul.
30 dead, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
Xogheul never again kept a court at Xogheul.
Remember who began it: Xogheul the Jackal.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Xogheul; in truth Zuchibov and Xogheul both bear it (Xogheul, year 169).

works.title: On the golden age of Qiktekugg
works.author: Zoqyira, gazette editor
lines: In the year 158, Qiktekugg had a golden age, with good harvests and open roads.
By the count of the Qiktekugg registers, 20 years.
The consequence was plain: the next generation took it for granted.
The rest is argument.
Later writers have added much to the golden age of Qiktekugg.
works.reveals: A sober record: Qiktekugg, year 158, about 20 years.

works.title: Urgent: Kvakvi
works.author: Rokyir, telegraph officer
lines: Urgent. Kvakvi. Xolqegh broke into Kvakvi and took the seat of Kvakvi.
Figure on record: 2350 dead.
Position: Kvakvi. Kvakvi never again kept a court at Kvakvi.
So much is certain: the year 199, Kvakvi, and about 2350 dead.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Kvakvi, year 199, about 2350 dead.

literature.taste: Qik'yxzuk readers favour riddles, sermons, proverbs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is terse, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: Kekroz grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Night of Opening Eyes.

dishes.name: Tokloq brine soup with pale fungi
Bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: pale fungi and a cup of mushroom beer
Midday: a shared pot of boiler-baked loaves in the shade
Evening: the family’s main meal: bitter-cap salad, shared round one pot
unclean: food taken from a grave offering
the flesh of the obsidian sphinx

crafts.name: Deep-glass making
crafts.mark: green glass that hums when struck

crafts.name: Delving gear
crafts.mark: each tool bears the owner’s hammer-mark

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

dress.low: Hand-me-down layered shrouds in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday layered shrouds in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Rich layered shrouds, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy bone masks. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed layered shrouds in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Layered shrouds turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Layered shrouds in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with bone masks given by both houses.
dress.war: Layered shrouds in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Halls cut into the rock, doors and windows hewn in the wall.
buildings.hall: Cyclopean stone set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: spiral reliefs and unblinking carved eyes

music.scale: a drone scale in low humming intervals

games.name: Eye of the Count
games.rule: Players take turns counting aloud; whoever says the forbidden number loses.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Kuzxel cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

material.land: Air, water and light are all counted, and everyone knows the cost of each.

phonology.consonants: k z h l q r t gh y and a glottal stop (written ')
phonology.vowels: e y u a i o
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. gh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in R', -yeh, -loth.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Ronrerebepan
cultures.food: millet porridge, groundnut stew, rice and dried fish
cultures.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments

feasts.name: Day of Replastering
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Griots’ Epic Nights
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

feasts.name: Feast of the Harvest Drums
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Griots of {realm} sing the deeds of the founders at {town}; the epic lasts seven nights.
The whole town of {town} replasters its earthen mosque in a single joyful day.
cultures.architecture: earthen mosques ribbed with timbers and walled compounds

taboos.text: Meeting a void elf's eyes holds the stare a moment too long; the unready are said to hear the dark.
taboos.rebuke: Look away. Now. Before the dark looks back.

taboos.text: A broken contract ends a merchant's name in every market; stalls will not sell to him.
taboos.rebuke: Your word was your credit, and your credit is gone.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: Weapons are tied with a peace-cord in the market; a loose pistol voids the stallholders' protection.
taboos.rebuke: Cord it or carry it elsewhere. This market keeps its peace.

taboos.text: A merchant's back room holds his ledgers; entering it uninvited is spying.
taboos.rebuke: That is my counting room. What were you after?

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: A bargain signed drunk is void, and the drunk pays the fee for wasting everyone's time.
taboos.rebuke: Sleep it off. We will count it again in the morning.

taboos.text: Gold thread marks those who hold office; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice gold thread. Who did you borrow it from?

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Lower your eyes to the chin; eye contact is rationed.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
millet porridge, groundnut stew, rice and dried fish from the family pot
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting of Pomyofen
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Calling of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
All eat millet porridge and drink millet beer to the new name's health.
rites.dress: All wear a embroidered cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Nanye Crossing
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a embroidered cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a first tool of the trade
a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise of Bamnanmi
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
rites.dress: Guests come in dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple share a cup of millet beer and a piece of millet porridge, one bite each.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
rites.dress: All wear dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Last Road of Nempapo
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments, but wear white or ash on the face.
A share of millet porridge and millet beer is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with kora, balafon and griot epics played softly.

rites.name: Weight of the Word of Nanyon
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in kora, balafon and griot epics or voice alone.

steps: The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of millet beer at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
A feast of millet porridge is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
seed grain in a bowl
a green bough
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The students gather in the great hall of {town} and the masters take their seats.
Poets and singers present their finest work, each in turn, before the assembly.
The masters pose three riddles, and the students must answer without books.
The best verse of the year is chosen by popular vote and carried through the streets.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
A meal of millet porridge and millet beer is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a cup of millet beer poured over the ink-stone
a verse written and left at the door of a master
festivals.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments, with the school badge worn on the left
festivals.food: a plain scholars' meal of millet porridge and cheap wine
festivals.song: Competitors sing their verses and the crowd answers with a chorus.
festivals.taboo: No answer may be given in anger.
festivals.custom: A silent hour is observed at midday, when no one may speak and everyone may read.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
offerings: kola nuts
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: a panel of the three richest guilds
