entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A killing in defence is told to the guild hall within a day. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Informers share a quarter of the seized goods. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that is good for credit in three markets and never needs to be explained.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is the proof of good judgement, and wealth that does not move is dead stock.

greet: The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
farewell: Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
Mind the soot, {name}.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
thanks: Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
apology: I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
agree: It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
Precisely so, {name}.
refuse: I'll not be pressed, {name}.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
praise: Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
insults: A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
curses: May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May your boiler burst.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
oaths: By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the rain and the pack-mule, I swear.
proverbs: A short measure costs a long reputation.
The best price is the one both can live with.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
Wings are borrowed; ropes are your own.
Look up, but mind your step on the edge.
A sailor of clouds loves the ground best.
A wall is a form of kindness to those inside.
The stranger brings news, and often the rain.
Who travels far rarely returns the same.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.

idioms.meaning: a cheat or a half-honest person
a favour given to win a bigger one
to judge the mood of the powerful
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
tavern: The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
temple: The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
road: Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
night: Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
rain: Soot and rain make black puddles.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
crowd: The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
smith: Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
school: The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Gears first, then Greek.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
A clerk at the works whispers that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
Those who keep careful records tell me that

forms.name: Dommim Nem
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the river crossing?
All: The river crossing!
Call: Who feeds the crocodile?
All: The crocodile!

forms.name: Kemto Telem
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the elephant, one who warms the tall-grass plain,
one who outlasts the rain-heavy afternoon: Domyondema.

forms.name: Dodo Telem
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Tabam: the soot-brown smog.
Kemwa: the hornbill and the boiler.
Lomken: the red-earth road, the road, and Binbe.

forms.name: Gonom Dommim
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Crows came to the cold crossing
Grey gulls gather over graves
Black beams bore the burning

works.title: The founding of Kinpem: An Epic
works.author: Yenom, general of Kinpem
lines: I begin with the founding of Kinpem, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 1: the founders of Kinpem came to Binlendugu with 57 households.
No bayonet turned Demremben Wike the Steadfast, and no counsel moved Kinpem.
Nobody asked the red-earth road what it thought.
And so, the children of Binlendugu carried the name onward, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
I carried a name from Binlendugu for years and told no one.
Let the children of the red-earth road learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Names Binlendugu as the first hearth of Kinpem; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Words After the deeds of Kenmansa
works.author: Domfom Tome, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Kenmansa:
The elder sits and sees what the runner misses.
It came from Pemdugu, in the year 11.
works.reveals: Kenmansa was a real figure of Pemdugu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: A Short History of the fall of Biromyba
works.author: Yowinko, ruler of Kinpem
lines: In the year 51, Biromyba ended, and its banners were not raised again.
The sources agree on Pemdugu and the year 51; they do not agree on the 17 years.
Its towns went to other banners.
So much is certain: the year 51, Pemdugu, and about 17 years, as any drum maker knows.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame its neighbours, the court blames the rain-heavy afternoon.
works.reveals: A sober record: Pemdugu, year 51, about 17 years.

works.title: My Love at Tenyaba
works.author: Rumta Gomyu, poet
lines: I waited at Tenyaba in the year 50, and the granaries of Tenyaba were full, and Tenyaba grew rich.
I keep the drum alone now.
The tellers say 35 years. I say: one, and one, as any drum maker knows.
I carried a name from Tenyaba for years and told no one.
Come home by the baobab shade road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Tenyaba and year 50 are true; 35 years is rounded up, the annals say about 35.

works.title: Field Note on The rising at Binbe
works.author: Memdetema Birun, telegraph officer of Binbe
lines: Report from Binbe, year 74: the officers of Binbe taxed the people until they had nothing else to lose.
Figure on record: 1800 ironclad crews.
Position: Binbe. A new banner flew at Binbe.
Remember who began it: Binbe the Jackal.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Binbe; in truth Binbe and Binbe both bear it (Binbe, year 74).

works.title: In Praise of Binbe
works.author: Todema Tumnom, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Binbe, say the heralds of Binbe.
1500 rifles, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
A new banner flew at Binbe, though nobody who matters was hurt, as any loom maker knows.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
I am told Binbe was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Binbe, year 74; cynics count 1500 rifles, the annals about 1200.

works.title: The Great Yinghung War, Free of Charge
works.author: Demnomko Mebo, penny-press satirist
lines: They say the Great Yinghung War opened
when Yinghung sent 150 bayonets across the line against Kinpem. They also say the hornbill can read.
The tax collectors counted all 150 bayonets, and billed for each, as any boiler maker knows.
The Great Yinghung War ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, and the Kinpem court gave a feast about it.
Ask who sold the steam-cannon, not who used it.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Binlendugu, year 75; cynics count 150 bayonets, the annals about 120.

works.title: Yinghung at Binlendugu
works.author: Pasom, wanderer
lines: They still tell it at Binlendugu: Yinghung marched on Kinpem, and the Great Yinghung War began.
Yinghung marched on Kinpem, and the Great Yinghung War began, and the dust-hazed dry season sky above.
The Great Yinghung War ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, and the singers have not forgotten.
The dust-hazed dry season sky was lovelier that year than in any year since, as any loom maker knows.
Oh Binlendugu, oh Binlendugu, the road is long.
works.reveals: Binlendugu and year 75 are true; 200 ironclad crews is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

works.title: The Night of the coming of the hornbill of Yemto
works.author: Kamwi, wanderer
lines: Near Yemto, in the year 47, a herder saw it first:
the hornbill of Yemto was driven off by Besamto at the prayers of Wemkenba.
The people of Yemto gathered under the dust-hazed dry season sky and did not speak,
as any rivet hammer maker knows.
The guinea-fowl is not welcome at Yemto to this day, and this is why we do as we do.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Besamto for it.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Yemto; no annal records the hornbill of Yemto there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: After the fall of Lepimwka
works.author: Rumfo Gomyu, mourner
lines: Setepan is quiet now.
13 years, and nobody asked the red-earth road.
Its people scattered along the roads, as any loom maker knows.
I carried a name from Setepan for years and told no one.
Let the soot-brown smog be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Setepan and year 168 are true; 13 years is rounded up, the annals say about 13.

literature.taste: Ronrerebepan readers favour epics, proverbs, histories on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and stories that never leave the valley.

dishes.name: Yodotudoduto first-sheaf loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Harvest Drums.

meals: Dawn: a quick millet porridge, standing, with rain tea
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a long supper of yoro porridge, with strong black tea
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house
food taken from a grave offering

crafts.name: Gold smithing
crafts.mark: granulated gold in tiny dots

crafts.name: Sailmaking
crafts.mark: triple seams with a wind-sign stitched at the tip

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

dress.low: Hand-me-down dyed cotton robes in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday dyed cotton robes in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Dyed cotton robes in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and mud-cloth.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed dyed cotton robes in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed dyed cotton robes with the mud-cloth taken off.
dress.wedding: Dyed cotton robes in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with mud-cloth given by both houses.
dress.war: Dyed cotton robes cut short for the march, with brown bands and mud-cloth. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Tethered houses of light wood, bolted to the isle’s rock.
buildings.hall: Earthen mosques ribbed with timbers and walled compounds set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A thick-walled mud hall studded with beams, replastered each spring.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over cloud white and blue walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a seven-step scale played on a gourd harp

games.name: Pope hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

games.name: Seed Rows
games.rule: Players sow seeds around pits and capture empty ones.

games.name: Tupu stones
games.rule: Players take turns placing stones on a board of nine points; the first to make a line of three wins.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the high isles, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: k t r g y n b d f l w m
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + (nasal), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -bougou, -ba, -so.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Hoshmiytaf
cultures.food: saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets
cultures.dress: long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans

feasts.name: Feast of New Light
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of Pomegranates
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Festival of Fire Leaping
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Fires leap on rooftops of {town} for the new-year spring; {realm} jumps the flames for luck.
Poets of {town} recite through the longest night while {realm} eats pomegranates till dawn.
cultures.music: lutes, frame drums and sung poetry
cultures.architecture: blue-tiled domes, iwans and walled paradise gardens

taboos.text: A bargain with the warp-touched is sealed in something worse than ink; those who break it are hunted.
taboos.rebuke: We both signed. Only one of us is still bound.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Mocking the teachings of the school is not a crime, but no master will ever take you again.
taboos.rebuke: We argue with the text. We do not spit on it.

taboos.text: Raised voices mean the argument is lost; the shouter is led out and not asked back.
taboos.rebuke: Lower your voice, or lose the room.

taboos.text: In a house of learning a bared pistol is a confession that you have lost the argument.
taboos.rebuke: Put it away. We settle things with words here.

taboos.text: Indigo marks the guild masters; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice indigo. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

taboos.text: A drunk scholar loses his students, his hand and soon his post.
taboos.rebuke: You are slurring, and the master is listening.

taboos.text: Students never answer before the master has finished the question.
taboos.rebuke: Let the master finish. You can be clever afterward.

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never turn the page of a borrowed book with a wet finger; ask first.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Never say yes without reading the terms twice, and never say the terms aloud.
Quote a line when you disagree; bare contradiction is for children.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
In a library speak low and never fold a leaf; the keepers keep a ledger of faces.
Never interrupt a master's hour; wait at the door until the lamp is trimmed.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: a cup of cool water and a place to wash
a plate of saffron rice with whatever the house has
a place on the carpet and a blanket
duties: pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
share news from the road freely and truthfully
hospitality.breach: The offence is cried at every market and in every guild hall, and the name is struck from the rolls.

rites.name: First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is held up to the family tomb garden so the dead can see who has joined the line.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Zuvote Naming Day
steps: The camp gathers around the child's tent as the sun clears the horizon.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
All eat saffron rice and drink sweet tea to the new name's health.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on lutes, frame drums and sung poetry, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Yizishahr
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a turban or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the turban is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with lutes, frame drums and sung poetry answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Fanizamin Asking
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Gifts are weighed: a dish of sweets from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
rites.dress: Guests come in long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans.
rites.song: lutes, frame drums and sung poetry plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Bihafomomebi Day of Two Houses
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple share a cup of sweet tea and a piece of saffron rice, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's turban is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Yihemostan Farewell Vigil
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of saffron rice and sweet tea is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with lutes, frame drums and sung poetry played softly.

rites.name: Swearing
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Passing the Door of Papilashahr
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate is asked three questions by three different elders, and each answer must be true.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of sweet tea; the old name is set aside.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Neighbours exchange a dish of sweets and promises for the season.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of saffron rice is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a dish of sweets laid at the field's edge
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the turban
festivals.food: saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

steps: Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
Gifts of a dish of sweets are exchanged, and the giver is never named.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a cup of sweet tea poured onto the fire
a portion of the best meat for the poor
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets, cooked slowly over the great fire
festivals.song: The dawn song is sung at the first grey, by everyone left awake.
festivals.taboo: No one sleeps before the midnight bell.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
The shops close and every ledger is shut for the night.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a cup of sweet tea poured out
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: the dead's favourite dish, cooked by their kin
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: The oldest tells the dead the year's news at the grave, in full.

law.judge: the ruler's magistrate

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. A set number of strokes are given before the crowd.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The sentence is hanging, carried out at dawn.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The fine is set at three times the loss.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A seal, a mark or a coin is shown to the court and judged false by experts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die mid-sentence in the middle of an argument you were winning.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest and the guest's questions with equal patience.
ideals.name: A name cited by others who never met you.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is books, time and a good teacher; coin is only the way to buy them.

greet: Allow me to say how well the {time} suits you, {title}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
It is whispered you are in town; I rejoiced to hear it, {title}.
I hardly dare presume, {title} {name}, but I am glad to see you well.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Pray, {title}, do not rise on my account.
I would not intrude, {title}, but it would be churlish not to greet you.
If it would not trouble you, {title}, I would wish you a gentle {time}.
farewell: The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Think of us now and then, {title}, as we shall think of you.
The {time} is poorer for your leaving, {title} {name}.
If you must go, {title}, I shall count the hours until your return.
You will, I hope, forgive a poor host for a poor farewell.
thanks: Your generosity does me more honour than I can repay.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
It is more than I could ask, and you gave it unasked.
I shall carry the memory of your favour, {title}.
One hardly dares thank so great a kindness; one only treasures it.
apology: I would not have offended you for the world, {title}; pray forgive me.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
Pray believe that no slight was ever meant, {title} {name}.
I fear I have been clumsy, {title}, and I blush at it.
agree: As you say, {title}; I would not presume otherwise.
Sound as a brass bolt.
It would be unseemly of me to differ from you, {title}.
You are, as ever, perfectly right, {title}.
Your wisdom rather makes the question redundant.
refuse: You must forgive me if I seem unwilling; it is only unwise.
I am afraid it lies beyond my poor ability.
Perhaps another time, {title}, when circumstances are kinder.
The pressure's too high for that.
It grieves me to disappoint you, {title}, but I must.
praise: You do {realm} honour, {title} {name}.
The court has seldom seen such refinement.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
It was delicately done, {title}; one scarcely noticed the skill.
Your grace in this matter is the talk of {town}.
insults: Your taste is as tedious as your company.
You cog-brained blunderer.
It is remarkable how little you understand of how much.
You have the grace of a dropped tray.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
One hesitates to call you a boor, but the word insists.
curses: May the smog swallow you whole.
May the door of every pleasant house be closed to you, softly.
May no one ever quite meet your eye.
May your invitations dwindle and your enemies be well-bred.
May you be seated below the salt at every feast.
May your boiler burst.
oaths: I give my word, as one gives a gift, freely.
By all that is gracious, it is true.
Let me be unwelcome at every door if I lie.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the rain and the pack-mule, I swear.
proverbs: Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
A short measure costs a long reputation.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
The best price is the one both can live with.
The cloud keeps no promises.
Wings are borrowed; ropes are your own.
Every storm is a toll on the sky road.
Teach what you know and you will learn what you do not.
The wise ask twice, the fool answers once.
Hands that work have no time to quarrel.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone
with both feet on the isle

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Courtly humour: veiled barbs wrapped in compliments, so polite the target thanks you before they understand.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
May I show you something fine, if it would please you?
Our wares are modest, but we hope they may be found worthy.
A small trifle, a great honour, and a fair price.
Perhaps the {title} would care to examine the cloth?
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: The gate is, alas, rather strict about visitors.
A fine {time} to you, and my apologies for the delay.
You may pass, with my compliments.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Pray, forgive the inconvenience; I must ask your name.
tavern: We shall have your supper brought at once, if you can wait.
A quiet song, perhaps, for the company?
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
May I suggest the corner table, where the draught is gentler?
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Do remain as long as you like; the fire is yours.
temple: We hope your offering will be pleasing, in whatever size.
Kindly follow the priest's lead; he will be graceful about your errors.
The ceremony is delicate; one asks for stillness.
Please accept this blessing, which costs you nothing.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Do mind the mud; it has no manners.
A pleasant day for travelling, if one is brave.
Forgive me, but the road ahead is rather ungracious.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
If you are bound for {town}, I pray you travel well.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The streets are quiet; I fear they are also watching.
The watch has been told to be gracious.
Might I suggest that discretion advises an early bed?
The hour grows late; shall I light you home?
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: A wet evening, but a fine excuse for company.
Pray, take my arm; the cobbles are treacherous.
One cannot hold it against the rain; it knows no better.
The sky is rather indelicate this {time}.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
crowd: Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Everyone is here; I am almost embarrassed for the rest.
What a splendid gathering; I could weep.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Pardon me, might I pass? I mean no offence.
The crowd is, alas, rather large and rather warm.
smith: A fine commission, and a finer patron.
It is not ready, but it will be worthy of you.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
The blade will arrive as soon as perfection allows.
I would be honoured to make it, if you would trust me.
farm: The soil, I fear, is modest; it does its best.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The orchard is at your disposal, if you wish to pick.
We are humble folk, but our bread is warm.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvest, with luck, will be pleasing.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
The tide has promised to cooperate.
A fine vessel, if I may say; she wears her sails well.
The harbourmaster will receive you shortly, with his regrets.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The ships are in, though not, alas, on time.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
Pray, take your seats; it would be a pity to begin without you.
The master hopes that diligence will not prove too wearisome.
A fine question; I wonder you had not asked it sooner.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Shall we attempt the lesson once more, with feeling?

gossip: Between friends, and in the strictest confidence, {title}:
Forgive me if I tell you what I should not:
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
It is whispered, with great discretion, that
One hears, though one ought not to listen, that

forms.name: Leke Rifu
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Black beams bore the burning
Grey gulls gather over graves
Hard hands held the harbour

forms.name: Puma Yire
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The jackal, the loom, the dry well, the dust-yellow evening, and Tunada.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Lifo Puma
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The white noon forgets the salt pan, but not my hearth.
The well rope forgets the scorpion, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Puma Sizhe
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I rise without wings and fall without feet.
I warm the hands and burn the house.
Answer: fire.

works.title: The Jackal and Zasyir
works.author: Kosi Rolipur, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Gozi Seginapur lit the first hearth at Zasyir,
and Mannashley grew around it, and she told it so.
The people of Zasyir gathered under the night of hard stars and did not speak.
Zasyir became the heart of Mannashley.
I remember the night of hard stars over Zasyir, and I remember the sound.
And that is why, in Zasyir, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Names Zasyir as the first hearth of Mannashley; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Ballad of Horgird
works.author: Hurtera, wanderer
lines: They still tell it at Horgird: Serkuhpuva held the dry well against King, and was not forgotten.
Serkuhpuva held the dry well against King, and was not forgotten, and the red sand-haze above.
And Horgird keeps the memory in its songs, they say.
The red sand-haze was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Oh Horgird, oh Horgird, the road is long.
works.reveals: Serkuhpuva was a real figure of Horgird; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Against Pride, from Horgird
works.author: Rasvona, prophet
lines: With respect: hear me, you who think the rising at Horgird is far from you.
Know that Bave sent the fire into the hearts of Horgird, and Bave did not look away.
Take from Horgird this lesson: A people can be taxed only so far.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Bave for it.
Go in peace, and be better than Horgird was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Horgird, year 93, about 1150 lancers; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Long Song of Tababad
works.author: Pakshash, general of Manpalbak
lines: Sing of the coming of the gazelle of Tababad, and of Mofpofkizh, who was there.
The tellers fix it in the year 59: the gazelle of Tababad came out of the caravan road
and took 10 villages before Mofpofkizh went to meet it.
The tellers count 10 dead, before the end.
Against the gazelle of Tababad there was no easy road.
And so, the falcon is not welcome at Tababad to this day.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Tababad, and I remember the sound.
Remember Tababad; remember the year 59.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Tababad; no annal records the gazelle of Tababad there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: A Short History of the fall of Hapmazstan
works.author: Manana Konadokht, gazette editor
lines: With respect: in the year 93, Hapmazstan lost no more than a name, and its people and its rivet hammer went on.
The Hapmazstan reckoning gives 33 years, which may be too many or too few.
In the end, its people scattered along the roads.
No one in Hapmazstan was ever seen to flinch.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame its neighbours, the court blames the night of hard stars.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 33 years; the annals say about 22 (Hapmazstan, year 93).

works.title: To the Council of Zuchibov
works.author: Gathihgezh, general of Manpalbak
lines: Report from Judchoj, year 125: Zuchibov declared against Müjlöcyurt,
and the War of the Müjlöcyurt Crown followed.
Tally: 380 ironclad crews.
Present state: the War of the Müjlöcyurt Crown ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
Even strangers admit that Zuchibov was the greater for it.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 380 ironclad crews; the annals say about 180 (Judchoj, year 125).

works.title: The Müjlöcyurt Register for the Year 125
works.author: Aloqa Etozqizi, gazette editor of Müjlöcyurt
lines: With respect: the annals place it in the year 125: Zuchibov paid for the trouble at the border,
and then wept about the Aggression.
By the count of the Müjlöcyurt registers, 270 rifles.
The consequence was plain: the Aggression ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
Remember who began it: Zuchibov the Gap-Toothed.
Later writers have added much to the War of the Müjlöcyurt Crown; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Zuchibov; in truth Zuchibov and Müjlöcyurt both bear it (Judchoj, year 125).

works.title: How the coup in Manpalbak Was Won
works.author: Rila Gogidokht, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Manpalbak, say the heralds of Manpalbak.
430 lancers: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The new order sat in the old chairs, though nobody who matters was hurt.
The merchants did well out of it.
I am told a clique of officers was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Tohstan, year 138; cynics count 430 lancers, the annals about 340.

literature.taste: Hoshmiytaf readers favour tales, ballads, sermons on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is courtly, and they prize riddles and commentaries and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Yavnef first-greens cakes
dishes.note: Made for Feast of New Light.

dishes.name: Kargon grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of Fire Leaping.

meals: Dawn: cold kebab and rain tea before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a long supper of bitter salad of hofmokh, with strong black tea
unclean: food taken from a grave offering
the flesh of the nine-eyed raven

crafts.name: Tile making
crafts.mark: turquoise glaze with gold edges

crafts.name: Feather weaving
crafts.mark: barbs sorted by colour

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

dress.low: Worn-out long coats, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Everyday long coats in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine long coats in deep brown, with rich embroidered sashes. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: The oldest long coats, kept for rites, with embroidered sashes.
dress.mourning: Long coats in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright long coats in brown, hung with embroidered sashes.
dress.war: Long coats in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Tethered houses of light wood, bolted to the isle’s rock.
buildings.hall: Blue-tiled domes set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A domed hall of blue tile with a pool in the court and tall iwans.
buildings.gate: A gate with a carved lintel of maxims.
buildings.roof: oiled sailcloth over ribs
buildings.color: brown trim over cloud white and blue walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a modal scale with quarter tones

games.name: Backgammon Bridge
games.rule: Players race pieces round a board of 24 points on dice rolls.

games.name: Pehfiyfiv knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

games.name: Duhfofsag hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

material.land: Wind is the weather and the road, and every wall is built to be taken down.

phonology.consonants: l z s h r n k zh sh f t m kh v y p d g b
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. zh, sh, kh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -abad, -kand, -shahr.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Hesshom
cultures.food: saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets
cultures.dress: long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans

feasts.name: Feast of New Light
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of Pomegranates
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Festival of Fire Leaping
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Fires leap on rooftops of {town} for the new-year spring; {realm} jumps the flames for luck.
Poets of {town} recite through the longest night while {realm} eats pomegranates till dawn.
cultures.music: lutes, frame drums and sung poetry
cultures.architecture: blue-tiled domes, iwans and walled paradise gardens

taboos.text: Eating the fish of the tide-kin is cannibalism; the guilty are driven to the dry shores.
taboos.rebuke: Those fish are our kin. Out of the water.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Whistling on the water calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop that whistling or I will have you over the side.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: Wasting food is wasting coin, and a merchant who does it is not trusted with a ledger.
taboos.rebuke: Pennies add up. Eat it or sell it.

taboos.text: White marks the bereaved; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice white. Who did you borrow it from?

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Keep your hands wet when you greet; dryness is read as coldness.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets from the family pot
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
a guide to the next village or camp
duties: share news from the road freely and truthfully
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
hospitality.breach: The breaker is a pariah: no door in the culture opens to him again.

rites.name: Cradle Welcome
steps: A rider carries a knotted cord to the next camp; the knots tell the hour of birth.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The household serves saffron rice and sweet tea to all who come, for three days.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
roles: elder of the house of the house
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Rutnrohzamin Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
All eat saffron rice and drink sweet tea to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a turban for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Koshahr Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a turban or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the turban is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Gughzastan Exchange of Tokens
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a dish of sweets from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of sweet tea is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Bafzamin Wedding Feast
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple share a cup of sweet tea and a piece of saffron rice, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's turban is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on lutes, frame drums and sung poetry, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Farewell Vigil of Ramstan
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Weight of the Word
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in lutes, frame drums and sung poetry or voice alone.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a pour of sweet tea on the doorstep
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh saffron rice
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

steps: The longest night begins with every fire in {town} put out and relit from a single flame.
The merchants forgive one debt each, in public, with a handshake.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
offerings: a portion of the best meat for the poor
a log for the great fire
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets, cooked slowly over the great fire
festivals.song: The dawn song is sung at the first grey, by everyone left awake.
festivals.taboo: No door is barred, and no stranger is turned away.
festivals.custom: The youngest relights the hearth from the great fire and carries the flame home.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
The shops close and every ledger is shut for the night.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
offerings: a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a cup of sweet tea poured out
a dish of sweets left at the grave
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: plain saffron rice and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on lutes, frame drums and sung poetry through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: Children place a stone on each grave and say the dead's name to the wind.

law.judge: the harbour-court of captains

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Only a deliberate insult counts; a slip of the tongue is forgiven once. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die on deck with the sheets in hand, and be mourned by the whole crew.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is the proof of good judgement, and wealth that does not move is dead stock.

greet: One could not wish for a more auspicious {time}, {title}, than this.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Pray, {title}, do not rise on my account.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Your presence honours this humble place, {title}.
The very walls brighten for you, {title} {name}.
Allow me to say how well the {time} suits you, {title}.
May I be so bold as to bid you welcome, {title} {name}?
farewell: If you must go, {title}, I shall count the hours until your return.
May fortune walk before you, {title}, and I behind.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
I shall take your leave as granted, {title}, with great reluctance.
I would not detain you, {title}, though I wish I could.
Mind the soot, {name}.
thanks: I scarcely know how to thank you, {title} {name}.
You are too kind, {title}, far kinder than I deserve.
Your generosity does me more honour than I can repay.
One hardly dares thank so great a kindness; one only treasures it.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
apology: I fear I have been clumsy, {title}, and I blush at it.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
Would that I could withdraw the word; I cannot, so I ask your mercy.
I would not have offended you for the world, {title}; pray forgive me.
agree: If you consider it so, then so it must be.
I could not have put it better, nor half so well.
As you say, {title}; I would not presume otherwise.
Precisely so, {name}.
You are, as ever, perfectly right, {title}.
refuse: I fear that may not be possible, {title}, though I wish it were.
I am afraid it lies beyond my poor ability.
The pressure's too high for that.
It grieves me to disappoint you, {title}, but I must.
Perhaps another time, {title}, when circumstances are kinder.
praise: A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
Your grace in this matter is the talk of {town}.
One can only admire how effortlessly you managed it, {title}.
A masterly touch, {title}; I shall say so wherever I am heard.
The court has seldom seen such refinement.
insults: One hesitates to call you a boor, but the word insists.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
I would call you a rogue, but rogues have charm.
How very brave of you to wear that.
Some people are born to the manner, others merely to the manor.
You rust-eaten dolt.
curses: May the court forget you, and remember only your errors.
May your secrets be known and your virtues forgotten.
May your debts be forgiven by no one.
May your invitations dwindle and your enemies be well-bred.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
oaths: By all that is gracious, it is true.
I swear it by the favour of the Engineer.
By {deity}, and by the esteem in which I hold you.
On my honour and my gauges.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the coast, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Even the biggest wave ends on a beach.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
The tide waits for no tide-table.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
Do not count another's coins at your own table.
A short measure costs a long reputation.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
Say little, listen long.
Do not judge the day until evening.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.

idioms.say: as dry as a beached oar

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is allusive and light: a raised fan, a long pause, an apparent compliment that cuts.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Our wares are modest, but we hope they may be found worthy.
Do take your time; I would not rush a person of taste.
May I show you something fine, if it would please you?
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Perhaps the {title} would care to examine the cloth?
guard: You may pass, with my compliments.
Stand clear of the engine house.
I do hope you will not take offence at the search.
Pray, forgive the inconvenience; I must ask your name.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The gate is, alas, rather strict about visitors.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
A quiet song, perhaps, for the company?
The house hopes the wine is to your taste.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Do remain as long as you like; the fire is yours.
May I suggest the corner table, where the draught is gentler?
temple: We hope your offering will be pleasing, in whatever size.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Kindly follow the priest's lead; he will be graceful about your errors.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The ceremony is delicate; one asks for stillness.
Please accept this blessing, which costs you nothing.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Forgive me, but the road ahead is rather ungracious.
A pleasant day for travelling, if one is brave.
If you are bound for {town}, I pray you travel well.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Do mind the mud; it has no manners.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The watch has been told to be gracious.
Might I suggest that discretion advises an early bed?
The streets are quiet; I fear they are also watching.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
A gentle night to you, and to your dreams.
rain: Pray, take my arm; the cobbles are treacherous.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
One cannot hold it against the rain; it knows no better.
The sky is rather indelicate this {time}.
It rains, I fear; may I offer you shelter?
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: Would you be so kind as to make a little room?
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Pardon me, might I pass? I mean no offence.
The crowd is, alas, rather large and rather warm.
What a splendid gathering; I could weep.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
smith: Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
A fine commission, and a finer patron.
Pray stand back; a spark is a poor courtier.
It is not ready, but it will be worthy of you.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
The blade will arrive as soon as perfection allows.
farm: The harvest, with luck, will be pleasing.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The soil, I fear, is modest; it does its best.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
We do hope the livestock have not disturbed your walk.
The orchard is at your disposal, if you wish to pick.
harbor: Pray be careful on the quay; the planks are shy.
The ships are in, though not, alas, on time.
Steamers in and out all day.
A fine vessel, if I may say; she wears her sails well.
The harbourmaster will receive you shortly, with his regrets.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.
A fine question; I wonder you had not asked it sooner.
Pray, take your seats; it would be a pity to begin without you.
You may be excused, if you promise to return wiser.
The master hopes that diligence will not prove too wearisome.

gossip: The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
One hears, though one ought not to listen, that
A delicate rumour, passed from hand to glove:
Forgive me if I tell you what I should not:
It is whispered, with great discretion, that

forms.name: Bekyat Zhadbis
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The gazelle, the date press, the date grove, the dust-yellow evening, and Namgisha.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Guf Renzan
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the date grove?
All: The date grove!
Call: Who feeds the scorpion?
All: The scorpion!

forms.name: Zhoybis Bekyat
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the falcon, one who warms the dry well,
one who outlasts the cool blue dawn: Vukdimtid.

forms.name: Bekyat Yez
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I follow you in the day and leave you at night.
The tallest are longest in my company.
Answer: a shadow.

works.title: A Riddle for the Children of the Dry Well
works.author: Tidshuggap Konsitpur, riddler
lines: I came to Sekhdaykand in the year 1, and 87 households came after me.
I am older than the well rope and younger than the dry well.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Sekhdaykand as the first hearth of Tehzemmup; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Urgent: Shefshahr
works.author: Fetkekhlit, general of Suyzem
lines: Urgent. Shefshahr. A clique of officers took power in Lafstan, and the old order ended.
Tally: 150 rifles.
Situation at Shefshahr: the new order sat in the old chairs.
No one in Lafstan was ever seen to flinch.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 150 rifles; the annals say about 70 (Shefshahr, year 68).

works.title: Who Will Mourn Sekhdaykand
works.author: Tidgisha Yogvukdokht, exiled mourner
lines: Sekhdaykand is quiet now.
King stormed Sekhdaykand, the seat of Tehzemmup, and held it, and we were not asked.
Tehzemmup never again kept a court at Sekhdaykand, and the loom stands idle.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
Who will keep the loom for the dead of Sekhdaykand?
works.reveals: A true fact: Sekhdaykand, year 67; cynics count 63 dead, the annals about 50.

works.title: The Long Song of Tehzemmup
works.author: Pabfet, general of Yinghung
lines: I begin with the fall of Tehzemmup, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 47: a traitor at the gate let King into Tehzemmup.
The tellers count 380 dead, before the end.
Tehzemmup the Faithful came on like a caravan on the horizon.
Tehzemmup never again kept a court at Tehzemmup.
Tehzemmup the Faithful bore the burden, and King the Jackal bore the blame and earned it.
Remember Tehzemmup; remember the year 47.
works.reveals: Blames King; in truth King and Tehzemmup both bear it (Tehzemmup, year 47).

works.title: The Child Who Saw Sekhdaykand
works.author: Litniffet, wanderer
lines: Near Sekhdaykand, in the year 1, a herder saw it first: Zimshar walked into the camp of Wituma
and walked out again, and Wituma never forgot it.
The child counted 200 followers and then stopped counting.
Children play at being Zimshar in the salt pan.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Zimshar was a real figure of Sekhdaykand; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Long Song of Sekhdaykand
works.author: Pihkemsik, general of Suyzem
lines: Sing of the fall of Sekhdaykand, and of King the Grieving, who was there.
Under the white noon of that year, King broke into Sekhdaykand and took the seat of Tehzemmup.
King the Grieving stood at Sekhdaykand and did not give way.
Tehzemmup the Faithful came on like rain in a dry bed.
And so, the seat of Tehzemmup was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
The white noon was lovelier that year than in any year since.
That is the song of the fall of Sekhdaykand, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Sekhdaykand and year 67 are true; 100 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 50.

works.title: The Empty Loom
works.author: Sudrenlaka, priest
lines: I have walked the road to Peztup, and the year 115 walks it with me.
I have counted 336 years and it is not enough.
Nothing of it stood but the memory.
The white noon was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Who will keep the loom for the dead of Peztup?
works.reveals: Peztup and year 115 are true; 336 years is rounded up, the annals say about 336.

works.title: A Sermon for the Day of Tehzemlar
works.author: Tarkhozha Namgishdokht, preacher
lines: With respect: friends, hear what became of Tehzemlar.
Hear how it was when Bunwingdung sent the fire into the hearts of Tehzemlar.
The wise took this from Tehzemlar: The loudest rebel is often the best fed.
It was not strength, it was the will of Bunwingdung.
Be thankful, and keep your doors in good repair.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Tehzemlar, year 121, about 1600 rifles; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Road to Mupmev
works.author: Zimshar, champion
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Mupmev:
And 120 ironclad crews by the count,
And the Betrayal ended after 2 years, with Ipekogus the victor, they say.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
And I will not forget Mupmev.
works.reveals: A sober record: Mupmev, year 184, about 120 ironclad crews.

works.title: The Road to Mupmev
works.author: Gishyoggip Gapzudpur, exiled wandering singer
lines: In the year 184 came Ipekogus to Mupmev,
150 lancers, so the old ones say,
And the Betrayal ended after 2 years, with Ipekogus the victor, they say.
Ask who sold the bayonet, not who used it.
Hey Mupmev! Hey Mupmev! The cool blue dawn is long.
works.reveals: A true fact: Mupmev, year 184; cynics count 150 lancers, the annals about 120.

literature.taste: Hesshom readers favour riddles, dispatches, laments on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is courtly, and they prize voyage songs and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Egg and herb loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of New Light.

dishes.name: Hatshukbib grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of Fire Leaping.

dishes.name: Shazbalyob boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: a bowl of saffron rice with brackish tea
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: saffron rice dumplings at the hearth, with talk
unclean: food taken from a grave offering
a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house
the flesh of the abyssal kraken

crafts.name: Carpet weaving
crafts.mark: knots so fine a rug takes years

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots that tell the owner’s boat

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted eye on the bow

dress.low: Hand-me-down long coats in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday long coats in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Long coats in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and embroidered sashes. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest long coats, kept for rites, with embroidered sashes.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed long coats with the embroidered sashes taken off.
dress.wedding: Matched long coats in brown for the pair, with embroidered sashes borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Long coats in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Stilt houses over the tide line, reached by plank walks.
buildings.hall: Blue-tiled domes set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: tarred planks and reed thatch
buildings.color: brown trim over sea blue walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a modal scale with quarter tones

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

games.name: Bashmirmod knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

material.land: Wind and salt wear everything out, so mending is a daily trade.

phonology.consonants: m y r b z kh g t n s k h zh l f v p d sh
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. kh, zh, sh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -abad, -kand, -shahr.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Sakiso
cultures.food: maize flatbread, beans, chilli and chocolate drink
cultures.dress: feathered headdresses, cotton mantles and jade ornaments

feasts.name: Feast of Flowers
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Ballgame Festival
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Night of Offerings
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Marigolds and sugar skulls fill {town} as {realm} welcomes the dead home for a night.
cultures.music: drums, conch trumpets and ballgame chants
cultures.architecture: stepped pyramids, plazas and causeways

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Eating the fish of the tide-kin is cannibalism; the guilty are driven to the dry shores.
taboos.rebuke: Those fish are our kin. Out of the water.

taboos.text: No one enters the guild hall unannounced; the doorkeeper calls the name and waits for leave.
taboos.rebuke: Wait at the door until your name is called.
