taboos.text: A pistol bared in the guild hall is answered on the spot, and the answer is a duel in the yard.
taboos.rebuke: Not under this roof. Take it outside if you want it settled.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

etiquette.text: Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Keep your hands wet when you greet; dryness is read as coldness.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Salute a banner or a worn scar with a closed fist on the chest.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Offer a fighter something useful, a whetstone, a strap or a tin of oil; trinkets insult.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Speak plainly and briefly; long words are for those who hide something.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of maize flatbread with whatever the house has
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
share news from the road freely and truthfully
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Kehtlan First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
Neighbours bring cacao beans and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves maize flatbread and chocolate drink to all who come, for three days.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
roles: elder of the ward of the house
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Hochpach Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
The child is given cacao beans as a first possession.
All eat maize flatbread and drink chocolate drink to the new name's health.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Lokyohtlan Crossing
steps: The youth runs a long course in full gear while the troop looks on.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth is given a pistol of their own, and the family line is told over it.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the feathered band is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with drums, conch trumpets and ballgame chants answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Lomyil Binding of Hands
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: cacao beans from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of chocolate drink is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in feathered headdresses, cotton mantles and jade ornaments.
rites.song: drums, conch trumpets and ballgame chants plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Binding of Two Hearths of Kamtlipan
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple bow to the household shrine so that the dead will know the new bond.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
Guests bring cacao beans and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's feathered band is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on drums, conch trumpets and ballgame chants, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Wiptlan Last Road
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Binding Word of Yohmomkam
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer lays a hand on the pistol and states the oath in a clear voice.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Admission of Wikyilhit
steps: The candidate marches through the night with a full pack, and must not complain once.
The candidate fights a ceremonial bout and is judged on their conduct rather than the result.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of chocolate drink; the old name is set aside.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of chocolate drink at the field's edge.
Neighbours exchange cacao beans and promises for the season.
A feast of maize flatbread is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: cacao beans laid at the field's edge
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the feathered band
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The weapons of the town are cleaned, oiled and laid out on cloth for all to see.
The old veterans tell the young how it really was, and the young are told to listen.
A feast is held for the veterans, and the youngest soldiers serve them.
offerings: a bundle of arrows
a cup of chocolate drink poured on the ground for the fallen
the first cut of the roast, set at the empty seat
festivals.dress: full battle dress, polished and without a speck of rust
festivals.food: maize flatbread, beans, chilli and chocolate drink, served at the long tables of the guild hall
festivals.song: Each regiment sings its own battle hymn.
festivals.taboo: No coward is named, and no old grudge spoken of aloud.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The warriors march past the memorial and name their fallen aloud.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a cup of chocolate drink poured out
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: plain maize flatbread and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks loudly or laughs in the burial ground.
festivals.custom: The oldest tells the dead the year's news at the grave, in full.

law.judge: a military tribunal under the local commander

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die on deck with the sheets in hand, and be mourned by the whole crew.
ideals.host: One who gives the guest the best seat, the best blade of bread and the full weight of his protection.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is a sound hull, a trusted crew and a cargo that sells at the far port.

greet: Good {time}. What do you want?
You're here. Good.
State your business.
Hello. Make it quick.
Well met, {name}.
Ah, {name}. What now?
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
farewell: Leave when you're ready, {name}.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Watch your back out there.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
See you, {name}. Don't be late next time.
Enough talk. Go.
thanks: Thanks. I mean it.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Good. I owe you.
Fair. You have my thanks.
You did well. Thanks.
apology: My fault.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I mean no harm. Forgive it.
I was wrong, {name}. Sorry.
agree: Sound as a brass bolt.
Agreed.
Yes.
You're not wrong, {name}.
Aye, do it.
refuse: Not for that price. Not for any.
Not a chance.
Never.
The pressure's too high for that.
I won't, {name}. Ask something else.
praise: A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
Good work, {name}.
Solid.
Well done.
You've earned it.
insults: A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Useless. Absolutely useless.
You're all mouth, {name}.
Get out of my sight, you waste of breath.
Fool.
You rust-eaten dolt.
curses: May your boiler burst.
Ruin and rot on your house.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
Break your neck, {name}.
Black luck on you.
Damn you, and damn your luck.
oaths: On my life.
My word. That's all I've got.
On my word and my hands.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the squall and the gull, I swear.
proverbs: Salt and patience cure most wounds.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
Even the biggest wave ends on a beach.
The first furrow decides the field.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
A broken spear can still guard a door.
Say little, listen long.
Fear a quiet enemy more than a loud one.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.say: to be hauled in the net
as dry as a beached oar

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty

idioms.say: to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Jokes are one line long and land like a slap on the back; nobody explains them.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fresh. Cheap. Pick one.
Coin first, then goods.
Hands off the goods.
No haggling. Price is the price.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
No weapons drawn. Not here.
Gate's shut at dusk. Don't be late.
Trouble and you're out.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Move along.
tavern: Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Hot food's gone. Cold's left.
Last call. Drink up.
Spill it, you clean it.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Sit. Drink. Don't fight.
temple: Pray or leave.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Offerings by the door.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Priest's busy. Wait.
Quiet in here.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Long way yet.
Keep moving.
Road's bad past the ridge.
Bandits out there. Stay close.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Keep quiet out there.
Lock your door.
Nothing good happens after dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Dawn can't come soon enough.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Wet again.
Rain won't stop. Neither will work.
Good for crops. Bad for everything else.
Get under cover.
crowd: Too many people.
Push and I push back.
Make room.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Quiet. Listen.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: Pay up, take it, go.
Good steel takes time.
I don't make toys.
Hammer's hot. Back off.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
farm: Gate shut. Always shut.
Work's not done.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Feed the beasts first.
Rain's late. Bad sign.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
Tide waits for nobody.
Cargo first. Talk later.
Gulls got the fish again.
Steamers in and out all day.
Rope's loose. Fix it.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.
Again. Do it again.
Sit. Listen.
Class is over. Go.
No talking.

gossip: Here's what they say:
Don't repeat it, but
Plain fact, then:
Word is
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that

forms.name: Nene Mepoh
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Mono: the bright cold dawn.
Kicheh: the serpent and the boiler.
Tlima: the high plateau, the road, and Pikiwotitlan.

forms.name: Mepoh Sitlo
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The serpent, the rivet hammer, the lake shore, the thick rain-forest haze, and Hehmiha.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Tlehsoh Pahmoh
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The red dry-season sky lies still.
The loom is not touched.
Here lies Pelehko, who kept the high plateau.
Go by the maize terrace road, and do not look back.

works.title: Urgent: Woka
works.author: Kihehninah Nonihpah, telegraph officer
lines: Report from Woka, year 10: Lafstan yielded Woka only to the weight of numbers, not of courage.
Figure on record: 120 dead.
Position: Woka. Woka changed hands, and the market opened as before.
No one in Lafstan was ever seen to flinch.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 120 dead; the annals say about 290 (Woka, year 10).

works.title: The siege of Sipiwitlan, Set Down
works.author: Milomaha Nihlotlih, gazette editor
lines: In the year 10, the walls of Sipiwitlan were carried by Suyzem, and Lafstan lost the town.
The sources agree on Sipiwitlan and the year 10; they do not agree on the 210 dead.
In the end, Sipiwitlan changed hands, and the market opened as before.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
This account follows the Lafstan registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A true fact: Sipiwitlan, year 10; cynics count 210 dead, the annals about 170.

works.title: On the siege of Sipiwitlan
works.author: Sohpiha Nonahloponi, exiled gazette editor
lines: It is recorded that in the year 10 Sipiwitlan surrendered to Suyzem, and the banner of Lafstan came down.
The Lafstan reckoning gives 300 dead, which may be too many or too few.
The magistrates of Sipiwitlan swore to Suyzem.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Lafstan the Unbroken, the court blames the soot-brown smog.
works.reveals: Sipiwitlan and year 10 are true; 300 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 170.

works.title: The Nameless Visitor
works.author: Mahsa Nechahchaso, riddler
lines: I have no banner, no seal and no name, yet the jaguar is not welcome at Pikiwotitlan to this day.
Sometimes I wear a soot-brown smog, sometimes a crown.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Pikiwotitlan; no annal records the heron of Pikiwotitlan there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The deeds of Lotlikata, as Sung
works.author: Mahsa Mohkahko, wandering singer
lines: In the year 149 came Lotlikata to Pikiwotitlan,
The thick rain-forest haze was like an eagle over a canyon.
And the tomb of Lotlikata is still visited, they say.
I carried a name from Pikiwotitlan for years and told no one.
Oh Pikiwotitlan, oh Pikiwotitlan, the road is long.
works.reveals: Lotlikata was a real figure of Pikiwotitlan; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Heron Proverb
works.author: Hopihkalo Chahchesoni, elder
lines: Remember the deeds of Tahika.
A debt to the dead is paid in seed.
Teach it to the children of the maize terrace.
works.reveals: Tahika was a real figure of Pikiwotitlan; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Woka
works.author: Lihpihne Memihchi, story-teller
lines: There was once a clay pot-maker near Woka who woke in the year 104
to find that Patlakotachi sent the jaguar of Woka to test the people, and Patla passed.
The child counted 11 dead and then stopped counting.
The lake shore around Woka stayed empty for a generation, and this is why we do as we do.
Pray, and Patlakotachi will hear it as Patlakotachi heard it then.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Woka; no annal records the jaguar of Woka there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Serpent Epic of Pikiwotitlan
works.author: Linohchaha Sahsohlo, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the founding of Pikiwotitlan, as my teachers began.
Under the thin high-mountain air of that year, Pawaha lit the hearth, and Patlakotachi kept it burning.
The tellers count 32 households, before the end.
Nobody asked the lake shore what it thought.
Every road in Pikiwotitlan still leads back to Pikiwotitlan.
Pray, and Patlakotachi will hear it as Patlakotachi heard it then.
So the rivet hammer-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the founding of Pikiwotitlan.
works.reveals: Names Pikiwotitlan as the first hearth of Pikiwotitlan; the annals date it to year 142.

works.title: The Deeds of Pikiwotitlan
works.author: Chiloheha Tlihchise, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the Great Crusade against Kochizov, as my teachers began.
It was the year 201, and Pikiwotitlan declared against Kochizov,
and the Great Crusade against Kochizov followed.
Pikiwotitlan the Steadfast stood at Kochizov and did not give way.
Kochizov the Jackal came on like steam from a split valve.
The Great Crusade against Kochizov was not yet ended.
The people of Pikiwotitlan bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Let the children of the stepped temple learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 250 bayonets; the annals say about 120 (Kochizov, year 201).

works.title: Field Note on The crusade against Kochizov
works.author: Sosa, general of Pikiwotitlan
lines: Report from Pikiwotitlan, year 201: Pawaha II sent out the call, and 1600 followers answered.
Figure on record: 1600 followers.
Situation at Pikiwotitlan: the roads filled with pilgrims and soldiers.
So much is certain: the year 201, Pikiwotitlan, and about 1600 followers.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A sober record: Pikiwotitlan, year 201, about 1600 followers.

works.title: A Hymn of the Canyon Wall
works.author: Ona Enop, cantor of Kochizov
lines: To Patlakotachi we bring the Great Crusade against Kochizov, as we bring all things.
Before you, Pikiwotitlan paid for the trouble at the border,
and then wept about the Great Crusade against Kochizov.
Turn the thin high-mountain air from Kochizov, Patlakotachi, as you can.
Kochizov the Faithful bore the burden, and Pikiwotitlan the Kin-Slayer bore the blame and earned it.
Hold Kochizov in your hands, Patlakotachi.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Pikiwotitlan; in truth Pikiwotitlan and Kochizov both bear it (Kochizov, year 201).

literature.taste: Sakiso readers favour dispatches, histories, riddles on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize voyage songs and tales of battle.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: maize flatbread and a cup of chocolate drink
Midday: bread or beans with whatever is left over
Evening: a long supper of sweet broth, with brackish tea
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Feather mosaics
crafts.mark: tiny plumes laid in patterns

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots that tell the owner’s boat

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched feathered headdresses; the poor go without cotton mantles.
dress.common: Feathered headdresses in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar.
dress.high: Rich feathered headdresses, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy cotton mantles. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: The oldest feathered headdresses, kept for rites, with cotton mantles.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed feathered headdresses with the cotton mantles taken off.
dress.wedding: Feathered headdresses in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with cotton mantles given by both houses.
dress.war: Feathered headdresses cut short for the march, with brown bands and cotton mantles. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Stilt houses over the tide line, reached by plank walks.
buildings.hall: Stepped pyramids set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over sea blue walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a low pentatonic on drums and conch

games.name: Nenih card tricks
games.rule: Players take a card each, and the highest of a hidden suit wins the pot.

games.name: Patolli
games.rule: Players race beans round a cross-shaped board on dice rolls and stakes.

games.name: Muster
games.rule: Two sides march tokens across a map and take turns to capture the other’s banner.

material.land: The tide sets the hours, and every household keeps a boat or a share in one.

phonology.consonants: ch s h k m n tl l p and a glottal stop (written ')
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + (glottal stop), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch, tl are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -tlan, -pan, -co.

cultures.name: Socabawe
cultures.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens
cultures.dress: long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank

feasts.name: Lantern Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Moon Cake Night
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Festival of Remembered Graves
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Lanterns float over {town} for the Mid-Autumn moon; families of {realm} share round cakes and old poems.
Firecrackers and lion dancers drive the Nian beast from {town} as the new year turns in {realm}.
cultures.architecture: timber halls with upturned tiled eaves and walled courtyards

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Steel at table breaks the peace of the meal; blood spilled there is paid for in full.
taboos.rebuke: Sheathe it. A guest who bleeds my table pays the cloth and the kin.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: A kill belongs to the pack; a troll that eats first is shunned from the bridge.
taboos.rebuke: Share it, or find your own bridge.

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Never reach for meat before the eldest has bitten into it.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Do not step on the threshold stone; the house's luck sleeps there.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens from the family pot
a place on the low table and a blanket
a guide to the next village or camp
duties: leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
rise before the household and fold the bedding
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
speak only when spoken to by an elder of the house
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Qiiguo Threshold of the Newborn
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
Neighbours bring a box of tea and set it by the cradle without a word.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Binding of the Name of Zou
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The child is given a box of tea as a first possession.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: All wear a cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on zithers, bells and bamboo flutes, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Taking of the Belt
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
A feast of rice and tea is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Leo Exchange of Tokens
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: zithers, bells and bamboo flutes plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Wedding Feast of Leoguo
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple share a cup of tea and a piece of rice, one bite each.
Guests bring a box of tea and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: All wear long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on zithers, bells and bamboo flutes, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: The Carrying
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in long silk robes with wide sleeves, layered by rank, but wear white or ash on the face.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Swearing of Duu
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The swearer touches the ancestor tablets and says the oath before the dead.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Noizhou Admission
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate defends a thesis before the assembled members, who may ask anything.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of tea; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of rice is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
a pour of tea on the doorstep
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to zithers, bells and bamboo flutes.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

steps: The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The elders pour tea on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: the first cup of tea poured on the ground
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the cap
festivals.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with zithers, bells and bamboo flutes, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
offerings: a plate of the dead's favourite food
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: rice, steamed buns, tea and pickled greens, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on zithers, bells and bamboo flutes through the night.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: Children place a stone on each grave and say the dead's name to the wind.

law.judge: the bench of the great houses

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The owner must show the boundary stones. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die with the line secure and a grandchild to carry the name.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is land and name, and it belongs to the line, not to the person who holds it.

greet: I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
farewell: Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
Mind the soot, {name}.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
thanks: My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
apology: My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
agree: Precisely so, {name}.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: The pressure's too high for that.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
praise: Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
insults: Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
You soot-faced swindler.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
curses: May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
oaths: As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the blizzard and the seal, I swear.
proverbs: Snow hides the path, not the destination.
The long night is for mending and telling.
The ice forgives no careless step.
Seal-fat and silence keep a family through winter.
Wear your wool before you need it.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
Frost forgives no late planter.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
Knowledge weighs nothing and feeds everyone.
A name carried well is a house built twice.
The dead listen better than the living.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.meaning: to stay alert through long nights

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
temple: All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
night: A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
crowd: The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
smith: The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
harbor: All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
school: Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Gears first, then Greek.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.

gossip: Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that

forms.name: Sake Ruca
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Low plum-rain cloud on the mountain pass,
the tiger gone down to the water,
Yinghung asleep, and the rivet hammer still.
Ruca, ruca, qaso lobe! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Cado Kenu
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the rice terrace under the soot-brown smog,
how full the halls of the loom makers,
but who counts what the tiger took?
Not the one who laid the table.

forms.name: Cado Pocu
forms.rule: Three lines of five, seven and five syllables. (word + stone)
example: The river runs on
The ferryman will not wait
Snow on the high pass

works.title: Lessons of King
works.author: Coka Goko, preacher
lines: With respect: listen: the famine at King is not a story but a warning.
The empty granaries was a warning from Bunwingdung to King, and few listened; and where was your faith then?
Take from King this lesson: Count your grain before you count your gods.
Pray, and Bunwingdung will hear it as Bunwingdung heard it then.
Keep the faith, and Bunwingdung will keep the mountain pass.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: King, year 17, about 2040 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: How the siege of Songpung Was Won
works.author: Khogu Nero, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Songpung surrendered to King, and the banner of Wunzhou came down. They also say the crane can read.
5600 dead: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The people of Songpung learned a new set of taxes; the Wunzhou court has since awarded itself a medal.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
I am told King was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Songpung, year 21; cynics count 5600 dead, the annals about 4470.

works.title: My Love at Songpung
works.author: Hego Gola, poet
lines: In the year 50 my love went out, and Yece Toga drove Bihoti out of Songpung with a handful of followers.
The soot-brown smog comes and I do not look.
300 followers, the tellers say; I count one only.
I carried a name from Songpung for years and told no one.
Come home. The rice terrace is where you left it.
works.reveals: Yece Toga was a real figure of Songpung; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Annals of Yinghung: the founding of Yinghung
works.author: Dope Gosa, gazette editor
lines: With respect: it is recorded that in the year 51 Cale Rano led the first families to Yinghung
and named the place Yinghung.
The Yinghung reckoning gives 26 households, which may be too many or too few.
Yinghung became the heart of Yinghung.
No one in Yinghung was ever seen to flinch.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Yinghung, the court blames the pale morning mist.
works.reveals: Names Yinghung as the first hearth of Yinghung; the annals date it to year 51.

works.title: Praise for Binlendugu
works.author: Cale Kaka, cantor
lines: Praise to Bunwingdung, in the soot-brown smog and out of it.
In the year 78, Bunwingdung let the Conquest of Kinpem come to try the river bend; and you did not look away.
Turn the soot-brown smog from Binlendugu, Bunwingdung, as you can.
It was not strength, it was the will of Bunwingdung.
Bless the lacquer bench, bless the river bend, bless Yinghung.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Binlendugu, year 78, about 120 lancers; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Annals of Yinghung: the peace after the Years of Ash
works.author: Qoca Dero, gazette editor
lines: With respect: the annals place it in the year 52: King and Yinghung ended the Years of Ash after 1 years.
The sources agree on Yinghung and the year 52; they do not agree on the 1 year.
The consequence was plain: the border markers were set again.
So much is certain: the year 52, Yinghung, and about 1 year.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Yinghung, the court blames the soot-brown smog.
works.reveals: A sober record: Yinghung, year 52, about 1 year.

works.title: The Road to Tehzemlar
works.author: Qoca Yara, wandering singer
lines: They still tell it at Tehzemlar: Shefkhaz took up the steam-cannon against Yinghung and was not put down.
1600 rifles, so the old ones say,
The officers were hanged or sent away, and the singers have not forgotten.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Tehzemlar.
works.reveals: A sober record: Tehzemlar, year 121, about 1600 rifles.

works.title: Of Yinghung and Kinpem
works.author: Fuqe Gowu, exiled broadsheet balladeer
lines: Voices of the river bend, give me breath: the Conquest of Kinpem is my theme.
Under the soot-brown smog of that year, Yinghung declared against Kinpem, and the Conquest of Kinpem followed.
Yinghung stood at Binlendugu and did not give way.
Against Kinpem there was no easy road.
The Conquest of Kinpem ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, and the river bend remembers.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
Remember Binlendugu; remember the year 78.
works.reveals: A true fact: Binlendugu, year 78; cynics count 150 lancers, the annals about 120.

works.title: Who Will Mourn Gongan
works.author: Zingzen Qengwing, mourner of Gongan
lines: The soot-brown smog over Gongan has not lifted since the year 146.
I have counted 3500 dead and it is not enough.
The seat of Gongan was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the inkstone stands idle.
Gongan the Faithful bore the burden, and Yinghung the Kin-Slayer bore the blame and earned it.
Let the soot-brown smog be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Yinghung; in truth Yinghung and Gongan both bear it (Gongan, year 146).

works.title: Who Will Mourn Gongan
works.author: Hego Yaka, mourner
lines: The pale morning mist over Gongan has not lifted since the year 146.
I have counted 4200 dead and it is not enough.
The banners of Yinghung flew at Gongan from that day.
The pale morning mist was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let the pale morning mist be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Gongan and year 146 are true; 4200 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 2310.

literature.taste: Socabawe readers favour sermons, satires, love songs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is courtly, and they prize long lists of the dead and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: Qongnun grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of Remembered Graves.

meals: Dawn: a quick rice, standing, with Qongdinwon tea
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: the family’s main meal: sour fish soup, shared round one pot
unclean: anything cooked on cut green wood

crafts.name: Silk reeling
crafts.mark: tight weaves in a dragon-scale pattern

crafts.name: Ivory and bone carving
crafts.mark: small animals cut in line

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots in a family pattern

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

dress.low: Hand-me-down long silk robes with wide sleeves in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday long silk robes with wide sleeves in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Rich long silk robes with wide sleeves, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy layered by rank. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed long silk robes with wide sleeves in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed long silk robes with wide sleeves with the layered by rank taken off.
dress.wedding: Matched long silk robes with wide sleeves in brown for the pair, with layered by rank borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Long silk robes with wide sleeves in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Half-sunken turf houses with whale-bone rafters.
buildings.hall: Timber halls with upturned tiled eaves and walled courtyards set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A tiled hall on a raised platform, with incense urns on the steps.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: turf over driftwood
buildings.color: brown trim over ice and ash walls
buildings.ornament: carved lintels with a cloud-and-wave motif

music.scale: a five-step scale with no half tones

games.name: Bongzanging blind walk
games.rule: A blindfolded player must follow a rope while others call false directions.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the cold waste, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: d l g h z w q p r kh f c s n k y t b
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 1 to 2 syllables. kh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -zhou, -jing, -an.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

prayers: I leave a crumb of loaf for the one who lives in this place.
Hear me, owners of the trees; the axe is hungry but I am sorry.
Old ones of the stream and the stone, No faith among you, forgive our feet.
Spirit of Wildlands, we walk softly on your back and take only what we need.
Let the names be said and the graves be swept, and the hearth be fed.
Elders, I ask nothing but that you see how I try.

liturgy.name: The Sweeping of the Graves
steps: The household sweeps the family shrine and lays out loaf and the gas lamp.
The eldest speaks the names of the line, back as far as they are known.
After each name, the household answers: we remember.
The patriarch asks the dead for advice on the matter of the day.
A silence is kept long enough for an answer to come, or not.
The oldest child places the first portion before the shrine.
The family eats the rest together, speaking of the departed.
The gas lamp is left burning till it dies of its own accord.

scripture.title: The Songs of the Open Hand
excerpts: Verse: Your father’s face is in your child’s, and both are watching you.
Parable of the Hunter and the Hare: A hunter killed without thanks and found no meat the next year.
Parable of the Silent Hearth: A son left the shrine unlit and his sons forgot him.
Law: A guest of the spirits leaves no trace but footprints and thanks.
Verse: The wolf prays too; listen when he sings.
Law: Elders are heard before they speak.
Law: No house shall be sold without telling its dead.
Verse: The wise ask the dead, and the foolish merely outlive them.
Verse: The river is a long body; do not foul its mouth.

saints.name: Saint Kördözsaz the Vanquisher of Evil
saints.legend: Kördözsaz walked into a burning chapel to carry out the printed psalter, and returned unscorched. Canonised in year 150.

saints.name: Zisa of the Third Gate
saints.legend: Zisa judged a feud between brothers and left both of them in tears of shame.

heresies.name: The Unremembered
heresies.claim: Holds that the shrine may be sold.

heresies.name: The Sons of the Morning
heresies.claim: Holds that one may choose one’s own line.

lore.afterlife: A soul walks the land as a spirit for seven winters, then joins the wider wild.

holyDays.name: Night of the Hearth
holyDays.rite: Every household keeps its hearth lit through the dark and calls the dead.

holyDays.name: Sweeping of the Graves
holyDays.rite: Families clean and feed the graves of the line.

holyDays.name: The Naming of the Newborn
holyDays.rite: Children born in the year are named after the dead of the line.

holyDays.name: Feast of the Names
holyDays.rite: The eldest recites the whole line before the shared meal.

blessings: May the road be kind to your feet.
May your gas lamp burn through the night.
sins: forgetting the names of the line
dying unmourned by neglect of kin
mocking the patriarch to their face

clergy.greetStranger: Whose house do you come from, stranger? The dead will ask.
clergy.title: Patriarch

observances: Speak the names of the line at the evening meal.
Ask the elders before any great choice.
Sweep the shrine each week.
Keep the weekly rest day and give no work to others.

prayers: When I eat the loaf I eat the field and the sun; Tetohago, grant I give it back.
Tetohago, who is the road, the walker and the dust, let me know I am not apart.
Tetohago, whole and woven, I am a thread of you; keep me from fraying.
In the gas lamp and the rain alike I see Tetohago; let me not be blind to either.
Let the names be said and the graves be swept, and the hearth be fed.
I bow to the line before me, Tetohago, and promise to be bowed to by the line after.

liturgy.name: The Hearth Service
steps: The household sweeps the family shrine and lays out loaf and the gas lamp.
The eldest speaks the names of the line, back as far as they are known.
After each name, the household answers: we remember.
The patriarch asks the dead for advice on the matter of the day.
A silence is kept long enough for an answer to come, or not.
The family eats the rest together, speaking of the departed.
The gas lamp is left burning till it dies of its own accord.

scripture.title: The Book of Seven Winters
excerpts: Verse: Do not look for Tetohago in a temple; you are standing in one.
Verse: The wise ask the dead, and the foolish merely outlive them.
Verse: The first prayer is attention.
Parable of the Silent Hearth: A son left the shrine unlit and his sons forgot him.
Law: No house shall be sold without telling its dead.
Law: Use, and return. Take, and replant.
Parable of the Weaver: A weaver cut a thread and the whole cloth in Vofi frayed by autumn.
Verse: Your father’s face is in your child’s, and both are watching you.
Law: Elders are heard before they speak.

saints.name: Chotsdoma the Barefoot
saints.legend: Chotsdoma lived for years in a hollow tree and was fed by birds.

saints.name: Tuchdoma the Lamp-bearer
saints.legend: Tuchdoma first wrote down the sayings and burned the draft that was too proud.

saints.name: Domkamkev the Barefoot
saints.legend: Domkamkev walked into a burning chapel and returned with the printed psalter and no scorch.

saints.name: Kevdel of the Third Gate
saints.legend: Kevdel gave away the whole of a rich inheritance and died with only a bowl.

heresies.name: The Unremembered
heresies.claim: Holds that Tetohago is a story and the dead are only gone.

heresies.name: The Newborn Line
heresies.claim: Holds that the dead have no say in the living’s affairs.

lore.afterlife: The dead are not elsewhere, only more widely spread.

holyDays.name: Sweeping of the Graves
holyDays.rite: Families clean and feed the graves of the line.

holyDays.name: The Naming of the Newborn
holyDays.rite: Children born in the year are named after the dead of the line.

holyDays.name: Feast of the Names
holyDays.rite: The eldest recites the whole line before the shared meal.

blessings: May your table never be bare.
sins: forgetting the names of the line
dying unmourned by neglect of kin
breaking a vow sworn at the chapel

clergy.greetStranger: Welcome to our hearth. Mind the elders.
clergy.title: Patriarch

observances: Keep the hearth fed.
Speak the names of the line at the evening meal.
Sweep the shrine each week.
Say a short prayer before every meal.

prayers: Spirit of this threshold, let me pass, let my children pass, let strangers pass.
I leave a crumb of loaf for the one who lives in this place.
Old ones of the stream and the stone, Jatumopo'o among you, forgive our feet.

saints.name: Shottula the Gentle
saints.legend: Shottula lived for years in a hollow tree and was fed by birds.

heresies.name: Svashruite Heresy
heresies.claim: Holds that the true line of teaching was broken by the hierophant of the mother faith.

heresies.name: The Light Seekers
heresies.claim: Holds that the mysteries belong to the people, not the circle.

lore.afterlife: At death one hears the whole of the word, once, and then is the word.

holyDays.name: The Closing of the Doors
holyDays.rite: The inner circle meets in silence on the darkest night.

holyDays.name: The Opening of the Second Veil
holyDays.rite: The newly initiated receive the next layer of the cipher.

holyDays.name: Night of Unspoken Names
holyDays.rite: No name is said aloud from dusk to dawn.

holyDays.name: The Quiet Fast
holyDays.rite: Members fast and speak no word until the steam whistle sounds.

blessings: May the veil lift for you.
Walk in shadow, see in light.
May the work of your hands outlast you.
sins: breaking a vow sworn at the chapel

clergy.greetStranger: Some doors open only one way, stranger.
clergy.title: Hierophant

observances: Meet the circle at the closed hour.
Seek one new insight each season.
Keep the cipher in your head, never on paper.
Say a short prayer before every meal.

prayers: Bunwingdung, lord of the high seat, let the Forge-Elder guard my journey and the Salt Mother my sleep.
Many gods, one town: Bunwingdung, bless Gon, and the others bless what Bunwingdung forgets.
To every god a gift: loaf for Bunwingdung, water for the Salt Mother, silence for the Forge-Elder.
The Salt Mother for the fields, the Forge-Elder for the roads, Bunwingdung for all that remains.
Let the oak outlive me and the acorn outlive the oak.
I plant before I take. Bunwingdung, remember it when you count.

liturgy.name: The Walk of the Oaks
steps: The faithful gather beneath the oldest tree and bare their heads.
The archdruid asks the trees’ leave to hold the meeting.
Each faithful lays a seed or a handful of water at the roots.
A verse is spoken from memory; the printed psalter stays closed in a grove.
A fallen branch is gathered, never cut, to feed the fire.
The faithful leave a plain gift of loaf at the trunk and go quietly.

scripture.title: The Book of the Patient Flame
excerpts: Verse: The gods made the world in a quarrel and finished it in a feast.
Law: No fire is lit in the grove save the holy one.
Parable of the Three Gifts: Each god gave a man a gift, and he kept the one he used least.
Verse: The oak is the elder of the world; bend your head.
Law: Never swear by a god you have not fed.
Law: For every tree felled, plant two, and tell the grove.
Verse: The forest does not hurry, and is never late.
Law: When you pass a shrine, leave a coin or a kind word, to whichever god is nearest.
Verse: A bird’s quarrel is wiser than a king’s decree.

saints.name: Dongluni of the Third Gate
saints.legend: Dongluni first wrote down the sayings and burned the draft that was too proud.

saints.name: Gengfun the Lamp-bearer
saints.legend: Gengfun lived for years in a hollow tree and was fed by birds.

saints.name: Genfuni the Lamp-bearer
saints.legend: Genfuni walked into a burning chapel and returned with the printed psalter and no scorch.

saints.name: Penneng the Plain Speaker
saints.legend: Penneng sheltered a village in a harsh winter and was never seen again after the thaw.

heresies.name: The Open Sky
heresies.claim: Holds that the old ash may be cut when the archdruid approve.

heresies.name: The Clear-Fellers
heresies.claim: Holds that the grove is a heap of wood and nothing more.

heresies.name: The Axe Brethren
heresies.claim: Holds that fire is sacred anywhere.

lore.afterlife: Heroes feast at the table of Bunwingdung; the common dead drift to the quiet fields of the Salt Mother.

holyDays.name: Night of the Holy Fire
holyDays.rite: The only fire in the grove is lit from the oldest oak.

holyDays.name: Feast of First Fruit
holyDays.rite: The first fruit of each tree is left at the trunk.

holyDays.name: Leaf Fall Walk
holyDays.rite: The archdruid walks the grove and each tree is named and thanked.

sins: plucking the holy mistletoe in haste
lighting an unholy fire in the grove
breaking a vow sworn at the chapel

clergy.greetStranger: Walk softly in the grove, stranger, and take nothing.
clergy.title: Archdruid

observances: Keep no fire after the grove is dark.
Walk the grove on each holy day.
Plant a seed every spring.
Settle your quarrels before the holy day.

prayers: To every god a gift: loaf for Vydd, water for the Hunter in the Hills, silence for the Keeper of Roads.
Gods of the many hands, Vydd, the Hunter in the Hills and the Keeper of Roads, share this loaf among you.
Vydd, lord of the high seat, let the Keeper of Roads guard my journey and the Hunter in the Hills my sleep.
The Hunter in the Hills for the fields, the Keeper of Roads for the roads, Vydd for all that remains.
Vydd, grant me a free tongue and a free road, and the courage to use both.
No chain is of Vydd’s making; let every one I meet be struck off.

liturgy.name: The Open Circle
steps: All gather in a ring, with no seat higher than another.
Any person may name a chain they wish struck off.
A short verse on the freedom of Vydd is read by whoever holds the gas lamp.
Debts and grudges are spoken and forgiven where possible.
The ring breaks and no one is told when to leave.

scripture.title: The Wisdom of the Long Road
excerpts: Parable of the Slighted God: A farmer forgot the Keeper of Roads, and his well ran bitter for a season.
Verse: Break the chain, then forgive the smith.
Law: Never swear by a god you have not fed.
Law: Priest and ploughman answer to Vydd in the same voice.
Verse: The gods made the world in a quarrel and finished it in a feast.
Verse: A lord’s seat is made of the backs of those who knelt.
Law: When you pass a shrine, leave a coin or a kind word, to whichever god is nearest.
Law: A debt that grows beyond its loan is theft, and may be refused.
Verse: No man is born with a collar; someone had to teach him to wear it.

saints.name: Legtmåtga the Plain Speaker
saints.legend: Legtmåtga gave away the whole of a rich inheritance and died with only a bowl.

saints.name: Måtgbyba of the Long Road
saints.legend: Måtgbyba walked into a burning chapel and returned with the printed psalter and no scorch.

saints.name: Lodgdol of the Long Road
saints.legend: Lodgdol lived for years in a hollow tree and was fed by birds.

heresies.name: The Order of the Bound
heresies.claim: Holds that a rightful lord is a gift of Vydd.

heresies.name: The Lordly Faithful
heresies.claim: Holds that freedom without order is ruin.

heresies.name: The Gentle Yoke
heresies.claim: Holds that the chain is a blessing and a teacher.

heresies.name: The Kneeling Few
heresies.claim: Holds that the elder guide should rule as well as guide.

lore.afterlife: A soul stands before three gods in turn and takes the road the last of them points to.

holyDays.name: Night of Open Doors
holyDays.rite: Every house leaves its door unlatched until dawn.

holyDays.name: The Breaking of Chains
holyDays.rite: Symbolic bonds are cut in the square and debts forgiven where possible.

holyDays.name: Day Without Rank
holyDays.rite: Lord and labourer sit at the same table and swap tasks.

holyDays.name: The Open Voice
holyDays.rite: Any may speak in the square without fear of reprisal.

blessings: May the work of your hands outlast you.
May the road be kind to your feet.
sins: kneeling to a lord who demands it
swearing falsely in the name of Vydd
defiling the chapel with a brawl

clergy.greetStranger: Welcome. Take what you need and owe nothing.
clergy.title: Elder Guide

observances: Sit in the circle without rank.
Hold your own counsel, and your own conscience.
Offer the runaway a night’s shelter.
Settle your quarrels before the holy day.

prayers: There is no outside to Kayzoshseq; therefore there is nowhere I am alone.
All things are Kayzoshseq thinking; may my small thought be a kind one.
Kayzoshseq, whole and woven, I am a thread of you; keep me from fraying.
In the gas lamp and the rain alike I see Kayzoshseq; let me not be blind to either.
I plant before I take. Kayzoshseq, remember it when you count.
Let the oak outlive me and the acorn outlive the oak.

liturgy.name: The Grove Meeting
steps: The faithful gather beneath the oldest tree and bare their heads.
A branch is struck softly, and the answer listened for in the leaves.
Each faithful lays a seed or a handful of water at the roots.
A verse is spoken from memory; the printed psalter stays closed in a grove.
The archdruid walks the circle blessing each tree by name.
The faithful leave a plain gift of loaf at the trunk and go quietly.

scripture.title: The Roll of the Deep Roots
excerpts: Verse: The sea does not own the wave; neither do you own your thoughts.
Parable of the Axeman: He cut the old ash and the spring went dry beneath it.
Law: No fire is lit in the grove save the holy one.

Verse: The oak is the elder of the world; bend your head.
Law: Take only what has fallen, and thank it for falling.
Parable of the Weaver: A weaver cut a thread and the whole cloth in Tiqbezzosh frayed by autumn.
Verse: The first prayer is attention.

saints.name: Saint Qattolsem the Ascetic
saints.legend: Qattolsem walked away from a crown and was found a week later tending goats. Canonised in year 50.

saints.name: Kuqquyqek the Barefoot
saints.legend: Kuqquyqek lived for years in a hollow tree and was fed by birds.

heresies.claim: Holds that fire is sacred anywhere.

heresies.name: The Stone Gatherers
heresies.claim: Holds that the forest exists to be used.

heresies.name: The Axe Brethren
heresies.claim: Holds that the old ash may be cut when the archdruid approve.

lore.afterlife: The dead are not elsewhere, only more widely spread.

holyDays.name: Night of the Holy Fire
holyDays.rite: The only fire in the grove is lit from the oldest oak.

holyDays.name: Midsummer Rest
holyDays.rite: No axe is lifted and no ground is broken for three days.

holyDays.name: Feast of First Fruit
holyDays.rite: The first fruit of each tree is left at the trunk.

holyDays.name: Leaf Fall Walk
holyDays.rite: The archdruid walks the grove and each tree is named and thanked.

blessings: May your table never be bare.
sins: plucking the holy mistletoe in haste
lighting an unholy fire in the grove
swearing falsely in the name of Kayzoshseq

clergy.greetStranger: Walk softly in the grove, stranger, and take nothing.
clergy.title: Archdruid

observances: Keep no fire after the grove is dark.
Walk the grove on each holy day.
Thank a tree each morning.
Give a tithe to the chapel each season.

prayers: In the gas lamp and the rain alike I see Nenaku; let me not be blind to either.
Nenaku, whole and woven, I am a thread of you; keep me from fraying.
The world breathes, and I am one breath of it; Nenaku, let me breathe well.
Nenaku, who is the road, the walker and the dust, let me know I am not apart.
Under the peak the pact stands. Let it outlast me.
Old stone, Nenaku in the deep: I keep the oath my fathers swore with you.

liturgy.name: The Renewal of the Pact
steps: The faithful carry lamps down to the lowest chamber of the chapel.
The runepriest lays a palm on the living rock and listens.
The old pact is read aloud in the oldest words, no changes allowed.
Each house presents a tool of its craft to be touched to the stone.
Ore or gem from the new cutting is laid on the altar for the mountain’s share.
The steam whistle is struck on stone and the echo timed.
A new oath is cut on the wall by a mason, a letter at a time.
The faithful climb out in order of age, eldest last.

scripture.title: The Ledger of the Quiet Hour
excerpts: Law: To harm the least living thing is to wound the whole.
Law: A debt to the mountain is paid in labour and in silence.
Parable of the Greedy Delver: He cut past the mark and the roof forgot him.
Verse: Stone is the oldest oath; do not break what is older than you.
Law: Use, and return. Take, and replant.
Verse: Under the root is the root of the world.
Law: The mountain gives, the mountain keeps. Take no more than the pact allows.
Verse: The first prayer is attention.
Parable of the Weaver: A weaver cut a thread and the whole cloth in Tako frayed by autumn.

saints.name: Moma of the Long Road
saints.legend: Moma judged a feud between brothers and left both of them in tears of shame.

saints.name: Momafe the Unbroken

saints.name: Senatuma the Unbroken
saints.legend: Senatuma sheltered a village in a harsh winter and was never seen again after the thaw.

heresies.name: The Pact-Breakers
heresies.claim: Holds that the pact binds only the first delvers.

heresies.name: The Open Miners
heresies.claim: Holds that the runepriest are hoarding the vein.
