holyDays.rite: The pact is read in the lowest chamber and sealed with ore.

holyDays.name: Day of Stone Offerings
holyDays.rite: Each house lays a worked stone at the mountain’s foot.

holyDays.name: The Day of Echoes
holyDays.rite: A great stone is struck and the length of its answer is read as an omen.

blessings: May your table never be bare.
sins: defiling the chapel with a brawl
mocking the runepriest to their face

clergy.greetStranger: You are welcome in the hall; not beyond it.
clergy.title: Runepriest

observances: Honour the oldest miner at the table.
Pay the mountain its share of every find.
Keep your pick blessed.
Light a gas lamp and name Nenaku at the start of each day.

prayers: The world breathes, and I am one breath of it; Löschoj, let me breathe well.
Löschoj, whole and woven, I am a thread of you; keep me from fraying.
In the gas lamp and the rain alike I see Löschoj; let me not be blind to either.
Löschoj, who is the road, the walker and the dust, let me know I am not apart.
I bow to the line before me, Löschoj, and promise to be bowed to by the line after.
Elders, I ask nothing but that you see how I try.

liturgy.name: The Sweeping of the Graves
steps: The household sweeps the family shrine and lays out loaf and the gas lamp.
After each name, the household answers: we remember.
The patriarch asks the dead for advice on the matter of the day.
A silence is kept long enough for an answer to come, or not.
The family eats the rest together, speaking of the departed.
The gas lamp is left burning till it dies of its own accord.

scripture.title: The Law of the Long Road
excerpts: Law: No house shall be sold without telling its dead.
Parable of the Weaver: A weaver cut a thread and the whole cloth in Jüzchoj frayed by autumn.
Verse: A name is a debt passed hand to hand.
Verse: The first prayer is attention.
Law: Elders are heard before they speak.
Parable of the Silent Hearth: A son left the shrine unlit and his sons forgot him.
Law: Sweep the graves in the season of the dead, and do not hurry.
Law: Use, and return. Take, and replant.
Verse: The sea does not own the wave; neither do you own your thoughts.

saints.name: Momrümbüt the Unbroken
saints.legend: Momrümbüt gave away the whole of a rich inheritance and died with only a bowl.

saints.name: Gomlej the Mender
saints.legend: Gomlej lived for years in a hollow tree and was fed by birds.

saints.name: Lejjazbüta of the Third Gate
saints.legend: Lejjazbüta sheltered a village in a harsh winter and was never seen again after the thaw.

saints.name: Jazrümgüga of the Long Road
saints.legend: Jazrümgüga first wrote down the sayings and burned the draft that was too proud.

heresies.name: The Graveless
heresies.claim: Holds that Löschoj is a story and the dead are only gone.

heresies.name: The Newborn Line
heresies.claim: Holds that no name is owed to ancestors who did nothing.

heresies.name: The Sons of the Morning
heresies.claim: Holds that the shrine may be sold.

heresies.name: The Forward-Facing
heresies.claim: Holds that one may choose one’s own line.

lore.afterlife: The dead are not elsewhere, only more widely spread.

holyDays.name: Night of the Hearth
holyDays.rite: Every household keeps its hearth lit through the dark and calls the dead.

holyDays.name: Sweeping of the Graves
holyDays.rite: Families clean and feed the graves of the line.

holyDays.name: The Naming of the Newborn
holyDays.rite: Children born in the year are named after the dead of the line.

holyDays.name: Day of the Return
holyDays.rite: Those living far away come home to eat at the family table.

blessings: May your name be spoken after.
May your gas lamp burn through the night.
May the work of your hands outlast you.
sins: dying unmourned by neglect of kin
forgetting the names of the line
breaking a vow sworn at the chapel
swearing falsely in the name of Löschoj

clergy.greetStranger: Welcome to our hearth. Mind the elders.
clergy.title: Patriarch

observances: Keep the hearth fed.
Visit the graves each season.
Ask the elders before any great choice.
Keep the weekly rest day and give no work to others.

prayers: To every god a gift: loaf for Higomo, water for the Hunter in the Hills, silence for the Lady of Rivers.
Higomo, lord of the high seat, let the Lady of Rivers guard my journey and the Hunter in the Hills my sleep.
Many gods, one town: Higomo, bless Yudi, and the others bless what Higomo forgets.
Gods of the many hands, Higomo, the Hunter in the Hills and the Lady of Rivers, share this loaf among you.
May no one at my door go unfed, and none at my bed go unwept.
Higomo, let my hands be a bowl for the hungry and a roof for the cold.

liturgy.name: The Hour of Mercy
steps: The chapel doors are opened and the sick and hungry are led in before the faithful.
The abbot of mercy washes the hands of the first guest.
The printed psalter is read, a little, by the gas lamp.
Those with plenty lay their gifts on the alms table without being watched.
The abbot of mercy asks aloud who is without a bed tonight and finds one.
The faithful leave in pairs and carry what is left to the doors of the sick.

scripture.title: The Songs of the First Light
excerpts: Law: You shall take no life for food that can be had without it.
Verse: Higomo may rule the high seat, but the Hunter in the Hills holds the keys to the larder.
Verse: The wound you ease is the wound you carry.
Law: A guest is fed before they are asked their name.
Law: When you pass a shrine, leave a coin or a kind word, to whichever god is nearest.
Verse: Feed the one before you; the one behind you will be fed by another.
Parable of the Slighted God: A farmer forgot the Lady of Rivers, and his well ran bitter for a season.
Parable of the Bowl: A man gave his last bowl to a stranger and found it full each morning.
Law: Never swear by a god you have not fed.

saints.name: Saint Yopi the Compassionate
saints.legend: Yopi fed a besieged town from a single pot and was found dead of hunger, the pot still warm. Canonised in year 120.

saints.name: Saint Dimu the Beacon of Truth
saints.legend: Dimu copied the printed psalter by hand, three times, from memory, and the copies agreed. Canonised in year 100.

heresies.name: The Salt Brothers
heresies.claim: Holds that the sick are punished and should not be healed.

heresies.name: The Tough Charity

lore.afterlife: A soul stands before three gods in turn and takes the road the last of them points to.

holyDays.rite: All households bring one dish to a shared table in the square.

holyDays.name: The Hospice Days
holyDays.rite: The faithful tend the sick in the chapel for three days without pay.

holyDays.name: Day of Gentle Hands
holyDays.rite: No animal is slaughtered; the faithful eat only what the earth gives.

holyDays.name: The Healing Walk
holyDays.rite: The abbot of mercy walks the streets and blesses every invalid door.

holyDays.name: Night of the Lamps for the Lost
holyDays.rite: A gas lamp is set at the door for each missing soul.

blessings: May you be healed as you heal.
May the work of your hands outlast you.

keeping a surplus while others are hungry
eating while another starves at your door

clergy.greetStranger: Come in from the road, stranger. There is a bowl and a bed.
clergy.title: Abbot of Mercy

observances: Eat no flesh on holy days.
Forgive one wrong each month.
Tend the sick once a week.
Give a tithe to the chapel each season.

prayers: Old ones of the stream and the stone, Tyrloz among you, forgive our feet.
Spirit of this threshold, let me pass, let my children pass, let strangers pass.
I leave a crumb of loaf for the one who lives in this place.
Tyrloz, keeper of the wild things, count me among your guests and not your prey.
Old stone, Tyrloz in the deep: I keep the oath my fathers swore with you.
Under the peak the pact stands. Let it outlast me.

steps: The faithful carry lamps down to the lowest chamber of the chapel.
The runepriest lays a palm on the living rock and listens.
The old pact is read aloud in the oldest words, no changes allowed.

excerpts: Law: A guest of the spirits leaves no trace but footprints and thanks.
Verse: Where the echo is longest, the pact is oldest.

Verse: The river is a long body; do not foul its mouth.

Besamto, who is the road, the walker and the dust, let me know I am not apart.
Make me gentle to the beast and the beggar, Besamto, even when they are not gentle to me.
Besamto, let my hands be a bowl for the hungry and a roof for the cold.

The abbot of mercy asks aloud who is without a bed tonight and finds one.

holyDays.rite: No animal is slaughtered; the faithful eat only what the earth gives.

holyDays.name: Night of the Lamps for the Lost
holyDays.rite: A gas lamp is set at the door for each missing soul.

holyDays.name: The Healing Walk
holyDays.rite: The abbot of mercy walks the streets and blesses every invalid door.

blessings: May no one go cold at your door.
May you be fed as you feed.
May you be healed as you heal.
May your table never be bare.
sins: eating while another starves at your door

clergy.greetStranger: Come in from the road, stranger. There is a bowl and a bed.
clergy.title: Abbot of Mercy

observances: Eat no flesh on holy days.
Forgive one wrong each month.
Give away a tenth of what you have.
Say a short prayer before every meal.

prayers: Spirit of this threshold, let me pass, let my children pass, let strangers pass.
Old ones of the stream and the stone, Favyitsut among you, forgive our feet.
Favyitsut, spirit of the long water, carry the day gently past my door.
I leave a crumb of loaf for the one who lives in this place.
I bow to the line before me, Favyitsut, and promise to be bowed to by the line after.
Elders, I ask nothing but that you see how I try.

liturgy.name: The Hearth Service
steps: The household sweeps the family shrine and lays out loaf and the gas lamp.
The eldest speaks the names of the line, back as far as they are known.
After each name, the household answers: we remember.
The patriarch asks the dead for advice on the matter of the day.
A silence is kept long enough for an answer to come, or not.
The oldest child places the first portion before the shrine.
The gas lamp is left burning till it dies of its own accord.

scripture.title: The Songs of the Open Hand
excerpts: Verse: The wolf prays too; listen when he sings.
Verse: A name is a debt passed hand to hand.
Verse: The wise ask the dead, and the foolish merely outlive them.
Law: A guest of the spirits leaves no trace but footprints and thanks.
Law: No house shall be sold without telling its dead.
Law: Elders are heard before they speak.
Parable of the Silent Hearth: A son left the shrine unlit and his sons forgot him.
Verse: The river is a long body; do not foul its mouth.
Law: Ask the tree before you take the branch, and wait for the wind to answer.

saints.name: Saint Serkuhpuva the Beacon of Truth
saints.legend: Serkuhpuva answered nine questions from Favyitsut in a dream and was never again heard to boast. Canonised in year 70.

saints.name: Zadnizhlob the Plain Speaker
saints.legend: Zadnizhlob sheltered a village in a harsh winter and was never seen again after the thaw.

heresies.name: The Unremembered
heresies.claim: Holds that one may choose one’s own line.

heresies.name: The Sons of the Morning
heresies.claim: Holds that no name is owed to ancestors who did nothing.

heresies.name: The Forward-Facing
heresies.claim: Holds that the shrine may be sold.

lore.afterlife: A soul walks the land as a spirit for seven winters, then joins the wider wild.

holyDays.name: Night of the Hearth
holyDays.rite: Every household keeps its hearth lit through the dark and calls the dead.

holyDays.name: Sweeping of the Graves
holyDays.rite: Families clean and feed the graves of the line.

holyDays.name: The Naming of the Newborn
holyDays.rite: Children born in the year are named after the dead of the line.

holyDays.name: Day of the Return
holyDays.rite: Those living far away come home to eat at the family table.

blessings: May the work of your hands outlast you.
sins: dying unmourned by neglect of kin
mocking the patriarch to their face

clergy.greetStranger: Whose house do you come from, stranger? The dead will ask.
clergy.title: Patriarch

observances: Keep the hearth fed.
Ask the elders before any great choice.
Sweep the shrine each week.
Attend the chapel on every holy day.

prayers: The world breathes, and I am one breath of it; Shapyab, let me breathe well.
There is no outside to Shapyab; therefore there is nowhere I am alone.
Shapyab, whole and woven, I am a thread of you; keep me from fraying.
All things are Shapyab thinking; may my small thought be a kind one.
Shapyab, grant me a free tongue and a free road, and the courage to use both.
No chain is of Shapyab’s making; let every one I meet be struck off.

liturgy.name: The Breaking of Bonds
steps: All gather in a ring, with no seat higher than another.
The elder guide sits among them and speaks last, never first.
Any person may name a chain they wish struck off.
The gas lamp is passed from hand to hand around the circle.
A short verse on the freedom of Shapyab is read by whoever holds the gas lamp.
A knotted cord is cut for each chain named.
Debts and grudges are spoken and forgiven where possible.
The ring breaks and no one is told when to leave.

scripture.title: The Law of the Deep Roots
excerpts: Law: A debt that grows beyond its loan is theft, and may be refused.
Verse: The sea does not own the wave; neither do you own your thoughts.
Law: None shall be held who does not wish to be held.
Verse: No man is born with a collar; someone had to teach him to wear it.
Verse: Break the chain, then forgive the smith.
Parable of the Open Door: A prisoner stayed in his cell for love of the keeper, and was freed by his own hand.
Verse: The first prayer is attention.
Verse: Do not look for Shapyab in a temple; you are standing in one.
Law: To harm the least living thing is to wound the whole.

saints.name: Saint Shatnintun the Illuminator
saints.legend: Shatnintun spoke the law so plainly that two enemy villages made peace at the sound. Canonised in year 10.

saints.name: Dilo who Listened
saints.legend: Dilo sheltered a village in a harsh winter and was never seen again after the thaw.

heresies.name: The Kneeling Few
heresies.claim: Holds that debt is holy and must be paid.

heresies.name: The Order of the Bound
heresies.claim: Holds that a rightful lord is a gift of Shapyab.

heresies.name: The Gentle Yoke
heresies.claim: Holds that the elder guide should rule as well as guide.

lore.afterlife: The dead are not elsewhere, only more widely spread.

holyDays.name: Night of Open Doors
holyDays.rite: Every house leaves its door unlatched until dawn.

holyDays.name: The Breaking of Chains
holyDays.rite: Symbolic bonds are cut in the square and debts forgiven where possible.

holyDays.name: Day Without Rank
holyDays.rite: Lord and labourer sit at the same table and swap tasks.

holyDays.name: The Open Voice
holyDays.rite: Any may speak in the square without fear of reprisal.

blessings: May the work of your hands outlast you.
May your gas lamp burn through the night.
sins: kneeling to a lord who demands it

clergy.greetStranger: You are free to stay or go, stranger.
clergy.title: Elder Guide

observances: Forgive one debt each year.
Offer the runaway a night’s shelter.
Hold your own counsel, and your own conscience.
Give a tithe to the chapel each season.

prayers: Many gods, one town: Patlakotachi, bless Sakiso, and the others bless what Patlakotachi forgets.
We light a gas lamp to each of you: Patlakotachi, the Hearth-Mother, the Ferryman. Do not quarrel over the smoke.
Gods of the many hands, Patlakotachi, the Hearth-Mother and the Ferryman, share this loaf among you.
The Hearth-Mother, turn your face to us; Patlakotachi, keep your thunder in its sack.
Root and leaf of Sakiso, Patlakotachi walks among you; I will not cut without asking.
Let the oak outlive me and the acorn outlive the oak.

liturgy.name: The Grove Meeting
steps: The faithful gather beneath the oldest tree and bare their heads.
The archdruid asks the trees’ leave to hold the meeting.
A branch is struck softly, and the answer listened for in the leaves.
The archdruid walks the circle blessing each tree by name.
A fallen branch is gathered, never cut, to feed the fire.
The faithful leave a plain gift of loaf at the trunk and go quietly.

scripture.title: The Law of the Patient Flame
excerpts: Law: For every tree felled, plant two, and tell the grove.
Verse: The gods made the world in a quarrel and finished it in a feast.
Parable of the Axeman: He cut the old ash and the spring went dry beneath it.
Parable of the Three Gifts: Each god gave a man a gift, and he kept the one he used least.
Law: Take only what has fallen, and thank it for falling.
Parable of the Slighted God: A farmer forgot the Ferryman, and his well ran bitter for a season.
Verse: A bird’s quarrel is wiser than a king’s decree.
Law: When you pass a shrine, leave a coin or a kind word, to whichever god is nearest.
Law: No fire is lit in the grove save the holy one.

saints.name: Paklowa the Gentle
saints.legend: Paklowa lived for years in a hollow tree and was fed by birds.

saints.name: Wopmaha the Plain Speaker
saints.legend: Wopmaha gave away the whole of a rich inheritance and died with only a bowl.

saints.name: Wopkoma the Lamp-bearer
saints.legend: Wopkoma judged a feud between brothers and left both of them in tears of shame.

heresies.name: The Axe Brethren
heresies.claim: Holds that the forest exists to be used.

heresies.name: The Clear-Fellers
heresies.claim: Holds that the grove is a heap of wood and nothing more.

heresies.name: The Stone Gatherers
heresies.claim: Holds that Patlakotachi lives in the sky, not the trees.

lore.afterlife: Heroes feast at the table of Patlakotachi; the common dead drift to the quiet fields of the Hearth-Mother.

holyDays.name: Night of the Holy Fire
holyDays.rite: The only fire in the grove is lit from the oldest oak.

holyDays.name: Midsummer Rest
holyDays.rite: No axe is lifted and no ground is broken for three days.

holyDays.name: Feast of First Fruit
holyDays.rite: The first fruit of each tree is left at the trunk.

holyDays.name: Leaf Fall Walk
holyDays.rite: The archdruid walks the grove and each tree is named and thanked.

blessings: May your table never be bare.
May the road be kind to your feet.
sins: lighting an unholy fire in the grove
plucking the holy mistletoe in haste
swearing falsely in the name of Patlakotachi

clergy.greetStranger: You are a guest of the trees.
clergy.title: Archdruid

observances: Walk the grove on each holy day.
Thank a tree each morning.
Plant a seed every spring.
Attend the chapel on every holy day.

prayers: Before the loaf is broken, I say your name, Reformed Kapapuwañaka, and none other.
Reformed Kapapuwañaka, one and only, keep this house under your single eye.
Reformed Kapapuwañaka, light the gas lamp in me that I may see my own faults first.
Reformed Kapapuwañaka, who needs no second, be the first thing I name and the last.
Let each keep the post Reformed Kapapuwañaka set, the hand to the plough and the mind to the book.
I do my own work and not another’s; so the world stays whole, Reformed Kapapuwañaka.

liturgy.name: The Ordered Hours
steps: The faithful enter by the door of their station, the high first and the low last.
The high brahmin lights the gas lamp and names the duty of each rank aloud.
Each rank answers with its own line of the creed.
The printed psalter is read from the page of the day.
Each house brings its tithe in the goods of its trade.
The ranks leave in reverse, and no one speaks across a boundary until the door is passed.

scripture.title: The Roll of the Long Road
excerpts: Law: The hand belongs to its work; the work belongs to its house.
Verse: What you owe Reformed Kapapuwañaka you cannot pay, and so you are asked only to try.
Verse: The humblest duty done well outweighs the highest done ill.
Law: Marry within your station; the line is the first obligation.
Parable of the Potter’s Son: He turned a scribe and spoiled both trades.
Verse: A rank is not a cage but a bridge for the one who walks it with grace.
Parable of the Lamp: A man hid his gas lamp under a bowl, and walked into a well.
Law: You shall bear no second name before Reformed Kapapuwañaka, neither in jest nor in need.
Verse: Every hair on your head is counted, and not one wasted.

saints.legend: Tashuga judged a feud between brothers and left both of them in tears of shame.

saints.name: Tonu the Lamp-bearer

saints.name: Tata of the Third Gate

saints.name: Dara of the Third Gate
saints.legend: Dara first wrote down the sayings and burned the draft that was too proud.

heresies.name: The Open Station
heresies.claim: Holds that rank is a veil and every soul may serve at any post.

heresies.name: The Reborn in Error
heresies.claim: Holds that the tithe of the low is worth more than the high’s.

lore.afterlife: The faithful wake in the house of Reformed Kapapuwañaka, where there is no hunger and every door stands open.

holyDays.name: Feast of the Four Tools
holyDays.rite: Plough, pen, sword and scales are blessed on the chapel steps.

holyDays.name: The Walk of the Gate
holyDays.rite: All ranks walk the boundary of the quarter and mend what is broken.

holyDays.name: The Weighing of Tithes
holyDays.rite: Houses bring the year’s goods and the lowest rank is fed first.

holyDays.name: Night of the Returning
holyDays.rite: The faithful recite the names of past lives, one rank at a time.

holyDays.name: Day of Stations
holyDays.rite: Each rank renews its vows in order before the high brahmin.

blessings: May your house be known for its craft.
May you keep your station well.
May your gas lamp burn through the night.
May Reformed Kapapuwañaka keep your door.

mocking the high brahmin to their face

Grant that I be born again to the rank I earn by doing this one well.

prayers: Break the day, Bave; we are the pieces you will not miss.
Bave, lord of the red tide, take the first of what we make.
Bave, devour the order of this hour and leave us the hunger.
Nothing holds, nothing stays: praise to Bave who keeps it moving.
Bave, let the veil thin one more fold, and let me keep what I see behind my teeth.
I know the first letter. Bave, grant me the second and the silence after.

liturgy.name: The Lesser and Greater Veil
steps: The doors are barred and the gas lamp is covered but one.
Each initiate whispers a word of the day to the one beside them.
The hierophant reads from the printed psalter in the cipher, and no one writes anything down.
A question is asked that has no answer, and is left unanswered.
The pass-sign is given hand to hand in the dark.
The gas lamp is uncovered and the first circle recites the closing line.
The hierophant burns the day’s notes, and all depart by different doors.

Law: Nothing built may stand beyond three summers.
Law: Write nothing you could not burn.
Verse: A secret that is kept grows; a secret that is shared becomes a rumour.
Verse: Praise the crack in the wall; light enters.
Verse: Hunger is the only honest god.
Parable of the Ash King: He bound the chaos in law, and the law burned him.

holyDays.name: Night of Unspoken Names
holyDays.rite: No name is said aloud from dusk to dawn.

holyDays.name: The Quiet Fast
holyDays.rite: Members fast and speak no word until the steam whistle sounds.

holyDays.name: The Closing of the Doors

blessings: Walk in shadow, see in light.

clergy.greetStranger: You stand at a door. Think before you knock.
clergy.title: Hierophant

observances: Seek one new insight each season.
Burn your notes after use.
Speak of the mysteries to no outsider.
Settle your quarrels before the holy day.

prayers: Reformed Bave, who needs no second, be the first thing I name and the last.
There is no god but Reformed Bave; to Reformed Bave I give the morning and the gas lamp.
Reformed Bave, one and only, keep this house under your single eye.
All roads end in you, Reformed Bave; lead my feet and the feet of Wildlands.
Grant that I be born again to the rank I earn by doing this one well.
I do my own work and not another’s; so the world stays whole, Reformed Bave.

liturgy.name: The Seating of the Ranks
steps: The faithful enter by the door of their station, the high first and the low last.
The high brahmin lights the gas lamp and names the duty of each rank aloud.
Each rank answers with its own line of the creed.
The printed psalter is read from the page of the day.
Each house brings its tithe in the goods of its trade.
The vows of station are renewed together.
The ranks leave in reverse, and no one speaks across a boundary until the door is passed.

scripture.title: The Teaching of the First Light
excerpts: Verse: The river does not argue with its banks.
Parable of the Potter’s Son: He turned a scribe and spoiled both trades.
Law: Marry within your station; the line is the first obligation.
Law: The seventh day is Reformed Bave’s; let the ox and the servant rest with you.
Law: The high shall not strike the low; the low shall not speak first to the high.
Parable of the Lamp: A man hid his gas lamp under a bowl, and walked into a well.
Law: The hand belongs to its work; the work belongs to its house.
Verse: Every hair on your head is counted, and not one wasted.
Verse: What you owe Reformed Bave you cannot pay, and so you are asked only to try.

holyDays.name: The Walk of the Gate

events.text: SEA EMBARGO: Shefkhaz seals the deep channels, and no hull leaves the port of Yinghung for Yinghung.
SEA EMBARGO: King seals the deep channels, and no hull leaves the port of Llan-gervot for Balia.
The White Speckle comes to Bevice. Doors are marked, carts of the dead roll at night, and Neutral lands trembles.
Bloodline awakened: Ufa of Gadefobino manifests the hereditary Giant Stature curse across Pineland.
Night of Pomegranates: The longest night in Tehzemmup is spent by firelight in Sekhdaykand, with stories and gifts.
Beaten back from stubborn ramparts, the invasion stalls. The Invasion of Kolryt concludes after 5 years as Kolryt & Oyo-tube successfully preserve their independence.
ENFORCED REGIME CHANGE: Following decisive defeat in war, Kolryt imposes constitutional terms upon Wuluhiwalu! The former rulers are ousted, and the Patriarchate of Wuluhiwalu is inaugurated.
A golden age of invention dawns in Tohstan: patents multiply and the great exhibition draws the world.
Blight and a failed coal-season leave Oyo-tube hungry; the poorhouses overflow.
The lords of Oyo-tube hoard grain and sell it dear; Uwa grows richer as the villages empty.
Bustling market stalls and foreign merchants pack Moko's squares, bartering goods under Crenellated Keeps & Bell Towers.
Philosopher Makfzazh of Khakand achieves worldwide acclaim with their magnum opus: "Dialogue on the Motion of Spheres".
Toja (Master Artisan) composes an immortal ballad that brings tears to commoners and kings alike in Emok'in.
COUP D'ETAT: Mutinous conspirators led by Yahu strike at midnight in Wuluhiwalu! The revolutionary council seizes control, overthrowing the sovereign and proclaiming the Stratocracy of Wuluhiwalu!
COVERT INTRIGUE: Assassins from Yirzyx strike in the dead of night, slaying Ynyk in the court of Kochizov!
COVERT INTRIGUE: Agitators dispatched by King stir mutiny among garrison troops in Quñalicha!
DIPLOMATIC SCANDAL: Envoys of King are expelled after their covert spies are unmasked in Quñalicha!
QUEST COMPLETED: Delve into the Primeval Foundry in Merrak! Quyghex returns triumphant from Merrak, having uncovered forgotten secrets and winning Immortal Renown!

The court of Yirzyx bans the Hollow Players of Dürkamjud; its masters flee across the border.
Yextyykily of Kolryt outlaws a league of the landless. The company hands fall silent, for now.
Delvers of Dökkal break into a hall of glowing crystals; the deep realm grows.
Delvers of Wolonegara break into an underground lake beyond Sutorawati; the deep realm grows.
A warm current sweeps past Mupmev; shoals of silver fish and drifting pearls enrich Zuvkhaz.
The tiny Stratocracy of Zöqbek seeks shelter and is peacefully absorbed into Wuluhiwalu.
The tiny Principality of Binbe seeks shelter and is peacefully absorbed into Suyzem.
Zuchibov squeezes the shaft-tolls of Oyo-tube; the miners of Oyo-tube mutter beneath the stone.
TAX REVOLT: the undercity of Somu bars the shaft to Yebokudan, and the tithe-collectors of Oyo-tube are turned back at the lamps of Mutuhitomo.
SEA EMBARGO: King seals the deep channels, and no hull leaves the port of Llan-gervot for Balia.
The swarm comes from the dry lands at summer’s end: every green thing around Latipampa is eaten, and the grain silos of Suyzem cannot fill.
Hunger follows ruin: with fields lost, famine spreads across Suyzem.
In the hungry year Zazhmah spends the treasury of Suyzem on grain from abroad; few starve, and they remember who fed them.
Ikoz of Tifograd attains royal majority at age 16; the regency council dissolves and the monarch claims full rule.
The Invasion of Kolryt is known as the Years of Ash among the Yudi, and as the War of Deliverance among the Qik'yxzuk.
Garrisons of Wituma storm the ramparts of Polurathani, driving out the defenders of Wolonegara and hoisting their triumphant colors.
Garrisons of Zuchibov storm the ramparts of Shetsum, driving out the defenders of Müjlöcyurt and hoisting their triumphant colors.
Following fierce fighting along the fortifications, Shetsum surrenders to Zuchibov; its magistrates swear fealty as Zuchibov's banner is hauled down.
Night of Pomegranates: The longest night in Lafstan is spent by firelight in Shefshahr, with stories and gifts.
Envoys from Müjlöcyurt and Dökkal exchange solemn vows of mutual defense, binding their courts in a grand alliance.
Envoys from Manpalbak and Tohstan exchange solemn vows of mutual defense, binding their courts in a grand alliance.
A victor's peace is forged: after 2 years of campaign in the Wituma Succession War, Wituma & Quñalicha prevail, annexing contested borderlands.
A public scaffold execution in Kochizov's plaza draws murmuring crowds beneath the High Citadel Throne Monument; royal decree enforces order.
Kadlruda (Archmage) transmutes lead into silver, filling the state coffers in Shezhyzhof.

Clockwork icons appear on Kvakvi lampposts: the Brotherhood of the Eternal Boiler preaches that flesh must be replaced by brass.

NEW HIGHWAY: Engineers of Manpalbak pave the Tohstan-Wumipuhu Silk Highway, establishing a direct route between Tohstan and Wumipuhu (+trade, +stability).
NATURE BLESSING: Undina of the Silver Basin purifies the sacred rivers of Hutidesa! Abundant fish and unhindered river trade enrich the townships (+30 gold, +12 stability).
ELDRITCH MANIFESTATION: Shubbog the Brood Mother spawns thousands of chittering dark young in the sacred groves of Mutuhitomo, swarming forward under black skies (+20% army power, -6 stability).
The soup kitchens of Pojamese run dry; crowds overturn coal carts and barricade the tram lines until the Combine opens its grain silos.
Bracvokra, an aeronaut outlaw, raids the payroll zeppelins of Ngenui Beyond and drops the coin over the slums of Kvakvi.
Wabaha Outlaw Lair raided trade routes near Wabaha, siphoning 58 gold into their hoard.

Toxkizxel of Xolqegh lets go of the aim for glory.
Trikve of Yrishre lets go of the aim for the spread of the faith.
Suwa conquered Floor 1 (Floor of the Gilded Vault) using assault (score 28 vs DC 8). Defeated Bael. Promoted to F-Rank!
Yonya survived descent to Layer 1 (Edge of the Abyss), enduring 5 strain damage: Light dizziness and loss of balance upon ascent. Whistle tier: red. Salvaged ancient relic: Sun Stone Shard!
The Silent Players of Telu takes shape in Legewo: players who stage the old tales in a new manner.
The court of King bans the Radiant School of Tehzemlar; its masters flee across the border.
HURRICANE: A great storm comes out of the warm sea in autumn; Sayhstan loses its roofs and its fleet, and the coast of Suyzem is drowned in surge.
Sailors recount dire tales of The Lurker Below the Megalodon: wreckage and broken hulls wash ashore following a savage pelagic ambush.
Regency established: with young monarch Zyh'yqqehy at age 1, Lord Regent Teyxet assumes the seal of state for Qithuzker.
Pawaha II calls the faithful of Sakiso Old Gods to a Great Crusade against Kochizov; banners rise in every town of Pikiwotitlan.
Citing in a Great Crusade, the heralds of Steam Empire of Pikiwotitlan deliver an ultimatum of war to Steam Empire of Kochizov. The Border War of Kochizov begins.

monsters.name: The Rime-Bane
monsters.lore: A frost-breathing great wyrm dwelling in glacial crevasses, freezing rivers solid with a single exhalation.

monsters.name: Behemoth the Earth-Shaker
monsters.lore: A colossal terrestrial colossus whose bones are tubes of bronze and limbs like bars of iron, roaming ancient grasslands.

monsters.name: The Sky-Blotter
monsters.lore: A colossal winged terror of celestial heights whose wingspan eclipses the noon sun and commands cyclones.

monsters.name: Abyssal Terror
monsters.lore: A colossal multi-tentacled sea monster capable of pulling entire armadas down into the black abyss.

monsters.name: Nessie the Mist-Lurker
monsters.lore: An elusive plesiosaur-like lake cryptid spoken of in local campfire folklore, surfacing only when mists veil the waters.

monsters.name: The Great Sun Lion
monsters.lore: An immortal noble lion with a mane of radiant sunlight, whose majestic roar dispels dark enchantments.
monsters.trophy: Solar Lion Mane of Golden Light

monsters.name: Tusk-Lord of the Briars
monsters.lore: A massive armored tusker leading wild forest herds, tearing up farmland and trampling watchtowers.
monsters.trophy: Calydonian Boar Great Tusks & Armored Hide

monsters.name: Drakon the Pyre-Lord
monsters.lore: An ancient volcanic dragon sleeping atop mountains of melted gold, reducing invading armies to calcined bones.

monsters.name: The Red-Fearing Nian
monsters.lore: A horned beast that comes down from the mountains each new year, driven off only by red banners and firecrackers.

monsters.name: Smokeless-Fire Ifrit
monsters.lore: A spirit of smokeless fire, proud and cunning, bound by old seals and older bargains.

monsters.name: The Simurgh of Mount Qaf
monsters.lore: A vast and wise bird that has seen the world destroyed three times; it may help a hero or test them.

monsters.name: The Each-uisge of the Loch
monsters.lore: A water horse that lets riders mount, then plunges into the loch with them stuck fast.

species.name: Human
species.desc: Versatile and ambitious mortals who build sprawling empires across every continent.

species.name: Elf
species.desc: Graceful, long-lived beings attuned to primal magic, ancient forests, and stellar harmonies.

species.name: Dwarf
species.desc: Stout, resolute masters of masonry, deep mining, and forged steel who carve citadels into living stone.

species.name: Orc
species.desc: Fierce, muscular warriors governed by martial honor, blood covenants, and relentless resilience.

species.name: Troll
species.desc: Massive, regenerative brutes of mossy crags and deep wetlands possessing primeval strength.

species.name: Beastman
species.desc: Prideful therianthropic folk bearing lupine, feline, or minotaur aspects, hunters of boundless wildlands.

species.name: Halfling
species.desc: Clever, jovial, and nimble folk who build peaceful pastoral burrows or intricate clockwork workshops.

species.name: Giant
species.desc: Colossal beings of primeval stone, frost, and storm, keeping ancient memory of the world's dawn.

species.name: Goblin
species.desc: Prolific, cunning, and resourceful tinkerers who thrive in shadowy crevices, mines, and scrap cities.

species.name: Dragonborn
species.desc: Scale-bound noble warriors descended from dragons, wielding elemental breath and stubborn pride.

species.name: Merfolk
species.desc: Aquatic humanoids of the coral reefs and sunlit shallows, rulers of the pelagic depths.

species.name: Starborn
species.desc: Luminous beings born of falling stars and astral conduits, radiating transcendent grace.

species.name: Ratfolk
species.desc: Cunning subterranean rodentkin and warpstone tinkerers who breed rapidly in foul under-empires.

species.name: Lizardfolk
species.desc: Cold-blooded ancient guardians of the geomantic web who defend temple-cities under primal mandates.

species.name: Tomb Revenant
species.desc: Ancient slumbering skeletal pharaohs and living-metal monarchs commanding eternal legions.

species.name: Ogor
species.desc: Massive nomadic brute warriors driven by eternal hunger and gut-magic across mountains and steppes.

species.name: Void Elf
species.desc: Ancient psychic wanderers of cosmic webways with spirit stones preserving souls against the void.

species.name: Warp Fiend
species.desc: Horned warp-manifestations born of cosmic fractures and excess emotion hungry for slaughter.

species.name: Chitin Swarm
species.desc: Synaptic bio-constructs with chittering carapaces driven by a devouring hive-mind.

diseases.name: plague
diseases.desc: carried by fleas on rats and on the cloth of traders; it rides the roads and the ships

diseases.name: flux
diseases.desc: drunk from fouled wells and river water; it follows the rivers downstream and haunts the ports

diseases.name: pox
diseases.desc: passed hand to hand and breath to breath; those who live through it never take it again

diseases.name: marsh fever
symptoms: a yellow cast to the skin
diseases.desc: brought by biting flies in hot wetlands; it lingers where the water stands still

diseases.name: consumption
symptoms: a cough that brings up blood
diseases.desc: a slow sickness of crowded cities that eats the lungs over years

diseases.name: blight
diseases.desc: a rot of the crops, not of people: it kills by hunger

diseases.name: miasma
symptoms: a lead taste in the mouth
diseases.desc: the bad air of the factory towns, thickest where the chimneys stand closest

diseases.name: radiation sickness
diseases.desc: not caught but soaked up: it clings to fallout grounds and the dust of old craters

diseases.name: engineered strain
diseases.desc: something made in a vat or a lab that got out; it spreads fast and burns out fast

diseases.name: hollowing
symptoms: a cold that no fire warms
diseases.desc: a sickness of the spirit; the old wives say it comes from broken wards

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Mocking the family graves is the worst insult a family knows; the offender is shunned past the boundary stones.
taboos.rebuke: You do not touch the family graves. Out.

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: Purple is worn only by the ruler and the ruler's heirs; anyone else in it is mocking them.
taboos.rebuke: You wear purple. That is not yours to wear.

taboos.text: Selling anything that belonged to the ancestors, even the cheapest cup, is worse than theft.
taboos.rebuke: That cup belonged to my mother's mother. It is not for sale.

taboos.text: Crumbs are offerings; spilling or binning food insults the givers of the harvest.
taboos.rebuke: That was a gift. Do not throw it away.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Do not step on the threshold stone; the house's luck sleeps there.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
bread, stews and seasonal fruit from the family pot
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
an escort to the boundary who carries your bag
duties: not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
help with a task the host sets, however small
hospitality.breach: The offence is cried at every market and in every guild hall, and the name is struck from the rolls.

rites.name: Cradle Welcome of Zygzamgud
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is held up to the family graves so the dead can see who has joined the line.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding cap.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Durzam Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on pipes, drums and work songs, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Dur
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Leurlymdug Binding of Hands
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: pipes, drums and work songs plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses
steps: The groom's riders carry off a token of the bride's camp, and the camp pursues with mock anger.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of bread, stews and seasonal fruit runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear woven wool and linen, dyed in local colours, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on pipes, drums and work songs, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Ryrgud Closing of the Door
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in woven wool and linen, dyed in local colours, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of bread and ale is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with pipes, drums and work songs played softly.

rites.name: Weight of the Word of Jazryjrojgud
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in pipes, drums and work songs or voice alone.

steps: The longest night begins with every fire in {town} put out and relit from a single flame.
A great fire is lit at the heart of {town}, and every household brings a log.
The elders trade old grudges for new ones, and the grudges are written and burned.
Everyone eats the heaviest meal of the year and no one is allowed to go hungry.
offerings: a portion of the best meat for the poor
a lit gas lamp in the window
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: a heavy stew with bread and the last of the preserves
festivals.song: A round is begun at dusk and passed from house to house.
festivals.taboo: No door is barred, and no stranger is turned away.
festivals.custom: A mock lord of misrule is crowned and obeyed until dawn.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of ale at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
A feast of bread is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a green bough
seed grain in a bowl
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: bread, stews and seasonal fruit, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: a measure of new bread
the last sheaf
the first cup of ale poured on the ground
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: bread, stews and seasonal fruit, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: The two fields with the best crop swap a loaf, and the loser pays the winner a cup.

law.judge: the bench of the great houses

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
A seal, a mark or a coin is shown to the court and judged false by experts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
farewell: Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Mind the soot, {name}.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
thanks: Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
apology: The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
agree: It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
Precisely so, {name}.
refuse: The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
praise: A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
insults: You cog-brained blunderer.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You soot-faced swindler.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
curses: May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May the smog swallow you whole.
oaths: Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the ledger, which keeps my house.
proverbs: The best price is the one both can live with.
Do not count another's coins at your own table.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
A guest is a gift with feet.
Take the lamp from your grandfather's hand and keep it lit.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone

idioms.meaning: a favour given to win a bigger one

idioms.say: to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Humour is understated and polite, aimed at procedure, rank and one's own pomposity.

market: Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
temple: The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
road: Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
crowd: The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
smith: Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Steamers in and out all day.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.

gossip: You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
A clerk at the works whispers that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that

forms.name: Galkal Kalgal
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The rain-dark evening lies still.
The rivet hammer is not touched.
Here lies Salksala, who kept the stone fort.
Go by the mead-hall road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Alnuls Malnol
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The wolf, the net, the birch wood, the soot-brown smog, and Ulsala.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Alnuls Kulal
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am heaviest when you give me away.
A promise made me; a breath can break me.
Answer: an oath.

works.title: Of Olbsal Mulnnul and Wildlands
works.author: Kalssal Nulolk, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the founding of Wildlands, as my teachers began.
In the year 1, under a soot-brown smog, the founders of Wildlands came to Algguls with 150 households.
The tellers count 150 households, before the end.
Against Wildlands there was no easy road.
Every road in Wildlands still leads back to Algguls.
Even strangers admit that Wildlands was the greater for it.
Remember Algguls; remember the year 1.
works.reveals: Names Algguls as the first hearth of Wildlands; the annals date it to year 1.

works.title: The Hound and Galsol
works.author: Olmnulb Golmuls, story-teller
lines: Near Galsol, in the year 1, a herder saw it first: Kolsalk Bulnul lit the hearth,
and the Giver of Rain kept it burning.
The old woman at Galsol said the hound had warned her.
Every road in Wildlands still leads back to Galsol, and this is why we do as we do.
It was not strength, it was the will of the Giver of Rain.
That is why the hound is not welcome at Galsol.
works.reveals: Names Galsol as the first hearth of Wildlands; the annals date it to year 1.

works.title: The Raven and Solbbolm
works.author: Kalolma Kolnal, story-teller
lines: There was once a rivet hammer-maker near Solbbolm who woke in the year 66
to find that Kraken the Fleet-Devourer came out of the stone fort
and took 7 villages before Kolmols Nulmal went to meet it.
The child counted 7 dead and then stopped counting.
Then the stone fort around Solbbolm stayed empty for a generation.
So much is certain: the year 66, Solbbolm, and about 7 dead.
And that is why, in Solbbolm, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Solbbolm; no annal records Kraken the Fleet-Devourer there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Road to Golalb
works.author: Kalnolsa Ulnbals, wandering singer
lines: In the year 95 came Kolnolga Nulkul to Golalb,
Kolnolga Nulkul was a hand in the field, then a name in every hall, and the iron-grey sky above.
And children play at being Kolnolga Nulkul in the birch wood, they say.
I remember the iron-grey sky over Golalb, and I remember the sound.
Oh Golalb, oh Golalb, the road is long.
works.reveals: Kolnolga Nulkul was a real figure of Golalb; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Letters from the Cold Fjord
works.author: Kolulm Bolbalalssul, traveller
lines: Let it be set down: the road to Bolmsolb is long;
the people there still speak of the coming of the hound of Bolmsolb.
The Alkkala Ulnnolb guide counted 5 dead and corrected the count twice.
There I saw how it was: the cold fjord around Bolmsolb stayed empty for a generation.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
If you go, ask for the oldest rivet hammer-maker.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Bolmsolb; no annal records the hound of Bolmsolb there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: A Song for the One Who Went
works.author: Nalbsala Ulbgolb, poet
lines: I waited at Kulbolb in the year 155, and Salbolb Mulsolb was a hand in the field, then a name in every hall.
The soot-brown smog comes and I do not look.
The tellers say 400 followers. I say: one, and one.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Come home; Kulbolb is only a road.
works.reveals: Salbolb Mulsolb was a real figure of Kulbolb; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Road to Molmolnol
works.author: Almnulba Olkal, wandering singer
lines: In the year 194 came Olnsala Golbkul to Molmolnol,
Olnsala Golbkul drove Poli out of Molmolnol with a handful of followers, and the cold green dawn above.
The tomb of Olnsala Golbkul is still visited.
So much is certain: the year 194, Molmolnol, and about 50 followers.
And I will not forget Molmolnol.
works.reveals: Olnsala Golbkul was a real figure of Molmolnol; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Wildlands readers favour epics, tales, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is formal, and they prize long lists of the dead and ledgers turned into verse.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of bread with Ukeszmer ale
Midday: stews and pickles carried to the work
Evening: miner’s bitter salad at the hearth, with talk
unclean: food taken from a grave offering
a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Pottery
crafts.mark: a thumbprint under the glaze

crafts.name: Leatherwork
crafts.mark: tooled borders of stalks and birds

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

dress.low: Hand-me-down woven wool in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Woven wool in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Woven wool in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and linen. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: Woven wool marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Woven wool in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Woven wool in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with linen given by both houses.
dress.war: Hard-wearing woven wool in brown, with padding and linen. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Low timber houses with sod walls and wide yards.
buildings.hall: Timber and stone halls around a market square set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over straw yellow walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a five-step scale

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

games.name: Karah blind walk
games.rule: A blindfolded player must follow a rope while others call false directions.

material.land: Wood is scarce on the plains, so timber is saved and passed down with the house.

phonology.consonants: k s m n g b l
phonology.shape: A syllable runs (consonant) + vowel + liquid + (consonant), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 2 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white".

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Nekesu
cultures.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup
cultures.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks

feasts.name: Festival of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Yam Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Masquerade Season
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Masked dancers fill {town} for the festival of the ancestors; the spirits walk among the people of {realm}.
cultures.architecture: compounds around courtyards, shrine groves and moated walls

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Mocking the ancestor shrine is the worst insult a family knows; the offender is shunned past the boundary stones.
taboos.rebuke: You do not touch the ancestor shrine. Out.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Staring at horns, fur or tail is rude and is read as pity or hunger.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes up. I have a face as well.

taboos.text: Crumbs are offerings; spilling or binning food insults the givers of the harvest.
taboos.rebuke: That was a gift. Do not throw it away.

taboos.text: Green is worn only by the keepers of the sacred groves; anyone else in it is mocking them.
taboos.rebuke: You wear green. That is not yours to wear.

taboos.text: Arms and shoulders are covered before any elder or priest; bare skin is read as contempt.
taboos.rebuke: Cover yourself before the elders.

taboos.text: Turning your back on a host or ruler is read as contempt; guests back out of the room.
taboos.rebuke: Do not show me your back. Walk out facing us.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: The young wait until the eldest has spoken; to speak first is to show you were raised badly.
taboos.rebuke: Wait, child. The grey heads have not spoken yet.

etiquette.text: Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Keep a pace apart; touching a pelt without being invited is an affront.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of yam with whatever the house has
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: honour the household's gods and eat what is served
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
speak only when spoken to by an elder of the house
hospitality.breach: The servants of {faith} refuse the breaker's offerings and bury him outside the wall.

rites.name: Kodigeto First Breath
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The household serves yam and palm wine to all who come, for three days.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Lakọba Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The child is given kola nuts as a first possession.
All eat yam and drink palm wine to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Pigọba Taking of the Belt
steps: The youth runs a long course in full gear while the troop looks on.
The youth is given a pistol of their own, and the family line is told over it.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
A feast of yam and palm wine is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the folded cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Asking of Tiwakopuditi
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of palm wine is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: talking drums and call-and-response chorus plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses of Torufanopi
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The couple bow to the ancestor shrine so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring kola nuts and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A feast of yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: All wear wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Kodidose Closing of the Door
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Weight of the Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
Families gather at the ancestor shrine to tell stories of those who have gone.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a folded letter placed under a stone
kola nuts left at the grave
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: The oldest tells the dead the year's news at the grave, in full.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: kola nuts
the first cup of palm wine poured on the ground
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the folded cap
festivals.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange kola nuts and promises for the season.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: a pour of palm wine on the doorstep
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the eldest of each of the families involved

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The kin of the dead may take the blood-money or the blood.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The first blow decides who is at fault. The offender's kin pay the weregild, and the whole line is bound to peace.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Informers share a quarter of the seized goods. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is land and name, and it belongs to the line, not to the person who holds it.

greet: Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
farewell: The Engineer keep your gears turning.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
Mind the soot, {name}.
thanks: I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
apology: I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
agree: Sound as a brass bolt.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
refuse: Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
