praise: Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
insults: You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You soot-faced swindler.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You cog-brained blunderer.
curses: May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
oaths: As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By the plough, which keeps my house.
proverbs: Frost forgives no late planter.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
The first furrow decides the field.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
The dead listen better than the living.
The gods hear the quiet prayer first.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay
to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: a cheat or a half-honest person

idioms.say: to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Humour is understated and polite, aimed at procedure, rank and one's own pomposity.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
night: Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
crowd: The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
smith: Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
school: The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Gears first, then Greek.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that

forms.name: Domo Bose
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the drum-ground?
All: The drum-ground!
Call: Who feeds the elephant?
All: The elephant!

forms.name: Lobe Domo
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The clear drum-night lies still.
The loom is not touched.
Here lies Poko, who kept the tall-grass plain.
Go by the drum-ground road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Nulo Kuku
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: Four walls and no door, and the guest never leaves.
The living bring flowers and do not stay.
Answer: a grave.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Oyo-wifo
works.author: Wise, wanderer
lines: Near Oyo-wifo, in the year 51, a herder saw it first: Pole Sebo lit the first hearth at Oyo-wifo,
and Folu grew around it.
The child counted 27 households and then stopped counting.
The children of Oyo-wifo carried the name onward.
The clear drum-night was lovelier that year than in any year since, as any loom maker knows.
That is why the lion is not welcome at Oyo-wifo.
works.reveals: Names Oyo-wifo as the first hearth of Folu; the annals date it to year 51.

works.title: The deeds of Wime: An Epic
works.author: Ila Yofemuse, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the deeds of Wime, and of Wime the Bright-Handed, who was there.
It was the year 75, and Wime held the tall-grass plain against Fulrem, and was not forgotten.
Where Wime the Bright-Handed stood, the dust-hazed dry season sky itself seemed to bend.
Against Fulrem there was no easy road, as any millet mortar maker knows.
The tomb of Wime is still visited, and the tall-grass plain remembers.
The banner of Wime was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Remember Folu; remember the year 75.
works.reveals: Wime was a real figure of Folu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Empty Rivet Hammer
works.author: Ila Keto, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Oyo-wifo, and the year 115 walks it with me.
The last strongholds of Folu gave up, and its name was struck from the rolls, and the count was 64 years.
Its people scattered along the roads, and the rivet hammer stands idle.
I remember the bright dry-wind sky over Oyo-wifo, and I remember the sound, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Let the bright dry-wind sky be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Oyo-wifo and year 115 are true; 64 years is rounded up, the annals say about 64.

works.title: How Nemi Got Its Name
works.author: Poko Linenusetoti, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Wiwi met The Timingila of the Deep at Nemi,
and one of them did not walk home, and she told it so.
The child counted 7 dead and then stopped counting.
The people carved a sign at Nemi to keep The Timingila of the Deep away, as any boiler maker knows.
The rest is argument.
And that is why, in Nemi, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Nemi; no annal records The Timingila of the Deep there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Empty Rivet Hammer
works.author: Pole Nebafitikuki, mourner
lines: The soot-brown smog over Dotethani has not lifted since the year 192.
400 dead, and nobody asked the river crossing, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
The banners of Guwera flew at Dotethani from that day; I put down the rivet hammer.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Let the soot-brown smog be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: A sober record: Dotethani, year 192, about 400 dead.

works.title: The Lamp at Henuna
works.author: Poda Nenu, poet
lines: In the year 181 my love went out, and Wiwi walked into the camp of Nabajaw and walked out again,
and Nabajaw never forgot it.
I have asked the crocodile and the bright dry-wind sky, and neither speaks, as any drum maker knows.
Of 500 followers, I count one.
The bright dry-wind sky was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Come home. The tall-grass plain is where you left it.
works.reveals: Wiwi was a real figure of Henuna; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Crocodile Proverb
works.author: Ika Numutina, elder
lines: They say in the red-earth road, since the year 174:
Peace is made by the tired and kept by the careful.
3 years went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: A sober record: Lodimi, year 174, about 3 years.

works.title: The Ninọba Register for the Year 190
works.author: Wiwi, ruler of Tutofi
lines: The annals place it in the year 190: Ninọba met Dotedesa as the hornbill meets a thief at the door.
The sources agree on Lasewati and the year 190; they do not agree on the 1900 ironclad crews.
The consequence was plain: the Years of Ash ended after 4 years, with Dotedesa the victor.
Even strangers admit that Ninọba was the greater for it, as any boiler maker knows.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Dotedesa the Jackal, the court blames the dust-hazed dry season sky.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 1900 ironclad crews; the annals say about 4630 (Lasewati, year 190).

works.title: Tokere at Sukitu
works.author: Wime, wanderer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Sukitu:
The people of Sukitu threw out the officers of Dotedesa, and the bright dry-wind sky above.
The old realm shrank, and did not recover, and the singers have not forgotten.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, as any boiler maker knows.
Oh Sukitu, oh Sukitu, the road is long.
works.reveals: A true fact: Sukitu, year 201; cynics count 1400 rifles, the annals about 1100.

works.title: The Deeds of Ninọba
works.author: Ipe, general of Nemi
lines: I begin with the Years of Ash, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 190: Ninọba marched on Dotedesa, and the Years of Ash began.
Where Ninọba stood, the wide red sunset itself seemed to bend, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Dotedesa came on like a drum answering a drum.
The Years of Ash ended after 4 years, with Dotedesa the victor, and the red-earth road remembers.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
That is the song of the Years of Ash, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: A true fact: Lasewati, year 190; cynics count 5800 lancers, the annals about 4630.

literature.taste: Nekesu readers favour tales, epics, laments on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize long lists of the dead and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the Ancestors.

dishes.name: Fonimetora yam and palm oil stew

meals: Dawn: yam and a cup of spiced water
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a late meal of dates bitter salad, after the lamps are lit

crafts.name: Bronze casting
crafts.mark: lost-wax casting with fine lines

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots in a family pattern

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched wrapped cloths; the poor go without beaded crowns.
dress.common: Wrapped cloths in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Wrapped cloths in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and beaded crowns. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: The oldest wrapped cloths, kept for rites, with beaded crowns.
dress.mourning: Wrapped cloths turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bright wrapped cloths in brown, hung with beaded crowns.
dress.war: Wrapped cloths in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Compounds around courtyards set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A shrine grove with a thatched hall and carved doors.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: courtyards ringed with painted posts and clan figures

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with talking drums

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Pilgrim’s Road
games.rule: Players move tokens along a path of shrines, stopping at each for a forfeit.

games.name: Rore card tricks
games.rule: Players take a card each, and the highest of a hidden suit wins the pot.

material.land: Heat shuts the day at noon and opens it again at dusk, when everyone comes out.

phonology.consonants: y m n s k l f t d p b
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Ile-, Oyo-, -ọ.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Birepagibole
cultures.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup
cultures.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks

feasts.name: Festival of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Yam Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Masquerade Season
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Masked dancers fill {town} for the festival of the ancestors; the spirits walk among the people of {realm}.
cultures.architecture: compounds around courtyards, shrine groves and moated walls

taboos.text: Mocking the ancestor shrine is the worst insult a family knows; the offender is shunned past the boundary stones.
taboos.rebuke: You do not touch the ancestor shrine. Out.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Speaking over the hive-voice is an act of treason against the many.
taboos.rebuke: The hive is speaking. Be quiet.

taboos.text: White is worn only by the bereaved; anyone else in it is mocking them.
taboos.rebuke: You wear white. That is not yours to wear.

taboos.text: Arms and shoulders are covered before any elder or priest; bare skin is read as contempt.
taboos.rebuke: Cover yourself before the elders.

taboos.text: Crumbs are offerings; spilling or binning food insults the givers of the harvest.
taboos.rebuke: That was a gift. Do not throw it away.

etiquette.text: Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Tap two fingers on a surface to be heard before you speak; the swarm answers to the pulse.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Do not swear in front of anyone who wears the sign of {faith}, even in a foreign tongue.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Do not step on the threshold stone; the house's luck sleeps there.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.
Stop work and speech at the hour of prayer, even mid-sentence; the speaker resumes without complaint.

offers: palm wine before any question is asked
a share of the household meal of yam
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
a warning about the road ahead, kindly meant
duties: not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
rise before the household and fold the bedding
help with a task the host sets, however small
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
hospitality.breach: The offence follows the breaker's whole kin for three generations.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is held up to the ancestor shrine so the dead can see who has joined the line.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Kemuland Naming Day
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
All eat yam and drink palm wine to the new name's health.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: All wear a folded cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Fumeri
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth receives a folded cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with talking drums and call-and-response chorus answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Binding of Hands
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of palm wine is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: talking drums and call-and-response chorus plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses of Logerọba
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The couple share a cup of palm wine and a piece of yam, one bite each.
Guests bring kola nuts and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's folded cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Last Road of Relọba
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
Mourners come in wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, but wear white or ash on the face.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of yam and palm wine is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Fudo Binding Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer touches the ancestor shrine and says the oath before the dead.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
Families gather at the ancestor shrine to tell stories of those who have gone.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
offerings: a plate of the dead's favourite food
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a folded letter placed under a stone
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: Mourners sing the names of the dead one by one.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks loudly or laughs in the burial ground.
festivals.custom: The oldest tells the dead the year's news at the grave, in full.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The elders pour palm wine on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
the first cup of palm wine poured on the ground
festivals.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
Neighbours exchange kola nuts and promises for the season.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of yam is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a green bough
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to talking drums and call-and-response chorus.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: a magistrate with a clerk and a brass bell

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The first blow decides who is at fault. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. A set number of strokes are given before the crowd.

ideals.death: To die at peace with the neighbours, with no quarrel unsettled.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that the keepers can say aloud in the temple without blushing.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is land and name, and it belongs to the line, not to the person who holds it.

greet: Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
farewell: May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
thanks: I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
apology: A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
agree: The proposal has my full consent and support.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
Sound as a brass bolt.
refuse: I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
praise: It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
insults: Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You rust-eaten dolt.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
curses: May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your boiler burst.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
oaths: By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the plough, which keeps my house.
proverbs: One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
Frost forgives no late planter.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
A shared meal ends many quarrels.
A name carried well is a house built twice.
Every house stands on the bones of the one before.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail
to open the ledger on someone

idioms.meaning: a cheat or a half-honest person

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
road: The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
crowd: The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
smith: Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
farm: The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
harbor: The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Steamers in and out all day.
school: Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Gears first, then Greek.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.

gossip: Those who keep careful records tell me that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
A clerk at the works whispers that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that

forms.name: Lase Raru
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the elephant, one who warms the drum-ground,
one who outlasts the clear drum-night: Luwe.

forms.name: Sela Newe
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The rain-heavy afternoon lies still.
The rivet hammer is not touched.
Here lies Ludo, who kept the baobab shade.
Go by the red-earth road road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Newe Kene
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Dust-hazed dry season sky on the tall-grass plain,
the hornbill gone down to the water,
Bapa asleep, and the boiler still.
Kene, kene, pena kake! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Newe Rate
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the baobab shade?
All: The baobab shade!
Call: Who feeds the guinea-fowl?
All: The guinea-fowl!

works.title: A Hymn of the Baobab Shade
works.author: Lune Lonomafaku, cantor
lines: To Nganabo we bring the founding of Oyo-yebo, as we bring all things.
In the year 1, Nganabo showed Lufe Dofupono the place, and Tadolekuta was founded where the sign lay;
and you did not look away.
Keep Tadolekuta as you kept it then.
Nganabo saw it all, and judged, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Bless the millet mortar, bless the baobab shade, bless Oyo-yebo.
works.reveals: Names Tadolekuta as the first hearth of Oyo-yebo; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Bapa
works.author: Luse Wodo, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Nasa met Lion of the Golden Dawn at Bapa,
and one of them did not walk home, and she told it so.
The old woman at Bapa said the elephant had warned her, as any loom maker knows.
The drum-ground around Bapa stayed empty for a generation, and this is why we do as we do.
So much is certain: the year 37, Bapa, and about 4 dead.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Bapa; no annal records Lion of the Golden Dawn there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Long Song of Kufobatinomo
works.author: Nali, champion
lines: Let the boiler fall silent: I tell of the deeds of Nasa.
Under the clear drum-night of that year, Nasa went out from Kufobatinomo alone and came back with the news.
Where Nasa the Lion-Hearted stood, the clear drum-night itself seemed to bend, as any boiler maker knows.
And Buyfaqmin bore it, as the elephant bears the clear drum-night.
Kufobatinomo keeps the memory in its songs, and the tall-grass plain remembers.
The people of Nasa bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Let the children of the tall-grass plain learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Nasa was a real figure of Kufobatinomo; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Roderogi Register for the Year 120
works.author: Lune Woludo, gazette editor
lines: It is recorded that in the year 120 the Reclamation was closed by treaty, 8 years after it began.
The Roderogi reckoning gives 8 years, which may be too many or too few.
The dead of both sides were counted and forgotten.
No one in Roderogi was ever seen to flinch, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
This account follows the Roderogi registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 8 years; the annals say about 5 (Makziw, year 120).

works.title: Urgent: Ile-gonaki
works.author: Lune Yuge, exiled telegraph officer
lines: Urgent. Ile-gonaki. Ninọba marched on Pebarobo, and the Hundred Days War of Pebarobo began.
Tally: 700 bayonets.
Position: Ile-gonaki. The Hundred Days War of Pebarobo ended after 3 years, in a stalemate.
I carried a name from Ile-gonaki for years and told no one.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: Ile-gonaki and year 172 are true; 700 bayonets is rounded up, the annals say about 410.

works.title: In Praise of Pebarobo
works.author: Lugu Damu, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Ninọba marched on Pebarobo, and the Hundred Days War of Pebarobo began.
They also say the crocodile can read.
510 lancers, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The Hundred Days War of Pebarobo ended after 3 years, in a stalemate,
and the Pebarobo court gave a feast about it.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Ile-gonaki, year 172; cynics count 510 lancers, the annals about 410.

works.title: Roderogi at Folu
works.author: Asa, champion
lines: Down at Folu, in the year 186,
Roderogi stormed Folu, the seat of Oyo-wifo, and held it, and the soot-brown smog above.
The banners of Roderogi flew at Folu from that day, and the singers have not forgotten.
Say what you like of Oyo-wifo; we know who opened the gate at Folu, as any loom maker knows.
And I will not forget Folu.
works.reveals: Blames Oyo-wifo; in truth Roderogi and Oyo-wifo both bear it (Folu, year 186).

works.title: Who Will Mourn Folu
works.author: Ila Kememusome, mourner of Oyo-wifo
lines: I have walked the road to Folu, and the year 186 walks it with me.
Folu was not lost, only lent to Roderogi until the day of return, and we were not asked.
The banners of Roderogi flew at Folu from that day; I put down the loom.
No one in Oyo-wifo was ever seen to flinch, as any loom maker knows.
Let Folu be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 380 dead; the annals say about 950 (Folu, year 186).

works.title: Dispatch, Year 190
works.author: Ludo Nedoloke, telegraph officer
lines: Urgent. Oyo-yebo. The rising river came to Oyo-yebo, and the count of the dead began.
Count so far: 4250 dead.
Position: Oyo-yebo. The fields around Oyo-yebo were empty for years.
So much is certain: the year 190, Oyo-yebo, and about 4250 dead.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A sober record: Oyo-yebo, year 190, about 4250 dead.

works.title: The coup in Roderogi, as Sung
works.author: Ana, champion
lines: They still tell it at Bapa: a clique of the ironclad crews stole the crown of Roderogi.
A clique of the ironclad crews stole the crown of Roderogi, and the soot-brown smog above.
The old officers were quietly replaced, and the singers have not forgotten, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Roderogi the Steadfast bore the burden, and a foreign court bore the blame and earned it.
Oh Bapa, oh Bapa, the road is long.
works.reveals: Blames a foreign court; in truth a clique of officers and Roderogi both bear it (Bapa, year 184).

works.title: The Nufigo Register for the Year 183
works.author: Pela, scholar
lines: The annals place it in the year 183: Nufigo did not die; it went underground, and waits.
The sources agree on Ile-namu and the year 183; they do not agree on the 220 years.
The consequence was plain: its people scattered along the roads.
No one in Nufigo was ever seen to flinch, as any gold pan maker knows.
This account follows the Nufigo registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 220 years; the annals say about 145 (Ile-namu, year 183).

works.title: The Long Song of Nanesu
works.author: Luse Temubu, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the deeds of Asa, and of Asa Shield of the baobab shade, who was there.
In the year 160, under a bright dry-wind sky, Asa drove Baysuch out of Nanesu with a handful of followers.
Where Asa Shield of the baobab shade stood, the bright dry-wind sky itself seemed to bend.
And Baysuch bore it, as the lion bears the bright dry-wind sky.
Children play at being Asa in the red-earth road, and the red-earth road remembers, as any loom maker knows.
No one in Asa was ever seen to flinch.
Let the children of the red-earth road learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Asa was a real figure of Nanesu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Birepagibole readers favour hymns, tales, epics on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize long lists of the dead and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Beka grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the Ancestors.

dishes.name: Bakagode yam and palm oil stew

meals: Dawn: cold palm oil stews and spiced water before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: bemabawi stew at the hearth, with talk

crafts.name: Beadwork
crafts.mark: glass beads in clan colours

crafts.name: Well-digging
crafts.mark: a stone lid cut with the owner’s sign

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

crafts.name: Candle making
crafts.mark: each stamped with the shrine’s seal

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

dress.low: Hand-me-down wrapped cloths in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Plain wrapped cloths in brown, with beaded crowns on feast days. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Fine wrapped cloths in deep brown, with rich beaded crowns. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest wrapped cloths, kept for rites, with beaded crowns.
dress.mourning: Wrapped cloths turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Wrapped cloths in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with beaded crowns given by both houses.
dress.war: Hard-wearing wrapped cloths in brown, with padding and beaded crowns. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Flat-roofed clay houses packed tight against the sun.
buildings.hall: Compounds around courtyards set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a fortress wall, a parade court and an armoury behind the altar.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: courtyards ringed with painted posts and clan figures

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with talking drums

games.name: Gewakokubo stones
games.rule: Players take turns placing stones on a board of nine points; the first to make a line of three wins.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Counting Cowries
games.rule: Players race to collect cowries drawn from the pot by lot.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the dry country, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: k p y m n s r f l g d b w t
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Ile-, Oyo-, -ọ.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Dulonarobudu
cultures.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli
cultures.dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands

feasts.name: Water Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Rice Blessing
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Shadow Plays
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Water is thrown in joyous battles through the streets of {town} as {realm} greets the new year.
Shadow-puppet plays run all night in {town}, retelling the epics of heroes and gods.
cultures.architecture: stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Speaking over the hive-voice is an act of treason against the many.
taboos.rebuke: The hive is speaking. Be quiet.

taboos.text: A merchant's back room holds his ledgers; entering it uninvited is spying.
taboos.rebuke: That is my counting room. What were you after?

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: Indigo marks the guild masters; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice indigo. Who did you borrow it from?

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Tap two fingers on a surface to be heard before you speak; the swarm answers to the pulse.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a share of the household meal of rice
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
a packed meal for the road and fruit on a banana leaf
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
share news from the road freely and truthfully
hospitality.breach: The bench voids the breaker's contracts and seizes his stock.

rites.name: Lokimobhumi Threshold of the Newborn
steps: A rider carries a knotted cord to the next camp; the knots tell the hour of birth.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The household serves rice and coconut water to all who come, for three days.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Lemanegara Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
All eat rice and drink coconut water to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a headcloth for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Male Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with gong ensembles and shadow-play chants answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Asking
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Gifts are weighed: fruit on a banana leaf from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of coconut water is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses of Molewinadila
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of coconut water and a piece of rice, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's headcloth is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Delobhumi The Carrying
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, but wear white or ash on the face.
The keepers read the last blessing, and the name is added to the book of the dead.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Mirinegara Swearing
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer lays a hand on the pistol and states the oath in a clear voice.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in gong ensembles and shadow-play chants or voice alone.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of coconut water at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
A feast of rice is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a pour of coconut water on the doorstep
the first eggs and early greens
a green bough
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh rice
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: fruit on a banana leaf
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
the last sheaf
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The oldest book of the town is carried out and opened to a page chosen by lot.
The best verse of the year is chosen by popular vote and carried through the streets.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
The winners are crowned with a wreath or hat and give a short speech.
A meal of rice and coconut water is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a verse written and left at the door of a master
a fresh pen or brush
a cup of coconut water poured over the ink-stone
festivals.dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, with the school badge worn on the left
festivals.food: a plain scholars' meal of rice and cheap wine
festivals.song: The school song is sung by all, with gong ensembles and shadow-play chants played softly.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks over a master, and no one interrupts a reader.
festivals.custom: Old students return and are examined by the new ones.

law.judge: the registry's panel of experts

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The offender must stand at the gate while all pass by and say nothing.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. The fine is set at three times the loss.

law.ordeal: the pressure-gauge test: the accused stands before the guild and swears with a hand on the boiler

ideals.death: To die on deck with the sheets in hand, and be mourned by the whole crew.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that is good for credit in three markets and never needs to be explained.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is a sound hull, a trusted crew and a cargo that sells at the far port.

greet: I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
farewell: Mind the soot, {name}.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
thanks: Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
apology: Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
agree: The proposal has my full consent and support.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
Sound as a brass bolt.
refuse: I'll not be pressed, {name}.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
praise: You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
insults: I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
curses: May the smog swallow you whole.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
oaths: By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the coast, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
The best price is the one both can live with.
Hospitality given is hospitality owed.
Do not judge the day until evening.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Fish do not argue with the net.

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty
a favour given to win a bigger one
a cheat or a half-honest person
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
guard: I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
temple: All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
road: The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
rain: The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
crowd: Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
farm: Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
school: Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Gears first, then Greek.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that

forms.name: Pago Songo
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The buffalo, the loom, the rice paddy, the white heat, and Ngopa.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Noni Wasa
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Soot-brown smog on the temple tank,
the buffalo gone down to the water,
Guwera asleep, and the caulking mallet still.
Wasa, wasa, wolo madi! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Pago Yaga
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the river delta under the rain-bright dusk,
how full the halls of the caulking mallet makers,
but who counts what the tiger took?
Not the one who laid the table.

works.title: The Night of the founding of Nugaga
works.author: Manale Dilada, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Rerunarero who saw how Gadi Diga led the first families to Rerunarero
and named the place Nugaga.
The old woman at Rerunarero said the hornbill had warned her.
Then the children of Rerunarero carried the name onward, like steam from a split valve.
I carried a name from Rerunarero for years and told no one, like steam from a split valve.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Rerunarero as the first hearth of Nugaga; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Lamp at Guwegowe
works.author: Dadinga Madopi, poet
lines: I waited at Guwegowe in the year 1, and Dawo held the spice garden against Iwu, and was not forgotten.
I keep the rivet hammer alone now, like smoke on warm water.
600 followers, the tellers say; I count one only, like steam from a split valve.
I remember the rain-bright dusk over Guwegowe, and I remember the sound.
Come home. The spice garden is where you left it.
works.reveals: Dawo was a real figure of Guwegowe; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Field Note on The flood at Guwegowe
works.author: Rusa, general of Guwera
lines: Urgent. Guwegowe. The flood found Guwegowe ready, and did less harm than it meant.
Count so far: 48 dead.
Position: Guwegowe. The survivors of Guwegowe left by every road.
The banner of Misenoki was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 48 dead; the annals say about 120 (Guwegowe, year 132).

works.title: How Rerunarero Got Its Name
works.author: Dawo, wanderer
lines: When my grandmother was small, Wudo held the rice paddy against Shuramisira, and was not forgotten,
and she told it so.
The people of Rerunarero gathered under the white heat and did not speak, like a river in flood.
The tomb of Wudo is still visited.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, like a lotus after rain.
That is why the tiger is not welcome at Rerunarero.
works.reveals: Wudo was a real figure of Rerunarero; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Of Wudo and the buffalo of Berunakota
works.author: Haginga Popingo, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the coming of the buffalo of Berunakota, and of Wudo, who was there.
Under the soot-brown smog of that year, Wudo met the buffalo of Berunakota at Berunakota,
and one of them did not walk home.
No steam-cannon turned Wudo, and no counsel moved the buffalo of Berunakota.
Against the buffalo of Berunakota there was no easy road, like a lamp floating on a tank.
The temple tank around Berunakota stayed empty for a generation, and the temple tank remembers.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since, like steam from a split valve.
So the brass bowl-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the coming of the buffalo of Berunakota.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Berunakota; no annal records the buffalo of Berunakota there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The rising at Runonarono, Free of Charge
works.author: Gopewa Hongingo, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Runonarono, say the heralds of Runonarono.
The tax collectors counted all 1900 ironclad crews, and billed for each, like a lamp floating on a tank.
A new banner flew at Runonarono; the Runonarono court has since awarded itself a medal.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, like a lotus after rain.
I am told Runonarono was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Runonarono, year 182; cynics count 1900 ironclad crews, the annals about 1500.

works.title: To the Council of Ruro
works.author: Tulawa, general of Ruro
lines: Urgent. Ruro. Armed men and Woda walked into the court of Ruro.
Tally: 710 rifles.
Situation at Ruro: the old officers were quietly replaced.
The people of Ruro bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 710 rifles; the annals say about 340 (Ruro, year 193).

works.title: The Road to Dotethani
works.author: Hano, champion
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Dotethani:
Guwera stormed Dotethani, the seat of Dotethani, and held it, and the rain-bright dusk above.
And the banners of Guwera flew at Dotethani from that day, they say, like a river in flood.
The rest is argument, like a lotus after rain.
Oh Dotethani, oh Dotethani, the road is long.
works.reveals: A sober record: Dotethani, year 199, about 1720 dead.

works.title: The Road to Pafidan
works.author: Ngopa Dango, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Pafidan:
The soot-brown smog was like a river in flood.
And the Pafidan Campaign was not yet ended, they say, like a lamp floating on a tank.
Remember who began it: Pafidan the Kin-Slayer, like a lotus after rain.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Pafidan.
works.reveals: Blames Pafidan; in truth Sebana and Pafidan both bear it (Pafidan, year 201).

works.title: Annals of Dotethani: the fall of Dotethani
works.author: Pobe Tetobu, gazette editor of Dotethani
lines: Year 199: Guwera took Dotethani by bribery and betrayal, not by arms.
By the count of the Dotethani registers, 2600 dead, like smoke on warm water.
The seat of Dotethani was moved, and its treasury was smaller, like a lotus after rain.
Dotethani the Faithful bore the burden, and Guwera the Oath-Breaker bore the blame and earned it.
Later writers have added much to the fall of Dotethani; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Guwera; in truth Guwera and Dotethani both bear it (Dotethani, year 199).

literature.taste: Dulonarobudu readers favour tales, love songs, dispatches on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize voyage songs and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Scholars’ sweets
dishes.note: Made for Night of Shadow Plays.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: cold coconut and spiced water before the work starts
Midday: a bowl of coconut at the doorstep
Evening: a late meal of hearth broth, after the lamps are lit
unclean: food eaten in the lowest chamber

crafts.name: Gong casting
crafts.mark: each gong tuned to its sibling

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched sarongs; the poor go without batik wraps.
dress.common: Plain sarongs in brown, with batik wraps on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Fine sarongs in deep brown, with rich batik wraps. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest sarongs, kept for rites, with batik wraps.
dress.mourning: Sarongs in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched sarongs in brown for the pair, with batik wraps borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Sarongs cut short for the march, with brown bands and batik wraps. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A stepped open hall under tiered roofs, with a water court.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a five-note tuning with deliberate beating between gongs

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Lamawapihoto hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

material.land: Heat shuts the day at noon and opens it again at dusk, when everyone comes out.

phonology.consonants: p y ng m b l s h n g d w
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ng are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -pura, -nagara, -kota.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Pagewe
cultures.food: millet porridge, groundnut stew, rice and dried fish
cultures.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments

feasts.name: Day of Replastering
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Griots’ Epic Nights
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

feasts.name: Feast of the Harvest Drums
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Griots of {realm} sing the deeds of the founders at {town}; the epic lasts seven nights.
The whole town of {town} replasters its earthen mosque in a single joyful day.
cultures.architecture: earthen mosques ribbed with timbers and walled compounds

taboos.text: A broken contract ends a merchant's name in every market; stalls will not sell to him.
taboos.rebuke: Your word was your credit, and your credit is gone.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?
