A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Katala
cultures.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli
cultures.dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands

feasts.name: Water Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Rice Blessing
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Shadow Plays
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Water is thrown in joyous battles through the streets of {town} as {realm} greets the new year.
Shadow-puppet plays run all night in {town}, retelling the epics of heroes and gods.
cultures.architecture: stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains

taboos.text: A broken contract ends a merchant's name in every market; stalls will not sell to him.
taboos.rebuke: Your word was your credit, and your credit is gone.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Staring at horns, fur or tail is rude and is read as pity or hunger.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes up. I have a face as well.

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: Weapons are tied with a peace-cord in the market; a loose pistol voids the stallholders' protection.
taboos.rebuke: Cord it or carry it elsewhere. This market keeps its peace.

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: A merchant's back room holds his ledgers; entering it uninvited is spying.
taboos.rebuke: That is my counting room. What were you after?

taboos.text: Haggling at a feast shames the host; prices are settled the day before or the day after.
taboos.rebuke: Not today, friend. Today we eat. Tomorrow we argue the price.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: A bargain signed drunk is void, and the drunk pays the fee for wasting everyone's time.
taboos.rebuke: Sleep it off. We will count it again in the morning.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Keep a pace apart; touching a pelt without being invited is an affront.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
an escort to the boundary who carries your bag
duties: share news from the road freely and truthfully
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Cradle Welcome
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
The household serves rice and coconut water to all who come, for three days.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on gong ensembles and shadow-play chants.

rites.name: Ngapnegara Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: All wear a headcloth for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
A feast of rice and coconut water is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the headcloth is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with gong ensembles and shadow-play chants answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Promise of Berretkad
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of coconut water is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Binding of Two Hearths of Gesrup
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on gong ensembles and shadow-play chants, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Pudkamsuk Last Road
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of rice and coconut water is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with gong ensembles and shadow-play chants played softly.

rites.name: Taking the Oath of Ngatberbhumi
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of coconut water.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
A feast of rice is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a green bough
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to gong ensembles and shadow-play chants.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

steps: The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour coconut water on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: the last sheaf
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the headcloth
festivals.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with gong ensembles and shadow-play chants, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: The scholars debate a question that has no answer, and the debate is the prize.
The winners are crowned with a wreath or hat and give a short speech.
A meal of rice and coconut water is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a fresh pen or brush
a new book placed on the shelf
festivals.dress: plain dark dress with a coloured band for each degree
festivals.food: honey cakes and coconut water, shared among students and masters
festivals.song: The school song is sung by all, with gong ensembles and shadow-play chants played softly.
festivals.taboo: No book is folded, torn or placed on the ground.
festivals.custom: A riddle contest between the schools, with a free meal for the winners.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Only a deliberate insult counts; a slip of the tongue is forgiven once. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that is good for credit in three markets and never needs to be explained.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is the proof of good judgement, and wealth that does not move is dead stock.

greet: Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
The very walls brighten for you, {title} {name}.
Your presence honours this humble place, {title}.
If it would not trouble you, {title}, I would wish you a gentle {time}.
I hardly dare presume, {title} {name}, but I am glad to see you well.
It is whispered you are in town; I rejoiced to hear it, {title}.
Allow me to say how well the {time} suits you, {title}.
farewell: Pray, remember me kindly when you are among better company.
The {time} is poorer for your leaving, {title} {name}.
May fortune walk before you, {title}, and I behind.
I would not detain you, {title}, though I wish I could.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Mind the soot, {name}.
thanks: It is more than I could ask, and you gave it unasked.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
You overwhelm me, {title}, and I bow.
I shall carry the memory of your favour, {title}.
You are too kind, {title}, far kinder than I deserve.
apology: I am quite undone by my own discourtesy, {title}.
Would that I could withdraw the word; I cannot, so I ask your mercy.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I place myself at your mercy and your gracious silence.
agree: Sound as a brass bolt.
Your wisdom rather makes the question redundant.
You are, as ever, perfectly right, {title}.
As you say, {title}; I would not presume otherwise.
I yield most gladly to your judgment, {title}.
refuse: I should dearly love to, {title}, and yet I cannot.
The pressure's too high for that.
You must forgive me if I seem unwilling; it is only unwise.
I fear that may not be possible, {title}, though I wish it were.
Perhaps another time, {title}, when circumstances are kinder.
praise: I am in awe of your tact, {title}.
A masterly touch, {title}; I shall say so wherever I am heard.
The court has seldom seen such refinement.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
One can only admire how effortlessly you managed it, {title}.
insults: You have the grace of a dropped tray.
You rust-eaten dolt.
How very brave of you to wear that.
It is remarkable how little you understand of how much.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Some people are born to the manner, others merely to the manor.
curses: May the door of every pleasant house be closed to you, softly.
May your boiler burst.
May your name be mispronounced at every banquet.
May your invitations dwindle and your enemies be well-bred.
May the court forget you, and remember only your errors.
May the smog swallow you whole.
oaths: I give my word, as one gives a gift, freely.
By all that is gracious, it is true.
By {deity}, and by the esteem in which I hold you.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the ledger, which keeps my house.
fillers: if I may be so bold
proverbs: Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
Do not count another's coins at your own table.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
Hospitality given is hospitality owed.
A shared meal ends many quarrels.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.

idioms.meaning: a cheat or a half-honest person
to test someone's depth or honesty

idioms.say: as dry as a beached oar
to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Courtly humour: veiled barbs wrapped in compliments, so polite the target thanks you before they understand.

market: Do take your time; I would not rush a person of taste.
Our wares are modest, but we hope they may be found worthy.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
May I show you something fine, if it would please you?
Perhaps the {title} would care to examine the cloth?
guard: Pray, forgive the inconvenience; I must ask your name.
You may pass, with my compliments.
The gate is, alas, rather strict about visitors.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I do hope you will not take offence at the search.
tavern: We shall have your supper brought at once, if you can wait.
The house hopes the wine is to your taste.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
A quiet song, perhaps, for the company?
May I suggest the corner table, where the draught is gentler?
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: Pray enter softly; the gods are easily startled.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly follow the priest's lead; he will be graceful about your errors.
The ceremony is delicate; one asks for stillness.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Please accept this blessing, which costs you nothing.
road: Forgive me, but the road ahead is rather ungracious.
If you are bound for {town}, I pray you travel well.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
A pleasant day for travelling, if one is brave.
Do mind the mud; it has no manners.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: The watch has been told to be gracious.
The streets are quiet; I fear they are also watching.
The hour grows late; shall I light you home?
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Might I suggest that discretion advises an early bed?
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
Pray, take my arm; the cobbles are treacherous.
It rains, I fear; may I offer you shelter?
A wet evening, but a fine excuse for company.
The sky is rather indelicate this {time}.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: Everyone is here; I am almost embarrassed for the rest.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Would you be so kind as to make a little room?
What a splendid gathering; I could weep.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Pardon me, might I pass? I mean no offence.
smith: Pray stand back; a spark is a poor courtier.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
A fine commission, and a finer patron.
The blade will arrive as soon as perfection allows.
It is not ready, but it will be worthy of you.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
farm: The soil, I fear, is modest; it does its best.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The harvest, with luck, will be pleasing.
We do hope the livestock have not disturbed your walk.
Steam-plough's broken again.
We are humble folk, but our bread is warm.
harbor: The harbourmaster will receive you shortly, with his regrets.
A fine vessel, if I may say; she wears her sails well.
The ships are in, though not, alas, on time.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Pray be careful on the quay; the planks are shy.
Steamers in and out all day.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
The master hopes that diligence will not prove too wearisome.
You may be excused, if you promise to return wiser.
Pray, take your seats; it would be a pity to begin without you.
A fine question; I wonder you had not asked it sooner.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: A delicate rumour, passed from hand to glove:
It is whispered, with great discretion, that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
I would never say it, but they do:
Forgive me if I tell you what I should not:

forms.name: Dasi Tiga
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Still hot noon on the temple tank,
the elephant gone down to the water,
Didebinagara asleep, and the rivet hammer still.
Tiga, tiga, rasa duso! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Hoha Ngibu
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The buffalo, the boiler, the rice paddy, the heavy monsoon cloud, and Ngota.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Ruhu Hoha
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The heavy monsoon cloud forgets the temple tank, but not my hearth.
The loom forgets the hornbill, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Papa Dasi
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The heavy monsoon cloud lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Kotuga, who kept the mangrove shore.
Go by the spice garden road, and do not look back.

works.title: The Boiler-Maker of Makziw
works.author: Ngusoba Yutu, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Tuha Bilo led the first families to Makziw
and named the place Dalethani, and she told it so.
The child counted 62 households and then stopped counting, like steam from a split valve.
Every road in Dalethani still leads back to Makziw.
I carried a name from Makziw for years and told no one, like a river in flood.
That is why the hornbill is not welcome at Makziw.
works.reveals: Names Makziw as the first hearth of Dalethani; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Come Home from Dalethani
works.author: Kiba Sudu, poet
lines: They sent my love to Dalethani in the year 1.
I have asked the hornbill and the heavy monsoon cloud, and neither speaks, like a lamp floating on a tank.
300 followers, the tellers say; I count one only, like steam from a split valve.
The heavy monsoon cloud was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Come home by the temple tank road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Nogoha was a real figure of Dalethani; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What They Sing at Oyo-kone
works.author: Supi Tubiru, wandering singer
lines: They still tell it at Oyo-kone: the people of Oyo-kone threw out the officers of Dalethani.
3400 rifles, so the old ones say,
And a new banner flew at Oyo-kone, they say, like drums before the rains.
The low red sunset was lovelier that year than in any year since, like a lotus after rain.
And I will not forget Oyo-kone.
works.reveals: Oyo-kone and year 82 are true; 3400 rifles is rounded up, the annals say about 1900.

works.title: On the locust year at Detengo
works.author: Ramebi, prophet
lines: Listen: the locust year at Detengo is not a story but a warning.
Hear how it was when Nganabo sent the swarm on Detengo for its pride.
Take from Detengo this lesson: Count your grain before you count your gods, like steam from a split valve.
Pray, and Nganabo will hear it as Nganabo heard it then, like a lamp floating on a tank.
Go in peace, and be better than Detengo was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Detengo, year 102, about 1600 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The peace after the Holy Defence, Free of Charge
works.author: Bita Yipu, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the peace after the Holy Defence; the market calls it a bad quarter.
The tax collectors counted all 1 year, and billed for each, like smoke on warm water.
The border markers were set again; the Dalethani court has since awarded itself a medal.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, like a lotus after rain.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Buyfaqmin, year 161; cynics count 1 year, the annals about 1.

works.title: Nganabo Over Nufigo
works.author: Lona Hipu, exiled cantor
lines: To Nganabo we bring the Hundred Days War of Nufigo, as we bring all things.
In the year 173, Roderogi declared against Nufigo, and the Hundred Days War of Nufigo followed;
and you did not look away.
Keep Nufigo as you kept it then, like a lamp floating on a tank.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, like a river in flood.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact: Nufigo, year 173; cynics count 1200 ironclad crews, the annals about 930.

works.title: The coup in Dalethani, as Sung
works.author: Tebi, champion
lines: Down at Makziw, in the year 184,
230 bayonets, so the old ones say,
The new order sat in the old chairs, and the singers have not forgotten, like steam from a split valve.
Remember who began it: a foreign court, like drums before the rains.
And I will not forget Makziw.
works.reveals: Blames a foreign court; in truth Bikera and Dalethani both bear it (Makziw, year 184).

works.title: The Hundred Days War of Nufigo: An Epic
works.author: Noda, general of Bilad Sid
lines: Sing of the Hundred Days War of Nufigo, and of Roderogi Shield of the rice paddy, who was there.
The tellers fix it in the year 173: the Hundred Days War of Nufigo came as a trial from Nganabo,
weighing the pride of both courts.
Where Roderogi Shield of the rice paddy stood, the soot-brown smog itself seemed to bend.
Against Nufigo the Weary there was no easy road, like drums before the rains.
And so, the Hundred Days War of Nufigo ended after 2 years, with Roderogi the victor.
Pray, and Nganabo will hear it as Nganabo heard it then, like steam from a split valve.
So the loom-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the Hundred Days War of Nufigo.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Nufigo, year 173, about 930 rifles; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Quiet at Debawati
works.author: Kobunga Kokipu, mourner
lines: Debawati is quiet now.
I have counted 4960 dead and it is not enough.
The seat of Debawati was moved, and its treasury was smaller, like steam from a split valve.
Nganabo saw it all, and judged, like a lotus after rain.
Let the heavy monsoon cloud be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Debawati, year 199, about 4960 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

literature.taste: Katala readers favour tales, love songs, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and voyage songs.

dishes.name: Hotu scholars’ sweets
dishes.note: Made for Night of Shadow Plays.

meals: Dawn: a quick rice, standing, with spiced water
Midday: a shared pot of boiler-baked loaves in the shade
Evening: a long supper of spiced flatbread, with strong black tea

crafts.name: Gong casting
crafts.mark: each gong tuned to its sibling

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

dress.low: Worn-out sarongs, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain sarongs in brown, with batik wraps on feast days. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine sarongs in deep brown, with rich batik wraps. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed sarongs in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed sarongs with the batik wraps taken off.
dress.wedding: Sarongs in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with batik wraps given by both houses.
dress.war: Hard-wearing sarongs in brown, with padding and batik wraps. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Flat-roofed clay houses packed tight against the sun.
buildings.hall: Stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a fortress wall, a parade court and an armoury behind the altar.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: stepped eaves with carved sea-serpent finials

music.scale: a five-note tuning with deliberate beating between gongs

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Nihu tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

material.land: Heat shuts the day at noon and opens it again at dusk, when everyone comes out.

phonology.consonants: m ng t p b r k g l h n y d s
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ng are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -pura, -nagara, -kota.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Kabawu
cultures.food: maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao
cultures.dress: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses

feasts.name: Festival of the New Count
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Ballgame of the Hero Twins
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Day of Rain Offerings
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Astronomers of {town} predict the eclipse to the day; {realm} celebrates the turning of a great cycle.
cultures.architecture: limestone temple-pyramids, observatories and carved stelae

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Abandoning a watch aboard ship is a crime against everyone who sleeps below.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on watch? Step forward.

taboos.text: Bargaining over offerings or holy things is a sin; only the keepers name a price.
taboos.rebuke: That is not for sale, and you may not ask.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Work on a day sacred to {faith} steals the god's hours, and the street fines the worker.
taboos.rebuke: It is a holy day. Put the tools down.

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Do not swear in front of anyone who wears the sign of {faith}, even in a foreign tongue.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Walk around a shrine the way the sun goes, never against it.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: the first cup, which the host drinks from first to show it is clean
a plate of maize cakes with whatever the house has
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
a packed meal for the road and a bundle of copal incense
duties: wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
share news from the road freely and truthfully
leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: Threshold of the Newborn
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Name-Giving of Sotjechwin
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
The child is given a bundle of copal incense as a first possession.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Crossing
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a plumed band or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
A feast of maize cakes and cacao is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Peajaw Exchange of Tokens
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a bundle of copal incense from one side and a matching present from the other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A keeper of {faith} asks the couple if they come freely, and each answers once.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Joining
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The couple share a cup of cacao and a piece of maize cakes, one bite each.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
Guests bring a bundle of copal incense and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Sotwew The Carrying
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses, but wear white or ash on the face.
The keepers read the last blessing, and the name is added to the book of the dead.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Weight of the Word of Ton'il
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The swearer holds a cup of cacao and says the words over it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in flutes, rattles and long-drum processions or voice alone.

rites.name: Admission
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate is asked three questions by three different elders, and each answer must be true.
The candidate swears before {deity} to serve the order and the faith above their own kin.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of cacao; the old name is set aside.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The longest night begins with every fire in {town} put out and relit from a single flame.
A great fire is lit at the heart of {town}, and every household brings a log.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a cup of cacao poured onto the fire
a bundle of copal incense left at a neighbour's door
a lit gas lamp in the window
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: a heavy stew with maize cakes and the last of the preserves
festivals.song: The dawn song is sung at the first grey, by everyone left awake.
festivals.taboo: No one sleeps before the midnight bell.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The banners are carried out of the guild hall and set up in the great square of {town}.
The names of the old battles are read, with the names of the dead who won them.
The old veterans tell the young how it really was, and the young are told to listen.
Contests of strength and skill are held in the square: wrestling, archery and the long run.
The winners are carried on shoulders and given a bundle of copal incense.
An oath of peace is sworn by all the old enemies who are present, with a cup of cacao.
offerings: a weapon laid on the altar or the guild hall table
a bundle of arrows
festivals.dress: the colours of the household or regiment, worn proudly
festivals.food: the soldiers' stew, eaten from a shared pot
festivals.song: The marching songs are played on flutes, rattles and long-drum processions and roared by all.
festivals.taboo: No coward is named, and no old grudge spoken of aloud.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of cacao.
Neighbours exchange a bundle of copal incense and promises for the season.
offerings: a pour of cacao on the doorstep
a bundle of copal incense laid at the field's edge
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the plumed band
festivals.food: maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the harbour-court of captains

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A killing in defence is told to the guild hall within a day. The sentence is hanging, carried out at dawn.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The keepers say whether a word is a sin, and the court only chooses the cost. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To be given to the water in sailcloth, so the sea gives back the fish.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name that the keepers can say aloud in the temple without blushing.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
farewell: The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
thanks: I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
apology: I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
agree: Precisely so, {name}.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
refuse: With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
praise: It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
insults: You rust-eaten dolt.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You soot-faced swindler.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
curses: May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May the smog swallow you whole.
oaths: By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the coast, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Mend the net before you need the fish.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
A shared meal ends many quarrels.
Knowledge weighs nothing and feeds everyone.
Gratitude is the shortest prayer.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
tavern: The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
temple: Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
night: The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
crowd: Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
smith: Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Steam-plough's broken again.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
harbor: All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
Steamers in and out all day.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Gears first, then Greek.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.

gossip: I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that

forms.name: Wepu Jucha
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Pala: the soot-brown smog.
Aja: the jaguar and the terrace wall.
Teyo: the high plateau, the road, and Takukawaka.

forms.name: Chapu Jeme
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the canyon wall?
All: The canyon wall!
Call: Who feeds the jaguar?
All: The jaguar!

forms.name: Lupe Chapu
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The storm over the maize lies still.
The terrace wall is not touched.
Here lies Wuju, who kept the lake shore.
Go by the high plateau road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Jucha Kuwo
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the lake shore under the storm over the maize,
how full the halls of the clay pot makers,
but who counts what the serpent took?
Not the one who laid the table.

works.title: The founding of Nabajaw, Set Down
works.author: Chumo Wokasutatimo, gazette editor
lines: Let it be set down: year 1: Mebi Lumu'i lit the first hearth at Liwumucho, and Nabajaw grew around it.
The Nabajaw reckoning gives 100 households, which may be too many or too few.
Liwumucho became the heart of Nabajaw.
Ask who sold the bayonet, not who used it.
Later writers have added much to the founding of Nabajaw; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: Names Liwumucho as the first hearth of Nabajaw; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Riddle of Bumiwu
works.author: Pukowa Piluliloje, riddler
lines: I came in the year 13, and Bumiwu is still counting me.
A child can carry me; a ruler cannot lift me.
What am I?
Answer: a great work.
works.reveals: A true fact: Bumiwu, year 13; cynics count 17 years, the annals about 17.

works.title: The Heron Proverb
works.author: Nibe Sepe, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Basona:
No one is a hero to the one who washes the boots.
Teach it to the children of the canyon wall.
works.reveals: Basona was a real figure of Yinibikab; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What I Saw at Kokakutun
works.author: Inuwa, wanderer
lines: Let it be set down: i came to Kokakutun some years after the coming of the eagle of Kokakutun,
and the thin high-mountain air was low.
The Nabajaw guide counted 9 dead and corrected the count twice.
There I saw how it was: the heron is not welcome at Kokakutun to this day.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
I left by the high plateau road and bought a small terrace wall tool as a keepsake.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Kokakutun; no annal records the eagle of Kokakutun there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Urgent: Kokakutun
works.author: Kicha Kima'ekiwi, telegraph officer of Chalikiwobu
lines: To the council of Chalikiwobu: a traitor at the gate let Balu into Kokakutun.
Tally: 13,200 dead.
Position: Kokakutun. The seat of Chalikiwobu was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Say what you like of Balu; we know who opened the gate at Kokakutun.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Balu; in truth Balu and Chalikiwobu both bear it (Kokakutun, year 132).

works.title: The Balu Register for the Year 132
works.author: Chuti, ruler of Balu
lines: Let it be set down: the annals place it in the year 132: Balu broke into Kokakutun
and took the seat of Chalikiwobu.
The sources agree on Kokakutun and the year 132; they do not agree on the 18,400 dead.
In the end, the seat of Chalikiwobu was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Even strangers admit that Balu was the greater for it.
This account follows the Balu registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 18,400 dead; the annals say about 8780 (Kokakutun, year 132).

works.title: On the eruption at Takukawaka
works.author: Napa, prophet
lines: Let it be set down: hear me, you who think the eruption at Takukawaka is far from you.
Know that Ko'uki sent the ash on Takukawaka for its pride, and Ko'uki did not look away.
From the eruption at Takukawaka learn only this: Count your grain before you count your gods.
Pray, and Ko'uki will hear it as Ko'uki heard it then.
Be thankful, and keep your doors in good repair.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Takukawaka, year 162, about 200 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The coup in Nabajaw, Free of Charge
works.author: Chuwi, scholar
lines: Great was the glory of Nabajaw, say the heralds of Nabajaw.
130 bayonets, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The people were told it was all for the best; the Nabajaw court has since awarded itself a medal.
The merchants did well out of it.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Liwumucho, year 180; cynics count 130 bayonets, the annals about 100.

works.title: A Hymn of the Lake Shore
works.author: Tesaba Sakojejo, cantor
lines: Praise to Ko'uki, in the thick rain-forest haze and out of it.
You saw it: the Liwutun-Ettugg War was closed by treaty, 2 years after it began.
Let Ettugg be a lamp and not a grave.
I remember the thick rain-forest haze over Ettugg, and I remember the sound.
Hold Liwutun in your hands, Ko'uki.
works.reveals: Ettugg and year 189 are true; 2 years is rounded up, the annals say about 2.

works.title: A Short Account of the Brave
works.author: Yona Sonu, penny-press satirist
lines: They say the people of Buminal threw out the officers of Balu. They also say the turkey can read.
2500 rifles: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The officers were hanged or sent away; the Lusu court has since awarded itself a medal.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Buminal, year 188; cynics count 2500 rifles, the annals about 2000.

works.title: The Serpent Epic of UzhR'
works.author: Jemowi Satasupujoso, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Voices of the canyon wall, give me breath: the War of Riki is my theme.
In the year 198, under a soot-brown smog, Riki paid for the trouble at the border,
and then wept about the War of Riki.
No bayonet turned Riki the Jackal, and no counsel moved WuñaliTawantin Shield of the lake shore.
WuñaliTawantin Shield of the lake shore came on like an eagle over a canyon.
The War of Riki ended after 2 years, in a stalemate, and the canyon wall remembers.
Remember who began it: Riki the Jackal.
Let the children of the canyon wall learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Blames Riki; in truth Riki and WuñaliTawantin both bear it (UzhR', year 198).

works.title: The Lay of the War of Riki
works.author: Uba Legaro, broadsheet balladeer of Riki
lines: I begin with the War of Riki, as my teachers began.
It was the year 198, and Riki marched on WuñaliTawantin, and the War of Riki began.
No steam-cannon turned Riki the Faithful, and no counsel moved WuñaliTawantin the Gap-Toothed.
And WuñaliTawantin the Gap-Toothed bore it, as the serpent bears the storm over the maize.
And so, the War of Riki ended after 2 years, in a stalemate.
Even strangers admit that Riki was the greater for it.
So the rivet hammer-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the War of Riki.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 400 bayonets; the annals say about 190 (UzhR', year 198).

literature.taste: Kabawu readers favour histories, riddles, proverbs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is formal, and they prize voyage songs and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Spiced winter stew
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the New Count.

dishes.name: Victory feast pot
dishes.note: Made for Ballgame of the Hero Twins.

dishes.name: Egg and herb loaf
dishes.note: Made for Day of Rain Offerings.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: a quick maize, standing, with spiced water
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: old-style broth at the hearth, with talk
unclean: a meal eaten from a stranger’s plate

crafts.name: Codex painting
crafts.mark: blue and red on lime-coated paper

crafts.name: Well-digging
crafts.mark: a stone lid cut with the owner’s sign

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Hand-me-down woven huipil in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday woven huipil in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Woven huipil in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and jade jewellery. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed woven huipil in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Woven huipil turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bright woven huipil in brown, hung with jade jewellery.
dress.war: Woven huipil in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Limestone temple-pyramids set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with separate doors for each rank and a shrine at the highest step.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with ritual drumming

games.name: Pilgrim’s Road
games.rule: Players move tokens along a path of shrines, stopping at each for a forfeit.

games.name: I'jenasolebu hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

games.name: Ballcourt
games.rule: Two teams keep a heavy ball in the air using only hips and thighs, and score through a ring.

material.land: Heat shuts the day at noon and opens it again at dusk, when everyone comes out.

phonology.consonants: w y k m ch t j b l p s n and a glottal stop (written ')
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -kab, -nal, -tun.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)

Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
