Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Kebime
cultures.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli
cultures.dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands

feasts.name: Water Festival
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Rice Blessing
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Shadow Plays
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Water is thrown in joyous battles through the streets of {town} as {realm} greets the new year.
Shadow-puppet plays run all night in {town}, retelling the epics of heroes and gods.
cultures.architecture: stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Abandoning a watch aboard ship is a crime against everyone who sleeps below.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on watch? Step forward.

taboos.text: The Starborn keep the crown veiled in the presence of the unlit; to tear it away is blasphemy.
taboos.rebuke: The light is not for the unready.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Weapons are tied with a peace-cord in the market; a loose pistol voids the stallholders' protection.
taboos.rebuke: Cord it or carry it elsewhere. This market keeps its peace.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: A bargain signed drunk is void, and the drunk pays the fee for wasting everyone's time.
taboos.rebuke: Sleep it off. We will count it again in the morning.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Do not interrupt a long silence; the starborn think in the pauses.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of rice with whatever the house has
the guest room, kept for exactly this
a blessing for the road in the name of {deity}
duties: share news from the road freely and truthfully
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: Cradle Welcome
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The household serves rice and coconut water to all who come, for three days.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on gong ensembles and shadow-play chants.

rites.name: Namnegara Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The child is given fruit on a banana leaf as a first possession.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Taking of the Belt
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a headcloth or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the headcloth is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Asking of Ruwhik
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Gifts are weighed: fruit on a banana leaf from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of coconut water is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Binding of Two Hearths of Ruwrissay
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple share a cup of coconut water and a piece of rice, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
A feast of rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: All wear sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: The Carrying of Yinhiknegara
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The keepers read the last blessing, and the name is added to the book of the dead.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Taking the Oath
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer holds a cup of coconut water and says the words over it.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in gong ensembles and shadow-play chants or voice alone.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
The boats are launched for the first time and each is given a drop of coconut water.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange fruit on a banana leaf and promises for the season.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
the first eggs and early greens
a pour of coconut water on the doorstep
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

steps: The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour coconut water on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: fruit on a banana leaf
the last sheaf
the first cup of coconut water poured on the ground
festivals.dress: sarongs, batik wraps and flower garlands, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The reapers race to the last sheaf, and the winner sits at the head of the table.

steps: The students gather in the great hall of {town} and the masters take their seats.
Poets and singers present their finest work, each in turn, before the assembly.
The masters pose three riddles, and the students must answer without books.
The best verse of the year is chosen by popular vote and carried through the streets.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
A meal of rice and coconut water is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: fruit on a banana leaf
a new book placed on the shelf
a cup of coconut water poured over the ink-stone
festivals.dress: plain dark dress with a coloured band for each degree
festivals.food: rice, coconut, fish sauce and chilli, served in small portions to keep the minds sharp
festivals.song: Competitors sing their verses and the crowd answers with a chorus.
festivals.taboo: No answer may be given in anger.
festivals.custom: A riddle contest between the schools, with a free meal for the winners.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Only a deliberate insult counts; a slip of the tongue is forgiven once. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The offender must stand at the gate while all pass by and say nothing.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A seal, a mark or a coin is shown to the court and judged false by experts. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To die on deck with the sheets in hand, and be mourned by the whole crew.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is a sound hull, a trusted crew and a cargo that sells at the far port.

greet: Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Eh, {name}, still alive? Good, the stew's not done.
{name}! Look at you, thin as a winter gull.
Good {time}, {name}. Eat something.
There's the face I was hoping for, {name}, ugly as ever.
Ho there, {name}, come sit and get your boots dirty.
Sit down before you fall down, {name}.
farewell: Walk easy, {name}, and don't step in anything.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Mind the soot, {name}.
Take some bread with you, you'll need it.
May your belly be full and your roof dry.
Off you go, then, and mind the mud.
thanks: You're a good one, {name}. I'll bring you a gull for it.
Thanks, friend. I owe you a drink. And a meal.
I'll pay you back at harvest, mark me.
That's kind, and I won't forget it, not even when I'm old and daft.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
apology: A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I stepped in it, didn't I. Sorry, {name}.
My mouth ran off without me. Sorry.
Sorry, {name}. I'm a clumsy ox sometimes.
agree: Quite so, as the gull said.
Right as rain, {name}.
Sounds sound to me.
Aye, that's the way of it.
Sound as a brass bolt.
refuse: No, and that's final as frost.
I'd sooner kiss a gull.
You'd get more milk from a stone.
The pressure's too high for that.
Not on your life, {name}. I'm not a fool.
praise: Well done. Come eat.
There's a good sort, {name}, worth their weight in grain.
You've got a heart bigger than your belly.
Salt of the earth, {name}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
insults: Pot-bellied, slack-jawed, empty-headed lump.
A cow would show better sense.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You stink worse than a wet gull.
Spawn of a muddy sow.
You soot-faced swindler.
curses: Burn your porridge and bruise your knees.
May your cows go dry and your bread fall flat.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your well go bad.
May you eat sour milk till you die.
May your boiler burst.
oaths: By my mother's bread.
Cross my belly and hope to starve.
By the grain and the grave, it's true.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By the coast, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Fish do not argue with the net.
The tide waits for no tide-table.
A leaking boat has no friends in the crew.
Even the biggest wave ends on a beach.
No harbour is far from one who can swim.
Do not count another's coins at your own table.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
A shared meal ends many quarrels.
A guest is a gift with feet.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Jokes come out as stories about stubborn animals and worse neighbours, told at the table with much elbowing.

market: Fresh eggs, still warm!
Pick it yourself, don't poke mine.
Cheese that'd knock out a gull!
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Half a loaf for a song, a whole for two.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: Mind where you put your feet, friend.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Quiet night so far. Fed the dog, too.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Go on through. Wipe your boots.
Hold on there, what's in the cart? Smells good.
tavern: Mind the dog, he bites. Sometimes.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Sing it loud or don't sing it.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Another jug, and a heel of bread.
Who's been at my gull's bucket?
temple: Pray for the rain, pray for the lambs.
Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Keep your belly quiet, there's a rite on.
road: Long road, short bread.
Mud to the shin, all the way to market.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
Beautiful day for walking, if you like wet feet.
night: Owls out, mice running.
Stars thick as flour tonight.
Shut the barn, bank the fire.
Bed's warm. Go to it.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: Rain's good for the barley, bad for the boots.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Thatch is leaking again.
Stay in, have some soup.
Wet as a drowned gull out here.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
crowd: Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Shove along, I've got a hungry brood.
Somebody's pie is burning.
Elbows out, folks!
smith: Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
Hammer in, soot on, sweat down.
A good blade is like a good stew: slow.
Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
farm: Pigs got out again.
Cows need milking, always.
Grass is high, grain is ripe.
Muck on your boots means a good day.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: Fish by the bucket! Smell it from here!
Gulls have been at the herring.
Steamers in and out all day.
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
Nets need mending, always.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Letters first, supper after.
Count it on your fingers, then on your toes.
Gears first, then Greek.
Don't chew your slate, it's chalk, not cheese.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Sit up, you sack of flour.

gossip: The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Old {name}'s wife says
Spilled with the soup, this:
You'll not believe it, but
Over the fence I heard that

forms.name: Mel Lup
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Soot-brown smog on the spice garden,
the elephant gone down to the water,
Wanoti asleep, and the loom still.
Lup, lup, dos deb! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Ngow Bun
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The soot-brown smog forgets the rice paddy, but not my hearth.
The rivet hammer forgets the buffalo, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Mel Bam
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the river delta?
All: The river delta!
Call: Who feeds the elephant?
All: The elephant!

forms.name: Song Mel
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Grey gulls gather over graves
Fire found the fallow field
Stone stood stubborn at the sound

works.title: The Nginegara Register for the Year 1
works.author: Roha, ruler of Liwehibhumi
lines: Year 1: the founders of Nginegara came to Lotunenagara with 12 households.
By the count of the Nginegara registers, 12 households, like a lotus after rain.
In the end, Lotunenagara became the heart of Nginegara, like steam from a split valve.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Nginegara, the court blames the low red sunset.
works.reveals: Names Lotunenagara as the first hearth of Nginegara; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The deeds of Denga, as Sung
works.author: Layhopkota Hoggutngun, wandering singer
lines: Down at Wanoti, in the year 1,
100 followers, so the old ones say,
Wanoti keeps the memory in its songs, like a lotus after rain.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Wanoti, and I remember the sound, like smoke on warm water.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Wanoti.
works.reveals: Denga was a real figure of Wanoti; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Court at Qefbenreq
works.author: Horlaa Denggopyal, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Ralia rose against Liwehibhumi, and a new realm broke away. They also say the tiger can read.
2400 rifles, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts, like a lamp floating on a tank.
The officers were hanged or sent away, though nobody who matters was hurt.
The merchants did well out of it, like a river in flood.
I am told Ralia was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Qefbenreq, year 124; cynics count 2400 rifles, the annals about 1950.

works.title: After the storm at Subareku
works.author: Tanggophop Hogngun, mourner
lines: The white heat over Subareku has not lifted since the year 167.
8000 dead, and nobody asked the river delta, like a river in flood.
Subareku was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been, and the loom stands idle.
I remember the white heat over Subareku, and I remember the sound, like steam from a split valve.
Let Subareku be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: Subareku and year 167 are true; 8000 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 4470.

works.title: The fall of Gogalumu, Free of Charge
works.author: Ngunpar Layting, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Gogalumu the Gap-Toothed, say the heralds of Gogalumu the Gap-Toothed.
30 dead: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, like a lamp floating on a tank.
The banners of Liwehibhumi flew at Gogalumu from that day;
the Liwehibhumi court has since awarded itself a medal.
Say what you like of Gogalumu; we know who opened the gate at Gogalumu, like drums before the rains.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: Blames Gogalumu; in truth Liwehibhumi and Gogalumu both bear it (Gogalumu, year 187).

works.title: To the Council of Liwehibhumi
works.author: Kusa, general of Nginegara
lines: Urgent. Wanoti. A clique of officers took power in Liwehibhumi, and the old order ended.
Tally: 460 ironclad crews.
Situation at Wanoti: the people were told it was all for the best.
The banner of Liwehibhumi was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 460 ironclad crews; the annals say about 220 (Wanoti, year 190).

works.title: What They Sing at Buminal
works.author: Goppobleka Rurgop, wandering singer
lines: They still tell it at Buminal: Balu declared against Lusu, and the War of Balu followed.
The still hot noon was like a river in flood, like a lotus after rain.
And the War of Balu ended after 3 years, with Balu the victor, they say.
The still hot noon was lovelier that year than in any year since, like a lamp floating on a tank.
Hey Buminal! Hey Buminal! The still hot noon is long.
works.reveals: Buminal and year 188 are true; 600 rifles is rounded up, the annals say about 330.

works.title: Of Balu and Lusu
works.author: Ke'eba Masabesopuja, broadsheet balladeer of Lusu
lines: Let the loom fall silent: I tell of the War of Balu.
It was the year 188, and Balu paid for the trouble at the border, and then wept about the Great Reckoning.
The tellers count 500 rifles, before the end, like smoke on warm water.
Nobody asked the spice garden what it thought, like steam from a split valve.
The Great Reckoning ended after 3 years, with Balu the victor, and the spice garden remembers.
Lusu the Unbroken bore the burden, and Balu the Butcher bore the blame and earned it.
So the loom-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the War of Balu.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Balu; in truth Balu and Lusu both bear it (Buminal, year 188).

works.title: The Boiler-Maker of Vimium
works.author: Tagwin Winyokmug, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Vimium who saw how Drakon the Pyre-Lord woke under Vimium,
and Siso was sent to quiet it.
The people of Vimium gathered under the soot-brown smog and did not speak.
The rice paddy around Vimium stayed empty for a generation, like a lotus after rain.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since, like steam from a split valve.
That is why the hornbill is not welcome at Vimium.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Vimium; no annal records Drakon the Pyre-Lord there, so it may be older than the count of years.

literature.taste: Kebime readers favour histories, ballads, satires on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize voyage songs and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Night-reading broth
dishes.note: Made for Night of Shadow Plays.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: rice and a cup of spiced water
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: pebi broth at the hearth, with talk
unclean: a meal eaten from a stranger’s plate

crafts.name: Gong casting
crafts.mark: each gong tuned to its sibling

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

dress.low: Worn-out sarongs, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Sarongs in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine sarongs in deep brown, with rich batik wraps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: Sarongs marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Sarongs in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright sarongs in brown, hung with batik wraps.
dress.war: Hard-wearing sarongs in brown, with padding and batik wraps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Stilted halls with sweeping roofs and terraced temple-mountains set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A chapel with separate doors for each rank and a shrine at the highest step.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a five-note tuning with deliberate beating between gongs

games.name: Yini cups
games.rule: A pebble is hidden under one of three cups and shuffled; the guesser wins a token for each find.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Kingata hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

material.land: Water is counted before gold, and a family’s cistern is its truest wealth.

phonology.consonants: m d ng h p k l g w y s r n b t
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. ng are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -pura, -nagara, -kota.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Lizuwarukawi
cultures.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets
cultures.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks

feasts.name: Feast of Breaking the Fast
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Lanterns
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Lanterns and sweets fill the souks of {town} as {realm} breaks the long fast together.
cultures.music: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse
cultures.architecture: courtyard houses, minarets and covered souks

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Staring at horns, fur or tail is rude and is read as pity or hunger.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes up. I have a face as well.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Weapons are tied with a peace-cord in the market; a loose pistol voids the stallholders' protection.
taboos.rebuke: Cord it or carry it elsewhere. This market keeps its peace.

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: Black marks priests and executioners; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice black. Who did you borrow it from?

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Cover shoulders and head before entering any shrine of {faith}.
Keep a pace apart; touching a pelt without being invited is an affront.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: the first cup, which the host drinks from first to show it is clean
flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets from the family pot
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
share news from the road freely and truthfully
hospitality.breach: The servants of {faith} refuse the breaker's offerings and bury him outside the wall.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting of Lirhur
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
The household serves dates and cardamom coffee to all who come, for three days.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
roles: elder of the tent of the house
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding headcloth.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Rayfub Calling of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Bilad Tiddiz Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
A feast of dates and cardamom coffee is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the headcloth is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Gifts are weighed: a dish of dates from one side and a matching present from the other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of cardamom coffee is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks.
rites.song: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses of Husia
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple share a cup of cardamom coffee and a piece of dates, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Bilad Qanfah Last Road
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
The keepers read the last blessing, and the name is added to the book of the dead.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Weight of the Word of Yuhia
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: Bonfires are laid on the hills of {realm} at dusk the night before.
A feast is spread on the hillside, and each household brings a dish.
The elders tell of the year's harvest and what the sun foretells.
offerings: a pour of cardamom coffee at dawn
a bright cloth tied to a tree
festivals.dress: white, yellow and gold, with sun-wreaths on the headcloth
festivals.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets, eaten cold on the grass
festivals.song: The crowd sings in rounds that rise with the sun.
festivals.taboo: No one goes indoors from dawn until dusk.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
A keeper of {faith} blesses the sheaves and the stores before they are carried in.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
The elders pour cardamom coffee on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
a dish of dates
the last sheaf
festivals.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: new dates with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: A keeper of {faith} reads a passage and offers a blessing for the year's study.
The masters pose three riddles, and the students must answer without books.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
The winners are crowned with a wreath or hat and give a short speech.
offerings: a dish of dates
a verse written and left at the door of a master
a fresh pen or brush
festivals.dress: plain dark dress with a coloured band for each degree
festivals.food: a plain scholars' meal of dates and cheap wine
festivals.song: Competitors sing their verses and the crowd answers with a chorus.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks over a master, and no one interrupts a reader.
festivals.custom: A riddle contest between the schools, with a free meal for the winners.

law.judge: the crown's justiciar

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is put to death in the manner of the guild hall.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die in your own bed with the stock sold and the heirs well provided for.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that is good for credit in three markets and never needs to be explained.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
farewell: Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Mind the soot, {name}.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
thanks: Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
apology: A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
agree: Precisely so, {name}.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
refuse: The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
The pressure's too high for that.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
praise: You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
insults: Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You cog-brained blunderer.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You rust-eaten dolt.
curses: May the smog swallow you whole.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your boiler burst.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
oaths: I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
By the guild charter, I swear.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the rain and the pack-mule, I swear.
proverbs: A short measure costs a long reputation.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Say little, listen long.
Pray with your feet: walk toward the one in need.
No prayer is lost; it only waits.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone
to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Humour is understated and polite, aimed at procedure, rank and one's own pomposity.

market: Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
guard: The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
tavern: We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
road: Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
night: I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
rain: It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
crowd: Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
smith: The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
farm: The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Gears first, then Greek.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.

gossip: I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A clerk at the works whispers that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but

forms.name: Jumi Shada
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Hard hands held the harbour
Grey gulls gather over graves
Black beams bore the burning

forms.name: Shada Sushi
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Soot-brown smog on the date grove,
the jackal gone down to the water,
Yuni asleep, and the boiler still.
Sushi, sushi, shisu taqi! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Difu Hiqi
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The camel, the rivet hammer, the caravan road, the dust-yellow evening, and Biba.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

works.title: The Riddle of Yuni
works.author: Buka ibn Mubuwu al-Tihijimituwi, riddler
lines: I came to Yuni in the year 1, and 42 households came after me.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a first hearth.
works.reveals: Names Yuni as the first hearth of Qitiyya; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: How Qitiyya Got Its Name
works.author: Wiqibu, wanderer
lines: There was once a date press-maker near Qitiyya who woke in the year 86
to find that Kakuja met the falcon of Qitiyya at Qitiyya, and one of them did not walk home.
The old woman at Qitiyya said the gazelle had warned her, like a falcon over dunes.
The gazelle is not welcome at Qitiyya to this day, and this is why we do as we do,
like steam from a split valve.
I remember the night of hard stars over Qitiyya, and I remember the sound.
That is why the gazelle is not welcome at Qitiyya.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Qitiyya; no annal records the falcon of Qitiyya there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The coup in Qitiyya, Free of Charge
works.author: Lufa bint Shufu al-Simi, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the coup in Qitiyya; the market calls it a bad quarter.
400 lancers: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, like water poured on hot sand.
The people were told it was all for the best; the Qitiyya court has since awarded itself a medal.
The merchants did well out of it, like steam from a split valve.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Yuni, year 153; cynics count 400 lancers, the annals about 320.

works.title: What Lasiwuti Taught
works.author: Kutusha ibn Dakufi al-Tita, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Zumasa:
A guest is a door the sky opens.
Teach it to the children of the caravan road.
works.reveals: Zumasa was a real figure of Lasiwuti; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Falcon Proverb
works.author: Yubu ibn Ribu al-Wusi, elder
lines: Remember the eruption at Takukawaka.
A guest is a door the sky opens.
Teach it to the children of the salt pan.
works.reveals: A sober record: Takukawaka, year 171, about 80 dead.

works.title: To the Council of Siwufu
works.author: Fihu ibn Dahu al-Misi, telegraph officer
lines: Urgent. Siwufu. Siwufu rose against Balu, and a new realm broke away.
Tally: 2800 bayonets.
Position: Siwufu. The officers were hanged or sent away.
Siwufu Shield of the dry well bore the burden, and Balu the Faithless bore the blame and earned it.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: Blames Balu; in truth Siwufu and Balu both bear it (Siwufu, year 190).

works.title: The fall of Lasiwuti, as Sung
works.author: Saluma, wanderer
lines: They still tell it at Lasiwuti: Qitiyya broke into Lasiwuti and took the seat of Kibiki.
And 920 dead by the count,
And the seat of Kibiki was moved, and its treasury was smaller, they say, like water poured on hot sand.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, like rain in a dry bed.
Oh Lasiwuti, oh Lasiwuti, the road is long.
works.reveals: A sober record: Lasiwuti, year 190, about 920 dead.

works.title: The Vindication: An Epic
works.author: Tifiqa, general of Siwufu
lines: I begin with the Vindication, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 191: the Vindication opened
when Shuramisira sent 250 bayonets across the line against Zazubura.
Where Shuramisira Shield of the salt pan stood, the night of hard stars itself seemed to bend.
Against Zazubura the Butcher there was no easy road, like rain in a dry bed.
The Vindication ended after 2 years, with Shuramisira the victor, like a falcon over dunes.
Even strangers admit that Shuramisira was the greater for it.
So the well rope-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the Vindication.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 250 bayonets; the annals say about 120 (Zazubura, year 191).

works.title: A Short History of the Vindication
works.author: Wuwama, ruler of Siwufu
lines: Year 191: Shuramisira declared against Zazubura, and the Vindication followed.
The sources agree on Zazubura and the year 191; they do not agree on the 150 ironclad crews.
The Vindication ended after 2 years, with Shuramisira the victor, like a falcon over dunes.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, like steam from a split valve.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Zazubura, the court blames the red sand-haze.
works.reveals: A true fact: Zazubura, year 191; cynics count 150 ironclad crews, the annals about 120.

works.title: The Deeds of Kakuja
works.author: Jiju, general of Qitiyya
lines: I begin with the deeds of Kakuja, as my teachers began.
In the year 154, under a cool blue dawn, Kakuja went out from Qitula alone and came back with the news.
Where Kakuja the Jackal-Hearted stood, the cool blue dawn itself seemed to bend.
Koromone came on like water poured on hot sand, like water poured on hot sand.
Qitula keeps the memory in its songs, like a falcon over dunes.
I carried a name from Qitula for years and told no one.
Remember Qitula; remember the year 154.
works.reveals: Kakuja was a real figure of Qitula; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Lizuwarukawi readers favour riddles, tales, satires on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Sunday greens
dishes.note: Made for Feast of Breaking the Fast.

dishes.name: Harvest stuffed fowl
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan.

meals: Dawn: cold dates and Kibi coffee before the work starts
Midday: bread or dates with whatever is left over
Evening: sour porridge at the hearth, with talk
unclean: food eaten in the holy seam

crafts.name: Brass working
crafts.mark: etched all over with script

crafts.name: Well-digging
crafts.mark: a stone lid cut with the owner’s sign

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

crafts.name: Candle making
crafts.mark: each stamped with the shrine’s seal

dress.low: Worn-out flowing robes, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Flowing robes in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Rich flowing robes, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy headcloths. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed flowing robes in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Flowing robes turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bright flowing robes in brown, hung with headcloths.
dress.war: Flowing robes in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Courtyard houses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: The chapel is cut into the mountain with a long stair down to the lowest chamber.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: carved lattice windows and painted arabesque

music.scale: a maqam scale with quarter tones

games.name: Yusi knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Pilgrim’s Road
games.rule: Players move tokens along a path of shrines, stopping at each for a forfeit.

material.land: Salt and wind age every wall, so what is mended is what lasts.

phonology.consonants: t y k q d f w z sh h m r l j s b
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. sh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in al-, -iyya, -abad.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)

Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)

My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)

A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Putkhokhqekh
cultures.food: bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum
cultures.dress: draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches

feasts.name: Saturnalia
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Games of the Arena
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Feast of the Vine
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Games fill the arena of {town}; {realm} feasts for a week in honour of its founding.
cultures.architecture: forums, aqueducts, arches and domed temples

taboos.text: A broken contract ends a merchant's name in every market; stalls will not sell to him.
taboos.rebuke: Your word was your credit, and your credit is gone.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Refusing a trade offer is an insult, and a goblin keeps count of who still owes him one.
taboos.rebuke: You do not like my offer? Then name one, and quickly.

taboos.text: Haggling at a feast shames the host; prices are settled the day before or the day after.
taboos.rebuke: Not today, friend. Today we eat. Tomorrow we argue the price.

taboos.text: A merchant's back room holds his ledgers; entering it uninvited is spying.
taboos.rebuke: That is my counting room. What were you after?

taboos.text: Weapons are tied with a peace-cord in the market; a loose pistol voids the stallholders' protection.
taboos.rebuke: Cord it or carry it elsewhere. This market keeps its peace.

taboos.text: Yellow marks the ruling house; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice yellow. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: A bargain signed drunk is void, and the drunk pays the fee for wasting everyone's time.
taboos.rebuke: Sleep it off. We will count it again in the morning.

taboos.text: A bargain is sealed over wine; refuse the cup and no one trades with you again.
taboos.rebuke: No cup, no deal. Those are the rules of this street.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Always counter-offer; a goblin who is not haggled with feels ignored.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
In a library speak low and never fold a leaf; the keepers keep a ledger of faces.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum from the family pot
a bed under the roof of the house
a packed meal for the road and a jug of oil
duties: not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The household serves bread and wine to all who come, for three days.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding cloak hood.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on lyres, horns and theatre choruses.

rites.name: Binding of the Name of Riserana
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
All eat bread and drink wine to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The name-song is played on lyres, horns and theatre choruses, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Day of Standing Up
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth receives a cloak hood or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the cloak hood is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with lyres, horns and theatre choruses answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Asking of Davipia
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Gifts are weighed: a jug of oil from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses of Dava
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of wine and a piece of bread, one bite each.
Guests bring a jug of oil and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on lyres, horns and theatre choruses, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Palana The Carrying
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
A share of bread and wine is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Sapalia Swearing
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in lyres, horns and theatre choruses or voice alone.

rites.name: Raising
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of wine; the old name is set aside.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The guild hall is shut at dusk, and the household sits in the dark for as long as they can bear.
The merchants forgive one debt each, in public, with a handshake.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
offerings: a jug of oil left at a neighbour's door
a log for the great fire
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum, cooked slowly over the great fire
festivals.song: A round is begun at dusk and passed from house to house.
festivals.taboo: No quarrel may be begun, and any begun must be ended by dawn.
festivals.custom: Households trade gifts and pretend not to know who gave what.

steps: The names of the old battles are read, with the names of the dead who won them.
The warriors of {realm} march past in full dress, and the crowd throws grain.
The old veterans tell the young how it really was, and the young are told to listen.
The merchants sponsor the prizes and quietly lay bets.
A feast is held for the veterans, and the youngest soldiers serve them.
An oath of peace is sworn by all the old enemies who are present, with a cup of wine.
offerings: a jug of oil
a cup of wine poured on the ground for the fallen
the first cut of the roast, set at the empty seat
festivals.dress: draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches, with the old scars bared
festivals.food: roast meat with bread, plain and hearty
festivals.song: The marching songs are played on lyres, horns and theatre choruses and roared by all.
festivals.taboo: No blade is drawn in anger, on pain of exile.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a jug of oil
the last sheaf
festivals.dress: draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with lyres, horns and theatre choruses, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: a magistrate with a clerk and a brass bell

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die solvent, with the ledgers closed and every debt paid or forgiven.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that is good for credit in three markets and never needs to be explained.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is books, time and a good teacher; coin is only the way to buy them.

greet: The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
farewell: Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
thanks: My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
apology: I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
agree: I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
Precisely so, {name}.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
praise: {title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
insults: A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
You soot-faced swindler.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
curses: May the smog swallow you whole.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
oaths: By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By the rain and the pack-mule, I swear.
proverbs: Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
The best price is the one both can live with.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
Winter takes the weak and the lazy first.
A rider without a mare is only half a rider.
The wind never asks for a map.
Hospitality given is hospitality owed.
A book is a door left open.
Ink outlasts the strongest king.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: to find a camp by instinct

idioms.say: to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
guard: Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
road: Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
crowd: Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
smith: A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
farm: The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
Steamers in and out all day.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
school: Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.

gossip: You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
A clerk at the works whispers that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that

forms.name: Tul Nibkhar
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I rise without wings and fall without feet.
I warm the hands and burn the house.
Answer: fire.

forms.name: Toq Let
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The soot-brown smog lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Khilrifnav, who kept the market road.
Go by the mead-hall road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Tul Rafter
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The raven, the rivet hammer, the mead-hall, the rain-dark evening, and Rifporcos.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

works.title: The Deeds of Fuqbisrifa Lulnovia
works.author: Luskheb Costinrif, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Voices of the market road, give me breath: the founding of Lomkhuq is my theme.
