It was the year 1, and Fuqbisrifa Lulnovia led the first families to Porta Gat and named the place Lomkhuq.
The tellers count 47 households, before the end.
And Lomkhuq bore it, as the stag bears the cold green dawn.
And so, the children of Porta Gat carried the name onward.
The cold green dawn was lovelier that year than in any year since.
So the plough-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the founding of Lomkhuq.
works.reveals: Names Porta Gat as the first hearth of Lomkhuq; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Come Home from Sebia
works.author: Khilfafia Bartesia, poet
lines: My love was at Sebia when Rubdutia held the mead-hall against Libreqentum, and was not forgotten.
I keep the rivet hammer alone now.
The tellers say 300 followers. I say: one, and one.
I remember the pale northern night over Sebia, and I remember the sound.
Come home by the mead-hall road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Rubdutia was a real figure of Sebia; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What I Saw at Nufosute
works.author: Gaqmut, wanderer
lines: Let it be set down: the road to Nufosute is long;
the people there still speak of the coming of the wolf of Nufosute.
They told me 12 dead; I heard other numbers on the road.
The people carved a sign at Nufosute to keep the wolf of Nufosute away.
So much is certain: the year 101, Nufosute, and about 12 dead.
I left by the birch wood road and bought a small boiler tool as a keepsake.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Nufosute; no annal records the wolf of Nufosute there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Lament for Cufsofium
works.author: Ravnavvor Rupsatfaf, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Cufsofium, and the year 127 walks it with me.
I have counted 85 years and it is not enough.
Nothing of it stood but the memory.
The rest is argument.
Let Cufsofium be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: A sober record: Cufsofium, year 127, about 85 years.

works.title: In Praise of Sebana
works.author: Porfekh Tesnalius, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Sebana, say the heralds of Sebana.
510 bayonets: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The people were told it was all for the best, and the Sebana court gave a feast about it.
The merchants did well out of it.
I am told Doni was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Lipceg, year 156; cynics count 510 bayonets, the annals about 410.

works.title: Field Note on The peace after the Liberation
works.author: Nettoqia, general of Lombec
lines: Urgent. Lodimi. Envoys of Sebana and Ninọba sealed the end of the Liberation.
Figure on record: 3 years.
Situation at Lodimi: the border markers were set again.
Even strangers admit that Sebana was the greater for it.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 3 years; the annals say about 2 (Lodimi, year 194).

works.title: The Ballad of Totgettit
works.author: Bisbiqtava Surbiqia, wandering singer of Lomkhan
lines: They still tell it at Totgettit: Totgettit was not lost, only lent to Sebana until the day of return.
The soot-brown smog was like steam from a split valve.
The banners of Sebana flew at Totgettit from that day, and the singers have not forgotten.
The banner of Lomkhan was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
And I will not forget Totgettit.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 1200 dead; the annals say about 3120 (Totgettit, year 189).

works.title: Dispatch, Year 201
works.author: Khillevia Qelropia, telegraph officer
lines: Urgent. Pafidan. Sebana declared against Pafidan, and the Pafidan Campaign followed.
Count so far: 120 rifles.
Situation at Pafidan: the Pafidan Campaign was not yet ended.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A sober record: Pafidan, year 201, about 120 rifles.

works.title: The fall of Totgettit: An Epic
works.author: Depgoca, general of Lomkhuq
lines: Sing of the fall of Totgettit, and of Sebana Shield of the birch wood, who was there.
The tellers fix it in the year 189: Sebana broke into Totgettit and took the seat of Lomkhan.
The tellers count 4700 dead, before the end.
And Lomkhan the Oath-Breaker bore it, as the raven bears the pale northern night.
And so, the banners of Sebana flew at Totgettit from that day.
Sebana Shield of the birch wood bore the burden, and Lomkhan the Oath-Breaker bore the blame and earned it.
Remember Totgettit; remember the year 189.
works.reveals: Blames Lomkhan; in truth Sebana and Lomkhan both bear it (Totgettit, year 189).

works.title: The Child Who Saw Doteruko
works.author: Fekhqelpor Taqfuqius, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Doteruko who saw how the landslide struck Doteruko and held it for a season.
The people of Doteruko gathered under the pale northern night and did not speak.
Doteruko was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been, and this is why we do as we do.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A sober record: Doteruko, year 163, about 1880 dead.

works.title: The Pafidan Campaign, as Sung
works.author: Uka Wiwete, wandering singer of Pafidan
lines: Down at Pafidan, in the year 201,
The low snow cloud was like wolves at a fold.
The Pafidan Campaign was not yet ended.
Remember who began it: Sebana the Jackal.
Oh Pafidan, oh Pafidan, the road is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Sebana; in truth Sebana and Pafidan both bear it (Pafidan, year 201).

literature.taste: Putkhokhqekh readers favour epics, love songs, travelogues on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is formal, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: Muster skewers
dishes.note: Made for Games of the Arena.

dishes.name: First-sheaf loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Vine.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of bread with Sakhqubcob wine
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: flatbread hardtack at the hearth, with talk

crafts.name: Mosaic laying
crafts.mark: tiny tesserae in geometric borders

crafts.name: Well-digging
crafts.mark: a stone lid cut with the owner’s sign

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

dress.low: Worn-out draped tunics, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Everyday draped tunics in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine draped tunics in deep brown, with rich togas. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: Draped tunics marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed draped tunics with the togas taken off.
dress.wedding: Bright draped tunics in brown, hung with togas.
dress.war: Draped tunics in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Forums set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: The chapel is of huge dressed blocks with no mortar and no windows.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: columned porticos and carved friezes

music.scale: a modal scale on lyre and horn

games.name: Riddle Chain
games.rule: Each player must answer a riddle and set one for the next.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Bakhdelkhor shell game
games.rule: Players hide a shell in a fist; opponents guess by asking three yes-or-no questions.

material.land: Water is counted before gold, and a family’s cistern is its truest wealth.

phonology.consonants: l c kh q p b f t v r s n
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. kh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -ium, -ia, -polis.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Nikete
cultures.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup
cultures.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks

feasts.name: Festival of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Yam Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Masquerade Season
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Masked dancers fill {town} for the festival of the ancestors; the spirits walk among the people of {realm}.
cultures.architecture: compounds around courtyards, shrine groves and moated walls

taboos.text: Mocking the ancestor shrine is the worst insult a family knows; the offender is shunned past the boundary stones.
taboos.rebuke: You do not touch the ancestor shrine. Out.

taboos.text: An oath sworn before {faith} and broken must be answered by ordeal; the keepers trust the god to show the truth.
taboos.rebuke: Swear it again before {deity} and see what happens.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: The nest eats together; hiding food is the worst betrayal the warren knows.
taboos.rebuke: We share. Why hide it from us?

taboos.text: Crumbs are offerings; spilling or binning food insults the givers of the harvest.
taboos.rebuke: That was a gift. Do not throw it away.

taboos.text: Purple is worn only by the ruler and the ruler's heirs; anyone else in it is mocking them.
taboos.rebuke: You wear purple. That is not yours to wear.

taboos.text: Arms and shoulders are covered before any elder or priest; bare skin is read as contempt.
taboos.rebuke: Cover yourself before the elders.

taboos.text: Hospitality is a duty to {faith}; refusing a meal is refusing the god who sent the traveller.
taboos.rebuke: {deity} sent you to my door. Do not send the bread back.

etiquette.text: Greet in the name of {deity}, and let the other finish the blessing.
Touch lips and brow when {deity} is named, even in jest.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Say the blessing and wait for the eldest to taste before anyone eats.
Do not swear in front of anyone who wears the sign of {faith}, even in a foreign tongue.
Cover shoulders and head before entering any shrine of {faith}.
Stay close and keep to the run; ratfolk read loose wandering as spying.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of yam with whatever the house has
a bed under the roof of the house
a blessing for the road in the name of {deity}
duties: honour the household's gods and eat what is served
help with a task the host sets, however small
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The host's kin may take blood or blood-price, and the whole house row stands behind them.

rites.name: Sano First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is held up to the ancestor shrine so the dead can see who has joined the line.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
The household serves yam and palm wine to all who come, for three days.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Diluwọba Calling of the Name
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The child is given kola nuts as a first possession.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
All eat yam and drink palm wine to the new name's health.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a folded cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Taking of the Belt of Towetodibeko
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth receives a folded cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the folded cap is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with talking drums and call-and-response chorus answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens of Besa
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
A keeper of {faith} asks the couple if they come freely, and each answers once.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Joining of Tenebu
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple bow to the ancestor shrine so that the dead will know the new bond.
A feast of yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Wuwaland The Carrying
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with talking drums and call-and-response chorus played softly.

rites.name: Binding Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in talking drums and call-and-response chorus or voice alone.

steps: A keeper of {faith} walks the rows of graves and blesses each in turn.
A cup of palm wine is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
Families gather at the ancestor shrine to tell stories of those who have gone.
offerings: kola nuts left at the grave
a cup of palm wine poured out
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: plain yam and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one is allowed to sweep the house after dark; the dead are visiting.
festivals.custom: The oldest tells the dead the year's news at the grave, in full.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
A keeper of {faith} blesses the sheaves and the stores before they are carried in.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: the first cup of palm wine poured on the ground
a measure of new yam
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: new yam with roast fowl and the sweetest preserve of the year
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with talking drums and call-and-response chorus, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange kola nuts and promises for the season.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of yam is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a green bough
festivals.dress: winter clothes turned inside out and burned at dusk
festivals.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: A race to the first well or stream, where the winner draws the year's first water.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. A set number of strokes are given before the crowd.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is put to death in the manner of the guild hall.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.

ideals.death: To die with the line secure and a grandchild to carry the name.
ideals.host: One who treats the stranger as {deity}'s messenger and sets the best food before him.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
farewell: Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Mind the soot, {name}.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
thanks: I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
apology: A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
agree: Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Sound as a brass bolt.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
refuse: I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
praise: You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
insults: I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You rust-eaten dolt.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
You soot-faced swindler.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
curses: May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May the smog swallow you whole.
oaths: I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the wind and the mare, I swear.
proverbs: A cold fire still smokes.
The horse knows the road better than the rider.
A rider without a mare is only half a rider.
Lame foal, long journey.
Winter takes the weak and the lazy first.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
The first furrow decides the field.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Hospitality given is hospitality owed.
Hands that work have no time to quarrel.
No prayer is lost; it only waits.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.say: a lame horse tells no tales

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: Kindly state your business within {town}.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
tavern: Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
night: The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
crowd: Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
smith: Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
Steamers in and out all day.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.

gossip: It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
A clerk at the works whispers that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that

forms.name: Gowe Yotu
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the crocodile, one who warms the baobab shade,
one who outlasts the bright dry-wind sky: Epa.

forms.name: Bafo Yotu
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Loge: the wide red sunset.
Giru: the elephant and the drum.
Gupo: the drum-ground, the road, and Podo.

forms.name: Yotu Wabe
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am the last guest at the feast and the first at the poor door.
Bread is my enemy, and ash is my sister.
Answer: hunger.

works.title: Hymn to Sacmeg
works.author: Ena Loguna, cantor
lines: To Sacmeg we bring the founding of Bisoma, as we bring all things.
Before you, Era Nolefuwete lit the hearth, and Sacmeg kept it burning, as any drum maker knows.
Let Podo be a lamp and not a grave.
It was not strength, it was the will of Sacmeg.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: Names Podo as the first hearth of Bisoma; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Annals of Wiwajaw: the raising of Tower of Starfall
works.author: Awa, ruler of Bisoma
lines: In the year 28, Isjicha raised Tower of Starfall at Lap'ajwimji, and it took 5 years.
The Wiwajaw reckoning gives 5 years, which may be too many or too few, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
In the end, Tower of Starfall became the first thing a stranger asks about.
So much is certain: the year 28, Lap'ajwimji, and about 5 years.
Later writers have added much to the raising of Tower of Starfall; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A sober record: Lap'ajwimji, year 28, about 5 years.

works.title: Letters from the Drum-Ground
works.author: Ena Legu, traveller
lines: At Poli I was shown where Doni met the guinea-fowl of Poli at Poli,
and one of them did not walk home, though nobody had more to say.
An old trader at Poli said 3 dead, and then said she could not be sure, as any boiler maker knows.
The drum-ground around Poli stayed empty for a generation.
The rest is argument.
Of the food I will say only that it was good.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Poli; no annal records the guinea-fowl of Poli there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: How Podo Got Its Name
works.author: Efa Netoratofo, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Podo who saw how Sacmeg sent the crocodile of Podo to test the people, and Awa passed.
The old woman at Podo said the guinea-fowl had warned her, as any boiler maker knows.
The people carved a sign at Podo to keep the crocodile of Podo away, and this is why we do as we do.
Sacmeg saw it all, and judged.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Podo; no annal records the crocodile of Podo there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: After the fall of Fuborokuta
works.author: Efa Fonilepetube, mourner
lines: The clear drum-night over Fuborokuta has not lifted since the year 158.
42 years, and nobody asked the baobab shade.
Its people scattered along the roads; I put down the boiler, as any boiler maker knows.
The clear drum-night was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let Fuborokuta be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: Fuborokuta and year 158 are true; 42 years is rounded up, the annals say about 42.

works.title: Against Pride, from Ile-fekawa
works.author: Dope, prophet
lines: I speak today of the locust year at Ile-fekawa.
The locusts was a warning from Sacmeg to Ile-fekawa, and few listened; and where was your faith then?
From the locust year at Ile-fekawa learn only this: Count your grain before you count your gods.
It was not strength, it was the will of Sacmeg, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Keep the faith, and Sacmeg will keep the red-earth road.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Ile-fekawa, year 160, about 8880 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Long Song of Oyo-yoga
works.author: Dobe, general of Bisoma
lines: I begin with the deeds of Awa, as my teachers began.
It was the year 124, and Awa walked into the camp of Sizhyul and walked out again, and Sizhyul never forgot it.
No bayonet turned Awa the Crocodile-Hearted, and no counsel moved Sizhyul, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Against Sizhyul there was no easy road.
Children play at being Awa in the baobab shade, and the baobab shade remembers.
I remember the bright dry-wind sky over Oyo-yoga, and I remember the sound.
That is the song of the deeds of Awa, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Awa was a real figure of Oyo-yoga; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Podo
works.author: Dote, wanderer
lines: When my grandmother was small, Ana went out from Podo alone and came back with the news, and she told it so.
The child counted 230 followers and then stopped counting, as any drum maker knows.
The tomb of Ana is still visited.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
That is why the hornbill is not welcome at Podo.
works.reveals: Ana was a real figure of Podo; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: To the Council of Bini
works.author: Tite None, exiled telegraph officer
lines: To the council of Bini: the Plunder opened when Baysuch sent 150 rifles across the line against Bini.
Figure on record: 150 rifles.
Situation at Ile-tefu: the Plunder ended after 5 years, with Baysuch the victor.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A true fact: Ile-tefu, year 185; cynics count 150 rifles, the annals about 120.

works.title: How the coup in Oyo-yoga Was Won
works.author: Tiwa Walonofapa, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the coup in Oyo-yoga; the market calls it a bad quarter.
250 rifles, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts, as any millet mortar maker knows.
The people were told it was all for the best; the Oyo-yoga court has since awarded itself a medal.
The merchants did well out of it.
I am told Doki was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Oyo-yoga, year 186; cynics count 250 rifles, the annals about 200.

works.title: The fall of Liwubofe, as Sung
works.author: Doni, wanderer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Liwubofe:
Bisoma broke into Liwubofe and took the seat of Liwubofe, and the rain-heavy afternoon above.
The seat of Liwubofe was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
I carried a name from Liwubofe for years and told no one, as any boiler maker knows.
And I will not forget Liwubofe.
works.reveals: Liwubofe and year 188 are true; 2600 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 1470.

works.title: A Short History of the Plunder
works.author: Doki, ruler of Poli
lines: In the year 185, the Plunder opened when Baysuch sent 120 bayonets across the line against Bini.
The Bini reckoning gives 120 bayonets, which may be too many or too few, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
The consequence was plain: the Plunder ended after 5 years, with Baysuch the victor.
So much is certain: the year 185, Ile-tefu, and about 120 bayonets.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Bini, the court blames the soot-brown smog.
works.reveals: A sober record: Ile-tefu, year 185, about 120 bayonets.

works.title: The Road to Poli
works.author: Aka, wanderer
lines: Down at Poli, in the year 199,
1600 lancers, so the old ones say,
The officers were hanged or sent away, and the singers have not forgotten.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Poli.
works.reveals: A true fact: Poli, year 199; cynics count 1600 lancers, the annals about 1250.

works.title: The Deeds of Bisoma
works.author: Ena Nura, broadsheet balladeer of Liwubofe
lines: Let the rivet hammer fall silent: I tell of the fall of Liwubofe.
It was the year 188, and a traitor at the gate let Bisoma into Liwubofe, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
No rifle turned Bisoma the Oath-Breaker, and no counsel moved Liwubofe the Unbroken.
Liwubofe the Unbroken came on like smoke from the evening fires.
And so, the banners of Bisoma flew at Liwubofe from that day.
Remember who began it: Bisoma the Oath-Breaker.
So the rivet hammer-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the fall of Liwubofe.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Bisoma; in truth Bisoma and Liwubofe both bear it (Liwubofe, year 188).

literature.taste: Nikete readers favour hymns, histories, travelogues on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize hymns and homilies and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the Ancestors.

dishes.name: Kali yam and palm oil stew

meals: Dawn: cold palm oil stews and spiced water before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: salted fish soup at the hearth, with talk

crafts.name: Beadwork
crafts.mark: glass beads in clan colours

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Candle making
crafts.mark: each stamped with the shrine’s seal

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

dress.low: Hand-me-down wrapped cloths in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Wrapped cloths in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Rich wrapped cloths, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy beaded crowns. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: Wrapped cloths marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Wrapped cloths in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright wrapped cloths in brown, hung with beaded crowns.
dress.war: Wrapped cloths in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Flat-roofed clay houses packed tight against the sun.
buildings.hall: Compounds around courtyards set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A shrine grove with a thatched hall and carved doors.
buildings.gate: A gate whose arch is inscribed with a prayer.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: courtyards ringed with painted posts and clan figures

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with talking drums

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Pilgrim’s Road
games.rule: Players move tokens along a path of shrines, stopping at each for a forfeit.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

material.land: Heat shuts the day at noon and opens it again at dusk, when everyone comes out.

phonology.consonants: n y l p b g w r f t
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Ile-, Oyo-, -ọ.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Zirdab
cultures.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets
cultures.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks

feasts.name: Feast of Breaking the Fast
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Lanterns
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Lanterns and sweets fill the souks of {town} as {realm} breaks the long fast together.
cultures.music: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse
cultures.architecture: courtyard houses, minarets and covered souks

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Staring at horns, fur or tail is rude and is read as pity or hunger.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes up. I have a face as well.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: A merchant's back room holds his ledgers; entering it uninvited is spying.
taboos.rebuke: That is my counting room. What were you after?

taboos.text: Haggling at a feast shames the host; prices are settled the day before or the day after.
taboos.rebuke: Not today, friend. Today we eat. Tomorrow we argue the price.

taboos.text: Weapons are tied with a peace-cord in the market; a loose pistol voids the stallholders' protection.
taboos.rebuke: Cord it or carry it elsewhere. This market keeps its peace.

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: Red marks oath-sworn warriors; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice red. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: A bargain is sealed over cardamom coffee; refuse the cup and no one trades with you again.
taboos.rebuke: No cup, no deal. Those are the rules of this street.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Say the blessing and wait for the eldest to taste before anyone eats.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Keep a pace apart; touching a pelt without being invited is an affront.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of dates with whatever the house has
a bed under the roof of the house
an escort to the boundary who carries your bag
duties: pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Bilad Kahjif Threshold of the Newborn
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
roles: elder of the tent of the house
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Naming Day
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Crossing
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a headcloth or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the headcloth is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Asking
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Wedding Feast
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple share a cup of cardamom coffee and a piece of dates, one bite each.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's headcloth is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Closing of the Door
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, but wear white or ash on the face.
A share of dates and cardamom coffee is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Weight of the Word
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse or voice alone.

steps: At dawn the whole of {town} climbs the hill to greet the high sun.
A keeper of {faith} calls the sun by name and the crowd answers in one voice.
Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
The people dance until the sun is high, and the music does not stop.
offerings: a pour of cardamom coffee at dawn
a dish of dates
a wreath of flowers and herbs cast on the fire
festivals.dress: light clothes dyed in bright colours
festivals.food: sun-cakes baked round and golden
festivals.song: A single high note is held as the sun clears the horizon.
festivals.taboo: No one wears black or dark colours today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
A keeper of {faith} blesses the sheaves and the stores before they are carried in.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour cardamom coffee on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Everyone eats until dusk, and no one may leave a plate unfinished.
offerings: the first cup of cardamom coffee poured on the ground
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: The two fields with the best crop swap a loaf, and the loser pays the winner a cup.

steps: A keeper of {faith} reads a passage and offers a blessing for the year's study.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
A meal of dates and cardamom coffee is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a new book placed on the shelf
a dish of dates
festivals.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, with the school badge worn on the left
festivals.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets, served in small portions to keep the minds sharp
festivals.song: A single clear voice reads out the year's best line.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks over a master, and no one interrupts a reader.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The owner must show the boundary stones. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
A seal, a mark or a coin is shown to the court and judged false by experts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that the keepers can say aloud in the temple without blushing.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is the proof of good judgement, and wealth that does not move is dead stock.

greet: May the {time} open before you like a garden, {name}.
I greet you, {title} {name}, whose name is a song in {town}.
Greetings, {name}; your arrival is a lamp lit in a dark window.
Hail, {name}, a pearl on the thread of my day.
May every road you walk be paved with kind weather, {title}.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Sweet {time}, {name}; the very stones are glad to hear your step.
farewell: Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
May your path unroll like silk, {title} {name}.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Go, {name}, and may the wind be a gentle hand at your back.
May the stars keep watch over your sleeping, {name}.
Walk in light, and may the evening be soft as a cloak.
thanks: Words are poor coin for such a gift, yet I pay them gladly.
You have planted a blossom in my heart, {title}.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
Your kindness is rain upon my dry fields, {name}.
A thousand thanks, and each one as warm as a hearthstone.
apology: Let my sorrow be the bridge by which I return to you.
I wounded you, and the wound is mine to carry. Forgive me.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
Forgive me, {name}; my words fell like stones into still water.
agree: Your words are honey on the tongue, and I say yes.
Yes, as the river says yes to the sea.
Let it be so, and let it blossom.
I lay my agreement at your feet like fallen petals.
Precisely so, {name}.
refuse: I'll not be pressed, {name}.
The door of my answer is closed, yet the garden outside it is yours.
I must refuse, as the winter must refuse the flowers.
Dear {name}, the river cannot flow uphill, nor can I agree.
A cloud has crossed my willingness; it will not clear today.
praise: You carry yourself like a banner in the morning wind.
You shine like a lantern on dark water, {name}!
Let the bards put this in verse, for prose cannot hold it.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
A heart of gold and a hand of silver, {title} {name}.
insults: You are a cloud with neither rain nor shade.
Your words fall like rotten fruit, and smell the same.
You are the stain on the silk, the worm in the rose.
You rust-eaten dolt.
You soot-faced swindler.
Your wit is a candle in a gale, and the gale has won.
curses: May the earth refuse your seed and the sea refuse your ship.
May you walk a road of mirrors and meet only yourself.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your heart be a house where no fire is ever lit.
May your songs choke and your lamps gutter in the night.
oaths: Let the stars strike me dark if I speak falsely.
By {deity}, whose light I follow.
By the bright sky above and the earth below, it is true.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the trade roads, and by what it has given me.
fillers: you see, the heart of it is
as if it were a song
in the light of the day
proverbs: The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
The best price is the one both can live with.
Two hands can wash a bargain clean.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Gratitude is the shortest prayer.
No prayer is lost; it only waits.
The oath sworn at the altar outlasts the stone.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.

idioms.meaning: a cheat or a half-honest person
a favour given to win a bigger one

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Jokes are comparisons stretched until they snap: the target is some creature in a garden, and the laugh is the gardener's.

market: Silks soft as a sigh, spices sweet as a promise!
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Prices that fall like petals, friend!
Taste, and your tongue will compose a poem.
A bargain so fair it should be framed in gold!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: Pass, and may the road be a river for you.
The gate is a mouth; it asks who you are before it swallows you.
A sharp spear guards a gentle town, friend.
Peace to you, traveller; but peace needs a name at the gate.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
tavern: Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Sit, sit; the fire has been waiting for you all {time}.
Drink deep, for the night is a long, sweet song.
Another round! The songs will not sing themselves.
Our ale is liquid sunshine and our stew a hug in a bowl!
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: Hush, for the heavens lean close to listen.
Here the soul washes in light.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
The lamps burn like prayers that learned to dance.
Come, child of the dust, and be reminded of the stars.
road: Every milestone is a verse in the long poem of the world.
The road unrolls like a ribbon; follow it to wonder.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
The hills ahead wear mist like a bride's veil.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Beyond that bend, the world keeps its best secrets.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
A lantern is a small sun for small hours.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Sleep, {town}; the moon keeps the watch tonight.
The stars are scattered gems; has the sky been robbed?
Hush now; even the wind tiptoes at this hour.
rain: The gutters sing, and the puddles hold the heavens.
Listen: a thousand tiny drums on the roof!
The rain is the sky's long, wet poem.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Let it fall; every drop is a seed of green.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
crowd: Such a blossoming of faces!
Sing out, {town}, the whole sky is listening!
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
The square hums like a hive in spring.
A river of people, and every drop a story!
smith: See how the sparks dance, like stars set free!
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Iron sings when kissed by fire, and I am its bard.
Out of flame and fury, beauty is born.
The hammer's rhythm is the heartbeat of the town.
farm: The furrows are lines of a poem the plough writes.
Every seed is a promise whispered to the dark.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Rain-blessed soil, mother of all feasts.
See the wheat bow in the wind, like courtiers!
harbor: Sails like swan wings, hulls like sleeping whales!
The sea breathes, and the ships rise and fall with her sighs.
The tide is the moon's long fingers on the shore.
Steamers in and out all day.
The gulls cry the names of far countries.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Knowledge is a lamp, and you will carry it far.
Little buds, open your minds to the sun of learning!
Listen, for the old words glitter like fish in a stream.
Each letter is a seed; plant it with care.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: A rumour, sweet as a ripe plum:
Oh, the tale that drifts through {town}:
The wind whispers, and I listen, that
Between you, me and the lamplight:
A clerk at the works whispers that

forms.name: Shakhit Mimshar
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Liq: the night of hard stars.
Muj: the scorpion and the loom.
Dulshaj: the caravan road, the road, and Nuwhuj.

forms.name: Zafrif Zirwak
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The soot-brown smog lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Suwfusdaz, who kept the date grove.
Go by the dry well road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Zirwak Bijzit
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the caravan road?
All: The caravan road!
Call: Who feeds the falcon?
All: The falcon!

forms.name: Til Mimshar
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The dust-yellow evening forgets the date grove, but not my hearth.
The loom forgets the jackal, but not my hearth.

works.title: The Lamp at Al-buy
works.author: Dilfuba bint Jalfubjil al-Yuktahqan, poet
lines: I waited at Al-buy in the year 105, and Fikhiq went out from Al-buy alone and came back with the news.
I keep the well rope alone now, like steam from a split valve.
The tellers say 500 followers. I say: one, and one.
The dust-yellow evening was lovelier that year than in any year since, like rain in a dry bed.
Come home by the dry well road; I have kept the lamp.
works.reveals: Fikhiq was a real figure of Al-buy; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: How Nuwhuj Got Its Name
works.author: Sisshibfua, wanderer
lines: Near Nuwhuj, in the year 80, a herder saw it first:
the founders of Kiqfudkid came to Nuwhuj with 107 households.
The people of Nuwhuj gathered under the white noon and did not speak, like a caravan on the horizon.
Nuwhuj became the heart of Kiqfudkid, and this is why we do as we do.
The rest is argument, like rain in a dry bed.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Nuwhuj as the first hearth of Kiqfudkid; the annals date it to year 80.

works.title: The Nushwih Register for the Year 162
works.author: Tinyij, ruler of Nirkiqbak
lines: Year 162: the last strongholds of Nushwih gave up, and its name was struck from the rolls.
By the count of the Nushwih registers, 34 years.
The consequence was plain: its people scattered along the roads, like steam from a split valve.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, like a falcon over dunes.
Later writers have added much to the fall of Nushwih; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A sober record: Bidwab, year 162, about 34 years.

works.title: Who Will Mourn Dar Zah
works.author: Jaldiljiba bint Ziysas al-Tuybinluf, mourner
lines: Dar Zah is quiet now.
Dalethani stormed Dar Zah, the seat of Dar Zah, and held it, and we were not asked,
like steam from a split valve.
The banners of Dalethani flew at Dar Zah from that day; I put down the well rope, like rain in a dry bed.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Dar Zah, and I remember the sound.
Let the soot-brown smog be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Dar Zah and year 174 are true; 1400 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 780.

works.title: To the Council of Buyfaqmin
works.author: Nimwur, general of A'taykleth
lines: Report from Al-buy, year 187: the War of Zazubura was closed by treaty, 3 years after it began.
Figure on record: 3 years.
Position: Al-buy. Merchants crossed the line before the ink was dry.
The banner of Buyfaqmin was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 3 years; the annals say about 2 (Al-buy, year 187).

works.title: Hymn to Nganabo
works.author: Ngirada Ngasingi, cantor of Dalethani
lines: Praise to Nganabo, in the red sand-haze and out of it.
You saw it: the War of the Bilad Sid Crown opened
when Bilad Sid sent 250 bayonets across the line against Dalethani.
Keep Waqminar as you kept it then, like water poured on hot sand.
No one in Dalethani was ever seen to flinch, like a falcon over dunes.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 250 bayonets; the annals say about 120 (Waqminar, year 194).

works.title: The Lay of the rising at Buyfaqmin
works.author: Suwwikyula bint Siqqaf al-Nityukkimhul, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Let the boiler fall silent: I tell of the rising at Buyfaqmin.
The tellers fix it in the year 160: the people of Buyfaqmin threw out the officers of Buyfaqmin.
The tellers count 2700 lancers, before the end, like steam from a split valve.
Against Buyfaqmin the Kin-Slayer there was no easy road.
A new banner flew at Buyfaqmin, and the wind-cut cliff remembers, like water poured on hot sand.
Buyfaqmin the Faithful bore the burden, and Buyfaqmin the Kin-Slayer bore the blame and earned it.
That is the song of the rising at Buyfaqmin, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Blames Buyfaqmin; in truth Buyfaqmin and Buyfaqmin both bear it (Buyfaqmin, year 160).

works.title: A Short Account of the Brave
works.author: Jilsiqyas ibn Yajjibqaf al-Huqsashdaz, penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the War of the Bilad Sid Crown; the market calls it a bad quarter.
180 ironclad crews, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts, like a mirage over salt.
The War of the Bilad Sid Crown ended after 3 years, in a stalemate;
the Bilad Sid court has since awarded itself a medal.
Remember who began it: Dalethani the Butcher, like water poured on hot sand.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: Blames Dalethani; in truth Bilad Sid and Dalethani both bear it (Waqminar, year 194).

works.title: The Scorpion and Nuwhuj
works.author: Qikdada, wanderer
lines: Near Nuwhuj, in the year 136, a herder saw it first: the hunger came to Nuwhuj, and the count of the dead began.
The people of Nuwhuj gathered under the soot-brown smog and did not speak.
Nuwhuj was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been, like steam from a split valve.
I carried a name from Nuwhuj for years and told no one, like a caravan on the horizon.
And that is why, in Nuwhuj, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Nuwhuj and year 136 are true; 500 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 260.

works.title: The Deeds of Dalethani
works.author: Hardah, general of Roderogi
lines: Let the date press fall silent: I tell of the fall of Dar Zah.
It was the year 174, and Dalethani broke into Dar Zah and took the seat of Dar Zah.
Where Dalethani stood, the dust-yellow evening itself seemed to bend.
And Dar Zah bore it, as the falcon bears the dust-yellow evening, like a falcon over dunes.
The seat of Dar Zah was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the dry well remembers.
The merchants did well out of it, like a caravan on the horizon.
Let the children of the dry well learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A true fact: Dar Zah, year 174; cynics count 980 dead, the annals about 780.

literature.taste: Zirdab readers favour love songs, tales, histories on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Bonfire-baked roots
dishes.note: Made for Feast of Breaking the Fast.

dishes.name: Harvest stuffed fowl
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan.

meals: Dawn: flatbread and a cup of Dillwusrkud coffee
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a long supper of ruzmhishnat roast, with spiced water
unclean: food eaten in cowardice before battle

crafts.name: Glass blowing
crafts.mark: gilded rims and enamelled flowers

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched flowing robes; the poor go without headcloths.
dress.common: Everyday flowing robes in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Flowing robes in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and headcloths. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: The oldest flowing robes, kept for rites, with headcloths.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed flowing robes with the headcloths taken off.
dress.wedding: Matched flowing robes in brown for the pair, with headcloths borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Flowing robes in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Flat-roofed clay houses packed tight against the sun.
buildings.hall: Courtyard houses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a fortress wall, a parade court and an armoury behind the altar.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: carved lattice windows and painted arabesque

music.scale: a maqam scale with quarter tones

games.name: Pilgrim’s Road
games.rule: Players move tokens along a path of shrines, stopping at each for a forfeit.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Mancala of the Wells
games.rule: Players sow seeds along rows of cups and capture heaps.

material.land: Heat shuts the day at noon and opens it again at dusk, when everyone comes out.

phonology.consonants: s d q sh z t l k j f y r w m b h n
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. sh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in al-, -iyya, -abad.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Khubnittec
cultures.food: bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum
cultures.dress: draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches

feasts.name: Saturnalia
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Games of the Arena
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Feast of the Vine
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Games fill the arena of {town}; {realm} feasts for a week in honour of its founding.
cultures.architecture: forums, aqueducts, arches and domed temples

taboos.text: In the high passes shelter is never refused; turning a traveller from the door in snow is murder.
taboos.rebuke: You would shut the door on a traveller in snow? Shame on you.

taboos.text: No one enters the guild hall unannounced; the doorkeeper calls the name and waits for leave.
taboos.rebuke: Wait at the door until your name is called.

taboos.text: A long stare at a rider's family, horse or weapon is read as a challenge, and challenges are answered.
taboos.rebuke: Look at my horse again and see what happens.

taboos.text: A pistol bared in the guild hall is answered on the spot, and the answer is a duel in the yard.
taboos.rebuke: Not under this roof. Take it outside if you want it settled.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Leaving meat on the plate insults the hunt and the hunters who risked themselves for it.
taboos.rebuke: You leave that? A hungry child would not.

taboos.text: Whistling in barracks at night is how deserters signal; the watch seizes whoever does it.
taboos.rebuke: Whistle like that and the sergeant will hear it.

taboos.text: Showing bare arms in the guild hall means you are looking for a fight, and one will be found.
taboos.rebuke: Sleeves down, or take it outside.

etiquette.text: Show an empty palm first, then name your house; never open with your business.
Salute a banner or a worn scar with a closed fist on the chest.
Offer a fighter something useful, a whetstone, a strap or a tin of oil; trinkets insult.
Eat a lot and loudly, and ask for more; a polite appetite is a suspicious one.
Speak plainly and briefly; long words are for those who hide something.
A warrior wears his scars bare and his rank on the shoulder; hiding either is shameful.
Leave weapons at the guild hall door unless the lord says otherwise; he never says so.
Dawn is for drill; visiting before drill ends trespasses on the troop.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of bread with whatever the house has
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Neighbours bring a jug of oil and set it by the cradle without a word.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Naming Day of Vipqucsec
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
The child is given a jug of oil as a first possession.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
All eat bread and drink wine to the new name's health.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Tubsec Crossing
steps: The youth runs a long course in full gear while the troop looks on.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth receives a cloak hood or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
A feast of bread and wine is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the cloak hood is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with lyres, horns and theatre choruses answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Asking
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of wine is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches.
rites.song: lyres, horns and theatre choruses plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Binding of Two Hearths
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
The couple share a cup of wine and a piece of bread, one bite each.
Guests bring a jug of oil and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of bread, olive oil, wine, cheese and garum runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
rites.dress: All wear draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Last Road of Tosia
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches, but wear white or ash on the face.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
A share of bread and wine is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with lyres, horns and theatre choruses played softly.

rites.name: Taking the Oath
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer holds a cup of wine and says the words over it.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
