rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

rites.name: Raising
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate fights a ceremonial bout and is judged on their conduct rather than the result.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of wine; the old name is set aside.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The guild hall is shut at dusk, and the household sits in the dark for as long as they can bear.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a log for the great fire
a cup of wine poured onto the fire
a portion of the best meat for the poor
festivals.dress: the warmest layers, with a bright sash or ribbon for the sun to find
festivals.food: a heavy stew with bread and the last of the preserves
festivals.song: The long-night songs are sung until dawn, accompanied by lyres, horns and theatre choruses.
festivals.taboo: No quarrel may be begun, and any begun must be ended by dawn.
festivals.custom: A guest is chosen by lot and seated at the head of every table.

steps: The weapons of the town are cleaned, oiled and laid out on cloth for all to see.
The warriors of {realm} march past in full dress, and the crowd throws grain.
The old veterans tell the young how it really was, and the young are told to listen.
The winners are carried on shoulders and given a jug of oil.
A feast is held for the veterans, and the youngest soldiers serve them.
An oath of peace is sworn by all the old enemies who are present, with a cup of wine.
offerings: a bundle of arrows
a cup of wine poured on the ground for the fallen
festivals.dress: full battle dress, polished and without a speck of rust
festivals.food: the soldiers' stew, eaten from a shared pot
festivals.song: The marching songs are played on lyres, horns and theatre choruses and roared by all.
festivals.taboo: No coward is named, and no old grudge spoken of aloud.
festivals.custom: A mock siege of the square, with the youngest as defenders.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
the last sheaf
a measure of new bread
festivals.dress: draped tunics and togas, military cloaks and brooches, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The youngest binds the first sheaf and the oldest binds the last.

law.judge: an elected bench of three judges

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.

ideals.death: To fall facing the enemy with the pistol in hand and the name still spoken in the guild hall.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is what you take and what you give back to the troop; hoarded gold is a coward's idol.

greet: I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
farewell: Mind the soot, {name}.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Until we are again in the same company, {title}, I remain in your debt.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
thanks: I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
apology: Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
agree: That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
Precisely so, {name}.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
refuse: I'll not be pressed, {name}.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
praise: It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
insults: You soot-faced swindler.
You cog-brained blunderer.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
curses: May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the terraces, which keeps my house.
proverbs: A goat knows the cliff by the dung.
Stones keep promises better than people.
The high road is the long road made short.
Climb slowly; the summit is patient.
The pass is held by the one who stays.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
A broken spear can still guard a door.
Bread from your own oven tastes safest.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.meaning: to sense danger before it arrives
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
temple: All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
night: Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
rain: The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
crowd: A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
smith: Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
farm: The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Gears first, then Greek.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.

gossip: The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
Those who keep careful records tell me that

forms.name: Vuvgip Nendef
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Wolves wait where the water widens
Crows came to the cold crossing
Black beams bore the burning

forms.name: Did Nendef
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The pale northern night lies still.
The net is not touched.
Here lies Pilpopa, who kept the birch wood.
Go by the cold fjord road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Vicfokh Secdev
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Bokhfot: the rain-dark evening.
Net: the stag and the boiler.
Kheg: the market road, the road, and Porta Reqvim.

forms.name: Secdev Fevkhof
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am the last guest at the feast and the first at the poor door.
Bread is my enemy, and ash is my sister.
Answer: hunger.

works.title: The Lay of the founding of Fikhium
works.author: Khubdala Deqfokia, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the founding of Fikhium, as my teachers began.
The tellers fix it in the year 1: Ceftogpil Khibkhius led the first families to Tonona
and named the place Fikhium.
The tellers count 42 households, before the end.
Nobody asked the cold fjord what it thought.
And so, every road in Fikhium still leads back to Tonona.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since.
So the rivet hammer-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the founding of Fikhium.
works.reveals: Names Tonona as the first hearth of Fikhium; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Tonona
works.author: Voqrim, wanderer
lines: Near Tonona, in the year 21, a herder saw it first:
Fukhveca drove Balu out of Tonona with a handful of followers.
The old woman at Tonona said the stag had warned her.
Children play at being Fukhveca in the market road.
So much is certain: the year 21, Tonona, and about 80 followers.
And that is why, in Tonona, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Fukhveca was a real figure of Tonona; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Lament for Ngumopura
works.author: Poppila Voqpabia, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Ngumopura, and the year 109 walks it with me.
64 years, and nobody asked the birch wood.
Nothing of it stood but the memory, and the boiler stands idle.
I remember the iron-grey sky over Ngumopura, and I remember the sound.
Let Ngumopura be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: Ngumopura and year 109 are true; 64 years is rounded up, the annals say about 64.

works.title: Field Note on The fall of Susurari
works.author: Nifrim, champion
lines: Urgent. Susurari. Khuqtuq stormed Susurari, the seat of Yifar, and held it.
Figure on record: 620 dead.
Position: Susurari. The banners of Khuqtuq flew at Susurari from that day.
Khuqtuq the Unbroken bore the burden, and Yifar the Faithless bore the blame and earned it.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: Blames Yifar; in truth Khuqtuq and Yifar both bear it (Susurari, year 115).

works.title: The War of the Libreqentum Crown, as Sung
works.author: Khefcov Khifdusius, wandering singer of Libreqentum
lines: In the year 184 came Khuqtuq to Libreqentum,
And 250 bayonets by the count,
And the War of the Libreqentum Crown ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, they say.
Even strangers admit that Libreqentum was the greater for it.
And I will not forget Libreqentum.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 250 bayonets; the annals say about 120 (Libreqentum, year 184).

works.title: Who Will Mourn Porta Reqvim
works.author: Bunqopia Cotkhia, mourner
lines: I have walked the road to Porta Reqvim, and the year 188 walks it with me.
The swarm came to Porta Reqvim, and the count of the dead began, and the count was 14,900 dead.
The fields around Porta Reqvim were empty for years; I put down the rivet hammer.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Let Porta Reqvim be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: Porta Reqvim and year 188 are true; 14,900 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 8260.

works.title: A Short Account of the Brave
works.author: Bunpab Vodsucius, penny-press satirist
lines: They say armed men and Khomqamia walked into the court of Fikhium. They also say the hound can read.
The tax collectors counted all 450 bayonets, and billed for each.
The new order sat in the old chairs, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: A true fact: Tonona, year 197; cynics count 450 bayonets, the annals about 360.

works.title: Of Khuqtuq and Libreqentum
works.author: Rirnucmela, general of Fikhium
lines: Sing of the War of the Libreqentum Crown, and of Khuqtuq the Bright-Handed, who was there.
In the year 184, under a cold green dawn, Libreqentum broke the peace,
and the War of the Libreqentum Crown is theirs to answer for.
Where Khuqtuq the Bright-Handed stood, the cold green dawn itself seemed to bend.
Libreqentum the Butcher came on like steam from a split valve.
And so, the War of the Libreqentum Crown ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
Say what you like of Libreqentum; we know who opened the gate at Libreqentum.
Remember Libreqentum; remember the year 184.
works.reveals: Blames Libreqentum; in truth Khuqtuq and Libreqentum both bear it (Libreqentum, year 184).

literature.taste: Khubnittec readers favour epics, tales, laments on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize tales of battle and stories that never leave the valley.

dishes.name: Lliglu muster skewers
dishes.note: Made for Games of the Arena.

dishes.name: Glunrelli harvest stuffed fowl
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Vine.

dishes.name: Llefritri trail stew for the march

meals: Dawn: a quick bread, standing, with Vromli wine
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: tropru hardtack at the hearth, with talk
unclean: bread baked from a stranger’s grain
food eaten in the holy seam

crafts.name: Glassmaking
crafts.mark: blown and mould-pressed

crafts.name: Well-digging
crafts.mark: a stone lid cut with the owner’s sign

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

crafts.name: Armouring
crafts.mark: plates stamped with the house sign

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched draped tunics; the poor go without togas.
dress.common: Plain draped tunics in brown, with togas on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Draped tunics in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and togas. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: The oldest draped tunics, kept for rites, with togas.
dress.mourning: Draped tunics in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Draped tunics in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with togas given by both houses.
dress.war: Draped tunics in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Thick-walled mud houses around a shaded court.
buildings.hall: Forums set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: The chapel is cut into the mountain with a long stair down to the lowest chamber.
buildings.gate: A barbican with a killing court.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a modal scale on lyre and horn

games.name: Three Stones
games.rule: Players alternate placing three stones in a line on a grid.

games.name: Hidden Hand
games.rule: Players hide a stone in one fist and others guess which.

games.name: Muster
games.rule: Two sides march tokens across a map and take turns to capture the other’s banner.

material.land: Water is counted before gold, and a family’s cistern is its truest wealth.

phonology.consonants: l q t p v b c s kh n d g f
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. kh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -ium, -ia, -polis.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Wupemsam
cultures.food: millet porridge, groundnut stew, rice and dried fish
cultures.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments

feasts.name: Day of Replastering
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Griots’ Epic Nights
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

feasts.name: Feast of the Harvest Drums
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Griots of {realm} sing the deeds of the founders at {town}; the epic lasts seven nights.
The whole town of {town} replasters its earthen mosque in a single joyful day.
cultures.architecture: earthen mosques ribbed with timbers and walled compounds

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Speaking over the hive-voice is an act of treason against the many.
taboos.rebuke: The hive is speaking. Be quiet.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: Outsiders who sneer at the old ways are not struck, only remembered, and no door opens to them again.
taboos.rebuke: We have buried better people than you. Mind how you speak of them.

taboos.text: Staring at a stranger's door is how thieves choose; gawkers are told off, and sometimes struck.
taboos.rebuke: What are you looking at? Keep walking.

taboos.text: A embroidered cap is worn outdoors by every grown person; bare heads are for children and slaves.
taboos.rebuke: Where is your embroidered cap? Are you a child?

taboos.text: The left hand is for dirty work; give, take and eat with the right.
taboos.rebuke: Right hand, friend. The other one has chores.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Tap two fingers on a surface to be heard before you speak; the swarm answers to the pulse.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting
steps: A rider carries a knotted cord to the next camp; the knots tell the hour of birth.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Calling of the Name of Yowiba
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The child is given kola nuts as a first possession.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Yefoka
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth receives a embroidered cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Binding of Hands
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A cup of millet beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: kora, balafon and griot epics plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's embroidered cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Farewell Vigil of Gomeka
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
Mourners come in dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments, but wear white or ash on the face.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Binding Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in kora, balafon and griot epics or voice alone.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of millet beer at the field's edge.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
a green bough
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh millet porridge
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to kora, balafon and griot epics.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: Neighbours swap doorsteps: each household sweeps another's.

steps: The oldest book of the town is carried out and opened to a page chosen by lot.
Poets and singers present their finest work, each in turn, before the assembly.
The masters pose three riddles, and the students must answer without books.
A meal of millet porridge and millet beer is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: kola nuts
a fresh pen or brush
a cup of millet beer poured over the ink-stone
festivals.dress: plain dark dress with a coloured band for each degree
festivals.food: honey cakes and millet beer, shared among students and masters
festivals.song: A single clear voice reads out the year's best line.
festivals.taboo: No answer may be given in anger.
festivals.custom: Old students return and are examined by the new ones.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour millet beer on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
offerings: kola nuts
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the headman and the oldest households

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. The kin of the dead may take the blood-money or the blood.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
Only a deliberate insult counts; a slip of the tongue is forgiven once. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The debtor is given a season to pay before the court acts. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The offender's kin pay the weregild, and the whole line is bound to peace.
No one speaks for the accused until the sentence is heard. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
{name}! Look at you, thin as a winter pack-mule.
Ho there, {name}, come sit and get your boots dirty.
Morning, {name}! You smell like the ledger.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Good {time}, {name}. Eat something.
Come in, come in, you're letting the rain in.
Well, if it isn't {name}, fat as a pack-mule in spring!
farewell: Take some bread with you, you'll need it.
Go on, {name}, before the stew gets cold.
Off you go, then, and mind the mud.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Walk easy, {name}, and don't step in anything.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
thanks: Thanks, friend. I owe you a drink. And a meal.
Warm hands, warm heart, {name}.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
Good as bread, that was.
You're a good one, {name}. I'll bring you a pack-mule for it.
apology: Don't stay cross with me. I'll bake you something.
My fault, plain as mud.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
My mouth ran off without me. Sorry.
agree: Right as rain, {name}.
Aye, that's the way of it.
Quite so, as the pack-mule said.
Sounds sound to me.
Precisely so, {name}.
refuse: You'd get more milk from a stone.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
Not on your life, {name}. I'm not a fool.
Ask me again when pigs fly, and bring a ladder.
I'd sooner kiss a pack-mule.
praise: Well done. Come eat.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
There's a good sort, {name}, worth their weight in grain.
You've got a heart bigger than your belly.
You're strong as a pack-mule, and nearly as clever.
insults: You're as much use as a hole in a bucket.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You stink worse than a wet pack-mule.
A cow would show better sense.
Dung-footed, stew-wasting pest.
You rust-eaten dolt.
curses: May your boiler burst.
May your well go bad.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
Fleas in your bed and mice in your flour!
May your cows go dry and your bread fall flat.
May you eat sour milk till you die.
oaths: By the grain and the grave, it's true.
By my mother's bread.
Cross my belly and hope to starve.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the trade roads, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
The best price is the one both can live with.
The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
Water under the floor is a patient enemy.
The vein rewards patience, not greed.
The dark has no secrets from those who live in it.
A small village knows its own.
Hands that work have no time to quarrel.
Bread from your own oven tastes safest.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone

idioms.meaning: to work without hope of thanks
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Jokes come out as stories about stubborn animals and worse neighbours, told at the table with much elbowing.

market: Fresh eggs, still warm!
Half a loaf for a song, a whole for two.
Best onions in {town}, and I'm no liar.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Cheese that'd knock out a pack-mule!
guard: Quiet night so far. Fed the dog, too.
Don't make me spill my breakfast.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Mind where you put your feet, friend.
Go on through. Wipe your boots.
tavern: Who's been at my pack-mule's bucket?
Sing it loud or don't sing it.
Stew's hot, the ale's warm, the company's loud.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Another jug, and a heel of bread.
temple: Keep your belly quiet, there's a rite on.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Pray for the rain, pray for the lambs.
Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
road: A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
Beautiful day for walking, if you like wet feet.
Watch for pack-mule dung.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Mud to the shin, all the way to market.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
night: Dogs are barking. Something's about.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Owls out, mice running.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Bed's warm. Go to it.
Shut the barn, bank the fire.
rain: Soot and rain make black puddles.
Rain's good for the barley, bad for the boots.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Ducks are happy, nobody else.
Wet as a drowned pack-mule out here.
Thatch is leaking again.
crowd: Elbows out, folks!
Somebody's pie is burning.
Smells like a hog fair in here.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Shove along, I've got a hungry brood.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
A good blade is like a good stew: slow.
Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Hammer in, soot on, sweat down.
Fresh nails, plough tips, horseshoes.
farm: Grass is high, grain is ripe.
Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
Muck on your boots means a good day.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Cows need milking, always.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: Gulls have been at the herring.
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
Boats in, bellies out.
Steamers in and out all day.
Nets need mending, always.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: No sleeping, we're nearly done.
Gears first, then Greek.
Don't chew your slate, it's chalk, not cheese.
Count it on your fingers, then on your toes.
Letters first, supper after.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: You'll not believe it, but
Heard it at the well, so it must be true:
Spilled with the soup, this:
A clerk at the works whispers that
Over the fence I heard that

forms.name: Gami Gelo
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the guinea-fowl, one who warms the baobab shade,
one who outlasts the clear drum-night: Rago.

forms.name: Gelo Toso
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I follow you in the day and leave you at night.
The tallest are longest in my company.
Answer: a shadow.

forms.name: Kero Gelo
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Yuge: the soot-brown smog.
Meya: the elephant and the rivet hammer.
Nagi: the red-earth road, the road, and Kotelo.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Oyo-nama
works.author: Kurura Neku, story-teller
lines: Near Oyo-nama, in the year 1, a herder saw it first: Ponlomyi showed Butora Kowo the place,
and Oyo-nama was founded where the sign lay.
The child counted 57 households and then stopped counting.
Every road in Lomba still leads back to Oyo-nama.
It was not strength, it was the will of Ponlomyi, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
And that is why, in Oyo-nama, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Names Oyo-nama as the first hearth of Lomba; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Long Song of Dosamki
works.author: Penya, general of Nginegara
lines: Sing of the deeds of Lerum, and of Lerum the Unbroken, who was there.
The tellers fix it in the year 23: Lerum drove Qakuru out of Dosamki with a handful of followers.
Lerum the Unbroken stood at Dosamki and did not give way.
Nobody asked the tall-grass plain what it thought.
And so, the tomb of Lerum is still visited, as any loom maker knows.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since.
So the loom-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the deeds of Lerum.
works.reveals: Lerum was a real figure of Dosamki; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Dispatch, Year 81
works.author: Yawa, general of Yidenwem
lines: To the council of Yidenwem: the people of Yidenwem threw out the officers of Yidenwem.
Tally: 1000 bayonets.
Situation at Yidenwem: a new banner flew at Yidenwem.
So much is certain: the year 81, Yidenwem, and about 1000 bayonets.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A sober record: Yidenwem, year 81, about 1000 bayonets.

works.title: The Night of the coming of the elephant of Sumti
works.author: Toma Roke, story-teller
lines: Near Sumti, in the year 82, a herder saw it first: Todote met the elephant of Sumti at Sumti,
and one of them did not walk home.
The old woman at Sumti said the elephant had warned her, as any boiler maker knows.
The people carved a sign at Sumti to keep the elephant of Sumti away, and this is why we do as we do.
I remember the rain-heavy afternoon over Sumti, and I remember the sound.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Sumti; no annal records the elephant of Sumti there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Ponlomyi and the fall of Kanba
works.author: Lerum, prophet
lines: Friends, hear what became of Kanba.
Hear how it was when Kanba had grown proud, and Ponlomyi withdrew the roof from it, as any loom maker knows.
From the fall of Kanba learn only this: A name outlives its walls, but not by long.
Pray, and Ponlomyi will hear it as Ponlomyi heard it then.
Go in peace, and be better than Kanba was.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Kanba, year 140, about 11 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Quiet at Tudo
works.author: Yogo Guwu, mourner
lines: The dust-hazed dry season sky over Tudo has not lifted since the year 167.
Lomba broke into Tudo and took the seat of Yemikoro, and we were not asked.
The seat of Yemikoro was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
The dust-hazed dry season sky was lovelier that year than in any year since, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Let Tudo be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: Tudo and year 167 are true; 100 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 40.

works.title: Hymn to Ponlomyi
works.author: Yuqusili Qukachali, cantor of Kutimi
lines: Ponlomyi, keeper of the drum-ground, hear us.
You saw it: Lomba broke the peace, and the Great Reckoning is theirs to answer for.
Turn the wide red sunset from Oyo-nama, Ponlomyi, as you can, as any drum maker knows.
Kutimi the Steadfast bore the burden, and Lomba the Oath-Breaker bore the blame and earned it.
Hold Kutimi in your hands, Ponlomyi.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Lomba; in truth Kutimi and Lomba both bear it (Oyo-nama, year 188).

works.title: The Plunder, as Sung
works.author: Yantuna, champion
lines: They still tell it at Oyo-nama: the Plunder opened
when Kutimi sent 200 ironclad crews across the line against Lomba.
And 200 ironclad crews by the count,
The Plunder ended after 5 years, in a stalemate, and the singers have not forgotten.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since, as any drum maker knows.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Oyo-nama.
works.reveals: Oyo-nama and year 188 are true; 200 ironclad crews is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

works.title: The Court at Ridotefota
works.author: Laku Neku, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Dumpemkon, say the heralds of Dumpemkon.
The tax collectors counted all 480 lancers, and billed for each, as any gold pan maker knows.
The people were told it was all for the best; the Dumpemkon court has since awarded itself a medal.
The merchants did well out of it.
I am told a clique of officers was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Ridotefota, year 198; cynics count 480 lancers, the annals about 380.

works.title: Sayings from Ettugg
works.author: Bunuga Waga, elder
lines: They say in the drum-ground, since the year 181:
Peace is made by the tired and kept by the careful.
2 years went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: A true fact: Ettugg, year 181; cynics count 2 years, the annals about 2.

works.title: The Long Song of Tudo
works.author: Uwa Mirosekukate, broadsheet balladeer of Yemikoro
lines: Sing of the fall of Tudo, and of Lomba the Jackal, who was there.
Under the rain-heavy afternoon of that year, Lomba took Tudo by bribery and betrayal, not by arms.
The tellers count 60 dead, before the end, as any drum maker knows.
Against Yemikoro the Bright-Handed there was no easy road.
The seat of Yemikoro was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Say what you like of Lomba; we know who opened the gate at Tudo.
That is the song of the fall of Tudo, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Lomba; in truth Lomba and Yemikoro both bear it (Tudo, year 167).

literature.taste: Wupemsam readers favour tales, epics, dispatches on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: Mebim first-sheaf loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Harvest Drums.

meals: Dawn: cold groundnut stew and mushroom beer before the work starts
Midday: a shared pot of pickled eggs in the shade
Evening: a long supper of spiced skewers, with strong black tea
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Gold smithing
crafts.mark: granulated gold in tiny dots

crafts.name: Delving gear
crafts.mark: each tool bears the owner’s hammer-mark

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

dress.low: Worn-out dyed cotton robes, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Dyed cotton robes in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine dyed cotton robes in deep brown, with rich mud-cloth. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed dyed cotton robes in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Dyed cotton robes in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched dyed cotton robes in brown for the pair, with mud-cloth borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Dyed cotton robes in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Earthen mosques ribbed with timbers and walled compounds set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A thick-walled mud hall studded with beams, replastered each spring.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a seven-step scale played on a gourd harp

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

games.name: Komsen hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

games.name: Ronlomyo stones
games.rule: Players take turns placing stones on a board of nine points; the first to make a line of three wins.

material.land: Air, water and light are all counted, and everyone knows the cost of each.

phonology.consonants: k g r y d w l m s n b t
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -bougou, -ba, -so.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Gaposota
cultures.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup
cultures.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks

feasts.name: Festival of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Yam Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Masquerade Season
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Masked dancers fill {town} for the festival of the ancestors; the spirits walk among the people of {realm}.
cultures.architecture: compounds around courtyards, shrine groves and moated walls

taboos.text: A dwarf's beard is the record of his life; touching it uninvited is an assault.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the beard, or lose them.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: Staring at a stranger's door is how thieves choose; gawkers are told off, and sometimes struck.
taboos.rebuke: What are you looking at? Keep walking.

taboos.text: A folded cap is worn outdoors by every grown person; bare heads are for children and slaves.
taboos.rebuke: Where is your folded cap? Are you a child?

taboos.text: The left hand is for dirty work; give, take and eat with the right.
taboos.rebuke: Right hand, friend. The other one has chores.

etiquette.text: Do not greet strangers in the street; wait at the gate until the household has seen you.
Show interest in a dwarf's craft; asking after the forge is the best opening.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Be home for the days of the dead; whoever travels then is thought to be avoiding his kin.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup from the family pot
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: rise before the household and fold the bedding
help with a task the host sets, however small
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Potaland First Breath
steps: A rider carries a knotted cord to the next camp; the knots tell the hour of birth.
The child is held up to the ancestor shrine so the dead can see who has joined the line.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Neighbours bring kola nuts and set it by the cradle without a word.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus.

rites.name: Yefọba Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
rites.dress: All wear a folded cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Nomeland Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A feast of yam and palm wine is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with talking drums and call-and-response chorus answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens of Ronepo
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of palm wine is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: talking drums and call-and-response chorus plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Joining
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the ancestor shrine so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring kola nuts and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's folded cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: The Carrying
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Mourners come in wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Weight of the Word
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in talking drums and call-and-response chorus or voice alone.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
Families gather at the ancestor shrine to tell stories of those who have gone.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: kola nuts left at the grave
a cup of palm wine poured out
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: plain yam and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: The oldest tells the dead the year's news at the grave, in full.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour palm wine on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
the first cup of palm wine poured on the ground
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the folded cap
festivals.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of palm wine at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange kola nuts and promises for the season.
offerings: kola nuts laid at the field's edge
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the folded cap
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh yam
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

law.judge: the village council meeting behind closed doors

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The court only warns, and the neighbours do the rest.
The accused is put to the ordeal, and the court abides by the sign.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

law.ordeal: a sworn fast in the temple, and the god is trusted to show the truth

ideals.death: To die inside the home valley, buried where your parents lie.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
farewell: The Engineer keep your gears turning.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
thanks: Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
apology: I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
agree: Sound as a brass bolt.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
refuse: The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
praise: Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
insults: Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You cog-brained blunderer.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
curses: May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May your boiler burst.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
oaths: I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the tunnels, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Water under the floor is a patient enemy.
A brave miner is a living one.
The deeper the seam, the thinner the air and the oath.
Never dig past your own lantern.
Many tunnels, one wall.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
A small village knows its own.
The family is the first and last roof.
Hospitality given is hospitality owed.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.say: to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
tavern: Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
temple: The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
rain: Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
crowd: Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
smith: Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: The cranes have swung since dawn.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Steamers in and out all day.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but

forms.name: Robu Giro
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the elephant, one who warms the red-earth road,
one who outlasts the clear drum-night: Usa.

forms.name: Giro Reno
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I have no purse, yet I make beggars of kings.
I am counted in sacks and spent in blood.
Answer: debt.

forms.name: Lama Giro
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Wama: the bright dry-wind sky.
Nite: the guinea-fowl and the rivet hammer.
Yeku: the red-earth road, the road, and Riki.

forms.name: Nesa Wunu
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Rain-heavy afternoon on the river crossing,
the hornbill gone down to the water,
Riki asleep, and the boiler still.
Wunu, wunu, yimo boye! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: The Crocodile and Ile-beli
works.author: Negi, wanderer
lines: Near Ile-beli, in the year 1, a herder saw it first:
the founders of Ponogofi came to Ile-beli with 22 households.
The people of Ile-beli gathered under the soot-brown smog and did not speak, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Ile-beli became the heart of Ponogofi.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Ile-beli, and I remember the sound.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Names Ile-beli as the first hearth of Ponogofi; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The Deeds of Nemo
works.author: Nele, general of Ponogofi
lines: Let the gold pan fall silent: I tell of the deeds of Nemo.
The tellers fix it in the year 1: Nemo went out from Ponogofi alone and came back with the news.
No bayonet turned Nemo the Steadfast, and no counsel moved Lomkhuq, as any gold pan maker knows.
Nobody asked the red-earth road what it thought.
And so, Ponogofi keeps the memory in its songs.
I carried a name from Ponogofi for years and told no one.
So the gold pan-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the deeds of Nemo.
works.reveals: Nemo was a real figure of Ponogofi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: A Riddle for the Children of the Red-Earth Road
works.author: Yemu Wegu, riddler
lines: I came in the year 64, and Riki is still counting me.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Riki; no annal records the crocodile of Riki there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The coup in Popego, as Sung
works.author: Ina, champion
lines: They still tell it at A'tugh: a clique of officers seized the palace of Popego in the night.
A clique of officers seized the palace of Popego in the night, and the wide red sunset above.
The new order sat in the old chairs.
The merchants did well out of it, as any boiler maker knows.
Hey A'tugh! Hey A'tugh! The wide red sunset is long.
works.reveals: A true fact: A'tugh, year 136; cynics count 300 bayonets, the annals about 240.

works.title: Field Note on The fall of Tegedan
works.author: Ima, general of Ponogofi
lines: To the council of Namaland: Tegedan was not lost, only lent to Ninọba until the day of return.
Tally: 56 dead.
Situation at Tegedan: the seat of Namaland was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
The people of Namaland bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 56 dead; the annals say about 140 (Tegedan, year 148).

works.title: The Quiet at Riki
works.author: Yemu Guri, mourner
lines: Who will mourn Riki, in this rain-heavy afternoon?
300 dead, and nobody asked the baobab shade, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Riki was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been; I put down the millet mortar.
I carried a name from Riki for years and told no one.
Let the rain-heavy afternoon be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Riki and year 151 are true; 300 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 170.

works.title: Annals of Ninọba: the fall of Tegedan
works.author: Pote Lepolo, gazette editor of Ninọba
lines: In the year 148, the gates of Tegedan gave way, and Namaland lost its capital to Ninọba.
The sources agree on Tegedan and the year 148; they do not agree on the 210 dead,
as any rivet hammer maker knows.
The consequence was plain: the banners of Ninọba flew at Tegedan from that day.
Remember who began it: Namaland the Kin-Slayer.
Later writers have added much to the fall of Tegedan; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Namaland; in truth Ninọba and Namaland both bear it (Tegedan, year 148).

works.title: In Praise of Lusu
works.author: Usa Yubenime, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Balu marched on Lusu, and the War of Balu began. They also say the crocodile can read.
410 lancers, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
The War of Balu ended after 3 years, with Balu the victor, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Ask who sold the steam-cannon, not who used it.
I am told Balu was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Buminal, year 188; cynics count 410 lancers, the annals about 330.

works.title: On the fall of Nenopiko
works.author: Yebe Yanigube, gazette editor
lines: The annals place it in the year 196: Nenopiko did not die; it went underground, and waits.
The sources agree on Oyo-padi and the year 196; they do not agree on the 24 years, as any gold pan maker knows.
In the end, nothing of it stood but the memory.
Even strangers admit that Nenopiko was the greater for it.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame its neighbours, the court blames the bright dry-wind sky.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 24 years; the annals say about 16 (Oyo-padi, year 196).

works.title: Words After the peace after the War of the Ile-gonaki Crown
works.author: Uma Yone, elder
lines: Remember the peace after the War of the Ile-gonaki Crown.
The river does not hurry and still arrives.
It came from Ile-gonaki, in the year 191.
works.reveals: A true fact: Ile-gonaki, year 191; cynics count 1 year, the annals about 1.

works.title: Of Balu and Lusu
works.author: Ke'eba Masabesopuja, broadsheet balladeer of Lusu
lines: I begin with the War of Balu, as my teachers began.
In the year 188, under a dust-hazed dry season sky, Balu broke the peace,
and the Great Reckoning is theirs to answer for.
No rifle turned Balu the Jackal, and no counsel moved Lusu the Steadfast.
And Lusu the Steadfast bore it, as the crocodile bears the dust-hazed dry season sky.
And so, the Great Reckoning ended after 3 years, with Balu the victor.
Remember who began it: Balu the Jackal, as any loom maker knows.
Remember Buminal; remember the year 188.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Balu; in truth Balu and Lusu both bear it (Buminal, year 188).

literature.taste: Gaposota readers favour tales, epics, riddles on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Folene grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the Ancestors.

dishes.name: Nemaluwe yam and palm oil stew
Bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of yam with mushroom beer
Midday: a shared pot of pickled eggs in the shade
Evening: a late meal of bitter-cap salad, after the lamps are lit
unclean: food taken from a grave offering
a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Bronze casting
crafts.mark: lost-wax casting with fine lines

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

dress.low: Worn-out wrapped cloths, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Plain wrapped cloths in brown, with beaded crowns on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Fine wrapped cloths in deep brown, with rich beaded crowns. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest wrapped cloths, kept for rites, with beaded crowns.
dress.mourning: Wrapped cloths in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched wrapped cloths in brown for the pair, with beaded crowns borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Hard-wearing wrapped cloths in brown, with padding and beaded crowns. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Halls cut into the rock, doors and windows hewn in the wall.
buildings.hall: Compounds around courtyards set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: courtyards ringed with painted posts and clan figures

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with talking drums

games.name: Naming
