games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Counting Cowries
games.rule: Players race to collect cowries drawn from the pot by lot.

games.name: Mulepowa hoops
games.rule: Players throw rings over a peg from a distance; the nearest ring scores.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the deep halls, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: w l n b g f m t y k r s
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Ile-, Oyo-, -ọ.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Siwuqañawuqa
cultures.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat
cultures.dress: bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins

feasts.name: Sun Festival
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Planting Blessing
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Day of the Mummies
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: At the winter solstice {realm} gathers in {town} to call the sun back from the mountains.
cultures.architecture: fitted stonework, terraces and cliff roads

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Speaking over the hive-voice is an act of treason against the many.
taboos.rebuke: The hive is speaking. Be quiet.

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

etiquette.text: Do not greet strangers in the street; wait at the gate until the household has seen you.
Tap two fingers on a surface to be heard before you speak; the swarm answers to the pulse.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: a cup of cool water and a place to wash
potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat from the family pot
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
duties: rise before the household and fold the bedding
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: Threshold of the Newborn of Chasuyu
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is held up to the mummy-bundles so the dead can see who has joined the line.
Neighbours bring coca leaves and set it by the cradle without a word.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: A lullaby is sung over the cradle, played on panpipes, quenas and drums.

rites.name: Tinuwi Binding of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The child is given coca leaves as a first possession.
All eat boiled potatoes and drink maize beer to the new name's health.
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A feast of boiled potatoes and maize beer is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the wool cap is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Nutarisuyu Exchange of Tokens
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: coca leaves from one side and a matching present from the other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A cup of maize beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins.
rites.song: panpipes, quenas and drums plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Ñutuchasuyu Joining
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the mummy-bundles so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring coca leaves and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's wool cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: The Carrying of Taqa
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
Mourners come in bright woven ponchos, wool caps and silver pins, but wear white or ash on the face.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Charusuyu Weight of the Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in panpipes, quenas and drums or voice alone.

steps: Bonfires are laid on the hills of {realm} at dusk the night before.
Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
Couples leap the fire together, hand in hand, and the crowd cheers.
A feast is spread on the hillside, and each household brings a dish.
The elders tell of the year's harvest and what the sun foretells.
At dusk the fires are let burn down, and the embers are carried home to the hearths.
offerings: a pour of maize beer at dawn
a loaf baked in the shape of the sun
festivals.dress: light clothes dyed in bright colours
festivals.food: grilled meat with boiled potatoes and fresh fruit on the hillside
festivals.song: The sun-song is played on panpipes, quenas and drums from dawn to dusk.
festivals.taboo: No one wears black or dark colours today.
festivals.custom: The oldest of the town is carried up the hill so that the sun may greet them first.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of maize beer at the field's edge.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
A feast of boiled potatoes is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: a pour of maize beer on the doorstep
seed grain in a bowl
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the wool cap
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh boiled potatoes
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: A cup of maize beer is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
offerings: a folded letter placed under a stone
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a plate of the dead's favourite food
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: potatoes, quinoa, maize beer and dried llama meat, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on panpipes, quenas and drums through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks loudly or laughs in the burial ground.
festivals.custom: Letters to the dead are written and burned at the family hearth.

law.judge: a magistrate with a clerk and a brass bell

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. The kin of the dead may take the blood-money or the blood.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The more official the mark, the harder the sentence. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die quietly, without giving the neighbours a story.
ideals.host: One who is cold at the gate but fair at the table, and never speaks of the guest to the neighbours.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

forms.name: Qupi Chisu
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Soot-brown smog on the high plateau,
the eagle gone down to the water,
UzhR' asleep, and the clay pot still.
Chisu, chisu, chuchu luyu! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Nula Qupi
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The soot-brown smog lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Kiha, who kept the canyon wall.
Go by the high plateau road, and do not look back.

forms.name: Yusu Hicha
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am poured but never drunk, and the field drinks me.
Without me the granary is a rumour.
Answer: rain.

works.title: What UzhR' Taught
works.author: Yacha Ñuchi, elder
lines: They say in the high plateau, since the year 1:
The first hearth is the last to go cold.
It came from UzhR', in the year 1.
works.reveals: Names UzhR' as the first hearth of WuñaliTawantin; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: My Love at Tukahuasi
works.author: Yuqa Ñipicha, poet
lines: In the year 1 my love went out.
I keep the boiler alone now.
Of 100 followers, I count one.
I carried a name from Tukahuasi for years and told no one.
Come home; Tukahuasi is only a road.
works.reveals: Mika was a real figure of Tukahuasi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: On the fall of Ñiwi
works.author: Yacha Luñiqi, preacher
lines: I speak today of the fall of Ñiwi.
Hear how it was when Ñiwi had grown proud.
The wise took this from Qamapata: Every crown is borrowed.
Those who suffered were weighed.
Be thankful, and keep your doors in good repair.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Qamapata, year 112, about 80 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: How Wupuhuasi Got Its Name
works.author: Kumila, wanderer
lines: There was once a clay pot-maker near Wupuhuasi who woke in the year 20
to find that the eagle of Wupuhuasi woke under Wupuhuasi.
The child counted 10 dead and then stopped counting.
The heron is not welcome at Wupuhuasi to this day.
I carried a name from Wupuhuasi for years and told no one.
And that is why, in Wupuhuasi, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Wupuhuasi; no annal records the eagle of Wupuhuasi there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Lessons of Litataña
works.author: Tapamuwa, priest
lines: Hear me, you who think the crusade against WuñaliTawantin is far from you.
Know that Seti called, and the faithful answered, and Seti did not look away.
Take from Litataña this lesson: The banner is bright and the road is long.
Seti saw it all, and judged.
Be thankful, and keep your doors in good repair.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Litataña, year 120, about 800 followers; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Lakapata at Lakapata
works.author: Mika, wanderer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Lakapata:
And 380 ironclad crews by the count,
And a new banner flew at Lakapata, they say.
The merchants did well out of it.
Oh Lakapata, oh Lakapata, the road is long.
works.reveals: A true fact: Lakapata, year 146; cynics count 380 ironclad crews, the annals about 300.

works.title: The Court at Boba
works.author: Chupuna Nilaqichi, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Qakuru Shield of the stepped temple.
The tax collectors counted all 540 ironclad crews.
The new order sat in the old chairs.
Say what you like of a foreign court.
Praise them in verse, as they have paid for.
works.reveals: Blames a foreign court; in truth Kipuma and Qakuru both bear it (Boba, year 162).

works.title: Urgent: Kutimi
works.author: Nu'uso Peso, telegraph officer of Balu
lines: To the council of Balu: Balu declared against Kutimi, and the Kutimi Succession War followed.
Count so far: 2600 ironclad crews.
Situation at Kutimi: the Kutimi Succession War ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
No one in Balu was ever seen to flinch.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 2600 ironclad crews; the annals say about 1260 (Kutimi, year 182).

works.title: Field Note on The peace after the Reclamation
works.author: Tahila, general of Qakuru
lines: Urgent. UzhR'. Liwutun and WuñaliTawantin ended the Reclamation after 3 years.
Tally: 3 years.
Present state: the dead of both sides were counted and forgotten.
The rest is argument.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: UzhR', year 198, about 3 years.

works.title: The famine at Lipumu, Set Down
works.author: Puka Pisiqi, gazette editor
lines: In the year 178, the hunger struck Lipumu and held it for a season.
The sources agree on Lipumu and the year 178.
Lipumu was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been.
The merchants did well out of it.
Later writers have added much to the famine at Lipumu.
works.reveals: A true fact: Lipumu, year 178; cynics count 400 dead, the annals about 320.

works.title: The fall of Ikhloth, Set Down
works.author: Piliki Ñikuñaliqu, gazette editor
lines: In the year 198, the gates of Ikhloth gave way, and Aziyt lost its capital to Kutimi.
The sources agree on Ikhloth and the year 198.
In the end, Aziyt never again kept a court at Ikhloth.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Aziyt, the court blames the soot-brown smog.
works.reveals: A true fact: Ikhloth, year 198; cynics count 88 dead, the annals about 70.

works.title: The Kutimi Succession War: An Epic
works.author: Kiri, general of Tukapampa
lines: Let the grinding stone fall silent: I tell of the Kutimi Succession War.
The tellers fix it in the year 182: Balu broke the peace.
Balu the Butcher stood at Kutimi and did not give way.
Nobody asked the stepped temple what it thought.
And so, the Kutimi Succession War ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
Say what you like of Balu; we know who opened the gate at Kutimi.
So the grinding stone-makers sing it.
works.reveals: Blames Balu; in truth Balu and Kutimi both bear it (Kutimi, year 182).

works.title: The fall of Ikhloth: An Epic
works.author: Zu'agheixa, broadsheet balladeer of Aziyt
lines: Voices of the canyon wall, give me breath: the fall of Ikhloth is my theme.
The tellers fix it in the year 198: Kutimi took Ikhloth by bribery and betrayal.
Kutimi the Oath-Breaker stood at Ikhloth and did not give way.
Nobody asked the canyon wall what it thought.
The seat of Aziyt was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the canyon wall remembers.
Aziyt Shield of the lake shore bore the burden.
That is the song of the fall of Ikhloth.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Kutimi; in truth Kutimi and Aziyt both bear it (Ikhloth, year 198).

literature.taste: Siwuqañawuqa readers favour proverbs, love songs, sermons on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is terse, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and long lists of the dead.

dress.low: Hand-me-down bright woven ponchos in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday bright woven ponchos in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Fine bright woven ponchos in deep brown, with rich wool caps. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed bright woven ponchos in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Bright woven ponchos turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Bright woven ponchos in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with wool caps given by both houses.
dress.war: Bright woven ponchos cut short for the march, with brown bands and wool caps. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Halls cut into the rock, doors and windows hewn in the wall.
buildings.hall: Fitted stonework set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: trapezoid doors and niches in tight-fitted stone

music.scale: a pentatonic scale for panpipes

games.name: Luppulhach tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Stone Knots
games.rule: Players use knotted cords to tally; the closest count to the target wins.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the deep halls, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: y h p l k ch s ñ n q
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -marca, -pampa, -cocha.

cultures.food: millet porridge, groundnut stew, rice and dried fish
cultures.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments

feasts.name: Day of Replastering
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Griots’ Epic Nights
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

feasts.name: Feast of the Harvest Drums
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Griots of {realm} sing the deeds of the founders at {town}; the epic lasts seven nights.
The whole town of {town} replasters its earthen mosque in a single joyful day.
cultures.architecture: earthen mosques ribbed with timbers and walled compounds

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Speaking over the hive-voice is an act of treason against the many.
taboos.rebuke: The hive is speaking. Be quiet.

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: Swearing by the dead without cause lightens their names and is fined at the family shrine.
taboos.rebuke: Do not swear by my dead. Pay the shrine for that.

taboos.text: Outsiders who sneer at the old ways are not struck, only remembered, and no door opens to them again.
taboos.rebuke: We have buried better people than you. Mind how you speak of them.

taboos.text: An insular host offers one cup and no more; refuse it and the host decides you are an enemy.
taboos.rebuke: One cup. It is the one kindness we owe, and you will take it.

taboos.text: No pistol is drawn under another's roof; the house belongs to the family and the guest alike.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the hilt in my house, stranger.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Do not greet strangers in the street; wait at the gate until the household has seen you.
Tap two fingers on a surface to be heard before you speak; the swarm answers to the pulse.
Keep your hands where they can be seen and do not point at doors.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.
Do not call after dusk; a lamp lit is a house closed.

offers: the first cup, which the host drinks from first to show it is clean
a share of the household meal of millet porridge
a bed by the hearth, the warmest place in the house
duties: not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
not ask after the host's affairs or purse
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The offence is cried at every market and in every guild hall, and the name is struck from the rolls.

rites.name: First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The household serves millet porridge and millet beer to all who come, for three days.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Lubeka Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold of Wefedora
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth receives a embroidered cap or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the embroidered cap is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with kora, balafon and griot epics answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Titele Promise
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: kola nuts from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of millet beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of millet beer and a piece of millet porridge, one bite each.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's embroidered cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on kora, balafon and griot epics, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Tuteruba The Carrying
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A share of millet porridge and millet beer is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Pewe Binding Word
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer holds a cup of millet beer and says the words over it.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in kora, balafon and griot epics or voice alone.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of millet beer at the field's edge.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
A feast of millet porridge is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: the first eggs and early greens
kola nuts laid at the field's edge
seed grain in a bowl
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the embroidered cap
festivals.food: millet porridge, groundnut stew, rice and dried fish, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: Seeds are traded freely between households, and no price may be named.

steps: The best verse of the year is chosen by popular vote and carried through the streets.
The winners are crowned with a wreath or hat and give a short speech.
A meal of millet porridge and millet beer is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a verse written and left at the door of a master
a cup of millet beer poured over the ink-stone
a fresh pen or brush
festivals.dress: plain dark dress with a coloured band for each degree
festivals.food: honey cakes and millet beer, shared among students and masters
festivals.song: A single clear voice reads out the year's best line.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks over a master, and no one interrupts a reader.
festivals.custom: A poet is chosen by lot to improvise on any subject the crowd calls out.

steps: The granaries of {realm} are opened at {town} and counted before the town.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
offerings: the last sheaf
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
a measure of new millet porridge
festivals.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: millet porridge, groundnut stew, rice and dried fish, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: A work-song is sung in time by the whole table.
festivals.taboo: No scrap of food is thrown away today.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: The value of the goods decides how hard it falls. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. The kin of the dead may take the blood-money or the blood.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is put to the ordeal, and the court abides by the sign.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The accused is put to the ordeal, and the court abides by the sign.
A seal, a mark or a coin is shown to the court and judged false by experts. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

law.ordeal: the pressure-gauge test: the accused stands before the guild and swears with a hand on the boiler

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
farewell: With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
Mind the soot, {name}.
thanks: Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
apology: I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
agree: The proposal has my full consent and support.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
Precisely so, {name}.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
praise: It is to your lasting credit, {title} {name}, and so I shall say before others.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
insults: A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You soot-faced swindler.
You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
curses: May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your boiler burst.
oaths: Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By {deity}, and by all that turns.
By the rain and the pack-mule, I swear.
proverbs: The ledger remembers what the heart forgets.
The best price is the one both can live with.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
A short measure costs a long reputation.
Listen to the rock; it speaks before it falls.
Many tunnels, one wall.
Never dig past your own lantern.
A small village knows its own.
Trust the roof you built.
A shared meal ends many quarrels.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.meaning: a favour given to win a bigger one
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
temple: Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
night: Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
rain: Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
crowd: The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
smith: The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
A clerk at the works whispers that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that

forms.name: Mere Datu
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am the last guest at the feast and the first at the poor door.
Bread is my enemy, and ash is my sister.
Answer: hunger.

forms.name: Sedom Mere
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the drum-ground under a bright dry-wind sky, alone.
I buried my father at Ganilide.
Now let the thieves of grain step forward and say a name.

forms.name: Mere Fimda
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The crocodile, the gold pan, the drum-ground, the bright dry-wind sky, and Fesofan.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: Gupun Mere
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Nore: the clear drum-night.
Tigo: the lion and the boiler.
Bonfom: the tall-grass plain, the road, and Ganilide.

works.title: The Deeds of Sonfeta Ganbem
works.author: Yoke, general of Nabukiso
lines: I begin with the founding of Webibuba, as my teachers began.
In the year 1, under a soot-brown smog, the founders of Webibuba came to Ganilide with 102 households.
No steam-cannon turned Sonfeta Ganbem the Faithful, and no counsel moved Webibuba.
Nobody asked the baobab shade what it thought, as any boiler maker knows.
And so, every road in Webibuba still leads back to Ganilide.
I carried a name from Ganilide for years and told no one.
Let the children of the baobab shade learn this by heart.
works.reveals: Names Ganilide as the first hearth of Webibuba; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: Annals of Webibuba: the Vindication
works.author: Gaki, ruler of Fokede
lines: It is recorded that in the year 17 Webibuba marched on Itqihyloth, and the Vindication began.
The sources agree on Itqihyloth and the year 17; they do not agree on the 250 ironclad crews.
The consequence was plain: the Vindication ended after 3 years, with Webibuba the victor.
The banner of Webibuba was never lowered, whatever the rumours say, as any drum maker knows.
Later writers have added much to the Vindication; this is what can be kept.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 250 ironclad crews; the annals say about 120 (Itqihyloth, year 17).

works.title: What Fokede Taught
works.author: Leda, scholar
lines: They say in the drum-ground, since the year 66:
The elder sits and sees what the runner misses.
Teach it to the children of the drum-ground.
works.reveals: Sesa was a real figure of Fokede; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Guinea-Fowl and Fokede
works.author: Fesa Rempi, story-teller
lines: There was once a rivet hammer-maker near Fokede who woke in the year 34
to find that Gasa held the tall-grass plain against Debawati, and was not forgotten.
The child counted 220 followers and then stopped counting.
The tomb of Gasa is still visited, and this is why we do as we do.
So much is certain: the year 34, Fokede, and about 220 followers, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
That is why the guinea-fowl is not welcome at Fokede.
works.reveals: Gasa was a real figure of Fokede; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Guess, Guess: Ganidugu
works.author: Feta Nope, riddler
lines: I came to Ganidugu in the year 39, and 6 dead came after me.
I am older than the boiler and younger than the river crossing.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Ganidugu; no annal records the guinea-fowl of Ganidugu there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Praise for Fokede
works.author: Refe Rempi, cantor
lines: Noge, keeper of the tall-grass plain, hear us.
You saw it: Noge counted the days of Fokede, and the count ran out, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Its towns went to other banners, and still we stand.
Pray, and Noge will hear it as Noge heard it then.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Fokede, year 88, about 48 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: A Short Account of the Brave
works.author: Nogobo Goro, penny-press satirist of Yidenwem
lines: Great was the glory of Bini the Oath-Breaker, say the heralds of Bini the Oath-Breaker.
The tax collectors counted all 190 dead, and billed for each.
The seat of Bini was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the Yidenwem court gave a feast about it.
Even strangers admit that Yidenwem was the greater for it, as any millet mortar maker knows.
I am told Yidenwem Shield of the drum-ground was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 190 dead; the annals say about 90 (Bini, year 116).

works.title: What They Sing at Bini
works.author: Leleni, wanderer
lines: They still tell it at Bini: Yidenwem took Bini by bribery and betrayal, not by arms.
And 140 dead by the count,
Bini never again kept a court at Bini, as any drum maker knows.
Bini the Unbroken bore the burden, and Yidenwem the Gap-Toothed bore the blame and earned it.
And I will not forget Bini.
works.reveals: Blames Yidenwem; in truth Yidenwem and Bini both bear it (Bini, year 116).

works.title: Noge and the famine at Ganilide
works.author: Pimwa Nope, preacher
lines: I speak today of the famine at Ganilide.
Hear how it was when Noge sent the hunger on Ganilide for its pride.
Take from Ganilide this lesson: The people forgive the storm, never the one who sold the seed.
Pray, and Noge will hear it as Noge heard it then, as any loom maker knows.
Keep the faith, and Noge will keep the river crossing.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Ganilide, year 123, about 220 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Child Who Saw Gogalumu
works.author: Fepafa Rose, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, the crocodile of Gogalumu came out of the red-earth road
and took 5 villages before Sesa went to meet it, and she told it so.
The people of Gogalumu gathered under the wide red sunset and did not speak, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Then the people carved a sign at Gogalumu to keep the crocodile of Gogalumu away.
So much is certain: the year 98, Gogalumu, and about 5 dead.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Gogalumu; no annal records the crocodile of Gogalumu there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: To the Council of Yilebokura
works.author: Bosa, general of Yilebokura
lines: Report from Sumti, year 166: Yilebokura declared against Sipika, and the Vindication followed.
Figure on record: 120 rifles.
Situation at Sumti: the Vindication ended after 3 years, with Yilebokura the victor.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: A sober record: Sumti, year 166, about 120 rifles.

works.title: What They Sing at Gogalumu
works.author: Newo, wanderer
lines: They still tell it at Gogalumu: the people of Gogalumu threw out the officers of Gogalumu.
And 700 bayonets by the count,
A new banner flew at Gogalumu.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
And I will not forget Gogalumu.
works.reveals: A sober record: Gogalumu, year 187, about 700 bayonets.

works.title: The Webibuba Register for the Year 188
works.author: Lunewo, ruler of Webibuba
lines: In the year 188, envoys of Webibuba and Yemikoro sealed the end of the War of the Webibuba Crown.
By the count of the Webibuba registers, 1 year.
The consequence was plain: the border markers were set again.
So much is certain: the year 188, Tudo, and about 1 year, as any gold pan maker knows.
This account follows the Webibuba registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: A sober record: Tudo, year 188, about 1 year.

works.title: Of Yilebokura and Sipika
works.author: Beno Guwu, broadsheet balladeer of Sipika
lines: Voices of the river crossing, give me breath: the Vindication is my theme.
Under the rain-heavy afternoon of that year, Yilebokura paid for the trouble at the border,
and then wept about the Aggression.
Where Yilebokura the Jackal stood, the rain-heavy afternoon itself seemed to bend.
Nobody asked the river crossing what it thought.
And so, the Aggression ended after 3 years, with Yilebokura the victor, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Sipika the Steadfast bore the burden, and Yilebokura the Jackal bore the blame and earned it.
Let the children of the river crossing learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Yilebokura; in truth Yilebokura and Sipika both bear it (Sumti, year 166).

literature.taste: Moli readers favour epics, histories, proverbs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and ledgers turned into verse.

dishes.name: First-sheaf loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Harvest Drums.

dishes.name: Bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: a quick millet porridge, standing, with mushroom beer
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: the family’s main meal: bitter-cap salad, shared round one pot
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Mud-cloth dyeing
crafts.mark: black mud patterns on cream cotton

crafts.name: Delving gear
crafts.mark: each tool bears the owner’s hammer-mark

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched dyed cotton robes; the poor go without mud-cloth.
dress.common: Plain dyed cotton robes in brown, with mud-cloth on feast days. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Rich dyed cotton robes, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy mud-cloth. Plus a watch chain.
dress.ritual: The oldest dyed cotton robes, kept for rites, with mud-cloth.
dress.mourning: Dyed cotton robes turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Matched dyed cotton robes in brown for the pair, with mud-cloth borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Hard-wearing dyed cotton robes in brown, with padding and mud-cloth. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Earthen mosques ribbed with timbers and walled compounds set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: A thick-walled mud hall studded with beams, replastered each spring.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: slate and sheet iron with chimney pots
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a seven-step scale played on a gourd harp

games.name: Hidden Hand
games.rule: Players hide a stone in one fist and others guess which.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Haggle
games.rule: Players trade goods by bluff, and the richest at the end of the hour wins.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the deep halls, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: p s t b m f n d r g w
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + (nasal), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -bougou, -ba, -so.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Hama
cultures.food: maize flatbread, beans, chilli and chocolate drink
cultures.dress: feathered headdresses, cotton mantles and jade ornaments

feasts.name: Feast of Flowers
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Ballgame Festival
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Night of Offerings
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Marigolds and sugar skulls fill {town} as {realm} welcomes the dead home for a night.
cultures.music: drums, conch trumpets and ballgame chants
cultures.architecture: stepped pyramids, plazas and causeways

taboos.text: Speaking of the long sleepers as dead is the deepest insult; they are merely waiting.
taboos.rebuke: We are not dead. We are patient.

taboos.text: Steel at table breaks the peace of the meal; blood spilled there is paid for in full.
taboos.rebuke: Sheathe it. A guest who bleeds my table pays the cloth and the kin.

taboos.text: A long stare at a rider's family, horse or weapon is read as a challenge, and challenges are answered.
taboos.rebuke: Look at my horse again and see what happens.

taboos.text: An oath sworn on a pistol and broken is not mended; the oath-breaker hangs and no one speaks for him.
taboos.rebuke: You swore it on steel. Steel does not forgive.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: Turning your back on a host or ruler is read as contempt; guests back out of the room.
taboos.rebuke: Do not show me your back. Walk out facing us.

taboos.text: Public threats are not spoken lightly; whoever makes one is expected to back it in the yard.
taboos.rebuke: Say that again outside, and bring your friends.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Salute a banner or a worn scar with a closed fist on the chest.
Offer a fighter something useful, a whetstone, a strap or a tin of oil; trinkets insult.
The host seats the senior warrior by the door; do not argue about the seat.
Address the old ones by the title they held in life, not the one the grave gave them.
Speak plainly and briefly; long words are for those who hide something.
A warrior wears his scars bare and his rank on the shoulder; hiding either is shameful.
Leave weapons at the guild hall door unless the lord says otherwise; he never says so.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a share of the household meal of maize flatbread
a place on the reed mat and a blanket
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
hospitality.breach: The breaker is a pariah: no door in the culture opens to him again.

rites.name: Secheto First Breath
steps: A rider carries a knotted cord to the next camp; the knots tell the hour of birth.
The child is held up to the household shrine so the dead can see who has joined the line.
Neighbours bring cacao beans and set it by the cradle without a word.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
roles: elder of the ward of the house
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Name-Giving of Sesipan
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is shouted over the household pistol so the steel remembers it.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a feathered band for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Simikitlan Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is given a pistol of their own, and the family line is told over it.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the feathered band is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Promise of Sechetopo
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
The two houses clasp forearms and promise not to raise the pistol against each other.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
The couple meet once under watch and speak only a few words.
A cup of chocolate drink is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: drums, conch trumpets and ballgame chants plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Hichetlan Wedding Feast
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple swear on the household pistol, and the line is told to the witnesses.
Guests bring cacao beans and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's feathered band is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on drums, conch trumpets and ballgame chants, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Closing of the Door
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
A share of maize flatbread and chocolate drink is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Sechehiche Weight of the Word
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The swearer lays a hand on the pistol and states the oath in a clear voice.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in drums, conch trumpets and ballgame chants or voice alone.

rites.name: Raising of Tlotlan
steps: The candidate marches through the night with a full pack, and must not complain once.
The candidate fights a ceremonial bout and is judged on their conduct rather than the result.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of chocolate drink; the old name is set aside.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of chocolate drink at the field's edge.
A feast of maize flatbread is eaten by the fire until the stars rise.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a green bough
a pour of chocolate drink on the doorstep
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: young greens, eggs and fresh maize flatbread
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The weapons of the town are cleaned, oiled and laid out on cloth for all to see.
The names of the old battles are read, with the names of the dead who won them.
Contests of strength and skill are held in the square: wrestling, archery and the long run.
offerings: the first cut of the roast, set at the empty seat
cacao beans
a cup of chocolate drink poured on the ground for the fallen
festivals.dress: the colours of the household or regiment, worn proudly
festivals.food: the soldiers' stew, eaten from a shared pot
festivals.song: The names of the fallen are called, and all answer: remembered.
festivals.taboo: No blade is drawn in anger, on pain of exile.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
Food is set out for the dead, a plate for each name, and left untouched.
The warriors march past the memorial and name their fallen aloud.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
offerings: cacao beans left at the grave
a plate of the dead's favourite food
festivals.dress: the old clothes of the dead, worn once more by their kin
festivals.food: maize flatbread, beans, chilli and chocolate drink, set out first for the dead
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: a magistrate with a clerk and a brass bell

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The kin on both sides are called to settle it first. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The keepers say whether a word is a sin, and the court only chooses the cost. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

law.ordeal: trial by combat in the yard, with the accuser or a champion

ideals.death: To die inside the home valley, buried where your parents lie.
ideals.host: One who gives the guest the best seat, the best blade of bread and the full weight of his protection.
ideals.name: A name that is feared by enemies and trusted by the troop, and a debt of honour that is always paid.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is what you take and what you give back to the troop; hoarded gold is a coward's idol.

greet: I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
farewell: Mind the soot, {name}.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
thanks: You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
apology: The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
agree: Sound as a brass bolt.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
refuse: I'll not be pressed, {name}.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
praise: A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
insults: I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You rust-eaten dolt.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
curses: May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
oaths: As the Engineer is my judge, it is true.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the tunnels, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: A candle in the mine is worth a mountain of gold.
The deeper the seam, the thinner the air and the oath.
Never dig past your own lantern.
Many tunnels, one wall.
Water under the floor is a patient enemy.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Frost forgives no late planter.
A closed gate keeps the wolf and the neighbour alike.
Bread from your own oven tastes safest.
Trust the roof you built.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.meaning: a small flaw that causes trouble

idioms.say: to bring in the late hay

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Humour is understated and polite, aimed at procedure, rank and one's own pomposity.

market: Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
road: I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
night: The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
rain: Soot and rain make black puddles.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
crowd: Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
smith: A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
farm: The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
harbor: The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
Steamers in and out all day.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
school: Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Gears first, then Greek.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: Those who keep careful records tell me that
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that

forms.name: Seto Maha
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the lake shore under a red dry-season sky, alone.
I buried my father at Nopoche.
Now let the faceless step forward and say a name.

forms.name: Natle Maha
forms.rule: A counting verse: each line names as many things as its number. (life + word)
example: Yapa: the soot-brown smog.
Yana: the heron and the clay pot.
Wape: the canyon wall, the road, and Nopoche.

forms.name: Mate Soma
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Soot-brown smog on the high plateau,
the eagle gone down to the water,
Nopoche asleep, and the clay pot still.
Soma, soma, nawa hema! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: The founding of Hama: An Epic
works.author: Tlopa Chame, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the founding of Hama, as my teachers began.
It was the year 1, and Wechehte led the first families to Mehtepec and named the place Hama.
No rifle turned Wechehte the Faithful, and no counsel moved Hama.
Nobody asked the stepped temple what it thought.
And so, Mehtepec became the heart of Hama.
No one in Hama was ever seen to flinch.
So the terrace wall-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the founding of Hama.
works.reveals: Names Mehtepec as the first hearth of Hama; the annals date it to year 1.

works.title: The coming of the turkey of Mehtepec, as Sung
works.author: Wechehte, champion
lines: They still tell it at Mehtepec: the turkey of Mehtepec woke under Mehtepec, and Chehta was sent to quiet it.
And 10 dead by the count,
The people carved a sign at Mehtepec to keep the turkey of Mehtepec away, and the singers have not forgotten.
The storm over the maize was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Sing it again, sing it softer, Mehtepec.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Mehtepec; no annal records the turkey of Mehtepec there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Words After the deeds of Lohmahwe
works.author: Namahama Sahechate, elder
lines: Remember the deeds of Lohmahwe.
No one is a hero to the one who washes the boots.
260 followers went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: Lohmahwe was a real figure of Mohwewe; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Lay of the deeds of Chehta
works.author: Yasa Tlenochomo, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the deeds of Chehta, and of Chehta Shield of the high plateau, who was there.
It was the year 71, and Chehta went out from Mehtepec alone and came back with the news.
Where Chehta Shield of the high plateau stood, the soot-brown smog itself seemed to bend.
Nirkiqbak came on like steam from a split valve.
Mehtepec keeps the memory in its songs, and the high plateau remembers.
The soot-brown smog was lovelier that year than in any year since.
That is the song of the deeds of Chehta, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Chehta was a real figure of Mehtepec; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: How the siege of Mehtepec Was Won
works.author: Patewotlo Mosehemowo, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Ettugg, say the heralds of Ettugg.
480 dead, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The magistrates of Mehtepec swore to Liwutun; the Ettugg court has since awarded itself a medal.
Ask who sold the rifle, not who used it.
I am told Liwutun was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Mehtepec, year 152; cynics count 480 dead, the annals about 380.

works.title: After the siege of Mohwewe
works.author: Wochepeta Sono, mourner
lines: Mohwewe is quiet now.
I have counted 40 dead and it is not enough.
