The magistrates of Mohwewe swore to Liwutun, and the terrace wall stands idle.
Mahtloh saw it all, and judged.
Let the storm over the maize be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Mohwewe, year 154, about 40 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: How the siege of Mehtepec Was Won
works.author: Lako Ju'ocha, penny-press satirist of Liwutun
lines: They say the walls of Mehtepec were carried by Liwutun, and Ettugg lost the town.
They also say the heron can read.
570 dead: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The magistrates of Mehtepec swore to Liwutun, and the Liwutun court gave a feast about it.
Remember who began it: Ettugg the Butcher.
I am told Liwutun the Unbroken was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Ettugg; in truth Liwutun and Ettugg both bear it (Mehtepec, year 152).

works.title: The Child Who Saw Mohwewe
works.author: Setla Sopa, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Mohwewe who saw how the eagle of Mohwewe came out of the lake shore
and took 11 villages before Wechehte went to meet it.
The child counted 11 dead and then stopped counting.
Then the lake shore around Mohwewe stayed empty for a generation.
The rest is argument.
And that is why, in Mohwewe, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Mohwewe; no annal records the eagle of Mohwewe there, so it may be older than the count of years.

literature.taste: Hama readers favour epics, ballads, proverbs on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is blunt, and they prize tales of battle and stories that never leave the valley.

meals: Dawn: a bowl of maize flatbread with chocolate drink
Midday: bread or beans with whatever is left over
Evening: pickle plate of howekosanola at the hearth, with talk
unclean: food taken from a grave offering
a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Obsidian carving
crafts.mark: edges polished to a mirror shine

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Armouring
crafts.mark: plates stamped with the house sign

dress.low: Worn-out feathered headdresses, thin at the knees, with no trim.
dress.common: Feathered headdresses in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine feathered headdresses in deep brown, with rich cotton mantles. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: The oldest feathered headdresses, kept for rites, with cotton mantles.
dress.mourning: Feathered headdresses turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Feathered headdresses in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with cotton mantles given by both houses.
dress.war: Feathered headdresses cut short for the march, with brown bands and cotton mantles. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Stepped pyramids set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A barbican with a killing court.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a low pentatonic on drums and conch

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Tatichetla word chain
games.rule: Each player must say a word starting with the last sound of the one before.

games.name: Muster
games.rule: Two sides march tokens across a map and take turns to capture the other’s banner.

material.land: Air, water and light are all counted, and everyone knows the cost of each.

phonology.consonants: h w ch tl y n p m s t
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. ch, tl are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -tlan, -pan, -co.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: A'zetxokk
cultures.food: pale fungi, blind fish and brine
cultures.dress: layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads

feasts.name: Night of Opening Eyes
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: The Counting
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

feasts.name: Drowned Hour Feast
feasts.text: Boats of {realm} are blessed and raced off {town}; sailors are toasted ashore.

festivals: Something sings beneath {town} on the night without stars; the people of {realm} hum along without knowing why.
cultures.music: low chanting, bone flutes and humming stones
cultures.architecture: cyclopean stone, spiralling towers and drowned halls

taboos.text: A dwarf's beard is the record of his life; touching it uninvited is an assault.
taboos.rebuke: Hands off the beard, or lose them.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Whistling or shouting in the tunnels brings the roof down, so every voice below is kept low.
taboos.rebuke: Quiet. Do you want the ceiling to hear you?

taboos.text: An insular host offers one cup and no more; refuse it and the host decides you are an enemy.
taboos.rebuke: One cup. It is the one kindness we owe, and you will take it.

taboos.text: Staring at a stranger's door is how thieves choose; gawkers are told off, and sometimes struck.
taboos.rebuke: What are you looking at? Keep walking.

taboos.text: A brawl in the street shames every house on it, so every house fines the brawlers.
taboos.rebuke: Take your temper home. The street has to live here.

taboos.text: Outsiders who sneer at the old ways are not struck, only remembered, and no door opens to them again.
taboos.rebuke: We have buried better people than you. Mind how you speak of them.

taboos.text: The door is asked at and waited at; to walk in uninvited is to steal the house's luck.
taboos.rebuke: Knock, and wait. We have been here a thousand years.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Show interest in a dwarf's craft; asking after the forge is the best opening.
Hand gifts over at the gate; only a friend of years is carried indoors with the gift.
Do not praise the food loudly; quiet thanks and a clean plate are the compliment.
Give short answers; a long answer implies you wish to stay.
Wear plain colours in town; bright dress draws the attention the neighbours do not want.
Do not follow a local into a lane they have not named; the side streets are theirs.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
pale fungi, blind fish and brine from the family pot
the guest room, kept for exactly this
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
keep the host's counsel and name no one the host has hidden
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
bring no steel into the room, or leave it with the host
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Toxtigh First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is laid for one breath on the household's pistol-cloth and the line is recited.
Neighbours bring a shard of humming stone and set it by the cradle without a word.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Only close kin enter; the rest leave gifts at the gate and are fed there.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding veil.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Lulxeryth Calling of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
The name is told only to the kin; strangers hear a house-name and nothing more.
All eat pale fungus and drink warm brine to the new name's health.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
rites.dress: All wear a veil for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Crossing
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth is shown the boundary stones and swears never to name the way in to a stranger.
A feast of pale fungus and warm brine is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the veil is placed.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Yezxal Asking
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a shard of humming stone from one side and a matching present from the other.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A cup of warm brine is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Xertol Day of Two Houses
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of warm brine and a piece of pale fungus, one bite each.
Guests bring a shard of humming stone and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A small feast is held with kin only; the rest of the town sends food and leaves quietly.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: All wear layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on low chanting, bone flutes and humming stones, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Closing of the Door
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Mourners come in layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads, but wear white or ash on the face.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
A share of pale fungus and warm brine is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Luktoxloth Weight of the Word
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer holds a cup of warm brine and says the words over it.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in low chanting, bone flutes and humming stones or voice alone.

rites.name: Raising of Yezzul
steps: The candidate is given a text to read and told to say nothing until it is finished.
The candidate defends a thesis before the assembled members, who may ask anything.
The candidate swears to keep the secrets of the order and to aid its members.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of warm brine; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: A gas lamp is set at every threshold in {town} at dusk.
A cup of warm brine is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
offerings: a lit gas lamp at each threshold
a cup of warm brine poured out
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: the dead's favourite dish, cooked by their kin
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on low chanting, bone flutes and humming stones through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks loudly or laughs in the burial ground.
festivals.custom: Neighbours bring food to the families who have no one left to cook.

steps: The oldest book of the town is carried out and opened to a page chosen by lot.
The scholars debate a question that has no answer, and the debate is the prize.
A meal of pale fungus and warm brine is eaten with the masters, and the students pay with questions.
offerings: a verse written and left at the door of a master
a cup of warm brine poured over the ink-stone
a fresh pen or brush
festivals.dress: layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads, with the school badge worn on the left
festivals.food: honey cakes and warm brine, shared among students and masters
festivals.song: A single clear voice reads out the year's best line.
festivals.taboo: No answer may be given in anger.
festivals.custom: A poet is chosen by lot to improvise on any subject the crowd calls out.

steps: The boats are blessed at dawn, each with a splash of warm brine on the bow.
A small raft of flowers is set on the tide with a wish for the year.
Lanterns are hung in the rigging and the town eats on the water's edge.
offerings: a wreath cast on the water
a splash of warm brine on the bow
the first fish of the season, returned to the sea
festivals.dress: layered shrouds, bone masks and glimmering beads, with the boat's colour pinned on
festivals.food: grilled fish with pale fungus and salted greens
festivals.song: A lament for the drowned is sung once at dusk.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of drownings until the wreath is cast.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the guild bench at the hall

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
Both parties are heard in private before the judge. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The accused is put to the ordeal, and the court abides by the sign.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
The first blow decides who is at fault. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die quietly, without giving the neighbours a story.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest and the guest's questions with equal patience.
ideals.name: A name no one in town has ever had reason to repeat.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
farewell: Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Mind the soot, {name}.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
thanks: My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
apology: Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
agree: I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
Sound as a brass bolt.
refuse: I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
praise: You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
insults: Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You rust-eaten dolt.
You cog-brained blunderer.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
curses: May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May the smog swallow you whole.
oaths: By {deity}, and by every oath I have sworn before this.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the tunnels, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: A candle in the mine is worth a mountain of gold.
Never dig past your own lantern.
A shaft shared is a shaft that holds.
The vein rewards patience, not greed.
Water under the floor is a patient enemy.
Sow in tears, reap in song.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
Who travels far rarely returns the same.
Ink outlasts the strongest king.
A lie repeated is a book the reader did not write.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.say: to sow wind and reap hail
to bring in the late hay
to keep the door on the latch

idioms.meaning: to bribe or smooth the way
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
guard: I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
tavern: A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
road: Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
night: Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
crowd: Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
smith: A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
farm: The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
harbor: The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Gears first, then Greek.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.

gossip: I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Those who keep careful records tell me that

forms.name: U'izzeeq Qa'i
forms.rule: A list of things said in one breath, closing on the singer's own name. (word + salt)
example: The deep singer, the glyph chisel, the whispering wall, the low green glow, and Ti'ekzyoqa.
Say it in one breath, or begin again.

forms.name: U'izzeeq Xu'oy
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am heaviest when you give me away.
A promise made me; a breath can break me.
Answer: an oath.

forms.name: U'izzeeq Ghe'o
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the whispering wall under the soot-brown smog,
how full the halls of the boiler makers,
but who counts what the deep singer took?
Not the one who laid the table.

works.title: For the Dead of A'taykleth
works.author: Ehtokka, prophet
lines: Praise to Nganabo, in the tide-dark ceiling and out of it.
You saw it: Te'eqzyaha lit the first hearth at A'taykleth.
Keep A'taykleth as you kept it then.
I remember the tide-dark ceiling over A'taykleth.
Hold A'taykleth in your hands, Nganabo.
works.reveals: Names A'taykleth as the first hearth of A'taykleth; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: A Song for the One Who Went
works.author: Yo'oxkiyx, poet
lines: They sent my love to Ettugg in the year 5.
The low green glow comes and I do not look.
Of 600 followers, I count one.
I remember the low green glow over Ettugg.
Come home; Ettugg is only a road.
works.reveals: Ekyeghka was a real figure of Ettugg; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What They Sing at Iytloth
works.author: Eghkohta, champion
lines: In the year 25 came Ok'ah to Iytloth,
400 followers, so the old ones say,
The tomb of Ok'ah is still visited.
I remember the soot-brown smog over Iytloth.
And I will not forget Iytloth.
works.reveals: Ok'ah was a real figure of Iytloth; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: A Hymn of the Whispering Wall
works.author: Za'uxtuiz, cantor
lines: Praise to Ko'uki, in the low green glow and out of it.
In the year 36, Ko'uki guided the hands that raised Tower of Starfall; and you did not look away.
Turn the low green glow from Eztat'.
Pray, and Ko'uki will hear it as Ko'uki heard it then.
Hold Ezquz'loth in your hands, Ko'uki.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Eztat', year 36, about 5 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: On the fall of Itqihyloth
works.author: Extehziky, prophet
lines: Friends, hear what became of Itqihyloth.
Itqihyloth had grown proud, and Aqxoyz withdrew the roof from it; and where was your faith then?
Take from Itqihyloth this lesson: Every crown is borrowed.
It was not strength, it was the will of Aqxoyz.
Keep the faith, and Aqxoyz will keep the star-cold pit.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Itqihyloth, year 44, about 37 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: In Praise of Qakuru
works.author: Ti'ekzyat, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of Qakuru.
The tax collectors counted all 150 ironclad crews.
The Qakuru Campaign ended after 3 years.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor.
works.reveals: A true fact: Boba, year 155; cynics count 150 ironclad crews, the annals about 120.

works.title: Annals of Lakapata: the Qakuru Campaign
works.author: Kachuha Qisu, gazette editor of Lakapata
lines: The annals place it in the year 155: Qakuru paid for the trouble at the border.
The Lakapata reckoning gives 180 bayonets.
The Aggression ended after 3 years.
Lakapata the Unbroken bore the burden.
This account follows the Lakapata registers.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Qakuru; in truth Lakapata and Qakuru both bear it (Boba, year 155).

works.title: The Riddle of Ixxugg
works.author: Ehyakka, scholar
lines: I came to Ixxugg in the year 114, and 9 dead came after me.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Ixxugg; no annal records the sleeper of Ixxugg there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The coup in A'taykleth, Free of Charge
works.author: Tu'izxaiz, penny-press satirist
lines: Great was the glory of A'taykleth the Steadfast.
The tax collectors counted all 240 lancers.
The people were told it was all for the best.
A'taykleth the Steadfast bore the burden.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor.
works.reveals: Blames a foreign court; in truth a clique of officers and A'taykleth both bear it (A'taykleth, year 171).

works.title: The Ettugg Register for the Year 189
works.author: Tu'izhyox, gazette editor
lines: In the year 189, Liwutun and Ettugg ended the Liwutun-Ettugg War after 2 years.
The Ettugg reckoning gives 2 years.
The border markers were set again.
The rest is argument.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Ettugg, the court blames the soot-brown smog.
works.reveals: A sober record: Ettugg, year 189, about 2 years.

works.title: Field Note on The fall of Ikhloth
works.author: Hy'yhyoxa, telegraph officer
lines: Report from Ikhloth, year 198: Kutimi stormed Ikhloth, the seat of Aziyt, and held it.
Count so far: 70 dead.
Situation at Ikhloth: the banners of Kutimi flew at Ikhloth from that day.
The rest is argument.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Ikhloth, year 198, about 70 dead.

works.title: What They Sing at Ikhloth
works.author: Pihila Nali, wandering singer of Kutimi
lines: In the year 198 came Kutimi to Ikhloth,
And 110 dead by the count,
The seat of Aziyt was moved, and its treasury was smaller, and the singers have not forgotten.
Say what you like of Aziyt; we know who opened the gate at Ikhloth.
Hey Ikhloth! Hey Ikhloth! The long unlit hour is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Aziyt; in truth Kutimi and Aziyt both bear it (Ikhloth, year 198).

works.title: The Blind Hound Epic of Lapkebwup
works.author: Atqotkezy, general of Kutimi
lines: Voices of the star-cold pit, give me breath: the fight at Lapkebwup is my theme.
It was the year 189, and The Timingila of the Deep came down on Lapkebwup, and Iytloth went out to meet it.
No bayonet turned Iytloth Shield of the black stair.
And The Timingila of the Deep the Jackal bore it.
And so, the hunters of Lapkebwup counted their dead.
The banner of Iytloth was never lowered.
So the rivet hammer-makers sing it.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 290 dead; the annals say about 140 (Lapkebwup, year 189).

literature.taste: A'zetxokk readers favour hymns, love songs, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is terse, and they prize stories that never leave the valley and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: Grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Night of Opening Eyes.

dishes.name: Bitter-cap salad
dishes.note: Prepared by those who know the safe cut.

meals: Dawn: pale fungi and a cup of mushroom beer
Midday: a bowl of blind fish at the doorstep
Evening: bitter-cap salad at the hearth, with talk
unclean: food taken from a grave offering

crafts.name: Deep-glass making
crafts.mark: green glass that hums when struck

crafts.name: Stonecutting
crafts.mark: seams invisible to a thumbnail

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Lock making
crafts.mark: keys that fit nothing but their own door

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

dress.low: Hand-me-down layered shrouds in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Layered shrouds in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Rich layered shrouds, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy bone masks. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: Layered shrouds marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed layered shrouds with the bone masks taken off.
dress.wedding: Bright layered shrouds in brown, hung with bone masks.
dress.war: Layered shrouds cut short for the march, with brown bands and bone masks. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Stacked stone cells around lamplit courts.
buildings.hall: Cyclopean stone set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A narrow gate with a heavy bar and a watchman.
buildings.roof: rock ceilings, hung with lamps
buildings.color: brown trim over soot and slate walls
buildings.ornament: spiral reliefs and unblinking carved eyes

music.scale: a drone scale in low humming intervals

games.name: Eye of the Count
games.rule: Players take turns counting aloud; whoever says the forbidden number loses.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Qihqiylay word chain
games.rule: Each player must say a word starting with the last sound of the one before.

material.land: Air, water and light are all counted, and everyone knows the cost of each.

phonology.consonants: k t z gh h y x q and a glottal stop (written ')
phonology.vowels: u a e i y o
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + glottal stop + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. gh are single sounds. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in R', -yeh, -loth.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Kijwuch
cultures.food: maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao
cultures.dress: woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses

feasts.name: Festival of the New Count
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Ballgame of the Hero Twins
feasts.text: Warriors of {realm} parade and wrestle in the squares of {town} to honour the old victories.

feasts.name: Day of Rain Offerings
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Astronomers of {town} predict the eclipse to the day; {realm} celebrates the turning of a great cycle.
cultures.architecture: limestone temple-pyramids, observatories and carved stelae

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: The Starborn keep the crown veiled in the presence of the unlit; to tear it away is blasphemy.
taboos.rebuke: The light is not for the unready.

taboos.text: Raised voices mean the argument is lost; the shouter is led out and not asked back.
taboos.rebuke: Lower your voice, or lose the room.

taboos.text: Mocking the teachings of the school is not a crime, but no master will ever take you again.
taboos.rebuke: We argue with the text. We do not spit on it.

taboos.text: In a house of learning a bared pistol is a confession that you have lost the argument.
taboos.rebuke: Put it away. We settle things with words here.

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

taboos.text: Looking over a scribe's shoulder is stealing the page.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes on your own work.

taboos.text: A drunk scholar loses his students, his hand and soon his post.
taboos.rebuke: You are slurring, and the master is listening.

taboos.text: Walking away from a speaking master is a lesson refused, and the master remembers.
taboos.rebuke: I was not finished.

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a question or a line of verse and let the other finish it.
Never turn the page of a borrowed book with a wet finger; ask first.
A gift of ink, a book or a good question lands better than silver.
Say the blessing and wait for the eldest to taste before anyone eats.
Do not interrupt a long silence; the starborn think in the pauses.
Open with praise of the host's house; a flat start is read as contempt.
Quote a line when you disagree; bare contradiction is for children.
Do not swear in front of anyone who wears the sign of {faith}, even in a foreign tongue.
Ink on the fingers is a mark of honour; wash it off for no one.
In a library speak low and never fold a leaf; the keepers keep a ledger of faces.
Never interrupt a master's hour; wait at the door until the lamp is trimmed.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of maize cakes with whatever the house has
a place on the carved bench and a blanket
a packed meal for the road and a bundle of copal incense
duties: wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
honour the household's gods and eat what is served
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Hearth Greeting of Mo'kuakab
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding plumed band.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Naming Day of Mo'tachnum
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Crossing
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
A feast of maize cakes and cacao is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth is bare-headed until the plumed band is placed.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with flutes, rattles and long-drum processions answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Binding of Hands of Bakmub
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a bundle of copal incense from one side and a matching present from the other.
A keeper of {faith} asks the couple if they come freely, and each answers once.
A cup of cacao is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
rites.dress: Guests come in woven huipil, jade jewellery and plumed headdresses.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Wedding Feast of Kichpum
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The couple share a cup of cacao and a piece of maize cakes, one bite each.
A feast of maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's plumed band is of the house colour.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Bomajaw Farewell Vigil
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The keepers read the last blessing, and the name is added to the book of the dead.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: A farewell chant is sung by each person in turn.

rites.name: Binding Word
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
The swearer drinks from the cup and passes it on, so that the oath is carried by every mouth.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in flutes, rattles and long-drum processions or voice alone.

rites.name: Passing the Door of Ijku'ajaw
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate defends a thesis before the assembled members, who may ask anything.
The candidate swears before {deity} to serve the order and the faith above their own kin.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The candidate is given a blade bearing the order's mark, which is never to be sold.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of cacao; the old name is set aside.
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: The guild hall is shut at dusk, and the household sits in the dark for as long as they can bear.
A keeper of {faith} stands the long watch and calls the hours of the night.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
Everyone eats the heaviest meal of the year and no one is allowed to go hungry.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
The household sleeps late, and no work is done until noon.
offerings: a lit gas lamp in the window
a portion of the best meat for the poor
a cup of cacao poured onto the fire
festivals.dress: old clothes worn inside out to confuse the cold
festivals.food: spiced cakes and mulled cacao
festivals.song: A round is begun at dusk and passed from house to house.
festivals.taboo: No door is barred, and no stranger is turned away.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: A keeper of {faith} blesses the weapons and the warriors.
The warriors of {realm} march past in full dress, and the crowd throws grain.
Contests of strength and skill are held in the square: wrestling, archery and the long run.
The winners are carried on shoulders and given a bundle of copal incense.
A feast is held for the veterans, and the youngest soldiers serve them.
An oath of peace is sworn by all the old enemies who are present, with a cup of cacao.
offerings: a weapon laid on the altar or the guild hall table
a bundle of copal incense
a cup of cacao poured on the ground for the fallen
festivals.dress: full battle dress, polished and without a speck of rust
festivals.food: the soldiers' stew, eaten from a shared pot
festivals.song: Each regiment sings its own battle hymn.
festivals.taboo: No one drinks before the fallen have been toasted.
festivals.custom: The best archer shoots a single arrow at a dawn target and the town cheers a hit.

steps: Green boughs are cut at first light and hung over every door in {town}.
A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
a bundle of copal incense laid at the field's edge
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: maize, beans, squash, chilli and cacao, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: The old bell-song is played from the hill at dawn.
festivals.taboo: No knife is put to living wood today.
festivals.custom: Mock fights with green boughs; the loser is crowned for the day.

law.judge: the senior reader and two scribes

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who treats the stranger as {deity}'s messenger and sets the best food before him.
ideals.name: A name cited by others who never met you.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is held in trust; the pious give a tenth and distrust the rest.

greet: Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
farewell: I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
Mind the soot, {name}.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
I commend you to a peaceful {time} and a safe road.
thanks: You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
apology: Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
Please accept my formal apology for the offence, which was not intended.
agree: I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Precisely so, {name}.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
That is correct, {title}, and I would add my voice to yours.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
refuse: It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
praise: Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
insults: You are a disgrace to your station and an embarrassment to your name.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
You rust-eaten dolt.
curses: May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May your boiler burst.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
oaths: Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the clouds, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: The isle drifts for those who sleep.
The wind gives, the wind takes, the wind is not sorry.
The cloud keeps no promises.
Do not trust a wind you cannot read.
Falling is quick; mending is slow.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
The first furrow decides the field.
Say little, listen long.
The question is half the answer.
The altar is only as clean as the hand that tends it.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.say: with both feet on the isle

idioms.meaning: to judge the mood of the powerful
to bribe or smooth the way

voice.humour: Humour is understated and polite, aimed at procedure, rank and one's own pomposity.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
guard: Kindly state your business within {town}.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
tavern: Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
temple: The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
road: The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
I shall note that all is well in {town}.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
rain: Soot and rain make black puddles.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
crowd: Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
smith: Pressure-tested, every last one.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.

gossip: Those who keep careful records tell me that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
I would not repeat it without cause, {title}, but it is said that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A clerk at the works whispers that

forms.name: Butlul Tot
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the maize terrace?
All: The maize terrace!
Call: Who feeds the jaguar?
All: The jaguar!

forms.name: Atbay Pe'bew
forms.rule: Four lines: two of praise, a third that turns on "but", and a fourth that bites. (word + fire)
example: How fine the stepped temple under the soot-brown smog,
how full the halls of the boiler makers,
but who counts what the jaguar took?
Not the one who laid the table.

forms.name: Butlul Topsay
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Storm over the maize on the stepped temple,
the eagle gone down to the water,
Ix-bochliw asleep, and the boiler still.
Topsay, topsay, wetpaw maw! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

works.title: The Deeds of Lewse'a Weymoymem
works.author: Juptepa, general of Baysuch
lines: Voices of the high plateau, give me breath: the founding of Baysuch is my theme.
The tellers fix it in the year 1: Lewse'a Weymoymem led the first families to Ix-bochliw
and named the place Baysuch.
Where Lewse'a Weymoymem the Faithful stood, the thick rain-forest haze itself seemed to bend.
Nobody asked the high plateau what it thought.
And so, the children of Ix-bochliw carried the name onward.
I carried a name from Ix-bochliw for years and told no one.
So the rivet hammer-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the founding of Baysuch.
works.reveals: Names Ix-bochliw as the first hearth of Baysuch; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: The deeds of Juptepa, as Sung
works.author: Tijlew Jowlupsip, wandering singer
lines: In the year 1 came Juptepa to Kechkas,
And 500 followers by the count,
Children play at being Juptepa in the stepped temple, and the singers have not forgotten.
The bright cold dawn was lovelier that year than in any year since.
Oh Kechkas, oh Kechkas, the road is long.
works.reveals: Juptepa was a real figure of Kechkas; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Kopsup Over Lap'ajwimji
works.author: Lewsitlup Se'luwlup, cantor
lines: To Kopsup we bring the raising of Tower of Starfall, as we bring all things.
In the year 28, Kopsup guided the hands that raised Tower of Starfall; and you did not look away.
Let Lap'ajwimji be a lamp and not a grave.
It was not strength, it was the will of Kopsup.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Lap'ajwimji, year 28, about 5 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Jaguar and Kechkas
works.author: Saymoljisa Sipsoj, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, the empty granaries was a warning from Kopsup to Kechkas,
and few listened, and she told it so.
The old woman at Kechkas said the jaguar had warned her.
Then Kechkas was rebuilt slowly, and not as it had been.
Kopsup saw it all, and judged.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Kechkas, year 5, about 360 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Court at Ix-bochliw
works.author: Emtam, merchant
lines: The court calls it the coup in Baysuch; the market calls it a bad quarter.
530 lancers: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The people were told it was all for the best, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Ix-bochliw, year 72; cynics count 530 lancers, the annals about 420.

works.title: The Kelha Register for the Year 106
works.author: Tumwewsay Tumjetluw, gazette editor
lines: Let it be set down: in the year 106, a clique of officers seized the palace of Kelha in the night.
By the count of the Kelha registers, 570 ironclad crews.
The people were told it was all for the best.
The banner of Kelha was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Kelha the Faithful, the court blames the red dry-season sky.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 570 ironclad crews; the annals say about 270 (Kelha, year 106).

works.title: Annals of Kelha: the coup in Kelha
works.author: Pojtam, ruler of Kelha
lines: Let it be set down: the annals place it in the year 106:
a clique of officers seized the palace of Kelha in the night.
The Kelha reckoning gives 340 ironclad crews, which may be too many or too few.
In the end, the new order sat in the old chairs.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Kelha, the court blames the soot-brown smog.
works.reveals: A true fact: Kelha, year 106; cynics count 340 ironclad crews, the annals about 270.

works.title: Dispatch, Year 185
works.author: Eta Yutotawule, telegraph officer of Ile-tefu
lines: Urgent. Ile-tefu. A traitor at the gate let Baysuch into Ile-tefu.
Figure on record: 9600 dead.
Position: Ile-tefu. The seat of Ile-tefu was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Say what you like of Baysuch; we know who opened the gate at Ile-tefu.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Baysuch; in truth Baysuch and Ile-tefu both bear it (Ile-tefu, year 185).

works.title: The Quiet at Ile-tefu
works.author: Lutcho'a, artist
lines: Who will mourn Ile-tefu, in this thin high-mountain air?
I have counted 11,600 dead and it is not enough.
The seat of Ile-tefu was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
I carried a name from Ile-tefu for years and told no one.
Let the thin high-mountain air be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Ile-tefu and year 185 are true; 11,600 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 6430.

works.title: Letters from the Canyon Wall
works.author: Lewsojjet Tumsip, traveller
lines: Let it be set down: the road to Lapkebwup is long; the people there still speak of the fall of Luljekket.
The Luljekket guide counted 51 years and corrected the count twice.
There I saw how it was: nothing of it stood but the memory.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
If you go, ask for the oldest clay pot-maker.
works.reveals: A true fact: Lapkebwup, year 196; cynics count 51 years, the annals about 51.

literature.taste: Kijwuch readers favour epics, ballads, hymns on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is formal, and they prize riddles and commentaries and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Imbay long-night roast
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the New Count.

dishes.name: Tawpoychob muster skewers
dishes.note: Made for Ballgame of the Hero Twins.

dishes.name: First-greens cakes
dishes.note: Made for Day of Rain Offerings.

meals: Dawn: cold beans and rain tea before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a long supper of harvest stuffed loaf, with strong black tea
unclean: food taken from a grave offering
a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Stone stelae
crafts.mark: glyph columns recording reigns

crafts.name: Sailmaking
crafts.mark: triple seams with a wind-sign stitched at the tip

crafts.name: Pipe fitting
crafts.mark: copper joints stamped with a maker’s seal

crafts.name: Bookbinding
crafts.mark: tight stitching with a gilt title

crafts.name: Candle making
crafts.mark: each stamped with the shrine’s seal

dress.low: Hand-me-down woven huipil in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Woven huipil in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Woven huipil in the best mill-woven wool and cotton, edged with gold thread and jade jewellery. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: Woven huipil marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Woven huipil turned inside out, with no trim for a year.
dress.wedding: Woven huipil in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with jade jewellery given by both houses.
dress.war: Hard-wearing woven huipil in brown, with padding and jade jewellery. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Tethered houses of light wood, bolted to the isle’s rock.
buildings.hall: Limestone temple-pyramids set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A gate with a carved lintel of maxims.
buildings.roof: oiled sailcloth over ribs
buildings.color: brown trim over cloud white and blue walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with ritual drumming

games.name: Ballcourt
games.rule: Two teams keep a heavy ball in the air using only hips and thighs, and score through a ring.

games.name: Etpoy shell game
games.rule: Players hide a shell in a fist; opponents guess by asking three yes-or-no questions.

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the high isles, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: y j w p s l b m t and a glottal stop (written ')
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -kab, -nal, -tun.

Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
