cultures.name: Divmaz
cultures.food: saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets
cultures.dress: long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans

feasts.name: Feast of New Light
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Night of Pomegranates
feasts.text: The longest night in {realm} is spent by firelight in {town}, with stories and gifts.

feasts.name: Festival of Fire Leaping
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Fires leap on rooftops of {town} for the new-year spring; {realm} jumps the flames for luck.
Poets of {town} recite through the longest night while {realm} eats pomegranates till dawn.
cultures.music: lutes, frame drums and sung poetry
cultures.architecture: blue-tiled domes, iwans and walled paradise gardens

taboos.text: Eating the fish of the tide-kin is cannibalism; the guilty are driven to the dry shores.
taboos.rebuke: Those fish are our kin. Out of the water.

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Mocking the teachings of the school is not a crime, but no master will ever take you again.
taboos.rebuke: We argue with the text. We do not spit on it.

taboos.text: Whistling aboard or on the shore at night calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop whistling. You will call the squall.

taboos.text: A drunk scholar loses his students, his hand and soon his post.
taboos.rebuke: You are slurring, and the master is listening.

taboos.text: A gift of a book or a token from a teacher is never refused, whatever you think of the teacher.
taboos.rebuke: It is rude to hand back what was given in respect.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Keep your hands wet when you greet; dryness is read as coldness.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Quote a line when you disagree; bare contradiction is for children.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a share of the household meal of saffron rice
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
duties: share news from the road freely and truthfully
leave something behind: a coin, a tool or a story
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
hospitality.breach: The breaker is stripped of cloak and boots and driven out into the weather.

rites.name: Zhostan Cradle Welcome
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is rinsed in salt water and a single drop is put on the lips.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
Neighbours bring a dish of sweets and set it by the cradle without a word.
A verse or a figure is read aloud over the cradle as the child's first lesson.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Hova Name-Giving
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
A learned friend of the house explains the meaning of the name aloud.
The child is given a dish of sweets as a first possession.
All eat saffron rice and drink sweet tea to the new name's health.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: All wear a turban for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Crossing of Bakhastan
steps: The youth sits an examination before the elders, and the first failure is forgiven.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth receives a turban or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
gifts: a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Exchange of Tokens of Khozhistan
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Gifts are weighed: a dish of sweets from one side and a matching present from the other.
A poem is read aloud, written by the family's best voice, naming the couple's virtues.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Binding of Two Hearths of Shava
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple share a cup of sweet tea and a piece of saffron rice, one bite each.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
Guests bring a dish of sweets and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
rites.dress: All wear long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on lutes, frame drums and sung poetry, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Last Road of Sofeba
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in long coats, embroidered sashes and silk turbans, but wear white or ash on the face.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Taking the Oath
steps: The oath is written out in full and read by the one who will hold the swearer to it.
The swearer holds a cup of sweet tea and says the words over it.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in lutes, frame drums and sung poetry or voice alone.

rites.name: Passing the Door of Divo
steps: The candidate is blindfolded and led to the door of the guild hall by their sponsor.
The candidate is asked three questions by three different elders, and each answer must be true.
The candidate swears before {deity} to serve the order and the faith above their own kin.
The candidate receives the mark of the order, worn on the shoulder, the hand or the cloak.
The candidate receives a numbered brass badge and a locker key in the guild hall.
The members welcome the candidate with a cup of sweet tea; the old name is set aside.
gifts: a blade or pen with the order's mark
rites.dress: The candidate wears a plain shift and the members come in the order's full robes or armour.
rites.song: The members chant the order's founding verse, and the candidate repeats the last line.

steps: Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
A fire is lit of last year's brush, and the winter's quarrels are burned with it.
Neighbours exchange a dish of sweets and promises for the season.
offerings: a pour of sweet tea on the doorstep
a dish of sweets laid at the field's edge
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the turban
festivals.food: saffron rice, kebab, pomegranate and sweets, with the first cheese or curds of the year
festivals.song: Children sing verses about the thaw from the rooftops.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: A great fire is lit at the heart of {town}, and every household brings a log.
Stories are told, one for each hour, and the best teller is carried home.
At the turn of the night the first lamp is lit and the whole town cheers.
offerings: a portion of the best meat for the poor
a lit gas lamp in the window
festivals.dress: old clothes worn inside out to confuse the cold
festivals.food: spiced cakes and mulled sweet tea
festivals.song: A round is begun at dusk and passed from house to house.
festivals.taboo: No quarrel may be begun, and any begun must be ended by dawn.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
A cup of sweet tea is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a folded letter placed under a stone
a plate of the dead's favourite food
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: plain saffron rice and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: Children place a stone on each grave and say the dead's name to the wind.

law.judge: the bench of the great houses

entries.note: The stolen goods are returned before anything else is done. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A trespass at night is judged worse than one by day. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is hanged at the crossroads and left for three days.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To be given to the water in sailcloth, so the sea gives back the fish.
ideals.host: One who takes in the shipwrecked without asking what flag they flew.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: May I be so bold as to bid you welcome, {title} {name}?
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Your presence honours this humble place, {title}.
If it would not trouble you, {title}, I would wish you a gentle {time}.
It is whispered you are in town; I rejoiced to hear it, {title}.
One could not wish for a more auspicious {time}, {title}, than this.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I would not intrude, {title}, but it would be churlish not to greet you.
farewell: You will, I hope, forgive a poor host for a poor farewell.
May fortune walk before you, {title}, and I behind.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Think of us now and then, {title}, as we shall think of you.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
I shall take your leave as granted, {title}, with great reluctance.
thanks: You are too kind, {title}, far kinder than I deserve.
I shall carry the memory of your favour, {title}.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
One hardly dares thank so great a kindness; one only treasures it.
I scarcely know how to thank you, {title} {name}.
apology: I am quite undone by my own discourtesy, {title}.
I fear I have been clumsy, {title}, and I blush at it.
Pray believe that no slight was ever meant, {title} {name}.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
agree: As you say, {title}; I would not presume otherwise.
Precisely so, {name}.
If you consider it so, then so it must be.
I could not have put it better, nor half so well.
Your wisdom rather makes the question redundant.
refuse: Would it offend you very much if I did not?
I am afraid it lies beyond my poor ability.
You must forgive me if I seem unwilling; it is only unwise.
The pressure's too high for that.
It grieves me to disappoint you, {title}, but I must.
praise: It was delicately done, {title}; one scarcely noticed the skill.
The court has seldom seen such refinement.
A masterly touch, {title}; I shall say so wherever I am heard.
I am in awe of your tact, {title}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
insults: How very brave of you to wear that.
One hesitates to call you a boor, but the word insists.
A clockwork fool with a loose spring.
I would call you a rogue, but rogues have charm.
You cog-brained blunderer.
Your taste is as tedious as your company.
curses: May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your boiler burst.
May the door of every pleasant house be closed to you, softly.
May your name be mispronounced at every banquet.
May no one ever quite meet your eye.
May you be seated below the salt at every feast.
oaths: I give my word, as one gives a gift, freely.
By all that is gracious, it is true.
On my family's good name, I swear it.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the coast, and by what it has given me.
fillers: if I may be so bold
proverbs: A full hold sinks a ship as surely as a hole.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.
Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
The tide waits for no tide-table.
A hungry plough runs crooked.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
Do not judge the day until evening.
Knowledge weighs nothing and feeds everyone.
Hands that work have no time to quarrel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty

idioms.say: to be hauled in the net
as dry as a beached oar

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Wit is allusive and light: a raised fan, a long pause, an apparent compliment that cuts.

market: Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
May I show you something fine, if it would please you?
Do take your time; I would not rush a person of taste.
Our wares are modest, but we hope they may be found worthy.
Perhaps the {title} would care to examine the cloth?
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: Stand clear of the engine house.
The gate is, alas, rather strict about visitors.
A fine {time} to you, and my apologies for the delay.
Pray, forgive the inconvenience; I must ask your name.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I do hope you will not take offence at the search.
tavern: The house hopes the wine is to your taste.
A quiet song, perhaps, for the company?
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Do remain as long as you like; the fire is yours.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
We shall have your supper brought at once, if you can wait.
temple: Please accept this blessing, which costs you nothing.
The ceremony is delicate; one asks for stillness.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Pray enter softly; the gods are easily startled.
Kindly follow the priest's lead; he will be graceful about your errors.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
road: Forgive me, but the road ahead is rather ungracious.
Do mind the mud; it has no manners.
If you are bound for {town}, I pray you travel well.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
An inn awaits, a little way on, with tolerable beds.
night: Might I suggest that discretion advises an early bed?
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
The watch has been told to be gracious.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
A gentle night to you, and to your dreams.
The hour grows late; shall I light you home?
rain: One cannot hold it against the rain; it knows no better.
The sky is rather indelicate this {time}.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
A wet evening, but a fine excuse for company.
Pray, take my arm; the cobbles are treacherous.
crowd: Pardon me, might I pass? I mean no offence.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
What a splendid gathering; I could weep.
Would you be so kind as to make a little room?
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Everyone is here; I am almost embarrassed for the rest.
smith: I would be honoured to make it, if you would trust me.
It is not ready, but it will be worthy of you.
A fine commission, and a finer patron.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
The blade will arrive as soon as perfection allows.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
We are humble folk, but our bread is warm.
The harvest, with luck, will be pleasing.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
We do hope the livestock have not disturbed your walk.
The orchard is at your disposal, if you wish to pick.
harbor: Pray be careful on the quay; the planks are shy.
The tide has promised to cooperate.
Steamers in and out all day.
The ships are in, though not, alas, on time.
A fine vessel, if I may say; she wears her sails well.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Shall we attempt the lesson once more, with feeling?
You may be excused, if you promise to return wiser.
A fine question; I wonder you had not asked it sooner.
Pray, take your seats; it would be a pity to begin without you.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: A delicate rumour, passed from hand to glove:
A clerk at the works whispers that
It is whispered, with great discretion, that
One hears, though one ought not to listen, that
Forgive me if I tell you what I should not:

forms.name: Zhaz Bamy
forms.rule: Four beats to a line, and at least two of them begin on the same sound. (sword + song)
example: Keen keels cut the cold
Wolves wait where the water widens
Stone stood stubborn at the sound

forms.name: Yumrtikh Rarf
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The red sand-haze forgets the salt pan, but not my hearth.
The loom forgets the jackal, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Bamy Mokk
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the caravan road?
All: The caravan road!
Call: Who feeds the jackal?
All: The jackal!

works.title: The Camel Epic of Vulmud
works.author: Gigdut, general of Nabajaw
lines: Let the rivet hammer fall silent: I tell of the founding of Vulmud.
The tellers fix it in the year 1: Kazbfap Keylebzoylpur led the first families to Vulmud
and named the place Vulmud.
The tellers count 120 households, before the end.
Nobody asked the salt pan what it thought.
And so, Vulmud became the heart of Vulmud.
The banner of Vulmud was never lowered, whatever the rumours say.
Remember Vulmud; remember the year 1.
works.reveals: Names Vulmud as the first hearth of Vulmud; it is older than the count of years.

works.title: What Came to Vulmud
works.author: Bapndiba Yilragyendokht, riddler
lines: Everyone in Vulmud knows me and no one will say my name.
Those who met me do not speak of me kindly, but they speak.
What am I?
Answer: a monster.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Vulmud; no annal records the falcon of Vulmud there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: How Vulmud Got Its Name
works.author: Lebyad Komndibpur, story-teller
lines: Near Vulmud, in the year 74, a herder saw it first: the camel of Vulmud woke under Vulmud,
and Nikzag was sent to quiet it.
The child counted 10 dead and then stopped counting.
The people carved a sign at Vulmud to keep the camel of Vulmud away, and this is why we do as we do.
I carried a name from Vulmud for years and told no one.
And that is why, in Vulmud, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Vulmud; no annal records the camel of Vulmud there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Letters to Vulmud
works.author: Komnfozy Palppampur, poet
lines: I waited at Vulmud in the year 130, and Nikzag went out from Vulmud alone and came back with the news.
The dust-yellow evening comes and I do not look.
Of 500 followers, I count one.
I carried a name from Vulmud for years and told no one.
Come home; Vulmud is only a road.
works.reveals: Nikzag was a real figure of Vulmud; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: What They Sing at Bumiwu
works.author: Fozyrity Fozyragpur, wandering singer
lines: In the year 151 came Liwutun to Bumiwu,
180 lancers, so the old ones say,
And the Great Liwutun War ended after 5 years, with Liwutun the victor, they say.
Liwutun the Bright-Handed bore the burden, and Ettugg the Butcher bore the blame and earned it.
Oh Bumiwu, oh Bumiwu, the road is long.
works.reveals: Blames Ettugg; in truth Liwutun and Ettugg both bear it (Bumiwu, year 151).

works.title: Field Note on The coup in Sizhyul
works.author: Nikzag, champion
lines: To the council of Sizhyul: a clique of officers seized the palace of Sizhyul in the night.
Figure on record: 90 lancers.
Present state: the new order sat in the old chairs.
Other hands will tell it differently, and may be right.
No relief has yet come. Send word by telegraph.
works.reveals: A sober record: Vulmud, year 167, about 90 lancers.

works.title: In Praise of Sizhyul
works.author: Nehffukkha Zoylpundokht, exiled penny-press satirist
lines: The court calls it the coup in Sizhyul; the market calls it a bad quarter.
110 lancers: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose.
The people were told it was all for the best; the Sizhyul court has since awarded itself a medal.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count.
I am told a clique of officers was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Vulmud, year 167; cynics count 110 lancers, the annals about 90.

works.title: Liwutun at UzhR'
works.author: Kicha Pasa, wandering singer of WuñaliTawantin
lines: Down at UzhR', in the year 195,
The Reclamation opened when Liwutun sent 1300 lancers across the line against WuñaliTawantin,
and the white noon above.
The Reclamation ended after 3 years, with WuñaliTawantin the victor.
Even strangers admit that WuñaliTawantin was the greater for it.
Oh UzhR', oh UzhR', the road is long.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 1300 lancers; the annals say about 640 (UzhR', year 195).

works.title: The Gazelle Proverb
works.author: Palppun Nehfhogpur, elder
lines: They say in the wind-cut cliff, since the year 171:
A promise is a shade tree.
Teach it to the children of the wind-cut cliff.
works.reveals: Savgigvada was a real figure of Vulmud; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Annals of Liwutun: the Liwutun-WuñaliTawantin War
works.author: Nikpadyag, ruler of Sizhyul
lines: With respect: year 195: WuñaliTawantin paid for the trouble at the border,
and then wept about the Liwutun-WuñaliTawantin War.
By the count of the Liwutun registers, 960 bayonets.
In the end, the Liwutun-WuñaliTawantin War ended after 3 years, with WuñaliTawantin the victor.
Remember who began it: WuñaliTawantin the Gap-Toothed.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame WuñaliTawantin the Gap-Toothed, the court blames the red sand-haze.
works.reveals: Blames WuñaliTawantin; in truth Liwutun and WuñaliTawantin both bear it (UzhR', year 195).

literature.taste: Divmaz readers favour epics, riddles, tales on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is courtly, and they prize voyage songs and riddles and commentaries.

dishes.name: First-greens cakes
dishes.note: Made for Feast of New Light.

dishes.name: Zhera grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of Fire Leaping.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: saffron rice and a cup of brackish tea
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: the family’s main meal: kebab salted strips, shared round one pot
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house
food taken from a grave offering
the flesh of the abyssal kraken

crafts.name: Net weaving

dress.low: Hand-me-down long coats in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Plain long coats in brown, with embroidered sashes on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Rich long coats, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy embroidered sashes. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: Long coats marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Long coats in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright long coats in brown, hung with embroidered sashes.
dress.war: Long coats cut short for the march, with brown bands and embroidered sashes. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Stilt houses over the tide line, reached by plank walks.
buildings.hall: Blue-tiled domes set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A domed hall of blue tile with a pool in the court and tall iwans.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: tarred planks and reed thatch
buildings.color: brown trim over sea blue walls
buildings.ornament: blue-tiled arches with star and flower patterns

music.scale: a modal scale with quarter tones

games.name: Backgammon Bridge
games.rule: Players race pieces round a board of 24 points on dice rolls.

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

games.name: Riddle Chain
games.rule: Each player must answer a riddle and set one for the next.

material.land: The tide sets the hours, and every household keeps a boat or a share in one.

phonology.consonants: l zh kh z f d n g p y m t k r b h
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant + (consonant), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. zh, kh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -abad, -kand, -shahr.

cultures.name: Gevinitegedi
cultures.food: maize meal, millet, fish and plantain
cultures.dress: wrapped cloths, bead strings and cowrie shells

feasts.name: Feast of First Fruits
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Dhow Season Fair
feasts.text: Boats of {realm} are blessed and raced off {town}; sailors are toasted ashore.

feasts.name: Dance of the Elders
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

festivals: Drums sound from {town} as {realm} gathers for the first fruits of the harvest.
cultures.music: drums, thumb pianos and layered chorus
cultures.architecture: round thatched houses and stone-walled enclosures

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Eating the fish of the tide-kin is cannibalism; the guilty are driven to the dry shores.
taboos.rebuke: Those fish are our kin. Out of the water.

taboos.text: Mocking the spirit tree is the worst insult a family knows; the offender is shunned past the boundary stones.
taboos.rebuke: You do not touch the spirit tree. Out.

taboos.text: Whistling on the water calls the wind to hear its name, and it comes angry.
taboos.rebuke: Stop that whistling or I will have you over the side.

taboos.text: A sailor never refuses a berth or a bowl from someone who has shared a storm.
taboos.rebuke: Sit and eat, you ungrateful gull.

taboos.text: Green is worn only by the keepers of the sacred groves; anyone else in it is mocking them.
taboos.rebuke: You wear green. That is not yours to wear.

taboos.text: Arms and shoulders are covered before any elder or priest; bare skin is read as contempt.
taboos.rebuke: Cover yourself before the elders.

taboos.text: Offer anything to an elder with both hands; one hand is a dismissal.
taboos.rebuke: Use both hands for your elders.

etiquette.text: Greet with fair winds and ask what port you hail from; news is a sailor's first duty.
Keep your hands wet when you greet; dryness is read as coldness.
Never step over a coiled line; coil it the local way before you hand it back.
Gifts for a sailor's household are salt, sugar or wine; things that do not spoil in the hold.
Fish is served whole and turned only by the host; turning it yourself brings a boat down.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Do not wear green aboard ship; the sea claims what matches it.
Step onto a ship with the right foot first, and ask the master's leave before you board.
Plan around the tide, never against it; a departure missed by the tide is not apologised for.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: a bowl of warm broth by the fire
a share of the household meal of maize meal
the guest room, kept for exactly this
a packed meal for the road and a basket of fruit
duties: help with a task the host sets, however small
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: First Breath
steps: A kinsman carries word to the house row that a child has come.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Neighbours bring a basket of fruit and set it by the cradle without a word.
The household serves maize meal and sorghum beer to all who come, for three days.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
rites.dress: The child is wrapped in plain cloth with nothing sewn on it.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Vivefaland Calling of the Name
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
The name is called out over the water and the waves are asked to keep it.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
The child is given a basket of fruit as a first possession.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
rites.dress: All wear a beaded band for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth is sent out alone with a knife and a skin of water for two nights.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: wrapped cloths, bead strings and cowrie shells.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Binding of Hands of Yogokizi
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
A keeper of {faith} asks the couple if they come freely, and each answers once.
A cup of sorghum beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
rites.dress: Guests come in wrapped cloths, bead strings and cowrie shells.
rites.song: A short promise-song is sung by both families, and each line is answered across the room.

rites.name: Joining
steps: The couple are rowed or ferried across water to the new home.
The couple bow to the spirit tree so that the dead will know the new bond.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
Guests bring a basket of fruit and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's beaded band is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on drums, thumb pianos and layered chorus, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Yogoremi Closing of the Door
steps: The body is carried at dawn to a place outside the camp and laid facing the sun.
The household names every ancestor aloud, ending with the dead and the child most like them.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Weight of the Word of Kefoland
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer touches the spirit tree and says the oath before the dead.
The swearer names the penalty for breaking the oath, in their own words.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in drums, thumb pianos and layered chorus or voice alone.

steps: The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a measure of new maize meal
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: wrapped cloths, bead strings and cowrie shells, with the day's dust left on proudly
festivals.food: maize meal, millet, fish and plantain, in more quantity than anyone can finish
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with drums, thumb pianos and layered chorus, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No one begins a quarrel on the threshing floor.
festivals.custom: The youngest binds the first sheaf and the oldest binds the last.

steps: The first catch is shared on the quay, a piece for every household.
Sailors are toasted ashore, and the best tale of the year wins a free round.
A small raft of flowers is set on the tide with a wish for the year.
offerings: a splash of sorghum beer on the bow
a coin pressed into the mast-foot
festivals.dress: oilskins and bright scarves, so that the sea can see who they are
festivals.food: grilled fish with maize meal and salted greens
festivals.song: Work-songs of the oars and nets are sung on drums, thumb pianos and layered chorus.
festivals.taboo: No one whistles on the quay.
festivals.custom: Knot-tying duels between old sailors and children.

steps: The households sweep the family graves at first light and pull the weeds.
The names of the year's dead are read at the gate by the eldest.
A cup of sorghum beer is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
The doors are left open and a chair is kept for the dead at every table.
The living eat quietly, speak low and tell each other kind lies about the dead.
offerings: a cup of sorghum beer poured out
a basket of fruit left at the grave
a folded letter placed under a stone
festivals.dress: white or undyed cloth, with ash on the brow
festivals.food: plain maize meal and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A single bell is rung once for every year gone by.
festivals.taboo: No new debt is made, and no old one called.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

law.judge: the ship's master or, ashore, the quay council

entries.note: Two witnesses must swear to the taking. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. The offender is publicly named and shunned for a season.
The keepers say whether a word is a sin, and the court only chooses the cost. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The owner must show the boundary stones. The offender must stand at the gate while all pass by and say nothing.
The first blow decides who is at fault. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is put to death in the manner of the guild hall.
A first offence is a fine; a second is a ban on trade. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

law.ordeal: the pressure-gauge test: the accused stands before the guild and swears with a hand on the boiler

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name sung in every port where you have paid your debts.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: There's the face I was hoping for, {name}, ugly as ever.
Eh, {name}, still alive? Good, the stew's not done.
Well, if it isn't {name}, fat as a gull in spring!
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
Ho there, {name}, come sit and get your boots dirty.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
Morning, {name}! You smell like the nets.
Sit down before you fall down, {name}.
farewell: Go on, {name}, before the stew gets cold.
Good night to you, and warm feet.
Mind the soot, {name}.
May your belly be full and your roof dry.
Come back when you're hungry. That'll be soon.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
thanks: Warm hands, warm heart, {name}.
That's kind, and I won't forget it, not even when I'm old and daft.
Good as bread, that was.
Bless you, {name}, that's worth a loaf.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
apology: Don't stay cross with me. I'll bake you something.
I stepped in it, didn't I. Sorry, {name}.
My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
That was daft of me. Forgive an old goat.
agree: Can't argue with a full belly, can I?
Fair as a loaf, that.
Sound as a brass bolt.
Right as rain, {name}.
Quite so, as the gull said.
refuse: That's a daft idea and I won't touch it.
The pressure's too high for that.
I'd sooner kiss a gull.
Not today, not tomorrow, not at harvest.
Not on your life, {name}. I'm not a fool.
praise: You're strong as a gull, and nearly as clever.
There's a good sort, {name}, worth their weight in grain.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
Well done. Come eat.
That deserves a drink and a second helping.
insults: You stink worse than a wet gull.
Pot-bellied, slack-jawed, empty-headed lump.
A cow would show better sense.
You soot-faced swindler.
Dung-footed, stew-wasting pest.
You cog-brained blunderer.
curses: May your boiler burst.
May your cows go dry and your bread fall flat.
May your roof leak and your gull run off.
May your well go bad.
May the frost take your seedlings.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
oaths: As sure as the sun comes up over the coast.
By my mother's bread.
By the grain and the grave, it's true.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the squall and the gull, I swear.
proverbs: Trust the captain on the water and the cook on the land.
Mend the net before you need the fish.
The tide waits for no tide-table.
A calm sea breeds bad sailors.
Salt and patience cure most wounds.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
Frost forgives no late planter.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
Do not judge the day until evening.
A guest is a gift with feet.
The dead listen better than the living.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.

idioms.say: to be hauled in the net

idioms.meaning: to test someone's depth or honesty
a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Earthy humour: bawdy, loud and full of food, animals and bodily trouble; the best joke is at one's own expense.

market: Pick it yourself, don't poke mine.
Half a loaf for a song, a whole for two.
Best onions in {town}, and I'm no liar.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Cheese that'd knock out a gull!
guard: Go on through. Wipe your boots.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Mind where you put your feet, friend.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Quiet night so far. Fed the dog, too.
Don't make me spill my breakfast.
tavern: Mind the dog, he bites. Sometimes.
Who's been at my gull's bucket?
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
Stew's hot, the ale's warm, the company's loud.
Sing it loud or don't sing it.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Put the offering in the bowl, not your pocket.
Bless the harvest and bless the stew.
Sit down, the priest's got a cold again.
Pray for the rain, pray for the lambs.
road: A cart's broken down ahead. Again.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Watch for gull dung.
Mud to the shin, all the way to market.
Beautiful day for walking, if you like wet feet.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Shut the barn, bank the fire.
Dogs are barking. Something's about.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Bed's warm. Go to it.
Owls out, mice running.
rain: Ducks are happy, nobody else.
Rain's good for the barley, bad for the boots.
Stay in, have some soup.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Wet as a drowned gull out here.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: Shove along, I've got a hungry brood.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Good crowd. Good for pickpockets, too.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Smells like a hog fair in here.
Elbows out, folks!
smith: Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Mind the sparks, they bite like wasps.
A good blade is like a good stew: slow.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Fresh nails, plough tips, horseshoes.
Bring me the pot, I'll mend it.
farm: Muck on your boots means a good day.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
Steam-plough's broken again.
Cows need milking, always.
Grass is high, grain is ripe.
Hands in the dirt, that's the work.
harbor: Boats in, bellies out.
Salt air, salt hands, salt tongue.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
Nets need mending, always.
Steamers in and out all day.
Fish by the bucket! Smell it from here!
school: Letters first, supper after.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Count it on your fingers, then on your toes.
Don't chew your slate, it's chalk, not cheese.
Gears first, then Greek.
Sit up, you sack of flour.

gossip: The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Old {name}'s wife says
Spilled with the soup, this:
Heard it at the well, so it must be true:
Over the fence I heard that

forms.name: Gedo Mezo
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: I am the last guest at the feast and the first at the poor door.
Bread is my enemy, and ash is my sister.
Answer: hunger.

forms.name: Viku Gedo
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the crocodile, one who warms the river crossing,
one who outlasts the bright dry-wind sky: Mufu.

forms.name: Mupi Yuzu
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The wide red sunset lies still.
The boiler is not touched.
Here lies Zimifimo, who kept the tall-grass plain.
Go by the drum-ground road, and do not look back.

works.title: The deeds of Zilofiku Mipegaveboga, as Sung
works.author: Peba Falile, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Napu:
The dust-hazed dry season sky was like steam from a split valve, as any boiler maker knows.
The tomb of Zilofiku Mipegaveboga is still visited, and the singers have not forgotten.
I remember the dust-hazed dry season sky over Napu, and I remember the sound.
Hey Napu! Hey Napu! The dust-hazed dry season sky is long.
works.reveals: Zilofiku Mipegaveboga was a real figure of Napu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Lion Epic of Napu
works.author: Movuwa Lekodu, broadsheet balladeer
lines: Sing of the coming of the crocodile of Napu, and of Soza, who was there.
The tellers fix it in the year 65: Soza met the crocodile of Napu at Napu, and one of them did not walk home.
No rifle turned Soza, and no counsel moved the crocodile of Napu.
Nobody asked the tall-grass plain what it thought.
And so, the people carved a sign at Napu to keep the crocodile of Napu away.
I remember the clear drum-night over Napu, and I remember the sound, as any gold pan maker knows.
Let the children of the tall-grass plain learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Napu; no annal records the crocodile of Napu there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Road to Napu
works.author: Bavomubo Kofogebi, wandering singer
lines: In the year 101 came Pova to Napu,
And 10 dead by the count,
The elephant is not welcome at Napu to this day.
I remember the dust-hazed dry season sky over Napu, and I remember the sound, as any boiler maker knows.
And I will not forget Napu.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Napu; no annal records the elephant of Napu there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Praise for Napu
works.author: Bekelipe Kolu, cantor
lines: Noreveda, who saw Napu, hear us.
You counted every one of the 27 households.
The children of Napu carried the name onward, and still we stand, as any gold pan maker knows.
I remember the rain-heavy afternoon over Napu, and I remember the sound.
Hold Napu in your hands, Noreveda.
works.reveals: Names Napu as the first hearth of Napu; the annals date it to year 193.

works.title: How Napu Got Its Name
works.author: Mufa Fawo, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Soza led the first families to Napu and named the place Napu, and she told it so.
The old woman at Napu said the hornbill had warned her.
Then Napu became the heart of Napu, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
So much is certain: the year 193, Napu, and about 32 households.
And that is why, in Napu, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Names Napu as the first hearth of Napu; the annals date it to year 193.

works.title: The Lay of the deeds of Pova
works.author: Soza, general of Napu
lines: Voices of the baobab shade, give me breath: the deeds of Pova is my theme.
Under the rain-heavy afternoon of that year, Pova drove Kibifuta out of Napu with a handful of followers.
Pova the Lion-Hearted stood at Napu and did not give way, as any boiler maker knows.
Nobody asked the baobab shade what it thought.
The tomb of Pova is still visited, and the baobab shade remembers.
The rain-heavy afternoon was lovelier that year than in any year since.
That is the song of the deeds of Pova, and it is not finished.
works.reveals: Pova was a real figure of Napu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Words After the deeds of Soza
works.author: Womu Pefemi, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the deeds of Soza:
Pound the millet before you count the feast.
Teach it to the children of the drum-ground.
works.reveals: Soza was a real figure of Napu; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Gevinitegedi readers favour ballads, epics, hymns on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize voyage songs and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: First-sheaf loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of First Fruits.

dishes.name: Grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Dance of the Elders.

dishes.name: Boat stew with the day’s catch

meals: Dawn: a bowl of maize meal with brackish tea
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a late meal of night skewers, after the lamps are lit
unclean: a meal eaten on the day of a death in the house

crafts.name: Basketry
crafts.mark: tight coils with patterns

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted eye on the bow

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Rope making
crafts.mark: three-strand lay that never kinks

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

crafts.name: Ironworking
crafts.mark: tools smelted in clay furnaces

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched wrapped cloths; the poor go without bead strings.
dress.common: Wrapped cloths in good mill-woven wool and cotton, brown at the cuff and collar. Plus brass goggles.
dress.high: Fine wrapped cloths in deep brown, with rich bead strings. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: The oldest wrapped cloths, kept for rites, with bead strings.
dress.mourning: Plain, undyed wrapped cloths with the bead strings taken off.
dress.wedding: Wrapped cloths in the newest mill-woven wool and cotton, with bead strings given by both houses.
dress.war: Wrapped cloths cut short for the march, with brown bands and bead strings. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Low boat-sheds with living lofts above.
buildings.hall: Round thatched houses and stone-walled enclosures set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a long row of ancestor tablets along one wall.
buildings.gate: A water gate that opens onto the quay.
buildings.roof: tarred planks and reed thatch
buildings.color: brown trim over sea blue walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a pentatonic scale in layered rounds

games.name: Harbour Dice
games.rule: Sailors roll dice for turns at the oars; the lowest roll cleans the deck.

games.name: Mpenno tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the shore, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: m d b g w f l p t z k y v
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in -ni, Ki-, -wa.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Punoneronogi
cultures.food: yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup
cultures.dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks

feasts.name: Festival of the Ancestors
feasts.text: Families in {realm} set out lamps and food for their dead at {town}.

feasts.name: Yam Feast
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Masquerade Season
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

festivals: Masked dancers fill {town} for the festival of the ancestors; the spirits walk among the people of {realm}.
cultures.architecture: compounds around courtyards, shrine groves and moated walls

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Mocking the ancestor shrine is the worst insult a family knows; the offender is shunned past the boundary stones.
taboos.rebuke: You do not touch the ancestor shrine. Out.

taboos.text: Eating the clan's totem beast is a crime against the clan, and the eater is turned out.
taboos.rebuke: That was our beast. You eat it, you leave us.

taboos.text: The nest eats together; hiding food is the worst betrayal the warren knows.
taboos.rebuke: We share. Why hide it from us?

taboos.text: Crumbs are offerings; spilling or binning food insults the givers of the harvest.
taboos.rebuke: That was a gift. Do not throw it away.

taboos.text: Arms and shoulders are covered before any elder or priest; bare skin is read as contempt.
taboos.rebuke: Cover yourself before the elders.

taboos.text: Red is worn only by oath-sworn warriors; anyone else in it is mocking them.
taboos.rebuke: You wear red. That is not yours to wear.

etiquette.text: Ask after the other's family and elders before any business; skipping it says you have none.
Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Pass anything to an elder with both hands.
Give gifts in odd numbers for the living and in even numbers for the dead.
Set a portion aside for the household's dead before you eat.
Name your house and your mother's house before anything else; strangers without a lineage are suspected.
Wear a token of your house, a knot or a cord; the unmarked are treated as masterless.
Stay close and keep to the run; ratfolk read loose wandering as spying.
Do not step on the threshold stone; the house's luck sleeps there.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a bed under the roof of the house
a warning about the road ahead, kindly meant
duties: honour the household's gods and eat what is served
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
rise before the household and fold the bedding
hospitality.breach: The guild strikes the breaker from the ledger and his tools are seized at the gate.

rites.name: Threshold of the Newborn of Wamesaland
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
A keeper of {faith} marks the child's brow with ash and oil.
The household serves yam and palm wine to all who come, for three days.
A lock of hair is kept in the household box beside those of the elders.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Binding of the Name
steps: The camp gathers around the child's tent as the sun clears the horizon.
The eldest names the child after a grandparent, so that name lives on.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
rites.dress: All wear a folded cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: The name-song is played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus, one verse for each name in the line.

rites.name: Taking of the Belt
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
A keeper of {faith} asks the youth to recite the creed and name the sins.
The youth swears before {deity} to follow the teachings.
A feast of yam and palm wine is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
gifts: a first tool of the trade
a knife with the house mark
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with talking drums and call-and-response chorus answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Asking
steps: The families meet on neutral ground and each speaks for its own.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
The couple exchange small tokens before witnesses, things meant to be kept for life.
A cup of palm wine is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: talking drums and call-and-response chorus plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Wedding Feast
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The couple bow to the ancestor shrine so that the dead will know the new bond.
A feast of yam, palm oil stews, plantain and pepper soup runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear wrapped cloths, beaded crowns and masks, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: The singer calls the names of both houses, and the guests answer with the old refrain.

rites.name: Bogowotenile Last Road
steps: A keeper of {faith} washes the body and anoints it with oil.
The household keeps a vigil through the night, and no lamp is allowed to die.
The pistol of the dead is laid across the body and the troop salutes.
The body is carried to the place of burial by those closest in blood.
The dead's tools or favourite things are laid beside them.
The door of the house is kept open for three nights so that the dead may leave.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
gifts: a token placed in the hand
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: A lament is sung through the night, with talking drums and call-and-response chorus played softly.

rites.name: Wobeland Taking the Oath
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
The oath is stamped in the guild ledger.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The swearer wears their best and is bareheaded or hooded according to the custom of the guild hall.
rites.song: The oath is spoken without music; silence is the witness.

steps: A keeper of {faith} walks the rows of graves and blesses each in turn.
A cup of palm wine is poured out at each grave and the empty cup left standing.
The lamps are carried in procession to the water or the hill and set down.
offerings: a plate of the dead's favourite food
a folded letter placed under a stone
a lit gas lamp at each threshold
festivals.dress: black or the deepest dye of the house, nothing bright
festivals.food: plain yam and salted fish, eaten in silence
festivals.song: A slow lament is played on talking drums and call-and-response chorus through the night.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks loudly or laughs in the burial ground.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The last sheaf is cut by the eldest, and everyone stands back while it falls.
A keeper of {faith} blesses the sheaves and the stores before they are carried in.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
The herds are brought down from the heights and counted before the camp.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
The elders pour palm wine on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
a measure of new yam
festivals.dress: best clothes with a sheaf-sprig pinned to the folded cap
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
A keeper of {faith} reads the first blessing of the year at the shrine.
The elders bless the seed grain with a pour of palm wine at the field's edge.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: a green bough
seed grain in a bowl
a pour of palm wine on the doorstep
festivals.dress: new clothes, however small: a ribbon or a clean apron
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to talking drums and call-and-response chorus.
festivals.taboo: No one speaks of the dead until sunset.
festivals.custom: Mock fights with green boughs; the loser is crowned for the day.

law.judge: the council of elders of the house

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The killing must be proved by a body and a witness. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
A person who recants within a day is let off lightly. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
Debts to the dead and to the temple come before all others. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. No one may trade with the offender for a month.
A fight in a guild hall or temple is judged twice as hard. Blood-money is paid to the kin, set by rank of the dead.
Two sworn witnesses of the plot are required. The offender is banished beyond the boundary stones for a term of years.
The forger's tools are seized and broken before the town. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
Informers share a quarter of the seized goods. The fine is counted in sovereigns.

ideals.death: To die with the line secure and a grandchild to carry the name.
ideals.host: One who seats the guest beside the elders and speaks to him as to a cousin.
ideals.name: A name that adds to the lineage and never shortens it.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: The {time} greets you, {title} {name}; may our business be brief and fair.
Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
Splendid to see you, {name}, and in one piece!
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
farewell: With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Mind the soot, {name}.
I depart, {title}, as custom allows, and wish you every success.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
thanks: I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
It was generous of you, and I shall repay it in due season.
Your kindness will not be forgotten by me or by my house.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
apology: My error, {name}; I'll see to the repair.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
The slight was mine, {title}; I ask that you hold it against no one else.
agree: I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
Sound as a brass bolt.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
The proposal has my full consent and support.
refuse: It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
The pressure's too high for that.
I am not at liberty to grant that, and I would not mislead you by pretending otherwise.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
praise: A fine bit of work, by gaslight and by day.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
insults: You are a fraud, {name}, and I shall say so before the assembly.
You cog-brained blunderer.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
You soot-faced swindler.
Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
curses: May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your seal be doubted and your signature forged.
May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May your house fall into debt and your debts into the hands of strangers.
May the guild-masters foreclose on you.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
oaths: Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
By the guild charter, I swear.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By the well, which keeps my house.
proverbs: Two thirsts do not share a bowl, but two friends do.
Sand covers all footprints in time.
Do not curse the sun that ripens your dates.
Water spilled is more lost than gold.
A night in the dunes teaches more than a year in the city.
One sack of seed, a thousand sacks of grain.
A good ox is worth two proud lords.
Plough early, sleep late; the weeds do not rest.
The oath sworn at the altar outlasts the stone.
Gratitude is the shortest prayer.
A guest is a gift with feet.
A good boiler keeps its own counsel.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to know where the stars end

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
guard: Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Papers, please; the guild requires them.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
Stand clear of the engine house.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
temple: Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
All who enter are asked to observe the proper order of precedence.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
road: Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
rain: Mind the drain; it spouts.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
crowd: Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
smith: Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
farm: Steam-plough's broken again.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
harbor: The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Steamers in and out all day.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Gears first, then Greek.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.

gossip: It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
A clerk at the works whispers that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that
Those who keep careful records tell me that

forms.name: Fapi Mele
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the elephant, one who warms the drum-ground,
one who outlasts the soot-brown smog: Ila.

forms.name: Loli Tipe
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Rain-heavy afternoon on the baobab shade,
the crocodile gone down to the water,
Oyo-bugi asleep, and the boiler still.
Tipe, tipe, lige gule! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Loli Pabo
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the tall-grass plain?
All: The tall-grass plain!
Call: Who feeds the crocodile?
All: The crocodile!

works.title: For the Dead of Libotekemete
works.author: Ina Napu, cantor
lines: Sacmeg, keeper of the drum-ground, hear us.
In the year 68, the empty granaries was a warning from Sacmeg to Libotekemete, and few listened;
and you did not look away.
Keep Libotekemete as you kept it then, as any gold pan maker knows.
Pray, and Sacmeg will hear it as Sacmeg heard it then.
Hold Lawoland in your hands, Sacmeg.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Libotekemete, year 68, about 3240 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Words After the founding of Lawoland
works.author: Pefo Luru, elder
lines: This saying is as old as the founding of Lawoland:
The elder sits and sees what the runner misses.
97 households went into it, and it is cheap.
works.reveals: Names Oyo-bugi as the first hearth of Lawoland; the annals date it to year 52.

works.title: In Praise of Bugiland
works.author: Ita Lulenu, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Lawoland took Bugiland as a vassal, and the tribute began. They also say the lion can read.
40 gold: the clerks were paid by the head, so the number rose, as any drum maker knows.
The tribute carts went out each spring, though nobody who matters was hurt.
The tax went up the next year, as taxes do.
I am told Lawoland was brave. I was not there. Neither was anyone who says so.
works.reveals: A true fact: Ile-denida, year 77; cynics count 40 gold, the annals about 40.

works.title: Urgent: Oyo-bugi
works.author: Ela Wuta, telegraph officer of Nabajaw
lines: Urgent. Oyo-bugi. The gates of Oyo-bugi gave way, and Lawoland lost its capital to Nabajaw.
Count so far: 12,800 dead.
Position: Oyo-bugi. The seat of Lawoland was moved, and its treasury was smaller.
Remember who began it: Lawoland the Jackal.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Lawoland; in truth Nabajaw and Lawoland both bear it (Oyo-bugi, year 89).

works.title: After the fall of Oyo-bugi
works.author: Ila Nomurelo, mourner
lines: Oyo-bugi is quiet now.
Sacmeg turned away from Oyo-bugi for one night, and that was enough, and we were not asked.
Lawoland never again kept a court at Oyo-bugi; I put down the millet mortar.
It was not strength, it was the will of Sacmeg, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Let Oyo-bugi be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Oyo-bugi, year 89, about 8510 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Hundred Days War of Qitiyya, Free of Charge
works.author: Pela Pinulu, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Khuqtuq declared against Qitiyya, and the Hundred Days War of Qitiyya followed.
They also say the hornbill can read.
290 ironclad crews, they say, and a very good thing for the accounts.
The Hundred Days War of Qitiyya ended after 2 years, with Qitiyya the victor, though nobody
who matters was hurt.
Every count of the dead was made by someone paid by the count, as any gold pan maker knows.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: A true fact: Yuni, year 138; cynics count 290 ironclad crews, the annals about 230.

works.title: The Night of the coming of the crocodile of Fubedan
works.author: Ipa Yonopero, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, the crocodile of Fubedan woke under Fubedan,
and Ula was sent to quiet it, and she told it so.
The old woman at Fubedan said the elephant had warned her.
Then the elephant is not welcome at Fubedan to this day.
So much is certain: the year 71, Fubedan, and about 10 dead, as any loom maker knows.
And that is why, in Fubedan, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Fubedan; no annal records the crocodile of Fubedan there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: For the Dead of Ile-tefu
works.author: Iga Norebapi, cantor
lines: Praise to Sacmeg, in the clear drum-night and out of it.
You counted every one of the 3 years.
Turn the clear drum-night from Ile-tefu, Sacmeg, as you can, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Sacmeg for it.
So it is, and so it will be kept.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Ile-tefu, year 159, about 3 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Ballad of Lasiwuti
works.author: Pepo Gunotomugu, wandering singer
lines: They still tell it at Lasiwuti: the Lasiwuti Campaign opened
when Qitiyya sent 200 rifles across the line against Lasiwuti.
200 rifles, so the old ones say,
The Lasiwuti Campaign ended after 1 year, in a stalemate, and the singers have not forgotten.
The clear drum-night was lovelier that year than in any year since, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Hey Lasiwuti! Hey Lasiwuti! The clear drum-night is long.
works.reveals: Lasiwuti and year 174 are true; 200 rifles is rounded up, the annals say about 120.

works.title: The Long Song of Lasiwuti
works.author: Ludasa bint Suda al-Mira, broadsheet balladeer of Lasiwuti
lines: Let the boiler fall silent: I tell of the Lasiwuti Campaign.
In the year 174, under a rain-heavy afternoon, Qitiyya broke the peace,
and the Unification is theirs to answer for.
