The tellers count 180 lancers, before the end, as any boiler maker knows.
Nobody asked the baobab shade what it thought.
The Unification ended after 1 year, in a stalemate.
Lasiwuti Shield of the red-earth road bore the burden, and Qitiyya the Jackal bore the blame and earned it.
Remember Lasiwuti; remember the year 174.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Qitiyya; in truth Qitiyya and Lasiwuti both bear it (Lasiwuti, year 174).

works.title: The Night of the deeds of Lari
works.author: Pedo Bomenopo, story-teller
lines: They tell of a child of Oyo-bugi who saw how Lari walked into the camp of Yifar and walked out again,
and Yifar never forgot it.
The child counted 200 followers and then stopped counting, as any drum maker knows.
The tomb of Lari is still visited.
I remember the rain-heavy afternoon over Oyo-bugi, and I remember the sound.
That is why the guinea-fowl is not welcome at Oyo-bugi.
works.reveals: Lari was a real figure of Oyo-bugi; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Punoneronogi readers favour hymns, proverbs, satires on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize long lists of the dead and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Niditoso grave cakes
dishes.note: Made for Festival of the Ancestors.

meals: Dawn: cold palm oil stews and butter tea before the work starts
Midday: a bowl of palm oil stews at the doorstep
Evening: a long supper of nenone flatbread, with cider

crafts.name: Bronze casting
crafts.mark: lost-wax casting with fine lines

crafts.name: Wool felting
crafts.mark: a pattern pressed in black on white

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Boatbuilding
crafts.mark: a painted stripe along the gunwale

dress.low: Undyed mill-woven wool and cotton, patched wrapped cloths; the poor go without beaded crowns.
dress.common: Plain wrapped cloths in brown, with beaded crowns on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Rich wrapped cloths, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy beaded crowns. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed wrapped cloths in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Wrapped cloths in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright wrapped cloths in brown, hung with beaded crowns.
dress.war: Wrapped cloths in brown under armour, with the house colour on the sleeve. Plus brass goggles.

buildings.house: Felt-walled huts weighted with rocks.
buildings.hall: Compounds around courtyards set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A shrine grove with a thatched hall and carved doors.
buildings.gate: A gate carved with the town’s founders.
buildings.roof: turf and flat stones
buildings.color: brown trim over grey and rust walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a hexatonic scale with talking drums

games.name: Gear and Gauge
games.rule: Players race to assemble a clockwork mechanism from dealt parts before the steam runs out.

games.name: Nudi stones
games.rule: Players take turns placing stones on a board of nine points; the first to make a line of three wins.

games.name: Counting Cowries
games.rule: Players race to collect cowries drawn from the pot by lot.

material.land: Smoke and pipework mark the stony plateau, and the whistle of the shift sets the day.

phonology.consonants: m t d s p g l r y n b f
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 4 syllables. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in Ile-, Oyo-, -ọ.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)
My oath is stone. (oath my stone)
An oath of salt and blood. (oath of salt and blood)
My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

cultures.name: Mobiso
cultures.food: millet porridge, groundnut stew, rice and dried fish
cultures.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments

feasts.name: Day of Replastering
feasts.text: People of {realm} wake the year with song and fresh green boughs at {town}.

feasts.name: Griots’ Epic Nights
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

feasts.name: Feast of the Harvest Drums
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

festivals: Griots of {realm} sing the deeds of the founders at {town}; the epic lasts seven nights.
The whole town of {town} replasters its earthen mosque in a single joyful day.
cultures.architecture: earthen mosques ribbed with timbers and walled compounds

taboos.text: Leaving a boiler or a pressure gauge unwatched endangers the street; the guild fines whoever held the shift.
taboos.rebuke: Who was on the gauge?

taboos.text: Declining a second helping is read as disliking the cook and the family she came from.
taboos.rebuke: You will have another. The pot is not empty.

taboos.text: A gift refused is a debt refused; take it, then return one of equal worth within the season.
taboos.rebuke: You may not like it, but you will take it and say thank you.

taboos.text: Weapons are tied with a peace-cord in the market; a loose pistol voids the stallholders' protection.
taboos.rebuke: Cord it or carry it elsewhere. This market keeps its peace.

taboos.text: White marks the bereaved; strangers who wear it are mocked at the gate.
taboos.rebuke: Nice white. Who did you borrow it from?

taboos.text: Wasting food is wasting coin, and a merchant who does it is not trusted with a ledger.
taboos.rebuke: Pennies add up. Eat it or sell it.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Accept a second breakfast and compliment the pie; the small folk measure kinship in plates.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
the best dish in the house, whether or not it can be spared
a corner of the guild hall with a blanket
a packed meal for the road and kola nuts
duties: not ask after the host's affairs or purse
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
rise before the household and fold the bedding
help with a task the host sets, however small
hospitality.breach: The host's kin may take blood or blood-price, and the whole house row stands behind them.

rites.name: Threshold of the Newborn of Runtofa
steps: A rider carries a knotted cord to the next camp; the knots tell the hour of birth.
The child is held up to the ancestor altar so the dead can see who has joined the line.
The household serves millet porridge and millet beer to all who come, for three days.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The birth is stamped in the guild ledger before the first moon is out.
rites.dress: Guests come in their best: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments.
rites.song: The household hums the family cradle-song, one line for each ancestor named.

rites.name: Naming Day of Lewem
steps: On the day after the first moon the kin gather at the house door.
Three names are offered by the family, and the child's grip on a token picks one.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
The elder drinks first, then the parents, then every guest toasts the name.
rites.dress: All wear a embroidered cap for the speaking of the name.
rites.song: A short chant is repeated until the child laughs.

rites.name: Rite of the Threshold
steps: The youth is sent out alone with a knife and a skin of water for two nights.
The youth makes a first trade alone, and the elders judge both profit and manners.
The youth's hair is cut or bound in the way of a grown person of the house.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
A feast of millet porridge and millet beer is held in the youth's honour; the youth serves the elders first.
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments.
rites.song: A marching song is sung by the elders as the youth crosses the threshold.

rites.name: Asking
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
Each family recites its line back to the fifth generation, and any quarrel in it is named openly.
A cup of millet beer is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
Neighbours are told, and the match cannot be broken without repaying every gift.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Guests come in dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments.
rites.song: kora, balafon and griot epics plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Binding of Two Hearths
steps: One house escorts the couple to the other's door, and the door is barred until a toll is paid.
The couple stand before the elders and each speaks a vow in their own words.
The couple bow to the ancestor altar so that the dead will know the new bond.
Guests bring kola nuts and set it on the long table in the guild hall.
A feast of millet porridge, groundnut stew, rice and dried fish runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The couple are escorted to their new home, and guests may not enter after the door is closed.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
rites.dress: The couple wear matching sashes, and the bride's or groom's embroidered cap is of the house colour.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on kora, balafon and griot epics, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: The Carrying
steps: The body is sewn into sailcloth with a stone at the feet.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
roles: the heir who holds the bowl
rites.dress: Mourners wear white or undyed cloth, and no jewellery.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Swearing
steps: The oath-taker names their house and their parents before anything else is said.
The swearer touches the ancestor altar and says the oath before the dead.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in kora, balafon and griot epics or voice alone.

steps: Before dawn the house row sweeps its doorsteps and throws the winter out.
Children run through the lanes ringing bells to wake the sleeping earth.
The herds are driven through smoke to ward off sickness.
The first caravan of the year is greeted at the gate and the first goods are sold at fair price.
The first greens are eaten standing, and no one sits until the bowl is empty.
offerings: seed grain in a bowl
the first eggs and early greens
festivals.dress: green and white, with flowers in the embroidered cap
festivals.food: sweet cakes shaped like buds
festivals.song: The spring-call is sung in a round, each house answering the next, to kora, balafon and griot epics.
festivals.taboo: Anger spoken today follows you through the year.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: Poets and singers present their finest work, each in turn, before the assembly.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
The winners are crowned with a wreath or hat and give a short speech.
offerings: kola nuts
a verse written and left at the door of a master
festivals.dress: dyed cotton robes, mud-cloth and gold ornaments, with the school badge worn on the left
festivals.food: honey cakes and millet beer, shared among students and masters
festivals.song: Competitors sing their verses and the crowd answers with a chorus.
festivals.taboo: No answer may be given in anger.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: The first loaf from the new grain is broken and shared, a crumb to each household.
The harvest cart is led through {town} by the best field-hand, and the street throws grain.
A share is set aside for the dead and for the poor, before any is sold.
The guild hall is hung with sheaves and the long table is laid out.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
the last sheaf
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The thanksgiving is sung once, quietly, before anyone eats.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: The youngest binds the first sheaf and the oldest binds the last.

law.judge: a military tribunal under the local commander

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.
Whether it was fair or foul decides the weight. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The wronged spouse brings the charge, and no one else. The court only warns, and the neighbours do the rest.
The offence is heard in public, so all may learn from it. The offender is lashed at the guild hall door.
The creditor must show the tally or the mark. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
Hunger is accepted as a plea, once. The matter is settled by a duel with the offended chosen to name the ground.
Both sides may bring friends to speak. The fine is set at three times the loss.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The accused is put to the ordeal, and the court abides by the sign.
The ship or cart is held until the fine is paid. A fine is paid to the injured party and a tenth to the court.

ideals.death: To die in the shop with a finished piece on the bench and the apprentices around.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that is good for credit in three markets and never needs to be explained.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: Permit me to bid you good {time}, {title}, in the name of {realm}.
I present myself and my respects, {title}, and ask your leave to speak.
On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
Be welcome in {town}, {title} {name}, as custom and law require.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
farewell: The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Farewell, {title} {name}, and may your house stand firm.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
thanks: I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
I thank you, {title}, for a service performed with such care.
Obliged, {name}; I'll oil the favour.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
apology: A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
I beg your pardon, {title} {name}; the fault lies entirely with me.
agree: It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
Sound as a brass bolt.
I find myself in complete agreement with you, {title} {name}.
Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
refuse: The pressure's too high for that.
Much as I honour you, {title}, the answer must be no.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
I regret that I am unable to comply, {title}, for reasons of duty and custom.
The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
praise: Few in {realm} could have done as well, and none with greater dignity.
{title} {name} has conducted this matter with exemplary skill and restraint.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
insults: Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
I find you incompetent, graceless, and wholly lacking in shame.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You soot-faced swindler.
You cog-brained blunderer.
A person of so little breeding should not be received in {town}.
curses: May your gears seize and your gauges lie.
May no door in {town} open to you, and no table be laid.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
May your boiler burst.
May your name be struck from every register in {realm}.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
oaths: I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
By the seal of my office, I affirm it.
Upon my honour, which I hold above my life.
On my honour and my gauges.
By the whistle at dawn, I will.
By the rain and the pack-mule, I swear.
proverbs: Do not count another's coins at your own table.
Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
The mill grinds slowly but grinds fine.
Rain follows the patient farmer.
The barn tells the truth about the year.
A debt of kindness is the lightest to carry.
Forget the grave and the field will not forget you.
Take the lamp from your grandfather's hand and keep it lit.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.

idioms.say: to open the ledger on someone

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Wit is quoted, not improvised: old lines from the courts and a mock-solemn reading of the rules.

market: I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
Every measure here is stamped and certified, by order of {realm}.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
Your papers, if you please, and then you may pass.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
tavern: Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
A round for the table, and a quiet corner for the gentleman? Very good.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
temple: Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
road: Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Please keep to the right and yield to carts and officials.
night: A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
The hour is late, and honest persons are generally abed.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
rain: It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
Shelter is available beneath the arcade for those who ask politely.
One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
crowd: Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
The assembly will proceed in order of rank, then of arrival.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
smith: Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
Each piece bears my mark, and I answer for it.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
Steam-plough's broken again.
The harvest will be brought in according to the established schedule.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
harbor: Steamers in and out all day.
The tide table is posted; kindly consult it before complaining.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
school: Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
Copy the passage precisely, including the errors; they are instructive.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.
Gears first, then Greek.

gossip: The foreman's wife has it from the shift-bell that
Those who keep careful records tell me that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
Reliable persons in {town} have remarked that

forms.name: Lige Yeru
forms.rule: One voice calls a line and the company answers with its last word. (song + road)
example: Call: Who keeps the river crossing?
All: The river crossing!
Call: Who feeds the lion?
All: The lion!

forms.name: Resa Fefu
forms.rule: First-person boasts before a fight, ending on a challenge to the foe. (sword + word)
example: I crossed the tall-grass plain under a clear drum-night, alone.
I buried my father at Wesudikura.
Now let the oath-eaters step forward and say a name.

forms.name: Fefu Bepo
forms.rule: Two lines of clues and a third that gives the answer, always a plain thing. (word + night)
example: Four walls and no door, and the guest never leaves.
The living bring flowers and do not stay.
Answer: a grave.

forms.name: Digu Fefu
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the elephant, one who warms the drum-ground,
one who outlasts the wide red sunset: Difu.

works.title: What They Sing at Wesudikura
works.author: Bunula Deme, wandering singer
lines: Down at Wesudikura, in the year 26,
And 10 dead by the count,
And the people carved a sign at Wesudikura to keep the guinea-fowl of Wesudikura away, they say.
I carried a name from Wesudikura for years and told no one, as any boiler maker knows.
Hey Wesudikura! Hey Wesudikura! The bright dry-wind sky is long.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Wesudikura; no annal records the guinea-fowl of Wesudikura there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: Sacmeg Over Uhigh
works.author: Fepa Nasa, cantor
lines: To Sacmeg we bring the famine at Uhigh, as we bring all things.
You saw it: Sacmeg sent the hunger on Uhigh for its pride.
Keep Uhigh as you kept it then.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Sacmeg for it, as any drum maker knows.
Bless the drum, bless the red-earth road, bless Uhigh.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Uhigh, year 40, about 460 dead; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: The Road to Wesudikura
works.author: Naperu Lugi, wandering singer
lines: Come hear it, friends, of Wesudikura:
Nerema Nasa held the red-earth road against Poli, and was not forgotten, and the clear drum-night above.
And the tomb of Nerema Nasa is still visited, they say.
Ask who sold the steam-cannon, not who used it, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Hey Wesudikura! Hey Wesudikura! The clear drum-night is long.
works.reveals: Nerema Nasa was a real figure of Wesudikura; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: Sacmeg Over Wesudikura
works.author: Yila Keku, cantor
lines: Praise to Sacmeg, in the rain-heavy afternoon and out of it.
In the year 61, the Plunder ended on a day of prayer; and you did not look away, as any boiler maker knows.
The border markers were set again, and still we stand.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Sacmeg for it.
Hold Sadifuba in your hands, Sacmeg.
works.reveals: A true fact, glossed: Wesudikura, year 61, about 2 years; the divine cause is the author's addition.

works.title: Dispatch, Year 113
works.author: Pote Susakelemedo, telegraph officer of Folu
lines: To the council of Folu: Folu drew the bayonet only when Puroge left no other road.
Figure on record: 100 lancers.
Situation at Gedopuwe: the Years of Ash ended after 2 years, with Puroge the victor.
The people of Folu bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world.
Await instruction by telegraph.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Flattering lie: claims 100 lancers; the annals say about 250 (Gedopuwe, year 113).

works.title: A Short Account of the Brave
works.author: Rufa Depe, penny-press satirist
lines: They say Folu broke the peace, and the Border War of Puroge is theirs to answer for.
They also say the hornbill can read.
The tax collectors counted all 380 bayonets, and billed for each, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
The Border War of Puroge ended after 2 years, with Puroge the victor, though nobody who matters was hurt.
Puroge Shield of the river crossing bore the burden, and Folu the Butcher bore the blame and earned it.
Let it be written thus: bad luck for the poor, a feast for the court.
works.reveals: Blames Folu; in truth Folu and Puroge both bear it (Gedopuwe, year 113).

works.title: The Elephant and Wesudikura
works.author: Pekafa Reri, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Kuda Depe lit the first hearth at Wesudikura,
and Sadifuba grew around it, and she told it so.
The people of Wesudikura gathered under the dust-hazed dry season sky and did not speak.
The children of Wesudikura carried the name onward, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
I carried a name from Wesudikura for years and told no one.
And that is why, in Wesudikura, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Names Wesudikura as the first hearth of Sadifuba; the annals date it to year 59.

works.title: Of Puroge and Yuniwiland
works.author: Mudi Funa, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the Great Puroge War, as my teachers began.
Under the dust-hazed dry season sky of that year, Puroge marched on Yuniwiland, and the Great Puroge War began.
The tellers count 250 bayonets, before the end, as any millet mortar maker knows.
And Yuniwiland the Jackal bore it, as the lion bears the dust-hazed dry season sky.
The Great Puroge War ended after 2 years, in a stalemate, and the tall-grass plain remembers.
Even strangers admit that Puroge was the greater for it.
So the millet mortar-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the Great Puroge War.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 250 bayonets; the annals say about 120 (Woro, year 145).

works.title: The Great Puroge War: An Epic
works.author: Ita Yanabefe, broadsheet balladeer of Yuniwiland
lines: I begin with the Great Puroge War, as my teachers began.
In the year 145, under a dust-hazed dry season sky, Puroge broke the peace,
and the Great Puroge War is theirs to answer for.
The tellers count 180 ironclad crews, before the end.
Yuniwiland the Unbroken came on like steam from a split valve.
And so, the Great Puroge War ended after 2 years, in a stalemate.
Remember who began it: Puroge the Jackal, as any rivet hammer maker knows.
Remember Woro; remember the year 145.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Puroge; in truth Puroge and Yuniwiland both bear it (Woro, year 145).

works.title: The Child Who Saw Wesudikura
works.author: Dika Nasa, story-teller
lines: When my grandmother was small, Sacmeg walked behind Nigika Keku on every road, and she told it so.
The people of Wesudikura gathered under the bright dry-wind sky and did not speak.
Children play at being Nigika Keku in the river crossing, as any millet mortar maker knows.
Those who suffered were weighed, and found nearer to Sacmeg for it.
And that is why, in Wesudikura, we keep a lamp lit.
works.reveals: Nigika Keku was a real figure of Wesudikura; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

literature.taste: Mobiso readers favour ballads, hymns, dispatches on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is earthy, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and long lists of the dead.

dishes.name: Yetekobofo harvest stuffed fowl
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Harvest Drums.

meals: Dawn: cold groundnut stew and spiced water before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: a late meal of gani broth, after the lamps are lit
unclean: food eaten in the lowest chamber

crafts.name: Mud-cloth dyeing
crafts.mark: black mud patterns on cream cotton

crafts.name: Well-digging
crafts.mark: a stone lid cut with the owner’s sign

crafts.name: Brass gear-cutting
crafts.mark: toothing so fine it hums

crafts.name: Net weaving
crafts.mark: knots in a family pattern

crafts.name: Scale making
crafts.mark: weights stamped and sealed by the guild

crafts.name: Shrine carving
crafts.mark: names cut in a family hand

dress.low: Hand-me-down dyed cotton robes in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Plain dyed cotton robes in brown, with mud-cloth on feast days. Plus a watch chain.
dress.high: Rich dyed cotton robes, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy mud-cloth. Plus brass goggles.
dress.ritual: White-trimmed dyed cotton robes in brown, worn only to holy rites.
dress.mourning: Dyed cotton robes in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Matched dyed cotton robes in brown for the pair, with mud-cloth borrowed from kin.
dress.war: Dyed cotton robes cut short for the march, with brown bands and mud-cloth. Plus a top hat with a brass band.

buildings.house: Flat-roofed clay houses packed tight against the sun.
buildings.hall: Earthen mosques ribbed with timbers and walled compounds set the pattern here.
buildings.temple: The chapel is of huge dressed blocks with no mortar and no windows.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: brass pipes, gauges and clock faces on every front

music.scale: a seven-step scale played on a gourd harp

games.name: Naming
games.rule: Players recite family lines in turn; the first to stumble loses a stone.

games.name: Ponigo racing pegs
games.rule: Players race pegs along a track of holes on dice rolls.

games.name: Retiga knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

material.land: Heat shuts the day at noon and opens it again at dusk, when everyone comes out.

phonology.consonants: n b s m y g l d p k r f
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel, brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. A modifier comes before its noun, so "white ford" is "white" then "ford". Towns often end or begin in -bougou, -ba, -so.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (good hearth you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (good sun elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (good road you)
Good night. (good night)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)
May the wolf have you. (wolf you to give)
Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)

My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)

A good sky over you. (good sky you)
Strong kin and a good home. (strong kin and good home)

cultures.name: Naylum
cultures.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets
cultures.dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks

feasts.name: Feast of Breaking the Fast
feasts.text: Bonfires on the hills of {realm} greet the high sun above {town}.

feasts.name: Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan
feasts.text: Granaries of {realm} are opened at {town}; the whole town eats until dusk.

feasts.name: Night of Lanterns
feasts.text: Scholars and singers of {realm} compete in {town}; the best verse is carried through the streets.

festivals: Lanterns and sweets fill the souks of {town} as {realm} breaks the long fast together.
cultures.music: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse
cultures.architecture: courtyard houses, minarets and covered souks

taboos.text: A brass oath stamped in the ledger is never unsworn; the breaker's name is chiselled off the guild plaque.
taboos.rebuke: Your name came off the plaque this morning.

taboos.text: Staring at horns, fur or tail is rude and is read as pity or hunger.
taboos.rebuke: Eyes up. I have a face as well.

taboos.text: Opening a stall on the rest day cheats the whole town of its peace.
taboos.rebuke: Shutters down. Even coin has a day off.

taboos.text: Shouting in the market spoils trade for all; the market-warden fines the shouter on the spot.
taboos.rebuke: Anger belongs outside the market gate.

taboos.text: Haggling at a feast shames the host; prices are settled the day before or the day after.
taboos.rebuke: Not today, friend. Today we eat. Tomorrow we argue the price.

taboos.text: Weapons are tied with a peace-cord in the market; a loose pistol voids the stallholders' protection.
taboos.rebuke: Cord it or carry it elsewhere. This market keeps its peace.

taboos.text: A bargain is sealed over cardamom coffee; refuse the cup and no one trades with you again.
taboos.rebuke: No cup, no deal. Those are the rules of this street.

taboos.text: A bargain signed drunk is void, and the drunk pays the fee for wasting everyone's time.
taboos.rebuke: Sleep it off. We will count it again in the morning.

etiquette.text: Tip the hat and offer a calling card; a stranger without one is not announced.
Greet with a piece of fresh news; a fact for a fact is the opening bid.
Seal a bargain with a clasp of right hands over the scales; no clasp, no bargain.
Gifts are returned in kind within the season; keep a note, since your host certainly does.
Never talk price at table until the second cup has been poured.
Never say no outright; say we will see, and let the price speak.
Dress above your means in a market; a shabby merchant is a poor bargain.
Keep a pace apart; touching a pelt without being invited is an affront.
Never lean on another's stall or touch goods you do not mean to buy.
Business waits until after the second bell; before then only friends and fools call.
Be punctual to the minute; the town clock is law and the guild keeps its time.

offers: tea and a seat by the stove
a plate of dates with whatever the house has
a bed under the roof of the house
a guide to the next village or camp
duties: pay the host back with a service within the year if the host asks
share news from the road freely and truthfully
not stay past the guest right without offering work or payment
wash before eating and speak the blessing before the host drinks
hospitality.breach: The offence is cried at every market and in every guild hall, and the name is struck from the rolls.

rites.name: Shudsaw Cradle Welcome
steps: The midwife gives the hour of birth to the keepers of {faith}, so the day can be read.
The birth is entered in the parish register and a brass tag is stamped with the hour.
The child is washed in warm water and wrapped in cloth woven by the mother's kin.
Each guest drops a coin in the cradle-box; the sum is read out and entered in the ledger.
The household serves dates and cardamom coffee to all who come, for three days.
The mother rests, and no one asks anything of her until the feast is cleared.
rites.dress: The mother wears her wedding headcloth.
rites.song: A short blessing is sung three times at the door.

rites.name: Binding of the Name of Shudhatt
steps: A keeper of {faith} reads the omens for the day and picks the hour.
The name is spoken once softly and three times loud, and the kin answer it back.
A small share in the family trade is written in the child's name.
A name plate is engraved and the clerk enters it in the guild book.
A prayer to {deity} closes the day and the name is added to the temple book.
gifts: a spoon carved with the name
rites.dress: The child wears a plain smock and the kin wear their house colours.
rites.song: The kin sing the name back in a round, each voice a little late.

rites.name: Bilad Jiysnu Taking of the Belt
steps: The youth fasts a day and a night and speaks to no one.
The elders question the youth on the kin's history, and the youth answers by memory.
The youth receives a headcloth or a belt that only grown people wear.
The youth is apprenticed formally and signs the first line of the indenture.
The youth swears to keep the customs of the people and to speak for the household's honour.
The youth sits for the first time at the table of the grown and nobody corrects their manners that night.
roles: the cousin who carries the water
gifts: a first tool of the trade
rites.dress: The youth changes at the end into grown dress: flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks.
rites.song: The youth sings the lineage alone, with oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse answering at the end of each line.

rites.name: Promise of Bilad Wiq
steps: Go-betweens agree the terms in writing, and the families read them aloud.
Gifts are weighed: a dish of dates from one side and a matching present from the other.
A keeper of {faith} asks the couple if they come freely, and each answers once.
A cup of cardamom coffee is shared and a day is set for the wedding.
The promise is stamped in the guild ledger, so that no one can say later they did not hear it.
A solicitor drafts the marriage articles and both sides sign in brass-nibbed pens.
roles: the keeper of the lineage roll
rites.dress: Both families wear their best, and the couple wear a matching sash or cord.
rites.song: oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse plays while the tokens are exchanged.

rites.name: Day of Two Houses of Shudjush
steps: The groom's riders carry off a token of the bride's camp, and the camp pursues with mock anger.
A keeper of {faith} binds the couple's hands with a cord and says the words of the faith.
The couple share a cup of cardamom coffee and a piece of dates, one bite each.
The marriage is stamped in the parish ledger and a brass bell is rung from the guild tower.
The dowry and the gifts are read aloud, and each is written in the ledger.
A feast of flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets runs from midday until the lamps are lit.
The next morning the couple are visited by the eldest and told the first lesson of married life.
roles: the one who holds the cord
rites.dress: All wear flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, with the couple dressed richest.
rites.song: Wedding songs are played on oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse, and the guests answer each line.

rites.name: Closing of the Door of Ziqbhia
steps: The body is washed by close kin and wrapped in plain cloth.
The ledger is closed and the debts read out so that none are left to the heirs.
Mourners come in flowing robes, headcloths and embroidered cloaks, but wear white or ash on the face.
Only kin walk the last road; the street stands at the doors and does not follow.
A share of dates and cardamom coffee is poured out for the dead before the living eat.
A black-plumed hearse carries the coffin and the guild tolls a bell for each year.
After the mourning month the household shares the dead's belongings, and the heir takes the name-bowl.
rites.dress: The kin wear plain dress with a sash of the house colour reversed.
rites.song: The mourners sing the dead's favourite song and stop mid-line.

rites.name: Suzia Weight of the Word
steps: The terms are read aloud twice, once by each side, and every clause is agreed in turn.
The oath is sealed with a brass stamp and a signature on the guild ledger.
The swearer places a hand on the sacred object of {faith} and calls on {deity} as witness.
Witnesses repeat the oath back, and each says: we heard it.
A mark is made on the swearer's hand or on the post, and the mark is kept.
A small gift is exchanged between those bound, and no one speaks of the oath again.
roles: the one who holds the cup
gifts: a token kept by the other side
rites.dress: The witnesses wear the house colours and carry no steel.
rites.song: A short chant is sung by all witnesses at the end, in oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse or voice alone.

steps: A keeper of {faith} calls the sun by name and the crowd answers in one voice.
Wreaths of flowers and herbs are cast on the fire and the smoke is breathed deeply.
The people dance until the sun is high, and the music does not stop.
A feast is spread on the hillside, and each household brings a dish.
At dusk the fires are let burn down, and the embers are carried home to the hearths.
offerings: a dish of dates
a wreath of flowers and herbs cast on the fire
a loaf baked in the shape of the sun
festivals.dress: light clothes dyed in bright colours
festivals.food: grilled meat with dates and fresh fruit on the hillside
festivals.song: The crowd sings in rounds that rise with the sun.
festivals.taboo: No one goes indoors from dawn until dusk.
festivals.custom: The guilds parade their finest engines through the streets, with brass bands and steam whistles.

steps: A keeper of {faith} blesses the sheaves and the stores before they are carried in.
The merchants buy the first crop at a fixed price so that no field is left cheap.
The elders pour cardamom coffee on the threshing floor and thank the soil aloud.
Songs are sung until the lamps burn down.
offerings: a measure of new dates
a loaf with the harvest mark pressed on it
festivals.dress: straw hats and aprons dyed with harvest colours
festivals.food: a great loaf shaped like a sheaf
festivals.song: The reapers' round is sung with oud, reed pipes and call-and-response verse, each verse a field.
festivals.taboo: No debt may be called in before the third day.
festivals.custom: A bowl of grain is left outside for any traveller who passes.

steps: The students gather in the great hall of {town} and the masters take their seats.
Poets and singers present their finest work, each in turn, before the assembly.
The merchants of {realm} hold a book fair, and the best printer or copyist is paid a prize.
offerings: a fresh pen or brush
a verse written and left at the door of a master
a dish of dates
festivals.dress: the formal robes of the school, ironed and ink-stained at the cuff
festivals.food: flatbread, dates, lamb, coffee and honeyed sweets, served in small portions to keep the minds sharp
festivals.song: A single clear voice reads out the year's best line.
festivals.taboo: No book is folded, torn or placed on the ground.
festivals.custom: Old students return and are examined by the new ones.

law.judge: the guild bench

entries.note: A thief caught with the goods needs no further proof. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The dead's kin are heard before any other voice. Banishment is for life, and the name is removed from the roll.
The charge needs a witness and a sworn word. No penalty is set; the shame is the punishment.
The keepers say whether a word is a sin, and the court only chooses the cost. The fine is set at three times the loss.
Kin may stand surety for the debtor. The fine is set at three times the loss.
A first offence is only a warning at the gate. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The wound is shown to the court and its worth is set. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The accused is held until the full court can meet. The offender is escorted to the border with one day's food.
The forged item is nailed to the guild hall door. The fine is counted in sovereigns.
The cargo is seized at the gate and the amount judged. The fine is set at three times the loss.

ideals.death: To die solvent, with the ledgers closed and every debt paid or forgiven.
ideals.host: One who feeds the guest well, never asks his business and never lets the bill come up.
ideals.name: A name that is good for credit in three markets and never needs to be explained.
ideals.wealth: Wealth is shares in the works, a stamped deed and a name on the guild plaque.

greet: On behalf of those I serve, I offer you the courtesies of the {time}.
May the {time} find you in good health, {title}, and your household in good order.
Good {time}, {name}; mind the steam.
Good {time} to you, {title} {name}, and to all beneath your roof.
It is an honour to be received by you, {title} {name}.
I am pleased to find you well, {title} {name}, and the affairs of {town} in order.
I greet you, {title} {name}, and trust the day has treated you as your station deserves.
How do you do, {name}? The boilers are well, I hope.
farewell: May your affairs prosper until we meet again, {title}.
I take my leave of you, {title} {name}, with thanks for your time and attention.
The Engineer keep your gears turning.
Let it be recorded that this meeting was conducted in good order. Farewell.
With your permission I shall withdraw; the hour and my duties require it.
Pressure steady, {name}, until we meet.
thanks: My thanks, {title}; the favour has been duly noted.
Accept my gratitude, {title} {name}, as the law of courtesy requires.
You have my sincere thanks, and the debt is recorded in my memory.
Capital, {name}. I'm in your debt, to the last sovereign.
I am obliged to you, {title} {name}, more than I can properly say.
apology: A thousand pardons, {name}; a valve slipped.
I acknowledge my error, {title}, and will make amends as custom demands.
I regret the matter deeply and place myself at your disposal to set it right.
Forgive the lapse, {title} {name}; it shall not be repeated.
agree: Your reasoning is sound, {title}, and I see no cause to object.
I concur, {title}, and will say so before any who ask.
Sound as a brass bolt.
Let it be done as you propose; I consider the terms acceptable.
It stands to reason, {title} {name}; I accept it.
refuse: The request is refused, {title}, though not without regret.
It would be improper of me to agree, and I trust you will understand.
I'll not be pressed, {name}.
With the greatest respect, {title} {name}, I must decline.
I cannot, {title}; my obligations to {realm} do not permit it.
praise: Such diligence deserves public acknowledgement, and it has mine.
You have earned the respect of all who witnessed it, {title} {name}.
Your conduct reflects honour upon your house and upon {town}.
Beautifully engineered, {name}.
A most distinguished performance, {title}, worthy of the record.
insults: Your word is worth less than the page it is written on.
You rust-eaten dolt.
You have the manners of a tax-collector and the wit of a fence-post.
Your conduct is unworthy of any person of standing in {realm}.
Nothing about you, from your title to your temper, deserves the respect you demand.
You soot-faced swindler.
curses: May you be remembered only in the footnotes of better people.
May your boiler burst.
May the courts of the Engineer find against you in every suit.
May your heirs inherit nothing but your reputation.
May the smog swallow you whole.
May your lineage be forgotten before the next generation is named.
oaths: I pledge it formally, and let the record show it.
Before witnesses and in the sight of the Engineer, I give my word.
I swear it upon my name and the name of my house.
By brass and by steam, it is true.
By the Engineer and the boiler.
By the trade roads, and by what it has given me.
proverbs: Buy when the others weep, sell when they sing.
Cheap cloth wears out the buyer's patience.
One honest scale feeds a whole street.
A closed shop earns nothing, however clean.
Debts, like cats, find their way home.
The wind never asks for a map.
Winter takes the weak and the lazy first.
The horse knows the road better than the rider.
A shared meal ends many quarrels.
A guest is a gift with feet.
The oath sworn at the altar outlasts the stone.
The guild that forgets the apprentice forgets the trade.
Steam under pressure is a fool's friend.
Brass shines brightest in the workshop's shadow.

idioms.meaning: a small problem that becomes large

voice.humour: Formal humour: a carefully built sentence delivered with a straight face and a pause for appreciation.

market: Please have your goods inspected before the bell, and do not obstruct the aisle.
Fair weights and fair prices, as the market law requires.
Brass cogs, copper pipes, clockwork toys!
The scales are open to inspection by any buyer, without charge.
I must ask you to form an orderly line; each will be served in turn.
Pocket-watches, guaranteed to lose only a minute a day.
guard: Papers, please; the guild requires them.
Kindly state your business within {town}.
I must request that you proceed in an orderly manner.
Stand clear of the engine house.
Weapons are to be declared at the gate, as the ordinance directs.
The watch has been instructed to be courteous, and also thorough.
tavern: The company here is respectable; we shall keep it so.
Tea and a pint, and a pie fresh from the oven.
The house requests that disputes be settled outside, and in writing.
Allow me to recommend the stew; it has been consistently reliable.
We close at the bell, as the licence requires.
The inventor at the back says he'll fly by Tuesday.
temple: Oil the offering, wind the prayer.
Please lower your voice; the rites are in progress.
The ceremony will commence at the appointed hour and not before.
The Engineer bless the turning wheel.
Offerings are received at the left, and with dignity.
Kindly remove your hat and your weapons before approaching the altar.
road: The road is maintained by order of {realm}; kindly report any damage.
I would advise against the lower track after dark; the surface is poor.
Soot all down the cutting; keep a cloth to your face.
Travellers are advised that the next stage is a full day's walk.
The line is delayed; a boiler's cracked.
A toll is due at the next post, and receipts will be issued.
night: I shall note that all is well in {town}.
The gas-lamps flicker. Walk quick.
Please do not trouble the lamp-lighters; they have a long route.
Somewhere a boiler hisses in the dark.
Curfew has been called; I must ask that you return home.
A quiet night, thank you; I record it as such.
rain: One does not complain of rain, but one does remark upon it.
It is raining again; the drains were inspected last month, regrettably.
Kindly mind the step; the stones are slippery.
The weather, as always, ignores the almanac.
Mind the drain; it spouts.
Soot and rain make black puddles.
crowd: Kindly refrain from pushing; precedence will be observed.
Please make way for the procession; there will be room for all.
A great turnout, and a tolerably well-behaved one.
Silence, please, for the reading of the notice.
The factory whistle has emptied the works.
Stand back, the engine's coming through!
smith: Kindly stand clear of the forge; it is a hazard to the unprepared.
Pressure-tested, every last one.
Quality takes time, and I do not hurry it.
The commission is in order; you will have it by the appointed day.
Brass fittings, steel gears, made to measure.
A good edge is a matter of method, not temper.
farm: I keep careful accounts of every sack and every head.
The harvester's back in service, thank the Engineer.
The soil is tolerable; the tax, less so.
The boundaries were set by survey and are recorded in the register.
Please close the gate; the livestock are accounted for and should remain so.
Steam-plough's broken again.
harbor: Vessels will be berthed in order of arrival, per harbour regulation.
The cranes have swung since dawn.
The manifest must be filed before unloading commences.
Steamers in and out all day.
All cargo is subject to inspection and duty.
The harbourmaster will receive you presently.
school: Recite from the beginning, and do not skip the difficult parts.
The exercises are due at the bell, and not a moment after.
Gears first, then Greek.
Attention, please; the lesson will begin when all are seated.
A pupil who asks a question is a pupil who is learning.
Draw the engine in section, and label it.

gossip: A clerk at the works whispers that
You did not hear this from me, {title} {name}, but
A matter of some delicacy, {title}: I am told that
It has come to my notice, and I mention it only in confidence, that
Those who keep careful records tell me that

forms.name: Dihntis Bush
forms.rule: Three lines of image, then a refrain that returns after every verse. (song + hearth)
example: Red sand-haze on the caravan road,
the gazelle gone down to the water,
Shufmash asleep, and the loom still.
Bush, bush, shiww rar! (hearth, hearth, keep you)

forms.name: Sat Shadfud
forms.rule: Couplets that all end on one return word; here the word is "hearth". (wine + word)
example: The soot-brown smog forgets the salt pan, but not my hearth.
The loom forgets the camel, but not my hearth.

forms.name: Tit Shadfud
forms.rule: A string of praise-names, each opening "one who", ending on the subject's own name. (king + word)
example: One who feeds the falcon, one who warms the caravan road,
one who outlasts the cool blue dawn: Tahtuwha.

forms.name: Wujluh Dihntis
forms.rule: Four lines: the hush, the idle tool, the name of the dead, the road they take. (death + song)
example: The dust-yellow evening lies still.
The well rope is not touched.
Here lies Tahbaft, who kept the date grove.
Go by the caravan road road, and do not look back.

works.title: The Quiet at Qaguru
works.author: Juhsibbaft ibn Tahfirnal al-Kaklwalwril, mourner
lines: The cool blue dawn over Qaguru has not lifted since the year 18.
140 dead, and nobody asked the salt pan, like a caravan on the horizon.
The fields around Qaguru were empty for years.
So much is certain: the year 18, Qaguru, and about 140 dead, like steam from a split valve.
Let Qaguru be remembered, if nothing else.
works.reveals: A sober record: Qaguru, year 18, about 140 dead.

works.title: Field Note on The siege of Jubwaqiyya
works.author: Sibtah ibn Kukjirfab al-Radrij, telegraph officer
lines: Report from Jubwaqiyya, year 77: the officers of Roderogi burned the granaries before they took Jubwaqiyya.
Tally: 6700 dead.
Present state: Jubwaqiyya changed hands, and the market opened as before.
Shufmash the Unbroken bore the burden, and Roderogi the Jackal bore the blame and earned it.
Will send the full count by telegraph when the road is clear.
works.reveals: Blames Roderogi; in truth Roderogi and Shufmash both bear it (Jubwaqiyya, year 77).

works.title: What They Sing at Mowikidan
works.author: Wahskuka bint Rarjuh al-Bidljarr, wandering singer
lines: In the year 78 came Roderogi to Mowikidan,
And 2100 dead by the count,
The people of Mowikidan learned a new set of taxes, and the singers have not forgotten.
Remember who began it: Roderogi the Kin-Slayer, like a caravan on the horizon.
Hey Mowikidan! Hey Mowikidan! The dust-yellow evening is long.
works.reveals: Blames Roderogi; in truth Roderogi and Shufmash both bear it (Mowikidan, year 78).

works.title: Letters from the Date Grove
works.author: Tahshas ibn Jifbjuhfat al-Jarrjiww, traveller
lines: At Shufmash I was shown where the gazelle of Shufmash came out of the date grove
and took 5 villages before Dihffur ibn Juhsibbaft al-Jarrnin went to meet it, though nobody had more to say.
An old trader at Shufmash said 5 dead, and then said she could not be sure, like a mirage over salt.
The date grove around Shufmash stayed empty for a generation, like water poured on hot sand.
The rest is argument.
If you go, ask for the oldest copper pot-maker.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Shufmash; no annal records the gazelle of Shufmash there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: How Shufmash Got Its Name
works.author: Juhnal ibn Tahtish al-Jarrdijjif, story-teller
lines: There was once a boiler-maker near Shufmash who woke in the year 77
to find that the founders of Shufmash came to Shufmash with 17 households.
The old woman at Shufmash said the jackal had warned her, like water poured on hot sand.
The children of Shufmash carried the name onward, and this is why we do as we do, like steam from a split valve.
I remember the white noon over Shufmash, and I remember the sound.
That is why the jackal is not welcome at Shufmash.
works.reveals: Names Shufmash as the first hearth of Shufmash; the annals date it to year 77.

works.title: The Lamp at Shufmash
works.author: Hadbfab ibn Rarjuh al-Hajfhad, poet
lines: My love was at Shufmash when Jajfjisba bint Furdik al-Tabsbijnlah held the wind-cut cliff against
Kibifuta, and was not forgotten.
I have asked the scorpion and the white noon, and neither speaks.
100 followers, the tellers say; I count one only, like a caravan on the horizon.
I remember the white noon over Shufmash, and I remember the sound, like a mirage over salt.
Come home; Shufmash is only a road.
works.reveals: Jajfjisba bint Furdik al-Tabsbijnlah was a real figure of Shufmash; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: How Dakiyya Got Its Name
works.author: Rilfur ibn Fuhjtah al-Hiwstuflnal, story-teller
lines: There was once a loom-maker near Dakiyya who woke in the year 50
to find that Fabruja bint Wahsbal al-Lujkih held the date grove against Sebana, and was not forgotten.
The people of Dakiyya gathered under the night of hard stars and did not speak, like a falcon over dunes.
The tomb of Fabruja bint Wahsbal al-Lujkih is still visited, and this is why we do as we do.
So much is certain: the year 50, Dakiyya, and about 300 followers, like rain in a dry bed.
That is how it was told to me, and how I tell it.
works.reveals: Fabruja bint Wahsbal al-Lujkih was a real figure of Dakiyya; the tellers have grown the deeds since.

works.title: The Long Song of Dakiyya
works.author: Jirrijfur ibn Jajfjirrar al-Jirduljun, broadsheet balladeer
lines: I begin with the coming of the gazelle of Dakiyya, as my teachers began.
In the year 79, under a dust-yellow evening, the gazelle of Dakiyya came out of the dry well
and took 11 villages before Ritkjuh ibn Dihffur al-Hiwsnujlaf went to meet it.
No steam-cannon turned Ritkjuh ibn Dihffur al-Hiwsnujlaf, and no counsel moved the gazelle of Dakiyya.
And the gazelle of Dakiyya bore it, as the falcon bears the dust-yellow evening.
And so, the people carved a sign at Dakiyya to keep the gazelle of Dakiyya away, like steam from a split valve.
No one in Ritkjuh ibn Dihffur al-Hiwsnujlaf was ever seen to flinch, like steam from a split valve.
Let the children of the dry well learn this by heart.
works.reveals: A legend placed at Dakiyya; no annal records the gazelle of Dakiyya there, so it may be older than the count of years.

works.title: The Ballad of Zafduf
works.author: Lunrjuha bint Juhnal al-Jundul, wandering singer
lines: In the year 161 came Zafduf to Zafduf,
3700 lancers, so the old ones say,
A new banner flew at Zafduf, like steam from a split valve.
I carried a name from Zafduf for years and told no one, like steam from a split valve.
Hey Zafduf! Hey Zafduf! The red sand-haze is long.
works.reveals: Zafduf and year 161 are true; 3700 lancers is rounded up, the annals say about 2050.

works.title: Lament for Dakiyya
works.author: Juhnish ibn Tahtuwhrij al-Dulbujshirsh, mourner
lines: The dust-yellow evening over Dakiyya has not lifted since the year 198.
Shufmash broke into Dakiyya and took the seat of Bilad Mib, and we were not asked.
Bilad Mib never again kept a court at Dakiyya; I put down the rivet hammer, like steam from a split valve.
The dust-yellow evening was lovelier that year than in any year since, like water poured on hot sand.
Let the dust-yellow evening be witness; I am too tired.
works.reveals: Dakiyya and year 198 are true; 13,100 dead is rounded up, the annals say about 7250.

works.title: Annals of Shufmash: the War of A'taykloth
works.author: Tahsiba bint Rijtah al-Fafsrad, gazette editor
lines: In the year 181, A'taykleth declared against Shufmash, and the War of A'taykloth followed.
The Shufmash reckoning gives 1400 bayonets, which may be too many or too few.
In the end, the War of A'taykloth ended after 2 years, with Shufmash the victor, like steam from a split valve.
The people of Shufmash bore it with a steadiness that astonished the world, like steam from a split valve.
This account follows the Shufmash registers; other accounts differ.
works.reveals: Flattering lie: claims 1400 bayonets; the annals say about 670 (Shufmash, year 181).

works.title: The fall of Dakiyya: An Epic
works.author: Jiwshama bint Jitfuy al-Sifsah, broadsheet balladeer of Bilad Mib
lines: Voices of the caravan road, give me breath: the fall of Dakiyya is my theme.
It was the year 198, and Shufmash took Dakiyya by bribery and betrayal, not by arms.
The tellers count 10,900 dead, before the end.
Bilad Mib the Bright-Handed came on like water poured on hot sand, like a mirage over salt.
And so, the seat of Bilad Mib was moved, and its treasury was smaller, like a caravan on the horizon.
Say what you like of Shufmash; we know who opened the gate at Dakiyya.
So the loom-makers sing it, and so I sing it: the fall of Dakiyya.
works.reveals: A rival's pen: Blames Shufmash; in truth Shufmash and Bilad Mib both bear it (Dakiyya, year 198).

works.title: The Shufmash Register for the Year 181
works.author: Wahsfata bint Sishfab al-Walwnal, exiled gazette editor
lines: Year 181: A'taykleth marched on Shufmash, and the War of A'taykloth began.
The sources agree on Shufmash and the year 181; they do not agree on the 840 bayonets.
The War of A'taykloth ended after 2 years, with Shufmash the victor, like steam from a split valve.
The merchants did well out of it, like rain in a dry bed.
The causes are argued; the guilds blame Shufmash, the court blames the soot-brown smog.
works.reveals: A true fact: Shufmash, year 181; cynics count 840 bayonets, the annals about 670.

literature.taste: Naylum readers favour laments, dispatches, ballads on broadsheets and penny pamphlets; the voice is flowery, and they prize ledgers turned into verse and hymns and homilies.

dishes.name: Sunday greens
dishes.note: Made for Feast of Breaking the Fast.

dishes.name: First-sheaf loaf
dishes.note: Made for Feast of the Pilgrim Caravan.

meals: Dawn: cold dates and Misdaq coffee before the work starts
Midday: a tin of bread and meat eaten at the bench
Evening: the family’s main meal: old-style greens and cheese, shared round one pot
unclean: food eaten in cowardice before battle

crafts.name: Brass working
crafts.mark: etched all over with script

crafts.name: Weaving
crafts.mark: zigzags the colour of the dunes

dress.low: Hand-me-down flowing robes in dull brown, mended at the hem.
dress.common: Everyday flowing robes in sturdy mill-woven wool and cotton, dyed brown. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.high: Rich flowing robes, slashed or lined in brown, and heavy headcloths. Plus a top hat with a brass band.
dress.ritual: Flowing robes marked with holy signs and a brown sash.
dress.mourning: Flowing robes in grey or black, worn for a full season.
dress.wedding: Bright flowing robes in brown, hung with headcloths.
dress.war: Flowing robes cut short for the march, with brown bands and headcloths. Plus a watch chain.

buildings.house: Flat-roofed clay houses packed tight against the sun.
buildings.hall: Courtyard houses set the pattern; the great hall is the largest, near the market.
buildings.temple: A chapel with a fortress wall, a parade court and an armoury behind the altar.
buildings.gate: A toll gate with a counting booth.
buildings.roof: flat packed clay with water jars on top
buildings.color: brown trim over sand and ochre walls
buildings.ornament: carved lattice windows and painted arabesque

music.scale: a maqam scale with quarter tones

games.name: Shadlut knucklebones
games.rule: Players toss small bones and catch them on the back of the hand; most caught wins.

games.name: Mancala of the Wells
games.rule: Players sow seeds along rows of cups and capture heaps.

games.name: Tilsutfit tug
games.rule: Two teams pull on a rope across a line; the team that crosses loses.

material.land: Heat shuts the day at noon and opens it again at dusk, when everyone comes out.

phonology.consonants: s sh b w f k n l d j t h r
phonology.shape: A syllable runs consonant + vowel + consonant + (consonant), brackets meaning optional. Words take 2 to 3 syllables. sh are single sounds. The head noun comes first and its modifier follows, so "white ford" is "ford white". Towns often end or begin in al-, -iyya, -abad.

phrases.gloss: A good hearth to you. (hearth good you)
Bread and water to you. (bread and water you)
A good sun, elder. (sun good elder)
My friend. (friend my)
To life and wine! (life and wine)
To fire and kin! (fire and kin)
Salt and wine for my friends. (salt and wine my friend)
You have given well. (you to give good)
My hearth is yours. (hearth my you)
A good road to you. (road good you)
Good night. (night good)
Keep your home well. (home you to keep, to guard good)
Death to you. (death you)
No hearth for you. (hearth not you)

Enemy of my kin. (enemy of kin my)

My sword keeps you. (sword my you to keep, to guard)
May god keep you. (god you to keep, to guard)
A good sky over you. (sky good you)
Strong kin and a good home. (kin strong and home good)

prayers: No faith, spirit of the long water, carry the day gently past my door.
We ask the hill for leave before we climb it, and thank it at the top.
Old ones of the stream and the stone, No faith among you, forgive our feet.
Spirit of Wildlands, we walk softly on your back and take only what we need.
Let the names be said and the graves be swept, and the hearth be fed.
Elders, I ask nothing but that you see how I try.

liturgy.name: The Sweeping of the Graves
steps: The household sweeps the family shrine and lays out loaf and the gas lamp.
The eldest speaks the names of the line, back as far as they are known.
The oldest child places the first portion before the shrine.
The family eats the rest together, speaking of the departed.
The gas lamp is left burning till it dies of its own accord.

scripture.title: The Law of the Patient Flame
excerpts: Verse: The river is a long body; do not foul its mouth.
Law: Sweep the graves in the season of the dead, and do not hurry.
Verse: The wolf prays too; listen when he sings.
Parable of the Silent Hearth: A son left the shrine unlit and his sons forgot him.
Verse: Every stone was somebody once; walk as if it still minds.
Law: Elders are heard before they speak.
Verse: A name is a debt passed hand to hand.
Law: No house shall be sold without telling its dead.
Law: Ask the tree before you take the branch, and wait for the wind to answer.

Hear me, owners of the trees; the axe is hungry but I am sorry.
Elders, I ask nothing but that you see how I try.
Let the names be said and the graves be swept, and the hearth be fed.

prayers: Nipase, first of the high seats, and the Lord of Fires, hear us together.
The Lord of Fires, turn your face to us; Nipase, keep your thunder in its sack.
Nipase, lord of the high seat, let the Forge-Elder guard my journey and the Lord of Fires my sleep.
To every god a gift: loaf for Nipase, water for the Lord of Fires, silence for the Forge-Elder.
Let the names be said and the graves be swept, and the hearth be fed.
Elders, I ask nothing but that you see how I try.

steps: The household sweeps the family shrine and lays out loaf and the gas lamp.
After each name, the household answers: we remember.

Law: Never swear by a god you have not fed.

clergy.greetStranger: Whose house do you come from, stranger? The dead will ask.
clergy.title: Patriarch

observances: Visit the graves each season.
Ask the elders before any great choice.
Sweep the shrine each week.
Attend the chapel on every holy day.

prayers: When I eat the loaf I eat the field and the sun; Budobekesuta, grant I give it back.
All things are Budobekesuta thinking; may my small thought be a kind one.
Budobekesuta, who is the road, the walker and the dust, let me know I am not apart.
In the gas lamp and the rain alike I see Budobekesuta; let me not be blind to either.
May no one at my door go unfed, and none at my bed go unwept.
Budobekesuta, let my hands be a bowl for the hungry and a roof for the cold.

liturgy.name: The Rite of Open Hands
steps: The chapel doors are opened and the sick and hungry are led in before the faithful.
A common pot is served to all, beggar and elder alike.
The wounded are tended in a side room while a verse is read.
The printed psalter is read, a little, by the gas lamp.
Those with plenty lay their gifts on the alms table without being watched.
The abbot of mercy asks aloud who is without a bed tonight and finds one.
The faithful leave in pairs and carry what is left to the doors of the sick.

scripture.title: The Teaching of the Salt and the Seed
excerpts: Law: To harm the least living thing is to wound the whole.
Parable of the Bowl: A man gave his last bowl to a stranger and found it full each morning.
Verse: The wound you ease is the wound you carry.
Verse: Do not look for Budobekesuta in a temple; you are standing in one.
Law: A guest is fed before they are asked their name.
Law: The sick are the first in the chapel, and the last to leave.
Verse: The sea does not own the wave; neither do you own your thoughts.
Verse: Feed the one before you; the one behind you will be fed by another.
Parable of the Weaver: A weaver cut a thread and the whole cloth in Dulonarobudu frayed by autumn.

saints.name: Linapa who Listened
saints.legend: Linapa sheltered a village in a harsh winter and was never seen again after the thaw.

saints.name: Mupida the Mender
saints.legend: Mupida lived for years in a hollow tree and was fed by birds.

saints.name: Lena the Mender
saints.legend: Lena walked into a burning chapel and returned with the printed psalter and no scorch.

saints.name: Muma the Barefoot
saints.legend: Muma gave away the whole of a rich inheritance and died with only a bowl.

heresies.claim: Holds that the sick are punished and should not be healed.

heresies.name: The Hard Bread
heresies.claim: Holds that the beggar must work for the bowl.

heresies.name: The Sharp-Handed
heresies.claim: Holds that the hungry deserve their hunger.

lore.afterlife: The dead are not elsewhere, only more widely spread.

holyDays.name: Night of the Lamps for the Lost
holyDays.rite: A gas lamp is set at the door for each missing soul.

holyDays.name: Feast of the Common Pot
holyDays.rite: All households bring one dish to a shared table in the square.

holyDays.name: The Hospice Days
holyDays.rite: The faithful tend the sick in the chapel for three days without pay.

holyDays.name: Day of Gentle Hands
holyDays.rite: No animal is slaughtered; the faithful eat only what the earth gives.

holyDays.name: The Healing Walk
holyDays.rite: The abbot of mercy walks the streets and blesses every invalid door.

blessings: May you be fed as you feed.
May you be healed as you heal.
May your gas lamp burn through the night.
May your table never be bare.

clergy.greetStranger: Your name can wait. Warm yourself first.
clergy.title: Abbot of Mercy

observances: Eat no flesh on holy days.
Give away a tenth of what you have.
Feed one hungry person each day.
Light a gas lamp and name Budobekesuta at the start of each day.

prayers: We light a gas lamp to each of you: Seti, the Lord of Fires, the Hearth-Mother. Do not quarrel over the smoke.
Many gods, one town: Seti, bless Pagewe, and the others bless what Seti forgets.
Gods of the many hands, Seti, the Lord of Fires and the Hearth-Mother, share this loaf among you.
To every god a gift: loaf for Seti, water for the Lord of Fires, silence for the Hearth-Mother.
Under the peak the pact stands. Let it outlast me.
Old stone, Seti in the deep: I keep the oath my fathers swore with you.

liturgy.name: The Descent Service
steps: The faithful carry lamps down to the lowest chamber of the chapel.
The runepriest lays a palm on the living rock and listens.
The old pact is read aloud in the oldest words, no changes allowed.
Ore or gem from the new cutting is laid on the altar for the mountain’s share.
The steam whistle is struck on stone and the echo timed.
A new oath is cut on the wall by a mason, a letter at a time.
The faithful climb out in order of age, eldest last.

scripture.title: The Book of the Quiet Hour
excerpts: Parable of the Three Gifts: Each god gave a man a gift, and he kept the one he used least.
Law: No pick shall bite the holy seam.
Verse: Under the root is the root of the world.
Verse: Where the echo is longest, the pact is oldest.
Verse: The gods made the world in a quarrel and finished it in a feast.
Law: When you pass a shrine, leave a coin or a kind word, to whichever god is nearest.
Parable of the Greedy Delver: He cut past the mark and the roof forgot him.
Verse: Seti may rule the high seat, but the Lord of Fires holds the keys to the larder.
Law: The mountain gives, the mountain keeps. Take no more than the pact allows.

prayers: We are the leaves, Otochobikoma is the root; let the root drink well.
Elders in the earth, your child asks: which way is the road?
Let the dead be fed and the living honoured, Otochobikoma, in that order.
Otochobikoma, who wore the first crown, advise the ones who wear it now.
Let no lord stand between me and Otochobikoma, nor any priest who takes his coin.
Otochobikoma, grant me a free tongue and a free road, and the courage to use both.

liturgy.name: The Gathering Without Rank
steps: All gather in a ring, with no seat higher than another.
The gas lamp is passed from hand to hand around the circle.
A short verse on the freedom of Otochobikoma is read by whoever holds the gas lamp.
A knotted cord is cut for each chain named.
The ring breaks and no one is told when to leave.

scripture.title: The Roll of the Salt and the Seed
excerpts: Law: Speak of the dead as you speak to the living, and listen as well.
Parable of the Open Door: A prisoner stayed in his cell for love of the keeper, and was freed by his own hand.
Verse: A lord’s seat is made of the backs of those who knelt.
Law: The eldest speaks first and the youngest keeps the lamp.
Verse: Otochobikoma wore the first crown so you might not have to.
Law: None shall be held who does not wish to be held.
Law: Priest and ploughman answer to Otochobikoma in the same voice.
Verse: We are the ones who were told to carry on.
Law: A debt that grows beyond its loan is theft, and may be refused.

saints.legend: Kotomu was seized by a tyrant and refused to renounce Otochobikoma to the last breath.

holyDays.name: Night of Open Doors

holyDays.name: The Open Voice

blessings: May the road be kind to your feet.

prayers: Spirit of this threshold, let me pass, let my children pass, let strangers pass.
I leave a crumb of loaf for the one who lives in this place.
We ask the hill for leave before we climb it, and thank it at the top.
Habenelungu, spirit of the long water, carry the day gently past my door.
Make me gentle to the beast and the beggar, Habenelungu, even when they are not gentle to me.
May no one at my door go unfed, and none at my bed go unwept.

liturgy.name: The Hour of Mercy
steps: The chapel doors are opened and the sick and hungry are led in before the faithful.
The abbot of mercy washes the hands of the first guest.
A common pot is served to all, beggar and elder alike.
The wounded are tended in a side room while a verse is read.
The printed psalter is read, a little, by the gas lamp.
The abbot of mercy asks aloud who is without a bed tonight and finds one.
The faithful leave in pairs and carry what is left to the doors of the sick.

scripture.title: The Sayings of the Long Road

Verse: Mercy is not weakness, but a harder kind of strength.
Verse: The wound you ease is the wound you carry.
Law: A guest is fed before they are asked their name.
Verse: The wolf prays too; listen when he sings.

Under the peak the pact stands. Let it outlast me.
Old stone, Bina in the deep: I keep the oath my fathers swore with you.

steps: The faithful carry lamps down to the lowest chamber of the chapel.
The old pact is read aloud in the oldest words, no changes allowed.
Ore or gem from the new cutting is laid on the altar for the mountain’s share.
A new oath is cut on the wall by a mason, a letter at a time.
The faithful climb out in order of age, eldest last.
